I'm pretty happy with these headphones, I received a reviewer pair intending to use them as my work headphones, and hope to make use of the sound canceling capabilities. My previous head phones are [[ASIN:B002YOENAS Sennheiser PXC 310 BT Compact Noise-Canceling Travel Headphones with Bluetooth Technology (Black)]] so that is what I am comparing them to.

Sound---

I am very happy with the clarity of the sound from these headphones. The music is crisp and has decent highs and lows. The one thing I am a little disappointed with is there seems to be a lot of distortion when turned to just a moderately high volume. Which probably works well with my use at work, but I can't truly crank these headphones without getting too much distortion. Of course this is probably good for my hearing, but to continue the comparison to the Sennheisers, these have less capability at higher volumes.

When listening to these at lower volume though, they are very nice. I'm not a huge audiophile, but I can appreciate the sound quality these deliver.

Sound canceling appears to work fairly well. I can at least attest to the fact that I missed phone calls while listening to these, I am interested to see how the will work to cut airplane noise.

Design ---

I'm impressed with the way these headphones have been designed to fold for storage and transport. They are not as compact as my Sennheisers, but they do fold into a decent size and the nice leatherette case holds them well, with space to spare for extra accessories. The ear pieces swivel well to form to you head, the cable connects firmly and securely, and the battery compartment is well designed.

Also, I am impressed that they thought to add an adapter for an airline headphone jack. I am looking forward to having these to listen to on my next air trip.

Comfort---

The ear pieces are nicely padded that make a nice comfortable fit. I have historically only used ear buds so at times my ears seem to get warm due to the coverage of the ear pieces. The bar is padded but noticeable on your head, again for those used to earbuds this takes an adjustment.

Summary---

All in all these are nice headphones. I prefer my Sennheisers which do deliver a little better sound on the corded connection (less sound quality over Bluetooth.) However, I am happy with these, but not enough to justify the price savings over the Sennheisers.

To let you know where I am coming from on this review, I have two sons, 9 and 4. We do a lot of camping without mom, but want to share our adventures. So far, our trips have destroyed a Canon Powershot 450 (overly hydrated while canoeing) and a Powershot 980IS (smashed into ground during a fall.) So the idea of a waterproof, shockproof and hopefully kid-proof camera sounded perfect.

Purpose for camera: Rugged camera to take along canoeing, fishing, camping, and hiking for snapshots and quick, shareable movies.

I have never owned a camera in this class, and the one thing I am trying to keep in mind is the price point. This is not intended to be a high-end performance device, but more a rugged snapshot camera. I was a little suspect on 1080P on a hand held device under $175 (still am,) but the 5 MP camera is adequate for photos to email to grandparents and to show off our catches and camps to mom.

Design -

The camera is very nicely designed. It is physically attractive and comfortable in the hand. The winged doors lock into place well in their watertight positions and are, well kind of cool. The screen is adequate for playback and we spend a lot of time watching what we filmed over and over. The controls are spare, but easy to understand and operate. The four major flaws I found are; the embedded battery, lack of a flash, lack of lens cover, and no headphone jack for previewing sound.

Battery-

It is unfortunate that the design team decided to go with an internal non-removable battery. This seems to move the device into the "disposable" class since it is useless once the battery dies. I suspect that the battery can be replaced fairly easily, judging by the hex screws in the camera body, but there is a big difference between slipping a battery in and out and sending the camera out for replacement. Also, I can make a huge argument for being able to carry a back up battery. At least for now though, the battery seems to have a decent charge. We have filmed and played back films for at least two hours between recharges and have never seen the battery near empty.

Performance -

Image capture: 1080p is a lot to ask from such a small sensor. For that matter, so is 720p. So I am satisfied with the images I am getting, not great but what I would expect. I usually shoot Canon DSLR's (except when camping with kids) so I am at times frustrated by the lack of manual controls of any kind. Autofocus, autoexposure... with no way to change anything beyond file format and resolution. The images and video I am getting are a little noisy and especially so in low light. Blurring from camera or subject motion is common on stills. This is where the flash option would be nice. But in daylight, or decently lit interior shots the images are definitely passable. Again, judging this camera on its price point and function, it really is decent. If I want good stills, I'll go with a Canon 50D, if I want a snapshot of my kid pulling a bass into the canoe, this is perfect.

I am uploading a video with more details on picture and movie quality.

Sound: For a single source mike on the camera, it does pretty good. Definitely picks up footsteps or breathing, so don't film while walking up hill. Truly emphasizes if you are out of shape. Picks up ambient sound well and in tests in a light breeze, did fine.

Interface: I had the interface lock up on me once and I was unable to get it to power off or get out of a locked state. I had to use the small reset button to get it to reboot and clear the freeze. So I have thrown a very small paper clip in its case. Without being able to pull the battery, the reset button seems to have been the only option. Otherwise the device is very fast loading up, and the interface is intuitive and easy to use. Although occasionally when browsing I end up in fast forward or reverse when watching a movie and it takes a little to get it back to play or browse.

Summary:

All in all, I am really happy with this camera. It is full of limitations which you should understand before purchase. For the price, it is a decent camera and it fits our intended purpose to a Tee. My kids love the ability to take a movie, then watch it immediately. I like the feeling that it might survive the kids for a while. I feel like I'm being pretty critical of the camera, and I guess I am. But I'm giving it four stars because it does what I want it to, and after using it for a couple weeks, I really like it. Just don't expect the world from a inexpensive camera.

It's also the perfect desktop for any business with a marketing department. I watched this video and was totally hooked. I have been doing PowerPoint presentations for 24 years and this blows it out of the water.

What finally hooked me to it's creative potential at the office was watching two 3 minute videos on YouTube:
"HP Sprout Review" and "Using the Capture Feature on Sprout by HP" - amazing

Hook up was easy as I expected about 20 minutes to unbox everything and less than an hour to get everything running

Now, right now I am not in a financial picture to buy the 3D printer or imaging stand (even tho the prices are not outrageous),but I can still get a designed printed by establishing a free account with HP's 3D printing partner. FYI the Dremel is the highest rated model by '3D Engineer' just go to their sight and search "dremel-idea-builder-review" it gave me a lot of easily understandable information if I decide to go that route. You can also go to the Dremel site '3dprinter dot dremel' the videos there helped me learn a lot about how this 3D printing works. Lastly, I read a informational article at 'makezine' that you can find on the internet "dremel-3d-printer-idea-builder".

Ok, so the next stop on my journey of discovery was HP where I searched 'Sprout'. So I watched the videos and skimmed the tech stuff. WELL worth your time - I truly think it saved me a TON of time. If object design is your thing or you are looking to get your high school or college kid into computer design this desk top will hook them. It's just so creative! One tip when getting started, on the HP site I put a query of "Sprout" in the search engine and got a nice small list of use links PLUS a dedicated SPROUT FORUM for users where HP folks jump in all the time with helpful information and trouble shooting help.

Ok, I really wanted to so how the 3D works so I created a free account with the HP 3D printer partner Sculpteo - it could not be easier. First stop for me was searching the Sculpteo site for '3D Printing Price and Payment Methods' and 'help/#price-calculation'. You can see it doesn't have to be ridiculously expensive - but it can be - the larger the object the bigger the cost. The site is very user friendly and immersive, even if you don't plan to print right off take a look, it is fascinating. I have the 16GB - Received as a gift September 2011. Didn't use it much until by Sony Viao Laptop got infected SINCE THEN have used THE HP TOUCH 30 hours a week for the last 10 months.

Super easy to use - very intuitive - I spent 5 minutes reading the product over view and was good to go.

things I learned:
1. JUST TYPE function on the home page is like Google or Bing

2. FUNCTIONS - Press the arrow at the bottom left - gives you 4 choices at the top screen:
a. Apps -
* Kindle app is pretty cool
* Facebook app is not so cool
* Adobe works great
* Camera - several apps -tricky to use because the camera lens and view screen both faces you
* PHOTOS - awesome
* Maps - not so great
* email app for Yahoo - AWESOME
* QuickOffice - terrific for Word docs
* THOUSANDS OF OTHERS

b. Downloads
* HP CARE PACK
* HP APP Catalog - not really my thing but super easy to do if it is yours
* THOUSANDS OF OTHERS

c. Favorites (I use this the most)
* you use the 'arrow in the box icon' on the upper right to add
* you can delete and move once added by pressing & holding any icon
* press the blue 'DONE' in the upper right to make firm.
* have as many as you want you use the scroll function to locate and use (sounds more complicated than it is).

d. Settings
* icon for updates - right now I am on HP-webOS 3.0.5
* software manager
* WIFI - use this the most - and it is THE BEST when linking to new wifi sites - SUPER EASY
* Device Info - mostly use for reset - resets take a minute and I use on occasion when the devise seems to run wonky

battery lasts the 4+ hours, I charge at night when asleep

Add youu top 5 favorites to the bottom of the screen by dragging any icon

HELP function- I used the first 12 months and wish I had used it more as it was super helpful talking to a live person.

Had to get creative only once when the charger usb cord stopped connecting - I used my Samsung phone charger USB cord and connected it to the HP TouchPad cylinder recharger and it works like a charm (you can also buy another HP cord, for $30 I think).

When the Touchpad freezes: press the power and the open screen button at the same time and hold for a slow count of 20 - it will reset after a minute, the hp icon starts to come on in a minute and you are back to normal.

Pictures - SUPER SIMPLE - touch the picture and you get 'copy to photos'; 'share image' (via email) ; 'set wallpaper'

Pictures (viewing/auctioning/shareing) - go to Apps; Photos & Videos; select; you then see screen captures; profile pictures - wall papers; downloaded pictures; Miscellaneous pictures (which are like Downloaded pictures and I can't figure what the difference is); and if connected to Facebook any pictures you have there. To get rid of a picture you have a trash can in the lower right;

Screencapture is way cool - to make a jpeg of what you are viewing: press the power and the open screen button at the same time and let go - you hear a camera clink and your screen gives a round flash - lol -

When you have too many pictures or documents and you want to download/delete -use the use cord to link to a computer - it's that easy!

When using it with certain light sources, the filter seems to have no real effect at all, while with others it creates a subtle, soft glow around the subject. I am still working out the situations where it is most effective. I have had similar issues with filters like these with other lenses, and as such I assume the problem is in my lack of practice with them. It will take some time and practice to make my results more consistent, and for now I lay the fault on myself.

The build quality seems to be good. I have received filters in the past where the glass rattles in the frame which is unsettling. This one is tight and there is no play between the glass and the frame. It screws on to the lens securely and is easy to clean.

The asking price is quite reasonable. I have seen these filters priced much higher, and I have also seen much cheaper ones that do not work well. The pricing seems in line with the product, if not slightly low.

I have no complaints with this filter. The issues I have with it are probably my inexperience, and I will keep working with it to improve my results. I will return here and update my review if my impression changes. For now, though, I am satisfied.

I have had good success with Kingston products (in particular their SSD storage) so I was pleased to have the opportunity to work with this encrypted thumb drive. It has a lot of promise and it works better than other encrypted drives I have used. There is one drawback, at least for me - it does not support Linux (if it does, I haven't figured out how yet).

I have the 16GB version, and the thing is built like a tank. It has a metal casing around the inner workings and it can handle some abuse. That's good news if you keep these things in a briefcase or loose in a bookbag.

Setup is easy. When it is plugged into a Windows machine (I do not have access to a Mac so I cannot speak to that use case), the software is available and can be used to set up the drive with a password. That's pretty straightforward. If you forget your password, you can wipe the drive and start over but you cannot recover your data. So, choose your password wisely.

Copy rates seem to be decent - a little slower than similar-sized drives I have that aren't encrypted but not prohibitively so. It's a trade-off, and a small one at that.

When I popped this drive into my Linux machine, the kernel saw it immediately. However, all it could see was the setup partition which is approximately 100mb, a far cry from 16 GB. The drive is smart enough to hide its data from foreign OS-based systems so your data is safe. Linux is gaining users though, and being able to access the data from a Linux system would be good, even if there was a tedious process to get to the partition but still requiring a password. This is better than other encrypted drives I have used in the past which made the data scrambled but was still accessible. However, not being able to use this drive under Linux is a problem for me.

To be fair, it is not advertised as compatible with Linux.

This is a good drive and from what testing I have done it works well. That said, it does not support Linux and that is a negative for me. Hopefully Kingston will release a Linux-based version (or a software layer) for it in the future; for now it's only usable for me under Windows.

I prefer trackballs like this one to regular mice, and I like the fact that this one is bigger than average so I decided to give it a try. So far I am pleased with it, though it isn't perfect.

DELUX is not a brand with which I was previously familiar so I wasn't sure what to expect. My requirements are fairly simple - it has to work with a dongle and it needs to work under both Linux and Windows. It definitely meets both of those requirements nicely and it has not given me any issues. I usually do not use mice with Bluetooth connections so this feature, while useful for connecting to multiple systems, is wasted on me. The dongle, however, is immediately picked up by the Linux kernel as well as by Windows and I was able to plug this in and go with no delays and no effort.

This is indeed a larger trackball and it fits my hands wonderfully. I have the hands of a gorilla and finding mice and trackballs that fit me is a challenge and I usually end up settling for something that is less than ideal for me. In this case, the trackball feels good in my hands and there is no strain on my thumbs as I don't have to stretch my hand in weird ways to reach the ball properly.

Other reviewers have mentioned that this trackball tends to skip. I have not observed this issue, though I have not had it long and I have not tried to use it with the computer more than a foot away. I also have not tried connecting via Bluetooth, which is when I have had troubles in the past with pointing devices.

One thing that would have made this trackball better would have been quiet clicking of the buttons. This is not a quiet device in use, and after using a more quiet trackball it is quite noticeable.

One important oversight is that it does not come with a battery. It takes a single AA battery, and I expected one in the box. Every other non-rechargeable pointing device I have purchased has come with a battery in the package. I am not sure why the decision was made to not include one here.

This is a nice trackball and I will be using it quite a bit, particularly on my Linux system. It's a good size for me and so far it has worked well. It would have been nice if it was quieter when clicking, and I don't know why there was no battery in the package, but these are smaller issues. I'm pleased with this trackball.

I selected this clamp for working with my mirrorless camera. There are times when clamping to a surface or a pole is more practical than setting up a tripod or monopod, so this kind of solution is useful in those cases. It's a decent clamp system and it works well, though it does require some messing with it to get used to it if you've only worked with a tripod in the past.

This idea is simple here. This is a clamp system that includes a couple of adapters for attaching cameras and accessories so that the camera can be held steady without having to set up a big, bulky tripod or having to hold the camera by hand. It comes with two clamps that can be connected via the ball joint adapter so that the system can convert to an anchor support for a pole as well (not the intended use, but practical nonetheless).

Included in the kit is a 1/4" adapter that connects to a standard camera mount (like my mirrorless), and an adapter for connecting a GoPro. It can be used directly with a cell phone, but it is not ideal for that and does require being creative with the clamps (not recommended); better is using the clamp to hold a selfie stick which in turn holds the camera.

The clamps hold tight as do the ball joints. It takes a little bit of fiddling but getting this set up exactly as desired is possible so that you can get the perfect angle. Further, the system can hold a little weight and has no trouble at all holding my mirrorless camera steady.

It seems to be made well and so far I have not had any issues with loose screws, stripped components, wobbly connectors (when properly tightened) or slipping grips. It's still early on in working with this system but so far I see no red flags.

I am happy with this clamp set-up and I will get some good use out of it. It's a practical solution when a tripod or other mount is not workable. It's not particularly expensive, either.

I work in an environment where I cannot use wireless connectivity like Wifi or Bluetooth, but I can use my smartphone. This is a problem if I want to use my iPhone 13 for music since I can’t directly connect my earphones or speakers to it. I selected this adapter for this purpose and it has answered the mail for me.

This adapter is as simple as it looks - it connects to the lightning port on an Apple device and allows for connecting a 3.5mm jack on the other. There’s no set-up required or anything - it just works. There’s a momentary initial lag as the device is recognized but that’s a very small price to pay for the functionality.

It’s designed to present the 3.5mm port at a 90 degree angle from the base of the phone. This is a lot less likely to break or get caught on something which can damage the phone. And, it’s small enough to not add much bulk to the phone.

Some real thought went into this little device. It works well and requires no real thought - just plug and play.

I have wanted a backdrop for photography for a while and chose this one based on the brand name. I have some experience with Powerextra products, in particular their replacement batteries for a digital camera I own. Based on that previous experience I thought this would be a decent frame for a backdrop. It’s mostly good and I do like it but I found an issue with the clips.

This is a fairly simple frame - two tripods with cross braces on which to hang a backdrop. It assembles fairly quickly and also tears down just as quickly. I especially like that the whole things collapses down into a small package that is roughly the same size as a fishing rod carrier and is very portable. In a pinch the whole assembly can fit wholesale inside a duffel bag with other things too, though that somewhat defeats the purpose.

This is not a heavy-duty rig which should be obvious from the price. It’s a set-up that I would say is ideal for travel as it’s relatively lightweight and easy to store, but sturdy enough to work in fairly static environments.

The main issue I have with this set-up is the set of four clips that come with it. I opened one of them and one of the tips on the clamping end popped off and went flying. It was easy enough to replace it, and it happened again on another one of the clips. I realized two things about the clips - three of the four clips were assembled incorrectly which makes this much more likely to happen, and the tips can be lost fairly easily. The clips are the most easily replaceable part of the whole assembly so in the grand scheme of things this is not a showstopper but more thought could have been put into the clamp design (and assembly) without increasing costs appreciably.

This is not a perfect rid for setting up backdrops but it works well enough and the cost is very reasonable. Pay attention to the clip assembly, though, and ensure that the tips are installed correctly.

I have gotten more into creative photography and I have enjoyed playing with lens filters like these. I have worked with star filters in the past and I thought it might be fun to experiment with this light streak filter as well. So far I have no complaints, though it is the type of filter that should be used sparingly.

This is a gold streak filter that works in the same way as star filters, only it channels light in a straight line across the frame instead of in multiple directions. That is, it can make lights look smeared as if swept from one direction in a straight line. The color of the filter lines alters the light slightly and it has a mildly warming effect.

Some thought went into this filter and it allows for turning the filter (similar to a CPL) so that it can channel light in any single direction.

As with any filter like this, it should be used sparingly. It is possible to have too much of a good thing and as such this can easily be overdone. When used properly and used infrequently it can make some very striking and impactful photos.

It seems to be well made. There are no hitches in the turn when making directional adjustments, and the glass does not rattle loosely in the metal frame. I have found no damage to the glass or metal right out of the package either.

One question that might come up is, why should you use this kind of filter then it is easy to do the same thing in software? The answer is straightforward - it's fun!

This is very much a fun and useful filter but it is a special-use thing that should be used with some restraint. It seems to be well made and it does generate the desired effects. It is not particularly expensive either which is a plus.

I have worked a lot with active noise canceling (ANC) headphones and ear buds, and I was excited to try these as Sony has really come on strong in recent years in this area. I usually do not wear ear buds, favoring full-sized over-the-ear can, but sometimes ear buds are the right answer. I am not unhappy with these.

There are two aspects of these that need discussion - the ANC function and the sound quality. I’ll cover each of these separately.

The ANC function is good but is not top-notch. That is, it’s very effective at killing off ambient sound and it allows for listening to music at lower volumes without letting in surrounding sounds like fans and air handlers in an office or road noise in a car. It is not as aggressive as some of Sony’s other offerings, but still far and away better than cheaper headphones and ear buds available.

I like the fact that I can touch one of the buds and the mode switches to allow more ambient noise through for conversation. This is a common feature for ANC phones of any type anymore, and this pair of buds implements this well.

The default sound profile is good but not perfect. The bass is good and not overdriven which is a refreshing change from most phones I have used. The midrange is a little off, with sound being a little muddy and with the slightest of distortion if you’re looking for it. The highs are not sharp and also seem a bit muted like the midrange, though it is not severe enough to write these off by any means. I have worked with ear buds that have better balanced sound profiles, but I have also heard much worse. Now, all that said, with Sony’s application it’s easy to access an equalizer to better balance the sound as desired. I have had no trouble tweaking the active profile in the equalizer to get these to sound better depending on the kind of music I’m listening to.

These are Sony’s midrange buds, and are sold at a midrange price point. If these were priced like their top-end buds I would be hesitant to recommend them. At the price point, though, they’re a good option and are better than most off-brand or cheap ear buds available.

The last Blu-Ray player I owned bit the dust about a month after we got it and I have been quietly looking for another one to replace it. I was given the opportunity to try this one and I took it. It's not a bad player and it seems to work, but there are a couple of behaviors about it that I do not like.

It is as simple a player as it gets. It's not fancy and it doesn't do a lot of extras beyond basic player functions - pause, play, eject, skip, etc. At the end of the day it's all that's needed. It connects via HDMI which is fine, and the resolution and picture size can be tweaked in the menu system which is good. Playback is fine and I have had no issues with picture quality.

There are two things about this player that bother me, both of which are annoyances but neither are deal breakers. First, when the unit is powered on it asks for the user to set the language and voice prompting. That's fine the first time. But, this player does it every time it is powered on again and that gets irritating. Second, when a disc is put in and playback starts, there's a very brief hesitation in the sound within the first 10 seconds of playback. This hesitation is just enough to notice, and then it's gone, almost like it skips a quarter-second of sound or something. It doesn't happen again until an eject operation and a disc is inserted again. I have observed this with multiple discs.

There is no HDMI cable in the box. Keep that in mind when you buy - you'll need to either have a cable already or you'll have to buy one separately.

This is not a bad player and so far it is working better than our previous Blu-Ray player. It sticks to the basics and it gets them right. There are a couple of minor odd behaviors that bug me a little but at the asking price I can overlook those.

I do a lot with photography and I always keep my eyes open for good lighting solutions that will help me get the lighting effects I want or need for given situations. I saw this one at a reasonable price and decided to take a chance on it. So far I am very pleased with it. It meets the biggest requirement I have for lighting - it does not strobe.

So many LED lights have an issue with strobing, especially when they’re low-cost. This light is not expensive when compared to a lot of others, so even though it is marketed as a video light I was only cautiously optimistic. To determine this for sure, I set my camera to use the electronic shutter only, sped up the shutter speed as high as I could and pointed directly at the light when it was powered on. Strobing lights always show banding in pictures with higher shutter speeds when using the electronic shutter; this one did not (though the display on the camera sure did but that’s a different problem). This test proved to me that this LED light does not strobe, at least not slow enough for my camera sensor to see it at high shutter speeds.

This is a fairly large LED panel, designed for video use of course but I also can work just fine for photography or even general lighting in the right setting. It comes with a clamp mount and a pole so it can be attached to a desk or shelf, then the mounting head allows for angling the light as needed so it can light a surface at just the right angle desired. The mount is sturdy and there should be no issues with stability when it is set up properly.

The light is super-easy to adjust. There are two dials on the back for tweaking the brightness and the temperature range, and there is a remote included that does the same. The temperature can be adjusted from a warm 2800K to a blistering white 8000K and everywhere in between so you can get the lighting just right.

Power is via an AC adapter and there is no battery. So, this is not a travel light by any means, If you need a light to use in the field, unless you have a power generator with you then this light isn’t it. For a static setting in a studio or room, this light is very good.

One design decision that would have been nice would have been a detachable mount so it could be used with a standard tripod instead of a clamp mount. That’s not a big deal, especially at the price point, but it would have made this light so much more versatile. I have other lights that I can mount on a tripod, so I am not too concerned.

This is a very good video light, especially when considering the price point. It has excellent temperature range, it has a solid mount for stability, and it does not strobe. If you’re looking for a solid video LED light that won’t cost a fortune, this one is better than could be reasonably expected at the asking price. It’s an easy one to recommend.

I have a strong interest in photography and I always keep an eye open for lights and equipment that will help me take more creative or impactful pictures. I selected this light with the intent of using it for creative photography and so far I am pleased with it. I have other LED lights that have similar functions, but this one is different in a few ways that set it apart.

This is a wand light as opposed to a square LED bank. As such, the light distribution is a bit different. It can directly cover a longer (wider) area which is handy when putting together a mock-up with miniatures. It has a couple of mounting options too, utilizing either a miniature tripod (included) or magnetically attaching to a metal surface. I do wish a clamp was included such that it could attach to the tripod horizontally, but such clamps are available if they're needed.

This light is VERY bright and can easily light a small room when at full brightness. It can be dimmed to cast a soft light too which is good. It's not exactly the most ideal light source but it will work for general lighting in a pinch.

The temperature range goes from 2500k (very warm and orange-y) to 9900k (blistering cold white) and everywhere in between. Getting the color just right is relatively easy though it does take a little patience and experimentation to get it right. Do keep in mind that because this is an LED-based light, the temperature band setting is quite narrow and presents a different light profile, one that the camera can see but the human eye cannot. In addition to "natural lighting" modes it can be set for specific colors too such as purple, red, blue and so on.

Charging is done via a USB-C port, and the charging cable is included. I have not tried using this as a power source to charge my phone though the documentation doesn't say much about that. A full charge on this light lasts a while, though I have not drained it all the way down to find out how long it will last. Obviously the runtime is variable based on mode and brightness, and what is interesting about this light in particular is that it displays the estimated runtime on the screen based on current settings - this is a nice feature that I have not seen on a lot of these lights.

There are some creative modes for use with video or for special effects in a live setting, though the usefulness of these modes is dependent on the user. I personally will never use them. However, in the right hands these might be very useful for a project. There are several effects available, including police flashers, tube TV glow simulation, flickering candle and more.

The light comes with a nice canvas carrying pouch that provides basic storage and protection.

I really like this light and will be working with it more in the coming weeks and months. It has some nice features and it has good color and brightness ranges. It's not terribly expensive either.

I am usually not a big fan of on-ear headphones. I have learned through experience that Philips makes good headphones, though, and based on the brand name I selected this set of headphones to try out. So far I am pleased with them.

As mentioned, these are on-ear phones. For me, I prefer over-the-ear phones which are more comfortable most of the time, and that is probably the only complaint I have with these. After wearing these for a while I need to take them off for a short time before I can put them back on and keep going. This is true with most on-ear phones I have tried. For on-ear phones, though, these aren't bad and the ear fatigue is less than many I have used.

This particular set boasts an on-demand bass boost, and for me that's a huge plus. Most headphones have the bass boost baked right in and there's no way to turn it off. I don't care for heavy-handed bass (gives me headaches), so for me it is a feature I will leave turned off most of the time. However, there are times when the bass needs some help, and these deliver. When activated, there is a very noticeable increase in bass response that will certainly make some people happy.

So, about the sound profile... A set of headphones isn't worth any amount of money if they sound bad. These are fairly balanced phones when the bass booster is turned off. The highs are bright and clear, the midrange is warm and the bass is present but not overwhelming. The bass becomes front and center when the boost is turned on.

These connect via Bluetooth and they pair and establish connection quickly. I have no complaints.

These are good on-ear phones that work well. They're reasonably comfortable, and they connect well. The most interesting feature, to me, is the on-demand bass booster which is better than having a continuous bass boost that's built in. For me, that's a major positive point and is the reason I will continue using these. These sound good.

This is marketed as a tripod designed for the Nest camera, but I didn’t get it for that particular use. Instead, I selected it for two purposes – first as a low-profile support for a video light and second as a tabletop tripod mount for my camera that will fit in my camera bag. It is a decent little tripod, not perfect but good for my purposes.

This is a small-profile tripod, measuring about 12” (a little more) when folded up as it comes from the package. It is fully assembled and is completely ready to go. The legs are initially straight; they are bendy though and can be adjusted some to increase/decrease the height as well as wrap around things to secure the tripod in place.

The head has a standard mounting screw so it will fit most cameras and similar accessories. My video light uses this size of screw so it attaches very easily and securely to the tripod. There is an adjustment ring on the mounting screw that allows for getting the mount tight against the device to which it is attached, even when the whole screw does not fit. The head also has a ball joint so that it can tilt the device in any direction and secure it without issue.

It works a bit better than other bendy-leg tripods I have used. It seems to be more stable in most situations. In particular, when the legs are wrapped around something and it is suspended off the ground, it doesn’t slip quite as readily, though with enough weight it can be shifted which should be fairly obvious.

The one area where this tripod could be improved is in the feet at the ends of the legs. These are smooth, rubber feet and most of the time they’re adequate for keeping the tripod stable and still. That said, on an modest incline they are not non-slip enough to keep the tripod from shifting, especially when on a moving surface (I know, this is an unusual circumstance, but it does happen occasionally). It’s easy enough to work around this with some tacky adhesive like you might find in a classroom, but it would be nice if this wasn’t necessary. On smoother inclined surfaces there are better solutions.

This is a nice little tripod that works reasonably well. It is not perfect but it does work better than a lot of other small, bendy-leg tripods. It’s made well and it fits nicely in my camera bag. Consider this one if you are looking for a small tripod.

I enjoy photography as a serious hobby and I lean to the creative side of it. I selected this set of display boards with the thought of doing more creative things with my pictures and so far I am happy with them. I will say they're not ideal for all situations and environments, though, and they require some gentle care.

In a nutshell, these are plastic round platters that are matte finished on one side and glossy on the other. In the right lighting, these can make a photo really pop, particularly when using the black reflective surface. The white disk is good for darker subjects, while the black disk is better for reflection in low light situations.

There are a couple of things about these that merit mention. First, these are plastic platters and are susceptible to scratches. Once the glossy side is scratched, these are basically no longer useful in their intended roles (the black disk in particular), though they can be repurposed. More subtle though is the fact that the black disk shows dust easily and when used in dusty environments it is almost useless. I wiped the black glossy surface with a microfiber cloth, and I hit it with an air duster can, and I still had particles that required editing after the fact to remove from the final image after less than 30 seconds of set-up after cleaning.

I do like these display boards and I will get some good use from them. That said, these are not perfect and require some gentle care to keep them useful.

I have a Fuji X-T3 and I have not shied away from third-party lenses at all. I have been looking for good wide-angle lenses and I have been aware of TTArtisan for a while. I was curious how well this lens would perform and I decided to take a chance on it. So far I am very pleased with it though I am still working with it and learning that it can do.

This lens is a brick! Right out of the box I was startled at the overall weight. It has a lot of glass in it, but it also is all metal - very little (if any) plastic. Even the front lens cap is metal. In spite of the price, this is a solid little lens.

It is probably the tightest fit lens I have used. It requires a little pressure to get it to click into place and to remove it later when mounting on the camera body. I was a little concerned at first, thinking I could potentially damage the camera. However, it does fit and does not harm the camera in spite of how tightly it fits.

Optical quality seems to be good, though that varies a little with the aperture setting. At the widest settings (and f/1.4 in particular) there is a little softness in the corners and a slight vignetting. As the aperture is closed more the image gets sharper at the edges. This is not unusual or unexpected for wide-angle large-aperture lenses, and it is actually slightly better than I was expecting.

I have not yet had a chance to get out and determine the coma with this lens. I am waiting for a clear night so I can get a starry sky shot with the aperture wide open, which will highlight not only the coma but also the chromatic characteristics. If it is particularly bad I will come back and update.

As a portrait or landscape lens this one works very well. Initial exposures have worked out well, but I am still learning what this lens can do.

Are there better wide-angle lenses out there? Sure - and they cost a lot more too. For the price this lens is far better than expected and I am looking forward to working with it more. It is good enough that I am staring to look at other TTArtisan offerings.

I selected this mouse/keyboard combo to work with a laptop I use every day. I wanted a full-sized keyboard and I was less concerned about the mouse because I prefer trackballs anyway. So far I have no complaints at all about this combo set, though I am especially pleased with the keyboard.

This is a basic mouse/keyboard combo that connects via an RF receiver. The keyboard is a full-sized US layout keyboard, and the mouse is a basic 3-button mouse. These are marketed as having silent keys and clicks, and that interested me in particular.

The keyboard is indeed nearly silent. I love the quiet operation and I love the feel of the keys themselves - they have a soft-down feel when pressed. I read one of the other reviews that stated that the keys stick a little, and I have not found that to be the case for me. The mouse is also quiet and it seems to work well, though it is nothing special.

This combo works well under Windows 10, Windows 11 and Linux. I have not tried it elsewhere though I have no reason to believe it wouldn't work on other platforms.

I am very happy with this combo set and expect years of service from it. It does live up to the claim that operation is very quiet, the keys have a nice feel to them, and the combo is priced reasonably.

Most of the headphones with which I have worked have been active noise canceling (ANC) phones so I know a lot about those, but I also have other headphones too that I like. I was unaware that 3M even had headphones, and I was also unsure what their "Quiet Space" was all about. It's an interesting solution that works fairly well. Overall, these are good phones, though there's one area that could use some slight improvement and that's the sound profile.

These are over-the-ear phones and they are actually quite comfortable. I like how they feel on my head - they fit snugly and I can tilt my head without losing these phones, but they don't clamp down super tight either.

Build-wise, these are more substantial than the price suggests. I like the size adjustment in particular which is designed to last and should not fatigue with use.

I powered these on and they quickly paired and connected to my laptop. The range is good and I was able to walk a fair distance away without losing the connection or having the sound get crackly or having it skip. With no feed coming to them they eventually powered themselves off, saving battery but potentially frustrating the wearer if this is unexpected.

Just putting these on I was surprised by the amount of noise isolation. Without even turning these on they drastically reduced the ambient noise in the room, even effectively blocking out the sound of a running fan. I have had very few headphones that have as effective sound isolation as these, and that's a huge plus right out of the gate. The Quiet Space function adds to this, but not like ANC phones - it injects white noise into the cans so all you hear is a gentle but constant hiss that overrides most other noises. It's not deathly quiet with these on, but you won't hear most other sounds in the area when they're producing white noise. This is a very different approach to sound cancellation and it works.

The sound profile is the one area where these phones could use a little improvement, though these are not terrible and are better than some big-name phones I have used. The bass is not overdriven but it is not muted either, and this is refreshing since most manufacturers overdrive the bass. The highs are clear, though not shrill. The midrange, however, is flat to the point that music can sound slightly hollow. It's an easy fix with an equalizer and is better than one particular big-name manufacturer's similar flaw.

I like these phones and will be working with them more. They take a different approach to dealing with ambient noise and surrounding distractions than what ANC phones use, and they seem to work well. They're well made, comfortable and reasonably priced.

I don't have a lot of experience with HP peripherals, particularly mice, so I was on unfamiliar ground when working with this one. This has proven to be a decent mouse and so far I am pleased with it.

This is a big mouse so it is well-suited for people with large hands like me. I like the fact that it is comfortable to use for long periods of time and it doesn't cause my hands to cramp like some other mice. I have had many mice that have caused me some issues in use so it is something to which I pay attention.

The buttons work as expected right out of the box. This is a 7-button mouse - more buttons than I'm used to - and the buttons work as you'd expect - left- and right-click, forward page, back page, scroll, etc.

Finding the wireless dongle was a little frustrating at first. It is tucked underneath, hidden under a removable panel that is held in place magnetically. I did not understand that the panel came out, even though a graphic printed on the bottom showed where to push. Once I realized that I found the wireless dongle and was able to connect it just fine. Now that said, this mouse does not require the dongle but can use Bluetooth as well and can be used with three devices.

The scroll wheel can be smooth or it can be stepped, and that is controlled through a single mechanical button on the top of the mouse. This button tends to be a little fussy and I have had some minor issues getting the button to work as expected. It does work, it just requires deliberate and focused attention, not a half-attentive push. I am not sure if this is just my mouse or is an issue with the design overall. It's minor but noticeable.

And, this mouse works flawlessly under Linux as well as under Windows.

I like this mouse and will use it on one of my laptops. It fits my hand very well and it works as expected.

I have worked with a lot of ANC headphones, and I have a different pair of JVC phones that have served me well. I looked to these phones as a possible replacement for a dead pair of Bose QC-15 phones that finally just wore out. These are good phones that balance sound quality and ANC nicely.

The ANC function is what interested me most about these and I set about testing them. These work very well but they are not as aggressive as Bose or Sony when it comes to actively cancelling out low-frequency noise. This is a good thing in most cases as the aggressive ANC on Bose and Sony is actually uncomfortable when turned on. Where the two bigger players go all-out for maximum ANC function, these go for "good enough for most" and in terms of how they compare against other manufacturers such as Sennheiser, Philips, and other well-known brands they compare well. They cancel out the lion's share of low droning noises such as road noise and fans, enough so that turning on music at low volumes is still workable in noisy environments.

The sound profile is another important consideration and I have seen a wide variance in sound quality, particularly among ANC phones. These get the sound profile fairly close to right which is a refreshing change. The bass is present and strong but isn't pushed forward as with so many other headphones. The midrange is warm and gives music a decent depth. The highs are clear and bright without being shrill. These aren't audiophile quality phones by any means, but they are better than many I have used.

These are over-the-ear phones which is my preference. I also like that these fit snugly and don't slip off whern I look down which is also a personal preference but it's important to me. If you like a very light set of phones these probably are not quite the right fit for you; if you like a set that fits a bit more firmly, these are good in that regard.

These are comfortable too. The ear cups are padded nicely and I can wear them for a couple of hours before I need to take them off for a few minutes. Most headphones I have worn get uncomfortable after a while, and these do also but it is not as quick as with many.

My one complaint is the way these are powered on and off. Instead of a simple on/off button or switch, the cans swivel to power them on and off. I can see the potential for taking them off and leaving them powered on, resulting in reduced useful runtime.

I like these phones and have been working with them quite a bit of late. They're not a complete replacement for more aggressive ANC phones but they get the sound profile right and they are comfortable enough to wear for a long flight. These strike a nice balance between comfort, ANC capability and sound quality.

I have worked with K&F Concept filters in the past and generally had good experiences with them. They're good, mid-range quality filters at (usually) a budget price. I haven't worked with any black diffusion filters prior to this one so I have no basis against which to compare, but so far it seems to work as designed and seems to be made very well.

In a nutshell, this type of filter softens light a bit, causing some gentle halos around light sources, without impacting image sharpness or detail. Where I have seen the most noticeable impact is in images where there otherwise would be a lot of shadows and contrast; instead of stark contrast and strong shadows, the filter has the effect of brightening up the shadows somewhat and creating smoother color gradients. Sure, this can be done in software after the fact, but it is a lot easier to do this at the time the image is taken and it certainly is a lot less work.

The filter is very easy to install. This is my first magnetic filter and it is as easy to attach to my camera as I could have hoped. The threaded ring attaches to the lens in the same manner as a step ring or another filter, and the filter itself just snaps securely into place due to the magnetics. Removing the filter is just as simple, especially if you choose to leave the magnetic ring in place on the lens.

The assembly seems to be well made. I have had filters in the past that have been poorly constructed and rattle in the frames when shaken, or have been mildly blemished, or just felt cheap. This filter has none of those issues and appears to be well made.

This is a nice black diffusion filter. It's easy to install and use, and it just works. I will be using it more in the coming weeks.

I have used smart watches for a while now and I have seen a steady progression in the technology. This is my first Gen 6 watch. It is a big improvement from what I have used before (beyond just battery life) and so far I am pleased with it.

This is an Android-based smart watch, and it is similar in interface to previous smart watches I have seen and used. If you have used any generation of smart watch before this one the experience is very similar. I won't get too deep into the nuts and bolts of that or the WearOS app.

There are two big areas of improvement I have seen with this new watch. First, the battery life is much better than previous smart watches I have used which is very encouraging. I have a Gen 2 watch that I love but it lasts only about 3 days on a charge, and my Gen 5 is not much better. This one lasts several days before the battery runs out.

The more important improvement to me, though, is the way it doesn't interfere with the Bluetooth in my car. Previous watches messed up my ability to stream to the car's sound system to the point that the sound would sputter and simply die. I did trace it to the watch by powering off the watch completely after which the problem went away and would come back when the watch was powered on. This watch does not interfere at all and my car's Bluetooth works whether the watch is on or not.

This is a stylish watch, a bit more upscale than some of the others I have seen and used. The band is a non-stretch link band that is a little snug but not unworkable.

So far this watch works well for me. I am pleased with the improved battery life and even more happy that it doesn't mess with my car's Bluetooth connectivity.

USB-C cables are the one cable type I usually have trouble putting my hands on in my house, and I need them for charging my tablet as well as my video lights. I selected this one because I like cables with braided insulation and so far this one has worked out well for me.

This is a 6' cable which is just about right for my needs. It is long enough to reach my devices when I have it plugged into my USB brick on my desk without requiring rearrangement of everything on my desk just to make it fit. Longer would be handy but unnecessary, but shorter would make it a lot less useful for me.

I have not used it for data transfer, just charging up devices, and so far it has worked out well in that capacity. The connection is snug and I have not noticed any particular difference in charging speeds between this cable and the OEM cables that came with my devices.

I am especially pleased with the build quality. The cable is stiff (as to be expected) and it should hold up for a long time against kinks and twists. The junctions where the cable goes into the plastic casings for the connectors are tight and allow no play which is a big plus for me as these are the spots where I have had cables fail most often. Overall, I am not unhappy with the build quality.

This is a decent third-party USB-C cable that works very well for me. It is made well and it does a fine job charging my devices. It isn’t too expensive either, making it easy to recommend.

I do a lot of creative photography work and I look for tools and ideas that will help me along in that regard. I took a chance on this LED light, thinking it would be a good tool for adding color and light when I need it, and so far I am pleased with it.

This is not a very big light, about the size of an iPhone. It's small enough that finding a place for it in my camera bag takes little effort and it is always at the ready when I need it without requiring a bunch of storage. It comes in a carrying case and even the case is small. If you need a small light, keep reading.

This is advertised as a video light, so one of the most important things to consider is whether or not is strobes. A lot of cheap LEDs strobe which makes them inappropriate for video work (or high speed photography for that matter). This is not a super-cheap light, more expensive than many of the LED banks I have seen, so I assumed it would not strobe and this assumption was correct. When considering that it is a non-strobing LED that is priced around $70 (as I write this), this thing is a bargain - good video lights are often more than double the cost.

This light is a very interesting tool. I have other LED video lights, and these typically have a brightness setting, a few effects, and gel plates that can be used to tweak the color. This particular LED bank is different in that it allows for adjusting not only the brightness but also the colors, with RGB broken out into components that can be adjusted individually. So, if you need a really bright yellow light, a pale green light or a cool blue, this light can do it. Whatever color/brightness you need, there's a way to get it out of this light.

This light also has a number of effects that will suit a videographer. I spent some time playing with these and cycling through the different effect modes. There's lightning flash, police lights, faulty bulbs and more, and these can be adjusted like the solid modes can be. These modes are not really of any use to me at the moment, personally, as I do not do video work much at all, but I can see some things I can do with them for fun and I do like having them available should I decide to do any video work later.

When I received this light it was mostly discharged and I needed to plug it in to charge. The documentation says it takes about 2 hours to fully charge and that's fairly accurate. The display shows the charging level and it doesn't take too long from almost dead to fully changed.

Though I am unlikely to need it, I like that I can charge a USB device with this light, like it's a power bank. I have not tried charging/powering my camera with it yet, but I like the idea that I can do that.

This light comes with a hot shoe mount and USB-C charging cables. While it can be mounted on a tripod, a selfie stick is more versatile and makes getting this light in the right position easy.

This is a neat little light and it is worth more than the asking price in my opinion. It seems to work very well, it has a lot of neat creative modes and, most importantly, it does not strobe. If you need a well-priced LED light that works well for video and high-speed photography, this is a good one to consider.

I have worked with a lot of active noise canceling (ANC) headphones by a lot of manufacturers, including an older pair of Philips headphones. I’ve seen a wide variance in ANC implementation and sound profiles, and to be honest few manufacturers get theirs right. With this set of headphones, Philips comes close.

These are over-ear phones which I prefer over on-ear phones. They fit snugly but not tight, and they actually do a good job of sound isolation. Even if you don’t like the ANC function (which would defeat the purpose of having these phones), these do a surprisingly good job of sound isolation. The pads are soft enough and comfortable enough that I can wear these for quite a while without discomfort. After a bit of time they do start to get a little warm but not to the point that I need to take them off.

These connect via Bluetooth and they connect very quickly. The connectivity of these phones is absolutely amazing: this is the very first pair of Bluetooth headphones I have used that maintains a steady connection up two flights of stairs with closed doors in between the phones and the source. The connectivity alone makes these very much worth checking out.

The ANC function is very good though it is not quite as aggressive as that of Bose or Sony. It is strong enough to mostly drown out a droning high-volume fan (my baseline for testing), such that music at a low volume while the ANC is turned on completely drowns out the fan. While Bose and Sony go to the extreme for noise cancellation, and other manufacturers often have ANC that’s barely there, Philips has implemented a system that is good enough for most. I am pleased with the ANC and will use these phones when I travel next.

The ANC function on these phones can be turned off if desired. There is also a special “awareness mode” that is an in-between mode that doesn’t completely turn off ANC but allows more environmental noise in, and this mode is really designed for permitting conversation without having to turn everything off completely. It works fairly well though the noise this mode produces via the external microphone is slightly harsh and shrill.

The default sound profile is not exactly perfect but it is better than many I have used and heard. These do boost the bass by default though not to an uncomfortable level. Bass boost is very common in headphones and it’s often too aggressive, but these actually give a modest boost. The midrange is a little soft though present. The highs sound bright and clear but not piercing. As a result, the sound profile is not quite perfectly balanced but it still good.

The sound profile can be tweaked via an app. I found the Philips Headphones app, installed it and started messing with it. The app works better than the reviews have suggested and it does a decent job of adjusting the headphones on the fly. The mode can be changed as well as the sound profile to adjust for different could quality based on music type, and there is a custom setting so that the equalizer can be adjusted to taste. The only complaint I have with the app is that there is about a 1s pause when changing modes between ANC. Awareness mode and Off, though this gap does not occur when changing the mode via the button on the headphones.

I like these ANC phones. They’re not perfect but they’re better than average with a good ANC function and decent sound. The have absolutely incredible connectivity, and they can be adjusted to taste via an app. This is a pair to keep on the short list if you need Bluethooth headphones that maintain a connection a long way from the source and provide ANC in the deal.

I have a smartwatch that I have worn now for over a year and I have been pleased with it. I was unfamiliar with the idea of a "hybrid smartwatch" and was interested in this one from Skagen. It's an interesting concept and the watch itself seems to work well, but I have some frustrations with the software.

This is basically a traditional analog watch with some smartwatch functions built into it. The smartwatches I have used usually have a full digital face with all manner of things on the display, and depending on the face chosen it may or may not be easy to read. This watch keeps things relatively simple and has the hour and minute displayed with moving hands, and around the center are displays for steps, heart rate and weather-at-a-glance. The whole is clean and easy on the eyes. Now, that said, if you cannot read an analog watch this one might not be the best choice.

Charging requires the special cable that comes with it and it takes a relatively short time to charge. The run time is much longer than most smartwatches I have used, getting well over a week on a single charge where a smartwatch is often 2-3 days or less.

Skagen has a special app for interacting with the watch and it was easy to find in the repository. It installs quickly and guides through the setup without too much issue. It is good for activity tracking and limited health monitoring as well as limited customization of the face. However, I have had some difficulty with connectivity and staying connected through the app, such that it has been an annoyance. This is the biggest complaint I have so far.

So far this watch has managed to keep good time, connected or not.

Overall I am happy with this watch though I am less than thrilled with the app. Hopefully an update will correct the connectivity issue I see with it. Otherwise, this is a good-looking and functional watch.

I have been interested in a device that can find hidden cameras for a while as we do tend to travel periodically. This device seemed like a good one and I wanted to try it out before I travel again. It seems like a pretty neat device that works fairly well, but it is hamstrung by very poor documentation.

This does more than just find hidden cameras. It is able to pick up Wi-fi signals, wireless phone signals and more. The sensitivity is very much like working with a metal detector - turn it up too high and it becomes nothing more than a sight and sound show; turned too low and it hardly sees anything.

With the unit turned on and set to a reasonable initial detection level I set about looking for devices in my home office. I have several Wi-fi connected devices and I usually have my smartphone there too, and I messed with this detector until I found the level where it was able to find everything. I did not try going near the router which is in another room but I imagine that one would require another sensitivity adjustment.

Most of the functions are self-explanatory, but some took a little trial and error to figure out. This is where good documentation would come in handy, and unfortunately the documentation with this device is poor. It's sufficient to identify the different functions of the device and where to find different components, but the actual descriptions and explanations of the functions are written in very poorly translated English.

Aside from the documentation, it would have been nice to have a carrying case for this device for storage and travel. That's a minor gripe, though.

I am happy with this device, though better documentation would make it much easier to use right away. It has some useful functions that will appeal to wary travelers, and it seems to work well once you figure out the right adjustments.

I have worked with a lot of different headphones, mostly active noise canceling (ANC) phones but also more traditional phones. Over the years I have had several Sennheiser phones and they typically have balanced sound and good build quality. This set is a step down from many of the others with which I have worked, though they’re still decent.

My preference on headphones is over-the-ear phones which for me are more comfortable. These particular phones are on-ear, and these pinch a little after extended wear. They’re better than some of the other on-ear phones with which I have worked, but I still prefer over-the-ear phones. One preference I have is a headphone that clamps down fairly tightly when worn so they’re less likely to slip off when I tilt my head down; these are a lighter fit.

These are Bluetooth-only phones and as such cannot be used with non-BT devices. This is unfortunate but isn’t a deal-breaker. These connect easily and quickly.

These are not ANC phones, but they have excellent passive noise canceling which is quite surprising for on-ear phones. They reduce ambient noise in my office considerably, which us especially noticeable when running a large fan that I use to generate white noise. I am pleased with that aspect of these phones. These are still not as effective as a set of ANC phones.

The sound profile is fairly typical of Sennheiser phones, though the bass is mildly beefed up.. The trend with phones these days is overdriven bass, and these do increase the bass response a little bit but not to a headache-inducing level. The midrange is full and warm, and that’s a good thing as many times the increased bass comes at the expense of the midrange. The highs are bright and clear without being piercing. Overall, the sound is reasonably balanced, but certainly not audiophile quality.

Build-wise, these actually feel a bit on the cheaper side which is surprising. These aren’t exactly fragile, but they are definitely not of the same build quality as other Sennheisers I have used in the past.

These are probably best described as entry-level headphones. They’re not the highest quality, and they are not the most sturdy, but the sound quality is fine and the cost is right. The main thing I would change is the addition of an audio port so they could be used as wired phones.

I use rechargeable AA batteries frequently, specifically in my handheld GPS receivers, so keeping them charged up is sometimes a challenge when I have had more than one device in use. My previous charger only allowed for charging two batteries at a time, so I was excited to have the ability to charge eight at once. This charger works well for this, though it is on the slow side.

This is a very small and lightweight charger, without a lot of bells and whistles. It does not have a refresh option, it is simply a charger. The cost is lower than I would have expected, running about $13 as I write this.

I was startled when I opened the box and found that this is a USB-powered charger, not a AC-powered charger. It’s not even a USB-C device but a Micro USB device. My immediate thought was that it will be slow, and this thought was correct. To be fair, I missed the detail that it works via USB so that’s on me. The fact that it uses a Micro USB interface is listed as well, though it is buried in the details.

I popped in 8 batteries and let it go. I wasn’t sure how long it would take to charge them all, and it finished them at varying times over about a 4-hour period. Most had some charge already and finished earlier, while others had little power already and needed more time. It did charge them all, and it gave me a clear visual indicator when it had finished each battery. I’m not dissatisfied there.

While it is slower than my 2-battery charger that runs on AC power, it ultimately is faster as it can charge 4 times as many at once and the net time consumed is less.

The one improvement I would make for this charger would be to have it use USB-C instead of Micro USB, though that would likely drive up the asking price. Otherwise, I have no real complaints. This charger works well and it handles 8 batteries simultaneously. Price-wise, this is a good deal, too.

I selected this audio extension cable for the office, where I need to use headphones to listen to content but am unable to move the source. A 6' audio cable is often too short, and having an extension cable instead of a full audio cable enables me to use different headphone sets. So far, this cable has worked out for me.

This is a nylon-wrapped cable which I prefer to plastic-insulated cables for durability. Unlike many other nylon cables, though, this one has some flex to it and it is not stiff and prone to knotting or kinking like others I have used. The end connectors are attached with a plastic sleeve that is stiff enough to keep the cable from getting bent at the connector without some effort, and this should greatly help in making this cable last longer since the point of connection is usually the failure point for me with audio cables.

The main concern I had when adding this cable to my configuration is if it would work seamlessly or would it introduce static or a hum to output. While this might not be a huge concern in this case it was still something I made a point to check. The sound was identical with this cable in place as it is without it. Even when turning the connector on either end, there was no static. That's all I can really ask of it.

This cable meets a need I had and it works very well. It's made nicely and it doesn't impact sound quality, good or bad (unless replacing a bad extension cable). Based on my working with it I am happy to recommend it.

I use headphones frequently in the office, and I have found that audio cables are often the weak link when it comes to headphones. I have gone through several cables just from daily wear and tear. I looked to this cable as a replacement for my last failed cable. So far I am pleased with it.

I prefer nylon braided cables as they seem to be more durable and tend to last longer. They do have a tendency to be more stiff and inflexible, though. This particular cable has more flex than most other nylon braided cables I have used while it also feels more substantial. I have been pleasantly surprised with how much more flexible this cable is compared to most.

The weak point in most cables is where the cable itself joins the connector. I have seen so many that have a rubbery, flimsy sleeve at the connector, and these have a tendency to rip before the cable connection fails. This particular cable has a nice, hard plastic sleeve instead, once that does have a small amount of flex but is hard and sturdy enough that it’s not going to rip or fail without deliberate effort to damage it.

As a nice plus, I like that this cable is bright red where most others are plain black or white. There will be no confusing this cable for someone else’s in a shared environment. I have paired this cable with a set of Munitio PRO40 headphones and it works well and looks great.

It’s another big plus that it comes in different sizes too, so you can choose the size you need.

Sound quality with my cable appears to be unchanged from other cables I have tried - no buzz or hum with different electronics I have tried, no crackle or hiss. That’s really all I can ask.

So far I have no complaints with this audio cable. It works well, appears to be made well and it is brightly colored which makes it stand out and distinguishable from most other audio cables I have seen and used. It is priced reasonably as well. Based on my experience with it so far this is an easy recommend.

Note: There is more than one product attached to this listing. I am specifically reviewing the 18” light.

One of the things I have been researching for a while is ring lights. I have wanted one for a little while, but not the kind that sits on a desk and is only useful for making personal videos for upload. I wanted one that would be suitable for taking portrait photos and would be suitable for professional use. This is a nice ring light to that end and so far I am pleased with it, though I have not been using it long.

This is a large light, 18” in diameter which makes it quite a bit larger than most ring lights available right now. It is large enough that you can shoot photos or video through it using a full-sized camera with little effort, which is what I was looking for. It comes with a full-sized tripod (which it needs) as well as a nylon carry bag. It also comes with a mounting makeup mirror in the bag which is something I will not use with the ring light (I have other uses for it). In includes all of the hardware you need for mounting your camera, video camera or phone if you are a vlogger or content maker.

The very first thing I did with this light was point my camera right at it while using the electronic shutter, in order to determine if the LEDs in this light are strobing or not. I half expected these to strobe based on the price, but they do not which is a very good thing. It means steady, consistent light that does not flicker.

There are two adjustment knobs that are on the light assembly, one to control the brightness and the other to control the light temperature. The temperature range (speaking in generalized, observable terms rather than technical terms with numbers) allows for setting the light from an orangy golden-hour glow to a piercing frosty blue, and everywhere in between. So, though it may require some messing it allows for getting the light temperature just right based on skin tone and background. The brightness can be varied from a soft glow to bright enough to hurt your eyes when looking right at the ring. Thought not designed for such, this would work as a studio light in a pinch...

I do not have a light meter to check the actual light temperature or the lumens/lux output.

There’s a plastic cover over the LED array that helps to diffuse the lights and make them easier to face when using the light to illuminate a face for portraits.

The power source is AC 110/120. Some ring lights I have seen and used have USB-based power input instead. These tend to be smaller and less powerful.

Construction is good though I would stop short of saying it is solid and rugged. It is mostly plastic so it does have some flex to it but seems sturdy enough to handle getting moved around and jostled some. Because the housing is plastic instead of metal this is a lightweight unit and is easy to transport. This is a trade-off I have seen with tripods as well – lightweight for travel, heavier for less mobile work. This light seems geared for the traveler based on that.

Overall, I am pleased with this light. It is a bit better than I expected and it has everything you need in the package to be suitable for vlogging or studio use. It’s a big light so it does cost a bit more than a lot of the smaller, USB-powered lights out there but the cost is reasonable. If you’re looking for a ring light that can be used for either video content or of portrait work, give this one some consideration.

My son participates in an online meeting weekly, and he needed a new webcam to replace the one he was using. The old one worked but was not of good quality. Based on the asking price for this webcam I was not especially hopeful. That said, it has proven to be better than either of us expected.

It's easy to set up - plug it in and let the OS configure it. It's easy enough to use, too, by selecting the camera desired if there's more than one.

We have seen no issues with clarity or audio/video quality, which have both been solid and reliable. In his meeting, others have commented that his feed seems to be the clearest and most glitch-free.

At least one other reviewer noticed issues with lag and skipping. This has not been an issue for us and so far this little camera has performed well without incident.

The model we received did not have the mini tripod. However, it has a standard mount for a tripod and those little tripods are easy enough to find. If you already have a tripod of any size, this webcam will mount without issue.

Could it be better? Sure. But, improvement would drive up the cost, and the quality is good as it is. For the asking price, this is a great little webcam.

I selected this keyboard after doing a bit of research. I already have a solar keyboard (a Logitech) on my Windows system, and I needed a keyboard for my Linux system. I was a little hesitant to buy because I did not see any definitive information that it would work with Linux. I've had it several days, and I can say with some authority, it definitely works correctly under Linux.

The system in question is a Dell laptop running Peppermint Linux hosting a CentOS 8 VM. Most keyboards (with one notable exception) work on this system so I was hopeful it would work well, and it does. It behaves virtually identically to the Logitech keyboard and so far has given me no trouble.

Build-wise, this is a solid keyboard that should hold up to some abuse. It is sturdy and does not flex when I am typing. I like the fact that the dongle is held to the back of the keyboard magnetically so it can be transported with less concern of being misplaced when not in use.

One of the major issues I have with keyboards is that I have the hands of a gorilla and I frequently run into issues with hitting multiple keys at the same time, particularly with flat keyboards like this one. The keys are slightly bigger than average with this one, though, and hitting muliple keys simultaneously is less of a problem. This was an unexpected and welcome surprise.

Aesthetically, I love the feel of this keyboard. Most of the keys are concave and feel pleasant to the touch. Oddly, a good number of the keys on the bottom row are actually convex. While this is no issue at all, I do find it puzzling.

It is priced competitively against the Logitech too.
