I have worked with other Rii keyboards and every one of them has worked out well for me. The ones I have used prior to this one have been well suited for portability and are smaller than a standard-sized keyboard. This one is a little bit different – it is still small and it has a nice footprint, but it includes an integrated touch pad. It is also rechargeable, which is not new but it is different in how it works. I am using it to type this review on my Linux laptop.

First things first – it is compatible with Windows as well as Linux and Android. I will assume it is compatible with OSX but I have no way to confirm this as I am not a Mac user.

This is a wireless keyboard that comes with a USB dongle as well as a direct USB connection that allows it to charge when it needs it. I had hoped that the USB wire would allow for not only charging but for use as a wired keyboard, but this is not the case – the wire is just for charging and nothing more. I suspected that to be the case but it was worth trying. I am not sure yet how long the battery will last, but I do very much appreciate that this keyboard will never need new batteries.

I plugged the USB receiver into the system and the keyboard was ready to work immediately. There were no drivers that required installation and no fancy setup procedure. It is literally as simple and plugging it in and turning it on.

This keyboard with the integrated mouse pad is about as wide as my 15.6” laptop, so the keys are slightly smaller than that on my laptop but this has not been a problem for me so far. The layout is economized for the space so it is important to realize that the layout takes some getting used to and you are likely to make some typing mistakes at first.

I am no fan of touch pads at all, and this one has not won me over either. That said, it works well and it even has a removable tab on it when it comes out of the box that shows hot to work with it. It is very responsive and I like the fact that it is beside the keys and not below so I do not end up inadvertently tapping it. Even though the tab on the pad says to remove it for use, I left it on there because the pad is still very responsive anyway.

One really nice plus with this keyboard, to me, is that they keys are not shiny. They have a dull matte finish which makes them very easy to see even under direct light. On my work desk I have a bright lamp that I use to illuminate the whole desk and with some keyboards it makes it difficult to see the keys because of the reflective finish. This keyboard does not have that problem. As I use it more and I wear the keys (especially the space bar) I expect that to gradually change, but for now it is great in that regard.

Though this is a small and compact keyboard it works very well for me. I like the feel of the keys, I love the fact that it does not require batteries, the touch pad is convenient when I absolutely need it and the finish is perfect for my working environment. I am very pleased with this keyboard.

I have a set of Bose QC-15 headphones and I damaged the pads some time ago. I was able to find replacements, though the original Bose pads are quite expensive. I have been looking for good replacement pads that are less expensive and I have tried some off-brand pads in an effort to save money. So far I have found none that are an exact match though I have seen some that are quite close. These are a reasonable match though they are definitely different than the original pads, but at a fraction of the cost.

In appearance these are close to the originals though they are smaller and they do not fit exactly the same. When I put on the headphones with these pads in place, I have to fiddle with the phones a little bit to get them to fit right, more so than when these had the original pads. It’s a noticeable difference but it is not a real problem unless you have to have an exact match.

The pads are soft, but not as subtle and buttery as the original pads. They will soften over time with use, but brand new they are slightly more stiff.

The main difference I have found with these pads is that they do not do as good a job with passive noise canceling as the original pads. I replaced one pad with one of these new pads and put them on my head. With a fan on in the background I listened closely. The new pad allowed more ambient noise to reach my ear than did the original pad. As it softens I think it will fit a little better and will help with the noise isolation, but even new the Bose original pads did more for sound isolation. They still do a good job, just not as good.

So, why would you consider these? There are two good reasons to buy these. First, these are a LOT less expensive than the Bose replacements. At under $10 these represent a very significant savings over the manufacturer’s own replacement pads. Second, although these are different than Bose replacements, they do a good job of making the phones look new and they do the job well enough for most people. The phones are plenty comfortable with the new pads on and unless you are looking for difference you probably would not notice.

These are good pads to consider if you need replacement pads for your headphones and you don’t mind the small differences. If you have to have 100% identical pads, these aren’t what you’re looking for. If you are content with approximately 85% the same, these are a very inexpensive alternative to Bose replacement pads.

An air mouse is not something you would normally use with a PC-based system unless you are trying to save space or are giving a presentation in which case it is a convenient accessory. Such a mouse is a lot more useful for things like Smart TVs, though it is also useful for embedded systems like a Raspberry Pi. I have used several air mice and I was curious to see how well this one would compare to others I have used. So far it has worked well, under both Linux as well as Windows. I will state up front that I have not used it with a Smart TV.

At a glance, this little device looks like a TV remote and little more, but it is quite a bit more than that. It does work as a remote, of course, but it also works as a mouse with a full-up keyboard. On one side of this device there are all of the controls you would expect to find on a remote for a Smart TV remote – volume control, channel settings, mode buttons, play, search and more. Flip the unit over and there is a keyboard, with 38 keys and most regular keyboard functions accessible through function key settings.

The unit requires two AAA batteries, not included.

I decided to try it with my Linux workstation, running CentOS 7 with a 64-bit 3.10.0-series kernel. I did not have to load special drivers and I did not need to do any special configuration at all, it was just plug and play. I was able to move the mouse just by waving the device in front of the screen and several of the buttons on the remote side worked as I would have hoped – Home took me to the browser home page, volume controls worked, Search worked, the menu button brought up the menu for the current application with focus and more. The keyboard portion worked as it should and I was able to type, though I found it a little awkward after being used to a full-sized keyboard for so long.

I also tried it with my Windows 10 system and I got nearly identical results. It required no drivers, no special configuration, no extra set-up – it just works as expected. The buttons works the same under Windows as they did under Linux for me and I was able to navigate as desired.

This is a good air mouse that works well under Linux and Windows. It should work fine with smaller systems like the Raspberry Pi (which uses a derivative of the Linux kernel). As an added bonus, it is relatively inexpensive. If you need an air mouse, this one is worth some consideration.

I have a number of headphones and I have gotten quite fussy about them and how they sound and how they fit. I was interested in this set, as they resemble a set of Philips headphones I used many years ago and my experience with them was positive. The difference was that the Philips set I used was quite expensive and had active noise cancelling functions. These are a lot less expensive. While these are not the best headphones I have used they are well worth their asking price and I think they are a good set.

These are very striking-looking headphones and they really stand out. I have the blue set and they are by far the most eye-catching phones I have used. The paint is electric blue and the pads and headband are black. I like the overall design, The cord is long enough to make them useful for using at a workstation or desk without having to sit still, a problem I have seen with a number of headsets with very short cords.

There are two primary considerations I have when looking at headphones – comfort and sound profile.

The comfort is good. The pads are long and oval and they appear at first like they would pinch or otherwise not fit well enough to make a seal. I was mistaken. They are quite comfortable and they feel good when wearing them. I will say I personally prefer headphones that really fit tightly, and these are a lot softer than I prefer, but many people prefer lighter headphones so I cannot consider this a fault. They do get a little warm after wearing them for a while, though. Keep in mind that because these do not clamp down tightly, they are not the very best for noise isolation.

The sound profile is another matter entirely. The bass is strong and there is no problem there. The midrange is sorely lacking and as a result the music sounds like it is in a tunnel – this is a problem with many headphones and I specifically look for it. It can be corrected with an equalizer which is fine if you have access to such. I will say that it’s noticeable to me but I have worked with more expensive phones that sound a lot worse. The highs are fine and are clear. I have also noticed that as the volume gets boosted higher, the sound distorts.

Now, if these were expensive headphones I would be a lot more critical, but these are under $20. For a $20 set of headphones, these are just fine and they are very much competitive with others in their price range. They sound all right through they could be better, they are quie comfortable and I really like the price point. If you need an inexpensive pair of headphones, these are not a bad choice at all.

The cameras built into smart phones are getting more and more capable and they have impacted sales of point-and-shoot cameras significantly. I still prefer using a dedicated camera instead of using my phone, and part of the reason is that using my phone doesn't feel the least bit like using a camera. This case changes that and converts your iPhone 6/6s into a camera that actually looks and feels like a dedicated camera in your hands. This is not just a cheap plastic shell with a lens port on it; it actually provides some good protection for the phone.

I will start with the shell case itself. The case is a hard plastic shell, providing back and bumper protection for the phone. It snaps over the phone and holds well. It is not so tight that it is near impossible to remove, nor is it so loose that it runs a risk of letting the phone slip. Overall, it is snug and holds well. The shell itself is a hard, semi-rigid plastic that has a small amount of flex but very little. The bumper guard is a softer material though still quite stiff and it has added material at the corners to give it some extra shock absorption. This is better than the majority of shell cases I have seen and used, and on the shell itself this is a good case.

In the package is everything you need to turn your phone into a point-and-shoot camera: the shell case itself, two grip bases (one hard plastic, one wood), a carry strap, a lanyard, a lens kit and a thumb rest for when you are holding the phone. There is even a small screwdriver so you can change the grips. It requires no other equipment or tools.

I did not understand the purpose of the grips right away, until I removed the base plate from the shell and attached one. It made sense then – the case actually looks and feels like a camera, with a natural groove for your middle finger when holding the phone like a dedicated camera. I of course prefer the wood one, but the black plastic one better matches the shell.

I also was puzzled by the thumb rest (wasn't even sure what it was) until I attached it to the case and held it up. My thumb rested on it naturally and it was actually a little more comfortable than my regular camera.

The case comes with a small lens kit which is made up of a wide angle lens and a macro lens for close-up shots. I experimented with the lenses and took a picture of the field behind my house after a recent snowstorm and it definitely captured a wider view than without the lens in place. I then removed the wide angle lens and used the macro lens to take a picture of a fiber on a blanket, and it did a better job than my dedicated camera with a close-up lens. I have attached both of these pictures with my review.

The one thing this kit does not include is a screen protector. A lot of cases do not have screen protectors and you have to buy them separately anymore. I would suggest using a tempered glass screen protector to get the best possible protection to go along with this case.

This case is enough to make me seriously think about using my phone's camera a lot more. It makes the phone feel like a dedicated camera, it has some thoughtful features and it provides very good bumper, corner and back protection for the phone. Also available for this case are separate add-on lenses like telephoto and fisheye lenses so you can expand the capabilities even more. If you have an iPhone 6/6s, consider getting this case before you buy a separate camera.

I have a workbench where I frequently have little projects underway, and the issue I have had is a shortage of power outlets so I am frequently changing the configuration on my desk to account for this. I decided to use this surge suppressor/power strip on my workbench to resolve this issue and so far it has worked out well for me.

There are eight full-sized, grounded power outlets on this tower, and each one is spaced properly to handle a full-sized power adapter like what comes with many electronics. As such, there is no need to compromise when plugging in devices that have larger adapters, because there is enough room for all on this tower. Every outlet includes a ground plug too, which is great for devices that require one (in my house, it's about 50/50). With almost every other surge suppressor, I have had issues with oversized adapters crowding other outlets – this is not a problem with this one.

There are also four USB charging ports on this tower which is a really nice bonus. These are all 2.1A ports so they can output a full-speed charge to devices that can handle it, but most of my devices take a 1A charge so the 2.1A is lost on me. I have not yet put a meter on these ports to check the actual power output but so far these seem to output about the same as most other USB charging blocks I have used. Power output aside, having USB and AC ports together allows choice if you have a device that uses a USB adapter to plug into an AC outlet.

The circuit breaker button is on the bottom.

One thing I particularly like about this tower is that the outlets are one two circuits and there are buttons (on the top) that control each circuit. This may require a little logic when planning your power usage – if you want only/all lights on one circuit, place them so that they are controlled by a single button and you can then power them all on and off together.

This tower have allowed me to clean up my work area and it has enough outlets on it to cover my devices without issue. It is very easy to use and understand, it has plenty of outlets that are spaced apart nicely so there is no waste, and it includes USB outlets too. I have had no trouble with it at all and have no problem recommending it it if you are looking for a good power strip/surge suppressor.

Smart watches have gotten more popular with the release of the Apple watch. They tend to have a standard set of functions, such as access to instant messaging, email, time, alarms and a lot more, typically tied to your phone. Not all smart watches are alike, though, and offer different sets of functions, better connectivity and other various differences from one another. This particular smart watch offers the mainline set of functions, setting itself apart through the user interface which is more polished and clean than most others with which I have worked. That said, I have a couple of quibbles with it, leaving room for a little improvement.

This is a standard-sized watch with a rubber wristband that can actually fit a larger wrist like mine. I have trouble finding watches and watch bands that fit me, so the fact that this one fits me is a pleasant surprise.

Powering it on, the user is immediately greeted with a complex and fairly complete visual menu system with tiles for every function available to the user. This is a standard presentation for a smartwatch, but this one looks a bit more polished and clean than the others I have seen. Switching to other menu screens just requires a swipe gesture, as to be expected. I have big hands, and this means that, for me, using a stylus makes working with this watch a lot easier. This is not the fault of the watch but a reality of working with a small device.

My first issue with this watch came when I paired it to my phone. The date and time on the watch were off, so I expected that it would grab the time from my iPhone when I paired it. It did not. Instead, I had to dig for the clock application and manually set the time. I dislike this and think that having it set itself when it is paired is much more accurate and cuts effort on the part of the user. For Android users, there is an application to allow for syncing up the time, date and more, but iOS users are out of luck for now. To the manufacturer's credit this is made clear on the product listing so this is not a surprise. Regardless, I am of the opinion that the watch should fetch the time, not rely on being sent the time. In the grand scheme of things, though, this is an annoyance, not a deal breaker.

There is a fairly comprehensive list of functions provided by this watch in addition to time/date and phone answer. Through the menus the user has access to call logs and function, Bluetooth functions, a remote finder function, a pedometer, a sleep monitor, a reminder function to get up and move on occasion, calendar and clock functions, audio functions, video functions and a few more.

One of the interesting functions that this watch offers is a camera. So, I tried to use it and it complained that there was no memory card available. Reading through the limited documentation included, I was unable to find anything about a memory card. I finally noticed that the back of the watch has a small groove where it can be popped off, and when I removed the back I found the battery which is removable (replaceable - another pleasant surprise). Under the battery is a slot for a micro SD card.

Adding a memory card comes with a big catch. It requires removing the battery to get at the holder which in turn clears the clock and resets it to midnight 01-01-2015. So, adding the memory card requires me to set the time again. And again if I remove the card.

Although I think the time sync functions of this watch are lacking, it is otherwise a good smartwatch. The interface is professional and polished and the whole provides access to a large number of useful functions. It's priced well too. Overall, this is a solid offering worth a look if you are wanting a smartwatch.

Projectors for home use are typically set up for home theater systems. I have seen a number of systems set up with projectors suspended from the ceiling, and I have seen a few that rely on being mounted on a table top. This is a table top model and it is a very good and easy-to-use projector.

This is a 300-lumen projector which is fine for home theater systems, though it would be a little underpowered to use in a larger room or something like a small church. It is good for small presentations too and is a good option if you want to take it with you for meetings instead of keeping it permanently placed somewhere.

There are several input sources for which the projector is configured. For testing and experimentation I found it easiest to work with HDMI though I was able to use some of the other sources as well. It accepts VGA (which is great for older computer systems and other hardware), it can read files from an SD card or even a USB drive. Using a USB drive or SD card, this projector becomes very compact and portable and doesn't even need an external source of input.

This projector even has a pair of speakers inside so you can use this projector for the entire A/V experience, though you will get better sound from a dedicated sound system. This projector is capable of receiving sound as well as outputting it.

I used the HDMI input to feed the image from my computer to the projector and it did a fine job of displaying my desktop on the wall for me. I was also able to configure Windows to use it as an extended display so I could then look at PowerPoint on the computer screen and use the projector to output the slide show. This is very, very convenient and makes this configuration ideal for presentations. I was able to adjust the focus manually and get the image as sharp as I wanted too.

The remote with this unit is great. I have worked with several K&F Concept lenses and filters in the past and I have had excellent results with them. I am still very much a beginning photographer and I am still learning as I go but I have learned a lot in the process. One of the things I have especially come to appreciate is the fisheye effect. Up to this point I have only had the ability to work this out via software, so I was pleased to have the opportunity to work with this fisheye lens. So far I have had a lot of fun with it and I love how it works, though I have again learned a few things along the way.

A fisheye lens is somewhat similar to a magnifying glass with a great deal of distortion. The center comes out clear and the edges are distorted and warped, giving the effect of looking through a lens that is very thick in the middle and thins out towards the edges. Straight edge objects like sidewalks become warped and bent.

This particular lens is a chunky and hefty fellow, actually comprised of two lenses instead of just one. There is a large macro lens that can work independently of the fisheye lens and it is very good for taking very close-up shots. The fisheye lens attaches to this macro lens and relies on it.

I took several shots with the fisheye lens and I discovered something I did not realize though it is fairly obvious now. When using the minimum amount of zoom, the distortion is maximized and you get the most effect. The more you zoom in the more dampened the effect though it is still noticeable. I used the lens to take two pictures of the case in which the fisheye lens packs, one zoomed in all the way and one zoomed out all the way. For the one zoomed out, you can see the warping effect on the blinds over the windows and you even can see the entire image framed in a black circle. The image zoomed in has minimal distortion.

I should state that this particular lens is designed for 58mm threads. Make sure your camera can use it before you buy it. If you have a different thread size for your lens, buy the right sized fisheye for that lens.

This is one of the most fun lenses I have. It works great and it does a good job of giving the distortion you want with a fisheye lens, and it is not particularly expensive. I am very pleased with it and am looking forward to working with it for many years.

[[VIDEOID:9c7f474d82697dfd8035b3c7cf95ccc5]] I am a longtime graphics tablet user, having started with a Bamboo small. Since then I have had several tablets including a Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch, am Intuos4 and finally an Intuos5 Medium. All of the tablets I have used have been Wacom tablets; this is my first experience with another brand, and it is the first time I have even heard of Huion as a brand. To me it makes sense to compare this tablet with my Intuos5, with which it actually compares quite well for about 20% of the cost.

My test system for testing this graphics tablet is a Dell laptop, with an Intel i7 processor and 16G RAM, running Windows 10 and Corel Painter X3.

Comparing this tablet to the Intuos5 it is approximately the same size (both are medium tablets). They both look very similar at a glance and there are some distinct similarities in the pen and pen holder as well. In operation they are both similar but there are some very distinct differences, and each one has advantages over the other.

One of the differences between these two tablets is that the Huion tablet has a numbered gauge across the top of the writing surface and includes a replacement surface in the box; the Wacom does not. The gauge is not a big deal but it does make a nice measure if you are looking for consistency in length of lines. The replacement surface is another matter – it is easy to damage the surface and over time it does get scuffed, so being able to apply a new surface is a huge plus to me.

The pens are different and there is give and take with them. The Wacom pen is sealed and does not need batteries or recharging. It is also reversible and both ends can be configured for drawing. Typically one end it set up as an eraser. The Huion pen is rechargeable and is not reversible. I prefer the Wacom pen, but I like the feel of the Huion pen and it works well.

The pens both come with a stand, extra nibs and a nib extractor. The Wacom stand is slightly heavier, but otherwise they are functionally equivalent.

The software is obviously different, and I have been experimenting with the Huion software to learn how to configure the buttons. The Wacom software is a little more intuitive, btu I have found the Huion software to be a bit more versatile and it provides better control. Speaking of buttons, the buttons are a little different between these two tablets with the Wacom providing fewer buttons but providing a scroll wheel.

Both tablets have 2048 pressure levels, and the only real way to test the pressure levels and drawing capabilities of each is to use a drawing application and start experimenting. I loaded up Painter and selected some acrylic brushes and started playing. I was able to get very similar results using the same brushes and the application had no issues with recognizing the pen or the position on the writing surface.

Operationally, these two tablets are very similar. However, the Wacom is more expensive – a lot more expensive. The Huion tablet costs roughly 20% of the cost of the Wacom and to be honest when I compare these two it is hard to justify the cost of the Wacom when the Huion tablet works as well for so much less.

Working with the Huion graphics tablet has been an eye-opening experience. It compared beautifully against a Wacon tablet of similar size and capability. I am very pleased with this tablet and can heartily recommend it as an excellent alternative to more well-known brands.

The primary lens I have on my camera is a good 18mm-55mm lens and it does great for capturing images that are a foot or more away. When I get much closer than that my camera is unable to focus properly and I end up with a crummy shot and I either have to give up or back up so that it can focus – not what I want most of the time. These magnifying lenses are a good solution, but there are somethings you have to keep in mind when using them.

I will start with a statement that should be obvious: make sure you have the correct lens size when you are purchasing add-on lenses like this set. This particular set can be used only with a lens where the thread size is 55mm. If you have a lens that has a different sized thread, you should consider looking for this kit in a different thread size. You can use a ring adapter, but getting the right size at the start is better.

There are four lenses in this kit, a 1x, 2x, 4x and 10x lens, each increasing in power as the numbers suggest. You can somewhat view these as magnifying glasses for your camera, but that metaphor is not completely accurate. They do magnify the image for you, but they allow a closer shot as well and you can get very close to your subject when you have one of these attached to your lens. Perhaps a better way to describe them is to realize that they make your camera very nearsighted and your camera can see close-up well and distance not at all when using these lenses.

The main thing to remember about them is that as they go up the scale in strength they introduce a lot more edge distortion. This is most obvious with the 10x lens. If you take this lens and hold it so that you can see things through it clearly in the center, you cannot help but notice a large area around the edge of the lens that is distorted. The effect is less then you get it close to something on which you wish to focus but it is something to keep in mind. If there is too much distortion, use a less powerful magnification lens.

These particular lenses have a little bit of heft to them but they are not what I would consider heavy. Because they are glass they are a bit more substantial than resin or plastic lenses.

Overall, these are nice lenses. I have been able to use them for taking very close shots that I otherwise would not be able to take with my camera, such as ridge detail on a penny or dot patterns on magazine print. These are not real-world examples but they definitely show off the capabilities of such lenses. If you are looking for good magnification lenses for your camera, this is a good set that works well. Just make sure you have the right thread size before you buy.

I use a full-sized projector every week to give presentations to a fairly large group of people. This projector is configured to connect via a VGA cable across the room and is suspended from the ceiling so that it can be hung in front of a projection screen. A full setup like this is not always the best configuration for every situation and a smaller projector is a better fit for certain situations. This is one such projector and it works very well.

I have the ST-038 model. This is a very small projector, measuring approximately 6"x5"x2". Because of the size it also is very light and is ideal for putting on most shelves or light desks. Because of the size it is ideal for taking along for events such as business presentations, church functions and family fun nights.

This projector has a 1,000-lumen light source and it is bright enough to handle projections in an entertainment room. It is not really strong enough to work in a large auditorium though it will do in an emergency if brought closer to the screen. Overall, I would say this is a good unit for using in the home or with small businesses.

There are several input sources that can be used and the projector has no problem allowing you to select from them. I worked primarily with the HDMI input during testing. If you have an older computer you can use the VGA port to project as well. It is also able to accept video files from USB as well as an SD card so in that way it can be used as a stand-alone projector, either for slides or video. There is even an audio input and a headphone jack on there so you can make it more personal.

There are two ways to control this projector. There is a series of buttons on the top that allow you to change input sources, change picture settings, modify sound settings, set the clock and make other settings adjustments including updating the firmware. The other method of interacting with this projector is to use the remote that is included in the package which allows access to the same settings, using an IR signal between the remote and the projector (the IR sensor is a large red square on the back of the projector).

Using an HDMI cable I was able to use my laptop to project my desktop and subsequently my videos. Done correctly, this projector is a fine second screen and makes an excellent presentation screen for PowerPoint (this requires setting up the desktop to extend the display on the second detected monitor - this projector - and then tell Powerpoint to use the second display for playing the slide show). It works very well and I am pleased with it.

There are two manual controls on the side of this projector. One controls the focus and the other slightly adjusts the tilt of the image on the surface where it is being projected. The focus is unable to get a clear image if you set the projector less than 6'-10' from the projection surface - not too bad of a distance.

On thing you have to remember, though - this unit puts out heat and lots of it, though less than larger projectors. It can quickly warm up a 10'x10' room so consider ventilation when using this or any other small projection device. I was a little surprised too that when the projector is shut off the fan stops instead of running a little longer to cool down the light - not a big deal but noticeable.

I like this projector. It travels well, it has a lot of options for inputs, the controls are intuitive and the picture is bright enough for smaller audiences.

I listen to music all day at work and I also enjoy listening to music at home and as such I spend a lot of time with headphones on my head. This is a good-sized pad, able to comfortably handle laptops up to 17”. It has a total of 4 larger fans that move some serious amounts of air, and fans are paired two and two between a pair of switches. The frame is painted metal mesh and offers good support to the laptop it holds.

The switches that control the fans are dial controls and they provide variable fan speeds for each pair of fans they control. There are no graduations so you can set the speed anywhere within the range to suit you, though having that much control is probably not all that necessary. The fans run very quiet but on the highest speed setting really move the air. When maxed out and all four fans running at top speed the fans blew cooler air from between the frame and the laptop, telling me I had the speed up much higher than needed. For my particular system under my typical use load, it seems I only need to turn them on about half way.

I have worked with some chill pads that have flaws in either the fans or the bearings and they make awful amounts of noise. So far, the only noise this pad makes is a low-frequency hum. It is quiet enough that even with lower-end noise canceling headphones I can cancel out the noise completely. This pad is not silent even on the low end of fan speed but it is very quiet all the way through the range of speeds. I have been able to leave the fans on full speed all night and sleep through the sound.

I have not measured the temperature difference between when the fans are on vs. when they are not, but I have noticed that the internal fan does not kick in as frequently when doing video rendering as when the fans are off. It does turn on and it still hits high speed on occasion but it is noticeably less frequently.

This is an excellent chill pad for laptops and so far it has worked out exceptionally well for me. It is quiet, it moves a lot of air and my laptop’s internal fan does not kick in as high as often. Because there is a system in the house that is much more frequently used for gaming, I will be moving this pad to that laptop instead and will use the other pad for myself.

This is a solid little device and seems to be assembled well. It has a slight heft to it and it feels very solid - no give in the housing and no noise when shaken.

I have been learning more about photography and as time has permitted I have been improving my skill as an amateur photographer. I have worked with other types of filters, in particular CPL and FL-D filters, but before now I have never worked with ND filters. I have been able to achieve good results with it and so far I am pleased with this filter though I know I have more to learn about it.

A neutral-density filter is used to reduce light reaching the aperture without fiddling too much with the colors. This allows one to get creative with shutter speeds. This particular filter is adjustable and turns on the lens body face, allowing the photographer to increase or decrease the amount of filtering done. At the lowest setting the filter does very little filtering; when turned up to the maximum filtering level very little light gets through and a moire pattern appears so I do not recommend turning up the filter to this level.

To get a feel for how well this filter works I took my camera outside as a big thunderstorm approached and took some pictures of one of the cloud formations. I selected two pictures from that set, one where I did not use the filter and one where I did use it on about 1/4 strength. Although the filter evenly reduced light levels, the color contrast in the filtered image is much more pronounced and obvious.

The most common use for this kind of filter is to reduce the light levels, then take an extended exposure for a scene with motion, such as a waterfall.

This is a very nice filter and I could not be happier with it. It is very easy to use and it really works well.

I have worked with quite a few car kits and some work better than others. Most of them are rechargeable Bluetooth receivers that allow you to turn your car’s stereo system into a hands-free system for talking on the phone while driving, though some plug into the 12V power outlet for power. All of the others I have used have connected to the car stereo by way of the AUX jack. But, not all systems have an AUX input which makes those solutions useless in those situations. I had an FM transmitter solution years ago that allowed me to connect a CD player to my basic AM/FM radio and it worked but I had forgotten about that type of solution until now. This kit works with Bluetooth and FM to connect phones to cars and it works very well. It also has some nice features I wish other kits had.

This is a basic kit that works by allowing the phone to pair with it via Bluetooth and then uses a small, low-power FM transmitter to connect to the car’s audio system on any FM channel desired (I suggest using an unused frequency). Music can be streamed from the phone to the transmitter and from there it goes to the radio frequency in the car. It’s simple in concept and it works. No more AUX jack.

For power the transmitter plugs into a USB port, and the kit includes a 2-port 12V plug. This allows for powering the transmitter and still having enough power for another device like the phone or a GPS navigator. One port on the adapter is a 1.0A and the other is a 2.1A so if you have a high-speed cable and your device can accept a high-speed charge it will work with the adapter. Because the adapter has two ports and it allows for completely disconnecting the transmitter it can be used for charging two devices at once.

Regardless of where in the vehicle the 12V adapter lives, the kit comes with a magnetic pad for attaching the receiver so that the receiver can be mounted almost anywhere. This is important - it means that it can be put in an optimal spot so that when speaking it has the best chance for picking up the voice clearly which is a very good thing. In my car, the 12V outlet lives under the center console so other kits sometimes do not get the best reception for my voice.

Sound quality is clear for both caller and receiver, particularly because the transmitter can be placed anywhere. When there is no competition for the channel the sound is as good as an AUX-connected sound source.

This hands-free kit for the car is better than most others I have used as it is easier to place the transmitter to get clear voice transmission and it does not require an AUX port on the care stereo system to work. I am pleased with it and am happy to recommend it.

I selected this keyboard/touchpad with the idea of using it with my tablet. Admittedly I mistakenly thought it was a Bluetooth keyboard which would have made it suitable for my tablet but this turned out to be a misunderstanding on my part. That said, it has proven to be a very handy keyboard in more ways than I had originally planned. In particular, in addition to working with Windows and Linux it works with Raspberry Pi which opens a whole world of possibilities for this keyboard.

This keyboard is very small, barely bigger than a Hershey bar, and it has a full set of keys as well a touchpad and mouse buttons on the right side. This is sufficient for doing pretty much everything you’d want to do, including surfing the web, text editing and software development. Granted, the size makes it less than ideal for some of these functions but it does work as a full keyboard/mouse combination if you want to use it that way.

Right out of the box, the switch was on and the keyboard had completely drained its battery so it had to be plugged in and charged overnight. This was a surprise but was not a big deal, just unusual.

When connected to a Windows 8 system the OS recognized it and immediately it was usable. It required no special drivers, no configuration changes or anything else – just plug it in and turn it on. It worked the same under Linux as well.

The real test for this keyboard/mouse was on a Raspberry Pi system. The keyboard connected and worked without a glitch – expected since it worked fine with Ubuntu Linux but not guaranteed as the kernel was known to work but the hardware was not yet tested. With a second external keyboard connected it was possible to type on both at the same time and also to use the other keyboard as a regular keyboard and the other just as a mouse.

There are a number of other SBC types and designs out there, and there is no reason that this device should not work with any of them that have a Linux-based kernel. Embedded Windows system should also support it as well.

This is a very small but fully functional keyboard/touchpad combination that works with multiple configurations. It connects easily and so far has given no real operational issues. Keep in mind that this thing is extremely small, though, which is great for portability, mobility and economy of space but less pleasant for systems that aren’t being transported anywhere.

A good laptop chiller pad becomes important when you run a lot of graphics-intensive games or if you are doing anything requiring the CPU to run a heavy load. Heat is the enemy of a computer system and the fastest way to a dead laptop is to not deal with heat issues when there’s a problem. I had a chill pad some time ago and it was sub-par. This one by LotFancy is much better and it does a good job.

First off, this is a big chill pad, the same basic dimensions as my laptop but much thicker. I have a 15.6" laptop and this pad is almost a perfect and exact fit, with only a narrow area in the back that extends past the end of the laptop. If you want a small and petite chill pad, this is not the one you want. It does incline too with a metal bar and slots in the case so that the laptop can be angled up. This actually is good for exposing it to even more air.

This chill pad connects to a USB port so it can either be plugged into a port on the computer or into a hub. There are two ports on it and both seem to be the same in terms of how the pad operates. That is, the pad operates at the same speed regardless of which port is used. There are also two buttons on the pad for turning it on. One turns on the larger fan in the middle, and the other turns on all the other fans. Two green LEDs next to those buttons indicate that the pad is powered on and working.

This pad moves a lot of air and it does a good job of cooling the laptop. But, it does so very quietly which is a huge plus. I have it set up in my home office and the pad makes about as much noise as a desktop computer, maybe a little less. The sound it makes is a gentle hum.

When powered on each fan has a bright blue LED in it. While they look cool when there’s no laptop on the pad, they’re all but invisible when the laptop is sitting on top. There isn’t even much of a glow coming from the pad. I turned on the pad, turned out all of the lights and the glow from the laptop screen was enough to overpower any light that might have come from the pad. Except for the low hum I wouldn’t know it was even turned on.

This is a good chill pad. It works quietly and it moves a lot of air. Compared to other chill pads I have used this one is very good and I am happy to recommend it.

My wife loves birdwatching and our teenage son enjoys stargazing so we have an assortment of binoculars and inexpensive telescopes. Before this monocular I had never used one and even though I have not had it very long at all I am already very pleased with it. Though it is ideal for bird watching and field work, it also will work as an amateur telescope.

At roughly 7" long, this monocular is large enough to be usable but small enough to fit in a coat pocket or even in a briefcase. It comes in a nice, nylon-weave carrying pouch that even has a belt loop so carrying it into the field is easy and does not take up extra room. It also has a holding strap much like a camcorder does so it can be held more securely. It has a small metal tripod suitable for setting up on a desk or table. It’s not a big tripod - the legs extend to 7.5" - but is works well if you are recording or are seated and need a steady hand. Finally, it includes a microfiber cleaning cloth in the box for wiping the lenses safely without scratching them.

This is a waterproof monocular and everything about it showcases that. There are two rubberized caps for either end that cover the lenses and keep out moisture and dust when not in use. These are physically attached to the barrel (one by a rubber flap and one by a nylon cord) so there is no issue with losing the caps. Most of the barrel is rubberized as well except for the focus knob assembly and where it attaches.

I used it to focus on the tree line behind the house (roughly 30 yards away) and was very pleased with how sharp and clear I was able to get the image. From the front of the house I was able to focus on the stop sign at the end of the street and had no issue with getting fine edge detail even at a distance of roughly a football field. The focus is very smooth and easy to adjust and getting the image in perfect focus is not the least bit difficult.

Though I enjoy cameras and optical equipment and I have learned a good bit about optical equipment I am a far cry from being an expert, so I took this monocular to work and approached two teammates who are very well-versed in optics, photography and astronomy and I asked them to look it over and give me their honest opinion. Both of them examined it and expressed their approval. They both said similar things about it: the image through this monocular is very bright and clear, the focus is very smooth and it seems to be very well made. They both made a comment about the lens and that it was very good due to not having a darkened coating.

One of my teammates told me to try looking at the stars with it. I had not really considered this but knew this would be an excellent test for it so I went outside after dark and pointed it skyward. Though I can definitely see more detail through a dedicated telescope, I was able to make out some of the larger surface detail on the moon including the high point in the middle of a crater. I was hindered by the fact that it is a full moon right now so I will have to try again this weekend during the eclipse. I then picked out a planet and looked at it through the monocular. Though it is a little tough to make out, I know I found Jupiter as I could see three of the moons as bright spots not visible to the naked eye (I have looked at it through a telescope so I recognize it from seeing it already). Finally I discovered a cluster of stars I could not see without magnification. This monocular is certainly not as good as a dedicated telescope but it is sufficient when camping and it eliminates the need to pack a big, bulky telescope unless you want to see more detail.

This is a great tool for use in the field. It has very good range, the image is bright and clear and it even is sufficient for stargazing should you choose to use it for everything on the road. Great product!

Many cars on the market come with a rear-view camera that allows for seeing where the vehicle is moving when in reverse. Often the view appears on a dashboard screen. There really needs to be a better documentation set than this.

If you are not skilled in working with electrical systems, either plan on this taking a good while or have someone you trust install the system. I have worked on car electrical systems in the distant past so I had a vague familiarity, but it still took me a while to have everything set up and working.

Once wired the system is fairly straightforward to use. This is my first experience with rear-view video systems and though it gave me a little trouble setting up it was from lack of good documentation and inexperience, not from being a bad product. Once installed this is a nice and easy-to-use video system. Time will tell how long it works.

FOSCAM is a well-known name when it comes to security cameras and security equipment and they make a good variety of security solutions for home and business use. The F19803P camera is a wireless IP camera that is weatherproof, has night vision and can be accessed via smartphone. One configured and set up on the network it works great but the setup process can be a very painful one.

In the box is the actual camera, the antenna, power adapter, mounting kit, installation software and an Ethernet cable. The camera housing is roughly the size of a new roll of bathroom tissue - very small, compact and lightweight. The mounting kit is a small but solid painted aluminum bracket plus the screws needed to secure it. When mounted properly, this camera can be very inconspicuous.

Following the included directions, I installed the software first and then hooked up the camera to the router. According to the included documentation the IPCamera application should immediately see the camera and from there one can select the camera, log into it and manipulate it as needed. This did not work for me and the camera never did appear. I tried downing my firewall, I tried connecting to a different router and even tried directly connecting to the camera and still was unable to see it. I finally managed to reach the camera by opening the FOSCAM client software and telling it to search for cameras. When I did this, the camera finally appeared, and the IPCamera application showed it too. This works but runs contrary to the documentation.

I did get into the camera finally and was able to change the username and password. I also set up the wireless network settings and found other settings to adjust like IR timer, time source and more.

I found that the camera’s administration settings can be accessed as needed through the IP address and specifying port 88 (unless the port is deliberately changed). I strongly encourage assigning a fixed IP address to the camera via DHCP through the router; otherwise, the IP address can change and accessing the camera gets more difficult. I learned this the hard way, when I had the Ethernet MAC defined but not the WiFi MAC in my router’s DHCP table. My fault, but this was made more difficult by the IPCamera application still not seeing the camera and I had to let the client software scan again.

I made one more mistake and reset the camera via the reset button and it cleared everything I had set already: user name, password, everything. I was concerned that I would lose everything again with a power failure so as a test I unplugged the camera for a few hours and plugged it in again, and fortunately it retained its configuration.

The camera cannot see my 5G network, only my 2.4G network. However, even though my computer is on the 5G network it still can access the camera. Both networks are handled by my one router so I assume that this is normal. If you have a 5G network, make sure you also have the 2.4G network configured or keep the camera connected via Ethernet. The fact that it does not support 5G networks is not necessarily a problem but is worth knowing beforehand.

Once I made it through the configuration (which was all of two hours, most of it trying to figure out how to talk to the camera), the client software allowed me to add it to the configuration and stream a live video feed from it. The video quality is actually very good and when not in IR mode is in full color. When streaming IR video the image is straight black and white, but the image is very clear. Testing with the camera indoors I killed all the lights in the room and the IR kicked in, my intent being to see how clear the image is. The image is clear enough to read text off a white sheet of paper when angled right. Specifically I held up the instruction manual to the camera at about a 2' distance and was able to read the front page without difficulty. The only complaint I have with the IR is that it does not seem to kick in early enough; when in a dimly lit room the camera still tries to use non-IR and the result is a very dark feed. I have found no way to adjust this in the camera settings other than to set the IR to cut on at a specific time which may or may not be the most useful thing.

I like the fact that this camera does not need a specialized hub to work and can be run from a PC or MAC instead. This makes the system a lot more flexible and easier to manage.

The real power of this camera comes in the client software. It allows for adding additional cameras (the screen settings suggest up to 64 cameras) and monitoring all of them at once on one screen. Some of the camera settings can be manipulated such as setting up recording times, setting alarms and more. Adding a camera is as simple as running a search and then adding the camera to an area. There is even the ability to play back the video that has been recorded built right in.

This is a nice security camera and it works well. It has very good IR capability, it works wirelessly and has full-color video that is clear and workable. Configuring this camera can be very unpleasant, though once configured it’s a great solution. If you need a good outdoor wireless camera and you have some patience for an install that’s not necessarily smooth, consider this one.

There are a number of reputable brands available and I have tried several - Lew’s, Quantum, Daiwa, Mitchell’s, Shakespeare and more. Until recently I was unfamiliar with KastKing as a brand and had no experience with their fishing tackle, and in a short time I have come to realize I have been missing something important. I received a Triton 3000 spinning reel for test and evaluation and have been thoroughly pleased with it.

This reel has some heft to it, very solid and tight. It’s more substantial than many reels I have used but it’s also not the largest or heaviest either. In terms of size and weight, it falls in the middle of the pack of reels I have used for freshwater fishing and it’s a bit on the small size compared to many saltwater reels I have used. I have larger hands and the size it about right, but someone with smaller hands might find a smaller size (like the Triton 2000 or 2500) a better match. In terms of assembly, there is nothing loose or flimsy on this reel at all and there is nothing that required tightening or adjustment right out of the box (which has been a problem with some others I have used in the past). Overall, this is a solid and well-assembled reel.

Appearance-wise, this reel is absolutely gorgeous. It is a deep shade of purple, almost black, with chrome and nickel colors on the spool, bail and handle. Appearance is not really all that important but it certainly does add to the package, and this is a reel that you won’t be embarrassed to break out in front of others. It relies on simple elegance, not bright flashy colors to make its statement.

This reel has a good-sized spindle on it and it can hold a good amount of line. I put at least 150 yards of 8-lb test on this reel and there’s a lot of room for more. The spindle is tall, not deep.

Ok, on to the really important stuff - how does this reel perform?

This reel has 10 ball-bearings for forward reeling and the reel is about as smooth and quiet when retrieving as could be. Cheaper reels (cheaper meaning lower quality) tend to grind a little bit when retrieving or they make substantial amounts of noise, and some reels even have a clicker in them to mask the sound when retrieving. Some also feel hollow when retrieving, but the Triton feels solid and smooth without a hint of inferior build quality. As nice as the reeling forward is, one of the most important features in a good reel to me is a zero-reverse clutch and this reel has it down. When engaged, the reel will not reverse even a little and to me this is worth its weight in gold.

One very real issue I have seen with some spinning reels is a poorly shaped bail that interferes with the distance when casting. If the bail is too shallow and does not allow enough clearance to allow the line to fly freely off the spindle, it can seriously impact casting distance. Fortunately, this reel has a very wide bail that has plenty of clearance around the spindle and it does not impact the cast at all. I get very good distance when casting as a result. Instead of concentrating on distance, the angler can instead concentrate on accuracy (and after years of practice I am still working on improving my accuracy).

I tested the drag and am pleased with it as well. When tightening the drag the dial does not get more difficult to turn like on some other reels and the drag gradually makes the spindle harder and harder to turn. It is not a graduated turn, meaning it does not increase in steps so there is essentially a limitless variance in how tight the drag can be adjusted. The dial remains easy to turn all the way through the turning range until it is tightened completely, at which point it just stops.

When reeling, either forward or backward, this reel remains balanced and does not wobble much at all. It is hard to notice wobble when the reel is attached to a rod so I tried something when I had not yet attached the reel to a rod. Holding the reel in one hand by the assembly and giving the handle a good spin, I was able to feel the reel gyrating very slightly but not appreciably. I tried the same with another high-quality reel and it was similar. This is not the case with cheaper reels which may or may not balance.

I love the fact that the reel is mounted on an arm long enough to prevent the bail from whacking me on the knuckles when I retrieve. A reel mounted too close to the rod due to a short arm can have this unpleasant effect and I look for this problem specifically so I can avoid it. I also appreciate that the handle is far enough from the reel body to avoid hitting my hand.

In the box with the reel is a velvety microfiber cloth bag for storage and transport when the reel is not in use. This is the only reel I have ever had that has come with such and it’s a nice touch. The bag is useful for keeping the reel clean and also for keeping supplies with it, like a small container of lubricating oil, an extra spool of line or even an extra lure or two (though this is no substitute for a tackle box).

I am very hard-pressed to find anything to criticize about this reel. It is a solid and well-made, looks great and works like a dream. I believe I have found my new primary reel.

I have a 10" tablet and it primarily gets used as an e-reader and as a music streaming device. It's a great device and I love it, but I do get frustrated with figuring out where to put it when I am streaming music through it. Although it is a relatively small device it does take up some room on the desk when in a stand case. I have tried suction mounts to attach it to a window and that works fine but the window cannot move and when the window is cold the suction mount lets go. This flexible mount for tablets is a very good solution for my needs and is far better constructed than suggested by the product description.

This is a simple mount in concept and design. It is flexible coil tube with a screw-on vice clamp attached on one end and an adjustable frame-style bracket attached via a ball joint to the other. In the box the unit comes unassembled and requires less than two minutes to put together. When finished, the whole thing is approximately 3' long.

Everything about this mounting stand suggests that it is built to last and is designed to hold up under heavy use. The coil tube is about the heaviest I have ever seen: it is roughly a half inch in diameter and is exceptionally stiff which makes it well suited for supporting the weight of the tablet. The item description here says it will support 2.2 pounds but it will support a little more than that (though I would not try to put much extra on there, particularly if the coil is horizontal).

The coil attaches to the vice clamp via a threaded machine screw assembly and it has enough threading to allow the coil to turn 360 degrees without becoming detached. This allows the tablet to be swung around a work area in an arch without having to really do anything that requires any effort. While this is great, what really caught my attention is that the clamp itself can be screwed to the coil in two ways at 90-degree angles (top or side) so that the clamp can be attached to an anchored surface that is either horizontal or vertical. This is one of those design decisions that just makes sense but I have seen very few manufacturers make this kind of effort.

The coil is covered by a very heavy plastic sleeve which protects the tube and makes flexing the tube easier on the hands.

The mounting bracket is connected to the top of the flexible tube by a ball joint, similar to the kind of joints many GPS navigators use in cars to attach to the suction base. When I first attached the bracket to the coil I put it on upside down, which is not a big deal except that the weight of the tablet worked against the joint and it tilted downward slightly. The bracket itself is a standard slider with a lever that presses against the slider which then catches on teeth on the frame to lock it in place. There's a fair bit of padding on the bracket to protect the tablet when it's being clamped in and when the position is being adjusted.

This mounting stand is of such heavy construction that it suggests the stand was designed for industrial use. While it is just fine for home use and is not out of place in a professional office, it is a good for a manufacturing assembly line or even a busy retail location.

This is a great mounting stand for tablets in 7"-11" range. The whole stand is very sturdy and solid and is build to last. Based on my experience with it I can heartily recommend it to any one who needs a mounting solution for a tablet.

[[VIDEOID:1556b033e43375c050880cc164652923]] I wear headphones daily and I use them for listening to music more than anything else. I am very particular about my headphones and I usually use active noise canceling phones as they make travel more pleasant. They also help with listening in a studio. I received a [red] pair of these iP852 phones for evaluation and I have been absolutely blown away by them - for the price they are some of the best phones I have used.

As mentioned, I received a red pair of these phones, and they look exactly like the pictures. I wasn't sure what to make of them - they almost look like toys instead of real headphones. I had low expectations on these phones and I was not sure what they would sound like, but their looks are very deceiving, in a number of ways.

Normally I use over-the-ear headphones as I find them to be comfortable. These phones are on-ear phones so they do not completely cover the ears. Surprisingly, they are snug enough to stay put without effort and they are still quite comfortable. They do get a little warm after a time, but this has never really bothered me. I still prefer over-the-ear phones for comfort and listening, and this is purely a personal preference.

Construction-wise these seem to be well-made. One of the things I really, really like about these phones is that they have a braided cord, not a plain plastic cord. In my experience a braided cord is less likely to kink or fray. The cord is permanently attached to the phones though, so if it catches it's not going to simply pop out but probably will yank the phones off your head. So, please use caution.

The most important aspect of any set of phones is the sound profile. These are inexpensive phones - less than $25 on sale and less than $40 full price - and I expected inexpensive sound. Instead, the sound profile is far and away better than any other headphones I have used in this price range. The highs and especially the bass are solid and there is acceptable midrange. The midrange is the weakest point in the profile but I have used other headphones that sound much worse and cost a lot more. I love club tracks which hit a wide range of sound, and these phones sound really, really nice when connected to my computer and not using an equalizer. When I make adjustments with an equalizer, I can get the sound profile perfected.

I decided to put these against my favorite headphones - a pair of Monster Inspiration ANC phones which I use every day for listening to music. I wanted to see if these headphones could compete with a set of phones that cost more than 10x more. I was amazed that these phones do compete, and quite nicely, for a fraction of the cost. The Monster phones do have a richer midrange and come with ANC, but the sound difference between them is marginal when considering the price difference.

These are certainly not perfect headphones but for the cost they are nothing short of excellent. You can find better headphones out there but expect to pay more. These are a great deal.

I purchased these replacement pads for my Bose QC-15 headphones as the old pads were torn and needed to be replaced. I selected this set of pads based on the positive reviews here on Amazon with the thought that they would be the same as the original pads. While they look the same, they are indeed slightly different.

First things first - these pads are fairly easy to install though they do require a little persistence to get them to snap into place. The earphones themselves have small tabs around the edges designed to snap the pads' bases into place and hold securely, and if the pads are not snapped down they simply will not stay securely. The inner foam and cloth shield that covers the electronics is easy to install but I had trouble with the double-sided tape that holds them in place - the adhesive did not want to release the cover strip and I had real difficulty peeling that strip away without ripping the actual cloth.

Once in place, the phones look exactly like they did when they were new, but I found three differences. First, the phones no longer fit into the case as easily as they once did. Instead of just turning the cups to lay flat and simply putting them in the case, now I have to mess with them slightly to fit into the case properly, though they can be made to fit. More noticeable, though, is that the pads are not as effective as the originals for passive noise canceling. A fan that I have in my office used to be canceled out almost completely with the combination of passive and active noise canceling but is now more audible than when the original pads were in place. I would not say the difference is enough to render the earphones' ability to cancel noise completely compromised, but they are definitely not the same. Finally, these replacement pads are just a little less supple and soft than the original pads. It is not all that noticeable until comparing the original and replacement pads side by side. You have to really be looking closely for the difference to notice it, but it's there.

The difference in noise canceling ability is most noticeable when working in an environment with reverb. I use my phones to monitor sound coming through a professional sound board because these have always done an excellent job of eliminating reverb and leaving just what comes through the sound board. With these new pads in place, I can now hear a lot of reverb, even when I press the phones tight over my ears and have ensured that they completely cover my ears so it's not a gapping issue. The material is different, plain and simple.

These are not bad replacement pads by any means. They are very good, they are comfortable and they do make these phones look brand new again. That said, they were not manufactured by Bose and there are some differences. When considering the cost difference between these and Bose parts, the trade-offs balance out favorably. If you have to have an exact match with the original pads, these are very close but not 100% identical. If you are satisfied with a [roughly] 90%-95% match, these pads work nicely for a lot less than original manufacturer pads.

The point-and-shoot camera market has taken a nosedive due to the prevalence of camera phones that produce high-quality images. It is difficult to buy a mobile phone that does not include a camera, and since mobile phones have become so commonplace and essential anymore there's little need for the point-and-shoot camera for most users. However, what phone cameras lack is the ability to make optical adjustments like zoom and winde-angle - all of these adjustments are done via the phone's ability to digitally enhance the image it takes. The BTOOP lens kits change that and add capability to your camera phone.

The concept with this kit is simple and is very similar to add-on lens kits for more expensive cameras. A lens is attached to the camera lens that enhances the zoom, creates a fisheye effect or adds wide angle capability. The lenses attach by a clip that attaches to the camera with a hole over the lens and a thread where the extra lenses attach. It works better than I would have expected and the image quality does not suffer from this arrangement.

This lens kit comes with three lenses. My favorite of the three is the fisheye lens which works surprisingly well and makes great distortion effects. It is particularly effective for emphasizing the center subject in the image. The wide angle lens also works well and creates photos that have more area covered in them. This lens is ideal for landscapes and skylines. The third lens is the most amazing of all, the macro lens. Using the macro lens I focused on a penny and was astounded by the ridge detail I could see. I took the lens off the phone and put the phone back on the penny and the phone never could focus on the penny that close. The macro lens is absolutely wonderful for very close-up shots.

The kit comes with a small pouch for carrying the lenses and clip, and the pouch doubles as a microfiber cleaning cloth. It's washable too so it can be run through the wash when it becomes soiled.

This kit also works well with built-in tablet and laptop cameras. Taking video with the fisheye lens in place on my laptop is a fun use of an afternoon...

This is a very nice kit for easily and very affordably extending the capabilities of your phone's camera. It's very simple to use and it adds optical effects that cannot be achieved to the same degree with a phone's software enhancements. It's works well and I am happy to recommend it.

I did a good deal of research to find the right camera. I wanted a solid camera with a generous feature set but I didn't want to spend a huge sum either - my budget was roughly $500. At Christmastime the NX300 went on sale, enough of a sale to put it in my price range. After doing a little more research to make sure I had found the camera I wanted, I committed. So far I have been very pleased with it.

Every digital camera I have used before this one has been a point-and-shoot camera, the best of which was actually another Samsung. These types of cameras are great for casual use like a day at the amusement park or making memories on a day trip, but for making really exceptional photographs these cameras are usually ill-suited. Either the focus is flat (meaning everything is one-dimensional), the zoom isn't granular enough, the color is wrong or something else is off just enough to make the picture not quite perfect.

The Samsung NX300 is a "prosumer" camera, meaning it's a high-end consumer and low-end professional camera. Unlike point-and-shoot cameras it has an interchangeable lens system and can be manually focused. It has a good number of features I have not seen on less capable cameras too, such as Wifi connectivity, the ability to add color filters to the lens and much more. I'll hit the highlights.

Without the lens in place, this camera is about the same size and weight as a point-and-shoot camera, maybe slightly larger but not appreciably heavier. Adding the lens adds some bulk and heft to it but it's not as large as something like a Canon Rebel or a high end Nikon. To me this makes this camera a lot easier to carry around than some other models with which it competes, and that can be important when traveling. That said, if not used to working with a camera that has interchangeable lenses there's more to carry (particularly if you use more than just a single lens). A good camera case is a good investment.

This camera has several modes of operation, each optimized for specific shot types and accessible through the spin dial on the top of the camera. The one I use most when experimenting is Auto, which does most of the adjustment for the user and tries to calculate the best settings given the lighting and conditions. It's a good, general purpose mode for most situations. Smart mode is a good choice too, which has presets for a good number of predefined situations like optimized face shots, panorama views, night shots, light traces, silhouettes and several more. Of those smart settings, "Beauty Face" makes adjustments to portraits to compensate for imperfections and this is a great feature. There is a mode for giving the lens the highest priority when it comes to adjustment and that's the mode that gives the user the maximum control over zoom and focus. Manual mode gives the user good control over what to focus on automatically but the camera maintains most of the control. Shutter priority mode allows the user to adjust the shutter speed which is great for when a faster shutter is needed (like an action shot). Aperture priority mode adjusts the aperture width and thus the amount of light allowed in. Program mode seems to be roughly equivalent to Auto mode; I am still learning about that one.

The menu system on this camera is accessible through a nice touch-screen interface, providing access to all manner of settings. I will not go into great detail on the menu system as to do so would make this more of a novel instead of a review. I will say this, though - it is very easy to accidentally make changes when using the menu system if handling the camera in any but the most careful of ways. Just picking up the camera when it is turned on must be done with care as it is almost too easy to touch the screen and make changes without intending to do so. It's fantastic that the screen is sensitive and can be so easily manipulated but it's so sensitive that care is required.

One of the greatest things about this camera is that it can take pictures that have a 3-dimensional quality to them. The main subject of the picture in the foreground is clearly in focus and the surroundings at different depths are in varying levels of being out of focus, and this gives the photo a depth that usually is very difficult to achieve with a point-and-shoot camera. I spent an afternoon playing with the camera just experimenting with this and was thrilled at how natural and easy this camera makes it to take this kind of picture.

Built into the camera is the ability to connect to a Wifi network for uploading images to a smartphone or to share online. This is a nice-to-have but it is not a feature I personally need.

The lens system on this camera is what makes it shine. I bought the 18mm-55mm OIS lens with the camera and this is my first exposure to smart lenses. The lens assembly itself has smarts built into it and when the camera mode it set to give the lens the most control the lens controls the digital zoom and the focus. The focus ring on the lens allows the user to determine what specifically in the picture is in focus which allows for overriding the camera's idea of what should be the main subject of the picture. Sometimes the camera gets it wrong and by using the lens to override it's possible to get the focus just perfect, even on very distant shots or shots that are very busy.

Samsung occasionally updates the firmware for this camera - and the lenses - and updating is relatively simple. With a PC connection the firmware download to the camera is quick and the update is applied through the menu system.

Though this camera is more than capable of taking high-quality video I do not use it for such. I prefer using a dedicated video camera. That said, video recording is easy with the touch of a single button on the back of the camera, to the right and just above the touch screen. What little recording I have done with it has turned out excellent of course, but I will not use this function most of the time.

For all of the positive things I can say about this camera, I do have a couple of minor gripes. First, though it's convenient to have a removable flash I would have preferred to have the flash built-in to the camera body. It's a minor issue but it's worthy of mention. A printed manual would have been nice too, but at 200+ pages it is understandable why one is not included. At least it's on the CD in the package. It is common knowledge that the battery life is not great on this camera and that the only way to charge the battery (without buying a separate charger) is to plug in the camera, either with a USB charger or into the computer itself.

I have found the camera I really wanted. It is a highly capable camera with a really generous feature set and it takes amazing shots (with some practice). There's a learning curve with it if all you have used prior is a point-and-shoot, but the effort is worth it.

I ordered this lens and filter kit to go with my Samsung NX300 with the intent of expanding the capabilities of the camera without spending a fortune. I looked at several different kits before settling on this one, based on the price. I will admit to being a bit apprehensive about the cost in relation to the number of lenses and filters in the kit (presently this kit sells for less than $35 on Amazon as I write this) but my concern was ill-placed - this is a good kit.

I will start off by saying that I am not a professional photographer by any stretch of the imagination. I could be best described as an enthusiast who is trying to learn as I go.
