I have been using a converter box and analog TV ever since we were required to make the change to digital TV. My 29" SANYO analog TV was a gift and has been a great TV. However, I have wanted to make the change to a digital TV, as well.

Today I received the Samsung UN40H5003 TV and am very pleased. I also purchased the byone HDTV window antenna with a stand. Byone offers black, white, and clear antennas in a paper thin plastic. I bought the clear and mounted it on a byone stand, purchased separately. I liked the fact that this antenna offered a 20 ft cable since I needed to place the antenna in another room, and most of the antennas do not have cables longer than 10 ft. The TV and antenna arrived on time from Amazon and were packaged beautifully.

The delivery service brought the large shipping carton into my home. If you live alone, you will want to proceed very carefully so that you do not damage any of the items in the shippng carton or the Samsung TV box, but you should be able to gently move the Samsung box out of the shipping carton.

The instructions suggest that you assemble the stand first. Basically, a shell-shaped post slips onto the shiny black base and is secured using 4 screws.

Once that step has been finished, the other end of the shell-shaped post screws onto the back of the TV. This step is the most delicate step of the entire process since the TV has be to placed gently, face down, on a table or flat surface that is covered by a cloth. The post will be attached to the back of the TV. Instead of using a table, I used the Samsung TV box, lying flat on the carpet, as the table so that the TV was never at risk of falling more than a few inches.

The instructions are pretty simple as you begin to program the TV. Batteries are included with the remote, which you will use to turn-on the TV and scan for channels. The instructions suggest that all components (such as a DVD player) be added before the TV is turned-on.

The single most important step is to be sure to select AIR as the source if you are not planning to use cable or satellite, etc. To do this, you press the button labeled Source on the remove. Then you will follow the prompts as they appear. Many of the prompts are pre-selected (highlighted), so you simply press the Enter button, which is positioned at the center of the up/down/left/right arrows section on the remote.

There is a bit of a lag sometimes with the TV's loading of some channels. For that reason, it's best to re-scan often until you are sure that your TV has captured all channels within your viewing range. I don't know whether or not this lag is due to the antenna or the TV set.

If you get an antenna stand, as I did, you may find it hard to get the posts that support the antenna into the base of the stand. Just keep working with them. Eventually they pop into place.

The shipping carton was heavy, but the TV box inside the shipping carton was not heavy. I took the carton and box to the carpet and worked on the soft carpet, taking care to keep the TV set upright as instructed.

Everything looks great, and I'm delighted that I am able to get a few extra channels that I had not received before. I live about 35 miles south of metro Houston.

I want to add that Amazon shipped everything beautifully, as mentioned above. This TV is available at other stores, but I knew that Amazon would ship the item beautifully and would help me if there were any glitches with the shipping or delivery or return, if needed.

My neighbor Mariam and I are in our mid-sixties. Her husband recommended this device so that we could get help during long walks just in case Mariam, who has a heart condition, begins to feel bad. We have great Verizon coverage in our area, and she has been very pleased with her tests of the device.

I didn't have any problems during the activation of my device: I thought that the steps were explained clearly by the Customer Service representative, who talked with me clearly and politely during our approximately 20-minute telephone call.

I have not yet retired and like the fact that this device can travel with me to work and back.

The only problem that I encountered was that initially I could not get the device to turn off. Consequently, I really couldn't figure-out whether or not it was "on" because I didn't know how to tell the difference between off and on. After several days, the "off/on" button worked properly, and I've learned that a voice speaks when it powers off and on in a way that is similar to the procedure that a cell phone uses when it powers on and off.

Because of the problem above, the cell phone was actually "on" for several days. I didn't recharge it during that time. The unit has a small "ready" light that blinks to show that the device is operating properly. The device continued blinking all week, and I am re-charging the device now and hoping to restore the full battery charge, indicated by a steady green light on the battery indicator.

It couldn't be simpler. I understand that a cell phone can be used to call 911, as well; however, it takes awhile for my cell phone to power up. It's not always easy to use. This device is simple and, hopefully, works as well as promised.

I am pleased with the battery life and so far am pleased with everything. Hope it isn't needed but am glad to have it.

Before buying the Kindle Touch 3G, I visited a Target store to see and handle the different Kindle e-readers. I immediately loved the simplicity, elegance, and convenience of the Kindle Touch 3G.

My sole desire is to read books easily without any distraction by the device that I am using. The Kindle Touch 3G is simple to use: "intuitive" is the word that ideally describes the operating features of this e-reader.

You can swipe the page to turn (as with any paper page) or tap.

Two toolbars disappear while you are reading, but both are accessed simultaneously with a simple tap at the top of the screen. A functional toolbar (allowing you to shop at Amazon, see battery status, etc.) appears at the top; a reading toolbar (allowing you to change font, etc.) appears at the bottom. Both are easy-to-use: just tap the choice you wish to make.

You have only two buttons to click on a regular basis: the on/off button at the bottom edge of the device and the Home button (looks like a tiny speaker) located just beneath the viewing screen.

You must hold the on/off button for approximately 7 seconds in order to power-off completely; otherwise, the screensaver will appear indefinitely.

Other features are available and are easy-to-master; however, you can begin reading out-of-the-box if you have a Kindle on your PC. The system automatically duplicates your archived items.

If you do not have a Kindle on your PC, you can begin reading once you register by entering the email and password that you use at Amazon.com. It is VERY, VERY easy to register: very user friendly. The screen and enclosed guide "walk you through" the simple process.

The Kindle Touch 3G is elegant. I also bought the case ($39.99). Together, the two items are almost as slim as a DVD and case rented from a Red Box. The design is sleek, slim, and pleasing to use.

Convenient? I found myself yesterday racing to an emergency room at my doctor's request. While waiting to be seen, I pulled-out my Kindle Touch 3G, began reaading a Sherlock Holmes short story, and had "no worries" about battery life or connectivity.

I heartily recommend the Kindle Touch 3G to anyone with an older relative who loves to read and may not have WiFi access OR who needs larger type in order to better enjoy the reading experience.

The Canon ELPH 100 HS is beautiful, and the Smart Auto feature takes great, no-stress photos for the user who has little or no experience with camera equipment.

Before buying the Canon ELPH 100, I read reviews and did a lot of research online to find a point-and-shoot camera that I would enjoy within the under-$200 price range. There are a lot of good products from which to choose.

I next went to Best Buy, Office Depot, and Sears to hold different point-and-shoot cameras made by the major producers: Canon, Nikon, Sony, Olympus, etc. For me, these visits to different retailers is an important part of the process of buying a point-and-shoot digital camera for the first time.

Another important step is to learn whether or not the camera's software is compatible with your desktop computer. Because my computer is old (2006), I had to research compatibility with the different cameras that I liked. You can find the information at the product websites.

Canon has a very user-friendly website that influenced my purchase considerably.

I had XP Service Pack 2 on an older Dell Dimension E310. For the Canon, I had to download XP Service Pack 3.

I ordered the camera from Amazon.com. From the moment I opened the box of the Canon ELPH 100 HS, I liked everything that I saw. The instructions are clear and organized well.

Finally, I love the pictures that I am taking. No, they are not the same quality as those taken by friends and family members who own thousands of dollars worth of camera equipment. However, these photos are beautiful and fun to take.

I am practicing now so that I will be ready to take photos at baby showers and graduations in the next couple of weeks.

Is it easy to learn how to use the Canon ELPH 100 HS? It is VERY easy to learn how to use Smart AUTO. The sliding Smart AUTO button is on the top of the camera: you slide the latch to Smart AUTO, and you are finished. The camera "decides" whether or not to activate flash and also determines other settings.

To learn to use all of the optional features (P mode) is fun but not essential to photographing great photos right away.

Another reason that I bought the Canon ELPH 100 is that it is considered to be among the best in its price range -- and possibly THE BEST -- in low-light conditions. The only time the colors seemed to be distorted somewhat was when I took photos of pets sitting in a semi-darkened room while they were directly under the strong light of a table lamp. I found that the bright light from the lamp washed over all objects close to the lamp; the objects outside of the lamplight were fainter in color. Since then, I've taken the precaution of composing photos more carefully so that I am not creating a spotlight effect.

I read that the ELPH 300 could be a better choice if you plan to use the video features a lot. For me, the video features on the ELPH 100 are fine.

While in Playback (viewing photos that I have taken), I am learning how to use the displayed menus to select options such as Slideshow and Erase -- so far, so good. While not as easy as Smart Auto, the menus are fairly intuitive.

I have been very pleased. The sheen of the dog's coat, the warm expression in her eyes, and the mysterious, bold gaze of the cat -- all captured beautifully.

I love this unit!  I use it almost every day and am happy with it.  I mainly use it for a blue tooth device from my iPhone in listening to my Audible books.  For that is is absolutely perfect.  I occasionally use it to listen to my music from my iTunes on my phone, but usually use my Sound Bar for that.

LIKE: the picture is great, not perfect, but great-especially for the price. The audio is good, but could be better.
Dislike: Not all that thrilled with the cartoony cursor.

These are good binoculars, and they really give good value for the price-especially if you prefer the porro prism type.  I actually like porro types slightly better than the roof prism type, but these do not have the close focus that my Orion Otters have-nor my Vortex crossfires have.  That is why they only rated a 4 for me.  For me, the close focus is a must have, but if you do not require this, then these are very good binoculars.

Installation and setup is very easy.  Footprint is fine, although it takes up more space than an Echo Dot 3 did.  Sound is fine, but with less bass... Which is OK with me because I'm an old jet engine pilot and can't hear bass well anyway, and the Alexa response distance is shorter than my 3rd Gen Dots, but I have one in every room so no problem.  Just noticed that the blue ring which indicates it's working has gone out, but the unit appears to still be working fine, so who knows what the future holds?

Arrived on time and in good condition. The Echo Dot Table Holder was well packaged with explicit assembly and setup instructions... Went together easily.  Sturdy construction should give years of use with proper care.  Elevating the Echo Dot above the surface with the holder definately improves sound and quality range.  I'm very happy with this item.

It works well, and is very loud, but unless the molding of the door frame is absolutely flat with the door (no bevel, like mine has) it will not install properly as the magnet won't align with the alarm.

Easy to set up, configure, and link to WiFi.  Speakers are full-toned with good bass qualities, and the uplink with Alexa is completely reliable.  Alexa does all the work, you just sit back and enjoy.
Good, strong, cable that delivers a great picture and sound.

The very best mini-speaker system I've ever found for a laptop or netbook.  Makes an excellent extension speaker as well for the TV or sound system... Small, unobtrusive, and with plenty of volume and acceptable bass.  I really like this speaker and use it in many applications.

I use them primarily with my Kindle Fire HD.  They give me the freedom of movement and the audio and music quality I want, without the weight and bulk of studio headpgones.  Since I wear hearing aids in both ears, I can't wear earbuds, so these are the next best thing to carry with my tablet or netbook.  AND, did I mention they are WIRELESS??

It does what it says it will do... What more can I say?  Sets up easily without hastle, even setting up the Wireless Internet connection is automatic, and it works perfectly right off the bat.  The on-screen keyboard for entering passwords and searches is one of the most innovative and easy to use I've seen.  The voice (audio) search is excellent and requires no "training".  Perfect!!

I originally bought this because my usual Apple 'Superdrive' DVD drive was still being dominated by my gaming needs, and I was going to need a dedicated DVD burner. Since then, however, my old Apple drive has failed me on several counts, not being forwardly compatible with newer USB protocols, etc. This drive works perfectly with my newest Mac, and is smoothly compatible with my older Macs as far as I can tell. And as I now require yet another dedicated DVD burner and/or drive, I have just now ordered another of these at less than half the price of the newest Apple 'Superdrive'.
Exactly what I was looking for: a light-weight 3 foot audio extension cord for my tower computer head phones. No more tripping over a heavy and unnecessarily long  ten foot extension.

I adore these headphones. So light, but with great quality sound for the size and price. And no head aches, neck strain or ear fungus like I get from most headphones. I bought one pair and loved it so much I bought two more for other rooms and uses. I think I may need still more...

Also, unlike most headphones, they don't break when your husband accidentally sits on them. They just quietly fold up under him. I just wish there was a wireless version of these, with inbuilt volume control. (Hint..hint..)

Not too heavy, feels decently sturdy and fits my Samsung Galaxy TAB A8 nicely while leaving room for access to the power & volume controls, all four speakers, microphones, charging port and the earphone jack to be easily accessible.
I bought the wine color which is beautiful, deep and rich. I haven't had this long but I'm quite pleased with this cover. Highly recommended.

I bought the original Fire TV Stick in 2014 when they first announced it. I used it on and off but we had cable and a DVR so I put it in a drawer. Recently I had some financial setbacks and canceled all the cable services. At about that time Amazon sent me an email offering a major discount on the new Fire TV Stick with Alexa integration. I bought it, delivery took a while and was even delayed beyond the promised delivery date. Installation was cake. Plug the wall wart into an outlet, plug the HDMI extender (recommended for better streaming) and USB power cable into the Stick. Mine oddly wasn't preregistered to my account but that took only a few minutes time to resolve. The longest time drain was downloading and applying the numerous firmware updates that were available. That took the better part of an hour, hour and a half or so.
Once done and running everything's been fine. Any streaming quality issues I attribute to my cable company constantly needing to work on the equipment in the area. I often had problems with the cable TV quality dropping or cutting out entirely. The new Stick is a bit snappier than the old, it's got a bit faster CPU though, sadly in five years the storage hasn't been updated. It still has the same 8gb the original came with. Alexa integration is nice, though mostly good for asking for specific shows to be played or asking for the next episode to be played before waiting for the onscreen prompt. Getting the weather displayed as on a Show is a bonus.
I think the best part of the whole purchase is the Stick's remote controlling the power and volume of my television keeping me from needing two remotes to watch TV. With the bargain price I'm glad of the purchase. I don't think I'd have bought it at full price but I'm glad I did when it was for sale.

This speaker seems more designed for more modern music somehow. Maybe it's how current music is mixed. I'm not sure but newer music like Billie Eilish has much more bass than music from the 70s, Led Zeppelin, etc. and even heavy metal from the 80s such as Iron Maiden. The older music, streamed from the same source, comes across flatter with a duller sound. It doesn't sound bad just newer stuff is clearer, has sharper highs and clearer bass.
The speaker is stylish with a nice modern design. There are rubber feet to isolate the unit and keep it from moving. Controls are. . . difficult to use. They're on the back, out of the way. They're dark although somewhat intuitive. Wireless connectivity was easy although the connection drops and reestablishes a few times a week at random times.
Issues with the speaker. I use this in my bedroom. The power/Wireless light is on the front and is a brilliant bright blue. With no other lights in the room this is almost bright enough to read by. I've had to resort to putting a piece of black duct tape over the light so I can sleep at night. The speaker has a narrow band where it sounds good; with the volume low the tone is flat and dull. Crank the volume and something, I think the passive bass radiator, buzzes horribly. Inside that volume window where the sound is good it's pretty darn good but it has it's limits. Not sure if it's my app or the speaker but every, single, time it loses wireless connection for more than a few seconds my volume, bass and treble settings reset back to flat defaults. It's only a mild annoyance but it's there.

I had a Galaxy S4 for several years. It was suitable and did the job. . . mostly. I was having some battery issues and my phone wouldn't update past Android 4.4. I was running into apps that needed a newer version of Android. I could have bought something cheap but I decided to treat myself and found the blue Galaxy S9 on sale for a decent price. I have to say I'm loving this phone.
The 5.8" Quad HD+ Super AMOLED screen is GLORIOUS! I run this is high performance mode with the brightness cranked up. Games, movies, even YouTube and TikTok videos look amazing. The curved edge I worried might be distracting but honestly I only notice in a couple games.
Sound is really good for a cell phone it has stereo speakers. Volume is more than enough.
Performance from the Octa-Core processor and 4GB of ram have not struggled to run anything I've thrown at it.
The camera is great. Maybe struggling a little in very bright light with a light colored subject. Otherwise, night mode gives great low light results. Video shooting is very nice with great slow motion results and a nearly unique super slow-motion recording mode at a mind boggling 960 frames per second is a lot of fun to mess around with.
Battery life is good, I got most of a day is high performance mode and could easily extend it by cutting things back to save battery.
The fingerprint sensor is quick to unlock and easy to use. A trick I found online to improve performance of the fingerprint sensor is to register the same finger more than once. It really works like a charm.
The look is sleek and sophisticated though I'm protecting that glass body with a nice Otterbox Symmetry case. The only real minor negative to the whole thing is this weighs more and is larger than my S4, a little hard on my hands and pocket but really, it's worth it.
I can't express how happy I am with this phone. I'm even buying props and things to use in creative videos and photo shoots.

The OontZ Angle 3 PLUS speaker has incredible battery life, pretty good bass, somewhat muddy mid range and okay highs (if you use the right app with a good equalizer). I found playing straight from the phone's built in apps wasn't so great but I downloaded another app with powerful settings and controls that bring out the best of this speaker. The OontZ Angle 3 PLUS has two speakers and 10 watts of power. There's a passive bass radiator. I never really thought those added much. All in all it's a decent speaker that kicks up my shower and shaving time. I got this on a Lightning Deal for a nice discount. I would not pay the full asking price.

I like the size. It's small enough that I was able to put it on the far side of the mirror and I really have to crane my neck to see the body. That being said I didn't pull the trim and conceal the cable so that runs down almost in the center of the car. But after a few weeks I completely stopped noticing it. The screen shuts down to be less of a distraction and the status indicator lights aren't bright enough to be annoying, even at night. Installation was fairly easy. Hardest part for me was getting the static disc that goes on the windshield and is what the mount glues to (this is done so you're not putting super strong glue directly on the glass) off its backing paper. I ended up needing an Xacto knife to get it free. Clean the glass then the clear plastic disk applies to the glass with static cling. The mount sticks to this and the camera easily attaches to the ball socket and can be swiveled into optimal position before being tightened down.
There are many settings you can use to configure your camera, I suggest going over them carefully and making the changes you want before mounting the camera. It's small and the buttons are fiddly. Some options include recording audio or not (I've got a foul mouth and tend to sing horribly off key so I turned my audio off), video resolution I set it to highest for best possible details, clip recording length; the camera will film for X number of minutes before saving a clip and starting the next (once the memory card is full the oldest video is deleted to make room for new video) I have mine set to 3 minute intervals. There's a G force sensitivity setting that once triggered (by impact or even extreme braking) it locks the current recording so it can't be deleted, recommended is medium to avoid over sensitivity. Night recording can be set to color or black and white. It does a good job with color in most situations. There's a ton of other options so make sure you explore and see what there is you may want to change. I'm quite happy with this unit and feel safer knowing it has my back. . . by watching out the front.

Okay, yeah, it's got a 128 LED lights and that's more and better than the ones that have only 60. . . or 96 lights. I already had one nearly, no exactly identical light/speaker to this with 96 lights. Now maybe there's a visible difference between 128 LEDs and 60, there pretty much has to be. But I have my 96 light speaker in the same shower nook as the new, 128 light speaker and Other than the large 1 I wrote on the bottom of the original speaker (96 lights) I can't tell them apart. That being long windedly said they're beautiful however many lights they have. As mentioned I have them both in the same wall nook in my shower and when I take a shower at night I use only the simulated fire from the two lights and it is awesome. The two speakers will sync into a stereo configuration very easily. Just sync once each and then turn them on. The speakers have decent sound as long as you remember they're small drivers running 5 watts each. More than enough for a shower, bedroom or out on a deck or patio for a small party.
About the only thing I don't like about these units are the white rim ring light and button lights for vilume, power, changing songs stay on the whole time and they're quite bright. I understand that you'll need to find the control buttons but the bright white lights detract slightly from the fire effect. They should either be orange/red to to match the fire effect LEDs or turn off after a short period of time. Besides that I really enjoy having these around. They hold a charge for weeks. Granted I only use them a few times a week for showers but I've never run them out of charge I end up thinking I should charge them because it's been a month or more since the last time they were charged.
Fun, entertaining light with a decent speaker, can be paired into stereo configuration. Good stuff.

These are great for turning a single outlet into a multi-plug surge protected plug. The short plug reaches the floor and doesn't require bundling the cord or zip tying to shorten thing. My only dislike, and it's not a big deal is the plugs are arranged vertically meaning any device with an adapter is going to take two, possibly three outlets. Still, they're handy and give some sense of security against power surges.

Well, it has been running six plus hours a day 4 - 5 nights a week for a while now and although I know other buyers have had issues this TV has been great. Out of the box it was four screws to put on the two reasonably sturdy feet. Connectors for power and HDMI were easily accessible. Setup was confusing at first. This is supposed to primarily be a Roku/streaming TV although it can work just fine with you cable or satellite provider's set top box. Included instructions didn't have a bypass the online setup section but TCL support quickly walked me through getting the TV connected to the cable box. Image quality is stunning. I was honestly amazed at how bright, vibrant and saturated the picture is. Sound quality is good, nothing spectacular but it does go loud which was a necessity as my mother, the primary user, is going deaf and at full volume couldn't hear her previous TV. She hears this set perfectly and there's plenty of volume left if her hearing issues worsen. I would recommend this set to anyone looking for an affordable TV.

My 3D printer came with a lousy 256meg (yes, meg!) micro SD card. I wasn't able to keep a library of the useful items I print frequently let alone all the things I had sliced and planned on someday printing. With this 2gb card I have optimal compatibility and storage space for hundreds of models, far more than I actually want to keep on a card at once. I also have my slicing software and custom profiles for my printers saved in a separate directory. Handy! It doesn't come with an adapter but I have three or four laying around so it didn't matter. These small capacity, non SDHC U1/? cards are hard to find and often more expensive than much larger cards.

This is a review of the Archer AC900:
It's a good router. In many ways it's a very good router. Might not be the choice for a large family with a lot of bandwidth consumption but it does do a good job for our small family usage. I've had multiple devices online at the same time the living room T.V. was streaming an HD movie. That and good coverage is all I really need. With our previous router the Echo Dot at literally the other end of the house had problems maintaining a streaming signal. Since installing the AC900 it's streamed music all night, every night for the two plus weeks it's been up and running. Signal strength was dramatically increased everywhere in the house. Speeds are a little better but not by too much. I had more of a consistency issue than a speed problem with the old router. The router sits low and doesn't seem to have great cooling so I have it sitting on a brace that I made so it's now couple inches off the shelf it's on. Better and more efficient cooling and less chance for dust build up.
I was happy to see that using a web browser you weren't required to install any software to get into the router's management although there is an Android app to manage the router. I've found the web browser access have be as easy if not easier to use though rarely I have to reload the main page a time or two but I think that's my choice of browser and not a problem with the device itself.
The router is great, for the novice, intermediate or even expert user. Unpack it follow the easy set up guide (pick a decent password) then connect your devices and you're done if you want to be or you can dig deeper and have fine control over the router's many features. It may not be the perfect choice for every installation but if you don't need a lot there's no reason to spend a lot.
In the end the AC900 delivers a lot of bang for the buck.

It's a phone extension cord, 50 feet was a little long but less expensive than the 35' cord available at the time I needed a new phone cord to wrap around my bedroom. There's a big somewhat tangled ball of excess cord behind a speaker but hey, I saved a couple bucks buying the longer cord and the sound quality of VOIP calls is just fine. Good product, good value.

Some people have claimed the screen is square, it's not. Like all previous Kindles this is measured diagonally. It only appears square because the one side of the bezel with the buttons (also not loud as has been claimed and the touch screen works fine if the nearly inaudible click might keep a partner awake).
I really like the seven inch screen and design of this new Kindle it's much closer to a regular paperback page now. I do wish the boldness option was allowed to be applied to any book and not just those purchased from Amazon. I get plenty of books from other sites such as Baen and Project Gutenberg but they're not given the full functionality Amazon's books are. I don't think it's fair.
The weight and balance. In or out of the cover is almost perfect. I find I can comfortably read for hours and if either hand gets tired a quick flip and you're reading with the other. I've reversed the page turn buttons like on the old K3/Kindle keyboard the page forward button is more natural feeling if it's at the bottom I have no idea why Amazon has the default reversed. Holding it you're more apt to go forward than bsck plus if you need to go back you can just slide your finger towards the screen and use the touch screen to go back, then it's right back to the lower button to continue reading. I rather like this device. It's noy light years ahead of the Voyage or PaperWhite but it is certainly a few large steps ahead. I haven't and have no plans to test the waterproof claims. I like the idea because I'm disabled and on a walker my previous Kindles have gotten damp. Now i don't have to worry. I did pour a few drops of water on the cover. All but one rolled off. The one soaked in. Caveat emptor. Im happy with the purchase so far. It was a gift to myself for having quit smoking for 10 full years. I deserved it.

We have two PaperWhites with the lower resolution screen. Viewing just text there honestly isn't a LOT of difference until you look closely at the edges. I replaced my PaperWhite with a Voyage (an almost regretful purchase) back in October and while there is a huge difference the added sharpness of an extra 88 PPI and the two extra LEDs make a difference. Since I tend to read in dim light the sharpness mattered more than the number of lights. when my mother's refurbished PaperWhite started acting up (reboots, updates, nothing helped) jumping forward or backward two, five, a dozen pages at a single click and often when turned on would be on the wrong page we decided to upgrade her to the latest PaperWhite. She's used to using the touch screen for changing pages and the lighting in the PaperWhite was more than adequate. In fact if I was asked to choose, right now, which Kindle to buy as a replacement I'd stare lovingly at the Oasis, look closely at its price, and honestly buy the PaperWhite. Two extra LED and the page turn 'buttons' just aren't worth the extra cost of the Voyage. They lured me in last year but after having had them since October I realize I could easily make due with the PaperWhite and the price difference would buy quite a few books. Now that this has the same 300 PPI screen, the adaptive lighting I turned off the first day and never turned back on. The PaperWhite has all the features you truly need and often goes on sale for a great price. In fact we were discussing replacing my mother's somewhat malfunctioning refurbished model she said to buy one when it went on sale and I swear the very next day Amazon had the Kindles all on sale (except the Oasis, grr). He unit had done three years of hard labor, that lady can READ so I didn't feel bad about replacing it. She's quite happy with it since it looks and functions exactly like her old one though slightly sharper. It even fit her customized case. Quite happy with the purchase.

I've bought expensive USB cable. I've bought cheap USB cables. I've had braided nylon USB cables that felt like they were taking your skin off you hand when they rubbed against you. Other than the braided cable every single cable I use to keep my bedroom tablet plugged in with has split, torn or ripped at the point just above the micro-USB plug end where the cable meets the plug (no, I don't, as I've been accused in the past, yank on the cord. I always use a firm grip on the plug.) Some last a month or two. My old white Kindle charging cable started flaking apart the same day I put it in use. I'd probably still be using the braided cable which hasn't failed but won't stay plugged in.
They advertise that this cable lasts 10x longer and has a 5,000 bend lifespan. I've only had it a short while. There just under seventeen months left on the warranty. I'd honestly be ecstatic if it lasts that long. I'm tired of worrying about shorts or what might happen to the tablet if it goes from plugged to unplugged over and over. So, here's to hoping that this cable lasts as advertised.

Update May 2nd 2017 - Well, here we are a little over three months since I purchased this cable and although it has developed a permanent bend just past where it plugs into the tablet it show no cracking, no lightening of the covering which would show stressing. This has literally at just three months has doubled the average lifespan of my USB cables. This device which is plugged in 24/7 (unless I need to charge my eReader) gets used numerous times a day, it just doesn't sit there. I'm extremely happy with the durability of this cable.

Update August 10th 2017 - I am amazed. No other cable has ever lasted as long as this Anker. I've had cables fail the same day, the same week and as I've mentioned it has developed a distinct bend from the way it hangs from my tablet, kept in the pocket of the grab bar on my bed, the cable shows almost imperceptible whitening just above the connector from strain but no cracks, splits or crumbling. It also stays firmly plugged into my Fire tablet and on occasion it's fine with my PaperWhite as well. Will certainly buy this brand again. Very impressive quality.

Another rare five-star review. I have the full size Echo which I got when they were offered fot $99 to Prime members only. I have preached the virtues and benefits of an Echo since the day I received it. I was finally able to talk my mom into a Dot the other day. Normally she's got her television blasting to help her sleep and I worried about the Dot's smaller speaker not being loud enough. It's been a week and though there's been some learning curve she hasn't once had the TV on and she's sleeping better. Extremely glad I was able to talk her into a Dot. It's loud enough for her, she's only had to skip a few songs that were too soft. I'm glad she got it and she loves it.

I love this light, absolutely love it. I purchased a laptop without backlit keys thinking I wouldn't be using it all that often but a disability has led me to require the touch-pad on the laptop as using a mouse on my desktop had become a near impossibility. I had come across another flexible USB lighting system that was less than half the height of this light and also lacked the on/off function as well as the dimmer capability which I find extremely useful.
When plugged into my rear most USB port this light reaches just above the top of the screen on my 15.6" laptop and with the light dimmed somewhat it doesn't glare even where it's just an inch or so from the screen itself but sheds enough light that I can see the entire keyboard easily.
The neck is strong enough to hold its position while standing there as well as once it's unplugged and put on the table when the laptop is not in use. It does wiggle a bit at the USB port but I think all USB ports seem to have a little wiggle room built into them.
Control couldn't be easier though controls would have, to me, been more convenient. You quickly press/tap the end of the USB light bar very, very lightly to turn or off the light. Dimming the light requires holding the end as the light dims or releasing it and holding it again as the light brightens. Personally I think separate switches would be more convenient but the single switch works well enough.
I love this light. It's absolutely perfect for my needs and puts so much more light on the keyboard than the smaller light I previously used (shown in one of the photos I'll attach) plus the fact that I can turn it on and off as well as dim or brighten the light just adds to the usefulness of the light. This also works great with a USB power pack.
I received this light in exchange for my review.

I have been considering a laptop cooling station for quite a while now. I had really hoped to review the smaller N5 mode which appears much lower than the N3 I was asked to review.
The first thing I noticed is the unit expects your laptop to have a USB port on the left hand side. Okay, the cable IS long enough to reach one of the two USB ports on the left side of my laptop but just barely. The on/off button and the extra USB port that's part of the base which is powered by the laptop's port that powers the cooling pad are rather out of the way and hard to reach. The port is also USB-2 only so if your machine is like mine make sure you leave the USB-3 open for things that require USB-3 connectivity.
The single fan is very quiet, I wouldn't call it 100% silent but it doesn't make that much noise. When it runs it gives an attractive blue glow. . . which you really don't get to see because the laptop's on top of the cooling pad. There are two removable clips on the base end which can be used if you want to use any of the five higher positions to stand the laptop at and they'll hold your laptop safely in place.
I was a bit disappointed in the height of this unit. My laptop is ¾ of an inch from front to back to front sitting on the table. With the addition of this N3 laptop cooling pad the height increases to two inches at the wrist rest and two and three quarters of an inch at the monitor end. That makes using the laptop somewhat uncomfortable. In the instructions it mentions that if you want to use this stand you should consider using an external keyboard and mouse. . . Sorry, but if I wanted to use an external keyboard and mouse I'd have bought a desktop computer. I have a desktop computer I was just hoping for a small lift to the laptop and a bit of extra cooling.
This unit left me disappointed. It's too high, too hard to reach the additional USB port and on/off button. The adjustability is quite impressive you can raise the screen quite high, eye level or even higher, but I just don't want to buy and use an external keyboard and mouse. To me, that defeats the purpose of having a laptop in the first place. Being disabled I bought a laptop because I have such a hard time using a mouse and the touchpad on the laptop was a blessing. Some users may find this useful or handy but I honestly did not enjoy using this at all.
I received this in exchange for my review.

*Update*
I also received the N5 cooler to review (all items listed on the same product page share the same review pool) the N5 does not light up like the larger N3 reviewed above. The N5 has its power switch and USB ports far more conveniently located on the center of the back of the Unit. The N5 does not have the ability to adjust the height or angle of your laptop. It raises the front one and a half to one and a quarter inches in height in the front depending on how you position the laptop. In the back the laptop is raised between two and two and a quarter inches. My fifteen inch Asus laptop overhangs each side by about a half inch but that doesn't seem to affect cooling. Although the N5 lacks the light up fans and height adjustability I think it's a superior cooling unit that could even comfortably fit in your lap. The N5 is a solid four-star item while the N3 remains subpar.
I received this unit in exchange for my review as well.

Fifteen dollars? Are you kidding me? The outer bag is reasonably durable and decently padded enough to give adequate protection as long as you don't drop it off a cliff or play football with it. The zippers operate smoothly and feel sturdy. The shoulder strap has an okay pad, it's better than nothing. The strap hardware is hard plastic and somewhat cheap feeling. The inner material is a bit thin and chintzy feeling but it will keep papers and your laptop separated well enough. I have two portable hard drives in a soft case and two USB cables in the outer pocket and there's plenty of room with the laptop inside. This is more than enough for what I need and the price can't be beat for what you get.

My family got together and picked this up for me during Fuji's sale/promotion in March. This is going to cover Christmas and birthdays for the next few years :)

Build quality is top notch. The zoom, focus and aperture rings are all nicely sized and very... grippy. The zoom itself is almost, but not quite, too stiff. I noticed no creep whatsoever. Autofocus is, expectedly, a bit slower than the kit lens but still decent. Image stabilization is impressive enough for hand-held shooting in low light at full zoom. Image quality is impressive. The included hood is huge, seriously huge. It's actually a little hard to get the lens cap on with the hood on. Speaking of the lens hood; my one gripe with this rig is when fully 'on' the lens the hood tends to rattle a little bit. I've found that backing off the connection a 1/4 inch or so keeps the hood from rattling and still keeps it firmly in place.

It does make my X-E2 a little front heavy but it's not that horrible. I'm contemplating buying one of the extension grips from Fuji for the camera. A nicely padded neck strap is a definite plus when carrying a camera with this lens mounted on it. One thing I've had to pay attention to is when switching back to my 18-55mm lens I need to be careful of how hard I twist the barrel to zoom in and out this lens is MUCH stiffer to use than the kit 18-55mm that came with my X-E2. I worry I may break the smaller lens after using this lens for an extended period.

Highly recommended.

I've used this several times now with my Fujifilm X-E2 and it works great. Simple and easy to understand and set. The only problem I had was the case is a little narrow for my thick hands and setting the controller required a bit of juggling. The addition of a light was a nice feature and even helped getting things connected in pre-dawn light.
The case is a little flimsy, possibly easy to break but with care it should last. I found an old mesh pouch, I think I got a pair of promotional ping-pong balls in it, which holds the controller and cable when not in use and is perfect to hang the rig on my tripod when it's being used as an intervalometer which is my main use for this remote.

I do frequent, manual, backups of my important personal files to a pair of Seagate portable hard drives. This six foot cable gives me a bit more freedom on where I can put my portables, lets me use a rear USB port and keeps my drives away from the edge of the desk where I had to put them when I used the short cables that came with the drives.

I was surprised at how heavy duty this cable actually was. It's almost too heavy. I've found it hard to flex and keep in place and while my portable hard drives are weighty enough to stay in place I could see this cable dragging a lighter phone or other device off a desk.

I had no problems with fit or connections and while it may be my imagination (I've run my backups hundreds of times over the last couple years so I know how long it normally takes) it seems like data transfer might be just a bit faster with this cable than with the ones Seagate sent out with their drives.

This is a well made, possibly too heavy for light devices, cable from AmazonBasics. I have used AmazonBasics cables for quite a while now and never had a problem with any of them.

I've only had the Fujifilm X-E2 camera and 18-55mm lens for a short while and I've barely scratched the surface of it's capabilities. This is a camera anyone can use right out of the box but also one that you can spend years learning to master.

The retro look and styling are very attractive but they made it, for me at least who was used to an extended grip on the camera body, a little hard to handle. I found myself hitting the AE-L and AF-L buttons often and frequently by accident spun the exposure compensation dial without even realizing I had. I resolved this with the LensMate Thumb Grip designed for the X-E1/E2. It made a good camera great. I also added LensMate's brass soft release button to the shutter release. It does aid in smoother pressing of the shutter button but it also looks great on the camera.

The 18-55mm lens that comes with the X-E2 is a real pleasure to use. The zoom is stiff enough to let you feel in control but easy enough that you don't need brute force to use it.

Image quality, even at 100%, is outstanding. I've been getting so many 'keepers' that I've had to reevaluate my shooting style. I feel like I'm overshooting. In the past I was shooting three or four hundred images in an outing and getting maybe four or six shots I really want to keep and share. Now, with the X-E2 I'm finding two, three even four times that many shots that are worth keeping. I'm going to need a bigger hard drive!

Battery life has been pretty good for me. Even shooting in temperatures down in the 30's and 40's I had no problem taking well over three hundred images and still having battery bars left. In the times I've gone out all day wandering around the county I've yet to have to swap out the battery though I did purchase an extra just to have around.

Functionality, configurability and controls are extensive and a bit quirky but easy enough to get used to. As an example the Q button gives you 'Q'uick access to many of the more necessary and often used controls. You navigate around the Q menu with the 5-way controller but you make setting changes with the command dial. One of the features I found most interesting was the ability to constrain the ISO in Auto mode and set a minimum shutter speed. I also liked the ability to configure the four letter prefix for file names. All the 'extra' settings like special effects, double exposure, movie mode and panorama are accessed through the Drive button.

I did find a couple small negatives. Nothing to cause me not to want to use it but made me wonder. The odd menu systems. The pop-up flash is a bit anemic and is somewhat blocked by the 18-55mm lens. It's even worse when the hood is attached. The shoulder strap that comes with the camera... I know they're usually bad but this is cheap camera bad not quality camera bad. I put it around my neck, gave a tug, and then threw it away without putting it on the camera. I expected a little more quality there. The tulip lens hood that comes with the 18-55mm feels hard and brittle. It too could have been a bit better quality. I already mentioned the LensMate thumb grip that I think is an absolute must add item (it's really worth the cost). My big clumsy hands desperately needed it to aid in stability and control.

Where to start with a conclusion? This is an interesting mix of old school retro styling and modern camera technology. I think Fuji have really blended them together well. I can see myself enjoying this camera for years to come. Very highly recommended.

{Update}
Not wanting to pile on the negatives but I had intended to and completely forgot to mention the battery door. It's really kind of flimsy and feels like it could easily break. Also, with the way it's hinged I find it rather hard to get the memory card out of the camera because it's so close and parallel to the battery door's hinge.

This is my new favorite tripod head. With two controls for setting friction and locking the head in place it's amazingly versatile. The previous ball-head mount I had was either locked or fully loose which made camera control a little scary. With the Vanguard TBH-250 you can have free movement and maintain enough friction to keep your camera from flopping wildly about. You can also lock and unlock the horizontal movement of the head so you can take panoramic shots with ease.

The mount is threaded for 1/4" which is a sleeve that fits inside a 3/8" threaded fitting so the TBH-250 will fit on the majority of tripods on the market. The 3/8" thread fit my Dolica AX620B100 tripod perfectly and even fit, separate from the tripod and with a lot of finagling, in the bag that came with my Dolica tripod. A small tool was included to remove the 1/4" sleeve but a flat head screwdriver would also do the job.

The only thing I'm not crazy about is the camera mount. It's advertized as a 'quick shoe' mount but it's not that quick and if you're not careful it's not that secure. Slightly loosened you can reposition the mount forward and backward about an inch or thereabouts to get better balance. But loosen the camera mount just a slight bit more and the camera will easily pull free of the tripod head. There is a brass pin which keeps the mount from sliding out front to back and that's great but there's no locking or safety latch keeping your camera attached to the tripod.

While we're on the subject of the camera mount the screw holding the mounting plate to the camera requires a screwdriver, coin or in a pinch you can flip the tool for removing the 1/4" thread adapter and tighten the plate to the camera with that. I'm surprised that a tripod head of this quality doesn't include a butterfly nut to hand tighten the plate to the camera.

While I do wish it had a more secure mount and an easier way to attach the shoe to the camera I would still recommend this tripod head. It's very smooth, solidly built and feels like it will last for years.

I've been testing this speaker system with my 10" Samsung Galaxy Tab2 tablet which had no problems connecting to the speakers with and without the app from the Android store.

Appearance:
Their product description calls this 'fun, trendy and modern'. But to be honest this looks, to me, like an appliance that fell out of my grandmother's 1950's black, white and chrome art-deco kitchen. It's not unpleasant looking but I wouldn't call it modern. When I saw images of the system online I had hopes that the neon green ring around the face would light up. Sadly it doesn't. The handle is also fixed in place and doesn't retract or collapse into the body. It would have been a nice idea so you could stack or store this more easily.

Sound:
It doesn't sound bad. Especially for being just two 15 watt wide range speakers in a ported (holes to help the bass sound better) enclosure. The bass is a little flat and the high end sounds a little... hollow but it is a lot better than the speakers built into my tablet. I've tried a variety of music; jazz, pop, classical, rock, punk and everything sounded quite good. I found I had to use both the tablet's volume control as well as the speaker systems volume controls to get real volume out of the system. They operate independently of each other.

Drawbacks:
I don't normally comment on price with items received from the Vine program but at the time I'm writing this review Amazon is currently selling this item for over two hundred dollars. Maybe the Bluetooth equipment is expensive but to me that's a LOT for just two speakers in a box. I didn't pay that much for my four speaker bookshelf system or the subwoofer equipped speaker system connected to my desktop PC. Both of which have far superior sound quality.

The battery indicator light only seems to light up when the system is charging. I charged this a week ago and used it for several hours at a time but I have no idea how much charge is left in the battery.

The biggest problem I had with this speaker system was when doing anything other than playing music. I thought it would be fun to add big sound to the games I enjoy on my tablet but there's a distinct lag between doing anything and when the speaker plays the sound. I noticed it most of all in my favorite billiards simulator. You would strike a ball...and then hear it happen, even system sounds such as keyboard typing noises, a 'blip' when selecting things played a noticeable time after they happened.

The App:
I won't say much about the app here. It's completely unnecessary to operate this system with your Android device. It's just poor quality programming that appears to have been slapped together at the last minute. It also doesn't match the documentation and features such as Bass Boost which are in the instructions but don't exist in the app.

Speaking of the documentation. I opened the box and found a large booklet and for one, brief, moment I thought this item was fully documented in depth and detail... then I opened the instructions and found there's twelve pages of English instructions which are poorly written and lacking in detail. The rest of the book is comprised of numerous other languages each getting their own few pages. Ah well. Turn it on, turn it up. Enjoy the music.

I bought this as an afterthought when I ordered my [[ASIN:B005HSDL8S Garmin nüvi 50LM 5-inch Portable GPS]]. At that time it was less than $5 so I figured I had little to lose if it didn't work.

Then I tried this in my 2007 Hyundai Accent, using the right-hand of the two center console vents, and it worked great! It's better than the stock windshield mount or the beanbag mount I also purchased.

I can still easily see and easily read my GPS (the 5" screen really helps) but it's not right out in front of me distracting me. It also doesn't put the GPS in the way of any of the dashboard controls though it's a little close to the radio tuning knob which I never use anyhow.

I've driven several hundred miles with my GPS on this mount some of that over unpaved and horribly maintained dirt roads and it just stayed in place without a problem.

It's easy to mount. Slightly trickier to remove (requiring two hands). My only worry is it seems a bit fragile but I'm careful with my possessions so I think it'll last.

Highly recommended!

Years ago I bought a little 2MP 3X Zoom digital camera. It was a Kodak and it took great pictures. Several years after that I won a Kodak Z650 in an online contest and flat out loved the pictures it took. So when the stars aligned and Amazon had the Kodak Z990 on sale and my gift card balance was enough to afford it I jumped at the opportunity.

I really LIKE the Kodak Z990 and I'm sad that it will probably be the last Kodak camera I ever buy...

I LIKE this camera... I almost love this camera. While my Z650 almost never came out of Auto mode I find myself accessing the PASM controls and bracketing the exposure compensation when I use this camera.

It isn't that the Z990 doesn't take great pictures. It does. It just takes a little work to get them.

The camera is hefty, weighing in at 1 LB. 5 OZ. (593g) and feels substantial. To me it feels like what a camera should. The gripping areas on the front handgrip and rear thumb rest are lightly rubberized and the non-movable ring on the lens has a sturdy ribbed rubber covering.

The controls are reasonably easy to access and use. I like that you can use either the 5-way controller (similar to a Kindle's) or the clickable toggle wheel next to the thumb rest to access and control many of the camera settings. I like having the zoom controls on a ring around the shutter button. It feels easier to use than those cameras that have this control on the back. It also requires a very light touch as with 30x total optical zoom the lens and controls are very sensitive. At first you will find yourself zooming or going wide-angle past the point you wanted but with a little practice it becomes much easier to control.

The Z990 uses AA batteries (4) which, personally, I think is great. You can, in a pinch, get replacements at any convenience store, gas station or mega-mart in the US. It also comes with a serviceable if feature free slow battery charger and four Kodak brand rechargeable NiMH batteries. I've since replaced these with a smart charger and better batteries but out of the box they're enough to get you started.

Another great addition is the Optical View Finder. This is incredibly handy when shooting outdoors in bright sunlight. The 3" LCD screen is great but in direct sun it, like all LCD screens, becomes almost impossible to see.

I've, as of the time of this review, taken a bit over a thousand images and a handful of videos with my Z990 and I've barely scratched the surface of experiencing all the features and functions it has to offer.

Some notable features are:
Two panoramic image modes. One has the camera stitching two or three images together to produce the image and the other allows you to hold the shutter button and 'sweep' the camera to produce the panoramic image.
Multiple Kodak film time emulations - Kodacolor, Kodachrome, Ektachrome, T-MAX, TRI-X as well as standard B&W and Sepia modes.
In camera HDR mode.
Multiple burst modes.
Full 1080p video in stereo.
The camera can even emulates a Photo Booth taking four images in quick succession and stitching them together.

Nothing being perfect the Z990 has a few cons I feel need to be mentioned:
The memory card is stored in the battery compartment and the battery door is one of the few things I worry about breaking on this camera. It is light plastic and not easy to close with batteries installed.
To use a USB cable to transfer images from the camera to a computer the camera needs to be powered up requiring removal of the lens cap (because the cap mounts on the body not the lens). I don't like that it needs to sit with the lens exposed for no reason.
The lens isn't threaded so you cannot use any filters with this camera.
Preview mode, where the camera shows you the last image taken, cannot be disabled on this model, you can bypass it somewhat by 1/2 pressing the shutter once the preview displays but it would have been nice to be able to turn off this feature.

In conclusion:
While the Kodak Z990 Max isn't perfect it is an affordable bridge camera that takes excellent pictures day or night with an extremely powerful zoom lens, a host of useful features and controls that can only be topped by DSLR cameras. As Kodak's last hurrah, it's a pretty good note to go out on.

Thank you to all you wonderful Amazon reviewers. I'd never purchased a Bose product before, with the exception of possibly headphones at some point in time. We know the Bose sound is legendary, but I never really needed a Bose radio or CD player. The Solo caught my eye because I love my flat screen TV, but the speakers are only so-so at best. Like many other reviewers, I have trouble understanding some dialogue on TV. It's fine as long as there is someone around to annoy endlessly by asking "what did they say," but watching TV alone, I miss big chunks of the story & plot. The doctor says it's just "one of the vestiges of old age." Oh. Another one of those. Thanks, doc.

So, I wondered if the Solo speaker might help, and thanks to all my hard-of-hearing contemporaries here (or should I say THANK YOU), I saw all the reviews promising that I wouldn't have to ask "what?" every 2 minutes any more. I could jump for joy after hooking up the speaker and giving it a listen, although my doctor would probably advise against it. On my TV, unlike some others mentioned here, the TV speakers work along with the Solo speaker, so it's easy to mute the Solo and hear the difference between it and the TV speakers. It's amazing. The sound is rich, and big, and crisp in a way that my surround-sound system isn't. Most importantly, in answer to my wildest hopes, I can understand every single word of dialogue, even Christian Bale mumbling behind his Batman mask. No kidding. The Bose speaker took 20 years off my age, and reduced my waist by four inches. Ok, I am kidding about that.

As if all that isn't reason enough to get one of these gems, it has to be the simplest piece of electronics to hook up, set up & operate. It's simply two cords, one to the power outlet, and the other to the TV. They include all the cables in the box: digital optical, HDMI & RCA. Plug, plug, power. That's all. The remote is four buttons: power, mute, up & down volume. It's hard to believe that such intricate, complex sound can come from such a simple device. Thank you, Mr. Bose, wherever you are. Not only would I highly recommend this to my friends, I think everyone with a flat-screen TV owes it to themselves to get one. Seriously. This is the audio-visual experience I thought I was already having with 5.1 surround system.

Luckily, I havn't had any of those problems with the camera, and after several months, am perfectly happy with it. Yes, the camera has a plastic body, but it's been very durable while travelling and seems no flimsier than any other electronic device made today. The plastic body is one reason why the camera is so easy to take everywhere. It's light, compact & not a chore to haul around, which is nice.

Rather than a short battery life, I have been suprised at the long life of the battery that came in the camera. I bought an extra battery because I expected it to run out quickly, but I've never used it. I've never needed to. During a 4-day weekend in the mountains, I plugged the camera in at night, and was able to record any time and every time I wanted all day long each day.

The noisy zoom lens? I don't know. My model doesn't have a noisy zoom lens. I can barely hear it when I use it, and have never noticed the sound of the zoom during playback. Maybe it happens with some of them.

Granted, the built-in microphone doesn't produce the best sound, but it's been good enough for my casual use of video. The video has been clear, sharp & colorful. Would I use it to record a wedding? Probably not. To record my mother's belly-dancing recital? You bet!

The Cooler Master put the cord on the side of a small thumbdrive-like device which I hope will protect the cord connections. The fan is quiet enough and keeps my laptop cool, but it's probably the screened top and multiple larger vents on the bottom that let it air circulate better.

Unfortunately the pad is made of plastic, is thin, and when you set it down on an uneven surface--like my leather couch-- it hums louder hitting the plastic. I have been shooting Olympus cameras since 1978. I have always loved the lenses. With over 2,000,000 shots on my Olympus E-500 camera, I decided it was time to invest in a new camera.

I was reluctant at first to try the EM-1 for three reasons:
- The format is Micro-Four Thirds, not Four Thirds. I take 99% of my photos in the telephoto range, and that is what Four Thirds was optimized to use. Micro-Four Thirds is geared more towards wide angle lenses.
- The camera is mirrorless and uses an electronic Viewfinder (EVF).
- I have to use a converter to mount my existing Four Thirds lenses, and converters have a very bad history.

Out of the box:
The first thing that you notice when you pull the body out is that it is SOLID. The thing feels like it is built like a tank. I have not tried the "splashproof" and other claims, but just holding this body I can believe them. The camera fits well in my hand. My hands are a little large, and my pinky occasionally slides off the bottom. I may buy the grip/extra battery holder later if this proves to be a problem. YMMV.

Using Four Thirds lenses:
I have no Micro Four Thirds lenses and a lot invested in Four Thirds lenses, so using them was a key issue. Olympus has 1/17 or 1 MP of the sensor dedicated to phase detection auto focus, the only type of auto focus that will work with these lenses. I find that the system works very well. Focusing is fast and accurate.

Mounting the converter is easy, as expected. Once mounted, you use a button on the side to release the lens. This is a learning issue since I still normally hit the lens release button on the camera body. I anticipate little real problems with this since as soon as I try to put the cover on the back of the lens I realize my error.

Balance with the 12-60 mm Four Thirds lens is excellent. Holding the lens by the zoom collar, the weight is only slightly behind my left hand. I only have to support the body lightly with my right hand. I personally like that balance. Longer lenses like the 70-300 are also well balanced.

EVF:
I have used a mirrored SLR since 1978 and a rangefinder 35 mm camera and 126 film P&S cameras before that. As you might guess, I favor a direct view to see what I am shooting. EVF have issues with resolution and lag when moving to a different point of interest or following a subject, especially in low light.

The EVF has turned out to be great. I really like Olympus' implementation. There is some lag, but it is generally minimal. The "What You See Is What You Get" is a big plus in my book. Adjust the exposure compensation or manual exposure settings, and the view in the EVF changes to reflect what the image will look like. It is not perfect, but it gets 95%+ of what you will actually get. The display of settings is bright, clear, crisp, large, and surprisingly unobtrusive.

The EVF also allows a lot of changes in camera settings to be done without removing the camera from your eye. Use the two dials, and you can see where the focus points that you are using are. Hit the OK button on the back, and you can use the dials to adjust just about every setting while watching the selections you are making in the EVF. Ditto with the other buttons like HDR and auto exposure mode.

HDR:
I had the opportunity to use in-camera HDR while on a recent trip. The day was cloudy, and there was a lot of shadow against bright grey clouds. The in-camera HDR used a series of shots at different exposures and combined them in the camera. The results were better than HDR Pro in Photoshop CS5.5 IMO. I was much, much happier with the dynamic range and overall look of the images. the 10 fps shooting mode was also great for minimizing camera movement, ghosts and other problems associated with HDR.

Image stabilization:
The EM-1 has a five axis image stabilization system for the sensor. That means any lens becomes can be used. The fourth and fifth axes are for rotations. One compensates for the slight turn of the camera that often occurs when you press the shutter button. I had good success using IS in low light with my 70-300 mm lens set at 300 mm.

Scenes:
the EM-1 has many useful scene modes. I used landscape and panorama with great success. The artistic filters and story modes may also interest you. I prefer to do those types of things in post-processing.

ISO:
The camera has an almost insane 25600 maximum ISO. Yes, you get image quality degradation and noise at that ISO, but the in-camera JPEG processor can actually give you some relief from the problems at higher ISOs. I so far have found shooting up to ISO 1600 produces no discerned degradation. I tried ISO 6400 and found minimal issues.

For those who started with film and were in love with the "high ISO" 1000 film for low light shooting, this is a major and welcome advancement. For those newer to photography that have been using higher ISO cameras for a while, the speed may not be much of a gain, but the image quality should be.

The low end ISO is 200, which is the new normal. I do not find it to be a problem. I would rather shoot at a faster shutter speed than have an ISO 100 setting in most cases. There is an ISO LOW setting, but I do not plan to use it. If you regularly shoot in bright light and want lower f-stops, invest in a neutral density filter.

Back display:
The back display is slightly disappointing. It can only tilt up and down, not rotate so that you can see your composition when you are getting into the shot. It works well for shooting over crowds or getting a low angle shot.

On the plus side, the display is clear, bright and a touchscreen that can be used to select a point of interest for focusing and can be used to take the shot in live view mode. You can also use it to select settings to change. The next generation should be even better, and hopefully it will have a screen that rotates.

SD card:
One change from the E-500 that I do not like is the use of SD rather than CF cards. CF cards are nearly indestructible, and a good Sansdisk Extreme card works virtually anywhere, anytime and is virtually impossible to physically break. The xD card slot disappearing is no loss, but not having a second card slot is somewhat surprising given the high-end prosumer/professional positioning of this camera.

Controls and customization:
The controls are pretty well placed for me with the exception of the auto exposure lock button. That is right beside the viewfinder and too far to the left for my liking. You can do a lot of customization with the control buttons and dials, but there are limits. I have not made any changes yet because I am still learning the camera. Overall the defaults seem logical and useful.

This camera has two dials, one on the front and one on the back. The E-500 only had a back dial, so I am learning to use the two dial system. They work well for adjusting and selecting options. I think the second dial was a good addition. Both are conveniently located for my fingers.

Image quality:
All of this is meaningless if the image you get out is bad. The EM-1 does not disappoint. I know that there are people who insist that they need 48 MP or some other ridiculously large number. The reality is that 16 MP is a great size for printing full-size 300 dpi images on your printer or using a commercial photo printing service. If all you do is screen displays, it is about eight times more pixels than you need for a typical 2 MP monitor.

The quality of the EM-1 pixels is very high, and you get excellent out-of-the-camera RAW and JPEG images. I have no problems seeing fine detail at 100% and higher magnifications.

Summary:
This camera is a winner, and it works with my existing Four Thirds lenses so I do not have to invest another $3000+ in lenses to use it. I have a lot to learn, and it will take some time to get the most out of the camera, but out-of-the-box, using my E-500 techniques, it is already doing great work.

If you want a very good, moderate cost camcorder for moderate to bright lighting and can live with the controls, this is a good choice.

Update after living with this PC for half a year: Zero problems, fast, and works perfectly for my application (business use). And excellent value. VERY pleased with this purchase.
---

The PC itself seems to be a great value, and is working fine thus far. The system is plenty fast. The HDD is a bit busy/noisy, and spins a bit more than it should, as though the system is caching to disk constantly. I'm not doing anything demanding with it at all--just light MS Office use and surfing. That's it. No gaming, no video editing, nothing heavy. Note this system is intended for business use, and could not handle much in the way of gaming or video editing, as it has no video card. The on-board graphics use the system's RAM, so anything asking a lot from the system's limited graphics capabilities will slow the entire system down immensely. Luckily, I outgrew DOOM years ago.

The SFF case is heavy, but oddly a bit flimsy, with more flex than I had expected for the weight--especially the back panel--mine was oddly bent outward. I pushed it back in/straightened it (I had to in order to plug things in--the plugs were deeply recessed due to the bent real panel--very odd). The chassis itself is a joy to work with though, as the case pops open on hinges without turning a single screw--not even a thumbscrew, and everything is very accessible. The HDD's working vibrations and sounds are amplified by the plastic subframe the drive is mounted in, which acts like an amplifier for the vibrations. I worry a bit that the system's small case will have cooling issues. There just isn't much room in there, and there is only one small 3" system ventilation fan (+ the power supply's fan, and a fan over the CPU). There are vents on the front and rear of the system, but I would like a lot more ventilation--I would have appreciated a perforated lid. Heat is the enemy of all electronics, and my other systems all have more ventilation than this box. Of course, this is an off-lease corporate desktop workstation, and is not designed to have the long life of other systems. The components in the box are the cheapest possible variants thereof, and I do not expect this system to last more than 3-4 years at the most. That said, $269 for a branded Lenovo PC with a 3.2GHz Intel Core i5, 12GB of RAM and a 2TB HDD is a fantastic value. If it dies in 3 years, I will have gotten my money's worth.

Important note about the packaging: it simply was not enough protection. I guarantee the system took some hard knocks on its way to me. The UPS driver actually dropped it at my feet from a height of 1'--not kidding! The system is not packaged in an inner box within the shipping carton--the carton IS the box. The small Styrofoam corner blocks used to float the system inside the box are unusually rigid, so much so that they provide little in the way of cushioning, and one of them had cracked in half--meaning the PC wobbled around in the box during shipping. Also, the carton was sealed with "Microsoft Certified Refurbisher" packing tape, making it clear to all it contained a PC. They need to change the packaging--a desktop system simply needs more/better protection than this. I half expected it to be DOA due to the abuse it took on the way here from Arizona.

Alexa now has a deeper, fuller voice! The bigger speaker (compared to the Dot) makes a huge difference. Also, the mics seem to work better, even though they are supposed to be the same(?). Music however, is what it's all about. This little gadget fills the room with rich, full sound. Love it.

This case is exactly what I wanted: extremely durable shock-absorbing (read: drop-proof) protection without screen protection. Let me qualify that statement: I did *not* want screen protection. I love the pearl eink display on my graphite Kindle Keyboard, and it now has a big brother. I do not want a screen cover, as this would greatly reduce the screen's otherwise remarkable clarity, adding unwanted elements such as bubbles, surface scratches, and glare to the mix--no thank you. There is a reason I disliked reading on the iPad so much I gave it back (very reflective!). In fact, this OtterBox defender case came with a stick-on screen protector--no way. It would ruin that big, glorious pearl eink display.

A screen cover serves no purpose once you remove the device from your backpack/messenger/tote/briefcase for use. Assuming you transport your Kindle device safely in an appropriate sleeve (you put your other expensive electronic equipment--your laptop/tablet in one; your Kindle deserves the same amount of respect), the screen protector is completely unnecessary--the sleeve protects the screen during travel. THAT is when the screen needs protecting--when you are not using it, from the other goodies in your messenger bag/backpack (keys, pens, earbuds, and anything else rattling around in there). Yes, that's right--I'm talking about a Kindle in an Otterbox Inside a sleeve inside your briefcase. ...Inception-level protection. You got it. Better safe than sorry, right? What if they once again stop producing our beloved Kindle DX and something happens to yours? I do not want to have to replace my DX--especially if it has to be with a Fire device (5% the battery life, reflective, heavy, expensive--no thanks!). When you are holding your Kindle in your hand, reading, a screen cover only detracts from the experience.

What you see in my pictures is exactly what you get: a beefy, black rubber (not silicone--too easily torn; rubber is much stronger) form-fitting sleeve with an equally form-fitting outer plastic shell. Science geeks like me understand how this works, and just in case you are not one, here is the idea: if you drop your device onto the floor, the outer shell absorbs some of the impact energy generated by the device hitting the floor. It then disburses the remaining energy of the impact broadly into the rubber inner lining. The rubber lining then in turn disburses the now greatly-reduced impact energy into the device. In other words, by the time the force of the impact is filtered through two layers of protection, the second of which is very absorbent and resilient (rubber) the device inside absorbs little if anything of the original impact.

I feel very good about having my Kindle DX in an Otterbox Commuter. If I ever had one of those incredibly poorly-designed (read: seriously fragile) apple devices, such as an iPad or iPhone (which I do not, and am not ever likely to), it too would live in an OtterBox Commuter case. OtterBox = the best protection a device can get. I paid $18 including shipping for this. A great price, and worth much more in terms of peace of mind.
