This is one of my favorite patch cables, and I especially love the fact that they come in a variety of them to color-code by function. I received mine as a review sample and it is one of the best constructed patch cables that I have used.

Since I am using them is my music studio the best thing is they are low noise. Actually this is about noise-free as you can get. Part of the reason is the double shielding, but part is the overall construction.

I also love the precision fit. I use these to patch bluetooth receivers in some of my amps and PA mixers for backing tracks. Lesser cables that I have used had a sloppy fit, These have a firm feel inserting and removing.

Construction is top notch. Everything from the heavy duty strain reliefs to the plated tip, ring and sleeve are well made. I also love the flexibility of the cable itself.

If you are looking for high grade patch cable for 3.5mm male-to-male, this is it in my opinion.

Stephen M. Charme's incredibly helpful June 19, 2014 review covers this device in exhaustive detail. I'll attempt to not repeat him, so will confine my review to why I awarded my review sample five stars.

Foremost, I love the convenience of having an all-in-one power and charging station for my phone, tablet and a few smaller electronic items. It takes up one full two outlet wall connectors in my music studio where I am using it. One of the plugs is a dummy that does not draw electricity. This ensures that you do not overload a circuit as well as providing stability to the rather large unit.

At 15 Amps (1675 Watts) this is more than sufficient for the small amperage devices I am using (although I do have a 5 Watt RMS output tube amp plugged into it as well.) Where I live the power fluctuates too wildly to plug anything of value directly into a wall outlet, so this is essential.

It's also a convenience with respect to the swivel. Most of the devices I am powering with this use wall warts, and even with the swivel I can only plug four in at any given time. While that blocks two of the outlets, had it not swiveled I would have probably lost one more outlet.

I have found this so useful that I intend to order another to place in my gig bag for playing out. There is always a dearth of outlets on most of the small venue stages where I play, and the power in most of those places is usually abysmal. One of these for a small PA and keyboard will afford adequate protection as well as being conveniently small.

Capacity is more than adequate for my needs, and the price is right. But the real reason why I gave it five stars is this drive is absolutely reliable. I have tried other brands only to experience premature death of the drive, data loss and other frustrations. In fact, one would get so hot in large transfers that it was uncomfortable to touch. This one does not have those flaws.

I use a pair of these. One for backing up my documents on my ThinkPad T61 running Win XP, and the other as a portable music library. For the latter use I've plugged it into my Galaxy Note 3 phone and Samsung tablet via a [[ASIN:B00C7SK2J2 Micro USB OTG Host Cable to USB 2.0 Adapter]], as well as a number of PCs and laptops of fellow musicians.

Just about every operating system, from my Android phone to a friend's Win 8 laptop immediately recognized this as a drive as soon as it was inserted in the USB port.

I did not bother measuring the transfer speed because I mostly use this for streaming music via USB. I have never experienced a freeze or lag in playing, so, again, I am very pleased with it. The final reason why I am happy is the small form factor, which is about the size of a bluetooth dongle.

Bottom line is you can save a few bucks by purchasing a competing brand, but you will get what you pay for in my opinion. I've been using this brand for literally decades and have never had to worry about failure or other issues.

I received the universal model as a review sample and tested on a few devices. Those were a Samsung Galaxy Note 3 phone, a Samsung Tab 3 10.1 and iPad 2 tablets. It paired and connected to each effortlessly and without going through a bunch of technical steps like the earlier generation of bluetooth keyboards. I pressed the connect button on the keyboard, scanned for it in my devices and - viola! - they paired and connected at a touch of my finger. I love it when stuff is that simple.

The key feel has the tactile feedback that sets this apart from cheaper keyboards, In fact, I would say that the feel is equal to the one on my ThinkPad T61 laptop. It's about 9 3/8 inches wide, which gives a lot of typing space. A point of comparison is my laptop's keyboard is about two inches wider.

Because this has an aluminum casing it is not going to creep away while you are typing, and it also keeps the keyboard from flexing when you are handling it. Again, some other keyboards that I have used were flimsy and did not last very long. One final thing I love is the micro USB connector for the power cable is sturdy. I actually had a keyboard from another brand that failed because when I pulled out the charging cable the internals of the port came out with it.

I have been using my keyboard for over eight straight hours, untethered from a charging cable, and it's still going strong. In fact I am writing this review with it to test it. This is a five star product in my opinion because of construction, feel, and the fact that it does everything the specs claim for less than twenty bucks (at the time of this review.)

There are some incredibly detailed and helpful reviews of this keyboard, so I will stick to how I am using the review sample that I received, and a few of my impressions.

First, this is not a bluetooth device (it was described as such to me when I was asked to review it.) The only weak point is the documentation, which is terse, but well illustrated. Had it contained specs and compatibility data it would have been significantly more useful. However, this is not a major flaw.

I first tested it with an ancient ThinkPad T61 running Windows XP. It was immediately recognized and functional. My next test was to see if it would work with my Samsung Galaxy Note 3 phone running Android 4.4.2. I connected with wireless dongle via a [[ASIN:B00C7SK2J2 Micro USB OTG Host Cable to USB 2.0 Adapter]] and it worked. To be honest, that arrangement is a bit on the clumsy side for me.

My final test and where this keyboard shines is when I connected it to my [[ASIN:B00JA5DCNS Keedox® Quad Core RK3188 Android 4.2 Smart TV BOX]] running Android 4.2. This keyboard made a lot of sense connected to that box because I rarely used it prior. I was using a corded keyboard and it was a trip hazard. Plus most of in interaction with it included few keystrokes, so this mini keyboard is perfect. In fact I find myself using the TV box a lot more frequently now that I have this keyboard. I think of it as a smart remote control - which it is - and have quickly grown to love it.

As for prolonged typing, this would not be my favorite solution. However, that is subjective. I hated my Blackerry when I was required to carry one back in my consulting days too. But for occasional use this is wonderful.

Bottom line: I would have never guessed that this would be the missing link between me and my TV box. Had I only tested this with phones and tablets I would have probably written a single word review: meh. Now, though, I see the wow factor.

First, I will disclose why I gave this speaker only four stars: when the review sample I received arrived it was not very intuitive and the instructions were little help. In fact, it took me ten minutes of fiddling to realize that this is not a bluetooth device and it would have probably taken longer had I not read Comdet's May 27, 2014 review. Mind you I am not subtracting a star because it's direct connect only, but because they instructions were obtuse at best. That is a minor fix on the manufacturer's part and one I hope they rectify.

The sound is absolutely incredible. Not for it's size, but incredible period. The full spectrum of sound frequencies blew me away. The bass is what impressed me the most. Since this is a direct connect only type of speaker you will be listening to it fairly close, so the volume is more than sufficient.

One of the interesting features is you can daisy chain up to three of these together. To be honest I do not see the point since it's designed as a personal speaker, but the technology is embedded in the device and it can be done. This would have been more impressive had this speaker been bluetooth-enabled.

Controls are simple to use and cleverly designed to take up as little space on the unit as possible while still providing an array of functions. I love the SD card slot, but do not much care for the hardwired 3.5MM connector that plugs into a phone port on your tablet, PC or phone. A port and separate cable would have been a better solution since it's one less failure point. As it is, if you break the 3.5MM pigtail you are out of luck unless you can repair cables.

Quibbles aside, this has the makings of a five star product and especially the speaker technology that this is based on. The sound quality is incredible.

I have tested a number of in ear monitors (IEMs) from Brainwavz and other brands and the review sample that I received is the best in its price range that I have come across. In fact, it's best in sub one hundred dollar IEMs.

The best feature to me is comfort because I normally do not care for in ear style phones. I can wear these for hours without even noticing them, and they ship with an array of tips that fit just about any ear size.

However, sound ranks right up there with comfort because I listen to a lot of music from a critical perspective as well as enjoyment. Nothing interferes with the sound quality, including ambient noise from the cables or other physical factors, and they do a great job of isolation. Every album to which I listen comes across with no gaps in any of the frequency bands. You can hear any note (and sometimes flaws) that musicians and recording engineers made, which is extremely important to me.

What truly sets these IEMs apart from other phones in its class are is the attention to detail. The cord is tangle free and practically indestructible. I have yet to worry about breaking or wearing out the inner conductor like I do with some other brands I own (including some pretty expensive phones). The plug is gold plated for and at a ninety degree angle - nice touches - and the phones ship with a protective hard case ([[ASIN:B00HPPL1M4 Brainwavz Hard Earphone Case]]) that is not only convenient, but functional.

If I had to recommend a sub one hundred dollar set of IEMs to a friend or fellow musician these would be it. The performance, comfort and price make them a bargain in my opinion.

This speaker has some convenient features like hands-free calling and receiving calls, but it's the sound quality that makes it stand out.

Before I list the many things I love (and why I awarded this five stars) I want to toss out the one thing that is keeping this speaker from being totally perfect: the older generation bluetooth pairing and connecting process. The newer generation of bluetooth speakers automatically beacon their presence when you turn them on. This one requires you to hold down a multifunction button for six seconds before you initiate a scan on your phone or tablet. It's not a big issue or deal breaker, but this would be the perfect speaker otherwise.

It is all about the sound and the review sample I received from the manufacturer passed my usual tests with flying colors. Among the tests are playing a handful of favorite jazz albums. The main one I always use us Miles Davis' [[ASIN:B003GIK2LU Kind Of Blue]] because it exercises a speaker's ability to reproduce the full spectrum of frequencies in the low, mid and high ranges. A truly great speaker will also reproduce the nuances from the natural reverb effect of the 30th Street Studio in NYC where it was recorded. This speaker did!

As I listened through this speaker I wondered how it would sound with something a little more in your face than circa 1950s acoustic jazz. I grabbed some old rock albums, dusted them off and gave them a spin.

Since I am sixty-five my idea of rock is probably ancient music to many folks. However, back in the day the following albums did stretch the woofers in stereo systems: [[ASIN:B001NCT8X4 Fresh Cream]] (Jack Bruce's bass and Ginger Baker's double bass drum kit came through as though I were in a small club), and [[ASIN:B0011Z5IUK Led Zeppelin II]] (same for John Paul Jones' bass and John Bonham's drums, especially on The Lemon Song).

Part of the reason the sound is so full and rich is the 360 degree speaker coverage. Another factor is the design raises the main speaker cabinet about a quarter of an inch off the base of the unit. This allows the low end frequencies to reflect a bit and sound deeper. Do be aware, though, that this is not an exceptionally loud speaker. It's perfect for most listening up to five meters away. That's about fifteen feet, so you can crank it pretty loud relative to its size, but as you increase the volume beyond three quarters the fidelity drops if you are too close. At the three quarter mark and a distance of five meters you can hear every note and nuance in the older jazz recordings with which I tested this speaker, and pretty good fidelity with the older rock albums.

If you listen to music with a critical ear this speaker is one that you should consider if you are shipping for a bluetooth model. Obviously there are wired speakers that are better, but in the bluetooth domain this is one of the best that I have tried from a sound perspective.

When I first received a review sample I was dismayed because the specs claimed that it would only fit batteries that are between 42 and 71 millimeters in length. In inches that works out to be 1.65 to 2.79 inches.

In actual fact, that dimension should have read width instead of length because my long Samsung Galaxy Note 3 battery (which is in excess of three inches long) not only fit, but charged perfectly. I also tested this on an HTC Driod Incredible and it worked perfectly on that phone's battery as well. There is a spring-loaded arm that opens to accept batteries with widths within the range I cited above, and they hold the battery firmly in place during the charging cycle.

What I love is the ability to charge a spare battery while simultaneously charging a phone with a battery installed. That feature makes this perfect as a travel charger (the folding prongs add to the function for that use. It is also ideal as an office charger for folks who frequently spend most of their work day in the field.

Do heed the two prominent notices in the specs (1) it is ONLY for phone batteries, and (2) it will only work with batteries that have contact points on the end (not the front of back). Indeed, the contacts on your battery (the metal strips that mate with your phone) cannot be closer than 3/8 inch from the edge of the battery, nor more than 5/8 inch away. If they fall outside of that range then this charger will not work for you.

For batteries that do fit this charger will automatically detect the type and capacity and charge it properly. So there is some intelligence built into the circuitry.

These are great for those of us who have spare batteries for our phones and want to keep them charged and ready to go. It worked perfectly on the phones with which I tested it. Measure and examine your battery before ordering to save disappointment.

For bicycle enthusiasts this is an excellent speaker/radio combination that has decent sound and a lot of convenient touches. I received mine as a review sample from the manufacturer.

I'll cover the sound quality first. In a word, it's adequate. Not overly spectacular, but sufficiently loud to be heard over road noise while trekking through streets and paths. I do not view the quality as a problem because in most biking environments the sound level is more important than fidelity. Plus, the safety factor of having a hands-free solution is the major reason for getting one of these.

What impressed me is when I turned this on all I had to do is scan for bluetooth devices from my phone and it popped right up. I did not have to press a multifunction button and chant, hoping the device would show up like other bluetooth speakers - it was immediately there.

Another thing I love is the buttons are on the top of the case and when the speaker is turned on they light up blue. I have stationary speakers which have buttons that blend into the case so well I cannot readily find them, so this feature removes one major distraction when you are on the road. In the dark the lights are soft enough to not affect your night vision. The only improvement that I can think of is to use red lights instead of blue because those would actually promote night vision. Perhaps the designers will do that in the next generation.

Some of the other nice touches are the ample inside space for a phone and other incidentals, plus a ring clip on the outside for your keys. I also love the three point attachment to your handle bar and steering post. It is easy to attach and remove. In fact, that takes mere seconds.

Having a removable battery is yet another design factor that makes this a value. Most bluetooth speakers on the market have a fixed, internal battery that will eventually wear out. When the battery in this one inevitably dies you can quickly replace it with a new [[ASIN:B0006HP7NC BL-5C Extended Li-Ion Battery]] and you are good to go another 500 or so charging cycles.

Finally, the semi-hard case, heavy duty zipper and construction are all first rate and clearly designed by someone who understands the rigors of biking when it comes to gear. This entire unit is built to withstand the outdoors in most weather conditions.

This is a great way to use HDMI devices on TVs that have no spare HDMI ports or are not equipped with one. I tested the review sample that I received on a 2008 Sanyo TV that came equipped with two HDMI ports that I quickly occupied with a Roku and a Chromecast, and with a 2011 model Samsung. Both displayed the transformed signal from this box beautifully.

It has come excellent features like the array of color encoding schemes and outputting either the most common PAL and NTSC ones with the flip of a switch. I also love that this is powered via USB, which one of my TVs as, so it's one less wall wart.

Do be aware that this only converts in one direction: HDMI in (from Blu-Ray players, etc) to composite out via RCA jacks on a TV or monitor. I tested this going the other direction - RCA to HDMI - and it did not work. Of course it was not advertised as such, but I felt compelled to try anyway. I would love it if I could flip a switch and change directions of the signal transformation because I could then connect my old VHS player to an HDMI port on my TV.

Regardless of my personal wishes, this does exactly what it claims with no problems or issues, and that merits five stars according to how I rate.

The review sample that I received proved to be a nice, low-to-mid range In Ear Monitor (IEM). It can compete with much more expensive IEMs from both Brainwavz and competing brands. To keep my evaluation in this brand I am going to compare the review sample of this model to two other Brainwavz IEMs: [[ASIN:B009UNZ5WQ Brainwavz R1 In Ear Noise Isolating Earphones]] and the [[ASIN:B00G4UQ6U8 Brainwavz S1 In Ear Headphones]]. To provide some context please bear in mind that I listen primarily to acoustic jazz, so my listening needs may be vastly different from yours.

The first thing I do with I test phones or speakers is to play Miles Davis' [[ASIN:B00136JQMI Kind Of Blue]] to get a feel for how well the various frequencies are reproduced. That album has instruments in the low, mid and high bands, and these phones seemed to have more bass than the R1 or the S1. The mids and highs on those models, though, had more clarity. I tried a few other albums that had heavier bass and these definitely did a better job of reproducing those frequencies. When I switched to some tracks with female vocalists the R1 and S1 were better phones, and both of the other phones were clearer with higher register instruments.

From a comfort perspective these phones were a little lighter than the other two IEMs against which I compared them, although I would consider it a tie among them for overall comfort. These phones and the R1 had a value-added bonus in that a [[ASIN:B00HPPL1M4 Brainwavz Hard Earphone Case]] is included.

These are obviously designed for lower end audio gear like MP3 players, phones and tablets. For higher end audio in the audiophile range I would probably use the S1 model because to my ears that one sounds better. However, you cannot go wrong with this one for everyday use when you want to listen to your music without disturbing others.

Prior to receiving this review sample I was happy with in-ear type phones, but always grabbed headphones when I wanted to listen to music without disturbing others, These phones changed that. For one thing they are super comfortable. For another the sound is incredible. In fact I have been testing various phones - mainly from this brand, but also some Sennheiser models - and this is head and shoulders above the pack.

I'll be honest and disclose that comfort edges out sound when phones sound good enough. I will normally not quibble over a few hundred Hz one way or the other as long as I can wear the phones without noticing them. These are not only unobtrusive, but downright comfortable, which is a major reason why these have now replaced my trusty [[ASIN:B00ENZRS76 Brainwavz HM9 Hi-Fi Noise Isolating Headphones]].

Soundwise the specs do not begin to describe the richness, especially bass. In fact, when I read the 20 Hz to 20 MHz range I thought that the sound would be somewhat generic for phones in this range. I own a pair of IEMs (in-ear monitors) that go as low as 18 Hz at the same 95dB at 1mW sensitivity, yet these sound much deeper than those. I love the balance of sound across the frequency spectrum as though it's on a smooth continuum. Every one of my test albums I played through these phones sounded so good that I decided that it's time to hang up the headphones and go with these.

Part of the reason why I love these from a comfort perspective is the over the ear memory wire. I prefer that style, but not everyone does. They are definitely stiff and take on a shape that will be uniquely yours over time (and a very short time at that!) Also, while this ships with a [[ASIN:B00HPPL1M4 Brainwavz Hard Earphone Case]] the phones will not fit after you have contoured them to your ear. The case is useful for carrying around the array of adapters and tips that are included. In fact, the final reason I love these phones is the included triple-flange style silicon tips, which block out the rest of the world and allow me to focus solely on music.

If you love music and want to hear every note faithfully reproduced in their natural frequencies these phones are it. I can honestly say that I have not used a better set of phones from any brand in this price range, including some Sennheiser models that have a street price of fifty to seventy-five dollars more than these, so the value is definitely there.

I own a number of Brainwavz models, all of which compare favorably to more expensive in ear monitors (IEMs). I am going to compare the review sample of this model to two other Brainwavz IEMs: [[ASIN:B00G4UQ6U8 Brainwavz S1 In Ear Headphones]] and the [[ASIN:B009UNZ5WQ Brainwavz R1 In Ear Noise Isolating Earphones]]. What I will try to avoid is repeating the other reviews - many of which are excellent - and the product specs on this page. Here are my impressions of these phones. Bear in mind that I listen primarily to acoustic jazz, so my listening needs may be vastly different from yours.

The first thing I do with I test phones or speakers is to play Miles Davis' [[ASIN:B00136JQMI Kind Of Blue]] to get a feel for how well the various frequencies are reproduced. That album has instruments in the low, mid and high bands, and these phones seemed to have more bass than the R1 or the S1. The mids and highs on those models, though, had more clarity. I tried a few other albums that had heavier bass and these definitely did a better job of reproducing those frequencies. When I switched to some tracks with female vocalists the R1 and S1 were better phones, and both of the other phones were clearer with higher register instruments.

From a comfort perspective these phones were a little lighter than the other two IEMs against which I compared them, although I would consider it a tie among them for overall comfort. These phones and the R1 had a value-added bonus in that a [[ASIN:B00HPPL1M4 Brainwavz Hard Earphone Case]] is included.

My conclusion is these are nice low-to-mid range IEMs that can compete with much more expensive IEMs from both Brainwavz and competing brands. I am impressed with the quality, completeness of the solution and the way these sound on lower end audio gear like MP3 players, phones and tablets. For higher end audio I would probaby use the S1 model because to my ears that one sounds better. However, you cannot go wrong with this one for everyday use when you want to listen to your music without disturbing others.

Shortly after I received this as a review sample it quickly became a permanent part of my home studio. Right now my [[ASIN:B00ENZRS76 Brainwavz HM9 Hi-Fi Noise Isolating Headphones]] are mounted for immediate use, and I tested this with some smaller phones I also use like the [[ASIN:B0002F74E8 Sony MDR7502 Professional Stereo Headphone]] and they fit perfectly as well.

This is a tall, thin stand that measures ten inches tall with a relatively short five inch base. Despite the proportions this sits stably and is not apt to tip if you accidentally bump into it. I love the contoured top over which the phones rest. That holds the phones in a natural shape. For expensive phones that is not especially a problem because the over the head mechanisms on those devices are usually very well made.

The material (I am guessing plexi-glass) is 8mm thick (about a third of an inch), and is flexible. Complaints about the large logo are valid if you want a cleaner look, but since I am currently using Brainwavz headphones - and this is in my music studio - the aesthetics are a non-issue for me. I care more about function and convenient storage and this stand provides both of those.

For me the convenience of having my phones readily available is important because I use them often. This stand is an inexpensive way of accomplishing that.

This case came bundled with my [[ASIN:B009UNZ5WQ Brainwavz R1 In Ear Noise Isolating Earphones]] and I was struck by how nicely made and perfect it is. I will not parrot the other excellent reviews on this page with regard to physical characteristics, but will confirm that they are spot on.

Although these are bundled with a Brainwavz product do not let that deter you if you have invested in another brand because these will work with most of them. I tested the fit with the following phones and they are a perfect match:

[[ASIN:B001EZYMF4 Sennheiser CX 300 II Precision Enhanced Bass Earbuds]]
[[ASIN:B004PO10E2 Shure SE215-CL Sound Isolating Earphones]]
[[ASIN:B000XPG2QI Etymotic Research HF5 Portable In-Ear Earphones]]

Of course I also tested them with the [[ASIN:B00G4UQ6U8 Brainwavz S1 In Ear Headphones]] which I expected to fit and they did. Although many of the phones with which I tested these come with their own case, none of them are are as sturdy or as protective as this one. For low-end phones this will probably outlast the phones themselves, and will be ready their their replacement. For the higher end phones this is an investment - and an inexpensive one at they - for protecting the instrument from damage.

I had the opportunity to directly compare my review sample to the [[ASIN:B001EZYMF4 Sennheiser CX 300 II Precision Enhanced Bass Earbuds]], which is a highly regarded IEM (in ear monitor) in the same price range. This one actually sounded better to my ears although both were nearly identical in specifications.

This is my third Brainwavz phone model, and I have quickly come to regard this brand as a real contender in the market. I will not lie - I much prefer the [[ASIN:B00ENZRS76 Brainwavz HM9 Hi-Fi Noise Isolating Headphones]] model because I love over-the-hear style phones. However, this set of phones, at about a third of the cost, is also close in sound quality as the HM9. In fact, the bass in this one is much better than the HM9 (or the Sennheiser CX 300 II to which I am directly comparing these.)

For me comfort is everything because I listen to music much of my time. These are perfect for both pleasure listening where I sit back and enjoy the music for its own sake. These are also good enough for me to hear every nuance when I am transcribing or studying a track to learn. In that respect these phones are good enough for professional musicians, but I will admit that they would not be my first choice for plugging into a high-end sound system.

Since I spend more time listening to MP3 tracks than off vinyl these do the job since MP3 files lose some fidelity by their very nature. I will say, though, that these phones passed my basic test suite, which includes Miles Davis' [[ASIN:B00136JQMI Kind Of Blue]]. That is my reference model for sound because it contains high, mid and low frequency instruments that exercise any sound system. I listened to that album both from CD and from an MP3 file. Reproduction was superb.

Not only do these phones have respectable sound and comfort, the package is complete. They come with a zippered hard shell case, which protects the phones. However, they come with more extras that add to the value and provide versatility: a 1/4 adapter for plugging directly into standard headphone jacks, and an airplane adapter.

If you are in the market for mid-range IEMs give these serious consideration. In my opinion they are easily the equal of better known brands like the Sennheiser I mentioned and can be a better value if you need the extras that this set includes.

I wanted a spare charging cable for my Samsung Galaxy Note 3 phone and took a chance on this one. By that I mean that that other USB 3.0 cables that I have tried with the phone would charge it, but would not support full speed data transfers and synching. This one performed without issues and identically to my OEM Samsung cable that came with my phone.

The blue outer jacket is much thicker than the Samsung cable. Although it is slightly stiffer it's also pliable and easy to bend and coil. Part of the reason for the extra thickness is probably from the the foil and braid shielding. In fact, the shielding is one factor in this cable's ability to transmit data at such high speeds without error. Another factor is the gold plated connectors.

The bottom line is this cable seems to be the equal of the more expensive Samsung OEM cable. In my experience anyway. I have owned it for three months and it has been problem free in every respect.

I tested these on my Samsung Galaxy Note 3 phone and my Tab 3 tablet and was impressed with the sound. Note: I always test using a Miles Davis album titled Kind of Blue because the instrumentation covers the high, mid and low frequency bands. However, the acoustic bass in jazz is different than electric bass in modern music so factor that into my comments when making a purchase decision. I did try a few tracks on an album with with electric bass that were not as deep sounding. Bottom line: for jazz these are superb, and especially for acoustic jazz that was recorded in the 1950s, but I am not sure about other genres of music.

What I love is the comfort of the ear buds. Normally I avoid them, but I received these as a review sample so decided to wear them and listen for a few hours straight. I found that the small ear tips that shipped with these fir me the best, although the medium ones were comfortable too. The large pair were definitely 'large', so there is a tip size for everyone. I did not care for the foam tips, preferring the silicon ones, but that is my personal preference and not an opinion of which is better. I was able to wear these for hours without the chaffing or discomfort that other bud-style phones cause me. One note: once in-ear the tips eliminated a lot of ambient noise, which allowed me to listen critically to the music itself. That is a big plus for in home (or in studio) use, but I would not recommend wearing these while driving because it cuts down on outside noise to the point that you may be unaware of traffic situations.

Another thing I love is the relatively long cable, which is slightly over four feet long. In my home studio it allows me to practice to backing tracks on my tablet what is usually on a nearby music stand. I also appreciate the fact that the connectors are gold plated, which ensures a good, clean signal to the phones.

Bottom line: these are relatively inexpensive phones with performance that can compete with phones costing two to three times as much. The sound is superior for the types of music I enjoy, but the bass may be too light for some modern, bass and drum heavy music.

UPDATE August 18, 2014. I just received a newer model without the USB ports (the [[ASIN:B00KBO619E Arctic Breeze USA]]. Aside from the patriotic USA motif, this model has some improvements. First, the fan blades have a more efficient pitch and size, so it throws a nice breeze. I have mine running next to the earlier model and the difference between the two are significant.

A second feature is this newer model is safer. I can put my finger into the spinning blade and it will stop without as much as a nick. The earlier model that I reviewed below was a safety hazard around small children. This one has corrected that issue. In all other respects the two models are very close in specs. [END OF UPDATE]

About six months ago I tested and reviewed the smaller version of this fan: [[ASIN:B003XN24GY ARCTIC Breeze Mobile]]. When I was provided with this one as a review sample I was able to compare the two side-by-side. This one is hands down a more sophisticated and functional cooling solution.

I love this one because it is serious competition to my [[ASIN:B0000DJ27I Lasko #2500 12" Oscillating Table Fan]], and this one takes far less power to operate and the breeze can be focused. On warm days this is a godsend, but it also works to keep my hot running laptop cool. It's also so quiet that I cannot hear it three feet away.

A key difference between this model and the earlier one is this has a variable speed knob that allows me to go from a light 800 RPM to a very brisk 1800 RPM. One caveat is at the higher speeds this fan cannot be stopped with your fingers like the earlier model and there is no fan guard. This is a safety hazard if small children are around and is not a solution I recommend if that's the case where this will be used.

Another thing I love is the earlier model was a gooseneck that plugged directly into a USB port. This one has a cable that is just a little short of six feet and can be placed a lot more conveniently. The base is very heavy, so there is little chance of knocking it over, and the base also contains four USB ports. Note that these are 2.0 only.

You can plug this directly into your PC or laptop, but I also found that the Samsung wall charger that came with my Galaxy Note 3 will power this fan as well.

Bottom line is this is a great cooling solution for child-free work areas, and it will definitely cause rapid cooling at the full 1800 RPM setting.

I received a review sample and tested this on an ancient Acer One netbook running Windows XP. The netbook immediately recognized the wireless dongle that is included with this keyboard and I had the keyboard operational in minutes after inserting the included rechargeable batteries and charging them up.

Frankly, I thought I would hate the keys because they resembled the 'chicklet' style of a circa 1977 Commodore Pet's keys. These, though, have beautiful tactile feedback and are exceptionally responsive. You can touch type at at least 120 words per minute (my max) with no problems.

Although this key board comes with a retractable USB cable, that is for charging the two batteries that power the unit. This is strictly a wireless device, so you will need a spare USB port for the required dongle, and access to one or a wall charger that accepts USB cables to recharge the batteries when they run down. You can go two months between charges as long as you remember to switch the keyboard off between uses. There is an on/off switch on the underside of the board.

One final feature I love is this keyboard has some heft to it. It is not going to slide across your desk like some cheap, flimsy ones that I have tried in the past. The bottom line is of all of the portable keyboards that I have tested (well over two dozen), this one is the best of the bunch for me. The size and feel earn it five solid stars.

When I accepted a review sample of this holder I had visions of using it to entice my constant companion to sit in the back and play with her iPad. Indeed, this hooked right onto the two posts of the front seat headrest that would allow a backseat passenger to watch movies and do whatever else they use the iPad for. My companion did not take the bait, so I was left with a review sample that, frankly, I could not give away.

Necessity is the mother of invention and the best use for this mount was in my music room. This hooks into my [[ASIN:B000CDUDQG Belmonte Orchestra Stand Deluxe Black]] to mount an iPad and still have room left for sheet music and a [[ASIN:0961470143 The New Real Book - Volume 1]]. I have uploaded customer-supplied photos to show how this securely attaches to the stand and holds an iPad in place (it will work with any tablet up to 10 inches.)

I love how this holder allows you to place your tablet at practically any viewing angle, and also how it positively and absolutely holds the tablet in place. For the record, these claims apply equally to the dual headrest posts in my 2014 Outlander and to the music stand cited above.

Personally, the manufacturer is missing a major market because tablets are now common on stages and in studios and I suspect that there is a much larger market for this holder than significant others who refuse to be relegated to the back seat. I am so pleased with this holder that I have already recommended it to fellow musicians.

First, this is not a flimsy cable - the construction clearly indicates that this is built to last. I received a review sample and initially put off testing this splitter out. When I finally got around to it I was actually impressed with the quality of construction.

Most cables and splitters fail quickly because they are subjected to bending and handling, which eventually fatigues and/or cracks the inside conductor. This one has a heavy-duty strain relief on the male end and a thick housing for the female jacks that is practically unbreakable.

One additional advantage to the female end is the housing will also provide a modicum of radio frequency shielding. Another factor is the housing is .75 inches across with 3/8ths of an inch separation (center to center) of the female jacks. I thought this was a clever piece of engineering and is indicative of the overall attention to quality.

The cable itself is 2 9/16 inches with an overall length of 4.5 inches. All jacks perfectly mate. I tried a few 3.5mm cables with the female ends and all fit snugly, and the male end was a perfect fit not only into my phone, but a PA system that I own that has a 3.5mm input for playing backing tracks. The signals in a and out (I tested this splitter both ways) was crystal clear.

I love purchasing items that are made to last and this splitter easily qualifies as one of those. If you need one this is the one to get.

I received a review sample and put this through its paces right after I charged it. The first thing I noticed is the sound quality and the volume. My test music is [[ASIN:B00136JQMI Kind Of Blue]] because it has multiple instruments in the low, mid and high ranges. This speaker passed that test by allowing me to hear each instrument. I will say that the low end of the frequency range is a little thin. Not terrible, but I want to point that out.

For overall volume, this beats two other shower-type speakers I have tested in the past. The previous ones could not be heard clearly with water spraying and cascading in the background. This one can. It easily cut through the ambient shower noise and I was able to enjoy music in the shower.

The instructions consist of a single-sided sheet of paper that is clear and concise. Pairing this with my Samsung Galaxy Note 3 took seconds. Switching to FM radio is as simple as depressing and holding the On/Off button after you have turned the device on. I get poor reception no matter which radio I use in my area, but I did manage to find a clear station, so if you listen to FM radio that feature is as rock solid as the bluetooth speaker feature.

This is definitely waterproof. The power cable is a hybrid with a standard USB connector on one end and a tip type DC connector on the other. I tested it with a few wall chargers in the house and all work. The included cable is relatively sturdy, which is a plus given its non-standard configuration. Of course that configuration is one of the keys to ensuring that this speaker is waterproof.

Overall this is the best shower-style speaker that I have tested to date. The sound quality is a cut above most on the market, and the unit itself is perfect for listening anywhere. For example, the hanger hook would make this ideal for hanging off a rear view mirror in a car for hand's free calling, which this speaker also supports.

I received a review sample from the manufacturer and was pleasantly surprised when I opened the box. I was expecting an 'erector set' of many pieces that I would need to put together. Instead I received a complete solution that literally unfolded and snapped into place in minutes.

Set up entails the unfolding and snapping step, plus connecting the antenna to a powered booster box with coaxial cable in from the antenna and out to your TV. Once connected you need to go into your TV's settings, select antenna as the input, then do a scan for available channels.

Since I live close to a major metropolitan area - Orlando, Florida - I decided to test this at a friend's home in Ormond Beach, which is about sixty miles from Orlando and roughly the same distance from Jacksonville. This location tested the claimed forty mile radius for the device.

The true power was when I did a quick test by temporarily setting it up, plugging it in and seeing what channels were available. With the device sitting on the floor the first scan found seven digital channels. Bear in mind that this was laying on the floor for the initial test, which is hardly optimum.

Test number two entailed raising the antenna towards the ceiling (but not permanently mounting it) and moving it around to various spots in a 15x10 foot room. That increased the total channels received to twenty-two, including Orlando and Jacksonville channels that were twenty miles beyond the claimed range, as well as a few channels in Cocoa Beach (right at the edge of the range).

Note that in both tests the Central Florida terrain is relatively flat. In other geographic locations the results may have been vastly different.

Installation does require access to 110/120 AC power for the signal booster module. The mounting hardware that ships with this antenna is heavy-duty and complete. You can use one of the clamps to mount it to practically any pole of beam, but there is a pipe assembly that provides you with even more mounting options. The kit also includes fifty feel of high quality coaxial cable, with a removable double male connector in one end in case you need to run it even farther. You will need to purchase a second coaxial cable to connect the booster box's out port to your TV.

For outdoor mounting (or in a ceiling that is not close to a 110/120 AC outlet) I recommend running the longer cable from the antenna to the powered booster, which can be placed close to the TV. If you decide to place the booster closer to the antenna's coaxial connection make sure you can do with without using an extension cord, which could be a safety issue.

The bottom line is this antenna works beautifully. Since it picked up signals fifty percent farther than the claimed range it greatly exceeded my expectations. For the record, although I received the antenna as a review sample I donated it to a worthy cause after I completed my testing and had enough information to write this review. I do recommend it as a wonderful solution and an alternative to cable if local programming meets your news and entertainment needs.

I received a review sample and put these through their paces. I want to disclose that I enlisted the aid of a friend to test these because she loves ear bud style headphones and is a demanding consumer.

Both of us tested the sound quality and we were both impressed. For me the album [[ASIN:B00136JQMI Kind Of Blue]] is the acid test because of the number of instruments and the dynamics and subtleties of the music. After I connected these to the 3.5mm jack on my Galaxy Note II I was treated to spectacular sound quality. While these are not noise-canceling phones the ambient noises in my car were completely attenuated. My friend tried these out with her iPhone 4S and could not only clearly hear folks to whom she was calling, but they confirmed that she was coming in crystal clear on their end. That confirms that the microphone is of the same excellent quality as the phones.

I found these to be extremely comfortable, which is saying a lot because I am not an ear-bud person. In fact I fell in love with them, but gave them to my friend as a token of my appreciation for her help in evaluating them.

Construction is impressive. The 3.5mm is gold plated and the cable is heavy-duty with strain reliefs. Even the in-line mic switch is sturdy.

There are some wonderful touches in the packaging and included components starting with one of each size of ear gels (small, medium and large). The phones also come with a nice carrying pouch that is not only attractive, but also functional.

Overall these are premium quality earphones that will please even the most finicky audiophiles. They are a perfect solution for folks who use their phones as an MP3 player because you can immediately switch into answer or call more with a flick of a switch.

Two things up front: (1) I received this from the seller as a review sample, and (2) I have never used an over-the-ear headset before.

This was tested with a Samsung Galaxy Note II and an Apple iPhone 4s.

Since the product description contains specifications I will not recite them here. I will say that the installation instructions are slightly different from that the device displays. Where it claims that a blue light and green light will flash in an alternating sequence mine flashed orange and green. That set me back about ten minutes when doing my initial pairing, but when I figured out it paired and worked flawlessly. One other part of the install and pairing instructions that did not apply to my device was the need to enter a 0000 code to connect. Mine paired and connected without that step, but it may be how my phone is set up.

Once paired and connected the sound quality is crystal clear. Surprisingly so for me - but remember that I have never used this type of device before so have nothing against which to compare. It is extremely comfortable and after about five minutes I did not notice that I was wearing it. The big test came when I made a few calls. The folks on the receiving ends claimed that I was coming through loud and crystal clear.

While this is designed to be a headset for hand's free calling I tried listening to music through it. I did not care for that, but bear in mind that it was all going into one ear when I am accustomed to left and right phones or ear buds. The sound quality was excellent, but just not in stereo.

In addition to a volume control rocker button there is a multi-function button that is located inconspicuously on the mic part of the headset. This button allows you to answer, end or reject a call, and to redial the last called number. For answering a call you can do it using your phone or the multi-function button.

Out of the box this is designed to work with your right ear. I prefer my left, and at first could not figure out how to adjust it to work that way. I contacted the manufacturer and they showed me how - the mic can rotate on two planes and can, in fact, be adjusted for left ear use. I uploaded a a customer-supplied image that shows how to make the adjustment.

One final note: charge it for two hours (or until the indicator light on the device turns solid green) before trying to use it for the first time.

I have grown to love it despite my personal ear preference, and the packaging is so attractive that I am probably going to buy a few of these for stocking stuffers for the upcoming holidays. I have a feeling that some friends and family members will be pleased. I sure am.

I received a review copy of this receiver and put it through its paces. I am going to compare it to a receiver that I've owned since 2011 and have been thoroughly pleased with: [[ASIN:B0047T79VS Belkin F8Z492TTP Bluetooth Music Receiver]].

It's a complete solution: the box contained easy-to-follow instructions and two sets of cables: one 3.5mm male at each end and the other with a 3.5mm male splitting into two RCA males. Those are a nice touch because some speakers require one or the other. With my Belkin I had to purchase an adapter to use it with one of my powered speakers. So having a complete solution right out of the box is a plus.

The receiver looks like a wall wart that plugs directly into a wall socket. It's about two inches tall and 1.75 inches wide, so it does eat up come space. Since the speaker cable comes out the bottom of the device you are pretty much locked into plugging it into the bottom receptacle.

One feature I loved is this also has a port for USB charging that allows you to keep your phone or MP3 player fully charged while playing music.

This, of course, is based on later technology and it shows. I greatly exceeded the ten meter distance limit by taking my phone to the opposite end of my house, two rooms apart from the receiver, and still managed a clear signal. Believe me, on its best day the Belkin struggled to receive a line of sight signal within a ten meter limit. I even took my phone outside and could hear clear reception coming from my speakers inside my house.

While the instruction sheet will step you through connecting to and using this receiver I did not bother to read it. I opened the bluetooth settings on my [[ASIN:B00AB7FVCY Samsung Galaxy Note II]], scanned for new devices and when BrightPlay Home showed up in the list I tapped it to connect and started streaming music to my speaker. It took longer to unpackage the receiver than it did to start using it. It does not get any easier.

The sound quality is markedly better too. I switched back and forth between the Belkin receiver and this one - attached to the same powered speakers - and could tell the difference. Not by much, mind you, but it's discernible. I had a friend listen and she agreed.

Overall this is an excellent receiver that exceeded the recommended specs in the instruction sheet and it a breeze to use. If I had to replace this it would be with an identical receiver and that is the highest praise I can bestow.

I did not experience the problems cited in the October 20, 2012 review, although that reviewer came across as knowledgeable. Either I was lucky or that unit was a lemon.

Mine runs quiet with no signal distortion or bleed, and even the dual fans are whisper quiet. I have uploaded photos to show how I have mine configured.

Some of the things I love are the form factor, which is a tiny 1U, the flexible outputs (Speakon or binding post), and simplicity. Another thing that I love is you can start with a single amp, then add another if you need more amplification. For me 300 Watts is more than ample for any live venue with a 300-patron capacity - or more, since I play low volume jazz and blues.

Of course, the price is a major plus, especially considering that not only has my experience been positive, but a quick search will reveal that these enjoy a solid reputation for reliability and owner satisfaction.

I purchased a few of these as an impulse since I wanted to connect a pair of [[ASIN:B0047T79VS Belkin F8Z492TTP Bluetooth Music Receiver]] components to my stero and a pair of powered speakers. For the price I was expecting cheaply made and flimsy cables that would be great for mating the receivers to RCA jacks in the stereo and in the powered speakers. Suffice to say I got more than I expected - and especially for eighty-eight cents and free shipping.

For adapting 3.5mm to dual RCA the six inch length is more than adequate. What surprised me was the quality of the connectors, which are anything but cheap junk, and the gauge of the cable which is a step above what you would get at a dollar store. It makes one wonder how they can sell for such a low price and ship for free.

Even more impressive, they seem to be noise-free, which is something I cannot say about some of the adapters I've used.

I know that when something that's too good to be true should raise red flags, but in the case of these cables they are one of the rare instances when you get a lot more than you bargained for - and in a good way.

Up front I will say that these fill a niche for me that was made possible because of the two sets of RCA inputs in the back of the main speaker. I cannot speak to the value for general purpose use or compare it to similar or competing products.

I use my speakers to connect both a bluetooth receiver (a [[ASIN:B0047T79VS Belkin F8Z492TTP Bluetooth Music Receiver]]) for streaming music from my smart phone, and a netbook to my TV. Please see my customer-supplied images at the top of this page for photos that depict how.

The bluetooth receiver allows me to stream music from my Droid X smart phone to the speakers. This is an important feature for me because I have most of my music collection on that device.

Using the second set of RCA inputs, and a [[ASIN:B00004Z5CP Belkin Audio Y Cable Splitter 1-Mini Plug/2-RCA Plugs (6 Feet)]] I am able to transmit my netbook's audio to the speakers, while a [[ASIN:B0002AHT0M Standard 15-Pin VGA Male to VGA Male Cable]] connects the netbook to my TV.

Regarding the sound: these speakers pump out clear sound that allows me to easily enjoy the full richness of my music up to 25 feet away. It favorably compares to my larger, power hungry surround sound system in quality, clarity and volume.

A nice feature that I personally don't use is the headphone jack in the front of the master speaker. For folks who are connecting these speakers to a desktop or laptop system to extend their sound capabilities, this is a plus because at night or in an office it gives the privacy you may need.

My only complaint is the power supply, which is more like a brick. Because of its size it takes up three outlets on my surge protector - one for the power and the size blocking two more. Please see my third customer-supplied image at the top of this page to see in detail what I mean.

As you can see, my use is somewhat unique. If you are looking for a set of speakers for your laptop or desktop, plus a smart phone audio or MP3 player and do not need bluetooth streaming, then you can dispense with my configuration that uses the [[ASIN:B0047T79VS Belkin F8Z492TTP Bluetooth Music Receiver]] and replace that device with a simple [[ASIN:B00004Z5CP Belkin Audio Y Cable Splitter 1-Mini Plug/2-RCA Plugs (6 Feet)]] that will connect to the audio out jack on most smart phones.

If you have any additional questions leave a comment to this review and I will respond.

I purchased this model(Roku HD) for a friend's birthday and set it up a few hours ago. While I am not going to rush out (yet) and buy one for myself, I admired the design and functionality of this slick little device.

Here are my thoughts:

- Ease of set-up: easy for anyone who can operate a PC, Mac or smart phone. Once you plug it in, power it up and select the video mode to which it's connected the screen will walk you though the process.

I have an extensive technology background so I did not bother to read the manual beforehand and had no problems following what were simple on-screen instructions. And to Roku's credit, there were few of those. To be clear - you absolutely need a wireless internet router (WiFi) and a computing device to perform a few simple steps in order to install and activate the Roku HD. Including date entry and the time to explain some things to my friend for whom I was setting this up, the total time to get it running was less than 15 minutes.

- Establishing your account. You will need some form of computing platform to access the Roku site via the web and complete this step. It's relatively painless.

- Payment options: you can use a credit card or a Paypal account. I believe the latter is a relatively new option that shows that Roku is paying attention to complaints registered in these reviews. The Payment option is there to remove barriers to adding for pay services. Of course, it makes it so easy that you are almost lured into it. Smart move on their part. Just be careful because fees can add up.

- Remote Control - Information that needed to be entered with the remote is a bit awkward at first, but I quickly adapted to it. One note about the remote: it is what we engineering geeks call elegant. Simple, functional with only the essential buttons. I absolutely loved the Netflix, Pandora and Crackle bottoms to quickly get most users to popular services. I would have loved it if Hulu Plus had a button since that is the service my friend plans to use. But that would have detracted from the elegance factor.

- Manual: Although I did not need the manual to set ths device up, I did take the time to read through it afterwards to make sure my non-technical friend could depend on it if a problem arose. I was impressed with the clarity and how well the technical writing team made it simple, friendly and anticipated possible support problems by weaving in information that would preclude those.

The default channels were merely OK, but a good start. The free content, especially from Crackle It, did not excite me nor my friend who would be using it.

A word about economics: the friend for whom I purchased this and set it up wanted this so she could scale back on expenses. At one point she was paying approximately seventy dollars a month for cable service. She scaled that back to local channels that entailed a monthly recurring charge of three times the monthly fee of Hulu Plus. In fact, had she wanted, she could get Hulu Plus and Netflix's unlimited content for two thirds of what she is paying monthly for local cable channels, and nearly a fifth of the cost of her original subscription that did not provide near the content of Hulu Plue and Netflix combined.

It's easy to see that this device pays for itself in very short order if you deem that the content from the services that you can stream via the Roku is as good for your purposes as the content you are currently getting from cable or satellite services. Everyone will have a different breakeven point after which your return on the initial investment is substantial. If you are considering this device do a little analysis. Of course, make sure the services to which you will subscribe with the Roku meet your needs.

There are also services at various price levels that allow you to stream video, music and send photos directly from your PC or Mac to your TV via the service, which sends that content to your Roku. Four such services that you can easily find via a search of the web are: Roksbox, Play on, Chaneru and RoConnect.

This device is so cool that I was tempted to get one for myself. I have not subscribed to any cable or satellite services for nearly a decade, but I do purchase a lot of DVDs and spend far too much time on YouTube. I am still on the fence, but was disappointed in the lack of YouTube support, and was not impressed with the available workarounds and services. The most promising, RateRix, seemed to me to be kludgy and unreliable. I was also put off by Netflix, which wanted me to sign up before I could ascertain that they had the content I was looking for. One part of their FAQ mentioned that their mail service was still available and had vastly more videos than their streaming service. Since I watch a lot of foreign langiage films, as well as jazz performances and concerts I decided that the Roku would not meet my immediate needs. One other (and puzzling) deal breaker for me is the Roku will not stream my music stored on Amazon's cloud. That is odd considering that it will stream music from Pandora and video from Amazon, but not music from Amazon.

UPDATE (JULY 8, 2012): While my friend continues to love her Roku, I found an alternate streaming solution that gives me access to YouTube and even more content: [[ASIN:B00882OHL0 D-Link MovieNite Plus Streaming Media Player]]. See my July 8, 2012 review that compares and contrasts that device with the Roku,

I am an old curmudgeon who is set in my ways. This device certainly met the entertainment and economic needs of my friend, and I am sure that anyone who pays for TV services has the potential to greatly benefit from it. The device is beautifully designed, not only from an engineering perspective, but also from a human-factors perspective. The minute Roku works a deal with Google for a YouTube channel is the minute I purchase one. I have a feeling that will happen sooner than later. In the meantime, the smile on my friend's face when this was up and running is proof of its value.

I use this to adapt my [[ASIN:B0047T79VS Belkin F8Z492TTP Bluetooth Music Receiver]] to the input jack on my [[ASIN:B0036B8A20 Kustom The Defender 5H Class A Guitar Amp Head]]. This is a power-saving solution I discovered for listening to music through the amp in my music room versus firing up my power-hungry stereo system. I then play music via my bluetooth-enabled phone. It's a kludgy solution that keeps my power bill down. It also shows how this adapter can work in one of an almost limitless number of situations.

What I most like about this adapter is it is designed around a block with no dangling wires like, for example, a [[ASIN:B000068O4W Hosa YPR102 TRS Male To Dual RCA Female Y Cable]]. The key advantage is this adapter will not break at the weakest point - the wires. In the past I have had the wires on the Hosa-style adapters go bad or even break due to frequent handling. Every time you insert male RCA jacks into a Hosa-style adapter you are putting stress on the wires, which will eventually break down internally. In some cases the result is a noisy connection with intermittent static, but in others the signal is lost due to an internal break in the cable.

The design of this adapter has none of the above mentioned points of failure. However, it does have one disadvantage that the Hosa-style does not: it will not fit into cramped places. Since I am plugging mine directly into the front of an amplifier the design does not matter. If you were to use it as an adapter to an amp or mixer that connects at the rear, you may run into space problems. Also, my amp connection does not have space constraints to the left or right, so, again, the design is perfect for me. For connections that have knobs, or other components close to the 1/4" connection, you may find that only a Hosa-style adapter will meet your needs.

One final thing: while the design allows for stereo signal input at the RCA connection end, this adapter sums those signals into mono. That means that your stereo source will not be heard in stereo with this particular adapter. The Hosa model mentioned above will maintain stereo separation of the RCA signals, so if you want to maintain stereo, the Hosa is the way to go.

I mainly use [[ASIN:B002GOYU0O 12 pc Velcro Ties Reausable Electrical Wire Cable Strap]], which meet most of my needs. I also use these and like them a lot.

Where these come in handy, and even augment my preferred strap, is they are nearly immovable once you tie them to a brace of other anchoring point. For example, if you are setting up with a keyboard, the stand makes a good anchor point for cross-stage cable runs. This is especially true of Z-style stands like the [[ASIN:B0002F6JH6 On Stage 2 Tier Folding Z Keyboard Stand]] (although X-style stands work well). This does take some pre-planning because you do not want to interfere with other musicians or, worse, create trip hazards.

Because you loop the narrow end through the eyelet on the wider end and pull this strap has more holding strength than someone who is only running cables on stage and in a studio will ever need. Frankly, I augmented my preferred brand and model with these because of cost - and they are worth every penny. At 8" you can safely run more than a few instrument, speaker and microphone cables through one anchored to a frame like the Z-stand I mentioned above, and still keep the strap sufficiently loose to prevent stretching or breaking cables run through it.

Think of it as one more handy tool in your bag of tricks if running and managing cable is one of the things you do. I purchased a half dozen packs for my needs.

I use this both indoors and outdoors as a protected outlet for two keyboards (my other gear is protected by two rackmounted [[ASIN:B003TUO6U8 Merit Series Power Conditioner]]s.)

One rule of thumb I use is to not overload protected power strips. The two keyboards I plug into this does not come close to overtaxing this device or power outlets into which I plug it.

Some features I love include the 25 foot cord, which is heavy duty and os sufficiently long for any conceivable placement situation I will encounter. And because the cord is heavy gauge, and the housing is metal, this protected outlet is designed for rigorous use.

Tripp Lite's reputation for quality, reliability and safety is another reason I purchased this unit. I am a firm believer in safety and will not cut corners.

I live in Central Florida, which is notorious for power problems, so not using well designed protection is inviting disaster, which can be very costly considering my investment in the gear this is protecting. Thus far I have had zero problems, and judging from other reviewers I expect that to continue. This is a professional-grade piece of gear and it designed to protect your equipment and to last if properly cared for.

I purchased this for two specific reasons: (1) safety because too many accidents are caused by drivers with a phone to their ear, and (2) I love music and my Droid X has become my MP3 player (among other things as well as a phone.

Installation was a snap, although I did have to read the directions, which were clear and easy to follow. In less than 5 minutes after removing it from the packaging I was listening to music through my car radio!

This device comes with a fairly short USB charging cable that connects to a port on the head. The length made it inconvenient, and it was pretty flimsy too, failing after about three months. I added a [[ASIN:B0042X8XQO PowerLine 90310 Auto Socket Splitter with USB Power Port]] (which cleared my console in my 2008 Mazda 3 with the GOgroove and [[ASIN:B000S5Q9CA Motorola Vehicle Power Adapter micro-USB Rapid Rate Charger]] plugged in), and the combination, while unwieldy, has worked perfectly ever since.

Music and calls are reasonably clear. I do have to turn my radio volume up when a call comes in, but that may be an issue with my phone and not the GOgroove. And, like a hands-free system should work, when there is an incoming call or you wish to make an outgoing one, the MP3 player feature in my Droid X pauses the music until I am finished using the phone. After calls are terminated any paused music will automatically resume.

For long trips where you pass through areas with radio stations, your clear signal set in one location may start to degrade and you will notice static. That is caused by you coming into the range of a strong FM signal that is competing with the one you selected. You will need to seek and switch to a new frequency when that happens. For example, if I am traveling from, say, Ormond Beach, FL to Jacksonville, FL, I will need to change my frequency twice going up and twice again returning. It's the nature of any such device and there is nothing that can be designed into the GOgroove to fix it - at least not at the price point at which this device is selling.

I've had friends connect to it with their iPhones, and it works without a hitch. The icing on the cake is the GOgroove remains paired with my Droid X, and automatically connects to it as soon as I start my car if I am playing music. This is a convenient feature that I wish my [[ASIN:B0047T79VS Belkin F8Z492TTP Bluetooth Music Receiver]] that is connected to my home stereo had - I have to manually connect to that device anytime I want to use it.

Overall I am thrilled with my GOgroove and if it dies I would not hesitate to purchase another. In fact, I am considering purchasing a spare anyway because I spend a lot of time in my car and life without this wonderful gizmo would not be the same.

Range limitations notwithstanding, this receiver has dramatically expanded the usefulness of my Droid X by allowing me to play my music through my home stereo system, as well as through my friend's [[ASIN:B001DLTDQC Bose SoundDock Series II Digital Music System for iPod (Black)]] (using an [[ASIN:B000068O51 Hosa YRA154 1/8 Male To Dual RCA Female]] to adapt the Belkin to the Sounddock since my Droid will not fit the iPod cradle.)

One reason I do not have a problem with the range is I am usually in the room where the stereo is, and sit fairly close to where I have the Belkin receiver located. And, with the Bose rig, that is for taking out to the patio or in the kitchen, so I am in line of sight and pretty close as well.

The signal is consistently strong between my Droid X and the receiver, and the sound quality is more than adequate for my old ears. The only thing I would want is for the Belkin receiver to automatically connect with my Droid X in the same manner that the [[ASIN:B003PPGOC0 GOgroove FlexSMART X2 ADVANCED Wireless In-Car Bluetooth FM Transmitter with Charging, Music Control and Hands-Free Calling for ANDROID, iPhone, Blackberry and Windows Smartphones]] I have in my car does. As it stands, I always have to go into my Droid's settings and manually connect the paired Belkin before I can transmit my music stream to it.

Overall I am very pleased with this receiver and intend to purchase two more (one for a PA system I own, and a dedicated one for the Bose Sounddock.)

Prior to Alesis coming up with this and its larger sibling, the [[ASIN:B005NIVLX4 Alesis Mic Tube Duo Stereo Tube Microphone Preamplifier]], I was sold on the venerable [[ASIN:B0002D0KG4 PreSonus Tubepre Single-Channel Vacuum Tube Mic Pre]] as the "gold standard" in lower end tube microphone tube amps. I personally think this and the 2-channel model that Alesis offers are game changers, mainly because the features and reliability are on par with the PreSonus competing products, and the price point is significantly less. In other words, bang for your buck.

Before rushing out and getting one of these (or its larger sibling - or even the competing PreSonus), make sure you need it. I have found that on a reasonably decent PA system this product makes a dramatic difference with the older technology mics like [[ASIN:B000CZ0R3S Shure SM57 Microphone]] and the [[ASIN:B000CZ0R42 Shure SM58-LC Cardioid Vocal Microphone without Cable]], or the lower end SM58 clones that are bundled with PA systems and otherwise flood the market (the [[ASIN:B00009W40D NADY SP-4C Dynamic Microphone]] comes to mind). On the other hand, not only have I found that these tube pre-amps not very useful with more modern design microphones like the [[ASIN:B002SQJL9U Blue Microphones enCORE 100 Studio-Grade Dynamic Performance Microphone]], the [[ASIN:B00006I5R7 Sennheiser E835 Dynamic Cardioid Microphone]], etc. In fact, with the more modern designed microphones, which run much hotter in signal, a pre-amp in a live PA needs to have the gain turned to the lowest level in many cases or feedback becomes a problem.

If you do need one of these devices, I recommend - unless your budget is severely limited - that you consider the [[ASIN:B005NIVLX4 Alesis Mic Tube Duo Stereo Tube Microphone Preamplifier]] instead. The reason is for a slight increase in price you get an extra channel that you may not need now, but may find to be a requirement in the future.

I use this cable with my [[ASIN:B0036B8A20 Kustom The Defender 5H Class A Guitar Amp Head]] and my [[ASIN:B004XFHWKE Kustom Defender 15 Watt Class A Guitar Head]], both of which I connect using this cable to [[ASIN:B0036B8A2K Kustom The Defender 1 x 12 Guitar Extension Cabinet for 5H Head]].

The CBI cables are well constructed (built like a tank, actually), and the 1/4" fittings mate perfectly with the amps and cabs. I am sure that the clear, clean signals I get from my amps are because of the exceptional construction of these cables, which appear to be engineered to provide optimum signals over a wide range of conditions. They are sufficiently heavy duty to meet the rigors of constant use, and are components that can make or break your sound. I highly recommend this model, especially for connecting amps to cabs.

I was using an older 128 MB flash drive as the file system for e-mail on two older laptop computers. This allowed me to keep my mail synchronized on my primary home system and the one I take on travel. The problem was that I outgrew the 128 MB, and since both of my systems were older circa 2001 laptops that used USB 1.1 and ran under Windows 98 SE none of the gigabyte flash drives would work with it - all of the others required either USB 2.0 and/or Windows ME or 2000.
This drive, however, is backwards compatible with the older USB 1.1 interface, and a Windows 98 SE driver is available for download from the manufacturer's site.
Download and installation of the new driver went perfectly. It was literally done in a few mouse clicks. I plugged the drive into each machine and it was immediately recognized by both my Sony and IBM laptops. I also tried this on a Windows 2000 system and it was immediately recognized and assigned as a disk drive without drivers.
Not only does this device work as advertised with no problems, but it also leaves room for a second USB device on laptops that have adjacent ports (my Sony is configured like this). My old flash drive required me to use an USB extension cable in order to have room to plug in my mouse, so the form factor is yet another feature I like about this particular model.
One final feaure I very much like - you can encrypt files on this device, and since I am using it as an email file system the privacy and protection this affords me is important.
Highly recommended if you want a high-capacity flash drive that will work on older Windows 98 SE systems, or just a reliable and easy-to-install flash drive for any system. It will not work on Windows 95 and below systems (none of the flash drives of which I am aware will).

This device is a no frills, high-value peripheral that you can literally plug in and use to transport files or extend your file system.
Unlike some other USB flash memory devices that come with password protection and additional utilities, this one is simply storage with no features beyond that. The value stems from the cost, which is among the least expensive of the devices I considered. One unique feature that I especially like is that it does not require drivers for Windows 98 - all other USB flash drives I considered required them. ALthough I haven't tested it, the manufacturer claims that it is compatible with all versions of Windows from 98 to XP, and also for the Mac OS.
I initially purchased mine to use for transporting files, but found that the best use (for me) was to use it as file system extension for my e-mail client. This works remarkably well for me because I use both an IBM ThinkPad and a Sony Viao laptop (both of which are running Windows 98 SE) and synchronizing e-mail between the two machines is a chore. I now have my e-mail client configured to store my e-mail on the flash drive, and plug the flash drive into whichever of the laptops I happen to be using at the time. This alone makes the flashdrive invaluable.
Note that on some systems with side-by-side USB ports that the flashdrive may prevent you from using the other port because of its width. My ThinkPad has a port in the rear and one on the right side, so that didn't pose problems, but the Sony laptop's USB ports are close together and when the flashdrive is plugged I couldn't squeeze the connector for my mouse into the adjacent port - I solved this by purchasing a mini-USB hub that is powered by the USB port, but this is something you need to know before purchasing this particular flashdrive.
Despite that minor problem I am pleased with the device and am especially happy that I now have a solution to the e-mail synchronization problem that has plagued me for years.
So, I spend my days on the phone. This is a great headset. Comfortable and good quality sound.
Used this to mount and H4N PRO to a sound booth. Brilliant, beautiful and easy.

I use this cable at my workplace, it is a life saver. Ever so often, customers will have problems communicating with our equipment due to their laptop or a big list of different issues. We simply ship them one of this problems and their problem is fixed. Makes our life and their life easier. Thank you Sabrent!

I have had the latest gen Kindle DX since October 2010. I am a singer in a choir and use it to display my sheet music. It is well suited to my needs. The display is clear and crisp and is the size of a standard music hymnal. The catch is getting the music onto the device. Most publishers are starting to provide PDF versions of at least melody with accompaniment. However, being an alto in a choir, that isn't sufficient. I need the 3 or 4 part choral version. Also, it is formatted for an 8.5 x 11 inch page with headers, footers, and page numbers. I only need the music staff and lyrics. So I do it the hard way. I scan my (purchased & owned) hymnal or sheet music, crop it down to what I need, then convert it to a PDF. Lots of work, but the payoff is worth it. I no longer carry around 100+ lbs of sheet music and hymnals twice a week! Keep in mind this isn't for everyone. It requires a lot of time and patience, but once the music has been prepped and imported, it's done and ready when you need it. I assume after a year I'll have perhaps 80% of my library scanned.
