USB Type-C is just a super complicated situation all around. The ports themselves can be USB 2.0, 3.0, 3.1, 3.2, thunderbolt 3 or thunderbolt 4. I'm probably missing something there. That only covers data transfer speeds. For power, a Type-C port can be rated for multiple voltages and amperages. To protect the consumer from disaster (or they try anyway), each type-c product needs to be equipped with a chip that allows it to negotiate the speed and voltages. This includes the cables. The situation with cables is just as complicated. A cable may only be able to charge at 5v and not carry any data. They may carry only usb 2.0 data. Better ones may be rated for high speed data but not high wattage. Others have both high speeds and are rated for up to 100w. Good luck trying to find the right cable once all of them are dumped in a drawer somewhere.

This 240W USB C to USB C Cable 6.6ft is yet another odd one in the bunch. It is rated for high charging speeds but is only USB 2.0 for data. Why is it necessary though? I have a Dell Inspiron laptop that has a discreet NVidia RTX 3050 processor. This means that it has a high power demand.

This Dell was also designed to charge only from a USB type-c port and the input power must be 130w. So began my search for a charger that I can take with me when I'm away from my desk. I was able to find a macbook style charger that outputs 140w but I didn't own any cables that were rated for higher than 100w.

I came across this cable and connected everything up. During boot, the Dell's firmware still detected a low-powered charging device, but when I booted into Windows 11 and checked its power settings (after reconnecting the charger to the wall), Windows did not warn of an under powered charger as it normally would. I was then able to use this charging setup to play a graphics intensive game for over an hour with no sign of GPU or CPU throttling.

In the end, this cable allows me to have a portable solution for my laptop without having to lug around a standard laptop charger. It works.

Feiyutech is a brand that I've come to know for their camera accessories. Generally, their products have great build quality and is well-designed. I've had problems with their app working with LG phones but once I upgrade, that wouldn't be a problem anymore.

The FeiyuTech Official SCORP-C Camera Stabilizer is a 3-axis gimbal made for DSLR and mirrorless cameras. All of the axis arms are metal with high quality plastic in the body. The motors are quiet and there are plenty of buttons that control most aspects of the gimbal. There's even a video made by Feiyutech that explains the buttons very well. This SCORP-C model does not have an LCD screen.

The accompanying smartphone app is used to upgrade the gimbal firmware and for finer adjustments of the gimbal such as the follow speed and horizontal calibration. Control of the gimbal itself is also possible, but it is easier and faster to use the buttons on the device. It really is a good thing that the gimbal is designed to be operated without the need to fuss with a phone and app.

A few USB cables are included with this gimbal, which is designed to control the shutter of the camera that you own. Unfortunately, my Lumix GX8 is an odd model that just isn't well supported, even by Panasonic themselves. None of the included cables worked for me so this gimbal isn't able to control my camera. Not a big problem, though. If I really need wireless control of my camera, I can probably work out some sort of phone mount and use the Panasonic app. Just be aware that Feiyutech's list of compatible camera might be a little limited. They publish a compatiblity list. Just search for the term "Feiyu SCORP-C Lens Compatibility List"

With that said, the gimbal stabilization is great. Once your camera is balanced (search youtube for "Scorp-C Balancing" to see a video demonstrating this process), the motors are very, very quiet and the various follow modes help to create smooth motion in your videos.

Recently, I'm helping my daughter record videos and this gimbal has really come in handy. My camera doesn't support in-body stabilization for video and the lenses I have do not have in-lens stabilization. Gimbals are the best answers for my camera's limitations.

This portable power bank is quite beefy and has some real heft. It weighs 2.5 pounds without the case but with this heft, you get some real power.

It sports two Type-A ports at 18w max, a type-c port at 45W max, and a 110V AC output at 120W max. The type-a ports are fairly standard and isn't anything out of the ordinary. The AC output should be enough to power most laptops but you would still need your laptop's power adapter.

The type-c port was why I wanted this device. It can be used to charge this power pack at 45w, which means you can fully charge this thing fairly quickly (sorry, I haven't timed it). The 45w output of the port allows me to run my pinecil soldering iron at full wattage, which means that my soldering iron can go to 300 degrees within 10 seconds.

Another use I had for this thing was that I had a skunk that was breaking into the crawl space under my house and I needed a camera to keep an eye on the movements of the skunk. Rather than purchasing a motion sensing camera, I was able to take one of my WIFI cameras and power it with this thing. The battery not only lasted the entire night, it only went down by one light (out of 4 lights total).

Two things I wish this power supply had: An adjustable DC output with a barrel connector. This would allow charging of laptops without having to plug in the laptop's adapter. I would also have liked the type-c port to support 100w because many laptops that charge by Type-C require at least 60w output. Those laptops will trickle charge from this power bank but will complain about it being under-powered.

Docking station or second power adapter? That's the question one would normally ask when considering a travel solution for their laptop. A docking station that sits on your desk with all of your accessories and monitor plugged in is a great solution that leaves the OEM power adapter available to be left in your travel bag. In the case of my Dell XPS 17, a docking station really isn't available for an affordable price.

The XPS 17 charges via the USB type-c port just like most laptops out there today, but it requires a 130 watt input through that type-c port. Most type-c docks or even power adapters only go up to 100w. If you wish to force the issue, the Dell thunderbolt dock will cost you over $200.

This 130w power adapter was the best solution for me. It truly delivers 130w as Windows does not give a warning regarding a low-powered power source when it is plugged in.

I had an extensive test of this device a few weeks back where I used it for three days straight. Initially, I thought it felt a little hot to the touch, but after rebooting my laptop, that no longer happened. I believe it was a problem with Windows power management.

This adapter comes with a nice, braided cable on the USB type-c side (normal two-pronged power cable on the other). The cable isn't overly stiff and feels like it has good build quality.

There really isn't much else that needed to be said about this adapter. It outputs the power as advertised and it worked great when I needed it. This will be the adapter I take with me on travel and my other adapter stays at my desk. Love it.

The Xasla 15000mAh Electric Air Duster & Vacuum 2 in 1 is a great little device that works great for cleaning more than just a computer.

I wanted this thing for its blower functionality because it is always a good idea to clean out the vents in your computers once in a while to make sure they don't overheat. I have a laptop cooler that I use for my gaming laptop and that thing does get visibly clogged up with dust after about two months. It is great to have this thing around that I can just pick up and clean it whenever I want.

Obviously, this is intended as a replacement for canned air. Canned air can get into very narrow areas because they are equipped with a narrow straw to concentrate the airflow. Also because of how narrow the straw is, the air is very strong. The Xasla is not as powerful and the nozzle isn't as narrow as an air can's straw so it is not able to get into those deeper areas, but for the advantage of not having to worry about air running out in the middle of a cleaning and the convenience of having it available at all times, I think this is worth it.

The vacuum functionality is quite good as well. The first time I used this device as a desktop vaccum, I found that the suction was quite weak. Then I looked more closely at the device and found that there's a switch to change between blower and vacuum mode. After making the switch, the vacuum function worked much better. The difference between the two modes is that when the air exhaust is directed to the blower nozzle, there isn't a good amount of air flow to make a good vacuum. Moving the switch redirects the exhaust to a side vent that allows much greater flow.

This brings me to the only complaint about this device. The side vents was blowing on the desk while I was trying to vacuum up my desk. This is somewhat counter-productive, but in the end, it still got the job done.

One last thing about the Xasla 15000mAh Electric Air Duster & Vacuum 2 in 1. The battery handle is detachable and can be used as a battery pack for your phone. This is a nice bonus feature that can come in handy as well.

[[VIDEOID:385afc8b9bb77a3a87ae44bd958be49a]] This double din aftermarket car radio has some great features, most important of which are the wireless Android Auto, wireless Carplay, and steering wheel controls. On paper it all sounds great, and it's really affordable to boot.

The implementation of the whole thing is just a little bit janky, but we'll get to that.

Installation:
I purchased a wiring harness for my Toyota Sienna 2009. My car is not the XL with surround speakers or dvd player so the wiring is really simple. Surprising to me was that the wiring harness colors matched up to the colors of this radio's wires exactly. Just match the colors and connect them together.

For steering wheel controls, it is necessary to patch into three additional wires: sw1, sw2, and sw gnd, which I located by searching google for "2009 Steering Wheel wiring diagram". I found a diagram of the back of my factory radio and using that, found the pins that the three wires ended in.

This radio didn't fit the generic mounting bracket for my van. It was almost as if the screw holes for this radio was drilled upside-down. If I were to mount the radio upside down, all of the holes would have lined up, but right-side up, they don't. Fortunately, the mounting bracket is plastic so I was able to drill the holes that I needed in order to successfully mount the radio.

Operating System:
This radio runs a rudimentary operating system with basic radio functions. It also seems to have the ability to play music from a USB drive.

The configuration options are limited. I found that I am unable to adjust the backlight of the radio at all and the screen is actually quite dim.

Android Auto:
Pairing of Android Auto is very easy. Simply connect the phone to the radio via a usb cable and choose the android auto function. Follow any on-screen prompts and you are connected. Disconnect the cable and the radio will try to connect to the phone wirelessly (make sure wireless AA is enabled on your phone).

The performance of AA can be a little laggy when compared to my other car, but it works well enough to bring my old car into the modern age.

Honestly, I'm actually okay with most of these issues because it is still much better than the original factory radio that lacked bluetooth and GPS. Being able to connect my phone to use its smart functions is all I really wanted out of this radio and that's what it delivers. Plus, I can still use my steering wheel controls. I'm satisfied with this purchase

[[VIDEOID:6e49ad5f11d43ea1130e7014d1f00ce9]] I've always been interested in video projectors because I really wanted that theater experience at home. Previously, they have been out of reach because of the price of the devices as well as the price of the bulbs that required replacement.

In the last few years, LED projectors have really come down in price. When it became attainable for me, I started to try out various models and in the last two years, the prices have dropped to the $100-$200 range, even for native 1080p projectors.

As I've said, I have tried out various models and had problems with most of them, problems ranging from not being bright enough, 720p native, unable to fully focus the corners, or even that it needed to be very far from the screen to project a big picture.

The Vimgo Smart Projector is a stylish little projector that has a nice, vertical design that takes up less space than a normal projector. It has a good-sized speaker behind the cloth-covered side panels. The sound isn't high fidelity, but it can get pretty loud. Many other projectors barely comes with a 10w speaker or worse.

It is rated at 300 ANSI Lumen, which isn't going to work well in direct light but quite adequate when the lights are turned down. There are no dark corners and I find the picture to be evenly lit. The keystone functionality is great. You can adjust the "tilt" up and down as well as left and right. You can also zoom the picture out and if all else fails, each corner can be adjusted individually.

I really like that there is a motor that performs the focusing. With manual focus, I often get up and focus the projector, just to get back to my seat and figure out that the focus wasn't that great. With the focus controllable from the remote, I can sit close enough to really see if I got it just right.

The Android system works well for plex and jellyfin, which I have installed. Unfortunately, Netflix and Amazon Prime Video has DRM that prevents them from running on this projector, but that is easily remedied by projecting from your phone or with a FireTV connected to the HDMI (the USB port outputs enough amps to power the FireTV).

Here's a tip: Install the Android TV Launcher by downloading the APK file to a USB drive, then choose the USB app from the projector to install it. It is not only a better-looking launcher, it will also give you access to the full Android system settings. I wouldn't suggest setting it as the default launcher, though because I haven't found a way to launch the built-in launcher manually.

I also found that the Vimgo projector actually has a shorter throw distance than my previous projectors. I'm able to get a larger picture when set up at the same distance as my previous projectors. I actually had to zoom out to make the picture a little smaller to fit my projection screen.

So to conclude, the Vimgo projector does not have any of the problems that I found in my previous projectors. It is stylish and compact with a great picture and good-enough audio (for small gatherings, not for a home theater experience).

This HP Pavilion desktop is a solid, but basic PC that, while it can be considered a gaming PC with its discreet Radeon RX 5500 card, that isn't going to raise too many eyebrows with its specs. What's out of the realm of this machine would be 4K gaming and VR, but it can run most modern games at medium settings at 1080p.

That's not why I needed this machine, though. As a Plex server, this serves well. It is quiet and can transcode videos using hardware transcoding. Unfortunately, it only has a single slot for an additional hdd. As a video editing machine, it can handle 1080p videos, but will struggle with 4K. As a photo editing machine, it can edit pretty much anything from the devices you have, but if you work in print, you'll find this machine lacking. For emulation, this machine will work quite well for all classic systems and even some more modern ones. Of course, for everyday web browsing and watching videos, this thing will be more than enough.

Overall, this is a fairly priced machine that is a step up from the basic computers that one may find and the discreet GPU will help to make this machine last longer than those with embedded graphics.

These SUYUZREY 3.5mm Jack Wired Earbuds were for my daughter who needs it for her laptop when she is doing video conferencing during her group study sessions. This means that sound fidelity wasn't the primary purpose for their purchase.

These earbuds are comfortable for extended study sessions and with the included memory foam ear pieces, there's a good variety of sizes and comfort. Voices come through clearly and the microphone works well, but of course suffers the same problem as any other on-wire microphone: It can be a little far from the mouth and rubbing against the cloth can creating noise.

There isn't much else to say about a simple pair of earbuds like these.

The WEWATCH Video Projector with WiFi and Bluetooth is a basic projector that has all of the necessary features that one needs.

The description of this product may lead you to think otherwise, but this projector is not really a "smart" projector. It does not run on Android and the built-in user interface is quite basic. Yes, it will play videos and show photos from USB drives and it has WIFI... for whatever reason (I didn't really look into it because I simply plugged in a FireTV). The bluetooth, on the other hand, does have a function. I'll get into that in a bit.

So for video input, you have two full sized HDMI ports, a VGA (for those ancient laptops that your office may have lying around?) and a USB port which outputs enough amperage to run a fireTV, so no additional power adapter necessary.

There is no automatic keystone adjustment, but what is there works well. You can adjust the four corners up and down, although I found that it still seems to have some bloating in the middle no matter how I adjust it (could be a problem with my projection screen and projector positioning). A tip for doing the adjustment: If you aren't able to move the corners in the direction that you need, try adjusting the zoom first. By zooming out, it allows the corners to be pulled up or down more.

Audio is as expected in that it is not winning any awards. It can get pretty loud, but it still sounds empty. This is where bluetooth or the 3.5 mm headphone jack comes in. For wireless audio, you can either pair a bluetooth speaker/soundbar to the projector itself or you can pair the speakers directly to the FireTV or whatever dongle you're using. The advantage of pairing the speakers to the projector is that they will work for both HDMI inputs. If you really wanted to get full surround, you'll have to extract the audio out of the HDMI wire. Basically plug the HDMI into an audio receiver, then the audio receiver to the projector. The receiver can take care of decoding the surround depending on your setup.

For the brightness, the 1100LM beats out many other projectors of this price and resolution. You can really tell that the picture just pops. It will work well enough in a dimly lit room, but you can only truly appreciate it when the lights are completely off.

Overall, this is a low-priced projector that will work well for outdoor, temporary use, or even a permanent setup inside the home.

I listen to audiobooks to fall asleep at night so I wear "sleep" earbuds as to not disturb my wife. I usually buy the soft silicone type, which never have good audio quality, but does the job. They usually break withing a couple of months because I tend to tug on them a lot when I sleep so this time, I decided to try out these ceramic Wired Headphones with Microphone.

My initial impressions of these earbuds are that they have better sound quality than the other sleep earbuds that I've tried. They also have excellent build quality. There are silicone reinforcements at all of the wire connection points to protect them from failing due to tugging and the shape of the earbuds are as flat as possible.

When in my ears, these metal earbuds do not protrude at all, they lie flat. I tested by lying on my side to see if they would hurt but they seemed okay because nothing protrudes. Then after a couple of nights, I found that while direct downward pressure doesn't hurt, the earbuds do hurt when they are nudged from side to side, which happens when I'm shifting positions at night.

So overall, I'm still using these earbuds and have gotten used to them, but they do still hurt occasionally, depending on how much I move at night.

This 5-in-1 card reader is exactly what I needed. It is fast, well-built, and connects to everything that I own.

Being USB type-c, this card reader will read and write to your microsd or SD card at the maximum speed that it is capable of. I found that the speed is in line with my previous reader as well as my laptop's built-in reader.

This reader has connectivity for Type-A, Micro-usb type-b, and USB type-c. It means that I can use this reader for my phones, including any older models that support USB host-mode and all of my PC's, including my Dell XPS that only has type-c ports.

Connected to the phone, I can back up my pixel phone, without having to upload all of the pictures to the cloud. Connected to my computer, I can quickly transfer files to and from my mirrorless camera.

This product does exactly what I need it to do and with its metal build and protective caps, this will be a product that I will carry in my tech bag.

Super thin, huge 17" touch screen with colors that just POP, large touchpad mouse, and silent chiclet keyboard. These are just the initial impressions one would see at first blush when approaching this high-quality laptop. Look a little deeper and one would find that this Dell XPS 17 sports a powerful 11th generation I7-11800H cpu with a dedicated RTX 3050 graphics card with Nvidia's real-time ray tracing and 16gb of ram. A 512GB ssd rounds out the entire package.

The Dell XPS 17 is simply elegant and high-quality. I was able to upgrade this laptop to Windows 11 painlessly and the new UI just looks great on this screen. It runs silently during normal web browsing and video watching. When playing games, the fan kicks in and the cooling seems adequate, but I still have an external laptop cooler helping it along.

Speaking of games, this laptop will run the latest games, but being at the bottom of the RTX line of graphics cards, the screen's 3840x2400 resolution simply is too much for the 3050 to run at the highest quality. It means that one would either run at a lower resolution or lower quality. The resolution issue can be alleviated if one turns on DLSS for resolution scaling.

So that is one of the first problems I would point out with the specs that I have in this laptop. The RTX3050 paired with the super high resolution means one must compromise in some way. In addition, performance in VR is somewhat poor. Half Life: Alyx runs well at low quality settings but any higher and the screen stutters and can cause nausea -- this was tested through wired and wireless configurations.

The second complaint that I have for this laptop is that the only included ports are 4 usb Type-C ports, headphone jack and an SD card reader. It is great that the ports support up to Thunderbolt 3, but the fact that no Type-A ports are available, dongles will be a part of life. It's nice that Dell includes a dongle that sports an HDMI and a Type-A port, there is no ethernet or display port support out of the box.

A good 9-in-1 dongle will cost you at least $60 and even then, the quality could be questionable. I happened to have a 9-in-1 dongle, but the ethernet port seems to lose connection constantly. This means that either you take a chance with a $60 no-name dongle or you spend over $100 for a proven one.

This then brings me to the last problem that I want to point out. A gaming PC has very high power requirements. Currently, there is no Type-C product that will provide (or pass through) the 130W that the Dell XPS 17 will require. It means that the nifty dock that you bought to get the additional ports that you need? It won't be able to power the laptop. You can connect a 100W charger to the laptop, but you will get a warning from the operating system. So perhaps on travel, one can get away with trickle charging the laptop, but at home, you will always be stuck with taking up two ports, one for power and one for your monitor.

Overall, this is a GREAT laptop with high quality build, but at the current specs, some things just cause awkward situations that one needs to work around.

What sets the INNOCN 15.6" portable monitor apart from other type-c portable monitors is the built in battery and the touch screen features. In the box, a soft silicone case is included with a cover that folds into a stand, making it feel like an oversized tablet.

Other portable monitors with built-in battery are usually a little bit thicker or have a bulge at back of the screen. The INNOCN doesn't have that. It is a thin slab that is around 3/8" thick. I actually use it as a secondary screen on a daily basis and while the monitor has an all aluminum casing, there is almost no heat generated by the screen during use.

The touch capability of this monitor brings touch support to any Windows PC without the need for drivers but even more, connect this to an Android phone such as my LG V40 and not only does the phone go into desktop mode, the touch screen works to turn the phone into a 15.6" tablet! The built-in battery will help to keep the phone topped off and allow fully wireless (no need to plug into the wall, but there will be a wire between phone and screen) tablet.

My previous monitor was a LePow 15.6" type-c portable Monitor. It is representative of many other portable monitors on the market. Compared to the INNOCN, the INNOCN is a lot brighter and the colors more vibrant. The LePow was instant on but the INNOCN can take about 2-3 seconds to turn on after receiving a signal. Both have speakers that are tinny and quite weak, but serviceable if you're on-the-go.

If you are purchasing this monitor to work with the Nintendo Switch, you will be disappointed. The Switch is very picky about the conditions that must be met before it goes into docked mode, mainly a 19v type-c PD. The power output from this monitor simply doesn't supply that, even when plugged in to an original Nintendo power adapter (the adapter will serve to charge the screen, but will not supply the 19v to the connected switch). It will only work with the switch through a dock, which really defeats the purpose of a portable monitor. On the other hand, the LePow does actually does work with the switch. Connected a power adapter or portable phone charger to the LePow and the monitor will supply the necessary 19v to the Switch.

So overall, a great monitor for most uses, especially the ability to turn a phone into a large touchscreen tablet, but if you want a portable large-screen solution for the Nintendo Switch, go for something like the LePow

I've owned a few Lexar USB drives and Micro USB drives in the past and they have all had good quality and performance. I've attached the crystal diskmark performance below, but keep in mind that I am using the built-in microsd reader in my computer so speeds may vary as the reader has just as much to do with these benchmarks as the memory card itself.

I don't have any equipment that really stresses the microsd too much. The cameras that I have, while they can record up to 4K at 30fps, have generally had no problem writing to a U1 microsd. The Lexar, which I keep in my Osmo Pocket, is no exception, it has not had an issue recording video.

There is one key thing to point out about Lexar storage media that I've experienced in two of my past devices and that is the built-in expiration or time-bomb (if you don't agree with this philosophy). Lexar seems to have the philosophy that keeping your data intact is the most important when it comes to these products. Solid-state storage media has a theoretical limit to how many times they can be written to. Once that is hit, the media will be permanently damaged. Lexar has written into their firmware, a hard limit that once you write a certain number of times to their media, it will become read-only, keeping your data intact, but the storage unusable from that point on.

While I've experienced failed media in the past, I really only had this behavior with Lexar. I have to say, it did save my wife from losing the pictures on her phone if the card failed instead of becoming read-only.

Yi is a brand that I know previously from their action cameras. They also dabbled in a mirrorless micro 4/3 camera as well so they know their camera tech.

The YIIOT 3MP HD Floodlight Camera is a lot like other wireless cameras that are on Amazon. The big difference here is that it is powered by the mains power, which I prefer. I replaced my regular floodlights with this camera. Just as with all other wifi cams, a separate app will be required. The setup is fairly straightforward. Go through the setup process and have the camera scan the barcode that was generated. From there, you're set.

This camera features high definition picture and local microsd storage. Notifications are customizable but mostly it is fairly standard.

There is ONE feature that sets this, and other Yi cameras apart, though. Install the Yiiot app through Alexa and you will be able to view the cameras if you have an Echo Show, FireTV, or Fire Tablet. Very nice.

I'm no artist in any way but I do want to try getting into digital art. As a present to myself, I purchased the [[ASIN:B083W88L5H Huion Kamvas 13]] to get started. Huion is known for providing great quality in their products while keeping the prices affordable.

As anyone who has used a drawing tablet can attest, with the tablet taking up the main desk space, it's difficult to access the keyboard for all the shortcut keys that help to make the job easier. One option is to use an under-the-desk keyboard tray, but I really don't like doing that as I tend to kick the tray when I get in and out of my chair. Others purchase more expensive hotkey devices such as this one.

While the HUION Mini KeyDial KD100 does not have fancy led lights or e-ink display on the keys, it does have the basics of what one would need. The keys are laid out like the number pad on a full 101-key keyboard and the dial can be used to adjust anything that needs a kind of analog input (volume, zoom, brush size, etc). The keys are preconfigured for the most common shortcuts but each key can be customized.

The Mini KeyDial came in an oddly plain white box with the name Huion printed on top. It's almost like this is a rebranded white-box device but that really isn't a problem. It simply means that the unboxing experience isn't as satisfying as the drawing tablet itself. Once connected to the Huion drivers, the device feels fully integrated to Huion's ecosystem.

It is managed in the same driver/software that Huion uses for its tablets so that once you'll be able to get up and running customizing the buttons immediately.

Last thing to point out is that the dial on this device can support Microsoft's own RaDial drivers to emulate the dial that Microsoft introduced a few years ago for the Surface Studio, allowing it to interact natively with built-in Windows utilities.

Easy solution for better air flow. I primarily purchase smaller nuc style computers around the house. They usually have a small fan with minimal air flow. When my computer started to throttle due to heat, I purchased these fans to help cool it down.

The fans are fairly quiet and have good flow. The rubber footing help to reduce vibration. No need to think about how to plug the fan into the motherboard and how to adjust it's speed. It's plug and power on. That's it

What can a 256gb drive be used for? If one wishes to have storage space, we're talking in Terabytes, not Giga. For portable storage, a micro-sd card or usb pen drive has just as much storage for about the same price. So what niche does a 256gb, M.2 drive fit in?

There are two possibilities that I can think of:
1. A live-usb linux distro install. When combined with a USB 3.1 enclosure, this drive can be used to boot a PC into a linux operating system without affecting the internal drive of the computer. This can be useful for troubleshooting or simply testing out various distros. A drive like this would perform much better than a micro-sd or usb-pen drive.
2. Used as an internal OS drive for a computer. Even with Windows' requirements for space, a 256GB NVME drive will perform better than a traditional Sata drive, meaning faster boot up and faster app launching. It is always good practice to keep your data and OS separate, so for your pictures, videos, and other large files, put them on a separate drive, but use this drive to install your operating system on. This gives you the freedom to refresh your system without fear of losing data.

Specific to this Pioneer 256GB NVMe PCIe M.2 2280 Gen 3x4 Internal Solid State Drive, I currently have it in an external enclosure and am testing Windows 11 (which is only in Insider Preview at the time of this writing). I ran a crystal disk mark against it and posted the picture. I'm happy with this drive and how well Windows runs on it, even through USB.

The rise of home automation devices means that many of us have a lot more devices that connect to our wifi networks. While most of those devices use the 2.4Ghz frequency while devices like phones, tablets, and firetv use 5Ghz to stay out of each other's way, it still means that there are so many more devices to manage in a network and all of them are attempting to talk on the network. Not to mention interference from neighbors and their many devices.

This drives the need for beefy routers with faster CPUs to manage all of the chatter and radios that allow many more simultaneously connected devices.

The NETGEAR Orbi Pro WiFi 6 Tri-band Mesh System (SXK80) attempts to address these needs. Sporting the latest wireless Wifi 6 technology, most of the basic features that a router needs (QoS, DDNS, VPN), and 60+ device support, the SKX80 holds a lot of promise.

Unlike one of the upvoted reviews, I don't have a different AX system to compare this to so for me, this mesh router performs admirably. It is fast and has good coverage. In my time so far, I haven't had any dropped connections. Videos stream well and web browsing works fine. I don't normally do voice or video calls while walking around the house, but watching videos while walking seem to work well. My device will jump from router to satellite correctly and there is no disruption to the video playback.

The X300 Mini PC AMD Ryzen 5 3400GE would be the fourth Minisforum pc that I got over the past two years. They are a brand that I've really been keeping an eye on. Minisforum makes small form-factor pcs using the latest Intel and AMD mobile cpu's. Their computers are geared toward daily homework or office work use without taking up too much space. Most of them are VESA mountable.

The X300 is one of the bigger computers that I've seen from Minisforum. The entire chassis is metal and is well-ventilated. Whereas my previous compact PC's use laptop cooler fans, the X300 has a low-profile fan with 3-inch blades. During normal operation, the fan is very quiet.

I was surprised when I successfully booted up Biomutant, a 2021 game, and was able to play it at 1080p at a good framerate (sorry, I didn't turn on the FPS indicator...) at medium quality. Intel i5's would've had no hope of doing this without an additional graphics card (although, admittedly, I haven't had a chance to test the new Intel processors with their Xe graphics built in).

My son is learning to program games with Unity and Godot engines but had be previously unable to follow tutorials for 3D games due to the hardware limitations but with this PC, he will be able to expand into 3D.

The Mcoplus VM-M03 Metal Shotgun Video Microphone is the next step in my attempt to address sound quality issues in my videos. While a lavalier is good for a vlogging situation, it's not great for getting on location sounds.

I'm not a professional videographer or anything so I've included pictures of the frequency response charts from the microphone's instruction manual. In my specific case, the quality of this microphone vs the built-in mic of my phone or mirrorless camera is that it seems to pick up a little less of the unwanted ambient noise, but the biggest difference for me is of course, the wind noise reduction afforded by the fur cover.

This microphone is an affordable upgrade to the built-in mics of my equipment and fits my needs well. I can't say that my recommendation should be taken by anyone who actually does videography professionally.

The Skagen Men's Hybrid HR Jorn Smartwatch is an elegant watch first and smart watch second. It is considered a hybrid because it is a watch first. Even with almost no battery life left, it still serves as a traditional watch with a stylish, all metal body and actual watch hands with glow-in-the-dark inserts for visibility without a front-light. In terms of thickness, unfortunately, this watch isn't any thinner than other Android Wear watches I've used.

For the "smart" portion of the watch, the Skagen is equipped with an e-ink display, which means that once the watch face is drawn, no more power is drawn from the battery to keep that display. This means that the watch will last much longer than a regular, oled-display smart watch. It is easy to tell that this e-ink display is of high quality because it does not have the yellow hue that older e-ink displays had. It is quite similar in quality to the paper-white kindle.

Beyond the screen is the software. The Skagen watch pares down the smart functionalities to only what a user may actually need on a watch. No games, no maps, no speakerphone functionality. Instead, the watch will track your workouts, show you notifications, and control your music player. It really is everything I normally do on my Android Wear watch. There are many watch faces, and multiple complications for customization. One can even use a photo as the background for the watch face. I did find that any watch faces with numbers tend to crowd out the UI and there is very little room for complications.

[[VIDEOID:ccc625498e24d19dfedabac29060c0d1]] At first blush, the Baseus S2 Wireless Earbuds looks like the countless number of Airpod knockoffs out there... and how dare they charge 70 bucks for it?

I'm happy to report that beyond the shape of the earbuds, the Baseus S2 is a high-quality pair of earbuds that can hold its own against even Samsung earbuds. Over the years, I've used many, many wired and wireless earbuds but I've always kept my budget sub-100 dollars. Of all of them, the S2 is definitely the best so far.

From the nice metallic blue color, to the discreet capacitive touch buttons, these earbuds look great and the mic stalk isn't so long as to look odd in the ear. The case is sleek and comfortable to hold and provides a button to initiate the pairing function. Oh, and NO FLASHING LED LIGHT on the buds themselves. Overall, great build quality.

In terms of functionality, these earbuds do not have the annoyingly accented "pairing", "connected", etc. voice prompts. Just beeps to indicate its current mode, which I'll go into in a bit. The earbuds can of course be used together or independently. On long trips with my family, I like to keep one earpiece in, listening to my audiobook while still being able to stay up with the conversation in the car, then switch the earbuds when the battery runs low.

A nice quality of life function that is also an homage to airpods is that the earbuds will pause the audio if removed from the ear and resume when inserted.

While I normally don't read instruction manual, I needed to reference it to figure out the capacitive buttons. So here's what I found out:
-- Single tap: Left earbud for previous track and Right earbud for next track.
-- Double tap: pause/play (or just remove the bud from the ear).
-- triple tap: Google Assistant
-- Long press: Active noise cancellation function
-- simple beep: ANC and passthrough mode off
-- a slow rise base sound: DNC (passthrough mode) on
-- a slow lowering base sound: ANC on.
(the slow base sounds are like the movie sound effects when a scene goes from normal speed to slomo and back)

One feature that I had to actually search carefully to discover on the product description was that the case actually has wireless charging capability. They really should advertise that more.

The sound quality has a rich full tone. I did not feel like I was missing the bass or treble parts of the spectrum, but then I'm not one for heavy bass in the first place. The clarity is also very good.

Please enjoy my mini unboxing video.

When I purchased the [[ASIN:B08RRV6S6W Ulanzi battery handle]] to go with my DJI pocket, I was impressed with the quality of the product. When gathering together my camera gear for my vacation, I realized that I actually purchased a couple of other Ulanzi products previously. Since then, this brand has jumped out at me when looking for camera accessories.

This ULANZI MT-33 Camera Tripod had a convenience feature that I didn't realize it had when I ordered it. It is well thought out and has good build quality (with one minor caveat). It is a flexible tripod that is strong enough to hold my mirrorless Lumix camera and is equipped with a cold shoe socket as well as a 1/4" screw hole. The cold shoe can hold a microphone or small LED video light which the 1/4" screw hole can either mount another cold shoe or other camera accessories.

The convenience feature that I didn't know about is that the mounting head of this tripod can open up to become a phone holder. It's not a separate accessory that screws on to the quarter inch screw. The spring-loaded phone holder is actually part of the mounting head's design. What this means is that one can switch from taking pictures with a camera to filming with a cell phone without fumbling around with phone brackets.

In my pictures, you will see a screw with its tightening wheel. The screw is supposed to be securely seated in the wheel but it wasn't seated properly in the product I received and it came apart. It wasn't a big problem. Simply reassemble the screw and wheel back and then mount a camera to the tripod. By tightening the screw to the camera and keep turning. The tightening action will seat the screw back into the wheel and should not come out anymore.

I'm not a video blogger but it seems like I'm slowly collecting many accessories that make me think perhaps it's a shame for me not to be? I have the necessary tools for it... not everyone is made to be in front of the camera, I guess.

First, I want to say that I verified this to be a 2K camera. I had some confusion because there was a discrepancy between the title and the description.

Webcams are pretty much a requirement in these days of Zoom meetings and school classes. This camera has great image clarity and quality. The light has 3 levels of brightness but is fairly useless due to how small the light actually is. It simply isn't big enough to light up my face.

The camera also has a microphone so it is completely possible to do a hands-free setup by having a speaker plugged into the computer.

Overall, it does what I need it for, but the light takes away from the aesthetics of the camera. It wouldn't be a problem if the light actually worked as I hoped it would but as it is, it simply makes the camera look bulkier than it needs to be.

Years ago, not knowing what I was looking for, I purchased the [[ASIN:B017IS057O Albott 70 inch tripod]]. It was a good entry-level tripod that is quite traditional with it's pan-and-tilt head and quick release lock. As I started to build out my video and photo equipment (I'm still a total novice), I've found that I needed a tripod that was more compact and sturdy.

This K&F Concept TM2515M1 tripod is certainly not professional level, but it is a good travel tripod. With a ball joint, and a screw-lock plate, I found that it is more versatile than the Albott tripod. With the orange highlights, it is also much better looking.

I've included a few pictures comparing the two tripods. As you can see, with the K&F tripod, I do not compromise on any of the features of the other tripod while gaining a more compact and sturdy frame. The build quality of the K&F is great. All parts are metal and the tripod legs are tightly screwed, giving it a very secure feel.

From the pictures, you can see that compared to the traditional tripod, the head is smaller and easier to pack away, without that long handle to get in the way. The maximum height is comparable to my old tripod, but when packed away, the K&F is much smaller. The carrying case is also more rugged. It has a heavy-grade nylon and the zipper is nice and big. What I'm losing compared to the traditional tripod is the monopod height but I'm not a tall guy, so I would never use the mono fully extended anyway.

The K&F has the upside-down feature that is common among tripods of this kind. It allows one to shoot videos and pictures from a much lower angle without risking the safety of the camera. I can imagine a low-to-the-ground timelapse on the bank of a river looking at boats on the river.

Form really follows function on this one. The orange highlights accentuate all the joint locations and the all round design gives this tripod just a sleek look overall.

I'm quite satisfied with my purchase and the sub-100 dollar price that was exactly what I was looking for.

I don't know how it happens but I somehow ended up buying over 20 pairs of bluetooth headphones over the course of my life. I'm also finding that I can't pass up a good pair of bluetooth headphones.

So of the over-head style bluetooth headphones, I've run across problems with short battery life (had one pair that lasts only 3 hours), too tight against the head, presses on the ear (supra-aural) and gets sweaty, active noise cancelling that can't turn on independently of the bluetooth function, and no carrying case.

This pair of RCA Active noise cancelling headphones don't have any of those problems. I sit at my desk all day with an air outlet behind me that is constantly blowing. I'm able to use them the entire day with music playing without the batteries running down. I don't keep the noise cancelling on the entire time but when I do, the fan noise is completely blocked out. Being circumaural headphones, the ear cups completely surround my ears and do not press on them. In addition, the spring isn't too tight to make me feel like my head is being squeezed in a vice.

As far as sound quality, because the speakers are not pressing against the ear, the sound seems to have a wider-room feel, making me feel even more like I don't have headphones on.

Overall, I'm quite satisfied with this purchase and don't feel the need to splurge and buy the much more expensive Sony and Bose products.

[[VIDEOID:2e7c0a6adbe4e28b15ec850150bf83ab]] Please check out the pictures that I provided for size and picture quality comparison between the TOUMEI Mini Projector and the [[ASIN:B008BUQ16S Vivitek Qumi Q5]].

**If you read through the entire review, I hope that I can provide some information that may help you get the most out of this projector.

THE REVIEW
I already owned a QUMI Q5, which was $500 when it came out and I really like the projector but I found that I did not take it with me very often when I travel because while the projector is small, it did not have built in battery and could not be powered by USB, requiring me to bring a power adapter. It also did not have Android so I had to bring a separate device such as a laptop or firetv. What this meant was that I ended up having to take up a lot of space in my bag for all the accessories necessary just to make the QUMI work.

The TOUMEI solves both problems for me. It has a built-in battery that should run for a couple of hours and can be charged using a USB charger (which I would bring with me anyway). Just remember that you need a charger with a high amperage (2.1A at least). With the built in Android, don't need to bring an additional media device. All I need to pack is the projector and its remote control. With the HDMI port, I still have the option to connect a laptop or FireTV to the projector (see caveats)

As you can see in my pictures and video, the TOUMEI looks just as good, if not better, than the QUMI when projecting a 30" picture. Fun fact: The TOUMEI was running on battery power when I was filming my comparison video. Projection brightness isn't lowered because it is running on battery power.

So for my use, the TOUMEI deserves its 5-Stars. I also want to give props to TOUMEI for updating the projector from Android 4 to Android 7.1.2. That's a 3-version jump! With that said, the projector is not perfect.

CAVEATS:
- Netflix not supported (See tips for workarounds)
- In HDMI mode, there are no keystone controls and auto-keystone doesn't work. This means you are forced to front-project and the projector must be level to the screen. I wrote an email to TOUMEI support and they were quite responsive. Unfortunately, they do not have a solution for this.
- Bluetooth mouse doesn't work very well. I've tried two bluetooth mice with the project but the pointer jumps around the screen, making it hard to use. Using a logitech usb mouse/keyboard worked well and mouse movement was smooth.

TIPS:
- Streaming apps: There is a builtin app called freeclick. From there, you can install a version of Amazon Videos and Youtube that works with remote control navigation. You can also install Netflix from there, but it is a very old version that was designed for touch/mouse input (see Netflix tip).
- Better UI: I was able to install "Leanback Launcher for Fire TV" (search google and click on the xda-developers link). Leanback is the codename for the launcher that is built in to Android TV. It is a more modern-looking launcher than what the projector came with. Also install "TV App Drawer" from the Play Store to show all apps that the Leanback Launcher hides.

- Better UI Alternative: I also tried out ATV Launcher from the Play Store and that is a launcher that looks just like the Leanback launcher but has more options but some are locked unless you purchase the PRO version.

NETFLIX:
The newer versions of the Netflix app no longer support any Android boxes that aren't on their "white list" so only version 4 or earlier work (Netflix is at version 7 as of this writing). So while the Netflix that is included with the projector works, it is old and you really need a mouse to use it. There are a few workarounds that you can try though:

- Miracast: While there is a builtin app for casting an android phone to the projector, it is buggy and doesn't retain the phone's aspect ratio, stretching the picture out. Instead, install AirScreen from the Play Store. The popup ads can be annoying unless you pay to remove them but AirScreen is the most stable Miracast receiver software I've used. It also supports Apple Airplay, Google Cast, and DLNA. With AirScreen, you can cast Netflix from your phone to the projector.

- FireTV: With the HDMI port, you can connect a FireTV to the projector and take advantage of all the great services that Amazon provides. Just remember that in this case, you cannot adjust the keystone in any way and ceiling mounting or rear-projection modes are not available.

- Kodi: As opposed to what you may have read, Kodi is not illegal. It is simply a great video player that supports addons. There are some addons that are bad, but Kodi itself is not illegal or malware in any way. So basically, only install Kodi either from their official website at kodi.tv or through the Play Store.

Kodi has a Netflix plugin (Search "Netflix Add-on [input-stream]") and click on the Kodi Community Forum link. Again, this plugin is not illegal and does not circumvent Netflix security in any way. You are still required to provide your Netflix login. I will not go into the installation instructions here because it will make this review even longer than it already is.

I hope that I was able to help some of you with my review and tips. Thanks for reading!

In the last month, I purchase 3 different 128gb flash drives for $30 on separate sales that came up. So when the price is the same, it all comes down to speed when comparing these drives.

Drives:
-- [[ASIN:B00FE2N1WS PNY Turbo 128GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive]] (Newegg Deal)
-- [[ASIN:B00IVEI6CG HP x702w 128GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive]] (Fry’s Electronics Deal)
-- [[ASIN:B00S5V5PJC Lexar JumpDrive S75 128GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive]] (Costco Deal)

Useable Space (NTFS Formatted):
-- PNY - 119GB
-- HP - 116GB
-- Lexar - 119GB

Benchmarks (Crystal Disk Mark):
-- PNY:
Sequential Read (Q= 32,T= 1) : 87.825 MB/s
Sequential Write (Q= 32,T= 1) : 77.465 MB/s
Random Read 4KiB (Q= 32,T= 1) : 6.178 MB/s [ 1508.3 IOPS]
Random Write 4KiB (Q= 32,T= 1) : 0.829 MB/s [ 202.4 IOPS]
-- HP:
Sequential Read (Q= 32,T= 1) : 132.768 MB/s
Sequential Write (Q= 32,T= 1) : 57.274 MB/s
Random Read 4KiB (Q= 32,T= 1) : 7.834 MB/s [ 1912.6 IOPS]
Random Write 4KiB (Q= 32,T= 1) : 1.718 MB/s [ 419.4 IOPS]
-- Lexar:
Sequential Read (Q= 32,T= 1) : 97.070 MB/s
Sequential Write (Q= 32,T= 1) : 108.641 MB/s
Random Read 4KiB (Q= 32,T= 1) : 7.035 MB/s [ 1717.5 IOPS]
Random Write 4KiB (Q= 32,T= 1) : 0.938 MB/s [ 229.0 IOPS]

Conclusion:
PNY is the most popular on Amazon because it has the lowest price normally, but when you are able to find deals that equalize the price, it no longer looks that great. I ran Windows To Go on both the PNY and HP. The PNY had a lot of lag because of the low read speed. HP ran well because it has the best performance with 4kb files out of all 3.

The Lexar is a good drive with great write speeds. Good for uses where you are copying in more than you are reading out.

My preference is the Lexar for the size and the great write speeds. The HP is great for web developers to store their projects on because it performs well for reading and writing small files. The PNY is good because it stays at a low price for the most part.

This is a combined review of two of the lowest cost “Active Noise Cancelling” earbuds on Amazon:
[[ASIN:B004K09H32 Audio-Technica ATH-ANC23 QuietPoint Active Noise-Cancelling In-Ear Headphones]]
[[ASIN:B00SA5JCWO Egghead 1010 - Active Noise Cancelling Earbuds with Travel Pouch]]

PRICE
The price difference as of May, 2015 was $14 with Audio-Technica being the more expensive unit.

IN THE BOX
Both products contain:
--Earbuds
--Multiple silicone earbud cups
--Airline headset adapter
--Carrying Pouch

Audio-Technica contains in addition:
--Battery
--Pair of foam earbud cups. Not memory foam, just normal foam. I have not tried these.

Egghead:
--Mute button: In addition to the ANC on/off switch, Egghead has a nice mute button that turns off Noise Cancellation while it is pressed down.

SOUND QUALITY
I am not an audiophile so the sound from both headsets were good to me but the difference comes when you factor in the fit of the earbuds.

FIT
Both sets sit deeply in your ear and from pictures of both products, you will see that beyond the earbud, they have a circular piece before the actual connection to the wires.
--Egghead: The earbuds are attached straight to the circular piece so the fit is actually straight out away from your ears.
--Audio-Technica: The earbuds are angled forward so the circular piece actually serves as an anchor that sits nicely in your ear lobe and further cuts out outside noise. The additional foam earbud cup may make the difference for some people when it comes to a comfortable fit.
--Kids: I purchased these for a trip that the family will take. The kids usually have a hard time with normal earbuds not fitting in very well but they were able to keep the Audio-Technica earbuds in using the smallest earbud cups. The kids are 6 and 9.

NOISE REDUCTION
Here is the main event. I want to make a few points about Active Noise Cancelling: --Noise cancellation filters are designed to cancel out lower pitched, repeating noises like airplane engine rotors and car tires on a road, but it will not cancel out high or mid-range sounds like human voice. The same engine rotor and road noise also contain components of higher pitched sounds so NC filters will not cut out the noise completely.
--Using Noise Cancellation often feels like being underwater with your ears popping. It is a discomfort that you would have to get used to. The greater the cancellation effect, the greater the discomfort. Be prepared for this if you haven’t used NC before.
--ANC only works IF the inverted noise wave can overpower the noise coming in. If you are using a lawn mower and the noise it makes overpowers the “anti noise” because you’re standing right in back of the motor, you will not hear a big difference in the Noise Reduction effects.

Ok, so on with it. The Audio-Technica claims to reduce 90% of noise. I don’t have anything to confirm the claim but if we assume the Audio-Technica(AT) to be at 90%, my own assessment of the Egghead’s (Egg) noise reduction effects would be around 50-60%.

--Computer Fan Noise: Egg reduces the noise to slightly audible but you’d need to use toggle the mute button on it to really tell. AT completely removes the noise.
--Clothes Dryer: Egg takes the “edge” off the noise produced. You can still hear most of the noise standing about 3 feet away from the dryer. AT takes the bass tones completely out of the noise while leaving the higher pitched metal friction and buttons hitting the tumbler noise. In effect, with the AT, standing only 3 feet away, it sounds like you are actually 20 feet away.

So in conclusion, you have probably guessed that I think the additional cost of the Audio-Technicas are worth it. In addition to the benefits mentioned above, I have recently been able to get a great deal on a pair of [[ASIN:B00UETOW4C Harmon/Kardon SOHO II NC]] on ebay. The noise reduction effects of the Audio-Technicas equal or maybe even exceeds those of the Harmon/Kardons.

This SmartShell case is not just a magnetic cover for the iPad Air. It has a hard shell that protects the back of the tablet. To me, this is preferable to the magnetic cover because of the extra protection. The disadvantage is that you will not be able to take the cover off easily like the magnetic cover. It adds about 1/8" to each dimension of the iPad which is a minimal as you can get and still have protection.

My kids dropped the tablet on its corner near the volume buttons from about 2 1/2 feet off the ground. The plastic around the volume buttons cracked (it's the weakest part of the entire case) but the tablet was fine. No dents or scratches. A little super-glue to seal the crack and the case was as good as new. Had it been the magnetic cover, the tablet would have had a pretty bad dent.

This case gives you the "tablet" stand capability of the magnetic cover while providing more protection.

Almost weightless with a great fit, and good battery life, the Avantree AS8Q Earbuds are great exercise headsets. The only factors keeping it from being perfect is the sound quality and clunky button controls.

For contrast, I also have the “Chicklets” style earbuds that have been rebranded by many companies (e.g. ECSEM Mini Lightweight...). If these “Chiclets” earbuds worked well for you, the Avantree will be a nice upgrade.

You should get the Avantree AS8Q if you are looking for:
-- lightweight and moves with you (after tightening the headband, there is nothing on these earbuds that flap, swing, tangle, or stick to your neck).
-- in ear, not over-the-ear (earbuds are angled slightly forward so they will fit deep into the ear).
-- separate earbuds (buds are not held together by a rigid band like the Motorola S10).
-- sweat proof.
-- good battery life (5 hours, while the “Chiclets” style earbuds have 2 hours).
-- no controls that dangle from the wires (like the Plantronics Backbeat)
-- great noise isolation (Deeply seated earbuds means you block out most of the noise. I’m able to hear the music and audiobook over the sound of a basketball bouncing off hardwood floors in an enclosed court without having to turn the volume up high).
-- good bluetooth range (I keep my phone on a chair near center of the basketball court, on the sidelines, and I’m able to go to both sides of the court without any drop outs. “Chiclet” style buds did not have this range).

And you don’t mind:
-- Fair sound quality. Compared to even the “Chicklets” style earbuds, upper and middle frequencies sound a little muddy, and the bass sounds blown out. Ever stand next to speakers on the dance floor? They sound horrible, but step away and they sound fine. The earbuds seat so deeply in your ear that you feel like the speakers are right next to your ear drums. Yes, the design advantage is also the design flaw. For all the other qualities that these earbuds have, I can overlook the sound quality issues (because let’s face it, you get used to it).
-- Clunky controls. The rubber that covers the control buttons are designed to keep sweat out, but they also make it hard to push the buttons. I often press the power button thinking I’ve got it pushed down, but after 10 seconds, I realize the earbuds aren’t turning on (or off). Same with trying to skip tracks. By contrast, controls on the “Chiclets” earbuds are easy to press while still being sweat proof.
-- Controls that seem backwards. Volume up is toward the back of your head and volume down is toward the front. Skip FORWARD is a long press of the volume DOWN button and the volume Up for skip back.

Wishlist for next revision:
-- Reduce the size of the housing.
-- Hard plastic buttons
-- Active noise cancellation. Noise isolation is nice, but you really can't hear anything when someone is talking to you.

In conclusion, I thoroughly enjoy my workouts with these earbuds.

Video files are big and add up quickly to fill up your tablet. With a WIFI enabled hard drive, you can free up space but still have access to your movies and shows. With a USB 3.0 and Ethernet connection, the Macally enclosure not only solves these storage issues, it provides some side benefits as well. Unfortunately, with limited WIFI range and unstable firmware, there is plenty of room for improvement.

Macally has the following advantage over similar devices:
- Ethernet port AND USB 3.0: Other enclosures on the market either do not include ethernet or is not USB 3.0. This enclosure has both. With Ethernet, the enclosure functions as a portable router and NAS.

Good:
- Transfer speed: USB 3.0 means transferring large files is FAST. I get 60Mb/sec.
- Files On-The-Go: Files are shared via HTTP if you use the WifiStor app or SAMBA if you use a computer.
- Battery life: I get about 3 hours because I have a SATA drive, not SSD. Life can be extended using any cell phone charger pack.
- Functions while charging: Plug in to car charger and no worries about batteries during a long road trip.
- Portable router/Wifi Repeater: In a hotel room, share the ethernet connection with the rest of your devices or use the WIFI repeater function and log in to the hotel’s gateway page only once for all devices.
- Acts as a NAS: Plug this into your router using an Ethernet cable and you have a nice Network storage device.

Bad:
- WIFI range is short. Because of additional interference you’d get in a hotel room (other wifi hotspots), WIFI wouldn’t even work across the room.

- Desperate need of a firmware upgrade:
-- Need automatic switching between Ethernet or Wifi. If Ethernet is plugged in, use that as the Internet connection otherwise, use the last WIFI AP.
-- Need stability. When using WIFI as Internet connection, the unit crashes and requires a few reboots before becoming useable.
-- Need FTP Server.
-- Need UPNP/DLNA. While playing videos off SAMBA is possible, UPNP/DLNA is more widely supported on the IOS and TV’s.

Tips for iOS:
Don’t rely on the WifiStor app. Players like PlayerXtreme HD will stream videos directly from SAMBA shares. Share is \\10.10.10.254\WiFiDisk1_Volume1

Tips for Android:
Video is already supported because WifiStor will launch the correct player for each video, but my top choice is to use XBMC and connect directly via SAMBA.

When purchasing a bluetooth mouse, or any bluetooth device, an important factor is how well it connects and how well it STAYS connected. After all this time, the industry still can’t make up its mind about how bluetooth works:
- Microsoft with their mouse and Sony with their controller that pair without the need of a code (which Android’s bluetooth stack doesn’t support).
- Mice and keyboards that will not reconnect after it wakes from sleep mode.
- To this day, bluetooth devices still can’t wake a computer from suspend state.
So when I get a simple bluetooth mouse for a good price, and it actually works as expected, I was happy.

For my review, I’m comparing the Bornd mouse to the [[ASIN:B006428K7I Motorola 89519N Bluetooth Mouse]] which I got in a set that included the [[ASIN:B004L9MBH6 Motorola Wireless Keyboard for Motorola ATRIX and XOOM (Motorola Retail Packaging)]].

With the Motorola mouse, its frequency somehow conflicts with the Motorola keyboard, resulting in sticky keys, as in “I’m having a good daaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaay”. Conversely, the keyboard interferes with the mouse where the computer would actually lose connection with the mouse for a few seconds after typing, or lose connection completely.

What I liked about the Bornd:
- Pairing was simple using the button at the bottom of the mouse.
- Operating distance is about 5 feet, but this may be because of my computer’s bluetooth antenna
- Takes a single AA battery which lasts over a month of moderate use (2 hours per day)
- Mouse movement is good. No need to adjust mouse speed in the control panel.
- Accuracy is good. Editing images using Pixlr.com, I’m able to select precisely the parts of the image I need.

What gave me trouble with the Bornd:
- When you first put your hand on this mouse, you will not feel that it is very well built. The plastic is completely smooth and the mouse wheel seems to rattle when you shake it. I got used to it after a few minutes, though.
- The mouse reconnects with the computer most of the time, but sometimes it was necessary to turn the mouse off and on again after the computer reboots or if the computer was out of range for an extended period of time.
- Lately, I’ve been experiencing double-clicks when I click on the left mouse button once. I’m usually able to fix this by getting angry and slamming the mouse down a couple of times. This may indicate a build quality issue with this mouse.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

As with all security systems my advice is never use cloud based recording - this opens your entire network to not only the company who you are giving blanket access too but also to hackers. The same is true for WiFi. Obviously WiFi is more convenient but if your privacy is a concern this really needs to be taken into account. Hackers have become quite adept at hacking into WiFi cameras and being able to not only watch your feed but control your cameras and access your entire network. If you choose to utilize WiFi cameras take the time to understand your router and employ proper VPN protocols.

Due to my security concerns with WiFi cameras my current security system is completely run through a dedicated computer utilizing the Blue Iris software. While this may seem intimidating to some, it is well worth learning and utilizing for the huge advantages in privacy and security.

I’ve noticed many people have asked if this camera works with a Blue Iris and it does without any issue. Just update to the latest firmware. The remainder of setup within Blue Iris is straightforward. This IPC2387C supports PoE 802.3af and will work with 48V active adapters which are more expensive, but you can also rely on a PoE switch, which in my opinion is a much easier, straightforward option. Something to note, if you plan on powering via a DC cable this is not included.

The fixed lens size of 2.8mm provides decent field of view and the digital zoom is acceptable. The 1/2.8” CMOS 8MP image sensor is decent in low light, certainly not as good as 1/1.8” but I’ve found the low light capabilities average in comparison to other similar cameras. The LEDs must be illuminating objects to provide what is considered “colored night vision” which is misleading.

The camera has a built in microphone that allows for sound recording, though no speaker so two way communication will not be possible with this unit.

In terms of storage, the IPC2387C utilizes H.265 which is currently the best option for video compression. I have had this set up utilizing Blue Iris software which I definitely recommend.

When all things are taken into account this is a solidly build camera, suited to outdoor environments, decent daytime / nighttime resolution, fairly easily mounted, and setup in Blue Iris was reasonably easy and straightforward.

While I would prefer to have pan and tilt capabilities at this price point that is unrealistic. Overall I have been moderately impressed with this budget camera and would recommend it for many security situations.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential.

As with all security systems my advice is never use cloud based recording - this opens your entire network to not only the company who you are giving blanket access too but also to hackers. The same is true for WiFi. Obviously WiFi is more convenient but if your privacy is a concern this really needs to be taken into account. Hackers have become quite adept at hacking into WiFi cameras and being able to not only watch your feed but control your cameras and access your entire network. If you choose to utilize WiFi cameras take the time to understand your router and employ proper VPN protocols.

Due to my security concerns with WiFi cameras my current security system is completely run through a dedicated computer utilizing the Blue Iris software. While this may seem intimidating to some, it is well worth learning and utilizing for the huge advantages in privacy and security.

I’ve noticed many people have asked if this camera works with a Blue Iris and it does without any issue. Just update to the latest firmware. The remainder of setup within Blue Iris is straightforward. The RLC-522 supports PoE 802.3af and will work with 48V active adapters which are more expensive, but you can also rely on a PoE switch, which in my opinion is a much easier, straightforward option. Something to note, if you plan on powering via a DC cable this is not included.

The varifocal lens is a major feature that sets this camera apart from others. With an adjustable lens size of 2.8-8mm the optical zoom is excellent in comparison to digital zoom where pixels are simply enlarged. This will allow for this camera to be hung higher giving a better over view shot of an area while still being able to zoom in. The 1/2.7” CMOS image sensor is decent in low light, certainly not as good as 1/1.8” but I’ve found the low light capabilities strong in comparison to many similar cameras. The 18 IR LEDs do a decent job of illuminating objects in the fore and mid ground areas.

The camera has a built in microphone that allows for sound recording, though no speaker so two way communication will not be possible with this unit.

Unlike many similar cameras a mount is not required to be purchased separately. Mounting is fairly simple although care must be taken to mount so your lens is ultimately pointed in the direction you want as this camera does not pan nor tilt.

The varifocal zoom is not particularly fast so if you were trying to zoom in on action, such as a moving vehicle as it passed, you will likely miss it. Although if you have an area you want to focus on for a period of time it works fine.

In terms of storage, the RCL-522 utilizes H.264 rather than H.265 which will require more space to record the same data. Storage options include a MicroSD card slot with support up to 64GB - which I find lacking, cloud storage via FTP, the propriety Reolink NVR systems, or as I use set ups utilizing software such as Blue Iris.

When all things are taken into account this is a very solidly build varifocal camera, suited to outdoor environments, decent daytime / nighttime resolution, fairly easily mounted, and setup in Blue Iris was easy and straightforward. While I would prefer to have pan and tilt capabilities at this price point that is unrealistic. Overall I have been quite impressed with this camera and would recommend it for many security situations.

One thing to note, while the listing says that it provides color night vision - what really happens is when the lamp detects presence it turns the lamp on in order to record in color. True night vision - in the dark - is monochrome.

While the listing states that the device or app can be connected to Dropbox for free cloud based video storage I have yet to find where it’s possible to do that and the online guides do not refer to it.

This is an extremely high quality camera system built into a nice modern lamp. It has sleek lines and will compliment most any room’s decor. The lamp provides a very pleasant ambient light while also providing video and audio surveillance and security.

This is a product that I wouldn’t hesitate to recommend.
