That second time could have been due to the Android virtual machine being set up (it was right after trying it for the first time) and hasn't come back since, but I feel like it is worth mentioning sometimes there are quirks. But overall my experience has been positive and I enjoy using it, I just really strongly recommend getting one of their keyboard cases.

This does the job for those times I want to listen to my wired headphones but not lose my charging plug. Those who you who like to watch in bed know what I'm talking about! The problem however is if you wanted to use this for a headset with an inline mic for calls, this is NOT the adapter for you. The mic channel is not carried and it only uses the mic on the phone in my tests.
If that's not a requirement for you, it's great for just normal headphones.

After finally needing to retire my last phone with a headphone jack, it was time to try out some of these USBC to 3.5mm adapters. The good news is, it works really well and actually is small enough to leave attached to the end of my favorite set of wired headphones. You're not going to get audiophile quad-dac quality out of it like my old LG phones, but it will drive a normal pair of headphones just fine for music or videos.
HOWEVER, there are a couple of things to note:
1) It seems to support the audio out channels but not the microphone, if your headphones have one. You know how phone earbuds usually have an extra pin for the microphone on the tip (3 rings instead of 2)? I think this doesn't support that. I believe this jack is TRS instead of TRRS. Or even if it IS a TRRS, it's only telling my phone that the left and right audio channels are there. Which leads me to item #2:
2) It tells the phone a headset is connected even if it is not. And I think this also is related to #1, because it doesn't seem to care what's plugged into the other side of it, as soon you plug this adapter into your phone, even empty, the headphones icon shows up and all audio is routed out to the empty 3.5mm jack. Plug something in, you hear the sound. Unplug it, the sound goes nowhere. This is why I'm happy to leave it semi-permanently attached to my earphones, and just considering it an extension of them. You don't want to leave this attached to your phone with nothing plugged in.

In a nutshell, this is great if you want to listen to music. Not if you want to use a wired headset for phone calls.

This is a great way to continue using your wired headphones without giving up your charging port. It is a little bulkier than a straight USB-to-3.5mm adapter, but that's just how it has to be in order to make room for two plugs on a dongle like this.
A couple of things to note: The USB cable does not support data, only charging. But that's expected since it says so on this listing.
The thing that DID surprise me, however, is that it does not support the inline mic for calls. During a test phone call, the audio was coming from the phone's mic and not the headset, which we confirmed by tapping on the mic and then again on the phone (only the phone tap sound was heard). It actually says for calls on the listing, which I believe is a mistake. I'm guessing this unit supports TRS and ignores the extra pin for TRRS, so it's great for listening to music only and this is why I'm removing one star.

I love mini PCs and I've collected a few of them for different projects. The Celeron chip isn't a speed demon, but combined with Intel's GPU it is fast enough to drive 2 HDMI displays quite well, and like most other mini PCs out there, it has enough RAM and storage for light media consumption and internet tasks.
But there are few things that stand out with this model:
- This one is FANLESS. Without moving parts whirring, this actually manages to stay completely quiet while running.
- Also since the body is the heat sink, it doesn't need space for airflow and is therefore more compact as well.
However, not all of those changes are positive:
- There is no upgrade option for the storage like other mini PCs. Some of the popular boxes out there have an access door to add your own sata SSD drive for additional storage. This does not.
- The fanless design also sometimes means that in hot environments (such as attached to the back of a large TV display sign), there is no way to cool itself off other than throttling the processor. Most of the time this doesn't mean anything, but like all fanless computer designs it is extremely possible the unit will need to slow itself down to prevent overheating if used for extended periods of time. A fan unit has alternative ways to cool itself off at least.

But the biggest disappointment to me personally, is the lack of USB type C ports. It looks like this has one, but that look is deceiving. The port is just a PD input to run the unit. I actually like that it is using a standard instead of the circular DC ports that other mini PCs use, the PD power port is plentiful these days and you can use most laptop and other standard PD chargers to run this device. However, it still does not work as a standard USB-C for peripherals that are compatible with one. To be fair, most of these mini PCs I've tried oddly lack a type C port as well. I can't really detract any stars for that, but I got excited for a moment that this would have one only to see it is the power port.

These are excellent for listening to audio in a noisy environment such as an airplane or bus. I wasn't expecting much out of the noise reduction system at this price point but it was pretty decent. Even more useful, however, is the ambient noise mode which will allow you to hear some of the background noise in case you need to be aware (someone talking to you or if you need to hear traffic on a bike, etc). I've used modes like that on modern Sony headphones, and was surprised to find it on something in this price range.

But above all else, I'm most impressed with the comfort of these. The cushion feels premium, I don't know how else to describe it, but it reminds me much more of headphones from brand names that cost several times what this does. The build quality looks much better than my cheap wireless headphones too. The only thing I wasn't impressed with is the call quality with the microphone. But that's sort of par for the course, as only the truly name brand higher end ones seem to get that right- putting a mic by your ears and still somehow picking up your voice over the background noise is a neat trick that isn't copied well by other brands.
Otherwise, for just music and audiobooks with some decent NR and comfort, this is a great value!

Technics is a brand well known in audio gear, originally a sort of higher-end branch of Panasonic. They are known for pro equipment like DJ turntables, however I haven't seen them in a while and surely never seen them trying to compete in the consumer wireless headphones space before!
I own various wireless headphones, from cheap brands to industry standard Sonys, and I have to say- I usually understand why Sony is considered the industry standard for prosumer headphones. Others come close, but I've never actually felt like a product in the same price range could surpass it, until now. This set of earphones actually has pretty remarkable ANR, and they are actually more comfortable than my Sony sets ever were (to my ears at least, I can't speak for others). The sound quality is no slouch either, which is, let's face it, the reason you'd be interested in this at all.
I can't say for certain that it is BETTER than the Sony in sound quality, but it is at least as good, yet more comfortable to wear and actually sports a longer running time. I have to admit, I was ready to come here and say that these are overpriced when I first saw it, but I'm pleasantly surprised at how good these are. I shouldn't have been, Technics are quality and always have been.

I bought an Atoto F7 standard last summer, and while I loved the features for the price, there were some shortcomings that made me want to try their higher end S8 editions instead. I got a chance to swap it out for an S8 Ultra, and I'm very impressed so far.
Let me tell you, I had my reservations about a phone/tablet OS running as a car stereo, but Atoto has done an incredible job making this as smooth and user friendly and FEATURE PACKED as you could ever imagine. Android Auto works of course, if you want to use your phone connected to the display. Even better, WIRELESS Android Auto works as well! They don't advertise this since it is in beta as of the time I'm writing this, but after asking Atoto customer support about it I was given access to the new test firmware and it works surprisingly well with my Galaxy S10 phone. All I have to do is press the Carlink button on the screen, my phone can stay in my pocket, and within 10-15 seconds the Android Auto connection is displayed on the car screen as if I had plugged it in. It also has an excellent Bluetooth audio input for the microphone, which is something I struggled with on the F7 I purchased previously. My car has a convertible roof that creates extra wind noise on the highway even closed, and callers can hear me just fine! But of course, the biggest pro is the ability to run Android apps directly on the head unit without needing to connect my phone.
I preloaded offline maps for most of NY/NJ in Google Maps, so wherever I end up I can navigate home (even if I don't have reception up in the mountains), all without needing my phone connected. I can also stream youtube and other apps (for the passengers, obviously!) as well as install all kinds of cool automation tools and car diagnostics thanks to a bluetooth OBDii plug I already owned.

It's not without a few caveats, however. Some things to be aware of:
1) The unit has a 5 minute delay when shutting off. This is apparently to avoid data corruption in case of a power cycle (key removed and restarted, such as for example if restarting the car). If you plug anything into the USB ports, you'll see them still on and drawing power for a solid 5 minutes after you've left the car. My wireless charger, for example, continues to be lit up and charging if I use the head unit's QuickCharge port built in. Any other peripherals such as remotes or volume knobs, etc, will remain illuminated for those few minutes. While most apps (built in music player, youtube, etc) are able to receive the signal to stop playing when the power is shut off right away, third party apps (such as some podcast or other streaming music players) actually CONTINUE TO PLAY during this 5 minute delay unless you paused/stopped them before removing the key. It's only a few minutes, and the truth is I usually play podcasts from my phone streaming, which DOES shut off right away since the Bluetooth connection is severed immediately when the key is removed. However I was surprised to find out it didn't stop everything immediately and they don't tell you this in the instructions at all.
2) If you are using Wireless Android Auto / Carplay, it creates a wifi ad-hoc connection that your phone connects to. With Android Auto, this can take a pretty big hit off your battery, but it is worth it to not pull your phone out on a small drive. However, due to the 5 minute delay I mentioned earlier, you might find that your phone is still connected to the car for a few minutes after you've left if you are in proximity of it. My car is parked just outside my office window, so I was surprised my phone wasn't connecting to my office wifi at first, then a few minutes later the car finally shut off the wifi and my phone was able to connect to the local network as expected. That delay, once again, was a little bit unexpected since at first I did not understand what was wrong.
3) Bluetooth and Android Auto volume are not consistent. For some reason, when connected with Android Auto, the volume is louder. So if you switch between them you'll have to adjust. Again, none of these are deal breakers, but things I found odd.
4) Bluetooth streaming has limited control over track. This is the one that surprised me the most since the less expensive F7 is superior in this regard. For those who know about Bluetooth profiles, there's the streaming stereo profile which gives you some ID tag metadata, and then there's AVRCP, which is the part used for remote controlling the playback. It seems that if you're playing audio from a phone, you are only getting the first profile, and not the AVRCP one. I've included a picture to illustrate the difference. With track control like you get on a dedicated bluetooth headunits, it shows the duration of the file being played, and you can even scrub through it by holding the forward and reverse buttons (like you would on an old school CD player). I listen to a lot of audiobooks so I like seeing how far into the file I am. But on the S8, it just shows the name of the file and artist/title, and then dancing lines to the audio levels. To be honest, the dancing lines are kind of distracting as well, but I can just hit home to go back to the main screen and not look at them. There's not much point in staying on that screen if I don't get track duration info anyway.

All in all, I think these setbacks are largely due to the way Android works and was designed as an OS. Atoto has had to customize a lot of things to make it work as a head unit, since things like receiving a Bluetooth stream (remember, phones and tablets running Android transmit to OTHER speaker systems, the system itself wasn't designed to be a receiver!) and going into a specialized "sleep" that shuts off all critical functions when you leave (all radios and apps running shut off) yet starts back up within 2 seconds when you turn it back on, etc (this is not regular sleep which still runs background operations- you don't want to come back to a dead battery! but powering off completely means you have to wait longer for bootup)... I think these limitations are reasonable. Atoto support has been amazing and incredibly responsive, whenever I had a question or concern, they got back to me within 24 hours which is more than I can say about radios I've owned from Pioneer and Sony in the past.
I think with time and software updates, they can eventually find clever ways around most of those caveats mentioned above, in which case I'd update this review to 5 stars. For now, I'd say this is a solid buy for what you get, I don't think a better iteration of this product with these features exists yet today. The sound quality is better than my stock Toyota ever was (even using the JBL amp it came with), and all in all I'm super happy with it so far.

I know it sounds silly in this day and age, but sometimes we need to sing the praises of a music player that still gives you a traditional audio jack. That's where devices like these shine over using a modern cell phone- I like that this actually uses USB-C for charging so you can use a modern phone charging port but still use REAL headphones or your home stereo without an adapter.
This overall a good mp3 player. The headphone jack is a bit of a tight fit, and taking out the Micro SD can spring/project it a couple of inches if you don't take it out gently. The sound quality is good with a bit of extra reverb making a very open and uncondensed sound.
The user interface is a custom one, and you can find some that run modified versions of Android which feel a little bit more polished, but otherwise this does the job and seems pretty straight forward.

My daughter loves these for the their fit and the concept overall. She has small ears and said this is one of the first comfortable earbuds she managed out of the box. The sound quality is ok, but she really likes the mirror functionality of the case. The problem with that feature, however, is that the display stays on for too long sometimes. It will show her the battery level when she closes it, but then you can't turn it off right away- you have to wait for the display to time out so that you can use the mirror again. Kind of silly for a case that advertises using it as a makeup mirror. But otherwise it's a pretty cool set of affordable earbuds.

I love the concept of bone conducting headphones, and if you haven't tried a set before you really should! The sensation is a little unsettling at first but when you get used to it, you are rewarded with the ability to hear deep bass in your sounds without covering your ears completely the way ear buds and over-the-ear headphones require. They're not for everyone admittedly, but I love that I can feel/hear the sound and still be aware of my surroundings and able to respond if someone calls my name.
Good bone conducting headphones are easily 2x-3x the price of these, so keep that in mind. This is not going to be an alternative to a big name brand set. However, they aren't terrible either, and I kind of like them for the novelty of it at the price point.
If audio quality is your primary goal, understand that for the same money you can get a very decent pair of traditional headphones that will outshine this. But where's the fun in that?
4 stars for the novelty of it, but I give the sound quality and cost value only 3 stars.

I was skeptical because I've used multi-point bluetooth speaker arrays before that just sort of doubled-up a mono signal to different speakers. But this appears to be using the same Bluetooth 5 protocol that wireless earbuds utilize to send a proper dual-stream (left and right) channel for true stereo sound!
I did some sound tests that play only on each channel at a time, and it performed EXACTLY as intended! They look really cool and the lights add a lot of character to an evening garden party as well. The only issue however is that they don't get as loud as other speakers I've used. They are plenty loud for any sort of indoor space, but you can't really place these at either side of a backyard and expect to hear each other at maximum volume. You need bigger DJ-style speakers for that. But if you just want some background tunes to set the mood at a get-together on an average sized porch or deck, these are very nice and don't require any electrical outlet nearby.
I like them and intend to to use them more as the warm weather sets in.

I have a rather large LED panel that I like using as a key light, however it supports only AC power or V-mount, and with this I can finally use it wirelessly on an impromptu setup without access to outlets. I've used other accessories from Neewer and on my camera equipment, from cages to adapters and mounts, and I've always been impressed with it for the asking price. I'm happy to say this is the same experience I was expecting from them. The product does what it is supposed to and at a price that seems more than reasonable. If you need an affordable V-mount battery and charger with D-tap support, it's hard to go wrong with this option. The USB is nice to have too, but I didn't really need or use that option.

I was looking for a simple keyboard/mouse combo to use with a Windows 10 htpc attached to a projector. Pairing was simple enough- unfortunately, I needed to dig up a real USB mouse in order to pair, but that's true of all Bluetooth input devices. Unlike a unit that uses a USB dongle, you need some other form of input to initiate the process first. On my fire stick, I was able to pair it using the remote pretty easily as well. Once paired, you are able to use it like a directly connected keyboard or mouse by just powering it on in the future.
The lights are cool looking (and very nice when using in the dark with a home theater setup), and the keyboard is nice and large, easy to type on. However, the mouse was little bit too jumpy for my taste. It was difficult to nail icons with accuracy due to how erratically it moved. On Windows, I'm sure I could have turned down the mouse speed to make it better, but on my fire stick there isn't that kind of control available. I definitely would not use this as a keyboard/mouse replacement for a desktop experience due to the mouse experience, however it is ok for a presentation control or htpc that doesn't require a lot of pointing or clicking.
The only thing is that I KNOW there are smaller keyboard-only devices on the market if you aren't going to need the mouse that much, and ones that can use a USB dongle to avoid the pairing process. And if you want to use this with something like a firestick or Roku, one could argue the mouse part (which takes up a significant amount of real estate on the bar) is superfluous and doesn't have such precision control even if you DO want it (using Silk browser, for example). I sort of feel like you can get better options in all those scenarios, but it is OK at what it does. So 4 stars at best.

I've owned many different models of computer mouse over the years, and I have to admit I rather like this one. Your hand rests easy on it thanks to the subtle ergonomic curve, and it does exactly what you expect it to do and works as it should- no frills like extra mappable buttons that you forget exist and press accidentally (I'm looking at YOU, recently retired mouse that accidentally closed the page I was working on more than once and lost my work!). I like this exactly because it is a basic and professional feeling mouse without the bells and whistles that require a learning curve.

The ergonomic shape is much easier to palm and use comfortably than a flattened mouse, however it is clearly designed to be used in your right hand, so if you're a lefty-mouser, this might not be the right choice. It also reminds me heavily of my old favorite Logitech wireless mouse... I threw it away years ago because a corroded battery ruined the contacts inside, but it looked and felt almost exactly like this and was considered one of the best wireless mice for professional use at the time. Good job Amazon for making this one so affordable and keeping all the good stuff.

[[VIDEOID:b45226034e07b4e60a830fa1a8bc9e15]] A few years ago, the only reliable option for this was an adapter from a brand called Magewell. It was expensive and overheated if you streamed for too long with it. Now, streaming is much more of a thing and the need for adapters like this have skyrocketed. There are dozens of cheap ones out there but most of them weren't great quality. This version is not only from a brand gamers know, but it actually supports 4k and it's REAL 2160p resolved resolution (not just downsampled to 1080 like cheap adapters).
No drivers or settings required, desktop OS sees it as a 4k webcam, really very much plug and play performance. I'm quite pleased with it and would totally recommend it. Glad there are better options these days than yesteryear.

Ok, first things first: Don't expect these to be great audiophile-sounding headphones. They are not. Can you listen to music with them? Sure. But at less than 7 bucks per set, set your expectations realistically. Then be pleasantly surprised when they are surprisingly decent for private listening on a budget. No, you won't get full symphony dynamic range response- Where they shine is in quantity and availability. If you've got a room of people having zoom meetings with clients or kids at home in online classrooms, these are invaluable. They have integrated microphones for 2-way communication, and GREAT for listening to movies / shows on a trip. We have a large family and on a recent plane ride, we were able to take these along for in-flight entertainment. Plenty for everyone plus some extras if anything breaks or gets lost. They are kind of large but at least the ear parts pivot 90 degrees flat so that they fit in a backpack with other things. The cords are also flat which is great for wrapping and avoiding tangles if they get thrown into a box together. The colors are fun, each of my kids could pick a different color to their liking. I highly recommend these for classrooms or large families on a budget.

There are a lot of people in my house. Things like keys and remotes are ALWAYS getting lost, so a unit like this is very welcome!
We used to have a similar device over a decade ago that was much bulkier, mostly looked like an additional key fob on my keychain only bigger, and would chew through batteries quickly. I think we used it for only a month before just removing it from our car keys.
I like how much sleeker and slim looking this device is, a much more modern take on the item locator concept. The tags are actually so thin, it comes with adhesive hook-and-loop pads to attach to other non-keyring things as well, like the back of a remote control. The range is OK- unlike other products (such as Tile), the range seems to be only within a room or two away. From the front door, if my keys are in my bedroom, it would not ring. However as I passed from room to room, eventually when I get near the room they are in, it starts ringing. The flashlight feature is cute but not really useful.
Something to note: The fobs use watch batteries which are included, but the locator requires AAA cells, which are NOT. I actually didn't have any on hand and needed to go out and get some more to try this.

Otherwise, these are cheaper than a set of Tile or similar product locator fobs. And it doesn't require an app on your phone. I like it.

This is a very cool piece of computing hardware for specific uses. The fanless design means unlike other mini PCs that I've tried, this is actually silent! I'm surprised because the i5 CPU should generate more heat than the miserly Celeron that other mini PCs use, but the fins seems to dissipate heat rather well so far.
The 6 ethernet ports means this can make a pretty cool Windows-powered server for internet or file serving, and the fanless design means it can sit in a home users' closet and not make any audible noise either! While the CPU is pretty good, the GPU is pretty...not. If you look at the attached user benchmark, you'll see the CPU benched at about 74th percentile, but the GPU at a disappointing 4th percentile.
That means you won't really use this for things like games, not that anyone was expecting to. However, it does sort of limit this use for something like a media server using a platform such as Plex, as it would rely on the GPU for real-time media encoding.
For just playing back HD video it should be sufficient, and for other kinds of custom home server use and/or industrial use, this is a pretty interesting and useful product!

This is a great wireless mouse and keyboard set that frees you from cables. I just got a convertible standing desk, and knowing that I'm now able to easily convert without possible cable snag is exactly what I needed. The keyboard is actually really nice, it has a very comfortable click and is full sized with number pad, and even a dedicated calc button (something I was wary to give up on my full wired keyboard!).
The mouse is ok, but its going to take some getting used to compared to my old gaming-style mouse. There's a button to cycle through three options in dpi for speed selection, and the scroll wheel and clicking buttons work well enough, but I think I was spoiled by a very high end mouse before and this is just something I need to get used to. The movements feel a bit more muted than my old one. In no way is it BAD, believe me I tried a wireless mouse before this one that was just awful and would frequently disconnect and lag. This is consistent and works well enough for most things, I think the average user would be very happy with it.
The keyboard uses 2 AAA batteries and the mouse uses a single AA, both of which come included with the set (nice!). I like this pair and I'm happy with it so far!

First the good- this is a decent mini computer that is useful for MANY things! It is not going to replace a gaming desktop for high end applications, but it is plenty powerful for running browsers or work applications on two displays simultaneously (even has 2x HDMI ports which claim to support up to 4k each!). It's also an excellent option for a streaming HTPC or digital signage, and can be mounted to the rear of a monitor or TV with a standard VESA mount. With this, you can basically make any screen into an AIO computer!
It is plenty fast to respond thanks to the SSD, and has enough RAM and CPU power to multitask through everyday tasks pretty effortlessly.
Here's the downsides though:
1) No USB-C port. Or at least, not a NORMAL one. Sure, you've got plenty of USB ports (some fast 3.0 as well as some regular 2.0), but the omission of such a useful all-in-one C connection in a modern tech device is just odd. For example, I have a touch screen monitor and tablet that can connect via a single USB-C connection - otherwise it requires three separate plugs for power, hdmi and USB input. On my laptop, I can use the USB-C port and it does everything with a single cable. I thought this would be a PERFECT use for such a mini PC, but I'm stuck doing it the messy 3-cable way since there is not a USB-C port available. Makes it much more of a hassle.
Meanwhile, underneath the spare HDD bay, there IS a hidden USB-C port inside! However it is not a fully functional one. Not only is it in a bizarre difficult-to-reach location, I tried connecting some USB-C devices to it and while the system indicated something was connected, it could not operate it. I'm guessing this is nothing more than a USB-A connection in a USB-C housing, or perhaps not a full USB3.1 standard, and this is why it is hidden. Or, perhaps saved for the manufacturer for updates, possibly why it is not accessible to the outside.
So, essentually, no USB-C on a PC in 2021.
2) This seems identical to another Mini-PC I owned once, the ACEPC GK2. Same specs, same housing, even same weird USB-C inside the spare hdd bay. This isn't necessarily a con since I loved that mini-PC, however it died an untimely death when the SSD kicked the bucket without warning a few months into owning it. I found a support forum of other users claiming the same problem, and their official support's answer was to buy a new 2.5" SSD to place in the bay, which we had to buy ourselves. Very upset about that, and the computer is no longer sold here, so I can't even complain to anyone about it. So far so good on this unit, but I'm wary that this appears to be the same computer rebranded under a different name. I hope this won't suffer the same face in a few months. I'll keep an eye on it and report back if there are any issues.

We've been using an older first generation Portal and like it very much. I was not expecting to be so impressed with this one, but wow have they managed to improve almost everything about the original! It still has the very cool zoom-and-pan style camera feature that follows the subject, as well as all the fun filters and of course my kids' favorite, story time... but the polish and style of this unit is really premium. The speaker is fantastic and LOUD if you want it to be. The clarity and bass rivals my bookshelf speakers so well, sometimes the kids play music off it and I could have sworn they were using the speakers in the living room. But the biggest improvement over the previous generation is the ability to run off battery power and move around. The "portable portal" honestly makes so much sense, I wonder why the original stationary style ones came out first!
Make no mistake, it is NOT a tablet, it is not thin and won't fit in an attaché case nicely. It is wedge-shaped making it stand easily at an ideal angle, and even has a cut-out handle to pick it up and carry it to a better location for video chat. This is great for bringing it to wherever my kids happen to be congregating currently, and it can be put back up on the shelf when done to charge. Like the original Portals, it has Alexa built in and can act as an Echo for most things, however it is very tied into Facebook's ecosystem. That means that although it seems to run something akin to Android behind the scenes, this is NOT going to offer a standard App store, and even things like Youtube are not available for it (licensing issues with Google I'd suppose). However there is a browser, and you can navigate to YouTube and play it from the website just fine, although a proper app would be much easier to navigate. It does have Plex support, which I found interesting since I have a Plex server. I never thought I'd find Plex available where Youtube is not! Meanwhile, between Youtube in the browser, Amazon Music through Alexa and content on Plex, there are plenty of ways to make it a music streamer on that glorious better-than-it-should-sound speaker. And the camera works just as well if not better than the OG Portal!
Calls over FB Messenger or Whatsapp work well, and of course the camera / mic not only have a switch to toggle, but the camera has a physical cover that can slide over the lens in case you don't trust Facebook not to snoop. But that's another story.
All things considered, this is a solid product.

[[VIDEOID:39f57150f79275f153991c4d149bb17]] Ok, first the good things:
-This supports Android Auto and Apple Carplay (we only tested Android)
-It takes a measly single-DIN slot and gives you a fold out touch screen display to make things like the backup camera, phone UI, etc, possible which normally would not fit in a single DIN space.
-I can't stress this enough, but IT HAS A VOLUME KNOB. I can't even tell you how hard it is to find a modern radio with Android Auto / Car Play support that doesn't rely on touch screen buttons!

That being said, it has some issues. As you can see in the video attached, sometimes it takes more than one touch to navigate the touch screen options. A more annoying issue, however, is the AM radio. You can't pick a station that ends in a zero! So stations like 550 which we wanted to listen to, simply CAN'T be tuned in! Even if you try to manually type it in, for some reason the dial pad starts reducing available numbers as you pick, as if they don't WANT you to be able to pick a zero as the last digit. It's very strange!

I'd say for the user experience it should be 3 stars, but I'm adding a 4th because it's kind of rare to find a radio like this that fits in the space it does and offers these features. This Ford truck had a busted radio from the 90s, and this is a VERY welcome facelift and upgrade. I really like it and think for the price you're getting a lot of functionality. Of course you can't expect the polish or audiophile sound quality of a Pioneer or Alpine head unit, or even the mid-range quality of something like an Atoto, so for the price considering how unique of a product this is, plus the included camera, etc, I'd say it's a good value for a truck like this. I just wish the AM radio weren't so weird!

I wanted to use this to project sound at a small corporate gathering. Too small to use a full blown PA system, too big to use a standard bluetooth speaker. This is a really good in-between size! I was able to use the bluetooth mode to project music, as well as use a wireless mic system to project voice (using the hardwired receiver inputs on the back). The only thing is that the mic port on the back of this has some weird echo effect that I did not like. Thankfully the guitar port was very clean, so I switched the mic to that one.
It gets loud enough to get the job done, although I feel like I've gotten louder responses from other speakers this size before. It is still good enough for my intended purpose so I won't deduct any stars for that. The lights can be turned off if you don't like them, but they are pretty cool too. The only other caveat is that the buttons aren't easy to see. They are embossed rubber-on-rubber, and don't light up. So if you are in a dark room and trying to figure out which one is volume, it is more difficult than it should be to figure it out. I wish they had made those buttons more visible, either using a white text label or light up the buttons or something other than black-on-black buttons. But other than that, it's a great speaker, looks good and sounds pretty decent.
At 150 I'd argue there might be better options, but as of the time of this writing, the listing price is 99 dollars, which I think is worth it for a speaker with these features.

This is a great value for 2 "classic" wired earphones. They come with multiple tips so you can install ones that will fit your ears (we have small ear canals in my family), and they do a decent job blocking outside noise when properly fitted. They get plenty loud (like, loud enough that the warning on my phone makes sense to give), and the sound quality is fine. It's not audiophile quality, but I'm not expecting them to be. I'm expecting them to be functional at this price, and they definitely are that! I'm giving one to my daughter to use with her music player on the bus ride, and the other I'm using as a backup in my camera case for video gigs (I had my over-the-ear studio monitors die on a job once, so having a no-frills backup pair is welcome) and maybe to throw in a backpack when I don't want to charge my wireless earphones for my phone. Thank goodness some phones still have a standard 3.5mm jack! So glad they are still selling classic earbuds, and these are a great value at a great price!

I tried this out to keep some of my work equipment in (live production gear like adapters, laptop, cables), and I really like the different pockets inside to keep things organized, but most important to me is how it can be carried in 3 ways. It can be worn like a backpack, turned sideways like a briefcase, or put atop a rolling cargo suitcase / Pelican case, using the strap in the back to go over the handle of the case and hold it in place. If I'm traveling light, I can just carry it solo. Or wear it on my back. Or bundle it with my wheelie cases.
The lack of external pockets means you can really move this in any direction and things won't fall out, it's really well designed to be completely closed in any orientation. It's also evenly sized in all dimensions, unlike a bookbag or pack which gets wider in the bottom and thinner on top. This makes this bag a very useful companion for travelling with just about anything.

My son has been wanting a gaming monitor for higher refresh rates in his games for years now. Obviously we were excited to try this one out, and I have to tell you... I'm impressed.
I usually stick with name brands for my computer monitors, and for the retail price this is at, I wasn't expecting a whole lot. But the image quality is pretty sweet, the resolution at 2560 x 1440 is noticeably better than his old 1920x1080 one, and the 144hz refresh rate ain't bad either (a whooping jump over the 60hz his old one maxed out at, which is really what he wanted).
BUT WAIT, THERE'S MORE!

1) The monitor has SPEAKERS. He connected with the included display port cable and realized that a new audio device showed up on his desktop. I told him yeah, because DP and HDMI can carry audio so there's a 3.5mm jack on the back to plug in speakers. My LG computer monitors do that too, but they can't actually play sound. There's just a jack on the back to plug in speakers / headphones, and it just makes it easier to bring the plug closer than my desktop. But when he tried it, lo and behold, sound came out of the monitor like a TV! Holy cow, this could double as a media center for a fire stick or something because it has integrated sound! My son usually uses headphones for games and didn't like the look of speakers on his desk, so he's never had a way to play something out loud for another person to hear before. This is a VERY cool option to have!
2) There's an RGB strip on the rear of the monitor so it looks cool from behind! (see included photo).
3) There's a funky little projector circle that displays an image of a tiger head (seems to be the branding logo) on the wall behind the monitor. See included photo of wall to illustrate.

My son loved that projector thing and actually tried to find the logo online so he can make it his desktop background, but sadly the monitor doesn't seem to have any branding we can look up to find that logo, which is a shame. Otherwise, what an awesome product! More than I expected, so far we are very pleased with it!

[[VIDEOID:ef18b2bc61d2bf43363a5f3d51e2b5d8]] This is a pretty great tablet geared for kids. Inside of the "kid-proof" case is an Android 11 powered tablet with a comfortable-to-read 10" display, much better than the 7" Kindle Fire tablet that my kids used to use before this. It has the standard Google play store, yet still comes with plenty of parental control tools and a pretty great suite of software for kid friendly use (something I really liked about the Kindle OS).
It even comes with a USB OTG plug so that you can plug in accessories like a USB sticks, a keyboard or barcode scanner, etc.
The only thing that bothered me a little bit is that the case makes the buttons and USB port a little bit difficult to line up. To turn on and off the power, for example, you need to find the on button next to the volume buttons, which isn't immediately easy for a kid to find. I can imagine younger ones especially hitting every other button first. And the OTG adapter had some trouble fitting in the hole cutaway since the port didn't sit exactly in the middle of the case. The cameras were also cheap-phone quality, but then again I never expect good camera performance at this price range.
That being said, it does an excellent job at what it is designed to do: Be a kind friendly tablet that parents will be happy about.

I like this style of camera very much. It mounts under the lip for the license plate on my vehicle and gives a very factory-looking installation, unlike the bracket mounted or license plate style ones I have been using previously. I had tried a different variation of this (also from GreenYi) before, however I had some difficulty with the product due to the way it worked on my head unit. The 170 degree view was only if using the AHD mode, which my unit did not support. In the lower CVBS resolution (compatible with more devices) it was cropped down to only something like 100 degrees, which was far too narrow to see around me in the back.
THIS product, however, seems to keep the full 170 degree view regardless of resolution supported! Just cut the green wire to set your own grid lines on the headunit (if supported), and good to go. My only reluctance to give this 5 stars is the fact that it is *just* that much tighter than my 175 degree bracket / license plate camera I was using until now. That extra 5 degrees doesn't sound like it would make a difference, but it does to me. I can see the borders of my bumper on the 175, but with 170 the edge is just out of view. This camera looks nicer and is clearer than my 175, but I think I need to stick with my 175 for practical useful reasons.
I'm waiting to see a wider angle from GreenYi, maybe they'll produce a 180!

This is a great cable for use with my projector setup. I have a speaker tower that I use for sounds when watching a projected movie, but the trick is getting the speaker closer to the audience and away from the projector/laptop. This cable plugs right into the laptop and lets me put the speakers a healthy 15' away. It works perfectly for this, the sound is clear and the length is fantastic. I'm very happy with this product!

I have a kiddie inflatable bounce house with a similar blower system, so I was expecting this to be LOUD. Like, too loud for our usual outdoor sound system. But I'm pleasantly surprised to say the volume isn't all that bad... especially since you'll be sitting far enough away to see it that the sound becomes less and less of an issue. That being said, I think I didn't realize in my head just how HUGE this is! I have a large garage I wanted to test it out in first (big enough for a basketball hoop inside), and THIS WAS TALLER THAN THE GARAGE. It must be used outside, and they're not kidding about tying it down either! If there's wind, this thing will act like a sail and blow away. But when used correctly in the right setup, this is really an incredible screen. Much more fun that my old foldable or pull-down projector screen. You'll need a bright enough projector to present from far enough away, so I suggest using a real brand name high lumen one, the cheap made-in-china projectors tend to be optimistic about their brightness lumen rating, resulting in a picture that gets pretty dim when you're this far away. My trusty Viewsonic does a decent job, but I'd even try to get something rated for more light output if you can. The more the better. Great product, I recommend it!

I've been hired to do a lot of live stream jobs since the pandemic, and that usually means my trusty laptop with OBS installed + Magewell HDMI to USB adapter + camera/tripod. If they need multiple cameras, I need to lug along my Blackmagic ATEM box and have that do camera switching before the Magewell. It's a lot of equipment to set up, worth a LOT of money, and that's not even counting the internet connection, which sometimes I need to supply via cellular hotspot device.
This unit replaces ALL OF THOSE. I can't even begin to accurately describe how incredibly versatile of a tool this is, but considering the price of all that equipment individually, this is a STEAL at the asking price. Sure, OBS might still be able to pull more complicated tricks that the UI here can't, and the ATEM switch can support more cameras (including SDI cables), but most of the time this is truly all you need and even then some! And there is so much value in the simplified hardware setup here.
The unit seems to run a customized UI over Android, and I was able to do some live multi-cam switching with minor effects on Youtube live using the built in Cat5 port. I am blown away with how capable this is. The only downside is there's a bit of a learning curve since it is a very niche product and offers a LOT of functionality, so you have to familiarize yourself with the features and how it works. But once you do? This is an excellent tool for any streamer. Highly recommended!

These are great for taking an HDMI output and converting it to a standard SDI cable, great for long distance or for inputs that require it. I used this recently for a live multi-cam concert stream to bring a small camera (Sony A7S) into my Blackmagic ATEM mixer over to mix with other SDI cameras. I ran it over 150' of SDI cable and it worked perfectly with no noticeable lag. For the price this costs, it's a no brainer to have on a job like this.

I have an Android Auto head unit in my car, but it requires a direct connection to my phone to work. When I'm in a hurry, I usually throw my phone in the holster of the car and start driving... I don't have time to dig out the USB cable and carefully plug it in, it's an extra step that I often decide to skip and just stick with Bluetooth audio instead.
This cable changes everything! Now, the cable is magnetically hanging next to the phone already, all I need to do is wave it near the bottom of the phone and CLICK! It connects and starts Android Auto!
I had previously tried another similar magnetic cable, but it seemed to only work well as a charging device, it wouldn't send the data necessary for a connection like Android Auto over the USB cable. I'm happy to say, this one DOES, and it's every bit as wonderful as I hoped it would be! I can't speak yet for longevity, but so far I'm pleased with it. The unit comes with enough plugs and tips for my wife to have one in her phone as well, and of course enough cables for both of us to charge when not in the car as well. It IS a little bit of a finger magnet to have the little nub sticking out on the bottom of my phone, I wonder if eventually that will shorten the life of my USB port or the tip, but for now I'm very happy with it and would strongly recommend it for anyone in my position!

I have another similar stand that I have used for my projector and laptop. I wanted a second one so I could both at the same time (projector mounted next to laptop, both on their own stand).
Compared to my other one, I liked that this could fold up smaller thanks to the top being able to fold in half, however I found the whole thing a little less sturdy overall. The center pole would wobble a little, and the top part that folds was actually really annoying to unfold to set up because the screws need to be removed and replaced. Sure, they are thumbscrews and you don't need tools, but I found it annoying as they would fall out as I was trying to hold it in place and decided it was better to just leave it assembled. Which begs the question, why even bother folding it? I also found that if I used it with the laptop and typed, the whole thing would shake with my typing. If you want to use it as only a projector stand where it won't get touched, I think that's fine and it will work well enough. But if you want equipment to not wobble if touched, I'd look for a different one.

These are very good mid-range headphones. They look cool, are comfortable to wear, and have much better sound quality than the cheapo headphones you find on Amazon. Sure, they're not Bang and Olufson, but you're not paying that insane premium price tag either.
For what these are, they are excellent quality. Has support for different types of cable connections, and when used with a proper Quad DAC audio player, the sound quality is impressive for the money!

Anyone in photography will tell you that the bigger the light source, the better the light. Hard small harsh lights are the worst in regards to shadows and contrast, and make terrible eye reflections of the light. Ring lights are popular because they spread a more even and therefore softer glow, and have those signature round eye catch lights. But a GIANT ring light like this one? Makes a good thing even better!
I was playing around with it tonight, but in the effort of keeping my family private, I used a Darth Vader helmet as my subject to share. Pictures are labelled, one without the ring light as a control, then using it to create a side light and then again as a front light, and then a practical example of using it to cast a soft light on a scene (my kid playing- face edited out obviously).
I like that this light comes with a camera mount as well as a cell phone holder, and especially that it can run on either battery OR plug in power. In fact, it even comes with 2 Sony camcorder batteries to power it! It only comes with one charger, so thankfully I already have other chargers for that type of battery around my house as it appears to require both to be used at once (so charging them one at a time is very annoying). I wasn't expecting the batteries so I'm pleasantly surprised and would not deduct any stars from an otherwise fantastic product!

I work in corporate video and photography for a living, and sometimes we need to rig up some bizarre camera setups to get the job done. Recently I needed a mini XLR mixer to feed into my camera but had to keep the controls accessible without putting the camera in a cage. Well, this little adapter worked PERFECTLY! I clamped it onto the the monopod leg securely, and attached the mini mixer to the 1/4 20 threading on the back.
Today, I attached a rigged battery bank to this to test power a camera for the duration of a concert unmanned. There are so many ways to attach and use accessories with it, I'd recommend this in the arsenal of anyone working with cameras that may need to rig up lights, monitors, audio equipment, or anything else in possibly non-conventional ways. I love it!

This is a fantastic IPS panel display that actually closely matches my laptop display in clarity, brightness and size/position. That makes it great for a quick "second screen" when I need to make a portable workstation on the go! Ideally, it should be possible to run the entire thing off a USB-C connection, so you don't need any additional power/hdmi/usb/etc connection. They advertise that this is possible.
However I was unable to get that to work. For some reason, my HP laptop, despite having a USB-C port, would not recognize this as a monitor. Neither would my phone which also supports display port over USB-C.
I needed to use the hdmi cable adapter, and then I was able to use the USB-C for power from my laptop. Interesting to note that if you want to use the display's touch screen capability, use the monitor in USB-C instead of the strictly powered one, and it will support full touch screen as well as power the unit. I was nervous when the single-cable setup didn't work that it would require all three plugs to be used in separate- power usb, usb for touch, and hdmi for video signal. 3 cables would have been too much and I'd just never use it. 2 cables are doable. I'd think a low powered unit such as a Raspberry Pi might require separate power since it likely can't supply enough power for the monitor, but the mini PC and laptop I tried it with seemed to do just fine running the monitor and using the same USB for touch-input support. I really wish it only required the single USB cable, however. I was unable to get that working no matter what I tried.
For what its worth, I'd give it 4 stars since it adds a touch enabled second screen to my laptop, and also makes my miniPC into a kiosk for interesting use at events. But I wish I could get it working with a single cable like it advertises. That would make it 5 stars.

I wish I could give this 3.5 stars. It works, and helps in all the ways I didn't like my old one, so it is worth at least 4 stars. But there are some things about it that could really use improvement.
To explain, I had a nice backup camera that I installed previously which only ended up being about 100 degrees of view. This wasn't as wide as I hoped, and only showed me what was directly behind the car. THIS camera, however, is a full 170 degree wide, which even shows the edges of my bumper in the fisheye effect. I can see the space next to me, cars behind me, everything that I can't see well usually thanks to the cloth convertible rear view window I have. Thankfully they used the same wiring harness as my previous camera so I didn't need to re-run my power and reverse trigger from the rear light, all of that I could keep which made the wiring pretty painless.

But what I didn't like:
1) The camera is VERY noticeable and it sticks out pretty far. I found the license plate holder covered up the state label of my plate and stuck out too far (camera was beyond the frame of my car) so I used the 2nd mount it includes which can attach to the plastic area over my plate. But even that, because of the mounting bracket requiring space above and behind the camera, sticks out like a sore thumb and still sits the camera beyond the bumper. As in, if someone parallel parks and gives my car a "bumper kiss" (as they call it when parking here in NYC), I have no doubt it will damage the camera as it hits there before it touches my bumper. As you can see in the included picture, bumper kisses are common here.
I turned the camera down so it is at least not sticking out past the bumper, but more in line with it now. I still get a good enough view thanks to how wide the camera is, but I wish I could position the camera better with more choice. I'm forced to use it like this or risk damaging the camera.
2) The picture quality is just OK. The older camera I'm replacing may have only been 100 degrees and not wide enough, but the quality of the image was superior. This one looks more like an old cell phone in color reproduction and smoothness. That's ok, it does the job I guess, but the old one was more pleasant to look at, especially at night. This works well enough at night, but my old one spoiled me because I know it could be better.

All in all, its a decent product that honestly gets the job done. But I wish it had better ways to mount it directly to the car in a way that takes up less space / looks sleeker / doesn't protrude, and that the camera image quality was a little bit better, especially in low light. But it'll do the trick if you want a cheap wide angle.

There's a lot that I like about these Philips headphones. All the classic features you'd expect from a higher-end over-the-ear style wireless headset are there, including support for an optional 3.5mm jack with included cable in the box, and they even threw in an airplane adapter and carrying case.
It's got soft ear cups and padded head bar, and a pretty awesome NC system. Here's the thing: I own a pair of Sony WH-1000 headphones so I was expecting to be somewhat spoiled and biased about the sound quality and build. And I am. The Sonys are still some of the best and the standard by which I judge other headphones in this style. BUT... at the time of this review, the price of this Philips product is less than half of what I paid for my Sony. Are the Sonys better? A little. Are they twice the price better? NO WAY. This is far better quality in sound and build than the cheapo bluetooth headphones, and if I didn't try them side by side with my Sony, it'd be hard to tell them apart. The feature set are similar, including the app control which actually made the phone really easy to pair as well.
One thing I actually really like about these is that there are more buttons than the Sony alternative. A dedicated button for mute, a dedicated button for noise cancellation, and of course power/pairing. But there are also touch sensitive controls on the ear cups, which I did not realize at first. I have mixed feelings about touch controls, I feel like they are easy to accidentally trigger, but so far it's actually been pretty good.
I think for the current asking price of around 150, the pros are solid enough to be worth recommending.

I have an old Toshiba TV that I bought from a friend who moved, and never got the remote. I've also got some stereo equipment that is missing the remote. It's actually been really hard to find third party replacements that support these obscure products, so I've been using an old LG phone (V20) from back in the days of IR blasters to program them. It's annoying because the phone is getting old and clunky and the battery has to stay charged, but at least if I lose it I can use Google services to locate it.
This universal IR is the best, and replaced ALL of those features now! It actually pairs with my current phone via an app, and you're able to really easily program the different functions and devices, and thanks to the app's UI, it is easy to understand what you are doing. It works great with the audio equipment and Toshiba TV, and if I misplace the remote the app has a find feature! So cool! I'm very happy with this device and I recommend it. I'm going to go put my old LG V20 on ebay now because this was literally the only reason I kept it!

Ok, so I have to admit at first I was wondering why someone would spend this much on a Bluetooth headset that isn't a feature-rich entertainment one like those from Sony or a major fad brand like Beats, both of which I have some experience with. But this, no... this is actually something different. This is a serious tool for serious use with serious built quality and seriously useful features. Seriously.
For example, the telescoping mouthpiece means you'll get unparalleled mic quality compared to headsets that pick the mic up by your ears (looking at YOU, airpods!), both in clarity and isolation from background noise. You can also physically bend it out of the way, or use the button on the mic itself to mute. Try doing that with airpods. Then there's the button based features. Shortcuts and touch-sensitive buttons are cool on aesthetic devices, but the physical controls on this are an ergonomic user experience DREAM. Everything is easy to access and control, no apps or press-and-hold or counting LED blinks, etc. Sort of makes me miss the old days of phones with physical switches and buttons. When you want your equipment to get serious, this is the sort of user experience you expect. Then there's the charging rack. OMG I love that, I can store it on my desk and it's charging automagically. Pick it up and put it on, ready to go. Never needs to be charged because it's been charging in between uses. Finally, I'm really impressed with the USB dongle option. You see, the one thing I really dislike about wireless headphones is that you usually need to pair it with a device, then unpair it to switch to another device. For example, using my Sony headphones on my phone and tablet, if my wife wants to borrow them for a zoom meeting, I need to pair with her device but then also unpair with mine so that it doesn't keep trying to reconnect to it. Sometimes we just give up and use a wired headset to avoid that mess. Non-bluetooth wireless headsets have a dongle, which makes it easy to swap what you are connected to (no unpairing needed, just move the dongle) but then you can't connect to devices without a USB port like a phone. This is the best of both- you can pair it with your phone, but ALSO use the USB to quickly connect with your desktop or laptop without going through the process of pairing and unpairing. This is the kind of usability and professional quality I would expect from a brand like Plantronics, and all the while it works well as a stereo headset for music/gaming/etc as well. Very comfortable to wear for long hours, I'd highly recommend it for serious users.

Yes, this is not a Kenwood or Alpine. And no, this is not an Android head unit. But honestly, it's actually really overwhelmingly been a positive experience, especially for the price.
Sure, it won't be the top-shelf quality audio, but you're not paying the price tag for that either. Thanks to my Toyota's built in JBL amp, I can honestly say the audio quality is at least on par with the factory radio that came with my car, so no complaints there. It isn't the cheapest head unit either, but honestly you won't get the features and customer support that this has with those. I'd say this is places at that perfect ratio of quality to price is an incredible value.
It is NOT an Android head unit, which is a good thing in my case. I've played with those, and didn't like them. Android is great and offers tons of customization, but for a daily driver it is ultimately an OS designed for a phone/tablet that was tweaked to be a car radio. The versions I tried, for example, took a long time to boot up, occasionally required updates like a phone, had background tasks that sometimes slowed the unit down, and things like switching to rear camera would mute the audio. This one, thankfully has NONE of that. This is a custom OS built from the ground up to be a car radio UI, and it works the way you expect (not like a phone/tablet pretending to be a car). The icons and fonts aren't just chosen at random like the bottom-barrel units, this actually is aesthetically pleasing to use. And when I WANT my phone UI on the screen, Android Auto is actually pretty great with my Pixel 3A.
Things that I found:
1) The style now is strictly buttons, knobs are outdated apparently, even with big brand names. I hate that, I miss my volume knob and hate fiddling with buttons to adjust the sound. Thankfully, I spoke to their support team who was super helpful at not only troubleshooting the steering wheel controls, but alerted me to the existence of an add-on remote part that connects to the IR port behind the radio, and gives some additional buttons you may not have on your steering wheel (it works in tandem with, not instead of). But the best part of that remote? IT HAS A VOLUME JOG DIAL around the outside! Since it magnetically sits in a holder, I was able to take it out, place an adhesive magnet on the faceplate around my radio, and BAM! I now have easy shortcut keys as well as a volume wheel! I'm thinking maybe I'll modify it to look more like a traditional knob (perhaps 3D print a knob part and hide the unit behind the plastic with a hole, I'm not sure yet), but the fact that this is supported as an extra customization is pretty great!
2) The rear camera requires a trigger wire, not just being turned on to activate. This isn't a bad thing, once I figured it out (thanks to their patient support team!). In fact, this adds the ability to turn on the rear camera while driving if desired, which is kind of useful if there's a lot of stuff in your car limiting rear visibility.
3) The mic quality for calls is only so-so. This is the only real con that I have with the device. It isn't the microphone, I tried using a pro-level Sennheiser lav mic to compare, and it just sounds a little more muffled than I'd like, as if there's an aggressive noise cancelling algorithm taking out too much fidelity from my voice. I can hear the other caller fine, but I tested calling an echo line as well as having someone call me, and using my phone in speakerphone had better mic quality than both the built in mic and the mic I mounted on the A-pillar. It's ok, and it works if I need it, but I wouldn't carry a long conversation on it, I think the other person would get annoyed trying to hear me after a while. But that's not really what I bought this for, I wanted to stream bluetooth audio and have Android Auto for maps, and for that it is perfect!

This is a great concept- my office setup has dual monitors for work, and I find it difficult when I travel to go back to using a single monitor on my laptop. But with this, you can connect what looks like a 15" tablet (with it's own protective cover/stand) to the laptop, and get that oh-so-sweet dual display goodness!
On my 15" 10th gen i7 HP laptop, the display is almost exactly the same size and is close enough in color and brightness to feel like an extension of the desktop, which is nice.
However, the USB-C single connection did not work. That is, this device supports connecting in a couple of different ways- it can be powered by USB and connected to a video source over HDMI, or with a modern USB-C that supports dp, you can connect one cable for both. I liked that second idea and tried to do that since my HP laptop supports USB-C connections. Well, the screen powered on but then said no connection, and the laptop said it detected a USB device but threw errors about it being unknown. The only way I could make it work is by switching to the USB input for power only and using a HDMI cable from the laptop. This is fine, however it's a little cumbersome with two sets of cables required, and then along with the charger for the laptop to keep the battery from depleting (running another LCD takes battery power), it ends up kind of messy pretty fast. I really wish it at least had a rechargeable battery itself, or at the very least worked with the USB-C cable like it was supposed to. Oh well. Otherwise, it is still functional and useful, so 4 stars.

This card's R/W numbers aren't amazing, but I didn't really expect them to be. For the price, the fact that you get 2x cards with 64gb is impressive! I'm not familiar with this brand and I'm not sure if I'd trust it with mission-critical storage (flying a drone for work, for example) especially if it requires high speed data to read and write, but for something like a media player or dashcam/security camera recording, this would be a great option to throw in.

For now, I'm formatting one to use in a Raspberry Pi project and the other will probably go in my car's media player. Definitely a good deal for the storage space.

There's a lot to like about this kit, starting with the price. For the money, I've owned similar light kits to this before, but this one comes with batteries and chargers for wireless use as well as the AC plug adapters for constant power. Similar kits that I've owned required me to buy the Sony-style FP batteries separately. It also comes with a soft case, however I found the case very flimsy and not very protective (it comes folded up inside the box, there is no rigidity to it). BUT, I realized that the box it comes it is roughly a similar size to the case when unfolded, and sure enough it actually can fit inside the case perfectly! I'm not sure if this was on purpose, it was not obvious to me that this was the intention so maybe don't throw away that cardboard if you want to give your case some protective strength (see attached photo for carboard box inside carrying case).
As far as the lights themselves... they are pretty good. I was concerned about them being less densely populated than other LED panels I've used, however it appears that each diode puts out more light than I was expecting so overall it is a good amount of light for using with video for something like an interview setting.
Meanwhile, the colors and party mode are a bit different for me. I'm used to using light kits as a professional tool, and I think the multicolor part is a bit too gimmicky. It's cool to set a tone with a color like the way I'd gel a red light for a setting or something, but the party mode? I can't imagine a use for the strobe effect of it changing color constantly. I have DJ lights that can move to music and this has a mode for that as well, however it seems that the only option is to change color with each beat suddenly- no gradual fade or anything like that. The hard cut is kind of migraine-inducing distracting, so I'd honestly rather use a different light for party background style color changes. As a light kit, it's pretty good, but the selling point of using it as a sound-controlled DJ thing is iffy. Maybe a DJ at a bar mitzvah would find that option useful?

For the type of run-and-gun projects I do, if I can get away with plugging a mic directly into the camera ( often a single stereo 3.5mm jack these days) I will always prefer to do that than a dual-sound setup that needs to by synced in post. However, sometimes you need more than one mic, so what's a one-man-crew to do? Well, traditionally I would use a TRS break out cable, which essentially looks like a headphone splitter Y-cable, but splits the Left and Right channel into separate plugs instead of doubling them. That's great because I can connect one mic to Left and the other to Right, then split them up and remix in post as needed.
But this is much more elegant solution- It is essentially the same idea, splitting the L + R into two sides, but not only is it less messy since you don't have Y cables dangling, it also serves as a point in which to mount 2 coldshoe receivers directly to single shoe mount, essentially making this an all-in-one solution to turn a single mic input setup into a dual one. No additional hardware necessary behind the second mic. I love this solution, it looks more professional, it is more reliable, and I would definitely recommend checking it out if you're in the same boat as me!

I'm a big fan of the Mi Band series of trackers, and this is the first device that finally got me to switch to something else. If you aren't familiar, Xiaomi and Huami aren't big brands in the US compared to other countries, but these are solid high quality products and not your standard fare Chinese junk. I've tried a LOT of different fitness trackers and smart watches- Everything from Google WearOS, Fitbit, Apple, and all the way down to the cheap trackers from Chinese throwaway brands with obscure apps. For a long time I've said I liked the features and quality of the expensive brands, but found they all had major flaws (battery life being a major one- I don't want another thing to charge as often as a phone!). The Mi band from Xiaomi was super affordable and high quality compared to others in that price range, and had a battery that only required being charged once a month.
This is basically the smarter older brother of that band. It is compatible with Mi Fit, so all my data transferred right over, but it is so much nicer than the band. For starters, the notification system is easier to read and keep up with messages, but the benefits go far beyond a larger screen. The music control is a nice touch, I like being able to pause and adjust the volume without taking my phone out of my pocket if playing on a BT speaker while I'm doing dishes, for example. The tracking is pretty accurate compared to other expensive brands, and while it doesn't support apps like Wear OS and Apple Watches, it has all the fitness functions you'd need built in already, including some fun widgets beyond the expected ones like a stopwatch, phone finder and even a compass! And unlike cheap brands, the UI is responsive and smooth. Not the smoothest out there for sure, but more than acceptably smooth considering how much a flagship smartwatch costs compared to this.
It has support for voice commands, but I honestly found that feature kind of gimmicky more than useful. The higher end version of this includes a speaker which might make the command function more useful as sort of a digital assistant, not to mention the ability to take phone calls from your wrist. But the model I got to try out lacks the speaker, which is a fine compromise for a cheaper price tag all things considered. The battery life at first was just OK, a few days on a charge if using lift-to-wake functions, but just as on my Mi Band tracker of old, I found if I turn off auto-wake and rely on using the button to wake the display, the battery life goes from counting in days to counting in weeks. That's the killer feature of this device- the ability to leave it on to track fitness and sleep habits without having to charge it so often. I'll have to charge it more than my old Mi Band's monthly top up for sure, probably at least 2x a month, but that's still very manageable.
So that's it, after years of loving my Mi Bands and considering it the standard by which all practical fitness trackers should be judged, I'm finally moving on to an Amazfit watch. This is a difficult value to beat.

[[VIDEOID:5a1bce8644783f1974b4478fd2851303]] The good: This device works! See the video attached using a Sony mirrorless camera going into the HDMI input as a webcam, recorded in the Windows 10 Camera app of my desktop. I love this little light! A colleague of mine uses a similar cube from a different brand to do interesting lighting with his photography at night, and I was always impressed with how much light you can get out of a little LED these days! This little cube has a rubber gasket for the charging port to make it dust/water resistant, and SO MANY different mounting points, the possibilities are endless!
I used it recently on a live production to light the crew so we could see our equipment around the dark stage. I think I'm going to need more of these, what a versatile tool!

I got this for my teenaged son to use on his gaming PC. He had actually broken his previous gaming headphones and this seemed like a no-frills decent replacement for him to try.
The sound quality is actually quite good. Both the ear pieces and the microphone are crisp and clear, so no complaints there. However my son found it a little uncomfortable to wear compared to his larger over-the-ear style headphones before. The actual ear parts on this are smaller, which means they don't fully envelop your ears the way other ones do. On the plus side, this means it doesn't block as much external noise, which I like for him in our household (no more calling his name when he can't us!), but others may want more noise isolation. Also, the smaller ear pieces aren't as comfortable when worn as the larger ones.
I also didn't like that it didn't come with an adapter to break out for mic and speakers like other headsets do. I thought it would come with that as an option, as I've never gotten a PC headset that didn't offer either a splitter or TRRS combo adapter so you can use it with both a laptop that has mic/headphone combos as well as separate mic and headphone jacks commonly found on a desktop.
Thankfully I had an extra one lying around for him to use, so that wasn't an issue. But something to take into consideration. Others, I've got to give it at least 4 stars for working well and doing what it should. But there might be other options for the price worth considering as well if you want larger earphones or a breakout cable included.

Ok, as an owner of real "Brand name" home theater projectors (Viewsonic, Epson, etc), I'm usually not impressed with the budget no frills variations. They are often misleading with their specs, using different standards of measurement for lumens, or having much lower resolution than they claim ("supports 1080p" but really only shows 480 or 720, and downscales the 1080 input). This one actually seems better than the cheapos I've tried in the past. As far as I can tell, this might even be a real native 1920x1080 full HD resolution for a change! The picture quality is decent, although the colors might not be as vibrant or true as my Viewsonic, and it definitely lacks the contrast ratio and brightness of brand name projectors as well.
BUT, one thing that blew me away with this, was the on-board speaker. I've never used a projector's speaker for a presentation before, they are usually terrible hollow tin-sounding messes, like trying to crank up a laptop speaker to fill a room (which is pretty much what they usually are). This one actually has a half decent speaker that I could use for something non-audio critical. That is, I wouldn't use it to hear the cinematic score behind an epic movie, however for broadcasting a speech or presentation to a room of people, I might consider the speaker good enough to not bother plugging in any other sound to it.
One thing I really miss compared to real projectors, however, is the ability to adjust the throw in addition to the focus. My Viewsonic lets me adjust the picture size with one knob and the focus with the other, so I am able to make the thrown image be the correct target size within a small range of distances. With this, the only thing you can adjust is the keystone angle. Don't get me wrong, that's useful to have as well, but you are limited to having the projector sit an exact distance away to get a specific size throw. I'd rather have the throw adjustment.
The bottom line is, this still won't replace the quality and experience of using a brand name projector. Heck, even a 720p Viewsonic will look better than this even if it's full HD. But for what it is, I have to say it's a pretty good value!

This is an excellent power strip for those who need many things plugged in. If you have a workstation with multiple monitors, external HDDs, speakers, and other accessories, THIS is the strip to get! With 10 outlets, you already are starting off with more than the usual 6-8, but add to that the fact that these face AWAY from the center on opposite sides, so wall wart adapters (such as those found on AC/DC plugs for external HDDs or speakers) have enough room to NOT take up the plug next to it! And then beyond that, you get built in USB ports, and even a type-C port, which means you can avoid additional adapters for all your USB-charging things.
And if that wasn't enough? This thing also has the flat the type of plug, so it can easily fit in the outlet behind your desk or other furniture, and not require a gap in the wall.
Essentially, other power strips should take note: THIS is what every single one needs to be like. They took everything that anyone could ever complain about on a traditional strip/surge protector, and went ahead and fixed it. A perfect product!

I have a mess of wires by my TV- adapters and remote control receivers, etc. My Fire Stick has a USB breakout box for a remote keyboard as well as ethernet port, and then an HDMI extender for use with my projector as well as an HDMI to HDMI + audio to send the sound to my stereo system.
