It's a mess, and I used to keep it all inside of a shoebox. My wife wasn't a fan, it always looked kinda grungy. This plastic box is perfect however! All my adapters and cables can be wrapped up and contained in a neat little package that has holes made for this purpose, as well as being easy to open and rummage around if needed.
All that while having a wood colored top that matches the wood of much of our furniture. This is truly a great solution to a modern day problem!

This is a decent black backdrop for use in studio setups for photography or video. It can be held up using standard equipment like a rod and muslin clamps. I found, however, that the material has a touch of a sheen to it. It isn't a huge deal and honestly can be easily worked around, but it seems to reflect a little more light back at the camera than other backgrounds if you aren't careful. For example, a hair light that I've used before on other backgrounds spilled a bit onto this and it made a visible area of the frame brighter. I had to use some larger barn doors on the light to deflect it better, but the point is a more expensive and professional level material might not have needed that.
For the budget I'd say it is still good and worth using to get a black background on the cheap.

I wanted my card reader for work on my desk instead of attached to my desktop tower by my feet, and this is EXACTLY what I needed! With this USB3 extension cable, I was able to reach the required length to put my reader where I want it, all while not losing USB3 transfer speeds. Does exactly what I wanted, couldn't be happier with it.

I work with video equipment and can never have too many connection options at my disposal. I love that this comes with both a straight patch and an elbow shaped one! I tried out both to attach an HDMI splitter to a display over 10 feet of wire away by combining two HDMI cables, and had no problems connecting at the highest resolution of both devices. They work!

I got this for my son's gaming desktop to make it WiFi 6 compliant, as his aging wifi adapter wasn't doing so well with our new router. It claims to also have bluetooth, which would have been a nice addition but it requires access to a USB header on the motherboard to do that.
We have USB access heads on the board, however we were unable to reach it with the length of cable provided unless I removed / shuffled around some other expansion cards (to be fair, he has dual GPUs and TV input card already, so there isn't a lot of space to navigate wires). I find this requirement kind of odd, because I have not seen other BT/WiFi cards that require a USB port. I was told the USB access is for Bluetooth, as it communicates over the USB channels, and wifi doesn't need it. But that still seems weird. I know that you can add USB ports via PCIe, so I don't understand why this card needs USB on the motherboard- can't it supply its own I/O for that?
Regardless, my son didn't care much about bluetooth, the point was to get an internet connection upgrade, and for that it worked splendidly. Without the USB wire, the WiFi portion of the card works just fine, plug and play. His connection is faster and with less lag. The Bluetooth portion is disabled for now as a result, but that's ok. Eventually we'll source a longer cable or maybe play musical chairs with the PCI cards in there currently to make it work.

Really I think this product deserves 3 stars compared to other webcams, but the price is good enough that I think it deserves 4 for value.
The camera claims to be 1080p, however in my testing recording locally, there's no way this is resolving a FHD worth of pixels. I believe it is sending a 1080 sized feed to the computer, but the actual camera itself looks less sharp than 720 scaled up to 1080. I'd say it is better than those uber-cheap 480p cameras, but it is definitely NOT the resolution they claim. Secondly, this is a wide angle lens with a lot of distortion as you reach the borders of your frame. See included photo for examples of the fish-eye edge distortion. The microphone isn't all that great either, but that's to be expected when the mic is so far away from you. For good audio, I always recommend a desk mic instead of a webcam mic anyway. All in all, if you just need to show up for work meetings or classrooms on zoom, this will do the job just fine! But if you want to look professional, record a vlog or twitch stream, etc, you're going to want a webcam with better quality, resolution, and less lens distortion.

I was looking for something to give adequate cinematic audio to our projector movie nights that won't break the bank. In the past I've tried various sound bars but have never been all that pleased with the quality coming out of them once we turn it up to fill the room. This product, however, is astounding for the money. It has a real 2.1 speaker system, as there are two sets of woofer/tweeters for the left and right channels, as well as a decent subwoofer at the base of the tower. Sure, the sound is all coming from the same location so you won't really get the surround sound effect of having L+R on opposite sides of the room, but the clarity of the sound reproduction on this is better than my old 2-speaker setup and far better than any sound bar I've tried yet. It gets LOUD if you need it to, but unlike other speakers which can get loud, it doesn't seem to distort the audio or lose the treble in the deep bass. This is likely thanks to the dedicated subwoofer at the foot of the tower complimenting the smaller speakers above it. You may have to play with the EQ buttons to get the optimal setting for your listening experience, but I'm so surprisingly happy with this product that I'd consider that a minor issue.
The speaker supports bluetooth as well as aux inputs and other standard sources for a speaker of this classification. I tried the AUX input with the Quad-DAC feature of my LG phone to really push the speakers, and I was very impressed with what I heard. Then I connected it via bluetooth to our Firestick and put that in the projector, and a clean wireless projector movie night was had with excellent cinema quality sound. I do wish there was a way I could buy a second one and split the channels for L and R for a proper stereo experience, but honestly, I'm really just so pleased with the sound from this for the price that I can't say enough about that.

We got this to replace some broken Apple earbuds for someone in my family. You can tell they aren't Apple, but they also don't cost what Apple charges. The sound is actually super respectably good! And be careful, they're pretty good at isolating noise around you too! I lent them to a friend and had to chase them down the street before they could hear me calling their name!
They are pretty comfortable too, I'm comfortable recommending this product.

I've used Skullcandy products before and always found them to be on the mediocre side of a brand name, so I had what I'd think are pretty realistic expectations for this set. At first I just assumed this was their attempt to break into the now flooded market of inexpensive completely wireless earbud market. And you know what- it turns out that's not a bad thing at all.
These offer some impressive fidelity in sound, and unlike some other earbuds which crank up the bass to compensate for being tiny drivers, this actually delivers what I'd consider more realistic sound reproduction. It isn't too bass heavy, but the bass is still there. To be honest, that's something I'm used to hearing only on higher end speakers which don't have anything to prove other than just be good. I forgot how much I just wanted that in a headset. The battery life is pretty decent as well, not amazing but not terrible, slightly above average for what you'd expect for this style of headset. I was actually surprised to find the microphone was half decent as well, as I've never had a good experience with calls on earbuds before (the mic is just too far from your mouth to work well). These aren't going to be as clear separating your voice from the background as, say, a mic that is closer to your mouth (wired or protruding mic arm), or whatever magic Apple has in their airpods to pull off that directional sound, but honestly I was expecting worse and this surprised me. So, 5 stars for being an above average offering at an excellent price. I'd say that makes this a good value product!

I'm a fan of Panasonic's electronics, and have been since I first used their GH camera line for work, and the DVX prosumer cameras before that. I was excited for a chance to replace my working headphones with ones from Panasonic, however I found it interesting that the plug type was NOT MENTIONED on this listing! The last pair of headphones + mic that I ordered came with a USB plug. It worked fine on my laptop, but not on my phone or tablet, obviously. I want a regular headphone jack, as in 1/8" or 3.5mm (whatever you want to call it!) to be compatible with all my things, and not rely on the limitations of bluetooth.
I was a little bit nervous about buying this one since it doesn't say anywhere that it is, in fact, a standard TRRS headphone-jack sized plug, but I'm happy to report that it IS! And the sound quality is what I expected from Panasonic, a good value for the price. One thing to note, however, is that this requires both sides have a wire going to the plug. This is a seriously old-school design that I almost forgot existed. Modern headphones have a single point of cable that splits to the other side in the band, however this is more like earbuds in that there's a wire going to each side.
It's not a deal breaker, it works fine and some people may actually prefer that look, but personally I'm worried about it being another point of contact that could get snagged/rip/break/go wrong, and actually prefer the more modern single-side cable style. But this is still a great pair of traditional tried-and-true headphones!

I happen to use a D-Link DIR 1360 as my internet router at home, and while it does a decent job broadcasting signal around me, it is located at one corner of our home which means the opposite corner of the house has too many barriers for a fast signal. And if I want to take my laptop out to the porch? No reliability at all!
But with this placed a few rooms over from the router, it has greatly extended my network and the speed of things nearby it. It was super simple to set up, too! I'm not sure if that's just because I happen to have a D-Link router, but all I had to do was press the setup button on the router and extender while plugged in next to it, then once setup I could unplug and move it wherever I wanted to extend to. No app or IT knowledge required! Literally press the button, wait a few minutes for the lights to turn green, and good to go! The access point matches the original name of my router, so it is all completely invisible to the user. The device picks whichever device is closer / stronger and automatically connects to it without any user intervention, much like a cell phone. Now, this is only possible because my router supports this mesh-style setup. Otherwise you'll have to do one of those alternative SSID things where the device sees two networks and has to decide which one to connect to. The first was is preferable obviously, and just works better in addition to being cleaner.

With my laptop in my living room (on the other side of the house from my router), I used to get somewhere between 20-40mbps in my speed tests downloading. That's not terrible, but I'm paying for 300mbps service! But with this plugged in the middle of my home, that jumped to 80-90mbps reliably! Still not the 200+ speeds I get if only a room or two away from the router, but definitely an improvement by almost 2x... and spots outside on the porch that rarely had coverage before now do.

HOWEVER, like any extender, this WILL introduce some lag to your network. This is the part I was warning about in the headline, as most people think extenders will improve your performance across the board, which isn't true. While my download and upload speed improved, my Ping time degraded from 8ms to 14 (lower is better). That extra hop from the extender back to the router has a cost. Now, that difference shouldn't make a huge difference in most things, 14ms is still pretty respectable, however a larger ping lag can effect real-time performance like lag in multiplayer games and video call performance. Arguably, in those cases, a lower ping is more important than higher speeds. So if I'm having trouble with gaming lag or video call echo, I'd probably unplug this and go with the original weaker signal to the router directly. But if I'm going outside, or just streaming Netflix etc, than the download performance is more important than the ping. So, make your decisions wisely... I've seen too many people running multiple zoom devices over lockdown and think a wireless extender is going to solve their problems, but in fact just made everyone's zoom calls worse! But this isn't the fault of the device, that's inherent of how all extenders work. So, I'm still giving this 5 stars for being an excellent instance of what it should be: a way to boost transfer speeds and extend range that's dead simple to set up.

This is a good alternative to my lightweight travel stands. My larger lights were always wobbly on those, but this stand gives me confidence that my lights are secure when setting up on location. It feels well made and has many mounting options thanks to the removeable mount pin on top. I would not recommend this if you're looking for a small and light stand to travel with- this is better suited for applications that require a heavier payload on top. I bring one of these now for my main key light (heaviest light), and then stick to the smaller lighter ones for my fill and backlight (generally using smaller LED panels). This is definitely a good value for a strong stand.

This is a perfect budget friendly way to add quality sound to a projector! We sometimes use our Firestick to watch movies on the wall with the projector, however the challenge has always been how to get epic sound to go along with the epic looking visuals (projector speakers are terrible). The Firestick lacks any audio out ports, however it DOES have bluetooth! I had tried smaller cheap soundbars before, but they were all the battery-powered variety that don't really get loud enough or deep enough to fill a room with rich sound.
I was expecting this to be another similar experience, but I have to admit I'm pleasantly surprised with how loud and clear this is! It looks, behaves and (most importantly) sounds like a much more expensive sound bar, and really fills the room with the cinematic sound I wanted. I actually like it better than our 2.1 stereo system's sound, so I might take down those and just use this!

First of all, the signal quality is great over my 300' of CAT5e cable going from my entertainment system in front of my room to my projector around the back (cable goes behind walls and snakes around furnishings to get where it needs to go). It is fast and responsive, and the lag seems minimal if any. I love that it can also be used as a pass through, and that it only requires power on ONE side! My old HDMI extender required a power adapter on both the tx and rx side, but this can actually send power over the network cable (PoE) so that the other side does not need its own adapter. Now THAT's awesome!
This is one of the primary reasons I was interested in this, as there are two times I use such an adapter: When I use my projector instead of my TV for movies, and when moving a camera around at an event that I want to send a live feed back to a screen or streaming box for. Currently I have to supply power at both ends of the network cable, but I imagined ONLY needing power on the receiver, and having THAT power the transmitter. For example, in the case of the camera, I could have the screen receiving the signal send power to the transmitter by the camera using PoE and be somewhat more free of tethered power on that side. Also, when using the projector, I could turn on the outlet controlling the projector via remote and have it power on the transmitter behind the TV as well. Less wires and outlet spaces where already difficult / congested is good! THE PROBLEM, however, is that this thing misses its potential by only sending power from the TRANSMITTER! In other words, I can send power from the tx with PoE to the rx side, but the RECEIVER can't power the transmitter! It only goes the same direction as the HDMI signal. This, to me, was disappointing as that's the side I wanted to save from having more wires to plug in. Not the receiving side. That side is never an issue to supply power.
So I was a little upset about that. But otherwise, it is a solid product that seems to do what it claims to, and so far seems more reliable than my previous setup. If it could send power using EITHER side, it would be perfect! So close this time!

This is a great little capture device for streaming and recording content from HDMI sources! I've been asked to stream a lot of live events (graduations, benefit concerts, etc) since Covid19 started. With this, I can take the feed out of my camera directly into the box, and stream or record using something like OBS software on my laptop. The input is considered like a USB webcam to the system, so really anything, including Zoom or Skype, can utilize the content coming from a camera or other HDMI source.
I have a Magewell HDMI to USB box that I was using before this one, and while the quality of the stream was professional (excellent color and stream clarity), it actually would often overheat and drop frames. I actually had to put a cooling fan on it to prevent that from happening on a long event outdoors. But so far, this adapter seems to be better at handling heat- likely because the overall box is bigger so the heat can dissipate. Crazy because the Magewell cost a lot more than this. Also this one has an HDMI pass through, which the magewell did not! That means you can split this with another ouput, for example run it out to a TV, a camera monitor, projector, or external recorder like a Atmos Ninja. The magewell couldn't do any of that without a separate splitter sitting before it to copy the signal to multiple outputs.
Yes, there are cheaper capture card adapters out there, but in my experience they are a mixed bag of mostly unreliable performance and subpar coloring, and lack the features this offers. The Magewell might still be the most pro version of this I've used as far as color and clarity, but it is more expensive and only offers a single input with no passthrough, not to mention overheats easily. I'd definitely recommend giving this one a try!

My younger kids wanted a music player but they are too young for a phone so I looked into these dedicated touch-screen players. These are a big step up from the old mp3 players of my days. First of all, they have bluetooth so you can actually use modern wireless headphones which is awesome, in addition to regular 3.5mm headphones. The sound quality is excellent, and it even has a built in speaker for use without any headphones at all!
Granted, the speaker isn't very loud, but the fact that it HAS one is huge in my opinion! And my daughter thinks so too.
The user interface is a little bit difficult to figure out, things aren't very intuitive to find and sometimes it seems to respond with a bit of a lag, but kids seem to adapt to it pretty quickly. One thing I was not able to get working however, is the video function. The product details claim it can play video and indeed, there is a video function on the menu, however I could not get anything to play on it. It does not recognize any file extension other than avi, and none of the standard AVI codecs that I tried did anything. I have no idea what this thing can actually play so if you're getting it hoping to put little videos on it, you may be sorely disappointed!

I've heard a lot of wonderful things about the Sony noise cancelling sets like these, and let me tell you: it isn't just hype. The sound quality is excellent, and the noise cancelling is eerily amazing. I put it on my wife and kids with the noise cancelling off and then turned it on to demonstrate, and you can see each them suddenly smile like "whoa". Like my Sony studio headphones I use professionally for work, the actual fidelity of the sound it reproduces is excellent, and the microphone for calls is excellent despite being up by my ears and so far from my mouth (other bluetooth headphones I've tried were good for music only, the mic being up by my ears wasn't good enough to isolate my voice from ambient sound, but this definitely does a great job).
The app gives a ton of control beyond what I expected to really customize the experience. For example, I have mine set to auto-pause if the headphones are removed, and to turn off noise cancelling when it detects me speaking to someone, and then resume playback when the headphones are removed/replaced. These features are all customizable, as well as many more. But you need the app. And this is where the cons come in:
1) You really need the app to get the most out of this. I was thinking about pairing this with my desktop and/or TV, but without the app you have far less control, and to be honest I couldn't even get it to pair with my phone using just Bluetooth alone. There seems to be a way according to the instructions, but I couldn't figure it out without using the app installed.
2) For a set that costs this much, I'm surprised at how scuffed up it got after one fall from about 3 feet next to my car. Including pictures. This happened the day I got it. I'm not sure if there's anything that can be done about that, pavement is hard to recover from if anything is dropped, but it's something to keep in mind if you're spending this much money on a gadget. My studio headphones have been roughed around for years and held up fine.

All in all, I'd give it 5 stars if it weren't so reliant on the app to get the features going and/or more resilient to being dropped. Feels like I should deduct one for that. But as far as features and sound quality go, this is a solid 5 out of 5.

This may not be a high end DAC player like my expensive audio equipment or even my Quad-DAC LG phones, but it is an adorable little device that is more than capable of playing some high quality tunes on a budget. I have a 7 year old daughter who always wants to use my phone for music, so I figured this would be a good little player for her. It doesn't disappoint, we didn't even need to add a storage card since the internal 8GB is enough to load up plenty of songs from our library of mp3s.
I was actually hoping I could throw a couple of short videos on there for her too since it claims to also play that, however I have not been able to get that to work. It seems to only support AVI files, and I tried many different codecs and none are playable. The instructions are a joke, I wish it came with a demo file or something so I could at least inspect and see what codecs work. But otherwise, everything about this is pretty straight forward- connect via USB, drag and drop, use touch screen. Aside from the video, it really does just work as expected. I actually really like that it comes with a cool little watch band so she can wear it like a smartwatch and play music off it. I'm really pleased with the value of it.

I've been a fan of Panasonic's consumer electronics since their camcorder days, so I was excited to try these! I've owned many of the cheap Chinese wireless earbuds, and generally sound is good enough for music or listening to videos but I've never found one with a microphone decent enough for sound quality outside of the major brands (Apple, Samsung, etc).
Well, I'm happy to say these Panasonic 'buds don't skimp! They don't cost as much as the big players but the sound quality both for listening and microphone use is head and shoulders over the cheap knock offs. The noice cancelling feature is pretty amazing as well, and overall I'm very pleased with the feature set and quality of those features. But here's the caveat:
The ergonomics aren't great. Touch sensitive buds are difficult for me because I'm the kind of person who moves around a lot and needs to adjust my earbuds to keep them from falling out. But touch sensitivity means sometimes I'm accidentally activating things when I don't want to. I also didn't find some of the features intuitive and had to learn how to use them properly (changing noise cancelling modes for example). They also have rather bright blinking LEDs but you'll only notice that in a dark room. All in all, this is a good product that could be made better in a second edition. For the price, I think it fits squarely between the polished big name brands and the cheap knock offs. This is a good product, it works and doesn't exactly what it says. But it isn't perfect.

My 7 year old daughter LOVES these! They are cute and light up and fold to put away easily in a bag or backpack. She actually said the folding part of it made it feel less comfortable, but I'll admit I'm not sure what that means exactly. When I looked at them I couldn't find any part of it that would cause discomfort. Meanwhile, it comes with a spare battery for the light up part which is welcome, and sound quality is good enough for the intended use as a kid's listening device with some fun flair.

Ok, I have to admit I'm pretty impressed with this little camera. At first I thought I had to use the Haven subscription, especially after reading the reviews here which said it is necessary. I was kind of bummed about that at first but it turns out this is really useful even without! Sure, being able to record videos and store them in the cloud require a subscription as well as many of the advanced features, but you can still "arm" the camera to snap a photo and alert your phone when it detects motion, which it does splendidly even without a sub. The way I currently use it, it alerts my phone and I can then go to the live view and see and even interact with who is there (talk feature is really cool!).
On top of that, I set ours up with Amazon's Alexa voice service and it is EXTREMELY COOL! I think the speaker seems a bit louder than an Echo Dot, which surprised me. I'm mounting ours by the front porch so we can see people come to the door and interact with them, but we can also use it to play music via Amazon's Alexa when just sitting on the porch drinking coffee. That's an amazing perk that I wasn't expecting before we got it!
I do wish you could combine it with device music groups in Alexa (so I could say, for example, play this song on the everywhere group and it will play inside on our Echo and out on the porch with the Ecobee), but sadly only echo devices can be grouped. That's OK, I knew that before getting this as other devices in our home can't be grouped either (Facebook Portal or Kindles, for example).
If you want to spring for the subscription service, there's a TON of goodies and advanced features beyond even the cloud storage things. But even without that, the live view and photo motion alerts combined with the voice assistant / Alexa integration makes it worth it even just for the hardware alone!

They're not kidding when they say this is a speaker made for outdoor use. Unlike smaller bluetooth speakers made for a desk or small room, this is a serious 15w device that can crank out some surprisingly loud levels of bass that can vibrate the floor (I put it on our living room floor to test it and you could FEEL it across the room thumping). I used it today out on our wooden deck, and it was actually TOO LOUD at full volume, we had to turn it down a little. That's impressive out of a battery powered unit!
I have to admit, at full volume (which we used just to test how high it can be cranked), the audio was exhibiting some distortion, but that's expected for a unit this size. Keeping it a few notches below top, it was plenty loud and clear quality to the music. It paired easily with our phones, however it took me a bit to figure out how to unpair and pair again with a different device (hold the play/pause button until it says "disconnect" followed by "pairing"). The audio cable is a nice option to have as well, and the build quality seems rugged enough to take on a camping trip and survive unscathed. It claims to be IPX5 waterproof, and the thick rubberized feel to it prevents scratches and scuffs. Very impressed with it!

I have an NVME drive already installed in my system but I'd like some additional storage for media editing that doesn't resort to the latency and slow r/w times of a spinning disk. These SATA drives are PERFECT for that! I haven't put it inside my case yet, but in just a USB3.0 enclosure it seems to do quite well (picture of speed benchmark shown). Not quite the 500+ speed advertised on the box, but a 10-15% discrepancy is reasonable especially when using an enclosure and not doing sequential reads and writes. I'm sure once I set this up internally it'll perform even better.
Great to add some storage to a modern system, and of course especially great if your mobo doesn't support NVME and you need something with an SATA interface. Quality product from a quality brand name, I recommend it.

I've owned many affordable bluetooth speakers, but never one this size! I love this, the sound quality is FAR BETTER than anything I've used in this price range. The woofers deliver solid bass, and the directions really help fill a space with sound. I love that it even has a carrying handle and a place to plop your phone onto (great for Karaoke!). I'm a little confused by the Mic input, I thought perhaps this could work as an alternative to the line in... for example, I can line in for music, but also sometimes I'd like a mic-level input for using with a microphone. But the mic input seems to only get used for some sort of recording to TF card function, which I couldn't get to work anyway. Doesn't matter, I wasn't so interested in that feature, I was more interested in using it as an amp and thought that might be an interesting alternative use.
Using the speaker for both bluetooth audio or wired aux in worked very well. The FM radio is nice too, but I didn't try it much. All in all, the battery life seems pretty solid and this thing is incredibly powerful for a battery operated speaker. We usually don't max out the volume because that's too loud!

Wireless headphones are all the rage right now, but sometimes I just want a good wired pair. When I'm using laptop especially, using Bluetooth headphones introduces lag and another thing that needs to be charged. These are excellent premium feeling wired 'phones that include an inline mic and controls if your device supports it. When used with my desktop that offers only a TRS plug (only two lines), it works as just a pair of headphones, with decent sound quality and bass response. On my LG phone or laptop which accept a TRRS plug (3 lines), the mic works as an input as well. My laptop didn't respond to the volume control buttons, but I think most phones will. Regardless, I'm impressed with the quality and presentation for the money this costs.

So, let me start off by saying, this isn't the best quality webcam on the market. But for the price, no one is expecting it to be. And it is FAR from the worst! During the Covid Pandemic, all the regular brand name webcams were sold out so I found myself trying out a bunch of these no-name brands from Amazon. The last one I tried actually had a much harsher fisheye effect in the corners, as well as over-saturated color. This one seems far less cartoony and more realistic in color reproduction, as well as being somewhat more rectilinear (photo speak for straight lines being straight, not as much curved distortion). There is a bit of fisheye curve on the edges, but it is very usable and didn't make my ceiling look concave like my last one I tried. See attached images for examples of the room's wall distortion. It's there if you are looking for it, but not terrible when you're looking at a subject. The microphone is just meh. I have a desktop mic and the sound out of that was MUCH better, especially because you can get it closer to your face than the camera. But the fact that this HAS a mic is a good option in a pinch. I would just strongly recommend an external mic if you want people to hear you clearly. Also something I didn't know before trying this:
It is MANUAL focus! That means it won't follow and focus on you automatically, you have to twist the lens until you're sharp in the view. It actually isn't that hard to nail focus, the depth of focus is pretty deep so once you've set it for your standard sitting distance, you likely won't have to change it ever again unless you walk away from the camera. A fun side effect, however is that the focus lens gear lets you push it to EXTREME MACRO distances! So you can do insane closeups of things if you want to, for example, put a webcam on an ant farm maybe? I tried it out on my desktop speaker, and in one picture you can see the relative size of it compared to my desk and then the closeup you can see the detail of the scratched plastic where it says Harmon / Kardon. Ha, if nothing else this shows me I should probably get new desktop speakers too! These are beat up when up close! A fun and versatile camera for a good price. If you need autofocus tracking, this might not be for you though.

This is a pretty good value microSD card. I did some tests on my desktop to check speeds, they aren't the fastest ever but they are no slouch either. Pretty good for the money I'd say. I really like the painted graphic on the plastic, it is unique and fun, and probably a shame if you end up just leaving it in your switch all day! I used mine to record some drone footage today and it seems to be holding up great so far.  I got the 128GB version, of which 118GB is usable according to Windows (which sounds correct to me after format).

I really needed one of these for my desktop during this time of teleconferencing for work and school. I wouldn't say it's incredible quality, a selfie camera on a modern flagship phone will have better, but it is absolutely usable for zoom meetings, skype calls, and real time streaming, and allows me to use the comfort of my desk and dual-monitor PC setup.
As you can see in the image, the view is rather wide, which comes with a bit of barrel distortion (look at the wall curve where it hits the ceiling- I promise this is straight in real life!). It's not a fish eye distortion, but it's slight and noticeable on straight edges. It has an LED indicator that comes on to tell you it has power, and then another light that comes on to tell you when it is active. I like this, because you have a visual indicator that your camera is on so that you won't have to worry about covering it for hackers or things like that. There is a mic but personally I like using an external mic that is closer to my mouth. The mic is OK on this, and definitely useful if you don't have one already. All in all, it is very functional and a major upgrade over my XP-era VGA resolution webcam from forever ago. Just don't expect it to be amazing. It's a good value for the price.

There are fortunately many wireless headphones in this price range these days. Usually they are pretty similar, but this is one of the better ones. The first thing I noticed is how SOFT the ear cups are. It feels like something that belongs on a more expensive set, almost luxurious. That makes these much more comfortable to wear for long periods versus many of the other inexpensive headphones. The build quality feels good, and the sound quality is pretty decent too. Speakers of this size are usually pretty good at their bass response, and these are no exception. They naturally have a bit of noise isolation due to the cup design, and you have the option to connect a 3.5mm cable to use them as traditional wired headphones as well.
The one thing I DON'T like, is the microphone. Don't buy these for phone calls. The mic is too far from your mouth to separate you from background noises. Yes, I know airpods also have their mic far from your math but Apple has some sort of magic voodoo to make that work somehow. I've never liked the mic on any of these headphones, so I'm used to that by now. But I feel like these are marketed more for people who want to listen to music, and for that they are great and comfortable! I honestly wish they would disable the handsfree profile so that my phone wouldn't keep trying to use it for phone calls. Otherwise, a solid buy for this price!

I've owned many wireless headphones, so this isn't my first rodeo. I wanted something separate to leave paired with my work computer. Earbuds aren't comfortable for me to wear for long periods of time so over-the-ear style is important. I have to admit, I like these more than I expected to. The ear pads are soft and slow to reclaim their shape like memory foam- this makes them extremely comfortable to wear so I don't mind keeping them on for a good portion of my workday. It also has a rubberized cover for the charging port and 3.5mm jack, which is surprisingly nice to find on a headset in this price range!
The sound quality is about on par with what I expected for this price range- that is, it is very good. Not blow-your-mind-amazing like sets that sell for hundreds, but as good if not better than others in this price range. What I didn't like, however, is the microphone quality. Yes, it has a mic, but I'd like to pretend it doesn't. The mic is on the headset by my ears and doesn't seem to be directed towards my mouth. This makes my voice sound distant and muffled, with ambient background noise sometimes on the same level or louder than my voice is. For calls I'd rather use a different headset, but that's OK. This ends up being used paired with my computer rather than my phone. It is pretty decent at passive noise isolation as well, reducing sound around you naturally. The only things I wish were better are the mic and perhaps a physical on/off switch rather than a button, but honestly this is pretty normal for headphones in this price range so I essentially got exactly what I expected.
EDIT:
I loved these so much, I ended up getting another on in another color for a family member. A great value for wireless headphones.

I've been doing this for years with a DIY rig made out of an interchangeable-plate battery charger. I've even got a video on youtube with over 5k views demonstrating how it works on my A7S and a dummy battery. It is such a simple concept, since most of these smaller cameras have the same voltage requirements as the big NPF batteries, I couldn't believe the market hadn't embraced mass producing the concept.
I was so glad to see devices like this have hit the market, I had to try it! I'm happy to say, it not only works just as I expected it to (provided you have the right size dummy battery adapter), but they improved upon the design by adding USB ports and even USB charging! So now if I don't want to use my dummy battery on, say, my A7Rii, I can use this as a charger to top off the internal battery while recording speeches, AND top off my phone and/or power a recorder or monitor while I'm at it!
These guys thought of everything, even offering USB C or micro USB charging so that you can use whatever cables you happen to have around. So hats off to Power Junkie, for not only mass producing something we no longer have to DIY, but adding enough functionality on top of it to be so worth it.

It's so good to find more wired TRRS headsets hitting the market. For a while it seemed like only wireless ones were selling and the wired models were all low-end earbud styles or the kind that have the mic embedded by your ears instead of your mouth.
This is a good over-the-ear style set, with decent bass response and sound quality, as well as a mic on the wire. I really like the placement of a microphone on the wire, it is second only to the telescoping mic style you see receptionists and gamers using. It keeps the mic relatively close to your mouth (rather than headsets that put the mic by your ears) so you pick up your voice more than ambient noise in the room. Just keep in mind, it is a TRRS set which means it has the extra pin on the plug for a mic. It may not work properly in standard TRS headphone plugs (stereo only, designed for use with headsets without a mic), although some can work with both.
Most modern laptops support TRRS, as well as tablets and phones (if you're lucky enough to still have a 3.5mm headset jack!).

I got this for an event gathering and it turned out to be a real hit! Loading it up with different sounds really was a hoot, and it was plenty loud in a room together with other people. It doesn't get loud enough to use at an outdoor event in my opinion, or loud enough for a very noisy event event, but with a gathering of friends or in a classroom, it is plenty loud. Even the preloaded air horn sound effect is awesome.
My wife works in a school and can already see this being something she'll use in a classroom as well. A very versatile and fun product!

I'm so happy to see they are still making new brands of wired headphones... lately all the new designs and features have been found in wireless only, and sometimes I just want a good pair of wired 'phones, especially for use with my Quad-DAC headphone jack.
They are passive noise cancelling, which basically just means they cushion sound out mechanically with nice big ear muff style rings, as opposed to any kind of digital reverse-sine-wave trickery (which are hit or miss on cheap brands usually), and it has a really interesting "focus" mode switch, which changes the EQ of the mix to promote the frequencies used in spoken words better. This is an amazing feature for those of us who listen to audiobooks or lectures, which I do frequently. To be honest, I didn't notice a big difference between having that mode on and off, but it was nice to know someone out there is trying to make products catered for people who want to do more than just listen to music over Bluetooth.
The sound quality is pretty good for the price, and the presentation is actually really impressive. The materials feel really premium and even the box it comes in feels super fancy, which might make this a nice gift. I don't expect much out of mics that are embedded in headphones, and this pair didn't change my mind about that. The mic isn't close enough to your mouth to be of much use, picking up more ambient noise around you than you. If they wanted to include that as a feature, they could have made a removable arm like a gaming headset, but they don't need to. This is a good pair of headphones for those of us who just want to listen, which is their ideal demographic IMO.

I have a Crane 3 Lab that I tried this attachment on, and let me say this piece is impressively strong. I love that it has the groove teeth to lock it into place like an OEM attachment, it feels solid and won't move or budge an inch unless you loosen the teeth first. I guess I shouldn't be surprised with a brand name like Smallrig, I'm familiar with their other gear and they are reputable in this industry.
I see this is advertised to also attach to a Ronin S, which I also have but use less often. Honestly, it looks like it will attach and stay put as well, but it feels like it was really made for the Crane more than the Ronin. I love it, and intend to use it for mounting audio gear.

I want to give this 3.5 stars- 3 is too low and 4 seems too high, but I'll round up for now. I have mixed things to say about this camera. It isn't going to take stellar photos. They are either going to have a lot of motion blur or if you raise the shutter speed (sports mode) you're going to get substantial noise. The videos side is even worse. A modern cell phone or point-and-shoot is going to snap better photos and videos. BUT... you can take this to a water park and not care what happens to it, which is exactly what we did.
I'm including three examples shots here that I wouldn't have gotten without this camera (excuse the smiley face for privacy). One are kids about to go down a water slide, where I as the photographer am being rained on by nearby sprinklers. Then there's a slightly more epic shot of the giant bucket atop the slides crashing water down on me. This shot froze the droplets of water right before thoroughly drenching the photographer (me) a split second later. The last is from some of our underwater pool shots. These are all cases in which I would NOT have been comfortable using my real cameras or even cell phones- as waterproof as they claim some flagship phones are now, I wouldn't trust them to this. In my experience, even waterproof phones have trouble operating under water (the touch screen doesn't work properly), and we have ruined the charging port of another at a pool previously. But this is totally sealed and has real buttons that work just as well under water as above. For all those reasons, I actually LIKE this camera. It takes photos I literally would NOT have gotten otherwise.
Also, as a bit of personal experience, after going down a water slide and trying to video it, I actually dropped the camera into the pool at the bottom. I was able to run in and chase and grab it, and the entire time I was thinking I'm SO GLAD this isn't my phone!
I'm actually printing some of the photos as I write this and although they appear grainy on my screen, on 4x6 photo paper they look perfectly acceptable.
So why 3.5 stars? Well, the user interface is terrible. More than once I had to turn it off and restart to get back to photo taking because I couldn't figure out how to get out of the mode I was in. Also, it claims to have a 21megapixel mode, but I'm pretty sure it is just upscaling a smaller resolution. The noise at 21mp seems soft, like it took a lower resolution image and then scaled it UP to 21 mp. The 12 megapixels mode seemed much more true-to-pixel size, so that seems like a bit of false advertising. Then there's the video mode- keep it at 720 if you want any kind of normal playable frame rates. It also looks like less-than-HD that has been scaled up to fit, but at least it works at all. At 1080 HD, it was doing a variable frame rate thing that often slowed to a slide show and wasn't playable on my phone or laptop. I'm only able to play it back from the camera, which I wish I had known before I chose it for some things I wanted to remember.
Outside of those caveats, it is good for the specific use as a camera you can afford to get wet.

I know everything is cloud based these days, but a good USB stick is still indispensable in my opinion. For my job I find myself responsible for presentations in places that often have no reliable internet access, and being able to hand over the finished video on a stick like this is perfect. Just yesterday, I used one of these as a Windows installation media to fix a botched dual boot laptop without a CD/DVD drive. Now that I've fixed it, I might throw a live linux distro onto the stick for future use as a handy recovery system.
They aren't the fastest transfer speed available, but they are perfectly acceptable for daily use.

This is a good card if you're on a budget and want some CUDA acceleration for your desktop. Personally, I have some applications that require CUDA cores for proper operation (Photogrammetry and Adobe's Mercury Playback Engine), and it's not so much that I need the fastest performance out there as it is that I need some CUDA cores to merely EXIST at all for certain features to work!
This card is a great because much like the 1550 ti before it, it offers a decent entry-level gpu without costing significantly more than other components in your desktop. It is faster than the 1550ti, so that's nice, and does a decent job pumping out fps in light gaming if that's your thing.
One thing I didn't know beforehand and wish I did: This card does NOT support the Nevnc Turing engine. It only supports the (somewhat inferior) Volta one, which isn't as efficient in hardware accelerated video encoding. Since I bought this card primarily to compliment a home video editing setup, I wanted that feature. The new 1650 SUPER, which is a slightly more expensive card, DOES have the Turing engine, and when that showed up in a Google search I assumed this card had it as well.
Its a shame, I was looking forward to that but I'll have to wait until the next time I upgrade my GPU.

If you want to connect two wireless headphones to the same source, this is what you need!
I actually have tried two larger versions of this on our TV so my wife and I could listen with two headphones and not wake the kids. The larger ones require a cable and a place to put it, so it usually goes behind the entertainment system.
This one fits in the palm of my hand! It plugs right into the headphone jack and supports itself like that, all while running self-powered with batteries! That makes it super convenient to use on laptops, while travelling, in hotel rooms, etc. I like it so much better, I actually might replace our home TV one with this because it is so much neater looking and easy to plug in/remove. The bigger one requires too many cables and sometimes would create a ground loop feedback hum if I didn't have it set up correctly. This one hasn't had that happen yet, thanks to the internal battery avoiding grounding issues!
The range might not as good as the larger ones (big one had large antennae which could work rooms away, whereas this one needs to be in the same room it seems), but this very much serves its purpose and I wish I knew it existed before getting the other ones!

Full disclosure: I'm a Sony E camera fan and use them for work, so giving this Nikon 5 stars means a LOT from me.
I was skeptical about Nikon's entry into the mirrorless camera world, since in the past they saved their higher end specs for DSLRs, and didn't take the mirrorless market seriously (*cough* Nikon 1 *cough*). However the full frame Z cameras got a lot of positive acclaim, and this Z50, their first APSC crop sized mirrorless, is a heck of a lot better than any first generation product has any business being!
First let's talk about ergonomics- the camera feels great, not point-and-shoot tiny in your hands. Definitely smaller and lighter than a DSLR, but more substantial than a phone, as a camera should be. It has a touch screen, which is AWESOME for touch-focus and really helps avoid the "how to I change that setting" learning curve- generally, just press on the icon and you can change the setting. Yet it doesn't RELY on the touch screen, there are plenty of physical buttons and dials, many of which are customizable and can be assigned to functions you need more often. Essentially, this is a camera that's got more than one way to do most things and therefore will adapt to YOUR workflow rather than force you to learn its own. The screen can also tilt up or down, and lets you flip it around on the bottom to see selfie-style if desired. This is one area that seems a little odd for me- other cameras like the Sony A5100 flip UPWARDS, so you can see over the camera if taking a self portrait. Or the Panasonic GH series articulates sideways. This, only flips DOWN. Which means if mounted to a tripod, you can't see the display at all. That is alright since honestly most of the higher end full frame cameras don't even let you flip the display around at all these days. The fact that you can, even if in a silly orientation, is better than nothing and a welcome feature.
Image quality seems pretty great, the kit lenses are adequate. I really liked the 50-250, as 16-50 with variable aperture feels very limited in creativity (however this lens is necessary as a "walkaround" standard zoom length). To be fair, I'm spoiled by my pro constant f-stop lenses that I use on my other cameras, so I'm rarely impressed by the performance of budget friendly kit options. I'll admit that for kit lenses these really perform remarkably well, but I'm hoping Nikon rolls out some awesome affordable Z-mount DX lenses soon. Cropping in to view pixels at 100% zoom size, the image holds up and seems reasonably sharp. Nikon colors are there as well, which are admittedly excellent. As with any new system, there aren't a lot of lenses available yet unless you adapt from other mounts. Nikon has F-mount adapters for native adaption, and I've read good things about third party adapters for other camera types as well (Canon, etc... I've even seen a Sony EF adapter for sale!). Sadly, I don't have access to any adapters at the moment, so I'm stuck judging imaging quality by the included kits for now.
Now for video, this gets even more interesting. Nikon has done a bang-up job supporting popular frame rates and resolutions (4k at 24p? Hello filmmakers!). In my tests, the quality of the video was very clean and sharp. I haven't noticed much in the way of moire or aliasing yet, and it has a clean HDMI out option as well if you want to record externally or view on a bigger monitor while filming. Unlike certain other cameras (like the Sony a6300), it is able to keep the rear display ON while also using the external monitor / recorder, and also recording internally at 4k. Other prosumer crop cameras have turned off the internal display when doing all of those things at once. It does support a microphone jack which means you can use this for recording interviews, however it is missing a headphone jack to monitor the audio levels. That's a huge omission if you wanted to use this as a semi-pro video making tool.
Thankfully, I found a workaround: If you get a cheap HDMI monitor (they have for around $100 that can attach to the hotshoe mount), they often have audio jacks. I happen to have a couple by Feelworld that do exactly that, and I was able to plug headphones in and hear the audio while in recording mode live. Well, semi-live at least. When recording 4k, there was a brief delay in the A/V playback, I'm guessing because the throughput required for 4K creates some latency. But the point is that you COULD hear it, and therefore make sure the volumes are appropriate and audible, and thereby making it possible to use the Z50 as a more pro level tool.
All in all, this is an excellent entry into the market by Nikon. Whether you are a beginner looking to eventually start using semi-pro tools or a seasoned pro looking for a budget friendly walkaround or B-cam, this is a very impressive value.

This works great to split the audio signal out of an HDMI feed- we use it to send audio to our surround sound system while using our home projector for an immersive theater experience. We used to have an Amazon Basics version of the same thing, but it did not work very well- sometimes the Amazon version would need to be set via a button to change 5.1 or 2 channel or passthrough sound since it wouldn't always remember the setting after a power down, but this unit has a physical switch so it will be hardcoded upon power on. Also sometimes with the Amazon version the sound wouldn't pass through to the video device (it would always send sound out the analog audio jacks, but only sometimes also out the HDMI- it is supposed to do both). This one seems to consistently do both, as it should.
I'd like to also add that THIS COMES WITH EVERYTHING! It has Two HDMI cables, a digital audio cable, an analog cable, etc, ALL IN THE BOX. A fantastic package that does exactly what you want.

We have a minivan with a DVD entertainment system pre-installed. It predates the HDMI standard, so there are just RCA analog inputs in the back of the van. Since DVDs are pretty much obsolete, using this adapter we are able to plug in a laptop, raspberry pi or other digital video player to the car's system. I like that it is powered by USB, it is a convenient source of power especially when you don't have access to outlets (like in a car!). But you have to be careful about ground loop feedback. When powering it off a laptop, and the laptop is charging in the car, it can create either an audible hum and/or visual static distortion pattern on the video feed. This is common in DC circuits that share ground when working with analog equipment, unfortunately. I'm not sure if there's much that can be done about it other than try to run off batteries as often as possible (with this converter attached to a USB battery bank, the laptop on its own power, and the car running its own 12v DC). I have an older similar product looks almost identical that does the same thing so I'm guessing that's just a side effect of working with RCA inputs instead of digital ones.

This is a great tool for those who need to use prosumer equipment in more professional environments. HDMI is great at what it does, but it has limitations. Long cable runs and many professional live hubs and recorders require the more robust SDI cable format. I've found myself working live camera feeds, etc, more than once with prosumer grade cameras and laptops that needed to interface with our SDI equipment. Having these available means I can use SDI outputs even if my source doesn't have an SDI port. And while at first I wanted to remove a star for the lack of a proper power adapter (it just comes with a USB plug), I realize now this is a blessing. If I want to run it off a laptop, I have a power supply immediately available without another wall plug. If I need a wall plug, any standard USB charger will do, and those are plentiful.
Solid metal body seems durable, kudos to Amazon Basics for offering a good alternative for such a useful tool.

The Portal is sort of like an Echo Show but with different strengths and weaknesses. There is SO MUCH I could say about this device, some good and some bad, but I'll try to stick to the more important points here.
The killer feature, as you may know from their ads, as the way it can automatically zoom in/out and follow faces in a video call. So essentially, you can move around a room hands-free and it will find you and make sure you're in the shot. It's like having your own personal camera man on call.
In my experience with it so far, this worked fairly well. Moving left or right, the camera followed me. If more people enter the shot, it will zoom out to get them all in. It isn't without limitations however, and sometimes you'll move too far and it can't see you. Other times it got confused and lost me (if I move out of the frame and back in, that usually fixed it). For the most part, it worked as expected.
The sound is actually EXCELLENT considering this is the Mini edition. I was expecting the sound to be more like the Echo Dot, but this has a very large speaker on the rear which is able to drive very impressively deep bass without even approaching max volume. So that was a pleasant surprise.
While it has its own "Hey Portal" voice commands, it ALSO comes with Amazon Alexa built in. That's where it sort of starts acting like a Facebook-branded Echo Show, playing music, announcements, showing you answers to questions, turning on/off digital things, etc. All the things you want Alexa to do. However, I was sad to find that it isn't considered an Echo device for certain Alexa features, such as multi-room music groups, the Ring doorbell, and probably other Alexa Skills that aren't supported on non-Amazon hardware. So you can't really replace an Alexa Show with this if you need those features.
Now, some things that are better than the Echo Show: PRIVACY. I know, this is Facebook we're talking about, but I really like that they included a tab to disable the camera (by covering it up, not just turning it off), microphone, or both. It's like they realized that someone was going to complain they don't want Facebook recording them in their living room and thought ahead to add that. The Amazon devices with cameras don't have a dedicated cover built in. Then there's video calling to people OTHER THAN OWNERS OF ANOTHER DEVICE. The latest Show devices from Amazon have cameras too, but you can only call other Echo Shows or phones with the Alexa app running. The Portal can call Facebook and Whatsapp users, which means I can actually reach other people I'd want to chat with. This isn't a perfect implementation either, however... For Whatsapp, it essentially uses Whatsapp's web functionality behind the scenes to connect to your account. If you use Whatsapp web on your computer, it will log you out of the Portal and you'll need to log back in again after using it. This is an unnecessarily silly extra step. I use Whatsapp web a lot, so we ended up using my wife's Whatsapp account on the Portal to call our family and friends so we wouldn't have to keep logging out and in.
Then there's media like Youtube- much like the Amazon Echo devices, Google has decided not to allow an official Youtube app for the Portal either. However, there IS a browser, and you can go to Youtube on it. This makes for an awkward user interface (and not just because you can't control it with your voice), but once the video is up it works fine. It not only plays beautifully full screen, but you can even go back to the home screen and it will continue playing as a picture-in-picture overlay which can be moved around the screen by dragging. That's pretty neat. It's almost like they tried to support Youtube as much as possible without actually having an official interface to abide by Google's rules.
Other fun features include Facebook games like Draw Something, Chess, Super Baseball Batting Derby, etc, which you can play against other friends on Facebook or Portal devices. Then there's a bunch of photo effects which are really fun Snapchat-style filters that follow your face in augmented reality-style real time. These features can be used not only in the Photobooth app, but also on ANY call with the device. Then there's my favorite fun feature: Story Time! This feature is sort of like the snapchat photobooth AR-style effects mentioned above, however you read a story and it will animate effects over your face to illustrate as you go. This can be done on the Story Time app on the device locally or in a call to another person. My kids actually really LOVE that feature, and my 2 year old likes to read along with me when we do it. I'll admit they are very cute and sometimes I've laughed out loud when I didn't expect what happens next in the animation being done to me.

Honestly, as an Alexa alternative to an Echo Show, it is close but not quite a replacement. As a video chat device, it is better but only if your contacts are on Facebook or Whatsapp. And even then, Whatsapp is only good if you don't use Whatsapp Web. I'd consider it a 3 star device for those caveats, however the Story Time feature as well as the camera that follows you is really quite cool. Add that they considered your privacy with the flap cover and I have to give this at least 4 stars. It really has so much going for it, and I'm hoping they can iron out some of the software kinks to make it even better in the future.

Let me start off by saying I work in freelance video and I love how much I can fit inside this case! I've been using a Pelican 1510 as my go-to travel carrier, so that's mostly what I'm comparing this to. For starters, this is a longer case so in addition to my cameras, lenses, batteries and other accessories, it has a long open sleeve that can even fit a light stand or small tripod! For extra versatility, the whole interior can actually be pulled out (it has its own handle straps if you want to use it as its own carrier), which then frees up the ample storage space inside the case as a separate giant unit (see pictures to illustrate). There are also plenty of pockets on the inside, as well as the outside and front of the case. Of course, for a case this size there is the requisite wheels and carrying handle.
The only things I like better about my Pelican case, however, are the toughness and waterproofing. This bag comes with a rain cover which you can keep inside the case, however I don't like the idea of having to carry around a cover inside the bag, then take it out and put it on if it starts raining. The Pelican cases are air tight by simply closing them, no rain cover needed. The Pelican cases also are tough enough that they can be stacked under other equipment, thrown into a corner, sat on, stood on, etc, and 99% of the time come out unscathed. That's more than I can say for this bag. I bring this bag on gigs that I'm not worried about those things happening, because I can fit what I normally take in 3 separate bags into just this one. You could get a Pelican style case in this size, however it would cost quite a bit more than the asking price of this one. I think for the price this is a great tool to keep your stuff organized and ready to go whenever you are!

I go through these quite often, sometimes attaching a laptop to a sound system for presentation, or when plugging in modern 3.5mm monitoring headphones to older mixer equipment. The ones I have tend to fall apart eventually after a lot of repeated use, but this seems to be holding up so far!
Sound transmission seems solid, and they have been holding up well so far, so I'd say this gets 5 stars for being exactly what it is supposed to be.

So many things I love about these. These appear to be as rugged and well built as I'd expected from a brand name like Cobra. I love that they include a flashlight, and especially that the units are USB rechargeable! Such a convenient way to power things these days, I wish more electronics ditched the AAA batteries thing like this!
The range might be a bit exaggerated, but to be fair I live in a very wooded area surrounded by hills and valleys. I found that around my neighborhood it worked great but if I went a few miles away, the sound was mostly just unintelligible crackling. We could still hear that someone was trying to say something, but that's it.
On the flip side, we started hearing someone else's conversation the next day... we were just testing it so we didn't bother changing the default channel, and it turns out someone else must have gotten some talkies on the same default frequencies. I have no idea how close they were, but my kids pointed out that someone was talking and we didn't press any buttons and then we all heard it. "Dad? Do I need to come in? I'm playing outside", and then a few seconds later "ok, but don't ride into the street". Then some clicks of singing and other noises- clearly someone else communicating with THEIR kid was coming through to us. I pressed the talk button and said "Hi- this is the default frequency for these walkie talkies, so we should both probably change them!" and then promptly picked another channel. So, that's kind of neat because I have no idea where these other people were, we live in a pretty urban area with houses spread out and I know it wasn't someone from my block. Yet we heard them clear as day. So, I'd say these are pretty good at what they do, but maybe don't rely on the full extent of their listed range.

This little drive really impressed me. I work with large media files for broadcast, and always find myself looking for more hard drives to transport and backup. I usually get the larger desktop style drives because I was always under the impression that you get more capacity and speed for your money, with the caveat that you need additional sources of power (USB alone does not supply enough power to run a desktop drive motor reliably). But this little fellow not only looks like a shrunken version of one of my desktop profile Seagate drives (see picture, same pattern and everything), it offers the same 4TB capacity AND the ability to be powered directly from a USB port without additional power . And while the random access speeds aren't quite as zippy as a desktop one (see attached benchmark), the sequential speeds are actually HIGHER than my desktop sized equivalent. Thinking about the physics of it, that sorta makes sense- the physical bits of storage are closer together because it is a smaller sized platter, but the ability of the read head to move around and hit random access data points might be limited to a slower speed to fit this size.
If you're a numbers guy, here's the breakdown:
This drive:
Seq Read/Write: 144.2 / 101.2
512k: 66.86 / 66.46
4k: 1.069 / 5.596
4K QD32: 0.448 / 5.761

My older larger (but same capacity) desktop version:
seq: 98.83 / 77.26
512k: 157.9 / 51.31
4k: 1.489 / 6.422
4k QD32: 0.537 / 6.519

Obviously neither can compete with an SSD which easily smokes any of these drives in speed AND in energy efficiency, but this is an incredible bang-for-your-buck storage option if you need a lot of storage space, and it seems to compete fairly well with it's larger desktop sibling. And possibly best of all, it doesn't need another source of power off your outlets.

I built a home office a couple of years ago and ran a network cable during construction where I thought my desk would go. Turns out I like it better facing a different direction, so now I'm on a wall without an Ethernet jack. Well, that's where this fantastic flat Cat 7 rated cable comes in! I love that it is flat and white so it can be cleanly mounted along the baseboards. You can barely notice it if you don't already know it is there. I like that it also comes with mounting hardware (plastic clips with nails) to help hold the cable in place along its run, as well as a velcro strap if you want to use it as a portable cable and not permanently mount it somewhere.
Connection seems to work as expected, I don't have the equipment to test high LAN speeds or if it really lives up to the Cat 7 spec claims, but for regular networking use it seems great so far! I might try to get something similar to run behind our TV for a stronger steaming media connection.

I'm running a 1080p projector for our home entertainment system, and have a high quality decades-old analog stereo system for sound. Without this Audio Extractor device, I used to be limited to source devices that let me separate the video from the audio (Fire TV box and other devices that offer both analog stereo and HDMI video simultaneously) since the sound has to go one way and the video feed another.
This device opens up possibilities such as more modern equipment that does away with analog connections entirely. A Fire TV Stick 4k for example, or Raspberry Pi board (yes, technically the Pi has analog outputs, but they are subpar and not recommended for high quality audio). I'm very happy with this device and the opportunities it opens for me. It works well for me with the 2ch setting and my equipment. I can't vouch for 5.1 as my system doesn't support that, nor can I vouch for 4k as my system doesn't handle that either. But so far it has worked well sending a stereo analog audio feed somewhere other than my projector when needed.

I got mine from Omega Distribution USA, and I have to say, I'm IMPRESSED! This thing looks and acts like brand new. I've bought good condition "refurbished" handsets before, but this is something special. I don't know where they found a V20 in such condition, with a battery that seems to be holding its original charge like this. In fact, it even seems to come with the original Nougat firmware- usually a phone that has been used recently would have been upgraded to Oreo already.
Only problem is that I was looking for a version that would work with T-mobile, and while this handset is unlocked from Verizon, it doesn't work as well as an actual T-mobile branded would be (that's the H918 model). So sadly, I have to return this gem of a phone and get the one with the correct bands and software for my needs. Its a shame, I wish I could keep it. But if you're looking for a Verizon model to use with Verizon service, this is EXACTLY what you want for a great price!
As for the V20 as a phone- if you know what it is already, you don't need me to tell you. It's one of the last great super phones ever made. Built like a tank, this phone is easy to repair yourself if need be (no glue or heat gun needed to open it up and, say, slap on some thermal paste to keep the CPU cool under a load)- I've seen walkthroughs to replace cracked screens, camera backs, vibrating motors, etc, that require nothing more than a small screwdriver. If the battery starts to go or you need more power than a stock one offers, you can easily replace them and get BIGGER capacity ones. IR blaster, second screen display (which is really neat!) HDMI out via USB-c, pretty much everything and the kitchen sink is thrown in here. They don't make them like this anymore, folks. This was the last of the greats. That's why people still have and use them in 2019!

I have an old latitude laptop from the windows Vista era that was pretty much considered useless. Someone recommended we try installing cloudready to turn it into a Chromebook, and now my kids use it as an internet machine (it's great for Google docs and YouTube as well as light chrome-based gaming).
Of course a machine that old had a battery dead as a doorknob, so they had to keep it plugged in 24/7. They were annoyed because the charging cable is actually quite short, so they were limited in where it could be used. When I saw how cheap this battery is, however, I decided why not splurge and make it into a portable machine again. They are SO happy now with it. If I had known how easy and inexpensive it would be to revive this old machine and make it useful again, I'd have done this a long time ago.
Note, the battery life isn't amazing. But to be fair, I don't recall how long the original would last either.

There's a lot I really like about these. Let me start off by pointing out, however, these are NOT USB SPEAKERS. They are simply powered off USB and use a standard headphone jack as the audio input. I have to admit, at first I was taken aback by how small they are, and assumed they must produce weak sound as a result (I'm used to a set of Harmon/Kardon speakers on my desktop which are bigger than these). But despite their size, they actually produce a really great and full sound, with an almost exaggerated stereo effect thanks to individual speakers pointing in different directions.
What I love most about it, however, is that it is USB powered. That means no additional plugs needed on my desktop, and in fact they are fantastic for boosting the audio on a laptop. In the included picture I'm posting with this, I have an old Dell Laptop that my kids use to watch things on, and these sound FAR better than the tiny built in laptop speaker. Since it is USB powered, it can be simply be run directly off the laptop itself, no additional wires or outlets necessary. Put one plug into an available USB slot, the other into the headphone jack. It makes a nice and neat looking portable setup. The thing is, I can't help but wonder why it isn't just a 100% USB sound system? I have a pair of headphones that I love using that are completely digital- it identifies as its own sound card when plugged in and requires only that one USB plug. I sort of assumed that this would be something similar to that and therefore require only that ONE plug to operate. In some cases, the digital sound systems are better than analog plug ones (interference, for example) anyway, so it seems strange to have an analog speaker system powered by a digital USB port. But I guess there can be interesting uses for this too.
For example, a device like an older phone with a headphone jack can connect to this which wouldn't work with USB. Or enhancing the speaker of an Echo Dot and powering it off a dual USB outlet (one for the Dot, the other for the speakers). It is definitely an interesting and useful thing to have around! And for the price, color me impressed!

My job has me working in video with small cameras, and sometimes I need to sync my audio recorder/receiver with a DSLR/DSLM. In my setup, this cable did an admirable job feeding clear audio to my camera from an external source. It seems to have a decent build quality, and the right angle is welcome because it makes it less likely to accidentally get pulled out by a cable tug.
My review is for the 4' length, which in my case is preferred to the longer cable. I'd honestly prefer even a 3' cable, not only is it less messy in my rig but less signal loss/noise attenuation on a shorter run is always preferable when working with recordings. Good value.

I work with video equipment for a living, and sometimes I need to wire up small cameras like DSLR/DSLMs to an external monitor or recorder on a job. Using a proper cable is important, especially one like this which goes from micro HDMI to full sized HDMI, rather than just using a regular HDMI and a micro-adapter on one end. Using adapters introduces more points of failure as well as distortion/possible signal loss at each connection point.
I used this on a job going from a Sony A7S to an Atmos Ninja recorder, directly from the camera to the recorder, no adapters needed, and it worked perfectly. Crisp clean signal as expected, and the setup was nice and neat looking.
If you need to connect a micro hdmi to a full sized port, you can't go wrong with Amazon Basics.

I've always wanted a wireless off camera monitor for director/crew use on our freelance camera operator gigs, or for when mounting the camera somewhere difficult to see like the side of a car. A few years ago, a solution like this would have cost upwards of $2k, but now thanks to products like this one we can do it on a shoestring budget!
I attached the transmitter to a USB battery bank and used gaffer's tape to attach to my camera cage with my Sony A7S inside. On the other side, I took a flash bracket and mounted a 7" monitor, and once again used gaffer's tape to sandwich the receiver to another battery supply and secure to the handle of the bracket. Note that the receiver isn't designed to run off USB power like the transmitter is (why, I don't know), so I had to use a modified cable to make one end a USB - it is still only 5v, but I think it requires at least 2amps so it is pickier about what battery bank will work with it. My smaller battery supply didn't crank out enough power so it won't start (blue light would just blink), but a larger battery supply that I have did just fine.
Once the two were wired up, as a proof of concept I fired up the camera and had a live feed in full 1080p on the remote monitor, which worked fine as long as I was in the same room as the camera. Pretty useful! If you look at the included image, you can see both units on the floor working, but I'll need some shorter cables to clean it up in the future (didn't have any short cable available for this test, so it looks messy).
The only thing I wish Sabrent had done better is include a mount for the transmitter to attach to the camera hotshoe. They claim it comes with one in the box, and even show a picture of it mounted to a camera but it does NOT! It comes with a bracket that uses a thumb screw to attach to something, but it will only fit into a hotshoe if you have an adapter for your shoe mount that will accept a screw through it. The thumb screw and shoe mount that they show in the picture are not included in the box, which disappointed me. No matter, I'd still need a battery supply for this so I had to attach it to a cage anyway. But I felt like that picture was misleading in the product's image.
