I also wish that they had made the receiver work off a standard USB plug as well so I wouldn't have to use a modified cable for it. It worked pretty well so I can't complain too much at the end of the day.
Although I was interested primarily in off camera monitoring, I discovered this device is very well suited to send your laptop's display to a TV. With the receiver on your TV wired up, the transmitter actually works like a dongle right out of the laptop's hdmi port, and just needs a short run of USB for power from the closest port. This is the cleanest use of this product that I can imagine, and it works well for that. Pretty amazing what it can do for the price these days!

As a freelance camera operator, I'm no stranger to these. This is clearly designed for us low budget video shooters using small DSLR style cameras, which is why it uses a Sony camcorder battery plate and designed with a hood for outdoor viewing. It has some pretty great features for the price point, including crop mark overlays, peaking indicators, and individual color channels. That being said, it can be used for all sorts of things, such as a Raspberry Pi monitor, backup camera screen, or even a second monitor for your laptop (that's a fun one!). It even has included sound, something a lot of these monitors do not, more on that later.
This is really designed for video use, and for that it does a pretty great job for the price. It comes with a hotshoe mount adapter to put on top of your camera, and uses standard batteries (most LED lights and other accessories also use these batteries, so you probably have some already if you work in video). The colors are vivid and sharp, more accurate than my Atmost Ninja 2 recorder screen, and nice and big for focus checking.
The hood is a nice touch as well, but it requires the snap on frame to attach, and the frame has a weird problem in which it partially obstructs the HDMI port. Maybe I'm just doing it wrong, but I found I needed to leave that corner off the frame if I wanted to use the HDMI plug.
Speaking of the HDMI plug, it comes with one included which I thought was pretty rad of them, but it isn't the more modern micro HDMI type, but the slightly older MINI one. That's the outdated kind that older devices use (such as 3rd generation Intel laptops or cameras like the GH2), but pretty much everything made in the last few years has been using the newer micro one. So it seems weird that they included this one. Personally, it will come in handy because I DO have a laptop that still uses that plug, but I don't intend to use it with this monitor. All my cameras that use that plug are long gone at this point.
Another couple of things to note: The focus peaking is pretty much useless. It oversharpens the image and thinks high contrast parts of bokeh are "in focus", which is weird. Thankfully my Sony cameras have peaking built in so that isn't much of an issue. Also, the screen is large enough and is HD enough resolution (not full 1080 but more than 720) that you don't really need peaking to tell what's in focus. You can see it with your eyes. Also, if using with a camera that is outputting a 16:9 image, you have to change the screen size setting from the default, which is to maximize the screen. Everything looked a little stretched because the display is a little taller than the output of my camera until I turned that off.
As far as sound, I mentioned earlier that this monitor has a speaker. That's good for when you want to review footage on the monitor, and even better if using with a Raspberry Pi or monitor for other things where it might be your only source of sound. It is also really useful if shooting with a Sony A6000 or similar smaller camera that doesn't have a headphone jack... this offers a headphone jack so you can monitor off the HDMI feed. That's pretty useful right there! But don't forget, when you turn the live view back on, you are going to get major feedback from the mic to the speaker unless you quickly turn the volume all the way DOWN first! Or just leave headphones in if that's how you roll.

It is important to note however that it will not accept a 4k signal. The actual resolution is 1280x800, and it will accept up to 1080p as an input, but more than that fails. At the time I'm reviewing this, it seems that there are similar monitors that can accept a 4k input for around the same price. I'm guessing they are updated versions of the same design, as there are no monitors that actually have that resolution for this price, rather they just accept the feed and down-sample to 1280x800, just like this one. So at the end of the day, it probably won't matter if it accepts 4k or not. Some cameras don't like outputting a different resolution than they are recording, so if you are recording in 4k and outputting 1080p, that might be an issue. Otherwise, this is a solid value.

Lexar used to be up there with Sandisk and other respected names in storage medium. These days the name was bought and rebranded, so I'm keeping my fingers crossed that this doesn't just kick the bucket one day!
So far so good, however. The drive is working, however I'm unable to get the full speed it claims due to my aging hardware requiring an adapter. I hope to test it on a newer computer I have in my office soon with a native NVMe slot and see if I can get it to reach the claimed speeds. With my adapted system, it is at least on par with the speeds I get out of my other internal SSD (SATA based), and with a USB3.1 enclosure, it makes a mean portable storage machine too that looks more like a USB stick on steroids than the bulky external HDs we used to rely on to carry information.
Hoping it holds up- for now I'm impressed with it.

I transfer large video files to take home with me for work each day (cloud storage would take too long to transfer), and this is much nicer than the SATA-2.5" SSD drive I used to carry around with me. I love the size of it, its more like a USB stick on steroids in size and style, but has capacity and speed you'd expect from a larger hard drive. I also like the USB C functionality since my desktop at work has a modern USB C port built in.
Unfortunately, I can't get the full speed out of the USB interface on my home workstation. These NVMe SSDs are capable of going so fast, but my internal SATA SSD clocks higher in benchmarks than this one, and I'm pretty sure that's because of my older USB 3.0 ports. It goes about as fast as my other full sized SSD over USB, but is much smaller and future proof. I dig it.

My daughter enjoys listening to music in bed and on car trips. The problem with traditional headphones are that they either fall our of her ears (earbuds) or are uncomfortable if she falls asleep (over the ear). This solves those issues. Although these are advertised as more of a eye mask with music, which I imagine would be a sensory experience to promote sleep, my daughter uses them more like a headband/sweatband to wear around the house. She just cleaned her room wearing them over her forehead and it reminded me of an 80's workout video. If it's cold outside, I think they'd make a pretty interesting alternative to keep your child's ears warm as well.
She says they are comfortable, and sound good, although I can't verify these claims since it doesn't really fit me. She likes them, so that's a win as far as I'm concerned!

My son wanted a computer for school work on his bedroom desk, but there isn't a lot of free space there. A wired mouse and keyboard looked very cluttered very quickly, so we looked for decent wireless options. I found some affordable Chinese ones, but my son wanted the ability to game every now and then and the cheap ones had reviews that claimed connection would sometimes die in the middle of use and require reconnect.
I found this one and remembered fondly that I used to use Logitech wireless equipment when I was in college and I always had a good experience with them. This model is no different, it handles his school work well and holds up to some light gaming without any noticeable hiccups or disconnects so far. And we can open the desk drawer and drop both the keyboard and mouse in when we are finished so he desk stays clean and uncluttered. I call this combo a win!

I have a larger hot tungsten kit that I use for big lighting jobs, but I found it tedious to use for talking head interviews and small spaces, not to mention needing outlets wherever I set up.
I decided to try these for a job in a warehouse (shooting video of people working), and the notion of it being battery operated was VERY appealing, since I did not want to run cables for power over hundreds of feet of warehouse. I was so impressed with these little lights that now I take them with me on other jobs too. They are so compact and fit so nicely into the included carrying case.
To be fair, they aren't a replacement for a tungsten kit if you're lighting a large area or want more bounce/fill/etc. LEDs simply aren't as bright (yet?), but these are far more convenient, and the light color rendition is very good. I do wish that they didn't require 2 batteries at a time to work (other LEDs I looked into only needed one at a time, these requires both for the correct voltage), and I also wish the case didn't have a big logo that reads "Great Video Maker" (kind of a cheesy name, isn't it? If it just said GVM that would be better IMO!). But these don't take away from how great the lights actually work, so 5 stars.

I previously owned a black pair of these and liked it enough to get a second pair (in red) for my son. The important feature? TF card reader for self-contained music. My son isn't allowed to have a cell phone in school yet, and finding a good music player that isn't more-or-less a phone is hard these days- but THESE HEADPHONES ARE ALSO AN MP3 PLAYER! I took an old Micro SD card from a discarded phone (about 4GB in size) and filled it up with music files. The headphones have little controls for start/stop/ff/rr, and they can be used like that without being tethered, wirelessly or otherwise, to anything else.
Then, in school, he can use it with the supplied aux cable for use in the classroom during computer time, and then at home with our tablets wirelessly over bluetooth. Its amazing how many different roles it plays, and he couldn't be happier with it. The only caveat is that unlike some of my other headphones in this style, this feels a bit weak in build quality, with very shiny plastic that probably will break in my son's backpack eventually. So far so good so I'm still giving it 4 stars, but if the build quality gave me a tad more confidence, I'd give it a 5. For the price I still recommend it, the sound quality is great and it does isolate background noise quite well.

I very much like that the default plug on this is a single TRRS with mic and stereo. I had another headset before this with separate speaker and mic plugs, along with a USB port to power it (light up earphones and mute button controls). When I wanted to use it on my laptop or mobile device which offers a single TRRS plug, it came with an adapter to use... however, it was WAY too much wire and always looked messy. I like how clean this is, I can even use it as a headphone for phone calls in noisy environments because the ear sets are decent about isolating noise from outside. Also since the speakers are larger than your average earbud, the bass response is very respectable. They aren't audiophile quality sound, but I wasn't expecting that from these. These are for gaming, but I think I'll also find myself using them to watch a movie and make phone calls with as well. Good deal!

These seem to be a pretty great option for over-the-head style headphones that fold for storage and are still affordable. My son's back to school list required a pair of headphones for some computer lab work, and he hates the earbud style ones. This is comfortable for both kids and adults, has a decent amount of noise isolation, and even has the inline mic for TRRS plugs like a phone if used in that type of setup. Extra points because they actually look more expensive than they are. My son loves them!

Bought this to replace an old laptop being used as a netflix player on a family member's TV. It was on sale for a few dollars less than an Amazon Fire Stick, so I figured it was worth a shot.
Pleasantly surprised by how great it is- the way you can search multiple sources for content, use your phone as a remote or as an audio channel (so you can plug headphones into your phone and mute the TV- how cool!), and even its selection of free content, was more than I expected. I didn't buy it for myself, but now that I've helped set it up, I've got half a mind to replace my android-based TV box with one of these!

My daughter loves this. Very cute, stylish looking headphones, and surprisingly comfortable to wear. My kids especially don't like earbuds, so the over-the-ear style like these are a welcome alternative. I was actually impressed at how much noise isolation they provide... it really blocks out the outside sound, you end up yelling when trying to talk without realizing, and that's not even when there is any music playing! Sound quality is OK- not as amazing as my brand name speakers, but good enough for what it is. A little echo-ey, but a worthwhile compromise for the over-the-head style and this level of noise isolation.

I love that this gives an almost factory level integration with the car- no matter what mode the stereo is in (even off!), when a call comes in or is initiated, it will switch over and play over the speakers automatically. When installed using the XM port, it will even use the XM's ability to send text to the display, telling you that you are now in Bluetooth mode, which phone is connected, caller ID and track information, etc. It feels as if the car came this way from the factory!
Except for two annoying caveats:
1) THERE IS NO WAY TO INITIATE A CALL WITHOUT YOUR PHONE. Sure, you can use the stereo controls to answer, hang up, and change tracks if listening to music, but there's no button to wake up the Google Assistant/Siri/etc and speak commands like on a factory installed Bluetooth unit. This is the most annoying for me because I really want to be able to que up a song or place a call without taking my phone out of my pocket. I tried to find a way around this by using the always listening "Ok Google" function of my phone, but it eats up my battery to have it always listening for the command. There's also the possibility of using an additional device, like the iSimple ISBC01 Blueclik, which acts like a remote control that connects to the phone using the BT keyboard profile, so you can connect to it and the BT45-HON3 at the same time without conflict. The ISBC01 offers a mic button which SHOULD in theory wake up your phone and launch the voice assistant (it simulates a long-press home button), but while I've heard people say it works for Siri on an iPhone, all it did was wake up the screen on my Android phone. It didn't actually activate the voice command assistant. I found I could install a button remapper app and make it work, but it only seems to work when the device is already on. Additionally, the iSimple device goes to sleep after 10 min of inactivity. So, when first getting into the car, I have to press the mic button on the iSimple to wake it out of sleep and connect to the phone, press it again to wake up the phone, then a third time to actually open Google Assistant. This is obviously not ideal and makes me feel like I could have taken my phone out of my pocket and done all this manually by then. It really makes me wish there was a way to to initiate voice commands from the BT45-HON3 directly, either via a stereo button or with a hardwire remote. Their newer BT45-AUX device actually ships with a battery powered remote, but I'm told it is not compatible with the HON3 version (it is a newer product and didn't exist when the HON3 was made). This makes me hopeful for a future version of this unit, but saddens me that it does not currently offer the features I'm looking for.
2) If using in XM mode, you have to use the tuner up/down function to change tracks and answer calls. The steering wheel controls in my 2010 Odyssey don't have channel up down, but rather radio preset up down (because the understanding is that in normal XM operation, you don't want to go up and down incrementally through 100+ channels, but rather to the next preset at a time). Jumping to the next preset isn't a function the BT45 recognizes, so you need to use the buttons on the stereo to incrementally go up/down a station to interact with the Bluetooth control. On my Odyssey, this is a tuner knob. It seems kind of silly to need to twist the knob right to answer the call or left to reject it when there are perfectly good controls available to my thumb on the steering wheel, but this is a limitation of how the XM buttons are laid out on my car. If using CDC mode instead of XM (which can be set using the dip switches), the up/down on the steering wheel buttons would work since in CD mode they would advance next track / prev track (which is what the BT45 unit is looking for). However, in CDC mode, you lose out on the text display. I like the text display for many reasons- caller ID is nice, as is the artist/title of songs when streaming with Spotify, but most importantly, since I share the car with my wife, it is nice when it displays which phone is currently connected. In our other car, we have bluetooth with no display. When we drive together, sometimes we don't know whos phone is connected and sometimes have an awkward moment pulling away from the driveway when we realize the OTHER person's phone is connected. Having a text display makes it easier to know what is really going on, so I decided I'll just compromise the steering wheel controls and use the tuner knob in return for the text. Its just unfortunate that I have to choose between the two.

Otherwise, the unit is danged near perfect. Connects quickly and sounds really good.

A couple of notes regarding installation:
The instructions want you to install it in the rear where the XM radio is. On a car as long as the Odyssey, I don't want to do that. Its too far from the driver so the BT transmission will have more interference, not to mention how annoying it would be to wire up the mic so far.
I chose to unplug the XM radio from behind the head unit because A) I only have a 3 month trial and don't intend to pay for it, and B) Whatever stations there are, I have access to much much more and arguably better content with my phone and streaming internet station for free (unlimited data plan). Once I have Bluetooth music streaming, I additionally have the benefit of notifications and GPS commands coming in over the radio, so for all intents and purposes, XM is useless in this age of affordable mobile data. And hey, if you really like XM that much, you can always use the XM app with your subscription and do it over Bluetooth. Then you still get notification sounds and GPS commands over the music.
Either way, I recommend unplugging XM and using the included harness to plug it in behind the stereo. Then you can easily fish mic wire behind your dashboard trim, up the A-piller, and over the rear view mirror, where they recommend putting it. I was able to use the included clip to secure it to the headliner, and tuck the wire behind the trimming using a plastic pry tool. Easy peasy and looks nice.

One more thing I did is I decided to plug in a USB cable to the charging port on the unit and drilled a hole in the storage cubby under the climate controls to fish it into. Now, I can open the cubby door and plug in my phone to charge if needed, and not have to see a single wire hanging anywhere in the car. That's nice. :)

I bought an HDMI switch and adapter to send my home entertainment content to either a flat panel screen or our projector. But this meant that instead of having a single HDMI cable from my player to my TV, I now had one going into the switch, another going from the switch to the TV, and another going from the switch to a CAT5 adapter to run the signal to a projector on the other side of the room. Normal sized hdmi cables were cluttering up my AV shelf, which is where these come in. Perfect, short run multi-pack was exactly what I needed. Cables don't need to be tied up to make them shorter, don't get twisted or tangled with other equipment and the short run ensures less signal loss over the course of all the connections. Very happy with this!

I bought this kit initially for the blower. As a mirrorless camera user, having a blower is a MUST. I picked this item because others were charging the same amount for the blower alone, and with this kit I also get a lens pen, cleaning cloths and whatever else you might need to keep your gear in top shape.
The quality of some components in the kit aren't necessarily the highest, but as freebies that come with a blower, they are pretty great and I'm glad I have them. Highly recommended if you own any sort of interchangeable lens camera system that frequently has lenses swapped. An absolute MUST if said camera is mirrorless, as they are practically dust magnets when the sensor is charged.

I bought this to use in an Atomos Ninja 2 video recorder for my camera after having a discussion with Atomos support to ensure compatibility. They actually told me this model should appear on their official "supported" list.
I already have an inexpensive larger HDD that I use for longer jobs (3+ hour concerts on a stationary camera, etc), but I wanted an SSD for jobs that I might require more shock-proofing if going off-tripod with the recorder. This is a perfect fit for that- performance is not the fastest on the market (Sandisk has other lines such as the extreme for that), but it is very respectable for an SSD in today's standards, and faster than my first-generation Intel SSD currently in my workstation. And if you're comparing to a mechanical HDD, we're not even in the same ballpark either way. These are FAST and solid. And I trust Sandisk a lot more than other brands out there.
In fact, I'm impressed enough with the quality-to-cost ratio that I might pick up another one to replace my workstation's older and smaller model. Great buy!

I have a camera cage that I used to mount directly to my Manfrotto QR plate, but would require tightening up frequently on a job (cage would start to have some play after an hour of use). I realized the cage has two mounting holes (originally designed for attachment to a rail system), so I put a second 1/4" screw in my QR plate, and now I have two points of security which not only prevents needing to tighten the screw, but the slight wobble is nearly non-existent now. I realized afterwards that these screws are not only useful for mounting UNDER the cage, but actually super useful for mounting TO the cage as well!
The cage is riddled with 1/4" holes, and in order to tighten an accessory like a microphone mount, the threading on the screw and cage and accessory need to be rotated usually. In other words, if the accessory is mounted in the wrong direction, turning it will also turn the screw, and tightening up the screw might once again move the accessory. These have clearance underneath the threaded part of the screw, so they can actually spin freely once inserted into the cage. That means I can hold an accessory in place while tightening the screw, and it will lock in tight the way I want it to face. Very versatile and useful part of any kit!

I got sick and tired of buying unique cages for each camera I use. This cage is great because it is the most universal design I've seen while still being solid and relatively compact, and most importantly: THE BATTERY DOOR CUTOUT FITS VIRTUALLY ANY CAMERA I'VE TRIED WITH IT! This was the biggest reason I wanted it. I happen to own many different types of cameras (Canon, Panasonic, Sony, etc) and all of them occasionally get used on jobs that require attached recorders, microphones, power supplies, etc. But until I found this, I needed specific cages that allowed access to the battery on each one, otherwise I'd have to remove the camera during a shoot to replace a dead battery, which is just unnecessarily complicated. I feel like this cage is a great addition to whatever I'm using now, and likely whatever I end up using in the near future.

As a few people pointed out, the rail system on the bottom has a knob that somewhat obstructs part of the battery door opening on some cameras (I noticed this on my A7s, other types of cameras may still get enough clearance). Someone on youtube showed that they were able to remove the knob to keep it accessible, but personally I just wanted the cage part. The cage itself has the same mounting holes as the bottom of the rail adapter, so you can just leave the rails off and attach a tripod QR plate directly to the bottom of the cage, which is what I usually do. I did one time try using the entire package decked out, with the rails, a matte box and follow focus attached... I got around the battery door problem by using a dummy battery with a DC wire that attached to an external power supply (I built my own adapter, I won't go into the details now but I'm pretty proud of it!). So I was able to swap batteries via an adapter mounted on the cage instead of under the camera. But this was a much more complicated setup than I usually work with. For normally daily use, I use the cage without the handle or rails, and with the camera attached it actually fits where my camera usually goes in my gearbag. I have the handle and rails handy if I ever need them, but the price is great for the cage alone!

This cooling pad is extremely silent, which is exactly why I wanted it. I bought one of these initially because I have a DLP projector that overheats on long presentations, and I wanted to help keep it cool. Obviously a model with loud fans and vibrations would be less than ideal, but this works well.
Only issue I have is that the USB power connection is short (so I need to bring an extension cord to reach a USB AC power adapter), but since it is designed for laptop use, that is expected.

I ordered these for my uncle because I have a pair but not the pro pair the only problem is he is having a problem with slight of echoing and sometimes sounding as if he was in a tunnel. I haven't talked to him the past few days but if he's gotten it to straighten up and get all that sound to stop I'll write another review and let everyone know

It was very easy to set up and use, so far I've had no complications while I'm using it. It does a really good job for cancelling the sounds from outside of the headphones. But it doesn't prevent other people from hearing your music lol. It's worth the price. Decent quality.

These aren't the most expensive speakers in the world but they can crank up pretty hard and still sound clean and clear without distortion. I use a projector attached to my laptop when we want to watch a movie. I have these speakers on the wall I'm projecting onto so when we're watching a movie I have the audio feed coming from my laptop, perfect for the 1/8" audio jack the transmitter uses.

The transmitter links quickly and without lag, the speakers are clear and don't distort unless theres a really heavy action scene turned up too loud. I tried a fan last summer that said it was quiet, but was definitely not. This one is actually virtually silent, like it claims! Second, and most important, I wish there were an on-off switch so I could angle the fan while it's plugged in, instead of having to guess first and plug in second.

EVGA ftw3 version runs super quiet. Can barely hear it run. At highest settings @ 6880 x 1440 resolution, it never runs hotter than 65c. As to whether 2080ti is worth it in general:

Increase in FPS performance- Too many people judge the 2080ti's merit on raw FPS numbers, saying its only x amount of percent greater in performance than the 1080ti. so its not worth it. But what they completely miss is that its not just about the raw numbers. Its about how those numbers translate into the EXPERIENCE of adding/using that component. The performance of the 2080ti is so much smoother, more effortless and frustration free, than the previous generation, that it was worth it for me to make the change.

Alernative Sli option- I tried 1080ti sli for about a month, it didnt affect the quality of my experience in a meaningful way. The presentation is still jittery and stuttering , making for a distracting experience. Support for SLI is inconsistent and it demands more power and space, creates alot more heat and noise. You can clearly see the poor quality of performance in side by side comparisons on youtube. Judge for yourself. Again, its not all about the FPS. A perfect analogy would be to cars- most high end races cars have respectable 0-60 mph speeds, but the experience and qualty of performance arent the same.

Price argument: Just because its expensive and someone cant afford it doesnt mean its a 1 star product. Check the quality, time and effort the reviewer put into the review and judge for yourself. It takes money, time and expensive R&D to make products such as these. Im not going to argue that its not expensive. It is. But consider that it beats two 1080ti SLI in quality of performance, then you realize it isnt. If you are salty that you cant afford it, try skipping some meals and dropping some vices and prioritize things differently. Seems everyone wants free things these days. I wonder if they would work without compensation.

Conclusion: Sure its expensive, but if you can afford it and you want quality performance, not just eye popping FPS numbers, which can be meaningless, get the 2080ti. Some just cant see the difference and thats fine. But for those who can afford it and have more discerning eyes, the upgrade is a must. My only complaint? It cant make poorly coded, inefficient games like Kingdom Come run better at the highest settings on a 6880 x 1440 setup. (Runs nearly every other game at the highest setting flawlessly at these high resolutions) Might have to wait for the next generation for that. Because of that and the "high" price it doesn't get a top recommendation but a very high recommendation.

Just a phenomenal cpu. This is probably the best upgrade Ive done, coming from an i7 7700k. I had 30 days to use and figure out if I wanted to stay with this or go with the latest AMD cpu.

Work- I used to have trouble running programs that were either too complex or inefficiently coded that it led to stutters, hitches, delays or freezes. One program that always caused massive trouble for me over the years was the Think or Swim trading platform. I originally upgraded to the i7 7700k and it could not handle more than 2-3 chart at a time running the time and sales and L2. Run some side charts and you could forget about trading, especially at the open when calculations need to be run at an extremely rapid pace. I even added a total of 32gb ddr4 3400 ram and it still wouldnt run properly. Arguably, the program is encoded really inefficiently requiring much more from the CPU than necessary. Ive tried many different trading programs and this one caused the most trouble. After stepping up to the i9 9900k I can now run this inefficiently encoded program on my main chart screen, with two different tickers having 4 different time frames each with its own L2 and time and sales, PLUS 15 side charts without a hitch! Also im running my browser with at least 5 tabs open and video/audio running. Absolutely amazing. I never thought I could get it to work like this.

Gaming- even if the cpu doesnt run at 100 pct it affects the quality of the experience of the gameplay, especially for demanding games, or just poorly coded, inefficient ones. RPGs fall into these categories. I.e., Kingdom Come Deliverance. Video and streaming is flawless as well.

Vs AMD- Performance isnt always about raw numbers, if there are too many peaks and valleys, it affects the quality of the experience. I havent personally compared it directly to the newest AMD cpu, but having looked at the side by side comparisons, AMD cpu seems to put out better numbers for work-related applications, but clearly on the gaming side, intel is superior. From my observation, the quality of the experience with Intel was greater because the frame rate was consistent with much less, if any micro stuttering, which you can see with the AMD chips. As a result, Intel's presentation was more effortless and smooth. With the AMD setup, you can see some graying/discoloring/hazy effects in demanding scenes. It seems like AMD is an overcharged chip that experiences these dips because of that, causing a deterioration in the experience. AMD is perfectly fine for work I presume, but not for me when it comes to gaming. Intel performs like a more refined, polished product. This is just based on my personal observation of their performance in these two different areas.

Overclocking- its perfectly fine using it the way it is. No need to overclock, but of course you can overclock it. I run mine 16 hours a day without any problems. Top recommendation at the asking price these days.

I have had this camera about a week and absolutely love most things about it. Super fast focusing, great low light performance, awesome pictures, superb macros, stunning lcd display, great body, and the list goes on. You've seen it all in the other reviews. It's a wonderful camera that I can carry with me for strolls and spur-of-the-moment shots. I would love to have been able to use this for street photography, but because Canon saw fit to do away with the articulated tilt screen, this is not so very practicable now. It's so much easier to get great candid shots of people when you're not so obviously balancing a camera out in front of you at chin level or higher, trying to compose your shot. With a tilt screen or articulated screen you just casually hang your head to look down at the screen, and a quiet, incognito, stealth shot, with the camera hanging low in front at chest level, is so much easier to carry off discreetly and without bringing attention to yourself. With a fixed screen - not. Huge disappointment in that department. What was Canon thinking? Did someone at the design meeting say: "Gentlemen, perhaps we should step back a pace. This camera is so awesome that if we included the tilt screen, like we did for its last 3 predecessors, we'd leave the competition choking in our wake. That would not be fair. Gotta keep the competitors healthy and happy. Let's ditch the tilt screen." How logical was that???

So, now I'm faced with trying to decide between this camera and its close competitor the very cool, but somewhat slower-to-focus Nikon P7700. Also, the Nikon's flash is virtually unusable on macro photos because it casts the lens' shadow over your subject. Even though the Nikon also has a 20x zoom lens in its favor and many other awesome features, that slower focus is kind of off-putting... After all, usually you want to actually capture "that" moment, not the one that comes 2.5 seconds later. Also, I love macro photography and really resent that shadow. Who designed that flash anyway???

Hence, my dilemma. What to do...? What to do...?

This is the most amazingly satisfying electronics product I have ever bought. The features are many and easy to learn. I especially enjoy some of the audio and video adjustment features: Audio: DRC setting helps bring up quieter sounds while controlling loud peaks. Great for taming those annoying audio surges in 'background' music or battle scenes, etc. The Dialog feature lets you adjust the dialog perception so that you can hear the voices better over the background sounds in the soundtracks. Video: You can adjust the Sharpness, Brightness, Contrast, Gamma, Hue, Chroma Level and BNR (block noise reduction). Each one has several levels to choose from and you get to sample it as it adjusts, so you can skip back and forth and compare the difference before you decide what to settle on. The USB mode has great, easy to navigate menus. You can also record to your thumb drive from a CD that you are playing. There is a choice of different bit rates to do this and you can record individual tracks or all tracks. Very user-friendly menus for all these choices. This unit has too many features to list, especially for someone like me, who is not quite fluent in tech terminology. Suffice it to say that it performs all the functions beautifully, the manual is very user-friendly and not only tells you how to adjust/change the various settings, but also explains the technical terminology in real English, so you know what those settings actually do when activated. I do love the region-free feature too. But for me, this is more ho-hum, since I already owned one - a far inferior quality Philips one. About the only thing I can think of to improve the user-friendliness of this product would be to have an alphabetized index in the manual. But, since it's only a 61 page manual, it's not such a big issue overall. Another suggestion I would have would be to allow to record audio from DVDs also. So often, the audio track on a DVD sounds so much better than the soundtrack that is published on CD (i.e.: Brassed Off, Eyes Wide Shut), although I recognize there may be some copyright issues with that concept. For the record: I am getting a second unit for my upstairs TV. Have I mentioned that I love it...? This is a really great product!!!

This is the most amazingly satisfying electronics product I have ever bought. The features are many and easy to learn. I especially enjoy some of the audio and video adjustment features:
Audio: DRC setting helps bring up quieter sounds while controlling loud peaks. Great for taming those annoying audio surges in 'background' music or battle scenes, etc. The Dialog feature lets you adjust the dialog perception so that you can hear the voices better over the background sounds in the soundtracks.
Video: You can adjust the Sharpness, Brightness, Contrast, Gamma, Hue, Chroma Level and BNR (block noise reduction). Each one has several levels to choose from and you get to sample it as it adjusts, so you can skip back and forth and compare the difference before you decide what to settle on.
The USB mode has great, easy to navigate menus. You can also record to your thumb drive from a CD that you are playing. There is a choice of different bit rates to do this and you can record individual tracks or all tracks. Very user-friendly menus for all these choices.
This unit has too many features to list, especially for someone like me, who is not quite fluent in tech terminology. Suffice it to say that it performs all the functions beautifully, the manual is very user-friendly and not only tells you how to adjust/change the various settings, but also explains the technical terminology in real English, so you know what those settings actually do when activated.
I do love the region-free feature too. But for me, this is more ho-hum, since I already owned one - a far inferior quality Philips one.
About the only thing I can think of to improve the user-friendliness of this product would be to have an alphabetized index in the manual. But, since it's only a 61 page manual, it's not such a big issue overall.
Another suggestion I would have would be to allow it to record audio from DVDs also. So often, the audio track on a DVD sounds so much better than the soundtrack that is published on CD (i.e.: Brassed Off, Eyes Wide Shut), although I recognize there may be some copyright issues with that concept.
For the record: I am getting a second unit for my upstairs TV. Have I mentioned that I love it...? This is a really great product!!!

For starters – I really do like this monitor. The picture is nice, it seems to be well designed and well packaged, and the support email address was very responsive when I registered my warranty. I performed a very non-technical color comparison using colored bars in a spreadsheet (see photo), and the external monitor seems to be on par with the display on my primary personal laptop as well as my work laptop. I am pleased with the brightness, which seems to be the primary complaint for most USB-C monitors.

The only disappointment that I have pertains to the advertised weight of the monitor. Supposedly 1.43lbs.

I spent several days evaluating many products and narrowing down my selection, and I chose this model specifically because of the advertised 1.43lbs weight. By comparison, there are a number of similar monitors on Amazon with 300nit brightness and which sell for $40usd to $50usd less than this one. However, those monitors are all advertised as weighing more than this monitor, which is specifically why I chose this brand. Weight is extremely important to me for a portable setup and I was willing to pay extra for the lightest one I could find.

Advertised as 1.43lbs, in reality it is 1.6 lbs (see photo) – the same weight advertised by the other brands. But, when you add the cover (which is required to get this monitor to stand up without an extra stand), the weight is 2.6lbs. There are other monitors which have an integrated stand with a total advertised weight of 1.6lbs - 1.7lbs.

I did end up buying a separate stand which is very lightweight and larger than competing products. I am very satisfied with how well is support the monitor.

https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B08K2W4X2V

So in the end, I really like the monitor, and the company is very responsive. But I would probably look at another option if I had to do it over again and was concerned about total weight. I probably could have saved some money and ended up with a lighter option that works as well.

I’m 40 and have high frequency hearing loss. I hear almost nothing from 1kHz & up in my right ear and 4kHz and up in my left ear. I only experience issues in loud environments(restaurants, etc) or when there is a lot of background noise, but I recently started experiencing low frequency tinnitus that was irritating so I started looking for solutions. I went to see an ENT doctor and went through the motions only for him to confirm that I have poor hearing for my age and it’s up to me if I want some expensive hearing aids. No way I’m dropping 5k... I began by just looking for something to relieve the tinnitus and ran across many people saying that noise canceling headphones helped. I then went to the Bose website and low and behold they had the Hearphones which also had noise canceling. I started reading reviews then first then I stopped by the store with my kids and tried them out. My son was across the store and I could hear him talking to his sister. I could also hear every word of the conversation of people not far away. I removed the Hearphones and could not hear my kids or the people talking. I did this a few times... tuning in on people, music, etc then removing the buds. Tried the noise canceling and the rumbling in my ears was almost gone. Needless to say, I was impressed. I discussed the warranty with the salesman...30 day return, 90 exchange for something else, & 1 year free replacement(btw the 1 yr starts replacement over every time you replace them). I was sold. I purchased them with the intention of using for 30 days and returning if I could do without them.

I have now had them for 1 month. Here is my experience... at first I hated the neckband and was considering returning, but I got used to it and now don’t notice it. I use them for 1 hour workouts every morning, driving in the car for phone calls, music, podcasts, noise canceling at work, so pretty much all day. The neckband twists a little while working out or running and you need to shift it back in place, but it’s not a big deal for me. I would prefer the Soundsport Frees for working out, but I can’t bring myself to spend another $200 for headphones when these are $500. The noise canceling is fantastic for the gym & office and allows me to listen to music at a much lower level, which saves what I have left of my hearing in the long run. I used the soundsport wireless for 1 year before getting these and the sound quality of the hearphones is better, plus the noise canceling, and it has the music boost/phone call boost. I gave my soundsports to my wife and now use these exclusively.

Hearing:
When there is a lot of noise I can put them on and hear every word of a conversation that I would normally not hear or tune all the noise out via the noise cancellation. I recently went to a concert and was shocked at how much I enjoyed the concert more while wearing them. I could hear the guitar strings, vocals, and so much more while having a conversation with my wife. Amazing! I even use them while listening to the stereo in my car because it sounds so much better. I am always surprised at the sounds that I miss while not wearing them.

Sound: Classic Bose sound. The best headphones I’ve owned and I’ve had a few nice sets including the Bose soundsports & Bowers & Wilkins. I enjoy music much more since having them.

Phone calls: Phone calls are so much better, I talk on the phone more now because I’m not struggling to hear the other person and I hear them in both ears.

Overall: They simply work great. One of the best features is the directivity. When you set it to front or focused it ignores the rear microphones. While at the same time merging the left & right sound together. You hear a little of the left in the right ear and vice verse which helps with conversations. If Bose can ever put this technology in earbuds like the Frees they probably could not keep them on the shelf. If you have hearing loss or tinnitus and love music buy the Hearphones. If you love music and have no hearing loss buy the QC30 or QC35 for the noise canceling feature.

There are other fun Easter eggs that I didn’t expect...Wearing these while listening to music creates a “karaoke” effect and you can adjust the world volume so that it increases your voice to blend with the music coming through the headphones. I also played my guitar and found that more enjoyable. I could hear the notes in more detail as well as hear my voice in more detail while playing. These are also great if you like to people watch. When you are in a mall or restaurant you can hear random people’s conversations from across the room in detail, while they think you are wearing headphones and not listening at all. If you have hearing loss and/or enjoy a premium set of headphones these are for you. I have not used any other hearing devices to compare, but there are plenty of other reviews that will provide that information.

- Noise canceling is superb. It has almost stopped my tinnitus altogether. Especially good in situations like moving the yard. Before the noise of the mower was exhausting , but now it does not bother me.

Negatives:

(Later: The manufacturer has changed the visual so it indicates that it's not HDMI. However, it still says REGION FREE and it is not. )

(Even later: If you contact the manufacturer at the e-mail posted in "Questions & Answers" OR on the booklet that comes with the DVD player, they will send you a PDF of the instructions. For the record, here are the instructions to make it Region Free:

Connect RCA cables and turn on unit. Do not put a disc into it, or leave the unit open with no disc.
Type 5168. This brings up a menu that includes the choice "Region"
Go to "Region" and press Enter.
Choose "Test 0." Press enter.
Press setup button to exit, or get back to the left menu if enter has not already taken you there and go up or down to Exit Setup and then hit Enter.

This played all my British DVDs and my one Australian DVD, because Australia was the only company that released TNT's wonderful Alan Arkin film COOPERSTOWN on DVD.)

I was hesitant to order these headphones because they had no boom mike. My husband's previous headphones, from Turtle Bay, had a plastic headband, and several weeks ago the plastic headband on the side of the phones that had the boom mike snapped in half. We had to tape the outside shell of the headband shut with electrical tape so that he could still use them to work with or play music on, so that the headphones sat cockeyed on his head. Luckily these Sony headphones turned up so we could try them out, but he was wary about the lack of external mike because their most important use was his taking phone calls when he teleworked. He needed to be understood by his callers.

All his fears have been unfounded. He uses them for his work, 10 hours a day. The people he speaks to over the phone can hear him perfectly, despite the lack of a boom mike, and he can hear them clearly as well. He charges it overnight and they last through the entire ten hours of his shift. Even better, these headphones do what his Turtle Bay phones did not: he can use them via bluetooth without the bluetooth shutting off when he doesn't use it. He was using the Turtle Bay headphones with a wired connection because if he didn't use them for over 20 minutes the bluetooth would shut itself off.

The noise cancellation function is excellent. When it is off, he can still hear external noises, but once on he can't hear much of anything. I shouted at him at one point and he did not hear me. If you were working, especially in a noisy office, these would be ideal, and they should be useful on a long airline flight as well. (Having no crying baby to test this with, he can't vouch for these covering a whiny child.)

As for the music, he said it sounded perfect right out of the box, without using the Extra Bass, better than his old Sony wired headphones. He listened to a favorite Moody Blues song and said he could hear when the riff changed channels from one guitar to the other, and the sound effects changing from ear to ear. Next he engaged the Extra Bass and listened to a Moody Blues selection with a heavy bass portion and loved the results.

At this moment we are totally satisfied with these headphones. Time will tell if they will stand up to weeks of work calls and listening to music. However, my husband says there is definitely one thing wrong with them: THE SIX INCH LONG CHARGE CORD. Really, who makes these things? Luckily we had a multipack of USB C charge cords we got here on Amazon.

I try to take a mile to mile-and-a-half walk each morning with our dog, to keep both our weights down, and since I walk the same route every day, after a while it gets a bit monotonous. Sure I can watch the weeds at the side of the road as they progress through the seasons--presently the privet and the honeysuckle are in sweet bloom, later on I want to see if the thistle plant blooms this year, in the fall the leaves make a carpet of color--but most of the time, dull, dull, dull. So I've taken to listening to a podcast while I walk, and was using the nice set of Jabra earphones I have, but they are too heavy to walk with; they work fine if I'm sitting still but if I move they fall out of my ear (I do mean my ear, because the traffic is so bad and I have to cross a busy street, I only keep one in). So I wanted a light pair to walk the dog in. These are great! The sound is nice and clear and very full even if I only have one in, and I love the fact that three sizes of earpads are included. I am using the largest ones and they are a nice tight fit. No having to push them back into my ear every three minutes. Very happy with these.

Tried these out just recently. The first charge took something like six or seven hours, so yes, it will be showing red that long! Supposedly after charging you can get 13 hours of use out of them,but I don't think I'll ever have the chance to try them out that long; I just don't listen to music/other stuff for marathon sessions like that. While the fact that they're not Bluetooth and you have to find a place for the base station might put some folks off, on the other hand they work just fine once you plug everything in. Used them to listen to a tuba concert from Boston on YouTube and that sounded good, so expect even better things if I use them to listen to CDs or watch a DVD in privacy.

Please note that they are not noise-blocking, if that is important to you.

I've had this little speaker for two days and love it. I don't know what NFC is; all I know is that it paired beautifully via Bluetooth to my phone and is playing CDs that I ripped to MP3 with a nice fidelity, especially after I tweaked the equalizer app in my music player.

I actually wanted this for a special reason. I still have lots of records and cassette tapes, especially Christmas ones and old soundtracks, like my original STAR WARS LPs, and wanted to be able to play them in our living room. However, the only record player/cassette player we have is in another room, and it is not Bluetooth enabled (it's from the 1990s). I ran a line in cable and a power cord along a wall to another small speaker I have and have set it on a bookcase shelf at the entrance to the living room and this setup works wonderfully, but I wanted a better speaker. This one fills the bill admirably, and I will swap them out when I have a minute.

I'm not a big audiophile, so I can't give you decibel commentary or hifaluting audio reviews. However, it sounds nice and does what I wished it to do, and that's quite enough.

I don't believe I have fully plumbed the depths of this gadget's usefulness. I've only loaded one skill so far. However, I have enjoyed what I've done on it. I can ask it the temperature outside when I get up, or before I go to walk the dog so I know what to wear outside. It has a good range, too; I can call from downstairs in the foyer and it will still respond. (Unless the TV's on too loud.) I've had it set timers while washing clothes or baking cookies. While I was decorating the Christmas tree I had it play Perry Como and Bing Crosby and the Ray Coniff Singers. It's not so good on "Wolfram-Alpha" type questions: for instance, I tried to ask it what date was 7 weeks from January 8 and it didn't get it. It WOULD, if I phrased it carefully enough, tell me what date was 7 weeks from the current day (which was January 3). I haven't played JEOPARDY on it or used it to order anything yet.

I will come back and do a further review when all the Christmas/New Year's hoopla is out of the way, but my husband got interested when he saw this gadget arrive in the mail and spent around an hour installing it (most of the hour spent trying to find somewhere to plug it in). He said installation is baby simple--plug it in the TV, plug in the power cord, then follow the instructions on the screen. You will need a computer, a tablet, or a smartphone to do the setup. However, I am automatically subtracting one point off the final rating because, although Roku states during the setup that there are many places you can access through its gadget for free, you are REQUIRED to give it a credit card number in order for your registration to complete "just in case" you want to order something that costs money in the future. This is like saying you can't surf Amazon and pick out a couple of books without registering first. I'd say you should allow your customers to "cross that bridge" when they come to it, not force them to supply a credit card, especially since Roku stresses in their advertising that there is no subscription cost!

Update: April 2017...I have taken this Roku stick off our guest room television and put it on the main TV because it gets Britbox, which I signed up for today. I am really happy with it, but must warn that the stick itself must be in plain view of the remote and you must aim the remote directly at it or it won't respond. Otherwise there is great reception and the remote is very easy to use. I found some interesting looking channels including one for the Great Courses.

This is my second Bracketron purchase, the first having been from Radio Shack. I'm sorry to give poor Radio Shack even less business by not buying my replacement unit there, but really--$35 at Radio Shack, only $12 on Amazon? I'm saving for retirement here, guys, give me a break.

Anyway, I like this unit because it works on my air vent rather than having it dangling from or standing on a suction cup. I know through bitter experience how quickly these suction cups lose their suction; I'm not risking breaking a $200 smartphone. I plug my phone into the power cord, wire it for sound, and while I'm using the GPS listen to podcasts or music. With a little finagling, it's just on the correct angle to see with a quick glance while you're driving. Using voice commands I can make a phone call without having to take my hands off the steering wheel. Waze guides me through traffic. Rick Steves keeps me entertained. I love my Bracketron.

I received this item yesterday and immediately set it to charge; however, you can connect to Bluetooth and set everything up while it is charging, which is what I did.

Connection was ridiculously simple: turn on Bluetooth on your device (in my case a Galaxy Nexus), turn on the WAE-PTP05, which immediately shows up on your Bluetooth screen, you tell them to pair, and you're done. The next time you turn on device and speakers they pair immediately.

I am not an audiophile; I can't tell you about megahertz levels and give you minute techy details. What I can tell you is that the sound is excellent. I tested a range of input: soft instrumentals, lively Celtic tunes with vocals, a lush film score, and several different spoken word podcasts, most featuring men with baritone voices. All sounded super. One of the soundtrack items had little, soft bells in the background and they could be heard quite well. My husband, who was in the kitchen when I initially tested it, could still hear it clearly--he can't hear the television at the same distance--and was impressed.

The bass response, something I always check out in speakers, is excellent. In fact, the bass is so good that I've upset the dog. We have a fifteen-year-old dog whose hearing is not as acute as it used to be, but she does react with unease when we put the subwoofer on our home theatre system on. This unit made her act the same way as she does when we turn on the subwoofer; I didn't have it on very loud at all and I still had to turn it down so she would relax.

You can also download a free app which will give you a music interface and an equalizer for different music styles (rock, pop, etc.). Frankly, I find the interface too cluttered (YMMV), but it's easy to navigate after about five minutes and you can set a custom setting on the equalizer. I haven't yet tested battery life, but the sound, in short, is worth the price. I would wholeheartedly recommend these speakers.

This keyboard arrived today and I couldn't resist immediately pulling it from the box and setting it up. It comes with the required batteries, so you don't even have to hunt them up. The instructions are two tiny pages, which is how simple it is. I don't think it took me ten minutes, and I could have cut half that off had I remembered to immediately turn on the tablet's Bluetooth and go to the Bluetooth setup so I could pair the two. :-)

This has a "Chiclet" keyboard, but the keys are very responsive. It is the same size as the laptop-style keyboard that goes with my husband's Asus tablet; he has large hands and still feels he can type on it comfortably. The top of the keyboard has four function keys specially programmed to work with Windows 7 / 8, but the rest work as on a regular keyboard: "end," "home," etc. While the keyboard has an off/on switch that works with the function key, it also comes with a thick, rubber-coated (or "rubberlike," perhaps) cover which turns on the keyboard when you take it off and then turns it off when you put it back on. It fits snugly and completely covers the keyboard, protecting it. In addition, the cover bends in the middle so you can use it as a stand for your tablet.

I used it to write in Facebook and Blogger, and also tested it with a Word document in Documents to Go. Very comfortable to type with, although it suffers from the same problem with my tablet that my fold-up Freedom Pro keyboard does: when I use it in Blogger or Facebook, it types the first TWO letters of a sentence as a capital letter rather than one. I think this may be a problem unique to my Galaxy Tab 2 10.1. I did notice that the CTRL i combination for italics and the CTRL b combination for bold does not work with this keyboard, which I do find problematic and why I did not rate the keyboard as five stars. Otherwise I am very happy with it.

After purchasing my tablet, I had found a case for it at Walmart, very sturdy, adequately padded, and with the ability to tilt the screen. However, the mechanism to tilt the screen was established with velcro, which after a while did not hold as well as it did in the beginning. In addition, at least one of the little elastic straps that held the tablet in the case pressed on the power button, sometimes with bizarre results. I therefore considered this Belkin case with interest.

Upon receiving, I immediately fitted the tablet into the case, and was delighted when it was held snugly and kept from slipping out by a flap which tucks under the tablet. All the buttons except the charging button were close to a cutout so that button could be accessed easily. In addition, the cover of the case has little grooves at intervals so that the tablet can be propped up to be viewed at various angles.

As other reviewers have mentioned, it's a very sturdy and thick case, which does increase the weight of the featherlight Galaxy Tab somewhat. And as I have been careful not to drop it, I do not know how well it protects and from various heights...and nor am I likely to test! But it appears very solid, and the elastic cord sewn into the case cover keeps it closed well.

Drawbacks: there's no hole for the charger, so you must charge with the case open. Nor can you charge when using the tablet propped up. And you can only prop horizontally, not vertically, although I doubt if that is much of an issue for most of the things you would want to do with the tablet propped up.

In short, it's not perfect because of the case having to be open to charge, and I also wish there was some way to keep my stylus inside; the case is so tight that I have to hang it outside, exposing the tip to dirt and damage. But otherwise it works well for me. Your mileage may vary!

I thought long and hard about a tablet, knowing that for me it would basically be a toy. Plus I already had a Nook Color. When the iPad2 reduced in price, I thought about getting one of those, but decided against it for the following reasons: (1) no Flash--and yes, I know HTML5 is going to make that obsolete, but in the meantime many websites have a lot of money invested in Flash animation and even restaurants use the silly format to show you their menus (geez, just give us a LIST already--I don't need pretty pictures to find out if you serve something I can eat) and (2) I'm already invested in the Android market and would have to buy many iPad apps that I already have free from Android.

I have not even used it for a week yet, but this a preliminary review with some information I saw requested in other reviews (not necessarily here at Amazon).

UPS delivered this a little before 6:30 p.m. I immediately plugged it into the charger and left it alone. It was charged by 10 p.m. (it might have been earlier, but the unit was away from me and I heard no bleep or flash that might have have indicated the charge was finished). So it does not take six or eight or ten hours to charge as I have seen claimed on other sites. By midnight I was attached to wireless, had gotten into all my accounts and Android apps and was happily surfing and rearranging my home screen.

I used this over the weekend at a science fiction convention. I did not use it constantly, but turned the screen on and off all day for about a 12-hour period, reading Facebook and blogs, checking the news and weather, looking at the convention schedule online, playing short You Tube videos, etc. Nothing excessive, but sometimes did have it on for a half hour to 45-minutes at the time. I also do not have a lot of widgets going, like the Accu-Weather and news widgets that come pre-loaded on the home screen. (They delete easily.) In that 12-hour period it never got below 78% on the battery. It's very quick and fast and responds to a Targus stylus (rubber tipped) wonderfully, much better than my Nook color. The resolution of the screen is impressive. Maybe it's not the new iPad's "retinal display," but it's very, very sharp and bright, even though I keep my brightness turned down to save power. I downloaded the Nook app and the magazines I subscribe to look gorgeous and are simple to read; if not, a tap of the screen makes the text bigger. The unit also comes with Zinio preloaded, an app I plan to use to subscribe to non-US magazines. Kindle books look nice as well, but to me this is too large for marathon reading sessions. I prefer my Nook Color for that. Like my Android phone and my Nook Color, it connects to wireless like a dream, which is more than I can say for my laptop.

Things that might lead you to choose another tablet: (1) The camera is nothing special. It takes good close ups, but further away was problematic. However, I was in a low-light situation each time. Taking photos outside may be totally different. Why Samsung chose to remove the flash I have no idea. Silly, really. But who buys a tablet to take pictures with? (2) With a stylus I can tap to enlarge an image (like Google Maps), but not make it smaller and there is no plus or minus sign on the screen as on my Android phone. (3) Blogger doesn't work in the browser; you have to download the Blogger app, but that works well. iExit doesn't work on it, either. Rats. (4) As at least one other person mentioned, the screen cap button is right in a place where you can hit it easily. I thought of a good use for it this weekend (took a screen cap of the online schedule for the convention I was at, made a short-cut of it to the screen, then pulled up the screen cap for reference rather than going to the web page all the time). Very convenient! (5) Hate the pre-loaded websites in the browser, but I have seen this on other tablets. Apparently we the public are stupid (or lazy) and can't find our own favorite websites and bookmark them. [eyes roll], and (6) my Bluetooth keyboard won't work with it right now because there is as yet no driver for Android 4.0 (Ice Cream Sandwich).

I hope to check back with further comments.

[A few weeks later after I bought this, my husband found an Asus Transformer (TF300) at a good price. It appears to be just as good as this Samsung and the camera is better. It has a zoom and does take a better photo. So if you were looking for a tablet with a better camera the Asus Transformer may be for you. Note: It doesn't have a flash either.]

It’s not hard and will make since after you read the directions. There is downloadable software which supports all the features. It works well but I don’t intend on using much. It isn’t required to be downloaded in order to use the keyboard. The usb transmitter is small and can be stored in the keyboard if not being used.

I find comfortable to use. It did take a bit of time to get use to the key design but I expected this. The key are quiet but not whisper quiet.

I have used it over a week now for work and I have had no issues at all. All key work well and the battery has not needed to charged once. I use it up to 10 hours a day. It is easily charged via the USB cord and you can use while charging with no issues.

Based on other mechanical keyboards I have used, I consider this one above average and price reflects that. I have no issues with price or functionally. I’am happy with the keyboard and interfaces well with me and my work environment.

Perfect fit under my computer monitors and takes up little space. Also the quality of sound is rather nice. Pairs very well with my existing speakers / bass combo. Also like the fact that I can bluetooth my phone to the speaker if I want to listen to something else while working on my PC. Directions were very helpful on how everything gets setup

ARTECK HW086MW162 Wireless Keyboard and Mouse combo, still charging that's why there are cables. Pen in the photo for size reference, along with the box it came in.

Unboxing was “frustration free” as advertised. I recycled my Logitech cord that connected to my desktop and inserted the USB receiver in it and it worked.

I plugged in the Micro USB charging cable to the keyboard and mouse. Only one Micro USB charging cable came with the combo so I used an extra Android Micro USB charging cable to charge both at the same time.

I was able to use the keyboard and mouse in a few moments. My computer automatically updated the files needed in a few minutes.

All in all the unboxing and set up was quick and effortless. Now I am going to explore the keyboard.

This keyboard has no number side keyboard that makes it smaller.

It has a blue function key to access page up, page down, home, and end, on the lower right where the left, right, up, down keys are.

Along the top with the F keys are blue function commands:

Escape has “Media” – when pressed opened Wave Pad, a NCH program I have installed.

F1 has an >/||, which did nothing when pressed

F2 has |<<, which did nothing when pressed

F3 has >>|, which did nothing when pressed

F4 has a speaker symbol )x, That mutes sound

F5 has a speaker symbol - which lowers volume

F6 has a speaker symbol + which increases volume

F7 has a symbol for home, which opens a new browser tab

F8 has a symbol of a magnifying glass that opens a search side window and uses Bing for search, when I clicked on one of the search results it opened a new Chrome tab. I had Chrome already opened.

F9 has a symbol for a folder, which did nothing when pressed

F10 has a symbol for power which turned off my computer. Since I had programs opened my computer asked for permission so I canceled.

F11 has “insert” on it which is pretty self explanatory

F 12 has “PrtSc” for print screen

The action on the keyboard is nice and a lot quieter than the Logitech keyboard I am replacing. The mouse action is good and also quiet.

For less than $23 this is a good keyboard and mouse. I never used the number keys on the side of my Logitech keyboard, which needed batteries, as did the mouse that came with it. The mouse had begun to do double clicks when I clicked once and the keyboard “enter” would stay down. That's why I replaced them for this Arteck Keyboard and Mouse combo. To be able to stop buying and replacing batteries and the small space it takes up, along with it is quiet, makes my money well spent.

I found set up of this system (3 outdoor, 2 indoor cameras) very easy. Total of two hours for install of all components, initialization, customizing settings, signing up for Blink service, and adding local storage. I used double stick heavy duty tape to mount the cameras. This allows me to relocate until I find the best locations. I carried a camera close around our home to check for any signal weak spots. No issues outside or inside our 1 story ranch. Basement was even good. As an ultimate test I put the a camera about 70' from the Sync Module. It worked fine. Although I haven't checked out sensitivity distance of video capture from this camera. Video quality is satisfactory. Audio is ok, but not intending on using it. Jury is still out on the video capture sensitivity from there The activity zone feature is great. Basic is good for most cameras. Advanced is good for cameras that have flags, trees and or shrubbery that are easily wind active. One disadvantage is that the cameras are either all armed or all disarmed. (The reason for the 4 star rating) It would be nice to be able to arm/disarm on an individual camera basis. Also camera by camera scheduling would be great. BATTERIES!!! PLEASE NOTE BATTERIES!!!!: the instructions and notes are specific that alkaline batteries are to be used. Don't plan un purchasing rechargeable NIMH batteries. If you read the comments on NIMH rechargeable batteries you will see that they do not work with Blink cameras. I think that changing batteries, even on an annual basis, is better than running power/communication cabling to other cameras systems. I can relocate cameras as needed to meet changing needs without hassling with wires. I do have one camera mounted where it it will be exposed to sun, wind, rain, snow, whatever mother nature has in store. I will update on how that survives. I signed up for the annual blink service. I'll see if it was worth it in a year. For now it was a simple setup solution to check video capture and storage.

Initial comments: Arrived yesterday. Easy assembly. Tripod is adequate for this scope. No suggested position for the tube in the mount. No instructions on how to set the balance weight. Instructions are more "assembly" than "user". Finderscope setup is pretty difficult. There has to be a better way than three radial thumbscrews. There is enough flex in the tripod that tightening the finder dead center is futile. Seems like a ball and socket with a tension ring would be better. Initial use was in daylight siting an object some 50 yards away. Thru scope great detail and very clear. Never was able to get the object in the finderscope cross hair center point. But was able to consistently hit the same spot in finderscope. Initial use was of the moon just prior to sunset with clear skies. Great crisp/clear view. Could see the craters on the surface with great detail and shadows in them. From there I viewed various other bright objects. When it got "dark" (Viewing in urban skies) I was able to see various objects visible to the naked eye. Most impressed with what was seen that naked eye couldn't see. Started to set up the phone/camera mount. But then the clouds moved in. I will update in a few days after the next clear night.
Hole for charging cord is not quite large enough/positioned adequately.

Amazed at the video quality. Using the zones allows for eliminating nuisance video collection. Night vision is clear. Only nuisance is that as clouds move across the viewed area and shadows from trees come and go video will be recorded. I think a black color option would be advisable. Being white makes the camera stick out against our dark soffit.

The monitor feels a bit generic, but with the ease of its set-up, it all worked out fine. The only drawback is that the clarity of color and resolution of the monitor can only be seen with a direct, straight on view. Any other viewing angle gives a whitewashed view to the entire screen. That won't be a problem if this is your main screen. However, it might be an issue if you plan to use it as a secondary screen in a multi-monitor set up.  Also, the anchoring device to hold the monitor upright is at an extremely low angle. I had to prop up the two front metal feet up by about 3/4" to view it. So this is not a high end monitor by any means, but it is fine for a low end one.
