Compared to the Duracell Inverter we have, the quality of the battery hookups is a bit cheaper and thinner. However, this little inverter is adequate for the job of recharging ipods and cell phones. Although this unit says you have up to 175 watts, that is peak power. Consistent wattage is 130 so you want to be sure that what you have to use on this needs to be consistent with the 130 wattage instead. I would not go above that, as 175 is PEAK.

The unit is easy to use, you can plug it into the cigarette lighter in the car and it provides power to the USB port for easy recharging. There is a little fan on it and a light to indicates that it is working. I also tested out the battery usage, and it is great to use for campsites, or other areas where you might need to have a way to run simple 130 watt (or near it) electrical units or recharging of cell phones, etc.

The packaging was great- quick open and easy to get to. No struggling with plastic packages that are frustrating, etc.

This is a great simple inverter to have on hand for recharging of various USB friendly components. It worked quickly and efficiently.

These headphones had a mixed reaction in my household. My daughter at twelve likes to spend some time with headphones on connected to her MP3 player. She has literal headphones. I showed her these headphones- or ear buds with loops on them- and asked if she would try them.

Her reaction was that she did not really like them because they had a suction and made it feel uncomfortable on her ears. They did stay in place very well and allowed her to do a lot of activities she could not do with her headphones on. She just couldn't see to get past the suction feeling.

I, on the other hand, like the tight fitting ear rubberized buds because they lock into the ears and close out interfering noise which I appreciate when working outside and trying to block out annoying noise like our next door drummer on days when I just don't want to hear it.

The earphones are comfortable and do stay in place well for activities like gardening and running. They are nice.

Some people might not be able to get past the suction feeling, but if you can, these are nice and will stay in place during active times.

I am not a professional photographer. I can not go into great detail about all of the settings and fancy terminology that others can do so if that is what you are looking for, you won't find it in this review.

I AM an artist, however. I have spent the last 20 years taking accurate color specific photos which need to have accurate texture as much as possible for posting photos of my art in many different media.

When I was younger, I used to devour every inch of every tool that I had. I would learn it inside out and study it until it became like an extension of my hands. Unfortunately life has crowded out my time and ability to study things so I am forced to learn things off the cuff and fly by the seat of my pants.

This can be a problem, however, when it comes to having a very refined taste in photos with color and accurate texture, but only the time to run a quick set of photos.

When my Kodak camera broke, I was very upset. I had one of the nice Z series of Kodak cameras. Although low light photos were a nightmare, the color intensity and accuracy always delighted my senses- especially when taken outdoors.

The Canon G12 is both a huge step forward and a step back.

WHAT I LIKE

The step forward is that in low light, this camera is unbelievable! I can capture a photo in a pure dark room with a flash that I can not capture with most cameras in good artificial light.
There are a ton of settings with the G12. I can set them any way that I want to and that is really nice- except when I am in a hurry.

The auto setting is adequate, but not quite as colorful as I would have hoped.

The camera is solid and can stand on its own for self portraits and a timer.

The intense color setting does a great job in some instances

The camera is easy to hold and I have no problems adjusting to it

The back screen flipping around for self portraits is fabulous- I take a ton of those and this is a huge help.

The lens is FAST- retracts and goes out really quickly.

After not using the camera for a few moments, the lens does retract back again into the camera, but if you press the button lightly that takes photos, it comes out quickly again.

WHAT I DON'T LIKE
The camera can be a bit heavy and cumbersome when I am attempting to hold it with one hand out of necessity (when photographing my arm or hand).

The color capture of this camera is nice outside but in subdued light- photos look washed out. I am well acquainted with photo editing and do use it, but it is a bit more challenging with the G12.

The neck strap can sometimes get in the way when using one hand for photos- but it is a bit too heavy for a wrist strap- although I would like to have that security in case I drop it like I did my other camera.

The manual has to be printed out which annoys me to no end. For a camera this expensive, you would think they would include a manual. This makes it really hard to learn how to use this camera.

I know that some people feel you need to know photography rather than a manual, but I find that I would like to learn this tool, and am very frustrated without inclusion of a manual.

I have not used this camera at all near to its potential. As a point and shoot camera on auto- it is adequate and for most people would probably be just fine. For the other features, there is no manual at all, unless you print it out, which takes ink and paper.

I do love the camera so far, although the color saturation is not quite what I am used to, I will learn to work with it. The lovely low light capacity of this camera makes up for it, I guess.

I have given this four stars because of the lack of manual mostly and the auto mode not being quite as accurate as I would have hoped.

But the G12 is such a nice camera in other ways, it is still close to five stars despite my disappointments.

This Splat stuff is really interesting. When I first got the jar, it was filled to the top with gooey shivery bright orange goo that is the same type of thing we used to get at the toy store and throw against the wall and watch it roll down.

This glob of goo, however, is supposed to be used to clean crevices in your car- speakers, dials, switches, vents, etc, that you can not easily clean otherwise. I did not use this goo right away, and almost a month later, I was surprised to see that the volume of the Splat goo went down by half. It had shrunk- and no one had taken any out either.

It is a bit weird to get used to using at first too, but it quickly becomes easy to manipulate into little places you want to clean.

When using it, it really does work. Little switches and indented areas that gather a lot of dirt and dust were cleaned well with no residue. The only problems I had were two:

---Don't drop it on the floor or it will grab every single stone, piece of dirt, or garbage it touches.

---Don't let it touch the windows or it will leave a smudge that you can only see at night when lights are coming at you and it can be very distracting. It does wash off relatively easily- but it takes a bit of work to get it back to the way it was.

All in all, however, I like Splat. As long as I don't drop it or let it touch any windows in the car, it does a good job. It is only useable for 50 uses and that is not a whole lot- but it is biodegradable. I have not used it up yet so I can not comment on the biodegradability of Splat.

Product came with in 36 hours. Easy to put on any headrest fits large iPad and cell phones. I like the telescoping arm So one child or all four of my children can watch the same program or movie in car. A must have for long trips and to keep children quiet and occupied
This latest Echo Dot works extremely well and the overall sound quality is much improved over my previous Dot. The improvements in sound quality alone is reason to buy this unit.

Product arrived on time as advertised. Finished radio worked very well and  had reasonable selectivity. Sound quality and volume were much better than you would expect from a small self assembled radio kit. I highly recommend this kit, but I must add that the instructions though adequate are difficult to follow for an electronic assembly novice. All the information you need to successfully assemble a nice working AM radio are present, but inexperienced people will most likely need adult assistance.

Love this small radio and all it's features. Works perfectly for me and the sound is acceptable for a bedside radio / alarm. It doesn't have the sound quality of a Bose (which I own also) but it 's not intended to and isn't priced like a Bose either.

Accuracy is amazing. Very clear with all types of music; I listen mostly to classical music but also some pop and jazz. Very excellent highs and mids, and bass response not boomy like some of the popular speakers today. The bass goes far enough down that you might not need a subwoofer -- you might consider trying these out first before getting a sub.

Unless I rearrange the room a lot, I don't have room for large floor-standing speakers. I'm very happy with these as my primary front L+R. I might get the center speaker in the same series at some point.

First impression is that it's physically beautiful, with the amazing piano black finish. It's fairly easy to set up, but I spent some time trying to figure out how to get it to turn on without an on-off switch. Turns out you just have to turn up your music to a respectable volume. After I figured that out, I'm pretty happy.

Oh, it sounds just great. :)

And depending on your computer's configuration, it might support two graphics cards. This is a vertical stand that supports the end of your graphics card (the end without the video connectors).

You can also get a horizontal brace (a different product) but that would require available space below your graphics card.

I'll update this review as I get more experience with the radio, but my first impressions are very positive. It's an excellent value because of its huge number of useful features. However, some notable features are missing, especially SSB if that's important. Likewise, there's no connector for an external antenna. Other features, such as squelch, are shared with the numbered buttons, so they're hard to remember without referring to the (comprehensive) manual.

* AM, FM, and complete shortwave bands.
* Digital tuning, with fine tuning that's easy to use.
* Bandwidth selector that's amazingly effective. Strong AM stations sound amazingly good on the wide setting.
* It can charge rechargeable batteries. Or turn the charge switch off to use non-rechargeable batteries.
* AC power adaptor is included.
* Pretty nice leatherette padded case is included.
* Telescoping antenna is about 2 feet long.
* FM and AM work well. Not sure about SW yet. I need a directory, and I need to compare with better radios.
* Sound quality from the mono speaker is good at low volumes. At higher volumes, the 1 watt amplifier will start clipping. FM stereo is available when using earbuds.

More to come ...

This is a NAS drive, suitable for prosumer or professional NAS units. The concept of being a NAS drive is that if the drive encounters a read error (which happens every once in a while with any disk drive), you don't want the drive to take a possibly long detour into rereading the data and applying its error correction algorithms to recover the data correctly. Rather, you want the drive to give up quickly, and allow the remaining drives in the RAID array to reconstruct the data. So that means "fail early, fail often." The reason for this behavior is that if a drive in a RAID array takes too long to respond to a read request (while doing error correction), the NAS device might decide that the drive has failed, and fail it out of the RAID array, requiring a spare drive to be added needlessly to rebuild the RAID array.

However, my trouble was that Amazon's packaging was completely inadequate to protect the drive during shipment. I was astonished that anyone would ship anything like that, especially a delicate piece of machinery. The drive does seem to work, but I'll have a better idea of that over time.

There are two more considerations for NAS drives. You want to pay attention to whether the drive uses native 4k blocks, and probably all drives in your array should be the same in that respect. And some NAS devices are designed for one or the other. Seagate makes both conventional and 4k-native drives, and the product descriptions aren't clear in this respect. Do a search on the drive's model number and you can learn this information.

Also, consider whether the drive uses conventional magnetic recording (CMR) or shingled magnetic recording (SMR). For typical desktop use either is ok. For NAS use, you should always use CMR drives. Again, doing a search on the drive's model number should help you figure out what kind of recording method is used by each particular drive.

I bought the ATH-A990Z as an upgrade from a previous pair of AT 700x headphones. These ATH-A990Z headphones are superb in many ways, and I often use them to listen to high resolution streaming audio from Qobuz (24 bits, 96 kHz). It's kind of like going from mono to stereo -- once you hear the difference that high resolution can provide, it's hard to go back to ordinary CDs or MP3s, even though those can sound very pleasant.

The fit of the earpads and headband is very good, and I often wear them for hours without any fatigue. In fact, the overall experience is so good that I look forward to my listening time. The substantial ear pads are very effective in blocking out noise from my surroundings, and create a zone where I can enjoy even quiet passages in my classical music favorites.

The sound is a little bass heavy, so those who like the Bose sound will probably be very happy. I prefer a flatter response, and it's actually pretty easy to accomplish that with the Windows equalizer for my Realtek hardware in the Sound control panel. The highs are very light and airy, beautiful. The net result is entirely excellent, with sound that is very smooth and open. Just fantastic. At the price, the ATH-A990Z headphones compare very well to much more expensive alternatives.

A very fine hybrid radio, especially if you have local HD radio stations that have different programs on the subchannels. Controls are very convenient. My only complaint is that it's not stereo sound, and kind of pleasant but only moderate sound quality. If you're ok with that, then you'll be fine with this radio.

This is a very traditional old school CD player. Aside from the gimmick of being able to vary the speed of the playback, this is as ordinary a CD player as you could imagine. It looks like it's built very robustly, which is why I bought it. It has a remote control, but nothing else at all that would qualify as a modern feature. (No bass boost, karaoke mic inputs, etc. Just playing ordinary CDs.) But it does know how to play MP3 CDs.

If that's what you want, I bet you'll be very happy with this.

You might also consider the more expensive CD-200i, which doesn't have the speed control, but does have an iPod dock. And there's the very much more expensive CD-500 CD player with many more features that are useful in a studio setting.

This review is for the Raspberry Pi Ultimate Kit. The assembled parts are all first-rate quality, and you get enough to get started and do a few simple projects. I had the basics assembled and working in about 20 minutes.

Here's a list of additional things you'll need:
Keyboard, mouse, monitor, Internet connection

The Model B board included here has the RJ-45 connection for wired LAN, or you can use the WiFi dongle that's included in the kit. A wireless keyboard/mouse will be handy if you get a keyboard/mouse pair that share a single USB dongle. (There are only 2 USB ports; of course you can attach a USB hub if you like.)

And here are some things you'll probably want to have:
1. Books on what to do with a Raspberry Pi. There are numerous inexpensive ones here on Amazon, covering things like the Python programming language to little projects you can create with the thing. Lots of information also for free on the Internet -- the Wikipedia is a fine place to start.
2. The camera module, if you want to experiment with that.
3. A clever idea of what you want to do with the thing. :-)

I've been playing with this all day, and haven't gotten bored yet. Fun stuff. If all you want to do is to learn about Linux, or do Internet surfing, this is all you need aside from the keyboard/mouse/monitor and Internet connection (wired Ethernet or WiFi). The speed is a little pokey (single core ARM CPU running at 0.7 GHz), so it's more or less the equivalent of high end computers of about 15 years ago. But it works well enough, and you can build a complete system for around $220 or maybe a bit less, including the monitor. Don't expect it to be the equivalent of a traditional desktop or laptop -- no CD/DVD drive, no easy way to copy files or make a backup, and you can't install any Windows application software, although there are lots of interesting and useful Linux applications that work fine. (Keep your data files in the cloud.) But consider the coolness factor, which it has quite a bit of.

These are excellent earbuds. The sound is open, spacious, clear, and pleasant. I have listened to music for hours on these, and my ears don't get tired at all. Here's what I like and don't like.

The sound is open, with sparkling high frequencies and tight, precise lows. The highs sparkle so much that some listeners might think that the sound is too bright. I'm pretty happy with it. The midrange is clear, voices very easy to understand. The lows are not at all boomy, and not as powerful as earbuds that advertise things like "deep powerful bass." But the bass is solid, and for music that has lots of bass energy, these earbuds let it all come through. Overall I think the sound is very accurate, uncolored, and not at all leading to ear-fatigue. I'm very, very pleased with the sound. Pretty sweet.

The product packaging is pretty silly. It's completely overdesigned, with an outer box that separates to allow you to get to an inner tray. I puzzled over the package for about 3 minutes trying to figure out how to get into it, before I discovered a diagram on the side panel of the box. After I successfully extricated the earbuds ...

The plug has a novel oversized swivel that allows it to attach either straight or at right angles to your sound source. It's clever, but I prefer plugs that are visibly more protective of the cord. There's no bendy thing where the cord joins the oversized plug, so I'm concerned that over time the wire might break at the join. We'll see. Whether the swivel is straight or right angled, it's a large plug that I think might be uncomfortably large with some phones or MP3 players. I'm using it with a laptop computer, and it sometimes gets in the way a bit.

In the middle of the cable is a volume control barrel. Just like the plug, it's a classy-looking silvery metal color. But what it earns in form it loses in function, as the volume control slider is very difficult to operate. I have some earbuds that cost only 20% what these cost, and they have a volume control slider that very much easier to use than we have here. Nevertheless, the slider does a good job of controlling the volume when I can get my fingers to operate it.

The earbuds themselves are interesting because they have rather large metal pieces that support the part that fits in the ear. My first reaction was that they would be uncomfortably heavy, or that they might fall out of the ear, but they work remarkably well. I've listened for hours, and had to reposition the earbuds only occasionally.

The cable is typical plastic-coated cable that's heavier than some other earbuds have. It feels rugged, and it doesn't tangle easily. A cloth-wrapped cable would be much nicer still.

The earbuds come with a case that stores the earbuds and the included airplane adaptor. It's a rather large case -- it doesn't fit well into your pocket (for traveling), but does protect the earbuds very well. There's also a second very small drawstring bag, which I assume is for traveling, but it's just a bit too small and stiff to do that job well.

This is one of the modems that's on Comcast's recommended list for my cable system here in California. When the cable guy showed up to install my Internet service, he checked it out and said "It will work fine." After about an hour of pulling wires around my house, he hooked things up to the modem and I had very high speed Internet service. Pretty sweet.

I chose this model because its upload and download specs are well above what my cable Internet service needs, and because it has advanced features like IPv6. So I'm assuming they got the basic stuff right as well. Other reviewers have said this model runs hot, but I haven't observed that. I have it in my utility room which is in the basement where it's pretty cool to start with.

The lights on the front of the unit show what's going on, which is mostly useful as it boots up. They work well, and are also attractive to look at -- they had a good designer for that. The unit has only 3 connection ports on the back, one for power, one for the incoming cable, and one Ethernet RJ-45 out. If you want to hook up more than a single computer, you'll need to connect this single Ethernet port to a router, or wireless router. I have the cable modem connected into a 5-port NetGear switch downstairs, which is connected to an 8-port NetGear switch upstairs, which is then connected to my Linksys wireless router. My computers then use the IP addresses that the wireless router provides. (It won't work to plug additional computers into the switch that I connected directly to the cable modem because the cable company provides only one IP address. It's the wireless router that hands out additional IP addresses. Each computer that you're using requires its own IP address.) The wireless connection works well for my 2 computers and my Roku box for Netflix. (And the bandwidth available to Netflix is amazing. It spends virtually no time at all buffering before it starts streaming HD video.)

Oh, and of course I had to reboot everything (including the modem and the wireless router) for the new modem to be recognized. For now, I'm keeping my old DSL service as a backup Internet service. Not sure when I might decide to give that up.

This is pretty heavy, but not so large that it's hard to position. I have it next to my computer that I use to listen to Amazon streaming MP3 music. My main speakers are NHT Model Twos, and this subwoofer supplies an excellent bottom end to the music. I haven't played it loud yet, but I'm looking forward to trying it out on a movie soundtrack.

The power switch has three positions -- Off, On, and Auto. In the Auto setting, it turns itself on if it senses an incoming signal. When I'm playing music softly, I'm finding that it takes a while to discover that it should turn on. In my case, the subwoofer is sitting next to my desk, and it's not hard to reach the power switch. But keep this in mind if you want to hide it somewhere that would make the power switch hard to reach. (It's near the top of the rear of the cabinet.) There's also a phase switch, with two positions. There's no magic to that; just set it to the position that sounds best. As with all subwoofers, the placement in your room isn't critical, although the subwoofer's sound can be somewhat amplified if you locate it in a corner.

Update: I've had time now to use this with lots of different types of music, as well as TV and movies. The bass is very solid and tight, with no boominess at all. It blends beautifully, with plenty of power for my medium-sized room. This is very musical, adding firm support that's more than just "punch". This is surely one of the best values in powered subwoofers, and I'd buy it again in a heartbeat.

You get two types of noise cancelling with this. First, there's some noise blocking just from having these stuck in your ears. Then the active noise cancelling works quite well. But you have to have them stuck in your ears really firmly, which isn't too easy for me. I suppose it all depends on the shape of your ears. You get several sets of tips, but none of them seem to fit me quite right.

The active noise cancelling works better than I expected. It does a better job with low rumbles, like aircraft noise. It's not so good with voices, but it does give you a little bit of reduction there too. I use them in my office, in a somewhat busy environment.

The sound quality is very pleasing, but it doesn't have the sparkling highs or very deep lows that you get with more expensive earphones or earbuds. Nevertheless, the sound is smooth and well balanced, so it's comfortable to listen to.

For the price, I'm pretty happy.

This actually works pretty well. How well it works for you is highly dependent on your car, and your car's FM radio. It's important to have reasonable expectations for this -- if you want to hook up your MP3 player to your car stereo, the best way is through an Aux input jack. Now, if your car stereo doesn't have an Aux input jack, that's where this product comes in handy. (Another way to hook up your MP3 player is using a cassette adaptor, if your car stereo can play cassette tapes. These also work pretty well, if you can deal with a wire hanging out from the slot where you insert tape cassettes.)

This unit is smaller than I expected, and hangs out of your cigarette lighter with a cord that plugs into your MP3 player. The reception quality over your FM radio depends quite a bit on the position of the unit and the wire. I've found it works best to position the unit somewhere that works, like in the ashtray, or wedged between the seats, rather than let it dangle. If you let it dangle, then its position relative to your FM radio will keep changing as you drive, and that can make the reception quality change. Even small changes in the the position of the unit, an inch to the right or left, can make a big difference in the sound. Sound quality will also vary depending on where your car's radio antenna is located, either in the back of the car or in the front. You need to experiment with this to find the best location.

There's a "Pro" button that cycles through 4 sound quality settings. You'll want to try all four to see how they work. Sometimes the type of music you're playing will sound better with one of those four settings.

Set your MP3 player's sound output as high as you can to overcome static on the FM radio. You need to set the unit and the FM radio to the same frequency. The unit's ClearScan button makes it easy to find an unused FM frequency in your area -- you then tune the car's FM radio to that frequency and you're good to go. As you drive, if you find that you get increasing noise combined with your music, that's often an indication that you've moved into an area with another station, possibly a weak station, on that same frequency. At that point, you'll need to retune the unit (and the car's FM radio) to a different unused frequency.

The part of the unit that plugs into the cigarette lighter also has a USB jack where you can plug in your MP3 player's charging cord, so you can charge your player while you're in the car listening to tunes. Pretty handy.

Considering that my car's stereo doesn't have an Aux input, and that I don't want to replace or upgrade my car's stereo right now, this unit works great. I'm not expecting perfection with the sound quality, but it's pretty good. Better than most FM stations on the dial. Certainly good enough to make me happy to enjoy my own tunes.

This device is a WiFi repeater. That means that it picks up your existing WiFi signal and rebroadcasts it to extend the reach of your network.

I got this (and the [[ASIN:B004WPUHXO Amped Wireless High Power Outdoor 14dBi Directional WiFi Antenna Kit (AD14EX)]]) to extend my wireless network to my workshop, at the back of the yard, about 250 feet from the house. This is far enough away that I don't get even the smallest amount of the WiFi signal from the house. I wanted to watch TV while I work, and I also needed to be able to use a phone there. I could run Cat-5e wiring underground, but that would require digging a trench across the yard, and also running the Ethernet cable from the router inside the house to a demarcation point at the exterior of the house, which would be quite a bit of work. Using this repeater and antenna--two pairs of them, actually, the pair in the house and the other pair in the workshop--I'm able to get a very strong and fast network link in the workshop.

It's incredibly easy to set up. The antenna is designed to be mounted outdoors, and they recommend using 25 feet of [[ASIN:B004WW5WAA Amped Wireless Premium Outdoor 25ft Antenna Extension Cable (APC25EX)]] to connect the antenna to the Smart Repeater. Instead, I connected the Smart Repeater directly to the antenna with the short cable that comes with the antenna, and both are sitting in a closet at the edge of the house. In the workshop, I have the Smart Repeater and antenna sitting on a shelf above my desk. I would probably get an even better signal if I mounted the antennas outside, but it works just fine for me with the antennas inside. In the workshop, I aimed the second antenna in the general direction of the one in the house, and it works great. There are a few trees between the buildings, and the signal still gets through.

You use a Web browser to set up the Smart Repeater, and it's incredibly easy. It automatically scans to find your existing wireless network, and then lets you choose a name for the new wireless network that connects to the first. It took me about 6 minutes to set up, including 3 minutes for the device to reboot after configuration.

Without doing anything to really optimize things, I'm getting 2.5 Mbps downlink, and about half that uplink. This is slower than my router's upstream connection, but it works just fine. For comparison, when I'm in the house connected directly to my WiFi router, I get 19 Mbps downlink, and 1 Mbps uplink. So I'm getting much less speed downlink, but all the available uplink bandwidth. I guess I'll go experiment with mounting and aiming the antennas better. But even with the reduced speed, I'm really enjoying having the network and phone in the workshop.

For moderate priced earbuds, these are pretty good. The sound quality is much better than average, with smooth response across the range. The highs are detailed, and not shrill. The midbass is clear, with no unnatural peak that sometimes passes for "bass boost". The deep bass is natural, and not artificially strong. Very easy to listen to for extended sessions.

For comfort, these are pretty average -- not the best comfort, but not bad either. There are interchangeable ear tips you can try out for the best fit. There's a lot of personal preference as to what's going to stay in the ear comfortably. The earbuds are angled, so you have to pay attention to the left/right orientation.

This is advertised as "iPhone compatible", meaning that there's a mic with tiny + and - buttons attached to the left ear piece. I'm a BlackBerry guy, and I'm happy to report that the mic works fine with my BlackBerry Bold 9700. But the + and - buttons don't have any effect (they don't raise or lower the volume). However, pressing the small button between the + and - buttons will either pause the song that's playing, or mute a phone call. Pretty handy.

Sound isolation is not a strong point of this set. I wasn't sure what to expect, so I guess I'm not disappointed. Probably you'd want to look elsewhere if sound isolation is important to you.

Durability may also be an issue. The wire is very thin, and it feels fragile, especially where it connects to the earbud. I'll know in 6 to 12 months whether these will stand up to regular use. The 90-degree plug will take wear better for many people, depending on how it connects to your phone, MP3 player or computer. Comes with a little storage pouch, which is good protection for the set when not in use.

First of all, these speakers sound just great, they really do. I'll echo the comments that the cords are an awkward design, depending on where you place them in relation to your sound source and listening position.

The power on-off button is on the top of the subwoofer, but the volume up-down control is on one of the satellites. And the sub's level control is on the sub itself. I ordered the ‘1More True Wireless ANC in-Ear Headphones with Microphone’ for review and would like to share my thoughts.

I have been looking for a true wireless earbud with true ANC which until recently have been pretty hard to find. I have a few different earbuds that claim “Noise Cancelling” but really they just “Isolate” the background noise. I have had these 1More earbuds for some time now. I have tried and tested several other brands both before and after receiving these and I have to say that these have become my Go-to earbuds for many reasons including their true ANC features. I will lay out my Pro’s and Con’s in no particular order.

Pro’s
* TRUE ANC - Yes these actually are true ANC earbuds with two different level settings. Is it the best ANC I have ever tried? No, but these 1More earbuds are the first True Wireless ANC “earbuds” I have tried and for me, I am impressed. The ANC does not work as well as some of the over-the-ear ANC headphones that I have, but that is to be expected. Again, for my use and in my opinion, the ANC functions beautifully for such small True Wireless earbuds.

* SOUND - These are the best sounding earbuds I own. The Bass is a bit on the heavy side but not to the point of becoming muddy which I appreciate. The Mids are well balanced and the Highs are crisp and clean.

* PRESENTATION - 1More did an incredible job on the presentation and unboxing experience with these.

* DESIGN - This may be my favorite thing about these earbuds. The case that both houses and charges the earbuds is a beautiful small metal matt black pill shaped case that not only looks great but feels nice and solid in the hands. The lid stays closed via a satisfying strong magnetic click which in my opinion is the best option and design. I have had others that use a flimsy plastic tab to click closed, and they tend to break after only a short time which then you need to use rubber bands to keep the lid closed so the buds charge and don’t fall out easily. Speaking of magnets, the buds snap satisfyingly into their respected right and left sockets and hold quite tight with no worries that they will fall out unless you take them out. The design of the buds themselves were not as impressive initially. They seemed to look a bit awkward compared to the other buds on the market which are more sleek. However after using them, I quickly changed my opinion. They poke out a bit from the ears and are not very “stealthy” so to speak, but I actually really like the look. Plus unlike other earbuds that are hard to figure out how they position into your ear, these 1More earbuds are as simple as popping the case open, pulling the bud out and putting it into your ear the same way it was positioned in the case.

* PAIRING - I had zero issues pairing these to my Android device. It was quick and easy and once paired, they will quickly and flawlessly connect every time I take them out of the case. I also love that everytime I take them out of the case, they pair back up using the same volume level that I used last when wearing them even if my media volume is turned all the way up or down before taking them out of the case.

* CHARGING - I love the fact that these not only charge via USB C but they will also charge wirelessly which really surprised me. While I am talking charging, these also retain a charge for several weeks which is most definitely a Pro. I have had other buds that will not hold a charge while stored after a week or so. With these 1More buds, I can give them a full charge and know that they are ready to go even after several weeks of no use.

* SINGLE BUD USE - I love that you can use just one bud at a time. It doesn’t matter which one you take out first and put in your ear - it will automatically pair and be ready for use as a single bud. I use this feature a lot as I will put just one in my ear while I lay on my side in bed.

* BLUETOOTH 5 - This is huge if you like to watch any streaming media. I have other earbuds that only offer Bluetooth 4.2 and there is an annoying sync issue with these. With the 1More earbuds I do notice a slight sync issue right at the beginning of the video for maybe a couple of seconds. After that, they sync up perfectly and continue to stay synced up throughout the video. If you happen to pause the video then unpause it again takes a few seconds to sync back up, but this really isn’t an issue considering that once synced, they stay that way during the rest of the playback.

Con’s

* FIT - Though they fit well and there are several bud tip and wing sizes included to choose from, I have not found the “perfect” combo to where they are totally secure in my ears. Don’t get me wrong here, they do fit well but after a while I find myself pushing them back into my ears. This is usually if I am, say just doing housework and bending over a lot. If I am just standing upright and walking, there are no issues.

* APP - there is a 1More APP for these and it works great for updating the firmware or changing the ANC or passthrough settings but other than that, there isn’t much to it.

* TOUCH CONTROL - Now I have had these for a while and I still struggle with the “conveniently located button” on each bud. Sometimes I can get them to work and other times I can’t. For me this is probably the biggest con although I did not take away a star rating for this because it very well may just be me. I love tech and usually am pretty good about figuring things out but the touch controls on these are a little tricky or perhaps just a little finicky.

To sum this lengthy review up, in my opinion the Pro’s far outweigh the Con’s. This is an amazing quality product and well worth the price. Are they better than some of the other Top brands out there? I really don’t know for sure, but so far in my experience, they are the best True Wireless ANC earbuds that I own! They look, feel solid and sound amazing! I hope that this was helpful.

I ordered the ‘adidas RPT-01 Bluetooth Sport On-Ear Headphones - New’ for review as I am a sucker for wireless headphones. My initial thoughts right out of the box were that these are solidly built, lightweight and beautifully designed headphones. They look and feel "high end". I’ve now had these for nearly a month and feel that I am ready to share more.

First I would like to comment on the fact that these are touted as “Sport” headphones and my idea of “Sport” headphones are more of the "in-ear" earbuds, which fit much more securely and do better in the “head-shake” tests. I honestly don’t see these working for anything more extreme than jogging. Don’t get me wrong, they do fit well and are lightweight but just don’t quite pass the “head-shake” test haha. These are IPX4 Water Resistant which is a bonus, and the padded ear cups are removable and washable which is nice (though I have not been able to figure out how).

Pairing was super easy and they sound really good for “On-Ear” headphones which leads me to comfort of “On-Ear” headphones and wearing glasses. I wear glasses and I have issues with “On-Ear” comfort in general. These are no different. Though they are very light and comfortable at first, within only a few minutes of wear they get quite uncomfortable for me. With that said, my Son who does not wear glasses has zero issues with comfort and says that they are really comfortable to him. Also speaking of comfort, personally (after about 30min of wearing) my ears tend to feel like I am wearing Winter Earmuffs as my ears get quite warm. This isn’t a huge deal but I thought it worth mentioning.

Now on to my absolute favorite thing about these headphones. The single Toggle Button on the right earphone. This is so simple to use and can control pretty much everything. Long Press to turn the headphones On or Off. Toggle forward or back to go forward or back a track. Toggle up or down for Volume Up or Down. Short press to Answer and End calls. This innovation is absolutely incredible and makes this the easiest pair of wireless headphones I have ever used. The button on the Left Earphone has the ability to assign three different functions. For example a single click could activate your phones default assistant or double click to play your favorite Spotify playlist and three clicks could play a different Spotify playlist. So basically the left Earphone button can only be used to use your default assistant or play Spotify. My guess is that Adidas could eventually add other apps to this button (with a firmware update) but for now, you only have the two to work with. In my experience so far, this button is a little tricky. First off, the button does not protrude much and can be harder to get it to click, especially if you have large fingers. Once you figure out how to get it to click, the next issue is that you really need to click fast to get the triple click to work. I've gotten to where I can get the triple click to work nearly 80% of the time. It's not a big deal because there's really only two apps it can control. I did notice that if you use this button to start playing Spotify, the Spotify app does not actually open on your phone which kind of freaked me out. This means that the headphones will be all that you need to use to quickly start playing Spotify. If you need to access it for anything else (on Spotify) you'll need to actually launch it from your phone.

USB C charging! More companies need to get on board with USB C and I appreciate the fact that Adidas have included USB C charging which makes for super fast charging of the Adidas RPT-01 Headphones. I have not fully tested the advertised 40 hour runtime but I can say that I have used these a couple hours here and there over my time with them, and I have only had to fully charge them once.

The Adidas app is pretty basic but it does offer some nice eq presets with the option to customize your own. Personally I like to start with the Adidas preset which is "flat" by default. Then if you prefer, you can customize it. The sound is amazing but not quite comparable to some of the other higher end noise cancelling headphones which I won't name.

Overall, I do love the Adidas RPT-01 headphones and they definitely have a place in my collection. Really the only two complaints that I have is, the comfort issue while wearing glasses, and I feel that at this price point they should have come with a nice protective case.

I ordered the 'Soundcore Wakey Bluetooth Speaker Powered by Anker with Alarm Clock, Stereo Sound, FM Radio, White Noise, QI Wireless Charger with 7.5W Charging for iPhone and 10W for Samsung' for review and would like to share some of my thoughts after a few weeks.

First off, this thing is actually pretty amazing. The build quality is nice and aesthetically it looks clean. The sound quality is nice but not phenomenal. However for how small it is, it does produce decent sound and for a bedside alarm clock it does quite well. The wireless charging works great for my Galaxy Note 8 (and does in fact Fast-Charge) however there have been a couple nights to where my phone was not charged the next morning. The fast charger also works with my wireless earbuds which I attached an image showing the charge light on the Wakey, and the wireless earbuds case indicating charging. However for the wireless earbud charging, it does take some precise positioning to get them to charge. I noticed in other review that others weren't happy with the bright display light with no way to adjust it any dimmer than the lowest setting, however they must have updated that with a firmware update (which was super easy to do) as I had no issues with the display being too bright at night. I use the auto adjust setting which seems to work quite well as far as I can tell. Also I love the sleep mode sounds that you can adjust several (or just one) sound volumes to create your own personalized preference. I do wish that there were more sound options but the ones they provide are acceptable. I also wish that you could download and install more alarm sounds. Bluetooth connectivity is super quick and have never once had an issue with pairing it up to my phone. Really the ONLY issue I have with the Wakey is that to get the sleep mode sounds going, you need to connect with the app, and via Bluetooth connect to the device. No big deal right? Well my concern is that you will need to keep it connected for this feature to work. This means you will be connected to the Wakey ALL night and this kind of bugs me. It's just kind of creepy that the Wakey is connected to your phone all night while you sleep. I wish there was a way to just play your favorite white noise sleep sound by pressing a button on the Wakey device without having to always connect and stay connected to the app and your phone. I ordered the 'Jabra Evolve 65e UC & Link 370 Wireless Professional Earbuds' as I'm a sucker for trying out new wireless earbuds. I've tried various different types. I ordered the Acer Chromebook 15, Intel Celeron N3350, 15.6" Full HD Touch, 4GB LPDDR4, 32GB Storage, Google Chrome, Pure Silver, CB515-1HT-C2AE, 15-15.99 inches so that I might have a lightweight portable travel laptop to enjoy and use for travel and at home. I ordered the iHome Alexa Built-in Bluetooth Speaker Portable Wireless Waterproof Rechargeable Lights Up to Music, with Speakerphone, Passive Subwoofer, Carry Strap, Durable Shockproof Floatable Design (IBT158) to replace an old sub par portable speaker that I’ve had for years. The iHome is quite the upgrade with the built in Alexa, better sound and being waterproof. I’ve had this product now for several weeks and would like to share my thoughts.

I must say that the sound is pretty good and packs a punch in such a small size. It’s much better than the much smaller and several years old portable wireless speaker that I have been using. In fact there really is no comparison at all. Let’s just say that it is the best sounding portable wireless speaker that I personally have ever owned. My daughter who “borrowed” the older speaker some time ago (and she never gave it back) keeps asking to "borrow" the new iHome as she says, “it’s louder and sounds WAY better”. I absolutely agree with her. Plus the lights on this thing are a nice touch, and there are options (via a button on top) to cycle through and change the color options or turn them off.

Setting up the iHome for Bluetooth and Alexa was easy and very straight forward, and there has been no issues whatsoever. We are mainly an Android household however my oldest daughter uses an iPhone and everyone has had the same great experience. So far my only complaint is that the Bluetooth connectivity distance isn’t the greatest but with that said, none of my Bluetooth devices really have much range in our home so I am not going to knock points off for that. The sound out of this little guy makes up for the Bluetooth short comings and the bonus of Alexa being packed into this as well as the waterproof features make this a great value for the selling price.

One thing worth mentioning is that to use Alexa, you can’t just say “Alexa” to activate her. You do have to physically press a button on the iHome speaker to access her, which isn’t a huge deal breaker, but because of this, you can’t use other Alexa devices to make an announcement and have it broadcast to the iHome speaker. Being fairly new to the Alexa and smart home world, I am not going to hold this shortcoming against the iHome device. It actually makes sense that with this being portable, you wouldn’t want to have Alexa always listening and drain the battery while on the go. Speaking of Battery life, it's decent but not spectacular by any means. This is pretty subjective however as usually when I use the iHome, I'm listening to it at a pretty high volume ;)

Another observation is that this uses micro USB to charge, and I really would like to see more devices using the newer and better USB C charging capabilities.

As far as the “waterproof” capabilities go, I must report that I have yet to float the device in a pool or let the kids play with it outside while running through the sprinklers. I know that it says it’s waterproof and it absolutely looks like it would hold up to getting wet as it is very well built, rugged and quite solid, but I don't want to risk ruining this new toy that the whole family has been enjoying so much.

These Razer Hammerhead Duo Wired Earbuds sound pretty amazing once you get the right fit. They come with several different sizes of eartips and I had to go one size up from the originals installed. Overall, Razer has done well with these wired buds but at this point in time, with so many mobile phones removing headphone jacks, Razer needs to up their game with a truely wireless earbud ;)

Amazing speakers I don't regret this purchase it arrived early also the sound Is next level and i will be using it for all my audio setups now!

Beautiful 32 inch display monitor. I hook it up to my laptop with a supplied cable and up came a nice bright image. There's no speakers, so you'll have to deal with audio separately. Otherwise, nice monitor (you can't go wrong with Samsung)

At this price, these are an excellent set of speakers. Easy setup and good stereo sound. They're not going to compete with high dollar speakers, but they'll definitely be a step up from built in speakers in your laptop or other device. The 2 way system provides clearer highs and reasonable lows. And the build quality is good. Definitely worth the price.

This is a great basic laptop. Not exactly a "power" player, but it serves all the standard laptop needs, web browsing, bills, photo/video management, etc. The screen is a beautiful display, especially considering the price. The unit boots up fast and has adequate interface connections (2 x USB 3.0, mini hdml, etc).

What i like most is the size and weight. Its 13.3 inch screen is just big enough and its full size keyboard and track pad, coupled with its light weight (2.7 lbs) make it a great piece of nicely portable gear.

This keyboard is impressive. I'm using it with my iPad air 3 and its a perfect fit. The plastic is a little stiffer than some of the softer cases available, so getting the tablet to pop in and out requires a little extra effort and care, but once in, its solidly held in place and the whole thing seems very sturdy. When closed, it seems to offer very good protection, although, with the stiffer plastic, I suppose the case itself could potentially crack if subject to overly rough treatment.

As for the keyboard, it operates independently of the tablet... that is to say, it has its own on-off switch and it must be charged separately (in addition to the tablet). Since it connects via Bluetooth, it really doesn't need to be physically attached to work, just within Bluetooth range. (You could leave your iPad on a stand while typing on the keyboard in your lap, for example).

The keys themselves feel good, with adequate travel and response to the touch - you can actually "type" on it... although it is slightly smaller than a standard keyboard (as you would expect), its still comfortable enough for regular use. Also, there's a backlight for the keys which I kinda like... my laptop also has that feature and it makes it usable anytime, anywhere (out on the deck after the sun goes down, for example).

The fact that it can be twisted around and folded back on itself for simple tablet use makes it that much more usable. It does add a little heft to an iPad air, including some weight and some thickness, so if the thin form factor and light weight were key reasons for choosing the Ipad Air in the first place, this will negate some of that.

Personally, I like this keyboard - I intend to use it when traveling instead of lugging along my oversized laptop. Recommended.

I've always had good luck with Lenovo computers. The desktop I bought back in 2007 is still going strong, and so is the laptop I bought a few years after that. This IdeaCentre 3 is a basic desktop, but it comes with everything you need for years of computing needs. As for inputs and outputs, it has 8 USB ports, along with an hdmi port, a dvd-rom drive and an SD card slot. Of course there's wifi and Bluetooth both supported.

As for performance... its fast. Much faster than you would expect at this price point. Setup was simple and straightforward... it wasn't overloaded with ads upon arrival, either... just trials for ms office and mccaffee protection. And with the 256 m solid state drive, this thing is dead quiet! Nice!

It comes with a keyboard and a wired mouse... no monitor. Definitely a winner!

This is an interesting piece. Small enough to fit in a purse or pocket, it makes displaying what's on your phone easy to transmit to your TV. It does require wifi, but when i hooked into it, it showed exactly what was on my phone display. It even did the auto rotate this, switching from photo to landscape mode when i rotated my phone. If you have a service on your phone (Youtube, or whatever) it would allow you to transmit that to your TV. Of course, for sharing photos, or home videos, etc. It would be great. The one nit is that it gets its power from USB and the attached cable is relatively short, so you have to have a spare USB on your TV to power it. The only other option would be to buy a USB extension cord so you could reach a wall charger. Its a small issue, but important to note. Otherwise, it does a great job.

I've got several sets of wired headphones that I like to use with my smartphone, so I was disappointed to find my new Samsung S20+ came without a headphone jack. Thats where this adapter comes into play. Construction is sturdy and the size is small. I like to leave them attached to my headphones and then I can plug those into my phone just like I used to. The sound quality is good, and the only downside is that you can't charge while listening... although that's the phone's fault, not this adapter. This adapter does exactly what its supposed to do.

This is a great addition to my studio... I've been swapping digital cables around on a regular basis for years, trying to get the studio output to a selection of other pics and audio devices. With this little box, I can set it up so my studio output feeds three different devices at once. All I have to do is turn on the device!

It's a small little box, with a small footprint. That's a big plus for a small studio owner. Its solidly constructed, too. I expect itll hold up very well over time. Recommended!

This is a USB based studio mic that's mounted on a desktop stand. The mic can be swiveled in the stand to tilt forward or back as needed. The mic itself is solidly constructed... it feels very well made. The stand is similarly constructed and should sit firmly in place. Theres a headphone volume control on the front of the body, along with a mute button, and similarly positioned on the rear of the body is a polar pattern selector switch and a gain control for adjusting the mic's recording output. The pickup patterns available are:stereo, omni, cardioid and figure 8.

I have some typical studio mice, but this is my first USB based mic, so I ran it through some typical trials to see how it fared. First of all, I found the sound to be accurate and with just the slightest "edge" - which seems to give it a slight touch of presence, especially in cardioid mode. Playing with tv he polar patterns, I could tell a bit of change in tone as I moved in close or away from the mic when in cardioid or figure 8 pattern - the effect is expected for these patterns and, though slight, were definitely there. Omni mode (picks up sound from all directions) did not show this effect (you would not expect it to). As for off axis rejection, I tried singing off to one side and then the other. Again, it performed as expected with no rejection whatsoever in omni mode. Rejection was minimal in cardiod and figure eight mode, though. (I would have preferred more). Also, in cardioid mode (signal is picked up directly in front of the mic only), I found the directional pattern a little wide. I like to use this mode specifically to isolate what's directly in front of the mic from the rest of the room. It works as it should, but I would have preferred it to be slightly more "directional". Finally, for stereo mode... this probably had the most impressive sound. It truly delivered a stereo sound... evenly balanced, with no dropout in the center. I even snapped my fingers on either side to see if it would pick up properly... it performed exactly as it should. As for sensitivity, it picked up the central heating unit fans in the background (just like a studio mic should), so some form of noise reduction would be called for (or turn off the hvac). Self noise did not appear to be evident - another specification that would have been nice for them to share (I dont even know if self noise is an issue with USB mics- this one didnt seem to have a problem with it).

Most people that I know would be interested in things like diaphragm size... that kind of detailed technical information is lacking from any of the paperwork that comes with this mic. It makes reference to a three capsule head, which makes me assume theres 3 diaphragms in there with the pickup pattern selector turning them on and off as needed, but no other info is provided.

All in all, I was impressed with this mic... it sounds good and has great versatility. It simply plugs into your computer's USB port and you're good to go (you may have to select the mic through your systems settings page). I think it would be ideal for any desk top application, podcasts, etc. It even has a screw in stand mount on the bottom. The only thing missing is some kind of a shock mount system, like a spider mount, or something), to shield it from noises that may vibrate through the desk to the mic. I suppose, sitting it on some foam would serve to isolate it.

These are really nice headphones. The built quality is first rate and the sound is excellent. I would put them on par with my favorite (similarly priced) Sennheisers. Clean, clear highs - smooth solid lows, nicely balanced overall sound. The active noise reduction system is phenomenal. I had an air cleaner (with fan) sitting right beside me and it disappeared! The amazing thing is that the sound quality didnt change - it was excellent whether on or off
They paired easily with both my phone and my laptop... no issues there whatsoever. Powers up when unfolded, powers back down when folded.

They come with a USB charging cable, and a soft sided case. The controls are cleverly built in, with a pause/play in the center of the eight ear, volume up on upper portion, volume down on lower portion. Theres one button on the left ear... that turns the active noise reduction on and off.

The two things that I thought were negatives... one is that the overall size is suited for average sized heads. I have a rather large head (my hat size is xxl). These headphones fit, but they're snug. They do have really nice soft cushions which make them usable, but they could be just a smidge larger (my Sennheisers are bigger). The other thing that I consider a negative, there's no provision for "plugging in" to some of my older gear... its bluetooth or nothing.

This bluetooth speaker joins a long list of similar devices designed to bring big sound from a small device. It does this nicely. It boasts multiple speakers pointing in different directions (listed as "omnidirectional") including a passive radiator for extended bass frequencies. This wont give you the "thumping" bass tones that some people might enjoy, but rather a full range of clear and accurate, natural sound. Pairing was easy (as most bluetooth devices are these days) and it comes with it's own charger. Definitely recommended.

Nice bluetooth speaker. It's portable... charged quickly and seems to hold the charge well (still going strong after a couple hours.) Neither my phone, nor my echo unit had any problem pairing in bluetooth mode.

As for sound, I think the sound is good... maybe not great... but definitely good. Its sound is clear and reasonably accurate... In comparison to the echo dot (gen 3), the echo is definitely fuller sounding... with more low end. But then, the echo is less portable (requires ac power) so I guess that's the trade off. Since its physically bigger, I was thinking of using this as an alternate speaker for the echo, but I truly think the echo dot sounds better. So this'll get some use as a portable bluetooth speaker... but not as an echo speaker substitute.

It comes with a nice case and both "recharge" and "auxiliary in" cables. I posted a pic with an echo dot sitting on top of it for visual comparison. It's clearly bigger... but still a manageable size.

Nice case for my wife's laptop. The Targus case is of sturdy construction and is exactly the right size for her Acer laptop (in fact, it's a little snug). Zippered from both sides and a pouch for accesories on the front. The rear has straps for attaching to your roll around carry on bag. The 2 strap style handles join from either side to form a sturdy grip. Padding is adequate and should provide proper protection. Otherwise, this is minimal, size wise... which is a good thing. No worries about the laptop flipping around inside and it takes up little space when traveling

I bought a 17" laptop awhile back because I thought it would be great to have the nice large screen... etc... etc... I don't take it many places, but when I do, it's always a problem. I should have thought of that before, I suppose, but on vacations, I tend to just find a suitcase to squeeze it into. On a daytrip, it may end up in a random bag in the trunk - hardly a way to keep it safe. Well, I finally got myself a proper bag that seems to have been made for it!

The bag itself is not heavily padded. In fact, I would describe it as "adequately padded". That is, it has enough padding to protect the laptop, but not so much that I would get careless with how I handle the thing. As for fit? Perfect! The laptop goes right in without difficulty but still doesn't seem to flop around inside. It also has extra pockets both inside and out - on both sides of the computer compartment. The outside pockets are zippered - and there's a shoulder strap that comes with it as well. Plain black... it's understated, as it should be. I like it... I'd recommend it.

I'm somewhat particular about my music and my headphones and have specific things I look for. I'll try to touch on those items in this review.

Sound Quality: obviously most important. I look for solid bass (not boomy or hyped). And clear trebles (not sizzling or hyped). These headphones performed okay on both counts although it did seem the bass was a little hyped. I have some expensive headphones that these did not compare favorably to. I also look for general clarity in vocals... here, they did good... nothing nasally or buried in the mix. The exception came when turning on the noise reduction circuit. More on that later.

Comfort: okay, I have a big head (size xxl hat). So comfort is important to me. These headphones are adequate in that regard. I had to extend them fully, but at full extension they fit me properly and comfortably, sealing off around the ear. They did not completely surround my ears as some studio monitors do, but they did cover my ears. The padding is decent and I was able to listen for a reasonable amount of time before they became uncomfortable pressing on the perimeter of my ear. If your head/ears are smaller, my guess is they'd be plenty comfortable.

Noise reduction: I'm not used to using this feature and wasn't sure how to test it, so I simply sat down next to an air cleaner I have in my home and tried turning noise reduction on and off to see what happened. There was definitely a reduction in the noise... mainly in the lower frequencies. It didnt completely eliminate the sound of the blowing air, but what was left was a thinned out version of the original noise. It was definitely an improvement in the level of noise. The only thing I didnt care for was that there seemed to be an impact on the sound of the music also. Again, the noise reduction thinned the music and left it a little nasally.

Controls: straight forward controls. Theres a slider to turn noise reduction on and off and an adjacent button to activate the phone function. Since the phone button was just below the slider, I kept accidentally turning on the phone when trying to activate the noise reduction. Better button placement would have helped.

Overall, I was reasonably impressed with these headphones. Especially considering the price, they seem to do well. They come with a nice, soft sided carry case and needed cables. I expect I'll get some good use from these.

I'm coming to this machine as a Mac user who needed a light-but-powerful Windows machine for some specific business purposes.

Bottom line: I'm impressed.

First, the basics. This is a thin/lightweight model with a 4-core i7 CPU, a 14 inch screen, and Intel's latest integrated graphics. Its body is a black magnesium affair, good-looking and really lightweight. The black finish is satiny and looks a bit like plastic but is far more rigid.

This laptop is based on Intel’s new “Eco” i7 chipset that runs cooler and more efficiently than Intel’s recent offerings. I’ve hammered it pretty hard and it’s been stable, cool and quiet. My model's specs are quite good for a lightweight business laptop, with a proper 1TB NVMe SSD and 32GB RAM.

For comparison purposes, in terms of price and features it’s roughly comparable to a current-model M1-based MacBook Air. Now, an Air with 16GB RAM (which, given its ARM architecture, is functionally equivalent to about 32GB on a Wintel machine) and 1TB SSD lists for $1509 direct from Apple. The LG was about $1750 at the time of my purchase. It has no biometric login gizmo, which is okay because for some reason the Windows world has yet to implement one that works half as well as Apple’s TouchID. It has the expected webcam, microphone and speakers… all of decent quality and again comparable to the Air’s. It has two USB-C/Thunderbolt 4 ports and two USB-A 3.2 ports. There’s an SD card reader and of course some spiffy WiFi and Bluetooth. It has a 14” screen, slightly larger than the Air’s. Resolution is similar, and I have no complaints about color fidelity or brightness with either machine.

The differences are most obvious in the details.

Keyboard
Both machines have truly excellent keyboards. Both can keep up with my frenetic speed-typist pounding and have a good feel and throw. But the LG’s keyboard backlighting surrounds each key with an unwanted glow that looks a bit cheap. So, the keyboard scores maybe an 8 on the Apple scale of 1-10.

Trackpad
Similarly, the trackpad is the best I’ve used on a Windows machine but is still behind Apple’s in terms of the hardware’s fluidity and consistent behavior. Fortunately, on the software side, Windows has advanced mightily in terms of gestures and support of things like multiple virtual desktops, so this machine can replicate most of my Mac-centric workflow without too much getting-used-to, if you spend some time fiddling in the setup screens. Score: another 8.

Display
The screen is fine, glossy like the Air's but not as glasslike and flat. Intel's latest integrated GPU is more than adequate for my purposes, and I've noticed no stuttering or frame limitations. Another 8.

Construction
The magnesium chassis is stiff and solid while remaining commendably lightweight and thin. The bezels are very thin as well; the top bezel contains the tiny camera and two nearly invisible microphone apertures. It merits a 9 on the Air's jewel-like reference 10.

Power
Battery life is good, not up to MacBook M1 standards, but looks like I'll top 6 hours of pretty intensive multitasking use with the screen on full brightness. Charging is via USB-C. The LG charger is compact and comes with long AC and DC cables. Call this another 8, with the Air demerited to an 9 as battery-life leader Apple no longer provides a long AC cord.

Summary
So far so good. After two Dells that were unsatisfactory and poorly supported, two HPs that died young, and after watching Lenovo go downhill, this seemed a good choice.

I'd certainly recommend it if a Mac is not an option for your use. The Air remains my top choice and is a better value, and the Genius Bars are wonderful for support and getting questions answered.

So far there's been only one surprise: despite LG being a Korean company, this laptop is made in China... like the Air.

I bought the 1TB version of this NVMe SSD to do a Carbon Copy backup of my end-2018 MacBook Pro's internal 1TB SSD, which is about 80% full. Starting from scratch, after formatting in APFS (which is eye-blink fast to do), this drive did the full backup job in about 20 minutes! It showed no signs of thermal throttling.

If you have a Thunderbolt 3-equipped computer, this is a fantastic drive and an amazing value, based on my early experience. I'll update this review if anything changes, but so far, I'm delighted. It is a worthy companion to my beastly 6-core Mac, and that's the highest possible praise.

If you have a Thunderbolt 3-equipped computer, this drive provides speeds approaching the highest-end built-in SSDs. Case in point: I have a 2018 MacBook Pro with top specs. Its internal SSD is a screamer. And, as you can see from my screen shots, the X5 is right in the same neighborhood. These tests were run on my computer while it was running a bunch of other things (Word, Excel, VMWare Fusion, Mail.app, Safari with about 15 tabs open), so it represents real-world use.

And, as you can see, the X5 is really fast. If you need speed and have Thunderbolt 3, this is a great drive.

Installation was easy. My Mac recognized the drive right away. I could've just used it, but Samsung provides a utility on the drive for enabling its onboard encryption and keeping its firmware up to data. Recommended.

(But do make sure your computer has Thunderbolt 3. You can't tell just by looking at the ports, as TB3 is implemented as a superset of USB-C. So, Thunderbolt 3 is USB-C but the converse is not true. Similarly, previous-rev Thunderbolt interfaces aren't forward-compatible to TB3 devices. Some of the one-star reviews of this drive are clearly from folks who didn't know these issues.)

I love to read but held off buying a Kindle until now because I could not abide the resolution of early generations' screens. The fonts used to look penciled-in, jagged and coarse to my eye. Plus, I travel frequently and would need a backlight for reading on long flights, and the earliest Kindles lacked a backlight option.

Times change, and when I finally succumbed to the Kindle's siren call just ahead of a sun-drenched holiday where there'd be zero hope of reading poolside on my iPad or iPhone, I was happy to see that the Paperwhite model now comes with a high-resolution display and a backlight at a reasonable price.

Reading Experience

The fonts do look pretty nice now. There are about six or eight font choices you can apply, and you can choose their size and weight easily from a menu. I'm still experimenting to find a favorite. I'm a bit of a font snob but have no serious criticisms of the kerning and justification options (I prefer ragged right formatting to fully-justified, and most books allow this).

The backlight works well, is fully adjustable, and is nice and even save for a bit of faint scalloping at the far bottom edge.

Glare has been no problem at all.

Images look pretty terrible, but that's not what this device is for. It's a single-purpose tool for consuming textual books in any environment, and at that it excels.

There are lots of reader tools, such as word lookup and things like that. I haven't explored most of those options.

User Interface

I have a passcode set, and entering the passcode is weirdly slow; you must pause significantly between characters.

The touch interface works well, but there are some drawbacks to it. Mostly, it can be annoying to fumble the device and find you've lost your place in the process of grabbing it. That's less of a problem with the dedicated buttons on some other models.

I do wish the Goodreads option were removable from the menu as I have no interest in it and have accidentally tapped it a few times.

The single ads you see on waking the device don't bother me. They're static and inoffensive and go away with a swipe. I'm unmotivated to spend the $20 to eliminate them, but that option is there if they bug you.

Slightly more concerning is that occasionally the text has lacked contrast. But I've found that going into and out of a menu, which forces a screen refresh, can help that. (I have Page Refresh turned off to minimize the blinking effect that otherwise accompanies most page turns, limiting the blinks to chapter transitions. This may be the cause of the occasional contrast loss. Now that I've found what seems to be a work-around, I'll leave Page Refresh off.)

Connectivity

Both the WiFi and mostly-free 3G connectivity work well. So far I've tested the 3G in five countries with no problem. WiFi has worked well and I've had no problem connecting to hotel WiFi that requires browser input-- the Kindle's "experimental browser" has worked sufficiently well for that.

My understanding is that Amazon-purchased book downloads, syncing and updates are free over 3G even if you are roaming internationally. But, if you're roaming internationally, you will be charged a small amount for downloading documents other than Amazon-sold books. By the way, that downloading capability is a really cool feature (you can email .pdfs and non-Amazon ebooks in certain formats to your Kindle via a special Kindle email address Amazon automatically sets up for you) but one that I'd wager 99% of Kindle users don't use or even know about, much less use internationally.

Battery & Charging

Note that the vaunted Kindle battery life of umpty-ump weeks is based on benchmarking with an estimated usage of only 30 minutes per day, and I believe it includes Airplane Mode being enabled. But after my 12-hour flight that I mostly spent reading with the backlight on and Airplane Mode enabled, the device still has about 65% battery charge. Not bad!

I did not purchase a charger. I pack an Anker 10-port USB charger (which works off of any national voltage and frequency and is highly recommended!) to keep all my gizmos charged when I travel, and the Paperwhite has had no objection to that.

Bottom line

I'm liking my Kindle Paperwhite a lot. There has been no problem reading in the bright poolside sun or on darkened transoceanic flights, and the touch user interface works well enough for me. The unit seem solidly built and is a great bargain for serious readers.

UPDATE: I totally neglected to note how delightful it was to order this from Amazon and have it arrive fully configured and personalized for my account. This made the unboxing experience the rival of Apple's! Special kudos to Amazon for that.

UPDATE: I did the Kindle a disservice by calling its built-in illumination a "backlight". It's actually a "front light"-- the white LEDs shine along the front faceplate and their light is directed down towards the screen by a nano-machined pattern embossed into the back side of the faceplate. So, the light is reflected off the e-ink screen (just as ambient light is), rather than shining through the display as is the case with smartphones and tablets.

18 MONTH UPDATE: This continues to travel with me (in a little zippered hard-case) and so far, knock wood, no problems. It remains the only unit I've found with all the ports I need, including SD, VGA and HDMI. Five star review renewed.

Pros: Functional and speedy. Everything you're likely to need in one nice-looking, briefcase-compatible, USB-C-powered dongle that won't embarrass your gorgeous Mac. Lots of ports. For my purchase I selected the "Space Grey" option-- it is a pleasing metal finish, like Apple's Space Grey but with a slight rosy tinge that gives it a bit of uniqueness, yet it still complements the lovely Mac design. Cons: The USB-C cable is non-replaceable and, inevitably, will eventually fray and break. We'll see if that happens within the warranty period. I travel with a specialized battery charger that requires 12VDC input. That has necessitated carrying a separate power brick in addition to my Anker multi-outlet USB charger I pack for my iPhone and other USB gizmos. Besides the inconvenience of carrying the brick, my hotel rooms often lack enough power plugs!

This adaptor plugs into my Anker USB charger and provides a nice 12VDC current that works well with my specialized charger. I purchased an inexpensive, 8-piece barrel-connector adaptor set to ensure I'd have the correct connector for my charger. Works brilliantly!

The internet is full of off-brand power adaptors marketed as alternatives to costlier OEM chargers from major brands like Apple, Samsung and HP. But if you do a quick search you'll find teardowns from people like Ken Shirriff that show exactly why cheaper chargers are cheaper: hasty design, risky safety engineering, marginal components, interference-inducing layouts, equipment-endangering outputs.

The safety issues Shirriff identifies should be enough to convince any sensible consumer that their lives aren't worth a savings of a few dollars.

Name brands became name brands by doing several things right, starting with not electrocuting their customers. Think about that as you shop!
Great, well-priced collection of essentials.  Everything Just Works.  (Well, except the HDMI cable, which was DOA.  I have requested a replacement from the vendor.)

Works transparently with Raspberry Pi (which absolutely requires a powered hub for many USB peripherals).  I have a Logitech wireless keyboard and mouse connected via one little USB adaptor through this hub, along with a mini WiFi adaptor also connected to the hub.  The hub's power supply powers both, saving the 'Pi's scarce power.  Everything is recognized at boot by Raspian, and it just works.
