I will be keeping a close eye on this router, which I just purchased yesterday, because it seems too good to be true. So far, in my 24 hours of usage since purchasing it for $29 at Walmart (sorry, Amazon, I was in a hurry) I have found it to be flexible and powerful in my unusual application, which is remote and requires 100% uptime with occasional bursts of heavy usage. Mine is a factory-fresh rather than refurb unit, incidentally.

I'll admit I had some trouble believing a router this cheap could be as good as this one turned out to be (assuming it stays reliable-- but, the one I bought trumpets a lifetime guarantee on the box). I expected something dumbed-down, with seriously constrained functionality and annoying firmware. (This model's v3 hardware, although Broadcom BCM5356-based, is not compatible with alternative firmware such as DD-WRT due to its problematic NVRAM size.) It's a single-stream design, with an internalized antenna, potentially suggesting performance limitations. And it's from Netgear, which I've frankly not had great luck with before... but it's been years since I've tried one of their products, and the reviews here are generally good. Most of the negative reviews here relate to support experiences, but my networking knowledge-level is expert, so ...what the heck, did I mention it was $29? An easy roll of the dice.

Though my application requires custom configuration, I initially started the unit using its web-based wizard, which you access by connecting your computer (via cable or WiFi) and pointing your browser to 192.168.1.1. With the unit connected to my cable modem, it set itself up quickly and voila, Internet. For most people this would be good enough and the job would be done. Kudos to Netgear for delivering the product with WPA-2 encryption enabled! They provide a SSID and password on a printed label. So, you're good to go. And its default configuration is just fine for most folks' usage.

For my application, however, I needed to cable several devices including a VoIP adaptor (a la [...] and a server with several ports exposed to the Internet. The unit needed to be set to a specific IP address scheme, SSID and password. And a dynamic-DNS utility on the server needed to communicate with my DNS provider. ...To accomplish these and other advanced tasks, the browser-based configurator at 192.168.1.1 has an Advanced tab. Proceeding through the settings is straightforward and similar to other reasonably-configurable routers. The default settings established earlier by the wizard remain intact in the Advanced panes so you are starting from a known-operable configuration. All good.

So I proceeded through each of my customizations, taking care to click the Apply button after modifying any pane. Usually there's a ten-second delay during which the unit sets up the new settings; a few necessitate that the router reboot itself. Everything went smoothly.

So, for $29 I'd replicated an unusual configuration and everything was working. But how well?

Okay so my wife had to take an important international FaceTime call as I was finishing up. So, for a while there the server was downloading some massive updates, two ssh clients were talking to the server, VoIP was in use, six WiFi clients were doing whatever they were doing, a 3G microcell tower was initializing and downloading firmware updates to itself ...and FaceTime was running smoothly with a high frame-rate on her third-gen iPad. A nice acid test!

In particular, I did not feel the need to mess with the unit's default QoS settings... and additional props to Netgear for including QoS in a router this inexpensive!

So far, I'm impressed. It's hard to imagine a better value in a router. I'll update this review if there are any reliability issues, but so far, so good. So excellent, in fact.

Purchased this system because, at the time, it was the only way to obtain a 1080 Ti next day, but received a fabulous overall system which far exceeded my expectations.

For background, I usually prefer to build my own computers, but would have incurred a ~$500 penalty if I took that path this time because of the ridiculously inflated 1080 Ti prices.

Per the attached photo, my system is benchmarking at the 99th percentile for CPU (holding stable overclocked to 4.9+ ghz using the automated bios tool), and 99th percentile for GPU (slight factory overclocked MSI Aero, but haven’t tweaked further yet).

It’s a bit funny that the system only scored 98th percentile in the 2d benchmark. My guess is that the test isn’t taxing enough to bump the GPU out of power saver mode (some of the compute 2d tests later on run at over 1600 FPS). Note that with regards to these benchmarks, the system hardware was tested “as is” apart from the CPU overclock.

My only concern is not terribly substantial, because I had already planned to replace the HD before I placed the order on Amazon. The HD is only benchmarking at the 69th percentile. It’s actually benchmarking pretty far below average for the WD blue 250 gb ssd, but I’m not overly concerned because it will soon be replaced. You shouldn’t be concerned either because you’re buying this system for the 1080 Ti, not the starter hd.

The keyboard and mouse are acceptable starters. I’ll be replacing these soon as well (as almost everyone buying a $2000 system will be) but they were actually better quality than I expected. Phrased another way, I’m prioritizing the new SSD over new keyboard and mouse.

Overall build quality is good - the system runs fairly quiet (though not as quiet as an iMac, but to be expected with this kind of gpu power), and looks beautiful. It’s a bit time consuming to open the case, but one does so infrequently to the extent it’s a non-concern.

In terms of gaming performance, this system is overkill for playing anything at 1080p - you should expect performance close to 150-200 FPS at 1080p.

Have been playing on a 4K gsync monitor. Witcher 3 and AC Origins performance has typically been 40-45+ fps, with all settings maxed. Sometimes it will run surprisingly close to 55-60fps. Suffice it to say 4K ultra is a stunning experience for a (former) console peasant like me.

In summary, highly recommended. Definitely choose this system if considering versus an off the shelf model. You’ll probably receive this system before a competitor starts building an alternative box. Note, this system has increased in price since my purchase, but it’s not unexpected given current ram and GPU availability constraints.

These binoculars are all about quality in the largest field of view. If you want to see a wide expanse of nature or the heavens downrange from your position, these are the way to go. I got them specifically to frame smaller constellations and asterisms, the detail of which can be further examined with a scope. They help tremendously to put the object in the scope into context. Ordinarily, observing half a degree of field tends to abstract objects almost entirely from their surrounding. Since it's not practical to really "zoom" in using a single optical instrument, using these in combination with something of higher power is ideal. Don't get me wrong, I do have a zoom on the scope... it zooms from 25x to 50x -- amazing but you have to understand that this is a field of view of 2.4 to 1.5 degrees -- essentially like looking through a pipe to a drinkstraw. These Nikons however, show over 9 degrees field of view -- something which is unsurpassed in the highest-end binocular out there.

There are compromises necessitated by the optical principles used to make these function. They do not have a very flat field of view, meaning objects in the center of the field (circle) can be focused, but objects nearer the edge of the field are out of focus. This is because the focused field is curved not flat. This problem is also evident in most 10x50's for example. It's less of a problem in good quality 8x42's like Nikon's Monarch for example, and obviously the high end Swarovski, Leica, Zeiss etc. This problem matters more when you have a narrow field and highly magnified image where the subject tends to fill the field of view. It matters less when the subject is focused in the center of the field and the background surrounding it is slightly out of focus.

Still, even if you pay the biggest bucks for bright, flat, and sharp images from the top of the line binoculars, you'll still only see about 8 degrees true field of view, whereas these give you over 9 degrees. Furthermore, they give an apparent field of view of over 59 degrees, rivaling the top-of-the-line binoculars.

If you're looking for a handy, all-purpose binocular, the roof-prism 8x42's are proven to be far more popular for a number of good reasons (more compact, more magnification while not yet needing a tripod or IS like 10x does, more competition and choices etc.) But if you're looking for the best field of view with high quality optics, this is it, and fortunately it comes at a very reasonable cost. I don't know what other 7x35's are out there, but I can tell you this is far better than Celestron or Bushnell.

This is a great, inexpensive little webcam for personal video conferencing (Skype). The picture quality is not incredible, but still far better than what most people you'll chat with have with their iPad, phone, or the camera built into their laptop.

I've been doing videoconferencing and webcasts for some twenty years -- in the early days it was mostly Polycom units, but lately Cisco Telepresence. With Telepresence you have three 1080p 60" big screens. The monthly cost is enormous but often justified by savings in travel costs (if you say so). Personal IP services like skype aren't as dependable or as rich in quality but they're outstanding on a cost basis, especially if the DSL or cable ISP fee is sunk.

I was tempted to step up to the 1080 (C920) camera but I've resisted because already nobody that I conference with (for personal use) has anything near as good as this, and they may also have trouble receiving or displaying 1080 video. Some of them even have monthly byte transfer limits from their ISP. So I see the 1080 HD services as better if it's really going to work out on all ends. Short of that, the autofocus this camera has is great especially when it's going to be more than a face-cam. I use mine to conference a whole room with a family of four. The kids are walking back and forth, to and from the camera and focus stays good. Its reasonably wide-angle is good too -- wide enough to see the room at some distance, but not so wide it distorts faces badly in closeup. I need to test the audio more at the longer ranges. It has an auto-gain feature that seems to be working well. Again, unfortunately, even if I get great audio at the source, it ends up going through someone's laptop speakers or an iPad on the other end.

The most important and biggest improvements to video conferencing to make once you have an adaquate camera like this is in lighting and acoustics in the room. It's real common to see people on camera that are back-lit, with their faces in darkness and a room full of echoes, reverb and weird modes.

I needed to replace my aging WD NAS, which was struggling to keep up with my needs. After quite a bit of research and product comparisons, I decided to go with the market leader, and bought a NAS that seemed likely to be able to support my needs for several years, and offered some options for expanding the ways I use a NAS.

For context, I mainly use my NAS as "network-attached storage": I back up files, and I share files for use on our multiple home computers. I don't use it for remote access (security concern: I'd rather use cloud storage services for that), and I don't use it as a repository for a media server, or anything else like that.

I decided to use WD "Red" drives for this unit: based on specs and user and professional reviews, they seemed most likely to run reliably for as long as I needed. My previous experience with WD black, blue, and red drives has been consistently positive, whereas other vendors have let me down.

Installation and setup was very easy: I had the unit up and running within a few minutes. Copying files over from my old NAS took some time, but the performance of this Synology unit exceeded my expectations. I was also pleased with how much faster my backup jobs were. I was especially pleased when apps that use network files began running much faster: so clearly both read and write performance were much improved in comparion with the old system.

I also set up a USB backup. It took a little bit of reading in the Synology KB to learn how to do it right, but after that it was a breeze. I plugged in a USB hard drive in the back port (the front port can be configured for use with the USB Copy button), opened up the Hyper Backup app, and ran the initial backup to copy the entire NAS contents to the USB drive. Then I scheduled it to run incremental jobs every day, so now my paranoid backup demon is happy. (I save backup drives in a secure location to provide "disaster recovery"; overkill perhaps, but it buys peace of mind.)

One criticism: the unit came with only 2GB memory, which seems cheesy. And what makes is super-cheesy is the way they price their branded "compatible memory" at ridiculous multiples of the market price. I was able to buy a 4GB Samsung memory card for under $15, and it worked just fine. You can do a web search and see that others have upgraded using larger memory cards.

The Synology KB website is very good: it's well written and comprehensive. There's also an active user community, so there is a ton of information easily available. Overall I'm very happy with my Synology purchase, and would buy their NAS products again without hesitation.

I'm using this simply as an audio extractor, so can't review the video capabilities.  I have a Chromecast v3, and wanted to use it simply to stream Youtube music or recorded (FLAC/MP3) music from my library, and feed it into a DAC connected to my stereo amp.  I hooked it up, used a fiber cable to connect the audio into the DAC, and the results are quite satisfactory: the sound quality is very good, and I'm not experiencing any problems.  No issues with distortion or noise.

I needed a decent DAC to stream music into my stereo amp (a very good one, but old enough not to have an internal DAC), both from my MP3/FLAC library, as well as online sources. (If you're an "audiophile", you can stop reading now.) So I'm using optical (or coax) in, not USB. The headline specs are 768kHz/32bit max, but read carefully, that's for USB in. With coax/optical in you get 192kHz/24bit max. All I care about is CD quality or better, since like most people I can't hear the difference with anything higher, so these specs more than meet my need.

Specs aside, how does it actually sound? Very good indeed. The sound is perhaps just slightly different (wee bit brighter) from my very good CD player (with Wolfson DAC) -- but I'm not sure I could tell which is which with a blind test. I'm quite happy with it, even when I'm streaming FLAC-source classical music that I'm fussy about.

I think 100-150 is the sweet spot for DACs: if you choose carefully you can get a very good one for the money, and paying more isn't necessarily going to give you better sound. Do your research carefully, and enjoy!

I wasn't willing to pay the ridiculous Synology price for the official memory expansion card, so I looked at the specs, and decided that this Samsung 4GB card would meet my needs nicely, while still staying within the official 6GB maximum.

Installation is quite easy: you shutdown and disconnect the box, take out one of the drives (on the side with the memory card slot), carefully insert the new card at a slight angle, then press down gently until it clicks into place with the retaining clips. Then restart, and check the system info to confirm that you have 6GB memory. I experienced no problems throughout this process.

Note: if you do a web search, you'll see various sites discussing the addition of an 8GB or 16GB chip, supposedly this works because the system board supports it. I didn't go there because my system isn't going to be heavily loaded (I use it as a NAS, that's it), so it wasn't worthwhile for me. I seem to have sufficient headroom for all my anticipated needs, and the system performance is more than adequate.

I bought two of these, one to use with a Chromecast Audio, another with a Chromecast video (Gen 3, I think). In both cases this gizmo worked flawlessly: all I did was plug the USB-A end into a charger, an ethernet cable (from a switch) into that port, and finally the micro-usb end into the Chromecast. In both cases the connection just took a few seconds (the Chromcast light went white), and the Chromecast worked as it had been working before on wifi, but with a wired connection. (I verified on my wifi controller and my router that the connection was now wired.)

The price was just a tad higher than for some competing products, but I've bought Ugreen devices before, and they've been reliable. So I paid slightly more for peace of mind, and I'm quite happy with the product and the decision.

If you're looking to connect your Chromecast to your wired network, I can recommend this product without hesitation.

I compared this cable with the optical cable I got with a SoundBlaster sound card, that I've been using to connect a Chromecast Audio to an external DAC, which pipes the sound into a stereo amp. I played a Scarlatti sonata with this cable and the other cable, and can detect no difference with my ears. (I don't claim this is a lab test, but with optical fiber at these short lengths and this limited frequency range, there really ought to be no measurable difference that would matter to human ears.)

So I'd say these cables are just fine, and they're sufficiently well made that I'd have no qualms about using them. I have to say though that I disliked the thick wrapping they gave this cable, as if the fiber were extra thick (that's a joke), or needed extra protection (it shouldn't need this much). And this heavy braided wrapping makes the cable heavier and less flexible (as well as uglier!), so I'm taking off a point for it, since I can find other such cables that are superior.

I really like these headphones at first: the Soundcore app made them easy to configure and update, and in LDAC mode the sound was very very good. So that was great. But then I found that I couldn't wear them for long periods, and this might just be me, your mileage will definitely vary. I wear glasses, and after a while over-the-ear headphones can make my outer ears hurt, and can make them hot. (I have a pair of gaming headphones that I use for conference calls, that are a bit more comfortable, but even those I can wear for about an hour at most.)

So I'm rating these 4 stars, giving them full credit for sound and convenience, and taking a point off for discomfort, although that might just be a personal thing.

I had to laugh when I saw the gold tips on this cable: while gold connectors might make sense on cables that carry electrical signals (analog or digital), they're irrelevant for optical cables, the tips are just the mechanical connection into the socket which aligns the optical fiber-ends. So there's no difference between this tip and the black tip of other cables like this (such as the Amazon Basics one).

That said, this cable does fit into the proper sockets just fine, and works as well as the other such cables I've tried. I used it to connect my SBX4 sound card with an Fiio BTA30Pro DAC, and listened to it with earbuds as well as external speakers, didn't experience any problems. I didn't expect, and didn't perceive, any audio superiority to the Amz Basics optical cable I had been using, so there's no reason there to prefer one over the other. Physically though this one is just a bit more stiff, so I tend to prefer the more pliable Amz cable. If that's not a concern, I would recommend buying whichever is available and cheaper.

I needed to connect my desktop speakers (with the usual 3.5mm audio plug) to a DAC's RCA connectors, and this little product worked perfectly. It's hard to get picky about the sound from your basic desktop speakers but these work as well as I would expect: certainly the improved sound I get from my Sound Blaster X4 carries through just fine.

An alert reader would note that I could have connected the 3.5mm plug directly to the SBX4, and I did do that at first, but there were convenience reasons for me to move the plug to the DAC: this way I can just use one device to determine whether I'm listening to my headphone or letting the sound go to the speakers. (TMI for more people, I think.)

This is a very nice package, containing a decent DAC with a bluetooth receive/transmit capability (supporting AptX HD and LDAC). Now that I have it set up and connected, I'm very happy with the sound quality, both through the stereo amp to speakers, and through bluetooth headphones using LDAC. For the price, this is really an excellent value, I haven't found anything else nearly as good for this price.

Setup is a bit involved and tricky, and the documentation is quite poor. (Fiio has this reputation.) I hooked it up to my computer using USB, to update the bluetooth & DAC firmware. Then I used the Fiio Control app on my phone to complete the setup, choosing the desired EQ settings and BT codecs. Pairing the headphones was a bit tricky: I found very sketchy instructions on their forum (there's also a Youtube video), which worked after several tries.

But the end result is that I have excellent results for a very moderate price. So if you're a bit technically inclined and not afraid of doing some digging and figuring things out, check this product out. I would recommend it highly.

Overall rating 4.5, rounded up to 5. I don't think there's anything better for this price.

I wanted a "better" set of wireless earbuds for casual music listening: I wanted either AptX HD or LDAC, good battery life, and comfortable to wear for at least an hour or two. (I specifically ruled out over-the-ear headphones because I can't wear them very long, and ruled out wired earbuds for convenience. To me these are acceptable compromises.)

I was considering the Sony WF-1000XM4, but didn't want to pay that much for casual listening. I was also considering the new Soundcore Liberty 4, which on paper seems to be a great product. But I decided to try this "Liberty 2 Pro Upgraded" pair to see if was good enough for a lot less money.

So far I'm really very pleased: the sound is excellent for all my favorite music genres: classical, country, pop, rock, and latin pop, and after replacing the earpiece flaps and cushions I'm finding them very comfortable to wear as I work at my desk.

Important: to get the sound right, I had to do several things. First, I downloaded the Soundcore app, connected the earbuds, set the audio quality to LDAC (in settings). Then on my Android phone (Pixel), I went to the bluetooth advanced settings (usually hidden under developer options: do a web search for more details), and set the Audio Codec to LDAP, the LDAC quality to 900kbps, and made sure that the other BT settings (such as sample rate, bits per sample) were at the highest for good audio. Finally, I went back to the Soundcore app and played with the equalizer settings until I had what sounded best to my ears. The app has a neat little personal-hearing tester, which is worth a try, especially if your ears are getting older. After all this I had nice clean well-balanced sound. You might try different EQ settings for different music genres if you like, it does make a difference, but perhaps not huge enough to matter.

I've read many grumbles about LDAC, but I wonder if those are based on using the default settings: in my experience getting the settings right makes a very big difference.

PS It seems that the LDAC settings on Android go back to "best efforts" everytime the earbuds are disconnected. Quite annoying: I have to set them back to 900kbps every time. The other settings are stable.

This is a really great prosumer/SOHO router, from a brand that deserves to be much better known in the US. I found it very easy to configure through the Web GUI, and there are tons of easy-to-follow instructions on the Draytek website. You can also just try out the GUI for any of their routers right there on the website in what appears to be a live demo of each of their devices.

I was looking for a dual-WAN high-performance router with strong security features, high throughput with security capabilities turned on, and, most importantly, easy to configure through a GUI. I considered Unifi, but the user experience with their more recent product leaves me very sceptical about giving them my business. I tried out Mikrotik, which sells excellent hardware at very reasonable prices, but proper configuration required way too much time and effort (and trial & error), so I gave that up. Finally I learned about Draytek through a review from a UK-based site, and decided to check them out.

So far I've been very pleased. It took me about an hour to update the firmware and set up the router to be a secure gateway, and the throughput for my CenturyLink gigabit connection has been consistently impressive. I've searched the Draytek website for various recipes, and have tried them out: each one has been fairly simple and easy to follow.

The WAN failover is very simple to configure, but I haven't yet tested the functioning. I don't expect a problem with it, based on the "it does what it says" experience I've had so far.

All that said, this is by no means an inexpensive router. If you want the features, and you don't mind paying a little extra for ease-of-use, then you might want to give this one a serious look.

I don't care to create a "home theatre experience", I just want to have very good picture quality with decent sound. Also, I wanted to keep things simple, didn't want multiple units which I'd have to place somewhere. So I ended up with this soundbar, which fits nicely in front of the big Samsung QN90A tv, without obscuring anything or needing a lot of space.

I connected it using a good HDMI cable to the tv's ARC port, and went through the basic settings: not much complexity or hassle. Then I watched a few minutes of several different blu-ray discs, some with big orchestral sound. I did A-B comparison with the tv, and also asked a family member to opine.

Result: the soundbar was clearly better, producing a deeper richer sound with nice but not overwhelming bass (to me this is a good thing). Overall I was happy to keep it to enhance my AV entertainment.

Now, is it worth about $150? Probably. If I were to rethink the decision, would I have paid more for a soundbar with better sound? Maybe. I'd have to do side-by-side comparisons to be persuaded, since the many reviews I read weren't all that convincing, until I got into the much more expensive products.

I'd been looking to upgrade my tv to a bigger (75in) and better one. After doing some reading, I narrowed my choices down to this newer Samsung Q90A and the LG OLED C1, and then decided I'd stick with the non-OLED tech to get the higher brightness, and of course the somewhat lower price. (I've read that OLEDs aren't made as bright because of burn-in concerns.)

So far I'm very pleased with my choice. The picture is wonderful: my usual test is a 4K nature documentary, and I think Blue Planet 2 looks just amazingly good, although I've seen it before on a slightly older 4K Samsung tv. The brightness is great, which I needed for an open living room with big windows.

I like to turn off the Samsung "smart hub" thing, which I find intrusive and annoying, so I can't review any of that for those who are interested. Amazon, Disney+, and Netflix streaming content looks great (through a Fire TV cube), so I'm perfectly happy.

As for other features, the 4 HDMI inputs is nice, and just adequate for my current needs. I do think these bigger tvs should come with something like 6 or 8 (why not?) HDMI input ports so that you can have multiple players and game consoles hooked up without having to get a separate switch.

The sound from the multiple speakers is very good, probably as good as you can get from a modern tv. I'm considering getting a decent (but not overly expensive) soundbar to try, see if it makes the sound noticeably better.

I have a Sony UHD (non-HDR) bluray player, and an older Panasonic bluray player, that I wanted to hook up through a switch to my 4K tv (so I'd be using only one HDMI port). I also wanted at least one spare port on the switch to use with a computer or tablet or whatever. I was a little wary of buying a no-name product, but the description and the more knowledgable reviews convinced me to give this a try. (This is where Amazon's great return policy comes in: I figured I'd just return it if it didn't work as expected.)

I just plugged it all in today, and my conclusion is that you can pretty much ignore the most negative reviews: this works, and works well. The connection to the tv is trouble-free and glitch-free, with image quality being what you'd expect. (Make sure you're using good HDMI cables meeting the required spec, of course.) I didn't even bother using the remote: the auto-switch function works just as it should: when I turned a player on, the switch selected the right input port, the tv responded as you'd expect (also switching input as it should), and all was merry. No hasssle, just as you'd want. Recommended.

These earbuds are really very good. The sound is balanced and clear, and it's a pleasure to use them to listen to all kinds of music, from classical to rock/pop to country. They're more than adequate for phone calls and online conferences. They're pretty comfortable to wear: I have a difficult time with most earbuds, especially with the ones that need a large hard object sitting inside the earlobe, so I might wish these were a tad softer, but really I haven't had any trouble wearing them for an hour or so.

The little charge case is nicely made, and very easy to use. I use it for more than an hour or two per day, and at that level I think the box only would need charging every few days, making it pretty convenient.

Are they worth the price? I got these from the VIne program, so price wasn't a consideration for me, and I haven't compared these with other items in a similar price range. The sound is better than some very nice earbuds I have that cost quite a bit less, so at least I can say that they're delivering some value for the extra money.

I was expecting this laptop to be a bit under-powered, and not quite up to the mark in video and audio. I was completely wrong: this machine blew past my expectations. For a general use laptop, used for web browsing, word processing, and similar purposes, this is more than an adequate machine, this is really very good. The performance is more than acceptable: I haven't noticed anything being unusually slow or erratic, it just runs smoothly and fast. The display is 1920x1080 (so HD but not 4K), and clear and crisp for watching online video (for example). The audio too is surprisingly good: you can play music on it and enjoy the well-balanced sound, no cringing necessary.

Notes: 8GB memory, 256GB SSD. HDMI, USB-A, USB-C ports, SD card slot, and 2.5mm audio jack. Bluetooth & Wifi. No ethernet jack, you would need a USB-A or USB-C ethernet adapter if you wanted to use a wired connection. The wifi works quite well, so it's not a major concern.

For this price you're not getting a powerful workstation or a gaming machine, obviously. And you're not getting 4K video or tons of memory or disk storage. But if you're looking for a very good "normal user" laptop for yourself or a family member, this is definitely one to put on your shortlist. If you want to compare, I've also been pleased with the similarly priced Asus laptops.

I was looking for a 1TB SSD to upgrade the storage in my computer. Background: I have a tower computer I built about 3 years ago, and at that time I used a 500GB SSD for the system drive, and two 1TB hard drives for pretty much everything that didn't have to be on the system drive. Since SSD prices have fallen so much, I decided to replace one of the 2 hard drives with an SSD and use the remaining HD mostly for less frequently used files.

After reading a few professional reviews, I decided on the WD Blue, because it seemed to offer the best combination of adequate performance, reliability, and competitive price. I skipped on some cheaper options because of suspect reliability.

I'm quite satisfied with this drive: the performance is very good, as promised. I haven't run into any problems with the drive, and my experience with WD & SanDisk storage products has been generally positive.

Caveats: (1) Of course I can't predict how well it will do over the longer haul, that's where I relied on reviews and brand experience. (2) Yes, one can get more speed for more money, but for my normal use it wouldn't make any practical difference in overall performance.

Note: If I were building a new computer today I'd use an M.2 SSD for the main drive. In fact that's what I did in the new computer I recently built for my son.

I needed to retire an old tv, and bought myself a Fire TV cube and a 4K tv. The combination is absolutely terrific. The setup is so easy that it doesn't require discussion. The speech recognition (Alexa) works smoothly out of the box, and can do more things than I care to try out. 4K video from Amazon or Netflix or my streaming package (PS Vue) looks very very good.

I should mention that I have a high bandwidth (1 gigabit) network connection, and a gigabit wired network at home, and use an ethernet cable to connect the Fire TV. If you have a good wifi setup you can use that, but I much prefer wired connections for most things, especially streaming video.

If you're looking for the best streaming box available right now, I think the Fire TV Cube is it. Highly recommended.

Update: I corrected this review, since it seems that the HDMI not working is a limitation on my Asus computer (the USB-C device doesn't support the HDMI video transmission, and apparently Asus has no plans to update).

I needed this adapter for my new Asus laptop (Win10), which came without an ethernet port or an hdmi port. The ethernet connection worked really well, I was getting full gigabit connectivity, with no detectable difference from a direct RJ45 connection.

The USB3 worked very well too: I hooked up an external SSD and was able to get high speed file transfers without any problems.

However, I was not able to get the HDMI connector to work at all. I looked for a missing driver on the TrippLite website, but didn't find anything. Without that, the device just didn't detect the monitor plugged into the HDMI port. Just to make sure, I tested the setup using another computer, and everything worked immediately, so I though the problem was this adapter. Turns out that it's actually a limitation on my Asus laptop's USB-C port. I fault TrippLite for making this a bit obscure and not being clear about the requirements, but that's all.

I did not test the charge port.

Given that an important feature doesn't work, I can't justify giving this adapter more than 3 stars. It's excellent (5 stars) for the two ports that I used and did work.

For background: I don't have any affiliation with Ubiquiti, and I'm not a network engineer with inbuilt preferences or dislikes of networking equipment. I do have a lot of experience with all kinds of computing and networking technology.

For my relatively large house I've needed multiple wireless routers set up as wireless access points (WAPs), but over the years have gotten more and more frustrated with the limitations of this kind of setup. I could solve the signal distribution problem by setting up many WAPs, but I still had the problem that my devices wouldn't roam seamlessly from WAP to WAP as I moved around the house.

So this year I decided to look into a better solution. One option is a "mesh" solution like Eero, Orbi, or Google Home. Another option was to go with
wired WAPs, like these Unifi devices. After quite a bit of research, I decided to put my nickels down and try these "Pro" units. Why? Because I wanted (1) very strong wireless signals; (2) commercial grade manageability; (3) products already proved in the market, and favored by many experts; (4) products priced competitively.

I'm happy to report that after much tinkering and experimenting I'm absolutely delighted with these devices. I have three of them spread around the house, with a "Cloud Key" controller device (highly recommended) giving me management access from computer, tablet, or phone. I'm getting excellent bandwidth (usually at the max my phone/tablet will support), and trouble-free roaming. I'm able to see all relevant information, including interference information (from the pesky neighbors!) in the "console". I'm able to easily configure the networks, and updating the software and firmware is painlessly easy.

This is good stuff. Not for everyone, since you do have to be comfortable with technical details that would daunt the less experienced. But if you know how to set up your router/WAP, and either understand or are willing to learn about various networking details, then you might want to seriously consider Unifi access points.

I'm trying to decide whether I should buy two more AP-AC-PROs, or should save a bit of money and go with the Lites.

SSD makers give us these benchmark numbers that aren't all that useful for most of us not using well-equipped computer labs. I mean, how would I even verify that an SSD can achieve 500+MB/s read/write speeds anyway? I'd be using a test program that does a lot of intensive (and synthetic i/o), perhaps? I don't see the point in that, I want to make sure it serves my usual purposes. That means fast bootup times, fast operation when running my usual programs (including especially web browsers), and so on.

Some background ... I've been using SSDs on my family's several computers for some years now, and have built a few computers using SSDs as the system drive. The performance improvement is quite dramatic, even a bit amazing at first. It helps a lot when doing local network file transfers or cloud uploads/downloads, and also helps with normal everyday use, especially game playing.

For this drive ... I had a 250GB Samsung 850EVO SSD in my computer, and had no problems with it. When I received this 500GB SanDisk SSD from the Vine program, I thought it might be handy to get a bit more space on the system drive, put some more frequently used files there, and so on. I used a handy USB3 to SATA adapter, plugged into the computer, then used Macrium Reflect Free to clone the C drive to the USB drive. (This will take some time, dependent on how much data you have, and the overall performance of your system.) Then I swapped the new drive in for the old one.

Result: I now had a larger C drive. Performance? About the same as with the Samsung SSD, no surprise. Here are some numbers: HD to SSD copy ~145MB/s; SSD to HD copy ~85MB/s; SSD internal file copy 100-170MB/s (varied widely probably because of other system load). What about those 500+MB/s numbers? I suspect I could get closer to those if I were writing to/from system memory, but I don't care. It's the real world performance that matters to me.

The SanDisk management software (SSDdashboard) is easy to find on their website, and easy to use. It checked and told me my firmware was upto date, and told me my drive was connecting optimally to my system. It didn't mention anything about my AHCI setting (which is important), where the Samsung Magician software tells you clearly whether AHCI is activated.

So overall a fine SSD for the money, does the job, makes no noise :-)

Final word: I don't know any reason, other than price, to pick a SanDisk over a Samsung. In fact, I don't know for sure that you lose much by going to the less expensive brands like Crucial and PNY. Read the "expert" reviews on the web and judge for yourself.

The Roku Premiere player is easy to set up and has a well-designed user interface that requires no reference to a user manual. I connected it to the tv (using an HDMI cable), plugged it in, turned on the tv and selected the appropriate source. I was disappointed that there was no option to plug in a network cable for a wired connection (like there is for the Fire TV box; you have to go up to the Premiere+ to get that port). This might be a concern for anyone with a weak or problematic wifi signal.

The initialization was fairly simple: language selection, wifi connection (it supports AC as well as N), automatic detection of the tv display type, automatic software update, then a separate session on the computer to register the device and create a Roku account. I had another disappointment here: the account creation requires the entry of payment info, either credit card or Paypal. If I want to use the box just to watch my subscribed services, such as Netflix and Amazon, there's no reason for me to give Roku any payment information at all, it just increases the risk of malicious use. (If you really don't like this, you can sign up using a Paypal account, then go back into your Paypal account and rescind the Roku permissions.)

After that it was all plain sailing, and I had no complaints: streaming video was clear and glitch-free, the sound was good. All in all, a very nice streaming box for a reasonable price. For my money, however, I would consider upgrading to the Premiere+. Or, the Fire TV box, which is what I normally use at home.

Summary: Very good waterproof bluetooth speakers that work as advertised, and better.

Firstly the sound is really very good, considering the size of this unit. It's loud enough, without distortion or other oddness -- quite suitable for using outdoors, at the beach, or even on a boat.

It really is waterproof, and does float without any trouble. After trying it out on the beach, I was confident enough to take it sailing (with the phone in a waterproof bag, of course), which was novel and amusing.

Charges fast, pairs easily, comes with a carabiner clip.

If you're looking for a small bt speaker to use with phone or tablet, and use near or in the water is important to you, this is definitely one to consider seriously.

I've been pleased with the CaseCrown cases for the various Kindles I own, so decided to get this one for my iPad Air 2. It's well made, and fits the ipad very nicely. I had a little trouble with the little flap that needs to fold under the ipad (after it's been inserted) and then be attached to the bottom with velcro -- but with a bit of trial and error I got it in snugly, and have had no problem since.

It's nearly perfect for my daily use, and I have only two minor criticisms.
(1) The case looks a little askew, as if the pieces weren't cut exactly right. Makes finding the power button a teeny bit more work. But it's a minor defect. No other problems with the various ports and buttons, they're all easily accessible.
(2) The triangle "stand" position I make with the front folded back and pushed into a little flap on the back, requires a little fiddling, and doesn't always sit quite right. Making the flap a bit wider & deeper might have helped.

Finally, the wakeup/sleep function for the ipad works just fine, I've not had any problems with it.

Unless you're willing to pay up a lot more (I wasn't), this is a very fine option.

The drive delivers on the SSD promise: very fast access times, even on an older computer supporting SATA1 only. The computer boots up so fast it reminds me of old days before operating systems became so bloated. (Yes, I'm talking pre-history.)

However, as others have noted, the software supplied with it for migration is just terrible, it only works if everything is perfect. And the instructions and error messages are completely inadequate (mostly missing, really).

I wanted to do more than complain, however. I figured I'd share some experience and some tips, that might help another user.

My existing disk was a 1TB hard drive that had some bad sectors (hence my desire to replace). I removed enough data from it to reduce the usage down to about 160GB, figuring that was good for a 250MB destination disk. Then I tried the Samsung cloning software. Many times. It kept failing, sometimes early, often after a few hours. With no useful information (unless you count obscure error codes that are not documented to be information). I tried running disk defrag, achieved no useful result, other than a failure after the cloning reported 100% complete. Deeply frustrating.

I couldn't do a system image restore, because Windows (Microsoft is another producer of dumb and unfriendly software) will only do a restore to a disk of the same configuration. (Here the message is simply that it "can't find a suitable disk", you have to hunt to figure out why.) And I wasn't about to buy a 1TB flash drive.

And I wanted to give it one good try before settling for reinstalling from scratch, because I didn't want to spend several more days getting my computer back to where it was.

Solution: I highly recommend using defraggler (from Piriform) to clean up your disk. You might also find it useful to shrink your partition to the minimum possible, using the WIndows disk management tool. Then I highly recommend using the Macrium Reflect Free Edition to do an "intelligent" clone of your OS volume to the SSD.

After I did this, everything worked perfectly, no problems. Wish I'd known about these tools and all the gotchas ahead of time.

Another tip: If you want to set AHCI in the BIOS (yes, now I'm getting to advanced users), you may need to first enable the AHCI drivers, otherwise Windows will not boot up (you'll get a BSOD). Do a search for this, there's a Microsoft KB article.

Good luck!

I've tried many similar products, and most of them range from bad to horrible. In fact I recently returned one that had fallen apart during shipping (although it had been well-packaged). I have another one from a different brand (Monoprice), that has been quite satisfactory, having kept a hot-running notebook in good shape for more than a year.

Having had to "borrow" that one for another feverish computer, I needed another one, and after some hunting found this on Amazon. It has now been running for 10 days or so under an older 13 inch notebook that runs really hot, and has been doing a great job.

The pad appears to be solidly made, with no rattles or squeaks. The metal mesh top and well-vented plastic bottom provides plenty of ventilation -- it might actually do a great job even without a fan -- which is what you want to see. The large fan runs silently but moves quite a good volume of air (you can check the specs if you care about numbers).

Note that the USB plug provides a USB port, so you don't lose one by using this. Doesn't matter to me, but might to some users.

All in all, a good product I can happily recommend.

I've used this headset quite a bit over the last few weeks, for work-related conference calls. Although I really like my tiny BlueAnt headset for casual use, I find myself reaching for this one for the ease-of-use convenience and better sound.

Firstly, the setup and the usage is quite well designed, as simple as it could be. I was suspicious of the voice prompts & messages ("phone connected", "answering call", etc.), but have found them quite useful and not at all intrusive.

I find the cord attaching the control pod (has on/off, volume control, and mute button) is a bit too long for my tastes, but some might need a longer one, so can't complain. The controls themselves are very useful to have where you can see them, you don't have to try to find something behind your ear to manipulate while you're on a call.

The sound is excellent: what I hear is always very clear. What others hear, whether I'm in a somewhat noisy room, or in a car, is also reported to be very clear, I've never had to raise my voice or repeat myself. BTW, the mic boom swivels out of the way easily when needed.

I'd give it 4.5 stars perhaps, with half a star off for my personal discomfort with a large-ish earpad (makes my ear hot after a while). But that's nit-picking, and probably won't bother many people.

Well-made audio cable with gold contacts, does improve the sound over cheaper cables. I used it to connect a computer to my stereo (e.g., to listen to Pandora), and the sound was definitely clearer and brighter with this one than with the cheaper cable I'd used before (because that's what I had on hand).

One thing to note: my RCA plugs had very tight sleeves, so I was having trouble getting them on/off, and was worried about breaking the ports on the amp. I took a pair of small needlenose pliers, and gently stretched out the insides just a tad (there are six segments on the circular sleeve, so you need to do this in 3 places around the circle). After that it still fit snugly, but was no longer an effort needing a lot of muscle.

As others have pointed out, paying ridiculous prices for such cables is silly, they're mostly the same quality hardware with a lot more marketing. This price point is just about right in my opinion.

These are really great cables. I used one to connect from the analog audio output of the tv to a stereo amp, to get better sound out of much better speakers. And the results were really good. So if you need a 3.5 to RCA cable, these are among the best you'll find (I've tried others).

HOWEVER ...

The manufacturer name on the packaging was Monoprice -- in case you don't know them they're well known for low-priced good cabling and electronic components. I often buy direct from Monoprice, so went there to check on the price, and of course it's a lot less. But their shipping cost can be high, so depending on how much you're buying, it might be cheaper to get free shipping from Amazon, or pay Monoprice for shipping.

It pays to shop around, but also keep in mind that Amazon's service is excellent, even when you're buying from a third party.

I have several of the Logitech M510, and think this is the best general purpose mouse you can buy. It's comfortable in the hand -- I have a large hand, some in the family have larger hands, some have smaller hands, but everyone finds the mouse comfortable to use. It's precise, easy to configure, and I'm very fond of the tiny usb adapter.

I particularly like the fact that you only need use one usb adapter for multiple devices (the "unifying receiver"). In fact you can switch between different Logitech mice if you need to do so (e.g., for a portable).

As for the keyboard, I was a little wary of the "wave" shape, not having used one before, and having some mild carpal tunnel issues. But to my relief, the keyboard is really comfortable to use, the wrist rest is well placed, provides support just where I need it. The keys have a nice touch, not too light, not too heavy, so perfect for me. There are a number of programmable buttons on the keyboard, most of which I tend to use only occasionally, mostly because I forget I have them. But the volume control is very useful, as is the button to bring up the calculator.

Do make sure you install the Logitech SetPoint software (you can download from their website) to properly configure the devices. You'll need that to make good use of the unifying receiver, among other things.

So if you're looking for a good mouse keyboard combo, I can happily recommend this set. If you just want one or the other, I still recommend the M510 mouse, and one of the many Logitech wireless keyboards that you can buy separately. (For instance, I also have the K270 keyboard, and find it to be quite good.)

If you're looking for a BluRay player, and don't need 3D capabilities or a web browser, then this just might be the best buy available. As another reviewer has observed, it's the best player in this price range. I'm giving it 5* because picking some nits for something this good at this price just seems unreasonable.

I've been very pleased with my Samsung TVs and BD players, they have proved to be excellent in video and sound quality (which to me is 90% of the evaluation). I bought this one to replace an older Sony BD player that was getting cranky with newer disks (even after updating). With this unit after I plugged in HDMI, ethernet cable, and power, it automatically turned itself (& the tv) on, and presented a simple configuration screen, and followed with an online update. After that, it was a pleasure to sit back and enjoy a movie.

I cannot honestly tell you that the picture from this was better than the one from my 2 year old Samsung BD-C6500 player, If there were any differences, they didn't jump out at me. The box itself is smaller and lighter, and instead of LED controls, this one has little buttons. Although those LED controls are cool-looking, I have to admit that these clunky buttons are a lot easier to find and use. The remote is smaller as well, and comes with Netflix & Pandora buttons (I don't like that, but others might).

I didn't test the streaming features, and probably never will, since my TV has streaming capability as well, and I tend not to use streaming that much.

I like the way the Samsung BD players integrate with the Samsung TVs, automatically turning on/off, and setting the optimal picture settings. I wouldn't buy them just for that, but it's a nice plus.

I got this to replace the PSU for a Dell E521 (about 3 years old, psu started making a nasty noise). The power rating for the original is 305W, so this one at 460W is more than adequate. (An online calculator suggested that I needed 365W.)

I would describe myself as relatively inexperienced at doing this sort of thing: I've replaced cards & memory & floppy/cd drives, but this was the first time replacing a PSU.

Removing the old unit and attaching this one inside the box was easy (just needed a philips screwdriver). The connections were mostly easy, but presented two challenges, one minor, one major: (1) The motherboard connector (P1) for the old one was a one piece unit, this one had two pieces, so I had to make sure I was connecting them correctly. (2) There is a single SATA cable, with three connectors, but my cd drive and hard drive were far enough apart in the box that I could not connect them both. Solution I'm going to try is a SATA y-cable (essentially an extender) from monoprice.com. I'll post an update about this once it's done. (BTW, I highly recommend monoprice for anything they carry: ethernet cables/connectors, parts, network adapters, etc. etc.)

Once I had it all in there, I plugged the computer in and started it up: everything worked fine, and the PSU was delightfully quiet. So far so good -- I'll post updates if I run into any problems over the next year.

I got the newer variant of this (last 3 characters in model name are 20U not 10U), which is supposed to be the same except for more power for the T5xx series. (Lenovo website says both are compatible with my Lenovo T410 computer.)

I thought I had a serious problem because the ethernet port simply would not connect. But I've since figured out that it had to do with some configuration problems on our office network (I won't go into details here, but they were obscure).

The minor problem I find is that the sound seems muted, but I am not worrying too much about that.

So no issues: buy one if you have a compatible system. (Check compatibility on the Lenovo website.)

Especially for this price, this is an excellent keyboard. (I don't get what some of the negative reviewers are complaining about, unless their reviews are misplaced, are really for a different product.)

It's quiet, it has a good feel, is easy to use. You plug it in, Windows & Logitech do the rest. You type away happily. I don't expect much more from a basic keyboard.

No it doesn't make the coffee or automatically type my thoughts for me. So maybe I should dock it a few stars.

This is an excellent headset -- I have to say that I'm puzzled by all the negative reviews. (Which did make me hesitate for a bit.)

The pairing works, and easily, and the first time. I paired it with my Samsung Renown, and my iPhone GS, and now when I turn on the headset, it pairs up with both phones (as promised), answers whichever one is ringing or connects with the one being used for a call.

The sound is clear at both ends, without any of the ugly distortions you sometimes get with such devices.

I like it, am happy with the purchase, and consider it a great value at under $40. I continue to be happy with every BlueAnt product I've acquired.

I had low expectations for this, since I haven't had great experience with cooling pads. They only sort-of work in terms of heat dissipation, and tend to be noisy (or become noisy as the parts wear in).

This one has so far been a very surprising change from the past. It's very quiet, I'm not sure if what I hear is just my notebook, or the pad as well. So I was even more sceptical about the cooling, but it fooled me. So far, my hot-running Dell XPS has been running much cooler, even when I'm doing something cpu-intensive like playing chess.

So try it, you might really like it! (The price is a bit steep, in my view, but I guess you get what you pay for.)

Note on size: this is about 14.25 x 11 inches, large enough for a 17-inch laptop perhaps.

A good switch should require no real thought to install. You plug in, connect cat5e cables, and you're done. After that, it should work invisibly, giving you good throughput and no concerns whatsoever.

This one does that. If you need a modest-cost 5-port gigabit switch, I can recommend this one without reservation.

Notes: (1) If you don't need gigabit, you can get 100mb equipment pretty cheap right now. (2) Keep in mind that you use 1 port in a switch for the incoming cable, so a 5-port gives you connection to 4 devices, 8-port allows for 7 devices, etc. (Yeah, I know, it's dumb, but that's the way techies think.) (3) If you think you might need a couple more ports later, then definitely get the 8-port switch, since you don't pay that much more for the extra ports.

If you're concerned about expectations for the brand -- I am generally pretty happy with DLink products. I certainly haven't had any breaking right after 1 year of use, as I have had for some other brands.

This is an excellent HDMI cable, at a very good price.

Although certain vendors will urge you to spend large amounts on audio/video cables, all reliable and independent experts will tell you that the expensive cables don't give you anything extra (other than satisfaction of having spent more than your neighbor, perhaps). You should certainly get good quality cables -- but paying more than around $10 for a 6/8 foot HDMI cable is definitely not necessary!

This one might be just a wee bit better than other cables in this price range. I replaced the cable I had been using with this one (using Sony BluRay player with Sony LCD HDTV), and found that although the difference was slight, the colors were just a bit richer and the picture perhaps very slightly sharper. I wouldn't have paid more for that difference, but it's certainly pleasing to get it without having to pay more.

I've used other products with this brand, and have generally been quite satisfied.

I'm not going to compare these speakers with my Aperions, I'm going to compare them with my old pair of HK speakers that they replaced, and with other decent pc speakers we have in the house. I have to say that I'm a bit surprised by the other reviews -- judging by what I consider appropriate standards, these are really excellent speakers, with clear bright sound, reasonable bass (for their size), and surprisingly good stereo separation. Much better than the others I mentioned -- so much better that I was honestly impressed.

Whether they are worth $80 is more a matter of personal choice than anything else. I haven't compared a range of speakers between $50 and $100 to see if you get a lot more for a bit more money, or almost as good for a bit less money. If a credible reviewer has done that, great, use that info to make up your own mind.

This is (was) an excellent camera, if what you want is a pocket-able point-and-shoot camera. Very versatile, easy to use, excellent pictures every time.

Contrary to what Amazon says, the SD870 IS is the new model equivalent to this one. And it's available at a pretty good price right here. (I just got that one, but haven't used it enough to review yet. Check other websites for professional reviews, e.g., cnet.com.)

I replaced my old Yamaha receiver with this Onkyo amp, and also got the related tuner and single-disk cd player. I used them with my old speakers while my new ones (Aperion) were arriving, and my reaction was "Wow!" All of a sudden the sound was bigger, clearer, and brighter.

If you're looking for a stereo amp in the $5-900 price range, and care about sound, you won't regret buying this component. It's all it promises to be.

Just got this, so can't comment on reliability and longevity. However, it was easy to set up -- just plugged in an ethernet wire from my router, and it became visible on the network. It's quiet, and doesn't take up much room. Performance is decent with 100Mb network, I don't have Gigabit setup right now.

I didn't bother installing their software (you don't need to if you are familiar with networked servers & storage). I was able to log in (easily) through a browser on one of my machines, make configuration changes, and make it become a member of the workgroup. Seems to work fine with XP and Vista, so far completely trouble-free.

I haven't tried hanging usb drives off it yet, will do so and update this review. They also provided some backup software from Memeo that might be worth trying out.

I like it enough that I'm planning to get a second one to use as a mirrored backup.

Just to add my vote, this is an excellent DVD player. I use it with an older Sony LCD tv (XBR1, only goes to 1080i), and compared the picture, using a standard widescreen DVD, with my older Panasonic progressive scan Panasonic dvd player (480p output). The picture with this one is clearly superior.

As others have said, the whole thing reeks quality and attention to detail. A good quality HDMI cable is included, as well as standard video/audio cables in case you need them for troubleshooting. The packaging is a class above the industry.

If you want something for watching standard DVDs with a good HDTV, consider this one or the 981HD model.

I concur with the other reviewers, this is an excellent TV (Sony KDL-40XBR4). The picture is gorgeous, especially with HD input (1080i or 1080p). Even looks good when watching VHS tape! The only problem is that some analog tv channels just look plain bad (grainy and fuzzy).

The controls are sensible, configuration and customization (e.g., input labels, picture/sound settings) are easy. The remote is a bit bigger (longer) than I'd prefer, but that's a minor quibble.

Yes, possibly you'll pay more for this one than some others. And sometimes a know-it-all salesperson will tell you that X or Y has much better reviews from "experts". For my money, I always find that the Sony in the store has the best picture.

On LCD vs. plasma, perhaps that's more a personal thing. But I don't find the "black level" argument in favor of plasmas particularly convincing. And I like watching 4:3 without stretching, so I'm not about to risk burn-in on a plasma. So I only considered LCDs.

BTW, the EagleGL shipping service used by Amazon for this was ok. They gave us a 4 hour window and were more than an hour late, but other than that no problems. (Mine was easy -- ground floor, 10 steps from the front door. So might not apply for every case.)

I was sceptical of a "non-impact" punchdown tool, but it was really quite easy to use, and it does the job. I only would use this rarely, since I don't do this for a living, so getting something at a reasonable price was a factor in the decision. Unless you need a professional tool that you're going to use frequently (in which case get a Paladin), this will do it for you.

It's 4 stars instead of 5 because the Paladin I had borrowed and used once before had a more satisfying motion and was clearly a superior tool.

Very nice sound, better than the Philips product of similar price. However, some deficiencies make it a bit disappointing: (1) no digital volume control, so you can't set volume level for an alarm, and there is no progressively louder alarm; (2) (as someone else noted) if you want 2 alarms at 2 different times (e.g., 5am & 6am), they need to be on different music sources (e.g., 5am radio, 6am CD).

I'd still recommend it if the features don't make a big difference to you, since the sound is good and everything works well.

Bought this to connect my new Roku Ultra to my television. Great purchase! Excellent picture and sound quality!! Great Velcro cable holder, allowing one to keep cable neatly organized if entire length not needed.

I have had all sorts of earbuds, but must admit for the price these are simply wonderful--and absolutely beautiful! I tend to listen while sitting or lying down, and these have wonderful sound for such use. I also love the simple beauty of the wood.

On the other hand, I am not so sure these would be the best choice if you are jogging or working out --- they might not stay put.

So bottom line, if you are not working out and relatively still I think you will love these! Superb sound and a great price!

I bought this TV to replace a wonderful but very old Panasonic 32" CRT that finally gave up the ghost just before Christmas. It is a totally satisfactory replacement and I recommend it strongly.

I had admired the new LED screens, but as I began investigating refresh rates and looking at the displays in stores, I came to the conclusion I would prefer a plasma screen, but my space would not accommodate anything larger than a 42". Which made this model absolutely perfect. Sears had the best price, but they were sold out by the time I placed an order. However, Walmart had the next best price at $398, so I ordered one for pickup at a local store. As it turned out, they were out of stock locally, but were able to get one within 10 days. It was well worth the wait.

In comparison to similarly sized LED TV's, this model is slightly heavier ( just under 40 pounds out of the box). Of course, in comparison to the old CRT, it was much much lighter. The stand assembled easily and seems quite sturdy. 8 screws total and a ratchet and it was ready for cables to be attached.

This is an HDTV. I may eventually bite the bullet and get HD service from Comcast, but even with the normal, non-HD cable box, the image is wonderful and light years beyond my old CRT. And the sound is GREAT! Unlike many of the LED models I considered, the sound on this model is better than on my old CRT and no need to get a sound bar. Right now I have it hooked up to an older Panasonic VCR/DVD recorder/player (non Blu-ray), an Apple TV (for streaming Netflix and which uses one of the two HDMI connections) and my Comcast cable box. It was easy to set up and I am very satisfied with the image quality. Speaking of which, I used the settings provided by R. White in his review, although I changed the tint to a -3 rather than the 0 he uses, and strongly recommend you try them as a point of departure. I am now assessing universal remotes to replace the four I currently need to operate the various components and will probably settle on a Logitech Harmony model.

If you are looking for a good and serviceable TV and don't need a larger size than 42"' or more than two HDMI connections, or the other bells and whistles, this is a fantastic choice. I don't understand the relatively low marks it gets in its review by CNET; In my opinion, it is much better than the review indicates. The advantage with the plasma is you don't need to worry about the refresh rate and the picture is great no matter what angle you watch from. (Note that if the room in which you are will place this unit has a lot of natural light, you may prefer the LED.) Also, as other reviewers have said, for this size of TV, I really don't think the eye can distinguish between 720p and 1080, and the image quality is really quite satisfactory. With the addition of an Apple TV or Blue-ray player with WiFi, you have the equivalent of a smart TV without paying the premium for one. Even at $500, this TV is a very good buy and better than you will find most of the LED's of similar size. If you can find one for under $400, grab it! But you should move fast, because these are going quickly.

I bought this unit primarily for use in England but have also used it in the US.
