Winner for the price sounds quite nice. Battery lasts on LAX to Singapore flights.

Not a well known product and yes you have to load the app but I find they work well for me.
Hubby bought me a galaxy x tablet and I love it but the volume is very low.... These took care of the problem... Thanks :) they came VERY quickly!! Great customer service!!

These were delivered March 31, 2020 and already theres connectivity issues. Sound is great. Battery life is incredible but I think they should last longer than 4.5 months. trying to get help under manufacture warranty is a nightmare. would love to have them replaced but it's well past Amazon warranty also.
They are cute and work well. They aren't as noise cancelling as id like but the functionality is good.

I had purchased a unit from a big box sporting goods store installed on my boat only to discovered after use and research (Hummingbird website is pretty useless) that it did not have GPS which was one of my primary requirements. I purchased what I wanted and will sell the other. I recently used it on a very foggy morning and was able to follow a track about 5 miles down river to the fishing spot I wanted to go to. I passed safely by every channel marker along the route and turned into the creek opening without any mishap. There are bigger units with more functionality but this is a great unit for my skill level. Very satisfied.

This drive meets most of my requirements for a flash drive. There are so few well made flash drives that I gotta rate it as 5 stars simply for filling this niche fairly well.

First and foremost, I need a flash drive with a real SSD controller, not the cheapo craptastic "flash controllers" used by almost every other flash drive. Real SSD controllers offer things like better reliability (e.g. error detection and correction, wear leveling), higher performance (especially for random reads and writes), and secure erase. A real SSD controller should also mean that you can treat the flash drive just like an internal SSD. For example, it should support partitioning, and have software that lets you specify the amount of over provisioning. Maybe it also ought to support the TRIM command and S.M.A.R.T. drive performance and health monitoring?

Second, I need a drive that is physically robust. I want a strong case, with zero moving parts, and ideally it meets some good dust and water resistance standard (e.g. IP68; see trustedreviews's article on "IP67 vs IP68: Waterproof IP ratings explained"). Since the drive must have no moving parts, its connector must be protected by a cap, and to help avoid losing the cap, the drive must let you put the cap on the non-connector end when it is in use.

I am not sure where I stand about encryption. In principle, I support it. In practice, manufacturers always seem to use proprietary solutions, which makes them intrinsically bad; when closely examined by real security professionals, they usually turn out to be rubbish (e.g. Western Digital's line of "My Passport" hard drives ~2015). Furthermore, depending on how it is implemented, you may have issues with the host operating system (e.g. if some custom driver is needed).

So, how does the VisionTek 900903 measure up?

First, it claims to use "a high-performance Silicon Motion controller". Off to a good start. Benchmarks below go into further details, but the conclusion is that it offers decent performance.

Second, this drive is an all metal rectangular case ("tough aircraft-grade aluminum housing" according to the manufacturer). Its case is solid: there are no moving parts except for the cap, and the cap can be put on the rear of the drive when you have it inserted. Good, tho the cap could fit a tad more snugly. There are ridges on the drive that allow an excellent grip, which is a nice touch. Sole defects are the 4 corners of the case which are slightly sharper than they ought to be, and the drive seems to meet no official dust and water resistance spec.

Contrast VisionTek's case with that of a Sandisk Extreme Pro USB 3.0 128 GB (model #: SDCZ88) that I also own. The Sandisk case is only partly metal. The metal came from a sheet that was stamped and then folded. Part of the metal near the connector end, where the slider is, is dangerously sharp--an idiotic design... The metal is way too smooth (is hard to pull the drive out in some situations). The slider mechanism is made of plastic and is weak (I have had 2 drives fail on me).

Concerning performance, attached are 5 CrystalDiskMark screenshots. The first 3 benchmark this VisionTek 900903 under 3 different disk formats (FAT32, exFAT, and NTFS); default format parameters (e.g. Allocation unit size) were consistently used (tweaking might improve performance). For reference, in the other 2 screenshots, I also benchmarked my Sandisk Extreme Pro (SDCZ88) as well as my internal SSD (a Samsung 840 EVO).

The disk format does not make too much of a difference; to my surprise, NTFS came out slightly ahead in most categories (I would have guessed exFAT would be). To be sure, the differences are small enough that maybe this was just measurement noise (did not have time to try multiple runs).

Comparing the VisionTek 900903 to the Samsung 840 EVO, the Samsung is clearly faster in every test, altho the VisionTek's Sequential Read and 4K random Write are respectable for a drive so small. (You should probably ignore the Q32 = queue depth 32 results, as they are not relevant for most desktop users, only servers.)

Comparing the VisionTek 900903 to the Sandisk Extreme Pro, the VisionTek is faster in 3 out of the 4 tests. The Visiontek is much better in Sequential Reads, and blows away the Sandisk in random 4k Writes. (Is that due to it having a real SSD controller?) It only loses moderately in Sequential Writes.

The sole performance disappointment with this drive is its 4k random Reads. That's a sore spot for the Samsung 840 EVO too, indeed, even Samsung's latest and greatest PCIe NVMe 960 Pro has awful 4K random read performance. It must be hard to achieve with current flash technology. The Sequential Write performance of the VisionTek 900903 could also be a bit higher.

All in all, I am pleased with this drive.

Altho I hate its past case designs, SanDisk has just announced at CES its new Extreme Pro USB 3.1 flash drive, which claims to offer "read speeds up to 420MB/s and write speeds up to 380MB/s" (when attached to a USB 3.1 port). Those are surely its Sequential specs; the fact that they do not mention its random specs makes me suspect that they are still bad.

Another case design I dislike is Corsair's way too fat Flash Voyager GTX, as it causes port crowding. A tragedy, since it otherwise is one of the few flash drives that claims to use a real SSD controller.

Speaking of CES, some other announcements for the small storage enthusiast to check out are Longsyss SATA Disk in Package (SDP) and Toshiba's BG Ultra Mobile SSD.
Seriously this is the best portable speaker that I have owned so far. The sound quality is incredible, and for the price ?? I can not believe it, the bass especially. This is a must have.
Bought two for each of my sons.  They work great.  Easy to operate, decent radio sound quality and of course USD ports.  Would buy again if I needed another.

Video quality is nice, but as some other people have mentioned the volume really isn't loud enough.  Would like the mount to the seat back to be a bit more sturdy and with fewer small parts..  My son kicked it and now its won't stay in position.

I got tired of putting a hat over my old webcam whenever I wasn't using it since it didn't have a cap to hide the camera, so I decided to give this one a try. The pros? It's very easy to install, just plug in the USB and make sure to select the webcam for whatever video program you're using. The video quality is really good, and the audio is decent (I use a Jabra speaker for work calls). It has a green light to let you know when it's in use, and a sliding 'cap' to cover the video lens when you're not using it for privacy.
The cons? Once you place it on top of your PC or monitor, you can't really adjust it much; it does have a nice wide angle, but you can't really tilt it down or up very well.

This will keep your mouse cursor moving so your laptop/pc doesn't time out, along with any application such as Teams which shows your status. It's helpful for things when you're in meetings but not typing or clicking and don't want to be seen as 'away'. It does have a faint whirring sound, but other than that, it does move the cursor. I like that it has an 'on/off' button so you can choose when to use it.

The video quality of my laptop isn't the greatest, and since I'm on video calls a lot more, I figured I'd give this webcam a try. It comes with its own little tripod (and a cap for the camera), and is so easy to set up (plug in the attached USB cord). The video quality is decent - not the best, but better than my laptop's. The audio quality is... ehhh, you'll probably want to stick with what's available on your pc or use a headset.

The laptop arrived in a cardboard box that was a bit mangled, but the LG box is designed to protect the laptop. There's also plastic covers on the brushed metal casing. Set-up is easy as you plug it in and power it on, and the MS assistant 'talks' you through things, allowing you to use voice or keyboard control. It's Windows 10 on the laptop, but no MicroSoft Suite (you have to pay extra for that).
With a SSD and 8 RAM memory, everything is very fast and responsive - I can have multiple tabs open on my internet browser, be playing music and have an app or Windows up and nothing is slow at all. It wakes up out of sleep mode quickly, too, and there's a fingerprint sensor for log-in or I can use a pin or 'drawing picture' function (there's lots of security options available).
Music/sound - the speakers are on the back/around the hinge, so if you're on a flat surface, the sound is good (it's not a high quality 'music/entertainment' laptop). But if it's on your lap, it may be muffled a little, fair warning.
Image/screen - it has good resolution and images are clear/crisp, but due to the fact that it's so lightweight, it's not a glass surface and has a little 'give'. When touching it, it leaves a faint 'trail' behind, but that does fade away quickly.
Keyboard - keyboard has some nice 'give' to it and I had to use Fn+F8 to make the backlight work. It didn't light up automatically, but you can turn it on/off and adjust the brightness.
There's three USB ports, an HDMI port, one for headphones and a micro SD card and others, split between both sides. That's a nice amount for a new laptop.
This is indeed a lightweight computer. It's lighter than my older generation Surface. The touchpad is responsive and the battery does have a good charge (at least for now), depending on what you're using (how many apps, backlight, etc.). All in all, this is a great laptop for work, writing, some entertainment and anything you would need to take on the go due to its light weight and thinness.

These are rather pricey for what they do, which is cord free earphones/buds. The case which holds and charges them (with a USB cord) is rather nice and handy, and lights up (red or green) to let you know when they're charged. They also charge relatively fast, which is good, and have various molds to help ensure a good fit. But yes, you'll be charging these a lot if you use these daily or often, be forewarned. Also, the controls are a little tricky to figure out and you might fumble with them a bit, considering you're pressing the things, basically, no nice cord with clear buttons. The sound quality is decent, not quite what I'd expect for the price, since part of the price is for the cordless nature of these things (that and the internal storage and the google speak and...). So yes, they've got a lot of nice options to them which make them more than just earbuds.

These are very nice looking earphones with denim and fabric accents (denim on the band, fabric wrapped cord), recycled aluminum and even some 'wood'. All in all, very nice. They are lightweight as well and they fit comfortably - then again, I'm on the small side. The sound is good, nothing spectacular but consider the price range. The music I'm playing comes in nice and clear so I'm happy. You have a microphone feature with them to take calls, but being able to pause music or adjust volume would be nice as well.

This review is one of those times I really wish we could leave a partial star review - the View Sonic MHD 22" monitor is not QUITE a five star, but it's pretty good. The quality is a slight bit lacking compared to the higher end HD monitors... but you're not paying the higher price so there's some give and take. The image is nice and crisp, but the color (at least on the one I received) is a little washed out. Also, the manual controls/buttons are on the back of the monitor which can make for some awkward adjusting depending on how you set up the monitor. Those are the reasons for the lack of a five star rating.
That said,you get a nice, light screen that comes very well packed, and with an HDMI cable included in the box (looked all over on the page and didn't see anything about cables included, and know that not all equipment comes with cables these days). Set up is easy, and it has selectable presets for games, movies, etc, that have predefined settings to optimize for those activities. It holds up well to gaming and is a step up from using the laptop screen.

The Klipsch KG-300 Pro Audio Wireless Gaming Headset is a very nice headset and easy to install - right out of the box you can plug in the base via USB (batteries included in the headset) and start using them. The audio is pretty good for a gaming headset, with the sounds of the game coming through clear, and people on the other end can easily hear what is being said. The headset is mostly comfortable - they're not the lightest and a bit bulky/padded, but they fit well.
Now, for the price of this headset, one thing that did surprise me is how much background noise DID come through. While it is true that they don't claim to be noise cancelling, considering the price and the padding, I didn't expect to be picking up so much background noise while wearing them. Definitely won't have to worry about anyone sneaking up on you while wearing these.

This is a nice, average case for your Kindle Fire HDX 7" device. One of its advantages is it's lightweight and slim, so if you're looking for a case that won't add weight or bulk to your kindle, this is a good one to buy. It's also 'stiff', the bottom part being reinforced plastic, so it gives some support and protection (not much, but a little, it's not thick or too strong). You have holes for the sound and cut-outs for the power button and the sound buttons, and you snap the kindle into the case. The 'lid' folds over to protect the kindle in transport when it's closed, and an elastic keeps it in place (no magnets or anything, which would be an improvement or what I'd expect for the price, to be honest). You fold the cover back and bend it to put it in a horizontal position for viewing or use - it's a very thin crease to do this, so it's not the strongest 'catch' to hold it in position. Obviously it's not meant to stand in a vertical position.

So you have a very thin, lightweight case in a nice shade of blue (neutral color) that holds/supports the kindle well and makes it easy to transport it, it just doesn't give it much options to display it. Considering the price, you might want to look at other options....

The Asus has a sleek look with its silver brushed metal lid and slightly rounded sides. Between this and it being JUST under 5 lbs, it makes for an easy transport if you want a laptop to carry around.

I noticed immediately the ultra-fast sleep mode. As soon as the lid is closed the laptop goes into immediate hibernation. After opening lid and clicking to un-hibernate, the laptop is back to active within 2-3 seconds.

The touchscreen has a sleek design with a black outline around the active screen that frames the look of the screen nicely. If you put pressure on the top of the laptop lid it does not affect the screen at all which tells of the durability of the laptop casing. The touchscreen has very nice vibrant display graphics that allows it to be seen easily from various angles without too much glare.

The visuals of the screen are great, which make for impressive video viewing. Picture is great and graphics are very crisp whether it is a Powerpoint still picture on display or a movie. The audio is great, too. While not a gaming pc, this is a nice one for video/audio usage.

It is a very thin and elegant design. The DVD multi recorder fits nicely along the side panels along with three USB ports, a microphone jack, SD slot, network slot and HDMI port.

The grooved out design around the touch pad is a small detail that has a nice impact on the overall look of the keyboard and touchpad (the touchpad is a bit of a different design with the 'clicks', but honestly, at this point with various keyboards for various devices, I'm used to things being different and just roll with it. But FYI to buyer). Keyboard is nicely laid out with light/'chiclet' touch keys and touchpad is sensitive without being too touchy. Considering that I also have a Asus Ultrabook S500-CA with a twitchy as heck touchpad OOB, this is a welcome relief.

Battery life appears to be great as well. I had the machine in hibernate for approx. 6 hours after machine was fully charged and the battery was not even down past ½ charge after all that time. And while in use, it does last about 6 hours. Considering the size and weight, that's pretty good.

Now for some negatives (or at least not so greats).
Fan vent is on the bottom which can be seen as a negative to anyone that works with the laptop sitting on their lap. I would imagine that the fan would be blocked in this instance and would not function properly and possibly allow machine to overheat? Gonna need a cooler for this one while using it for any length of time.

No SSD at all?

It barely comes in under 5lbs. As stated, I also have a ASUS Ultrabook S500CA, which is a 15" screen and weighs less. It also doesn't have a DVD drive, so.... You're definitely adding weight here for that and a few other options (and losing USB and other ports).

No full Microsoft Office Suite/software (you'll have to pay to get more than a trial version or use something else). Just making that clear. - edited as before I had stated 'Windows'. Sorry for any confusion.

All in all, this is a responsive laptop with impressive visual and audio that can be useful to an everyday user. It probably has some drawbacks to someone needing serious processing (no SSD), but for a lot of users, this one is good. I like ASUS, I find them to be reliable laptops, their designs tend to be good, and this ultrabook is no exception.

For everyday use, I'd give this 4.5 -5 stars. Anything else, take off a star or two.

Okay, I have officially bought into Amazon's kindle crack. This is not my first kindle (or second, or...). This tablet is definitely an improvement over the previous versions, it's more responsive, it handles video and web browsing so much better than the previous Fire generation, and I love the slimmed down version.

The overall design is an improvement. The video quality is great, and music does play with a decent quality. Love the feature where it can display lyrics while playing song (if the mp3 has the information), thanks to the whole X-Ray/Lyrics feature. There's a lot of new touches here that are fun. I really appreciate the volume and the power buttons being on the opposite sides of the kindle now (don't know how many times I've hit the wrong one on my Fire >.<).

Also, being able to have more than two browsers open on Silk now w/out it crashing all of the time is a great improvement.

Some minor quirks - not sure if it's me or the tablet, but still trying to figure out how to get pictures already taken from my phone onto the tablet and directly into the photo folder.

Have installed several apps without a problem, downloaded files and opened them, so far so good. The kindle goes everywhere with me (literally, it's the perfect size to fit in my purse). I wish there were more cover options for the 7", but it seems to be increasing the longer the kindle is out, and I think a cover/case is a must for one of these. This is the kindle that I do take everywhere, and on a recent trip, I used this more than my Surface as it has my most frequently used personal emails installed on it (easy to set up), I can access my social accounts, my music, and of course my books.

The battery is... eh, decent. I can keep it on and play music for a few hours, video less, and use it to read books for most of a day. It could use some improvement.

All in all, it's a great tablet that you can take with you.

I was torn between the three and four stars, I'll admit. This case DOES get the job done, which is to be a slim case that helps the Kindle Fire HDX 7" fit well in my purse so I can carry it around and use it at work, etc., protect it and prop it up. I love the color choices and that it doesn't add bulk. The magnetic cover is okay, could be a little stronger but it does manage to stay close. The fit COULD be better, I find that I have to keep sliding it back up to help align up the power button or to make sure the power cord is fully seated in the Kindle. And you better plan on just using the screen if you want to play with the sound setting.

You will have to set/stand the Kindle in landscape mode, there is no portrait stand with this case. For the most part, that's fine if you're listening to music, watching videos or typing/reading, but if you need a game or a screen that is only portrait mode, you're going to want another case fast. Hence the debate on three or four stars. However, for the price, the fact that this is lightweight/slim and that it does a decent job for its limitations, I think it's a decent case. Just don't go buying it thinking it'll do everything or that it'll free up all of the buttons.

This is one of the smaller external HD's that I've received lately, and while the size and weight is nice for a portable HD, it does feel a little on the flimsy side (not as thick plastic) which would make me more concerned while carrying it around than with other HD's. That said, it looks nice, and more importantly, it works well. I'd just tuck it inside of something better than the little cloth bag they so kindly included with the drive. There's a small bluish/white light on the side that lets you know when it's linked, transferring and safe to disconnect.

It supports USB 3.0 connectivity, and is very fast in transferring files on my pc. There's very nice, detailed information on setting up the back-up functionality on the drive as well as any files you need (maybe too much - if you're just going to use the drive as a regular portable HD, then I'd delete the folders/programs to clear up space - or clean up after you get what you need off of it after setting up as a backup). I was a bit surprised to see that they send you to Dropbox for the cloud backup, considering that there's an associated cost for large file size storage (kickback much?).

So basically it's a small, lightweight drive that is very fast (if you've the right connection) and a decent price if you want to use it as a backup drive. It helps you back up to the cloud, but you'll be paying for your own storage.

I'm not the most tech-abled person out there, but I think I can manage to get by - I work with computers all day, I've owned several laptops over the years, bought into the Kindle crack (several different versions) and have a tablet. So I'm used to different types of tech and have been using Windows 8 for a couple of months (albeit on a Surface Pro). Seemed logical to give a touchscreen laptop a try, and Asus has a pretty good reputation.

The Asus Ultrabook S500-CA had some decent reviews, and the main draw (other than being pretty big for an ultrabook with not the greatest battery life) was that the touchpad is 'quirky'. Other people have commented on this, and yes, I HAVE to agree. I adore touchpads. I rarely use a mouse w/ a laptop because it's in my lap most of the time (yes, bad ergo). This pc might break me of the habit unless I get the touchpad reset properly. I can't tell you how many times my screen has zoomed out because of this touchpad. But it should be fixable (there's comments below on resetting). It's just annoying as all heck.

I also find that sometimes the touchscreen isn't very responsive. I don't know if it's the site I'm on, my browser (it seems to freeze up on the net most of the time) or what. Sometimes it won't let me close apps or is a pain to do it. Sometimes it doesn't let me scroll. I don't seem to have this problem w/ my Surface. But I'd say it works 95% of the time (I have to admit that I have a different web browser on the Surface).

Speaking of my apps, it's a pain how some of them pop up all the time when I don't want them to, and I have to spend a few minutes getting them to close (see screen).

These have been the most annoying issues w/ the laptop so far. Well, that and figuring out the keyboard. Having the number keys on the side causes the keys to be a little offset, and it took a few days to get used to it. But that's something that you can get used to (or I did). Other than that, it's figuring out where one of the two deletes are that's bugging me the most. Not the most intuitive changes there.

But the laptop is nice and light for its size. Screen graphics are pretty good (it's not the greatest for gaming, but for everyday use and video viewing, it's nice) as is sound. Speed has been decent. I'm still trying to figure out the why's of the HD partitioning, but maybe that's just me.

Quirks aside, it's a light, sleek pc that works well, is responsive (maybe too responsive) for the most part and is meeting my every day needs. The longer I use it and figure it out, the less quirks there are. I like the pc, I just wish it had a better OS on it. And a less sensitive touchpad.

I've tried a couple of high quality headphones and earphones lately, and have to say that these are probably the best. The sound quality is exceptional, for pc, iPhone and mp3 player listening, providing clarity and definition of both bass and tremble. It was easy to pick up elements to the song that other - lesser quality - earphones left out, and the Munitio earphones were comfortable to use (in part thanks to the three different sizes of earbuds that they provide to ensure the best fit).

The microphone and the control buttons work well with any Apple products, which is nice (one day it'll be great to come across a universal product), and the design is appealing with the thick, flat cord (which isn't entirely tangle-free but less likely to knot up like some other earphones I've come across, especially those which are fabric wrapped) and the bronze accents. Munitio provides a nice, flat bag to carry your earphones in which can be easily tucked into a pocket or bag.

There are probably higher end earphones that provide just as good if not better listening quality, but for the price, I'd have to recommend these.

I'll admit that I usually get by on the earbuds and don't usually pay a lot for headphones - most of the time I just use what comes with whatever music player I've purchased. These were available for trial so I figured 'why not'? I must admit that they are doing a very good job of convincing me to turn in my earbuds....

These aren't noise canceling headphones, but they do a very good job of muffling out the sound around you, which is great because a lot of time I do listen to music while in a noisy environment (traveling, work, etc). The sound quality itself is definitely an improvement over other head/earphones I've used in the past - I'm picking up more musical instruments and definition in songs. These are also very nice looking headphones. I received the white/ivory ones and while plastic, they appear solid and have a nice heft to them, with good padding and a thick cord that is less prone to tangling.

The downside (and the reason they didn't get five stars)? Well, they are pricy, and they are a bit bulky (you're not going to fit them in your pocket), although they do come with a nice bag and collapse somewhat so you can throw them in a backpack or bag to protect them while traveling. I also wish that the toggle to adjust volume/tracks for iDevices was lower on the cord - it's about shoulder level on me and I'm not a big person (but it works great w/ my iPhone). The headphones also exert a bit of pressure against the ears to provide a snug fit and block out noise, so I find myself adjusting them from time to time for a bit of relief, especially since I listen to music for a few hours at a time while working. They take some getting used to on that front. But overall, I think they're worth it for the quality and listening experience.

This really is one very nice looking cover. It makes me feel as if I am holding a real book instead of a tablet/ereader, and it does look a lot like leather (which it isn't). I really like the 'sleep' feature that this cover has, putting my Kindle to sleep mode when I close the cover, something I haven't come across in the other covers I've bought in the past. It does have a handy stand feature that lets you prop it up, in the horizontal position only. The fasteners to hold the cover closed and to keep the Kindle in place inside are rubber, but they do a decent job of it (and can be positioned to prevent any important ports/buttons from being covered). Of course, with this type of cover (fake leather, going for the appearance of a real journal/book), the speakers are going to be covered, but it doesn't have too much impact on the sound when you're using it.

There's been comments made on the smell of this cover, and I've noticed that pretty much all of my fake leather covers come with some sort of odor when they arrive. It usually dissipates after a day or two (longest might have lasted a week) and this was no exception - if anything, this was one of the 'better' smelling faux leather covers I've received. None of them were so awful as to be off-putting, in my opinion, but I'm aware that it's a personal thing, how much it affects you.

All in all, this is an impressive looking cover that has a few nice features and enough heft to provide some decent protection for your Kindle Fire.

As a person that appreciates style and appearance, as soon as I saw this UE Boombox I was impressed. It is a modern, sleek design that includes a long handle across the entire top of the boombox that adds to the portability of the speaker. It is shiny silver with a rubberized silver bottom and sides that assist in gripping it to whatever surface it is set on. The right side has a blue rubberized "quick hit" volume up and down panel and the left side houses the Bluetooth Pairing button, Power switch, battery indicator, and 3.5mm aux input (this cable is not included with the product).
According to the product specifications, two 0.5-inch tweeters, two 3-inch woofers, and four 2.6-inch passive radiators deliver the audio and it contains a rechargeable battery with a 6 hour life as estimated by Logitech. This battery is replaceable after it has reached the end of its lifetime. The battery charger is included with the product.
Pairing of my iPad and this UE Boombox was so easy I was actually really surprised. I removed it from the box, charged it for about two hours (which I later learned on Logitech's website was no necessary. It comes fully charged). After two hours, I followed the simple three step instructions to pair the UE Boombox which consisted of turning it on, waiting for the Bluetooth light to blink rapidly (took about 5 seconds) and then selecting the device under Bluetooth on my iPad. It worked just liked the instructions said it would! Sooooooooooo simple!
I played through many types of musical genres and again was very impressed. The bass is great on this UE Boombox. I do Zumba dancing and music like Pitbull and Flo Rida sounds fantastic on this (even blaringly loud). I also ran through Kidrock, Styx, Journey, and some Barry Manilow and the music sounded fantastic at all volumes. The bass is really deep and intense at loud volumes making this the perfect party boombox.
Overall, at $250, the Logitech UE Boombox offers a good-looking design and impressive output in this reviewer's opinion.

This is a great idea for a Kindle Fire - the kit comes with two speakers that really does improve the sound quality of whatever you're listening to.  You can charge the speakers by USB - either through your computer or an adapter, and the stand/cradle will hold your Kindle and allow it to charge as well (through your own charging device, it's not included in the kit).  The stand doubles as a case for the speakers, which allows you to easily carry them around if you want to take them and your Kindle with you to the office or somewhere else.

I bought this tv when a local store had them on sale, after deciding to get an internet tv. I am by no means an expert, but I have been impressed by this tv. I wanted a simple hardshell case to attach a carabiner to and sling my noise-canceling headphones off my backpack. This did the job. It was fine, I was pleased.

Then I came back from a December trip to Helsinki and somewhere between baggage claim at DFW and my front door, the case - with my beloved headphones, a battery bank, and my Apple rapid charge block - vanished.

I was heartbroken. I filed reports. I checked with my Lyft driver. I went through my backpack and suitcase over and over and over again. I poked the bushes around my apartment building. Nothing.

Fast forward four months to today. I took the trash out and as I came back up the stairs, I saw something dark colored under the feral cat shelter on my patio. In all these months I’d never noticed it. But when I lifted the shelter, there it was. Filthy, scratched up, covered in pollen - my headphone case. I believe I knocked it under there while I was looking for my house keys.

In the last four months the DFW area has seen torrential downpours, freezing sleet, and even snowdrifts. My porch often catches the brunt of these storms. And yet when I zipped the case open, my headphones and battery bank and charging block were perfectly fine. Not so much as a dust mote on them. Everything was still fully charged and absolutely totally functional. As if they hadn’t just spent four months outdoors in Texas’ wacky winter weather under a cat hutch. Completely perfect.

And the case may be fine externally as well once I take some Clorox wipes to it.

Anyway. Good case, STUPENDOUS dang value for the cost.

I use this to stream audio to my TWS headphones so I can listen to music, videos, and audio books while working out or doing projects around the house. I've been using it for about a month now, and I'm pretty satisfied with it.

As I am sure is the case with many, I purchased this after seeing it listed by the New York Times in their portable BT transmitter review list. It was bought specifically to allow me to transmit BT audio from my computer to my Sony WF-1000XM3 earbuds. As the Sony earbuds only support SBC with these, I wasn't expecting stellar audio quality - I usually use them for lectures or podcast-like content, or for fairly low-bitrate music anyway. I wanted to see if the advantages of true-wireless earbuds were worth the sacrifice in quality before I invested in a more expensive BT transmitter and BT receiver+high-end IEMs. As such, I do not use the receive function, and I do not use the battery on the unit - it is always plugged in via USB. I did briefly test the battery though and can confirm it lasts at least 30m.

Note: I went with this type unit, instead of USB, because I wanted to have the ability to test it in multiple environments, including while running and in the car for single-ear usage. Normally, I'd go with a USB solution for computer use in order to avoid the conversion of the audio from to and back from analog.

Initial Setup

Dead simple - I connected the Line Out on my computer to the input on the transmitter, and alternately, the HP out on my stereo receiver to the input on the transmitter. I also tried it with a Sansa Clip+ MP3 player. It worked in all cases, though with the WF-1000XM3 I had to keep the input volume on the BT transmitter under 30% and allow the headphones to do the real amplification, as otherwise the audio would distort.

BT Setup

Fairly simple. I put my earbuds into pairing mode, the transmitter into pairing mode, and they connected within 10s. Afterward, they maintained their connection for the most part, I've had to re-pair a couple times over the last three weeks, but that is mostly a learning curve. Re-pairing is easy - just hold the pairing button down for two seconds and place the receiving device in pairing mode.

Range

Unpredictable, and sensitive. If the transmitter is located on a desk, at least twelve inches away from other electronics, then the range is remarkable. I can leave the room, pass through the adjacent room, and enter into the next room - a total of maybe thirty feet, through two or three walls - and start to lose audio at the end. This is despite being only five feet from a wireless router. However, if I move the transmitter six inches over so it is next to my monitor, or a couple feet so that it is within three feet of the router, the earbuds will begin to drop out even at ten feet. So it is very sensitive to environment.

Audio Quality

Decent. Better than I expected, but I haven't used bluetooth audio in ten years. It can be hard to really gauge it, because the Sony WF-1000XM3 are true wireless earbuds and I can't A/B test them to compare BT quality to a cable. I would say that the BT audio quality is equivalent to that produced when my Sony earbuds are connected to my smartphone. While it is decent, it can't compare to wired earbuds of even fairly middling quality. You lose highs and lows. For dialogue content, lectures and the like, no issue.

Summary

Seems to be a great entry-level transmitter for the average consumer. I'm glad I bought it, because it is reliable and easy to use, and has shown me that the freedom of using wireless earbuds is definitely worth the hit to quality - I can always use my full circumaural headphones if I want to watch a movie or listen critically. Would recommend.

I purchased this for my '05 Subaru Outback, which was made before the days of USB ports and 3.5mm jacks being regular features of cars. I used this in conjunction with two other devices - an iSimple IS31 (ASIN: B002U5XPBE) and a YIPIN HEXHA Quick Charge QC3.0 USB Step Down Converter (ASIN: B0918CR35N), as well as a couple cable adapters. I installed it in the oddball center compartment above the Subaru's media console, so it is normally out of sight, and I can store any cables plugged into it in the compartment when no device is in use. The step-down adapter ties into a cigarette lighter which is inactive when the car is not turned on.

I checked my dimensions and runs first, deciding to install near the media console and run the wires behind the radio. I already had the iSimple and its own audio jack installed in the center console, so I was just going to tie this into the existing setup. Install was easy, if a bit fraught, due to the brittleness of 15+ year old vinyl and having one-shot at drilling the hole for it. I forewent the rubber gasket to I'd have a more flush mount, so you have to get the dimensions right within 1/16". I ended up using a stepper bit, and then an X-Acto to finish the hole.

The port sits quite nicely in place, the included nut makes it easy to tighten everything down. You might want a little bit of threadlocker on there so it doesn't vibrate loose, but it's not strictly necessary. You can shave down the back of this adapter a bit if you need the wires to make a tighter bend - I had to do so - but be careful, naturally. The port, even without the gasket, sits about 1/8" over the surface of the panel, so it isn't perfectly flush. However, it is tight enough that it is out of the way and will probably look more or less in place on a black panel.

For me, exercising care to get everything looking nice and clean and stock, it took about two hours total, not including the iSimple install - which was about two hours itself, with the same level of care - and the step-down converter, which was maybe 30m with the soldering.

So far the unit performs perfectly, power is transferred without issue - it seems to charge quickly, but I can't attest to full QC3 compatibility. The only odd-ball issue is that it looks like USB connectors don't seat all the way into the USB jack - some silver is exposed, more than you would expect. Not sure why this is, but it is the same with multiple USB plugs. Doesn't affect functionality, but might give you pause or encourage you to try pushing in hard to get it to seat fully.

Would recommend.

I installed this in my Outback after thinking about doing so for years. I've never used the sound system in my car and it felt like a bit of a waste, and I would like to listen to audiobooks and music on my commute or long trips. Previously I considered tying the audio into the wiring harness for the CD player in order to attain maximum quality, but it was sufficiently unapproachable that I put it off for years. I ended up going with the iSimple instead of a generic FM transmitter because I wanted to get the maximum possible quality at the maximum power, hopefully improving the battery life of my MP3 player (a Sandisk Sansa Clip+).

As for installation: I watched a video on Youtube by a guy named Dirtcheapdaily (How to add an auxiliary port to any car | Ep.81) which made the process very simple. It took me about three hours total from start to finish, and required that I remove the center console from the car and make some modifications on the workbench. However, I wanted my car to look stock, with everything hidden away - if you don't care about any of that, you could literally do this in 20m.

However, the steps I took were: remove some panels from center console and radio - pull antenna wires out from behind head unit- connect iSimple model to antenna wires via adapters to check length of wires - remove center console and bring to workbench - add velcro and attach iSimple to space inside center console where it won't interfere with anything - drill holes in wall of center console storage compartment - cut switch wires, feed through holes, resolder w/ heatshrink - feed audio wire through hole, solder to 3.5mm jack, seat in hole - trim, then solder power wires to back of cigarette lighter (only has power when ACC is on) - tie all wires down so they don't wander - return center console to car and temporarily reconnect to adjust gain and switch to best radio station, and make sure parking brake doesn't interfere with modules or wires - reassemble car and test one last time.

Regarding quality: after adjustment, I'd say the audio quality is pretty good. When the switch is on, there is no interference whatsoever from other stations. It is not as good as a true line in, but I don't see that as being very important as I frequently have the windows down, hear road noise, or have the car vents running, so for me fairly good is good enough. It is better than many external FM transmitters I've heard, and much more consistent.

I do wish the gain on the unit was a bit stronger, I have it maxed out an still have to crank my volume up to 50% if I have my MP3 player on ~50% volume, which isn't an issue it itself but at 20 the other radio stations are truly deafening. I wanted to add an AUX input to my '05 Subaru Outback via an iSimple transmitter, and this seemed to be what I was looking for. Since I like everything to look stock, I drilled out a hole for it in the wall of the storage compartment in the center console and mounted it right next to the switch that activates it. A 5/16" bit will do the trick, though if you have one, 11/32 makes it easier. For me, the panel was too thick to use the nut, so instead I just made barely made the hole big enough and press-fit the jack into it, then used some heat shrink tubing on the back.

Contacts could be larger, but soldering them up was a simple matter. I ended up using a bit of UV-activated glue to isolate the contacts and prevent a potential short, but hot glue, regular glue, or three individual sleeves of heatshrink will do the trick. If you are looking right at the back of the connector, the ground/chassis wire is on the bottom, the right channel (red, typically) is to the right, and the left channel (white, typically) is on the left.

Audio is fine, nice little snap when the connector goes in, retention isn't problematic in the least. Black bezel blends right into the mounting surface, like it belongs there. Durable enough that when I used the rubber-coated handle of my pliers to press-fit the jack into the panel, there was no damage at all to the surface of the jack.

Would recommend as a panel mount, it is compact, durable-feeling, and easy to use.

Would recommend.

I now have Supershieldz on three devices, and would recommend.

I only purchased a smartphone about a year ago, previously being in the flip-phone-for-life crowd, due to the requirements of a job I was on. Since then I have slowly been picking up the various accouterments of such devices, the latest being this magnetic mount. I bought it mostly so I can use Google Maps for navigation.

It is remarkably effective. I have a Motorola Moto X4, in a slim silicon case, and an 05 Subaru Outback. The kit comes with the magnetic mount, two metal plates with adhesive (a rectangular one and a little circular one), a clear adhesive interposer, and, as a nice surprise, an alternate, black bezel.

What you do is attach the metal plate to the outside of your case, the inside of your case, or your phone. If you choose the lattermost option, then you don't attach it directly to the phone, but to the clear adhesive interposer (just a clear plastic sheet with adhesive on both sides), likely to prevent surface damage and dampen shock/reduce possible strain. If you have one of those pop-socket devices, you attach the little metal circle to the center of that instead. Then, you fit the magnetic mount to one of the grilles of your car's vent system, wherever it is most convenient. Now you can mount your phone to it, the magnet clinging to the metal plate.

I attached the metal plate to the inside of my case. It is very thin - I would say 1mm or less - and even on my slim silicon case it leaves only a very slight rise, hardly visible from the outside. I also attached it about 2/5ths of the way up from the bottom of the phone, as recommended (the Moto X4 does not have wireless charging). The magnet adheres quite well to the phone - the silicon case actually slightly pulls away when detaching the phone from the mount - not nearly enough to dislodge the case, but enough to let you know that the magnet is really sticking. As the mount has a rubber pad, and my case has a rubber texture, the phone does not slide at all in any lateral direction, the shear resistance is quite high. I am not concerned about the phone just falling off during normal operation of the car.

The tines of the mount grip the vents quite well - I have only had the mount pull off the vents once when detaching the phone after parking. There are two sizes of gaps - narrow and wide - and the narrow gap seems to fit pretty well on the Subaru. I like how you can pivot the mount a little to the left or right, and use the vent's own hinge to pivot it up and down.

There are some basic shortcomings of design. Obviously you can only attach this to the vents of the car, which limits your choice of positioning. I tried putting it on the left vent, but that caught too many outside reflections. I tried the right vent, but my hand was mostly blocking the screen. I tried the left passenger-side vent, but found that this took my eyes too far off the road while checking the navigation. In the end, I went with the driver's side right vent, since it required the lease eye-movement to check navigation and it was actually helpful to have my had block the screen, so as to avoid distraction. The tines hold, but they are not as secure as a hard mount would be. Likewise, the magnet could, in theory, be bumped out of position by kids/pets/carelessness and fall down into the foot well.

However, I would generally recommend this, at least as someone's first mount, to get a feel for what they are looking for if nothing else.

I was trying to choose. Sony MDR-V6 Sony MDR-7506, ATH-M30, ATH-M40... I looked at everything. I found a youtube channel, which plays direct from CD sample, then crossover in sync to various model headphones resampling the sound from the each headphone as it's placed over a foam head. - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sj69-mWHV3E - The point is, they are trying to reproduce what is heard. Also, I found another youtube channel of a guy who shows various headphones sampled through a graphic analyzer, showing the frequency response.

All headphones add something to the signal. So what you hear on one model isn't the same, with another. But of all the head phones, the ATH-M40x was identical in sound reproduction to the original music. You couldn't tell the difference. Why is this important? Two reasons, if you are an audio engineer, you will have a truer sound, what you hear, is what you will get. It goes both ways, what you listen to, will be what the sound engineer intended for you to hear.

For music with base, it has good presence, and you can hear details that sound muddy on other head phones. I have been listening to a lot of head phones. You do understand muddy and clarity, once you hear it.

With that said, and having spent some time, in store sampling, (note: I must say that the Sonys are really good too. I tried and liked the MDR-V55 as well. It's a DJ headset so it's a bit more base. I felt they were very clear and better than the MDR-X05 hands down.)

The ATH-M40x, has removable cables. They are field repairable. And you can choose between three different cables, although two come in the box.

They are son tested and approved. Now I have to keep them locked up, joking. They are well built. Some say the ATH-M50x is better. It's also said the M50x sound the same as last year's model, and the M40x sound as good as last year's M50 model too. Which is it? The M40x is specifically flat sounding for audio engineering. The M50x is targeted for the audiophile, with a V shape EQ. The M40x is in the sweet spot, unless you have money to burn.
