My only problem is that if I leave my car stereo set to AUX and my phone is not plugged in, then I get static noise from the cable. This does not happen when the cable is not plugged in. This is easy to fix by turning the stereo off or turning it to a different audio source.

There are several different products in this listing with the reviews all mixed together. I got the soundbar for $50 with no separate subwoofer. I'm using this soundbar with a desktop computer and the soundbar placed below my 28 inch monitor. Since my PC is always right next to the speaker, I used the included USB audio cable. A wired connection is always more reliable than Bluetooth and often sounds better as well. The sound is as good or better than any other $50 speaker system that I have used. The higher frequencies are pretty crisp and clear and the bass is above average for this price level.

The soundbar is pretty bulky, so while it is portable, I probably won't do that much. Battery life is not great if you are using it unplugged, but fine for making presentations from your laptop, etc.

Budget-priced earbuds are complicated to review because, in my experience, all $200 earbuds sound significantly better than all $50 earbuds, but there is still a lot of demand for value-priced "good enough" products. I do own a couple of $200 earbuds and they do sound noticeably richer and clearer than these $40 earbuds. However, when I'm out jogging or traveling (eg airplane or train) or listening to voice podcasts, having the absolute best sound quality isn't really important to me. In those situations, features are more important to me, like active noise cancellation, equalization, good volume, good battery life, and easy access to the features. I'd rather use cheap earbuds that I don't mind losing somewhere along the way.

These earbuds have average quality sound for the $40 price. Where these Donner earbuds beat the competition is the features. I've never owned $40 earbuds with app control before. The user manual has a QR code to let you download the app. The QR code did not work, but I did find the "Donner Control" app in the Google Play app store and the app works fine on my Android phone. The app lets me pick from pre-programmed equalization settings or design my own. Adjusting the equalization for different types of music makes a significant difference in audio clarity. The app also lets me choose from 3 active noise cancellation modes. These features don't work as well as in $200 earbuds, but these are $40 earbuds and most $40 earbuds don't have any of these features or any app at all. You can control some of these features with the confusing set of triple-tap commands on the earbuds, but I can never remember those and would rather just tap the picture in the app.

The app also lets you download firmware updates from Donner. None was available when I checked, but this could be a great way for them to refine the features of the earbuds or even add new features. They ask you to give them your email address and create an account when you open the app, but I did not and the core features of the app still work OK.

Battery life for these earbuds is good for this price range (6 to 8 hours, depending on whether or not you use ANC). As with most budget-priced wireless earbuds, maximum volume is OK but not great. Bass is above average for the $40 price. Static noise is very low. The Bluetooth connection has been very stable for me, even when I'm 30 feet away from my phone or in a different room in the house.

I can't give these earbuds 5 stars because I can easily buy better sound quality with more money, but these are solid 4 stars for value at the current $40 price.

I'm replacing all my old frequently-used flash drives with SSD drives. SSD drives have become reasonably priced (for the capacity) and are much faster and much more reliable than flash drives. This brand is made in Taiwan and so far works just as well as the name brand drives. Read and write speeds are extremely fast. We get 500GB of storage in the same size as an old 64GB flash drive. It wasn't so long ago that 64GB flash drives would cost this much, too. Flash drives always seem to develop data errors with regular use (or with just age). I have yet to have a data problem with a SSD drive.

This cable works great for charging. It easily charges my USB-C tablet and laptop at full speed. It does contain an E-Mark chip, which modern USB-C require for high power charging.

The cable is well made with a sturdy casing and sturdy connectors.

Data transfer speeds with this cable are mediocre USB2.0 speeds. If you want high speed data transfer (including video streaming), you should get a USB3.0 or faster cable. This cable is only good for high speed charging.

This adapter works great to connect my Pixel 6 phone to the aux jack on my car stereo while I'm charging the phone via USB-C at the same time. I hear no static at all when the phone is not playing anything. Nice clean sound when the phone is playing something. Charging works fine, too. $15 is a great price if this adapter works well for you too.

I am more of a hiker than a bird watcher so I chose the 32mm binoculars. The 42mm size is about 50% larger and heavier. The 42mm lenses are brighter in low light situations (like sunrise), but I prefer the less bulky size and lower weight when I am carrying the binoculars on day-long hikes.

These binoculars are good quality for the price, comparable to name-brand binoculars in the $100 to $150 price range. Image quality is much better than cheaper binoculars that are usually distorted over much of your field of view and have poor brightness and contrast.

The magnesium chassis does make these binoculars a little heavier than average, but hopefully that also means better long-term durability.

I do have 2 complaints about these binoculars. First the hard rubber eyecups are noticeably less comfortable than the softer rubber used in other binoculars that I own. Second, the carrying case is bigger and bulkier than it needs to be. Did the company cheap out and use the same size case for both their 32mm and 42mm binoculars?

There is no warranty information included in the package. I did find the warranty on the company website. The warranty is much more restrictive than some name-brand binocular companies. That is something to consider, especially if you are hard on your equipment.

I notice that some other reviews are complaining that the strap is difficult to attach to the binoculars. I did not have any problem using the strap and the strap is comfortable and secure. See photo of how the camera is attached to the binoculars.

This is a very compact flash drive; just 1.5 inches long. It supports both USB-C and USB-A, so it is great for copying files between my Android phone (that supports only USB-C) and my PC (that supports only USB-A). I got the 32GB version and USB3 speeds are plenty fast for 32GB. The drive is fast, quiet, and doesn't get hot when I am using it. It is handy to have for both data backup and file transfer. It comes pre-formatted with exFAT, but you can change that to FAT or NTFS if you want. $10 price is reasonable for what you get. 5 stars.

This backpack is rated at 20 liters, but it seems roomier than that. Maybe that is because this backpack doesn't have lots of little pockets. There is only 1 big compartment and a padded laptop pocket in the bottom of that compartment. One big compartment gives me a lot of flexibility to haul different sized items, especially when I'm bicycling. The backpack is narrow enough to be very stable when I'm bicycling. Contoured padded shoulder straps and a chest harness make the backpack even more stable and comfortable. I love the rolltop closure which is sturdier and more rain-resistant than a zipper. The rolltop also allows me to adjust the height of the backpack, especially when I want to carry a taller item (like a musical instrument). Chrome is a top quality bike messenger brand that is very well designed and built. Their products are expensive, but I think they are worth the price if you use them daily.

This alarm is louder than other hand alarms that I have tried, but the 1000 foot audible range sounds like a stretch. It activates easily enough once I practice it a couple of times.

I do not like that it requires 4 LR44 batteries, which we do not have any of at home. You need a very tiny screwdriver to open the battery door. The instructions say the batteries will last about 1 year if not used, but I assume that using the flashlight regularly will kill the battery. Other hand alarms that I have tried are rechargeable, which is much more convenient.

These light stands are only 3 feet tall (3.5 feet with the lights attached), so they are designed for tabletop use, not for full-room use. The lights are not real bright, so they do work best illuminating your desk and/or a person sitting or standing near the desk. The lights in this kit do not have any batteries and have to be plugged in to a USB power source to operate; either a USB battery pack or a wall socket. All the pieces in this kit are mostly plastic, so are not real sturdy or real precise, but are adequate quality for the price (currently $38 for the kit).

If you're looking for a general purpose lighting kit to light up a room or a whole person (instead of just the upper half of a person), I recommend looking elsewhere for more larger powerful lights and taller sturdier light stands. This set is fine for desktop/tabletop/low-angle use only.

I'm using this adapter to listen to wired stereo audio on my Pixel 6 phone while charging at the same time, mostly in my car. Sound quality is good enough for car use. Power Delivery fast charging works great at the same time.

I have a Google Pixel 6 phone that has a USB-C port and no stereo audio port. Google sells USB-C to stereo adapters for $12 each. This one costs $8 and works fine with my phone. For the type of music I listen to and the quality of my speakers/headphones, I don't notice any difference in audio quality.

I've been using desktop PCs since the 1980s. In the old days we always bought the biggest PC cases so we could add more components like multiple disc drives, CD drives, extra I/O and networking ports, a bigger power supply, etc. These days, computers come packed with features and interfaces, internal storage is smaller and cheaper, USB3 is fast enough for external peripherals if we need them, and more and more computing is done in the cloud instead of on the desktop.

This little 5 inch x 5 inch x 2 inch box is all I really need for my desktop computing needs. The Intel i5 CPU is the same as what most mid-range laptops use. The built-in SSD and 16gb of RAM are faster than the hard drive and 8gb in our old PC that we replaced with this one. There is space to add a 2.5" SSD to increase the local storage space (I'm planning to add a 2TB SSD). The computer has plenty of ports; even a microSD flash card slot. The PC comes with Windows 11 pre-installed and it launched flawlessly when I turned the PC on.

There are 2 limitations for me. First is that there is only one memory card slot which currently contains a 16GB memory card. This is enough for most people (especially considering the mid-range i5 CPU) but if you want to add more memory, you must discard the 16GB card and replace it with a bigger card. Most PCs have 2 memory card slots so you can simply add a second memory card that adds to the first one. The second limitation is that the built-in graphics processor is not suitable for high-end gaming and there is no room to add a high-performance graphics card. If you are a hard core gamer, you should probably look elsewhere.

Considering the size and price of this mini-PC, I think it is fine as an everyday desktop computer for home or for the office. Students will probably want a laptop that they can carry to school, but a lot of adults prefer having a full-sized keyboard and screen and this mini-PC is cheaper than a comparable laptop if you have to buy a separate monitor in either case. If I want more power than my phone when I'm traveling, I bring a tablet instead of a more bulky and more fragile laptop.

My only real complaint about this mini-PC is that the fan is not super quiet and it runs a lot when I am multi-tasking with more than one program running.

There are a lot of USB microphones in the $99 to $139 price range right now including this AKG Ara as well as the slightly more expensive AKG Lyra and the popular Blue Yeti. Personally, I like the AKG Lyra the best out of this bunch. The AKG Ara is slightly cheaper, but the features are stripped down making it less flexible. In particular, the AKG Ara has a poorer sampling rate, worse low-frequency response, no stereo recording modes, and no mixing volume control, while the AKG Lyra has all of these features for only $25 more. The AKG Ara is fine if you have a hard $100 price limit and you don't think you'll ever need the extra features, but I would pay the extra $25 to get the AKG Lyra.

This adapter works great to let me charge my Pixel 6 phone and listen to wired stereo music at the same time. Sound quality is crisp and clear with good stereo separation. I mostly use it to plug into my car's stereo AUX jack, but I can also use it to listen to wired headphones.

This adapter works great with my Pixel 6 phone. I use it to listen to wired stereo audio while charging my phone at the same time. Amazon sells other adapters that try to do the same thing but some of the others work poorly, giving me very noisy audio or not charging my phone properly. This adapter charges my phone at the same speed as if I plugged the USB-C cable directly into my phone. Audio output is clear and noise free. The adapter looks sturdy enough for regular use. $15 price is reasonable. 5 stars.

I'm using this adapter with my Google Pixel 6 phone. It lets me charge my phone while listening to music through wired speakers at the same time. Charging speed is slightly lower than plugging the cable directly into my phone, but still very good (3.5A instead of 4A). Sound quality is fine.

I have a Google Pixel 6 smartphone which has a USB-C port, but no stereo jack. This gadget works great to let me charge my phone and play music through wired speakers or headphones at the same time. Sound quality is good with no noise or hissing like some other adapters have. $19 price is reasonable.

This is a sturdily built stereo splitter. Works great to connect my phone to two stereo speakers or headphones. Sound quality is fine with no noise issues. Price is a little high for what you get, though.

This is a handy light-duty adapter that you can mount to a camera cold-shoe or a tripod screw. The angle of the adapter adjusts in 1 dimension only (with a pivot, not a ball head). You have to use a hex wrench to tighten the pivot bolt, which is much less convenient than the lever or knob that most tripod heads have, so this head is best used for setups that don't need to be adjusted often. Mostly metal construction is pretty sturdy as long as you are only mounting lightweight equipment on it (like video lights, etc).

This adapter works well with my Pixel 6 phone. I can charge the phone and listen to stereo music through external speakers at the same time. Sound quality and stereo separation are good, except that I hear a faint buzzing when no music is playing. Amazon sells similar adapters that work just as well as this one for a little less money.

I have a Google Pixel 6 smartphone that has a USB-C port but no stereo headphone jack. These adapters work fine to connect stereo headphones or speakers to my phone. Sound quality is clear with good stereo separation and dynamic range no noise. These adapters cost $4.50 each while the genuine Google adapters cost $12 each. 5 stars for good performance at an inexpensive price.

My Pixel 5 phone has a USB-C output, but no wired headphone jack. This adapter works great when I want to connect my phone to my car's AUX jack. Sound quality is great. $15 price is reasonable for this product quality. 5 stars.

I'm a big fan of the 8x32 style of binoculars. These aren't as bright or powerful as the 10x42 or 8x42 binoculars on the market, but they are 1/3 to 1/2 less bulky and lighter weight. I'm more of a hiker than a birder, so when I'm hiking 20 miles, the extra weight and space in my backpack is very noticeable. Realistically, the larger 42mm binoculars are mostly brighter than the 32mm size at dawn and dusk, which is not when I'm hiking. 8x vs 10x is a personal preference, but a lot of people prefer 8x because the image is easier to hand-hold (in addition to the smaller size and lower weight).

Celestron makes a wide variety of binoculars, including a lot of basic-quality entry-level stuff that is not built very well and doesn't perform very well. This TrailSeeker ED model is a big step up from entry-level, both in price and performance. This model isn't quite as good as the top-rated 8x32 models like Nikon Monarch or Zeiss Terra, which both sell for around $400, but I think it is at least as good as any of the competition selling for under $300 that I have tried. I see a bright clear image with no noticeable chromatic aberration. Field of view is much better than most 8x32 binoculars and the image is sharp over a wider area than other under-$300 binoculars that I have tried. Field of view is very useful if your subject moves quickly or unpredictably (birds, wild mammals, sports athletes, etc). Build quality has been very solid and reliable for me so far.

Some people complain that the Celestron warranty is not as good as the competition and this is true. Some of the other brands have a "no questions asked" return policy for a good period time. Celestron's warranty is very limited in comparison, so definitely take that into consideration, especially if you are hard on your equipment.

The first couple of generations of Soundcore headphones were pretty mediocre. I'm glad the company keep improving their products. This year's models are really good for the price.

I got the Life A2 model. For $80, these earbuds come with features that I usually see on earbuds that cost more than $100 like equalization, noise cancellation, and upgradable firmware. These features all work great. I especially like the equalization that noticeably improves sound clarity.

Overall, the sound quality is great for earbuds that cost less than $100. Bass is not boomy, but great if you like a more natural sound. Stereo separation is excellent. Clarity at the higher frequencies is excellent when I set the equalizer to type of music that I'm listening too. Volume is better than average for true wireless earbuds.

These earbuds are on the larger side, but they don't stick out of my ears too much, so I don't constantly knock them out like I do with Apple-style earbuds. They are comfortable and secure enough in my ears.

I'm using an Android smartphone and the earbuds pair easily with my phone. Bluetooth connection has been solid. The Soundcore Android app is necessary to manage the equalizer and upgrade the firmware and both features work great. The app also shows your battery levels. Unfortunately, the app does spam me occasionally with unrelated Anker product announcements. I wish they wouldn't do that. Anker spams me enough by email.

These are very good travel headphones. Over-the-ear style is very comfortable when worn for hours at a time. The headphones are relatively lightweight and compact. They fold nicely into the included EVA soft-shell case, which fits easily into my carry-on bag.

The headphones pair easily with my Android smartphone. The Soundcore smartphone app is required for upgrading the headphones' firmware. The app also lets you customize the equalization to one of the presets or you can design your own. Depending on the kind of music you are listening to, the equalizer can make a noticeable difference in clarity and balance.

Unfortunately, the app spams me with notifications about unrelated Anker products. Hopefully this will not be frequent.

Noise cancellation works well. There are 3 modes: on, off (normal), and transparency that lets you talk to people around you without taking the headphones off. Noise cancellation can be toggled both from the app and from a button on the headphones themselves.

Overall, sound quality is good. More of a balanced sound than the boomy default effects that some headphones give. I mostly listen to acoustic music, so this works well for me. Clarity is good. Bluetooth connectivity has been great so far.

Amazon sells a lot of webcams for $20 to $30 that are really terrible. Most of those do not have autofocus, so video is never sharp. If there is autofocus, it is slow and often inaccurate. Some of the lenses and sensors on the cheap cameras and all of their microphones are sub-par so colors and contrast are washed out and the audio is muddy and dull.

This webcam costs $40, but I think it is actually worth buying while the cheaper ones are garbage. The autofocus on this webcam is fast and accurate. Colors and contrast and exposure look natural. Picture quality is sharp and clear. The microphone is reasonably clear for voices (as long as you are close to the camera), though not nearly as good as if you get a decent external microphone, though that will cost you at least another $50.

These earbuds sound good, but not as good as some $100 earbuds that I own and not much better than $80 earbuds that I own. Sound is crisp and clear, but bass is a little weak in rock and roll music. Volume is adequate, but not as loud as some other true wireless earbuds.

I downloaded the Yamaha Headphones Controller app from the Google Play app store. The app lets check for firmware updates (none available) and enable "listening care", which is a basic equalizer that improves music clarity a little. There are no settings for different listener preferences or music styles. There is no noise cancellation or equalizer profiles, which my $100 earbuds have. There is no ambience passthrough mode, which even my $80 earbuds have.

6 hour battery life is great, but my $100 earbuds have similar battery life with more volume.

These earbuds have a simple plastic look and feel. They fit in my ears securely and I'm not worried about knocking them out (like I am with earbuds that stick farther out of my ears).

In summary, these earbuds sound pretty good, but there are many cheaper earbuds that sound just as good and have more features.

This adapter works great to charge my Google Pixel 2 phone while listening to stereo music through wired headphones or the AUX jack on my car stereo. Sound is clear and noise-free. Amazon sells several similar products and this appears to be one of the cheapest at only $12 (compared to $15 to $25 for the others). 5 stars for value and performance.

This little adapter has the 3 ports I need to mirror my laptop display to a larger monitor. HDMI output carries the video the monitor, the stereo jack carries the audio to my speakers, and the USB-C port lets you charge your laptop if it has only one USB-C port. This adapter does get pretty warm when in use, but not burning hot.

Received 2 USB-C to stereo adapters as advertised. They work fine with my Google Pixel 2 phone. Sound is clear and noise-free. The housing and connectors look simpler and lighter weight than some other USB-C adapters that Amazon sells. Price is similar to the official USB-C adapters from Google.

I am using these headphones in the USB-C port on my Google Pixel 2 phone. They work great for the $17 price. Music is crisp and clear with good stereo separation and decent bass; better than expected for $17. Lots of volume. The package includes 3 pairs of different sizes of eartips. The silicone ear tips are not as comfortable (to me) as memory foam, but are very good for this price. The thin wire does tangle more easily than the thicker or flat cables of some other headphones, but I'll excuse that at this price level. 5 stars for good performance at a value price.

This USB-C to stereo audio adapter works great with my Google Pixel 2 phone to let me listen to music from the phone's USB-C port on my standard wired headphones. It gives me a nice clear noise-free signal. Unfortunately, the $15 price is twice as much as Google's official adapter that works just as well. Minus one star because of the price.

Amazon sells a lot of different memory foam eartips and these are above average in price. They work well. They have a stiff plastic inner sleeve so they attach to my earbuds securely. I find the foam to be much more comfortable than the silicone eartips that usually come with earbuds. Foam eartips also give me a better fit than silicone. Sound quality is great for me, but I think this is mostly because they fit well.

This backpack is surprisingly lightweight compared to my old heavy-duty Timbuk2 messenger bag. This backpack is made from a lightweight but reasonably sturdy and abrasion-resistant 100% polyester. Empty weight is 1.4 pounds according to my kitchen scale.

The rolltop is much taller than some other rolltop backpacks that I have seen. Total unrolled height is 27 inches, which allows me to carry bulky items that won't fit in zipper-style backpack. Musical instruments like a violin or ukulele will easily fit in here. So will bulky (but not too heavy) sports equipment. The rolltop is also more reliable than a zippered backpack for carrying school clothes or books.

The backpack has outside side pocket that are big enough to hold small-to-medium sized water bottles securely. The inside laptop sleeve has only minimal padding, but I usually carry my laptop in a padded sleeve anyway.

This backpack is not cheap, but it is well designed and very functional. My past Timbuk2 bags have given me years of use.

These fit better and are more comfortable than the silicone ear tips that came with my headphones. Since they fit better, I also get better noise isolation. Glad to see that a large set of tips is available at a reasonable price. I don't expect these to last as long as the silicone tips. I took a chance and ordered the smaller 4.5mm size and that works with some of my earphones, but is too small for others. I'm going to order the larger size as well and hopefully that will fit the others.

This is a fancier version of the popular Blue Yeti amateur-quality USB microphone with a much higher price tag ($170 vs $110). For the extra money, you get 4 condensers (instead of 3) to give you higher-resolution 24-bit audio (instead of 16-bit) plus a bunch of fancier control and display options. The new microphone has the same directional recording patterns to isolate the recording to your intended audio sources. Is the new microphone worth the extra money? If you really need 24-bit audio, then definitely yes. If not, the new display and control features are more convenient than a huge jump in functionality. The Blue Yeti is still a great microphone for amateur USB recording (podcasts, musical performances, etc). The new version is a step forward, but not worth the price for everyone.

My biggest complaint is that the new microphone uses the same ancient mini-USB interface as the old one. Modern ultralight laptops are moving to the USB-C standard and mini-USB is 2 generations old. You could use a USB-C hub to give you a mini-USB interface, but I wish all modern devices came with USB-C ports since this has been the standard for the last few years.

These earbuds work great with my Google Pixel 2 phone. My phone has a USB-C jack, but no standard headphone jack. These earbuds plug right into the USB-C jack with no adapter needed. Sound quality is very good for the $25 price - much better bass than the OnePlus headphones that I bought for about the same price. Volume and stereo separation are great. I get some noticeable hiss at high volumes, but not much distortion. 3 sizes of soft rubber ear tips are included and I find them to better than most rubber ear tips, but not as comfortable as the foam eartips that some more expensive earbuds use. 5 stars because the sound quality is great for this price level.

This microphone includes a smartphone clip stand. It works fine with my Pixel 2 phone when I connect it to the USB-C dongle cable that was included with my phone. Audio quality is better than phone's built-in microphone, but not as good as the more expensive Shure, Sennheiser, or Audio-Technica microphones that I have used. For voice recording, this microphone is adequate, but for live music performances, I recommend something better. One big advantage of an external microphone is you can aim it at the sound source, instead of relying on whatever direction your phone's microphone is pointing when you aim the camera.

There are a lot of cheap off-brand lavalier microphones on Amazon that work adequately for voice recording, especially at close range. Very hard for me to tell if this one is significantly better than the $10 products.

This is a handy device for people who driver older cars that have audio AUX jacks but no Bluetooth audio and you have a newer phone that has no headphone jack. The device is easy to install: just plug it into your stereo's AUX port and USB power port. The USB power could come from a basic cigarette lighter charger. If your charge has 2 USB ports, it can charge both the device and your phone at the same time. The device pairs like any other Bluetooth device. Audio volume and quality is fine for most factory-quality stereo systems. Price on this device seems to be higher than similar products that are sold on Amazon, but I haven't tried any of the others and can't rate their quality.

I've been using Chromebook laptops and Android phones and tablets for years, but until I saw this product, I didn't know that Chrome tablets were a thing. This Chrome tablet appears to be targeted at the classroom environment, where the teacher wants all the kids running the same Chrome web apps at the same time. That is different from the typical Android environment, where there is little built-in support for synchronizing multiple tablets.

If you are using these tablets in a classroom, they work great. The screen is is brighter and sharper than the Amazon Fire tablets (which are admittedly much cheaper). The pop-out stylus works well and does not need a battery. This is a smart Wacom stylus that is much more accurate than a cheap rubber-tipped stylus or using your finger. Unlike most Android phones these days, this tablet supports micro-SD cards for expandable memory and it has a headphone jack. The tablet has stereo speakers, but they are on the sides, so aren't as loud or clear as tablet with front-facing speakers. The tablet is a little thicker than an iPad, but it is also sturdier with a rubberized shell for easier gripping and drop resistance. The tablet is lightweight for the 10 inch screen size at barely 1 pound. The camera is mediocre, but I am always carrying my phone with its much better camera, so I just use that.

Speed is really good, especially startup speed, which only takes a few seconds (much better than Android tablets). The Chrome operating system gets regular system updates for security patches and new features, unlike the Android operating system on most tablets that often gets obsolete quickly.

If you're using this tablet stand-alone (not in a classroom), it is still pretty good. The Chrome operating system runs both Chrome apps and Android apps, so it is a little more confusing than a pure Android operating system. The application launcher shows both types of apps and figuring out which is which is a hassle. Also, sharing data between Chrome apps and Android apps is a lot more complicated than sharing data between 2 different Android apps. A casual user should think hard about buying an Amazon Fire 10 inch tablet instead of one of these, mostly because the Amazon tablet offers much of the same functionality of this tablet for 1/3 the price. The Amazon tablet is much slower and doesn't have as nice a screen and doesn't have the pop-out stylus and doesn't have access to the full Google Play Android app store, so you do get what you pay for.

There is no manual in the box with this tablet. I suggest that you go to the Asus website and download the manual for this product. The manual tells you where all the buttons and ports are and how to use the stylus.

The tablet comes with a bulky high-power USB-C charger, but if you already use USB-C for your smartphone or laptop, that will probably work with this tablet as well (as long as it is not too wimpy).

4 stars because the $330 price seems high for what you get. If the price was close to $200 or even $250, I would have given it 5 stars.

This is a nice moderately-priced USB hub for devices with only USB-C ports. It gives you 4 full-sized USB ports plus one USB-C charging port so you can charge your device when the hub occupes your USB-C port. Metal and glass construction looks and feels more durable than the mostly plastic products on the market and the connectors all feel solid. Data transfer rates are fast enough and reliable. This hub does not have any audio/video ports like you get with some other hubs; it just gives you the USB ports that you will use most often. It installs plug-and-play on my laptop and my Android smartphone.

These headphones are advertised more for business use than for music. The business features do work great. There is a bluetooth adapter included in the package so you can use the headphones with PCs that don't have built-in bluetooth. You can connect the headphones to 2 different bluetooth sources simultaneously so you can have a Skype call on your laptop and connect to your smartphone at the same time. There is a nice pass-through mode that lets you listen to your surroundings (or not) by pushing a button on the Jabra app.

Speaking of the app, the included manual is very skimpy and really unnecessary. To use these headphones you should download the Jabra app to your phone or PC and use the app to pair and configure the headphones. Many of the features are only available through the app.

Sound quality of the headphone is great for business use, very solid with no connection problems. For music, this is not the best I have heard from "true wireless" headphones. Some music-focused "true wireless" headphones that I own have better clarity and detail. The Jabra app does have an equalizer feature, but the effect is more subtle than what I get from other headphones.

These headphones are very comfortable and very secure, actually surprisingly secure for headphones that don't have any wings or clips. 3 different size ear tips are included, though no memory foam tips like you get with some headphones in this price range.

Battery life is 5 hours per charge and you can recharge twice with the included carrying case. That's good for "true wireless" headphones.

I would give these headphones 5 stars if the sound quality was better. It does have good business features and those are the main focus of this product. Bluetooth connection is very solid and build quality is great. 4 stars.

Necklace-style earbuds seem to be going out of style these days. They are bulkier and heavier and generally less comfortable than the more compact earbuds, but they do have important advantages. The necklace lets them hold a much bigger battery than compact Bluetooth earbuds, especially compared to the "true wireless" style and thus the battery life is tremendously better (up to 15 hours with the noise cancelling turned off). Sound quality of these earbuds is good: generally loud and clear with a good frequency range. Noise cancelling seems weak to me, though I've never been a fan of noise cancellation on earbuds, since the earbuds block so much external noise already. My main complaint is that these earbuds are much more expensive than LG or Motorola necklace-style earbuds that I have found to have about the same sound quality.

These are good earbuds for people who like boomy bassy music. I hear much more bass on these than with any of my other earbuds(even some very expensive ones). Stereo separation is great and I hear a lot of midrange detail on both channels. The main negative is that these earbuds lack brightness at the higher frequencies, so they are not too good for acoustic music.

Comfort is average for sports-oriented headphones. I like the ear hooks, which are a bit of a hassle to get into, but then are very secure when I'm running or working out. The hooks are comfortable enough. They also give you the option of using ear-wings, which I'm not a fan of, but I suppose some people like. The ear pieces come in 4 different sizes instead of the 2 or 3 sizes that most other brands supply. Picking the right size is important for getting the best sound quality.

The earbuds are sweat and weather resistant, which is great for sports. 11 hour battery life is tremendous and these charge pretty quickly as well.

This is a very nice USB microphone. I think it gives me clearer sound quality than the very popular Blue Yeti microphone that costs about the same. The polar patterns are great if you are trying to block out the sound from noisy equipment or if you are trying to record multiple sound sources with one microphone, like 2 people or a singer and a musical instrument. USB installation is very easy plug-and-play. The bright red light was obnoxious at first, but I got used to it quickly.

While the bright colors and lights obviously target this microphone at online gamers, it also works very well for other recording projects like podcasting and recording personal music performances. It works less well for video recording since the bright colors and lights are very distracting on video.

These earbuds are pricey, but they are easily the best sounding earbuds that I have ever tried. I listen to mostly acoustic music where detail is more important than boomy bass. The bass on these earbuds is great for me without being boomy. The higher frequency detail is incredible. I can hear things with these that just don't come through with other brands of earbuds. The quiet sections of a song are very quiet through these earbuds, so the soft sections are even clearer. Stereo separation is excellent so I feel like I'm right there in the room with the musicians.

Volume is excellent. With other brands of wireless earbuds, I usually have to turn the volume all the way up and even then the music is often too quiet. WIth these B&O earbuds, I never have the volume at more than 2/3 power.

4 hour battery life is average for premium true-wireless earbuds and somewhat better than the cheaper models. The charging case is compact enough to fit in my pocket (unlike some other brands) and works flawlessly. I love that is uses USB-C, just like my smartphone. It also supports wireless charging, which I don't use with my phone either. USB-C is easier for me to understand.

As with all earbuds, picking the right ear tips is an important part of getting the best sound. I love that they included memory foam ear tips in the box. The memory foam tips are the most comfortable and best sounding tips for me. I can listen to these for hours without any discomfort.

There is an official B&O Android app that connects to the earbuds that has a few interesting features. It shows the earbud battery life, which is nice to have, especially if I don't remember when was the last time I charged them. There are some listening modes, that are somewhat customizable (but not like a traditional equalizer, which would be easier for me to understand). There is also a transparency feature that lets me hear background sound through the earbuds (useful when walking on the street or listening for an airport announcement). The earbuds do work fine without the app if you pair them with your phone using the normal Bluetooth setup.

These earbuds are not designed for sports. When I'm running or working out, I use my Jaybird earbuds that are more secure in my ears and are waterproof. The B&O earbuds are more comfortable and better sounding than my Jaybirds, so I use them more often.

I use this adapter when I'm using my Google Pixel 2 phone in my car. The phone has one USB-C port that is used for both charging and stereo audio output. The adapter plugs into the phone's USB-C port and gives me separate USB-C charging and stereo audio ports so I can simultaneously charge my phone and listen to audio from my car stereo's wired aux port. Audio quality is fine. My phone charges fine. There are a lot of similar adapters on Amazon and this one is cheaper than most (currently $15). Works fine, delivers useful functionality, and the price is right so 5 stars from me.

These are the best earbuds that I have found for running or workouts. I hate cords flopping around when I'm running, so the "true wireless" style of earbuds is worth the price to me. The buds come with a variety of ear tips and wings to customize my fit and after I found the best combination for me, they are very comfortable and secure in my ears. I've never had a problem with them falling out.

Sound quality is pretty good out-of-the-box (clear and loud), but a little thin at the higher frequencies (especially noticeable with acoustic music). Fortunately, Jaybird has a great smartphone app you can use to equalize the sound. I was never very good at designing my own equalization profiles by ear, but the app has several ready made profiles so I just picked the one that sounded best with my favorite music (boosting higher frequencies more than lower frequencies).

4 hour battery life is really good for "true wireless" earbuds. That's almost as good as the Apple earpods, but these sound way better than Apple and also get much louder (which is probably part of the reason for the lesser battery life). 4 hours is plenty of battery life for running or workouts. The portable charging case is handy when I'm traveling, but not something I use every day.

These earbuds are waterproof, which is great for rainy days or people who sweat a lot. If you don't need waterproof, the older Jaybird Run earbuds are still available for about 1/3 less money and those are very similar except that they are water resistant instead of waterproof.

I notice that several people give these earbuds terrible reviews because there is a noticeable lag in the audio stream when they are watching videos. This has never been a problem for me, since I only use these earbuds for running and I never watch videos when running. If watching videos is important to you, then I think wired headphones are a much better choice for you.

This USB-C keyboard is kind of pricey for a basic functionality keyboard, but it does work fine. No batteries are required. The USB-C cable plugs directly into the USB-C port on my Android tablet and draws power from there. Android has built-in keyboard support so the arrow keys and function keys work fine. There is no mouse pad on the keyboard, but touching the tablet isn't too much of a hassle. The keyboard is very responsive (better than a Bluetooth keyboard). Typing long sections of text is much easier with a real hardware keyboard than with a touchscreen keyboard.

I've used a few other true wireless headphones in the $50 price range (mostly unknown brands) as well as some more expensive brand name models (B&O, Plantronics). This set is better than most headphones in the under $50 price range. Sound is clear and noise free. Volume is loud enough for earbuds, but not booming at full volume. Bass is kind of weak, though that is a common problem in this price range. 3 hour battery life is about average for this price range. Comparing $50 headphones to $100 headphones is not really fair, but if you do want to spend more money, most headphones will give you much better bass and richer overall sound quality. More expensive headphones also give me better battery life (usually at least 4 hours without any recharging). On the other hand, if I'm out running or riding on the subway, I'd rather use these $50 headphones instead of risk losing much more expensive headphones.

I am impressed by the build quality of these Soundcore headphones. They headphones feel solid. They are comfortable in my ears. The case is sleek and the recharging system works well. The buttons that control the headphones work easily and reliably. I do wish they used a modern USB-C charging system instead of the old-fashioned micro-USB.

This tablet installed easily on my Windows 10 PC. The tablet plugs into a USB port, but you should download the driver from the company's website to configure it. Also download the user manual since only a quick-start guide is included in the box. The tablet works well for me. It gives me much finer cursor control than a regular mouse when I'm drawing in PhotoShop or Microsoft Office or other graphics programs, though unfortunately not fine enough for really clear handwriting. Feels durable enough for this price level. They include a bunch of spare pen tips since those do wear out with use. It runs off of USB power, so no batteries are required.

As expected, these Duracell batteries fit properly and work great. A lot of the no-name batteries have sketchy quality. CR2 batteries are used in a variety of small electronic devices, especially camera equipment.

These are very good Bluetooth earbuds for sports use. Construction is very lightweight, but still very durable. Earpieces are very secure when I'm running or working out at the gym and more than comfortable enough for hour-long workouts. Sound quality is pretty good out-of-the-box, but a little thin at the higher frequencies (especially noticeable with acoustic music). Fortunately, Jaybird has a great smartphone app you can use to equalize the sound. I was never very good at designing my own equalization profiles by ear, but the app has several ready made profiles so I just picked the one that sounded best with my favorite music (boosting higher frequencies more than lower frequencies). There is no noise cancellation, but noise isolation is very good with the included foam eartips (not the default eartips).

I really do not like that you need a special dongle to recharge this headset. You can't just plug a standard USB cable directly into these, like with most Bluetooth headset. This may have something to do with the headset's waterproof rating, but other headsets I own are also waterproof and can still be recharged with a standard cable. I am concerned that the proprietary charging dongle will get lost or broken or I will just forget to bring it with me when traveling.

These are nice sturdy cables. Thick braided casing minimizes wear-and-tear and doesn't kink or tangle. Connectors fit securely in my devices and are stress-relieved. Having USB-C on one end and USB-A on the other end is great for transferring data between older and newer devices. Data speeds are very good. I cannot use this cable for charging since my USB Power Delivery chargers all require USB-C to USB-C cables.

Is your computer a little older and getting a little sluggish? There are 3 relatively easy and inexpensive ways to make it perform as good or better than new. First is to add more memory, though older 32-bit computers may be limited in how much memory you can add. Second do some housecleaning by removing unused software and reinstalling the operating system. Third is to install a solid-state drive like this one. It installs just like an old-fashioned hard drive, but runs tremendously faster. Install your operating system and frequently used files on here and your computer will feel like better than new, especially when starting up and when launching large application programs. This drive has been very reliable for me so far. In the long run, I expect it to be more reliable than a traditional hard drive (which is often the most fragile part of a computer).

I'm not a gamer, but I do type a lot and appreciate a responsive keyboard. This keyboard is much better than my old AmazonBasics mechanical-like keyboard. They keys respond more quickly and smoothly with this keyboard, so I feel faster and more accurate. There are a bunch of lighting modes that may interest the gamers, but those are easy to turn off for people who want to use this keyboard for business. You can also easily program in macro sequences for your favorite games. Price is reasonable for a nice mechanical keyboard. Plug-and-play installation on my Microsoft Windows 10 desktop PC. I just plugged it in to a USB port and it installed automatically with no special drivers to load.

These are great Bluetooth earbuds for sports use. Construction is very lightweight, but still very durable. Earpieces are very secure when I'm running or working out at the gym and more than comfortable enough for hour-long workouts. Sound quality is pretty good out-of-the-box, but a little thin at the higher frequencies (especially noticeable with acoustic music). Fortunately, Jaybird has a great smartphone app you can use to equalize the sound. I was never very good at designing my own equalization profiles by ear, but the app has several ready made profiles so I just picked the one that sounded best with my favorite music (boosting higher frequencies more than lower frequencies). There is no noise cancellation, but noise isolation is very good with the foam eartips.

I really don't like that you need a special dongle to recharge this headset. You can't just plug a standard USB cable directly into the thing. This may have something to do with the headset's waterproof rating, but other headsets I own are also waterproof and can still be recharged with a standard cable. I am concerned that the proprietary charging dongle will get lost or broken or I will just forget to bring it with me when traveling.

If you want a 10" tablet for reading books and watching videos/TV shows/movies and can't afford more money than this (price regularly drops to $100), then this is good product choice. Performance is fine for e-books and videos, but sometimes sluggish for intense game playing, photo/video editing or even text editing. The SD card slot lets you store lots of TV shows and movies and use the main memory for apps (which often work poorly if stored on the SD card). Kindle e-books sometimes work much better on the Fire tablets than on ipads or Android tablets, especially if the books have embedded audio or video. The user interface revolves around the books and videos that you bought from Amazon. With a considerable amount of work, you may be able to replace the user interface with a more standard Android launcher that focuses on your apps and files. Realistically, the performance of this tablet clunky enough that I don't recommend it unless you are mostly using it for e-books and videos, so maybe changing the user interface is not worth the effort.

You should also ask yourself if you are using the tablet for mostly e-books and videos, do you really need a 10 inch screen? The 8 inch Kindle Fire tablet has similar performance and a much lower price and is also lighter weight and less bulky, making it easier to use in many situations.

These are easily the best sounding Bluetooth earbuds that I have ever tried. Bass sounds natural without being artificially boosted like in some earbuds. Excellent clarity in the mid and upper frequencies. Acousting music and vocals sound really great. Overall volume can be louder than I ever want. 8 hour playing time puts those Apple earbuds to shame. A couple of minor complaints: I don't like devices that still use the outdated micro-USB connectors, especially now that USB-C is becoming widespread. At least they do include a cable. Also, the buttons are a little confusing with the big central button controlling on/off, play/pause, and phone answer/call/redial. I don't make many phone calls through my earbuds, but if you do, the controls may be a problem for you.

Chromebook prices range from around $100 to over $1000. Better Chromebooks have Intel Core CPUs for great performance. The much cheaper Mediatek system in this Chromebook gives it mediocre performance, especially for intensive games or for business users who open lots of tabs simultaneously and frequently switch between them. On the plus side this Chromebook has a useful 4GB of RAM, a sharp colorful IPS screen, a touch screen that works great with Android apps, a very responsive (for swiping) touchpad, and reliable WiFi (much better than my HP laptop). On the minus side, the white plastic shell looks and feels a little cheap, the screen is not very bright, and the touchpad's button feels a little clunky. In summary, if you can't afford more than $300, this is a good choice for casual users who only have a few tabs open at once and use it mostly for email, Facebook, web surfing, and streaming music or videos. If you can afford $350 to $400, you will have several choices with more powerful CPUs for more intensive users.

If you're an iphone user, you're probably wondering whether to buy these Pioneer wireless headphones or the Apple version. The Pioneer price is about 1/3 cheaper than Apple. The Pioneer earbuds fit in your ear, so you get much better sound and much better sound isolation. These are nowhere near as detailed or loud as similarly priced wired headphones, but that's true of all wireless Bluetooth earbuds. I will say the connection is stable and not noisy, so these are better than most cheap Bluetooth earbuds. There is some bass, but don't work well for bass-heavy music. Maximum volume is just OK. Battery life is only about 3 hours per charge (compared to 5 hours for Apple), then you have to put the earbuds back in the case for a 1 hour charge. 3 hours may be enough for you; you have to decide, but 5 hours is certainly going to be more interesting to most people. The charging case is much larger than the Apple charging case. The case is 3.3 inches long and 2.2 inches wide. These case is to big to fit comfortably in my pants pocket, so I would only carry it with me in a backpack or purse.

Usage is pretty simple. They paired easily with my phone as a normal Bluetooth device. The buttons on the headphones are easy to use. They are comfortable in my ears. They are secure enough so far, never feeling like they are going to fall out. They are not noticeably heavy like some earbuds can be. When in my ears, they are much less ugly than the Apple earbuds.

I would give these 5 stars for the price and performance if the sound and battery life were better. Frankly, I've tried a few different totally wireless earbuds and been less than impressed by all of them. Bluetooth headphones that have a wire connecting the two pieces can be had for much lower prices and have much better sound quality and much better battery life. Removing the wire just doesn't seem worth the downsides to me.

The Apple Watch is slowly gaining functionality and popularity, but it does not work with non-Apple smartphones. If you have an Android phone, your choices are Google Wear OS watches like this one, Samsung Tizen watches, and smart fitness watches like Garmin and Fitbit.

Samsung watches work best with Samsung phones since both devices require you to buy into the Samsung ecosystem, which has diverged quite a bit from the Google Android ecosystem. For example, you have to run Tizen apps on the Samsung watch and you have to use the Bixby assistant instead of the Google Assistant. Those requirements are going to be too much for many people using Android phones other than Samsung.

Garmin and Fitbit make some pretty good sports or activity tracking watches that also have some smartwatch features, like playing music or displaying notifications so you don't have to pull the phone out of your pocket everytime it beeps. Garmin and Fitbit also have much better battery life than any of the Apple, Google, or Samsung watches. The GPS and activity tracking features on Garmin watches are noticeably more accurate than the general purpose smartwatches. Garmin and Fitbit watches are more sporty than stylish, but some of the recent models try harder to be at least presentable in a casual workplace. These are definitely a good choice for some types of users, especially very athletic people.

Google does not make its own watches (yet); they release the watch software and allow companies like Skagen to use it in watches like this one. Google Wear OS phones mostly work the same, though they may have different hardware capabilities. This Skagen watch has GPS and heart rate monitor hardware, while others may not. The Skagen watch is definitely the best looking Google Wear OS watch that I have seen so far, perhaps the most stylish of all the most recent smartwatches that I have seen (better looking than the Apple watch as well). From the front, it looks like a regular Skagen watch, though from the side it is much thicker; maybe twice as thick as a regular Skagen watch, since this brand is usually known for very thin watches. The 40mm case size is about the same as a medium-sized men's regular watch or a large women's watch (many smartwatches are huge and out-of-place on medium-sized wrists). In my testing, the Google Wear OS features all work great on the watch. It synchronizes and interacts easily with the phone. Activity/fitness tracking is fine for casual use, but not accurate enough for serious athletes who want detailed measurements of their performance.

Battery life is the shortfall of most of these smartwatches. I get less than a full day of battery life if I do any GPS sports tracking and use the always-on-display, but I will get a full day if I only do one of those. Then I have to charge it every night (and cannot use it for sleep tracking). I've heard that Samsung and Apple get slightly better battery life. Garmin gets several days of battery life, so that is the way to go if you don't want to keep worrying about battery.

In summary, there is no single best smartwatch on the market right now. If you're looking for the most Google experience, this is probably the most stylish choice right now. A new smartwatch CPU that supposedly has better battery life was recently announced, but I don't expect any products to use that until mid-2019 at the earliest, if you want to wait until then.

There are a whole bunch of "brands" selling USB CD drivers that look exactly like this one. $16 price for this one is a little cheaper than many of the others. Basic functionality, but it works fine so far. Runs quietly enough once it warms up. Powered by the USB cable so no separate power supply is needed. USB cable slides out of the bottom of the case, so no separate cable is needed. No problems using it with any of my PCs or laptops with full-sized USB ports. No carrying case, so hopefully the metal body construction will be durable enough inside my computer bag.

Google should include one of these with their Pixel phones that no longer have 3.5mm headphone jacks. Works perfectly to fast charge my phone while playing music through the 3.5mm headphone jack. My car has a 3.5mm stereo input but no Bluetooth stereo, so this is perfect for long road trips. Metal construction seems durable, which is great for car use. Sound quality is fine. Fast charging works fine, too.

This microphone has a lot of options, so figuring out what modes worked best (or at all) with my smartphone took a while. I have a Google Pixel 2 Android smartphone, which is not well documented in the product literature. If you have an iPhone, you may find that setup is somewhat easier.

Here are the basic steps that I had to take to get this working with my Google Pixel 2 phone:
1. Charge the receiver unit using the included mini-USB cable (not the micro-USB cable). I am disappointed that they are still using mini-USB which is obsolete these days. Why aren't they using USB-C for charging, which is the international standard these days?
2. The receiver unit has built-in clamps to attach to a smartphone. You can also mount it to SLR camera's flash shoe or a tripod.
3. Install 2 AA batteries in the microphone.
4. Turn both the microphone and receiver unit on.
5. The microphone is pre-paired with the receiver. If you want to pair a second microphone (not included), you can do that at this point.
6. Use the screwdriver inside the microphone to set the gain level (so that the light on the receiver unit doesn't flash red for the highest volumes that you plan to use with the microphone). I set mine to about 75% of maximum.
7. Connect the receiver unit to the phone using the included micro-USB to USB-C cable (my phone has a USB-C port, but no 1/8 inch audio port).
8. The default Google Pixel camera app unfortunately does not support external microphones. I installed the "Open Camera" app which has a setting to use an external microphone. This is a very popular and powerful 3rd party apps. I'm sure there are others that will also work.
9. Start the camera and now you have a video camera with a wireless microphone. Range and sound quality are pretty good as long as I stay in the same room (and you generally will want the microphone and camera to be in the same room when recording).
10. I set the output volume in the Samson receiver unit to 4/5 since higher volumes were distorting. You have to experiment with this for the types of sounds you are recording.
11. Unfortunately, I could not find an audio-only recorder app that supported the USB-C digital signal coming from the Samson receiver unit. I can use the analog audio signal with the 1/8 inch audio cable connected to the Google Pixel audio dongle that came with the phone. I presume this is a problem with the audio recorder apps, not with Samson hardware.

I've only played the audio and video back on my phone and it sounds fine. If you're recording professional-quality music videos, you may want something better than this.

I'm generally pleased with this microphone. Some negatives: the microphone is big and heavy and the mostly plastic construction looks and feels a lot cheaper than it costs. The product has lots of different parts and no carrying case to store them in, except for the original and not durable retail package. I could not find any way to determine the remaining battery level of either the microphone of the receiver unit, so your batteries could easily die in the middle of a recording session. Replacing the microphone batteries is easy since they are AA, but charging the receiver unit is very slow. I have not compared the audio quality of the large microphone with the lavalier microphone, but the latter is a lot smaller and less bulky and may be a better choice for people recording voices and not music.

This speaker is designed for use in the shower. It has a rubberized splash-proof shell with a hang cord so you can hang it over the shower head. Large buttons make it easy to use when wet. For this purpose, sound quality is fine. You get good volume (for this size of speaker) if you are right in front of it. Not the most detailed sound, especially at the low end, but certainly fine for shower use. Sound quality decreases quite a bit if you are listening from an angle, however.

Ever since Apple started making iphones without headphone jacks, a lot of cheap lightweight mediocre bluetooth headphones have appeared on the market. I've tried a bunch, but have not yet found a set for under $20 with acceptable sound quality.

This one is lightweight and moderately priced and does have decent sound quality for the price. Maximum volume isn't super loud, but it is loud enough for me and distortion is tolerable. At moderate volumes, there is decent detail and decent base. There is no annoying his in the quiet sections of my music like some cheap headphones have. These headphones are lightweight and comfortable. The wraparound headphone style is very secure when I'm running and not too hard to put on or take off. 7 hours of battery life as very good for headphones that are so light. They paired easily with my Android smartphone and my phone shows the headphone battery power level on the home screen so I can easily remember when to recharge them.

These earbuds are cheap ($10) and look and feel like toys. Very lightweight all plastic exterior. I wasn't expecting much, but the sound is very good for this price level. At the moderate volumes that I like to use, the music does not sound distorted or tinny. Not as much detail as from a bigger heavier headphone, but this is fine for listening to MP3s on my cellphone when I'm jogging. The lightweight construction means it doesn't fall out of my ears as often as heavier earbuds. I have tried some of the other cheap bluetooth headphones from Amazon, and this is the best that I have used for under $10. It even uses one of the newer Bluetooth standards that shows headphone power level on my phone screen; as someone who is always worried about rechargeable devices running out of power, this is a really great feature. Unfortunately, battery life is somewhat less than the advertised 5 hours. Even at moderate volumes, I'm down to about 50% battery after an hour and a half. That's fine for a gym workout or a subway commute, but not for airline travel.

It comes packaged in a self-destructing pile of paper and plastic. I wish they had included a carrying case instead of all this garbage.

I use this cable with my Google Pixel 2 phone. So far, it works as well for me as the USB-C to 3.5 audio adapter that Google sells. The Google adapter is cheaper, but this one has a longer cable with a male 3.5 plug, which is handy for plugging in to my car's aux audio port.

Works fine to connect my Google Pixel 2 phone to my car stereo's audio aux jack. When I bought it, this was cheaper than the official Google adapter. Now the price has gone up and it is more expensive, so I wouldn't buy another one unless I really wanted the longer cable with male jack at the end.

Bought this tablet because it was the cheapest name-brand 10 inch Android tablet available on Amazon ($130 when I bought it). I use it to store and read sheet music and take notes in my music class. The class has hundreds of sheets of music, so this tablet is much more convenient than carrying that much paper. I mount the tablet on a floor stand a few feet away so I can play my instrument while viewing the music and the 10" screen size is great for reading at that distance. The tablet is faster and more responsive than I was expecting for this price, perhaps because of the 2GB RAM size (many cheap tablets have only 1GB of RAM). I use the 16GB of storage space for the operating system and apps. All my sheet music (several GB worth) goes on the SD card. Screen brightness and contrast isn't terrible, which can be a problem at this price level. This setup works great for me and it costs 1/3 of an ipad, so 5 stars from me.

After deleting most of the ASUS spam-ware apps, the UI for this tablet is clean and easy to use. Much less cumbersome than often frustrating UI on the Amazon Fire tablet.

We also have a 7 inch Kindle Fire (from 2015). This 8 inch Kindle (from 2017) is way better. It runs much faster and smoother and the screen is brighter and sharper. 1 inch size difference makes a big difference. This is a real bargain for $50. Added a $10 memory card to hold my media and this is all the tablet I need.

A couple of notes. 1) it is possible to install the Google Play app store on this tablet, but the user interface is very clunky. Many of the Google Play apps work much better than what comes with the Amazon appstore, though. 2) you can install some apps to your SD card instead of main memory, but they then load more slowly. I prefer keeping all my apps in memory and just storing data files (like audio and video) on the SD card.

Yes, all the Amazon ad-ware is obnoxious. It is spread over all the screens, not just the lockscreen. I am thinking about installing a 3rd-party Android launcher to remove most of it and give me a sleeker user interface.

Also, the speaker is really terrible. Very weak volume and poor sound quality; much worse than the sound quality of my Samsung phone. Plan on buying an external speaker or headphones for music or even for conference calls.

3.5 stars for user experience + 1.5 stars for cheap price = 5 stars

Like all dedicated gaming laptops, this is a big heavy high-powered machine. It is portable enough to lug over to your buddy's house for play dates, but it is too bulky and heavy to carry to work everyday. Construction is very good with an aggressive-looking aluminum case to match the aggressive-sounding "Legion" product name. Mechanical keyboard has decent (but not the best) travel and the large keys are backlit so you can easily play your games in the dark. Dolby Atmos audio works well for games, but is kind of thin for music or movies unless you hook it up to external speakers. This Y720 version has a 1080p IPS display, which is OK but not as bright or contrasty as some other laptops I have used. There is also a more expensive 4K display available, but I have not tried that.

Core i7 CPU with 16GB of RAm gives you really great performance. This machine is easily powerful enough for any games I tried on it. Even though performance is throttled somewhat when run off the battery, battery life is still less than 2 hours under heavy use (maybe 6 hours with light use).

For the money, it is hard to go wrong with these Lenovo Legions. If you don't want to spend more than $1000, the cheaper Legion Y520 is almost as good for most types of games and costs $300 less.

Very good headphones. Smallish ear pieces and the black plastic shell is not real attractive, but they feel solid and well made. Rubber ear tips are comfortable for long periods of time and 3 different sizes of replacement tips are included. Bass is very good and overall sound clarity is much better than with cheap headphones. Full volume is more than loud enough for me and distortion at the highest volume is tolerable (unlike with cheap headphones). Wrap-around cables can be a hassle, but these have thicker wires and don't tangle as much as others that I have tried. Wrap-around cables really prevent the earbuds from falling out when I am working out. A simple nylon bag is the only carrying case included in the oversized box, but better cases are available at dollar stores.

Yes, Apple is trying to kill off wired headphones, but wired headphones still have huge advantages over Bluetooth, such as not having to worry about battery life, being able to recharge your phone at the same time you are listening to music, and of course the sound quality of wired headphones is usually better than similarly priced Bluetooth headphones.

This is a big heavy Bluetooth speaker, easily the biggest one that I own. It is 13 inches wide and 6.5 pounds heavy (according to my scale). The photo shows the size of the NYNE speaker compared to second biggest Bluetooth speaker that I own, a Sony SRS-XB30 which is 9 inches long and 2 pounds. The Sony costs about the same as the NYNE speaker.

Comparing these 2 speakers, the NYNE is much louder at the maximum usable volume (before the distortion becomes annoying). The Sony, however, gives me better clarity and the Sony does have a usable bass booster feature for those times when you want some thump-thump with your music. The NYNE speaker can fill a good sized room with music at a good volume. The Sony isn't loud enough to do that, although Sony lets you sync multiple speakers to spread the music over a larger area (at extra cost for each speaker, of course). NYNE has no multi-speaker Bluetooth capability.

The NYNE is bulky enough that I'm not going to carry it with me for day-to-day use (even with the built-in carry handle). However, it is great for times when you need more volume, like an outdoor party or picnic with a good sized group. Both the Sony and NYNE speakers have rubberized exteriors and water resistance to protect them from abuse, which you're going to get from outdoor use and carry in your car. Neither speaker comes with a carrying case to keep them clean (unfortunately).

Yes, the huge NYNE multi-language instruction sheet is a hassle, but it really does not say much. If you've used any kind of Bluetooth device in the past, the only thing you need the instructions for is how to use the on/off switch and how to charge it. There are no special features like an equalizer or bass booster or multi-speaker Bluetooth syncing that you find in some other speakers.

Both the NYNE and my Sony use non-standard chargers instead of the USB cables you that your phone uses. I hate having to keep track of all these chargers. The batteries in these speakers are not tremendously bigger than what an ipad uses so I don't know why that can't use a more standard charger.

5 stars because the price is reasonable for the usable volume of this speaker. If you don't plan on using the speaker at maximum volume, however, I think a smaller speaker will be much more practical for you.

This is my second Sony action camera. The first one was the AS100, which was Sony's top-of-the line HD camera from a couple of years ago. This new camera has 4K video as well as "BOSS" optical image stabilization (the old one had only digital stabilization). The AS100 had good video quality for its time, but this X3000 model is tremendously better. The video is sharper, more detailed, has better dynamic range, and has less distortion (especially around the edges of the image). While the AS100 is great in bright conditions, the video quickly got muddy in low light (including cloudy days). The X3000 is also much better in lower light condition.

Battery life is mediocre in 4K mode (maybe 1 hour total). I use regular HD mode for longer videos (about 2 hours of battery life). I like that the battery door on this camera is on the side, so replacing batteries is pretty easy when your camera is mounted without the case.

I use these cameras mostly for road bicycling, which can get bumpy, especially on fast downhills on rough roads. Mountain biking and other sports can get even rougher, but I haven't tested that. The digital image stabilization in my old Sony AS100 was good at smoothing out bouncy video, but it did reduce video sharpness. The optical image stabilization in the X3000 is much better. Hard to say how much of the improved quality is from the 4K sensor and how much is from the better image stabilization, but the combination is outstanding.

There are several important ergonomic differences between the 2 cameras. Out of the box, the X3000 is noticeably heavier, especially since the camera is shipped inside the waterproof case. The camera weighs 4 ounces alone and the case adds 3 more ounces for 7 ounces total. In comparison, the AS100 was 3 ounces for the camera + 2 ounce for the case = 5 ounces total. The X3000 case is rated for 60 meters and the AS100 case is rated for only 5 meters, so this isn't really a fair comparison, but these are the only cases I have to measure right now.

As shown in the photos, the X3000 is slightly wider than the AS100 without the cases, but significantly larger with the cases. The cases also affect your sound quality and can lead to overheating in hot weather, so honestly, I do not use them on my bicycle. The case also makes changing your battery a bigger hassle. I have ordered the lens protector for the X3000, but don't have it yet. The X3000 lens protector is bulkier than the AS100 protector, which is shown in the photo.

I like that the X3000 now has 5 control buttons instead of just 3 on the AS100. Trying to navigate the AS100 menu system with just 3 buttons was so cumbersome in the field that I would always just pick my modes at home before going out, then just on/off in the field. The X3000 menu system is much different and takes some studying to master, but at least it is usable when you're outdoors and your buddies are waiting for you to get going.

The X3000 has louder beeps and brighter lights to tell you when you started recording. This was sometimes a problem with the AS100 since it had no indicator light on the top of the camera and the "on" button was a little finicky. The X3000 now has indicator lights on the back, top, and front so you can see it from different angles. The "on" button for the X3000 is also much easier to press.

Sony makes a bicycle handlebar mount for their action cameras, but it is bulky and plastic and not the most stable. I much prefer the K-Edge aluminum mount (shown in the photo) which is sleeker and stiffer and also mounts the camera below the top of the handlebar so the camera doesn't get in the way of my bicycle computer.

While I like the video and image quality of Sony cameras much better than GoPro (no optical image stabilization on GoPro), GoPro does have a couple of advantages over Sony. Most importantly (to me), GoPro can be mounted upside down so you can mount it underneath your bicycle computer (if you have a two-sided handlebar mount) to give you a less cluttered handlebar or give you more space for other accessories like lights. Also, there are a lot more accessories available for GoPro. Adapters for Sony are available, but some of these mounts just work better with GoPro because of the shape of the GoPro (eg the chest mount).

One last comment: Sony's remote viewer and finger camera mount is included in this package. I think this is real cute, but I'm not sure how much I will use it in real life. The remote viewer is really sluggish to use compared to a point-and-shoot camera. I used it to aim my camera when setting up my bicycle mount, but not much else. Changing camera modes is easy enough by pushing the menu buttons on the camera. Maybe the viewer will be useful if you want to record water sports (or in rainy conditions) and you don't have a waterproof point-and-shoot camera.

This is an excellent mid-priced medium-sized Bluetooth speaker. The speaker measures 9x3x3 inches and weighs 8 ounces (half a pound). Despite the moderate size, it does fill a medium sized room with great quality music. At medium volumes, the sound is very rich and well balanced. Sound starts to get a little tinny near maximum volume, but the distortion is tolerable, not painful like with cheap speakers. For the price, I think the sound is great. Volume is excellent for a speaker of this size. Sound quality is also excellent; probably the best I've heard for a speaker of this size. I do have some larger, more expensive speakers that sound better at high volumes, but I am very happy with this one for the size and price.

The "extra bass" button on the top of the speaker gives you a pronounced reverb effect which is fun for dance music, but maybe not something I want to use all the time.

This is the first bluetooth speaker that I have owned with built-in party lights on the front of the speaker. That's a cute feature if you're a group of lights at a party. I don't think the lights are synchronized with your music, however, which would be a more fun feature.

The speaker pairs easily with my Android phone (don't have an iphone to try). You can pair it directly with the Android bluetooth control or use the optional Sony SongPal app. The app gives you more features like syncing multiple speakers, a basic equalizer, control of the party lights on the front of the speaker, and a power-down timeout. Syncing multiple speakers would be great for increasing the volume and range of your music at an outdoor party. Some photos of the app are attached. The Sony SongPal Android app is a fairly large 44MB, but you don't need it for basic speaker use.
