This is not an expensive headset, so I didn't expect it to be wonderful. It works fine, after a year of fairly frequent use at my desktop computer. However, recently I have switched to using earbuds not just with my iPhone and MP3 player, but with my desktop and laptop, too. Earbuds are a lot smaller, more portable, and comfortable than a regular headset.

I have owned this shredder for over six years, and it has endured some heavy use. It is the second home-shredder I've owned, and it is much the better of the two. It is heavy enough that it doesn't tip over, but not so heavy it can't be hauled from room to room by someone moderately strong. The front compartment holding the shredded paper is easily removed--in an identical fashion to our dehumidifier's bucket. You pull on it and the bucket comes out with a forward motion. The sound the shredder makes when in action is loud, as one would expect, but not so loud that you need protective ear plugs, such as for when you are near a kitchen blender, blow dryer, leaf blower or lawn mower.

The main thing to be careful about is to not get impatient and overload the shredder blades. Yes, you can use the backup function to try and back out paper you have overloaded it with, but it is a pain. Secondly, be sure and feed paper in straight. If you feed it in crooked, that, too, is a prescription for a jam.

When I am shredding, I lay down either a bed sheet or a tarp and set the shredder in the middle of it. This helps me corral the scraps of shredded paper flying around when I empty the bucket into a trash bag. Another option is to shred in your garage or basement, if you have such spaces, and use a [[ASIN:B00005AXI1 Shop-Vac]] to clean up afterwards. If you do it inside your house, plan on having to use a regular vacuum to clean up after each use, because a mess is almost unavoidable no matter how careful you are since this shredder is turning private papers into confetti. That's great for the shredder's intended purpose, but it does have a tendency to give whatever room you are using a strong resemblance to Times Square on New Year's Eve.

When my husband recently purchased a [[ASIN:B0071N6AC6 netbook]], he wasn't using his Kindle Fire nearly as much, and I inherited it. I had recently dumped my cable TV service in favor of using the Fire to watch online the few news and TV dramas that I normally had used my TiVo to record. I found that my Internet connection through a wifi router has a really hard time playing videos via the Fire. It would often lose connectivity or freeze up when my iPhone was working fine using the same connection, playing the same shows.

The Fire has a gorgeous interface, though, for reading eBooks compared to my Kindle Keyboard. However, I've been using a Kindle app so frequently the past few months on my iPhone, that both the Kindle Keyboard and the Kindle Fire feel too cumbersome to bother with most of the time in comparison as an eReader.

For searching the Internet, the Fire has an easier interface than the iPhone, so I use it more often for that, unless I don't have it with me--I always have my iPhone with me.

I don't use the Fire for MP3. It is just too huge compared to my tiny MP3 player.

I don't have magazine subscriptions in electronic form, so I don't use it for that, though I know I could if I wanted to.

I understand the Fire can support PDF, but I haven't used it for that yet.

I have a pink MP3 player, and these go very well with it. They are a lovely, bright shade of pink. They fit very comfortably in my ears and work well for extended use during the day or sleeping at night.

The sound quality is excellent, both for music on my MP3 and watching movies and TV shows on my laptop.

I would definitely buy these again.

This adapter did it's job just fine to set up my [[ASIN:B005INJ4ZG My Zone Wireless Headphones]] to work with our TiVo. Unfortunately, the My Zone equipment itself is faulty, with too much static. I do not blame that on this adapter.

This handy device fits perfectly into my car's cassette deck and plugs easily into my [[ASIN:B000XQRAI6 MP3 player]]. An adapter like this allows me to use the speakers of my car to listen to music and audio books I've loaded onto my MP3.

This cassette-shaped adapter slides into my car's cassette player smoothly and easily. There is no sound distortion when I use it.

I owned an adapter similar to this one for years. It recently wore out from constant usage, which manifested as the adapter making a grinding noise and then popping itself out of the cassette player.

Since this is an inexpensive adapter, I am not expecting it to last indefinitely because it will get a lot of use. Currently, after a month of regular use it is working as well as the day I got it.

I would definitely buy this product again. It is a great value for the money. In fact, I am contemplating buying a spare right now to have readily on hand at the time this one eventually, inevitably, wears out.

My spouse uses a CPap and he makes the weirdest noises throughout the night! It makes it very difficult for me to get to sleep and stay asleep (I know - I sound terrible!). With this I can listen to white noise or something similar and never hear a peep from the CPap next to me. I still hear my alarm the next morning and there’s no discomfort as nothing is inserted into my ear canal. The speaker portion is padded enough to prevent my ear from becoming sore during wearing and my spouse never hears what I’m listening to. It’s a win-win.

Good high quality cable. I'm not going to claim that it makes the sound any better, but I do like my well build cables.

I knocked off one star since the installation was so hard. Seriously, the retaining clips don't have to be that tight guys.

Make sure to be very gentle when installing them, twisting back and forth while applying pressure to push them on.

If you just go and blindly smush them on as hard as you can there is a good chance that you will rip the RCA jack off the PCB that it is mounted to.

I bought this specific PCIe to USB adapter because I saw it doesn't need additional power from a sata power / molex power cable.

I used this to go to my Fiio E10k and it works great. My motherboard's USB ports were loud and had a lot of electrical interference.
When I plugged my DAC into this I was amazed at how quite it was.

I also used it to plug in my microphone's interface.

It is very small and compact as well.

I bought this in an "emergency" situation, where I needed a capable laptop quick so i could work remotely. it hits nearly every checkbox. The CPU is plenty powerful for my web dev/app dev work, and the mx150 is plenty powerful to play multiplayer games like league of legends, csgo, dota underlords, and gwent without any hassle.

The only thing I did to my device is I installed an application called "throttlestop" and undervolted the cpu. Once I did this my temps while gaming dropped from the mid 80's (already reasonable while gaming on a laptop) to the low 70's. Because of this my fan spins up less, and when it does its quiet, and it stays cool.

The only downsides to this device are the battery life could be longer (im getting like... 5-6 working hours), the laptop has no LTE option (very few laptops do, and ZERO with GPUs do), the right shift key is small and annoying. (biggest downside, very often hit up instead of shift because of this)

overall though, very good. I bought mine "used - very good" on amazon and it is like new and $400ish cheaper.

Deffo built for a 17" device, but for my 15" laptop it isnt too big. I wouldnt buy it for a 13" though. I bought it for my dell xps 9560 - it doesnt have heat issues, but it gets hot under load and im migrating it towards my main workstation so i want it to run cooler consistantly. dropped my load temps from 85c to 70c on low fan setting. high fan setting doesnt seem to make a significant difference and there is a small whine associated with it.

Both the low and high fans are audible, but the low fans are much quieter than my laptops fan under load.

The riser mechanism seems honestly pretty weak and flimsy, for me thats fine since i am going to use it with other monitors, but if you like to have your laptop elevated I dont think it would last long, particularly for a heavier laptop.

if you need a laptop cooler on the go, i wouldnt get this, it is probably thicker than your laptop.

additionally, I thought there was an extra USB port with it, there is not.

The Echo Dot has been a game changer for my household. My kid used to hog my phone to play her music, and then complain when it wasn’t loud enough to hear in the shower. Enter the Echo Dot. The voice recognition is fantastic. It plays music from Amazon Music as well as online radio stations. What’s worked great for us is combining it with Amazon Music Unlimited. I let the kid create her own playlist, and when she wants to blast music while she’s in the shower (which, by the way, it gets PLENTY loud), she just tells it to play her playlist and I’m free of my DJ duties. It’s also come in really handy when we can’t get to a clock to check the time, to set timers, and to check the score of the football game. This was a superb purchase!
Sound was very impressive. Easy to carry and transport. I just received it yesterday but seems to be very good with battery usage. Overall I am impressed with this product.

Tablet would constantly not recognize any sd card and would need to be rebooted to be able to see the card again. This happens frequently and was annoying to not be able to use the SD card as that is a main feature for a tablet. Contacted support to exchange with another unit and they monitored the tablet and said they found nothing wrong with it. Sending the tablet back for a refund instead and will find another tablet that works properly and has good support.

I'm leaving the original part up to show the process I has to go through to get a replacement unit. Since we have received the replacement it has worked perfectly and are very happy with the unit. The initial hoops we had to jump through were painful but eventually they were able to stand behind the product.

Overall this keyboard is great. The keys feel nice and they're quiet but not too quiet or soft or squishy. Enjoy typing on this keyboard, pushing the keys seems to take minimal effort and overall it's great.

The best part about the keyboard is that it separates and having the ability to give it a little separation is great. I miss it when I don't have it and it helps avoid torquing the wrists when you are typing. I also love the feel of the keys.

Now before my minor complaints understand two things: (1) I really like this keyboard and despite what I would consider minor defects, I would definitely buy another one. (2) please excuse the fact that I like my keyboards to be consistent and while Apple may not make the *best* keyboards I do use a laptop and I am used to their keyboard layout and feel.

The biggest thing that annoyed me when I purchased this keyboard was the positioning of the ⌘ (command) key. It seems to be shifted over a bit from what I'm used to. Normally I would hit ⌘ with my thumb but it's a little touch to do that on this one given the position of it. It's just something I'm having to get used to.

One minor downside to the keyboard is that the function key doesn't work the same way as the default apple keyboard, rather, the `fn` key is a toggle. I prefer for fn to work as a modifier because that is what I am used to on my laptop keyboard.

Another minor problem is the styling on the caps lock key. Like many people, I remap my caps lock to ctrl and and thus want caps lock to be a normal button. However, on this keyboard the caps lock key is missing the right part of the key so that you don't accidentally hit it when typing the `a` key.

Finally, the escape key and '`' (back tick) keys are in weird positions. The escape key is not as bad as the backtick. There is just something about the distance that I must go that is different from what I'm used to and I have been consistently hitting the `1` key instead. Life goes on.
Took a while to get...kinda forgot I ordered it..but arrived in perfect condition and sound is great..will order another soon

This review - such as it is - is for the TP-Link TL-SG2008 eight-port managed switch.

I don't know how helpful my review of this switch will be; I'm just a home user with techy inclinations who thought I was going to need a managed switch to connect and take advantage of the link aggregation feature of the Synology NAS I had on order...but delivery of the NAS was sufficiently delayed that I wound up rethinking the expenditure and deciding it was better I have that money in the bank than that I have a NAS right now...so I cancelled the NAS and am now using this switch unmanaged and for nothing more than relocating the Hue hub I had connected to the Ethernet port of my network extender...well, and providing six more Ethernet ports just in case I want to connect that NAS or any other Ethernet equipment to my otherwise entirely wireless network in future.

All that said, and my having barely dipped into the switch's managed features (I did create a link aggregation group (LAG) in anticipation of the NAS's arrival - easy-peasy - and then delete it when I nixed the NAS), I'm pleased with the purchase. This switch was quite a bit less expensive than Netgear's equivalent options, and I'm not seeing reviewers complaining of TP-Link's engaging in questionable moneymaking tactics the way Netgear does (required phone apps giving you a free trial before you're forced to pay for them if you don't want your switch to revert to an unmanaged state, expensive and ineffective paid support, etc.). I frankly only just noticed in the product description that this switch features static routing; I will likely take advantage of that, if only so I can log onto its web interface without having to chase its IP address around my network.

I find the documentation a little cryptic - it assumes a greater knowledge of networking than I possess - but I don't think it's anything I can't figure out with a few quick DuckDuckGo searches.

With the aid of a power strip, it has let me get my Hue hub off my kitchen counter (I have a tiny apartment and have to extend my landlord's wifi network into my apartment with a (Netgear) network extender, and right above my kitchen counter is the only place I can plug in the extender where both it and the devices I'm connecting to it get a good strong signal), and, being of techy inclinations, I do appreciate having a bunch of Ethernet ports available if ever I want them...and a few more blinking colored lights in my apartment (blinking colored lights are almost always welcome in my dwellings :).

I also like that, unlike with Netgear's switches, the ports are hidden away on the back of this unit, leaving the front panel (and its blinking lights ;) clean, neat and readily visible. (Whoever posted the photos for this unit on Amazon doesn't know the front of the switch from the back, and put a photo of the back panel as the main image. A little disorienting, that, and it makes questions arise until one looks through the rest of the photos and finds the image of the front of the unit.)

If one day I start using more of this switch's features and I remember to do so, I'll come back and update my review if such will be useful.

I bought a Netgear EX6250 in a brick-and-mortar store about four months ago and my experience with it has been good overall...though not without its complications. Past experience with late-model Netgear products can be helpful in getting this unit set up and operating as the process is not always straightforward. It took me (who has a lot of experience with Netgear products and home networking in general) rather a few tries to get onto the right track in the Nighthawk app to set the thing up - you can run into roadblocks due to aspects of the Nighthawk app's design being less than intuitive (I know I did). I can't remember specifics now...so you know what I'm going to do? Out of lovingfriendliness for my fellow Amazon customers, I'm going to reset the extender to factory settings and set it back up, taking notes along the way, so that I can relate my experience more clearly and in greater detail.

Okay, so:

First you want to jump online and download the Netgear Nighthawk app to your phone. I don’t know if this unit can be set up without it.

Next, plug the extender into power - somewhere where it’s in range of your router. After you first plug the unit in, or after resetting it using the little recessed paperclip button on the side, the power LED will glow orange for rather a long time - two to three minutes in my experience - before finally turning green. Green means “go” - but orange doesn’t. So you just have to wait until that light turns green in order to be able to proceed with the setup process. Good opportunity to focus on the breath. And the fact that patience is a virtue.

Once the power indicator turns green, launch the Nighthawk app and check the little circle confirming that you accept Netgear’s terms and conditions and that you’ve read their privacy policy…even though you probably haven’t. Then tap “I Agree”.

On an iPhone, at least, the next screen says that iOS requires that you enable local network access in order to be able to set up your extender (which at this point the Nighthawk app is calling a “router” because it doesn’t yet know any better - you haven’t yet told it what you want to set up). Obviously, since you want to set up your extender, you’re going to okay that local network access. Tap “Continue” and your phone will ask you if you want to allow the app to find and connect to devices on your local network. Tap “OK”.

The next screen asks you to allow push notifications. This one’s up to you. I think I’ve always allowed them and I haven’t seen one yet, let alone been annoyed by excessive/unwanted notifications that are, in the end, just trying to sell me crap or otherwise waste my time.

The next screen tells you Netgear needs access to your device’s location services to automatically connect to your wifi network. I always allow this.

Next you’re told you have to create a new Netgear account or log into an existing one. Do that.

Then you’ll be asked if you want to enable Face ID and you’ll also be asked…something else I forget because I just blazed past it, momentarily forgetting that I was writing this detailed description of the process. But…y’know. You can read (because you’re reading this), so…tap the things on your screen that accord with your wishes. :)

At last we come to a screen that says, “Let’s set up your Nighthawk”, and tells you what to do if the unit’s been set up before. I don’t think I’ve ever had any luck using the “been set up before” option, so I always reset the extender to factory settings (by pressing and holding the paperclip/pen-point button on the side of the unit until the power light blinks orange) when I have a problem with the connection (which I seldom do, and when I do it’s usually because the power’s blinked or something else explicit has happened to make me need to set the extender up again). If this is your first time setting it up, tap “Set up a Nighthawk”. Even though I don’t think this extender is technically a Nighthawk. Doesn’t matter - you can still set it up with this app.

Next you’re shown a rundown of what’s going to happen. Read that as you’re inclined, then tap “Get Started!”.

On the product selection screen that comes up next, tap “Range Extender”.

The app tells you where to plug in your extender. Follow its instructions and tap “Next”.

The next screen just tells you to actually plug it in now, and wait (…and wait…and wait…) for a solid (green) power LED. Do that, and when you’ve got the solid green power light, tap “Next”.

On the next screen, the app will ask you to let it join your extender’s network. Tap “OK”, and wait while your phone connects to your extender. When it does, the screen will change to display “Great, we found your extender”. Tap “Next”.

Tap “Next” on the next screen as well.

Now your phone will look for your router’s network (which is your pre-existing wifi network, the one you want to extend). I think what it’s doing now is acting as a liaison between your router and the extender - introducing them to one another, as it were. Because what happens next is that your extender looks for and - ideally - connects to your wifi network. (When you’re asked to allow…something…to join your network, tap “Join”.)

And if all has gone well, that’s pretty much it. You’ll see a screen that says you’re up and running, and…there it is: you’re up and running!

Obviously, all of that is how things are *supposed* to go. If they go otherwise…you’ll probably need to be able to apply a searing laser beam of logic to the process and figure out how to make it work (that’s been my personal approach and, lucky for me, it’s always worked so far), or else to contact the dread Netgear Support People. I hope for your sake the laser beam works.

Good luck and enjoy!

I see people raving up and down about the perfection and wonderfulness of these headphones; I’m not as completely blown away by them as those people are. Quality of construction does seem to be excellent (although because Amazon doesn’t lower all prices at the start of Prime Day but only lowers some of them well after Prime Day has begun, I had to send back the first pair I bought and purchase another pair to get a discounted price, and the piston things for extending and compressing the size of the headphones was smoother on the first pair I had) and they’re comfortable enough to wear for extended periods, but while it may be a limitation of Bluetooth (I don’t know), I haven’t noticed myself being amazed by their bass response. No, in fact I just now watched the video for Shake It Off and listened to a couple of Lana Del Rey tracks and these headphones are definitely lacking in bass response – as in, there’s very little, and what there is gets completely lost under any midrange and high-end sounds that may be playing at the same time. They’re tinny-sounding. I have to wonder what the people are listening to with these who are praising the sound quality so enthusiastically.

On the other hand, I don’t ordinarily listen to music anymore, but only to talks and lectures; While I’m watching movies is probably the only time I’m going to really want big bass, and I watched The Revenant last night and didn’t feel like I was missing anything…

So their construction is much more solid than that of probably most other headphones on the market, they’re comfortable to wear, and there’s a nice ecosystem of accessories out there, but I personally find the sound quality quite lacking and I’m going to have to decide whether to hang onto these or return them.

This is a smart case - no bra needed.

UPDATE: Wrong, alas. I mean, it’s possible to make this case put your headphones to sleep – at least with the version of this case that I have – but it’s such a precise, finicky, painstaking endeavor that it’s nowhere near worth the effort. I’ve taken to using my case just like everybody else does: with the bra inside.

My guess is that what these third-party case makers need to do is what Apple did with the bra: rather than a couple of dime-sized round magnets, they need to put in long, thin magnets that will connect with the sensors in the earcups no matter where in the case they fall. The bra puts the headphones to sleep every time without fail and without the user having to spend several minutes massaging the headphones into just exactly the perfect position so that they’ll go to sleep, so it can be done; the third-party case manufacturers just haven’t yet figured out how Apple did it.

Anyways: I was dreading this case having an horrendous stench to it, based on several reviews I've read. I'm happy to report that while mine has a smell and it is kind of chemical-y, I find the smell neither strong nor entirely unpleasant. It's pretty mild, strength-wise (and I'm sensitive to such things) and I find the smell has a sort of fresh quality to it, despite its chemical nature. Lucky me, I guess. But this, like the Apple bra, is basically half a case. You need the bra to put the headphones to sleep, and this case to give them adequate protection. Hard to believe in this day and age, but there it is. I guess if Apple included a case with these that did everything necessary they would probably charge an additional $200 for it…

I lived and breathed full-sized Kensington trackball mice from about 1987 until my last one stopped functioning and I couldn't find them anymore...probably in the late '90s. Tried some others; all had small, lightweight balls that gave none of the feel and control of Kensinton's...Expert Mouse? Was that what it was called back then too? Because it was the same general design as the current Expert Mouse, but the body was computer-case white.

Anyway, I had several of those (the quality going downhill with each iteration, as I recall) and loved them, and since they disappeared (as far as I could tell), I adapted, first to trackpads, which I've never liked much, and then back to traditional mice which don't give nearly the control of a trackball. Now, at last, it seems Kensington has again begun to produce truly worthwhile trackball mice, and this is one. Oh, it's _so_ good to have one of these again.

I'm doing that thing I hate when other people do it and reviewing the product as soon as I've gotten it up and running, without any kind of experiential history behind my assessment. I'll come back and update this in the future if necessary. But so far: I'm happy, happy, happy to have a real, full-sized Kensington trackball mouse again, with a heavy, substantial ball. There are only two things about this device that I'm not crazy about: In my old Kensington mice, the ball rested on physical rollers and I could give the ball a good spin and it would keep spinning for a second before stopping; it spun much more freely in its cavity than this ball does (so far...maybe that's something that will break in?) [Update: yes, after about three days of use the ball rolls more smoothly and silently than the old one on rollers ever did]. And the other thing is the scrolling mechanism. It's weird. Despite the KensingtonWorks software trying to make us believe otherwise, the "scroll ring" itself actually has nothing to do with scrolling, nor with anything else - the "scroll ring" is not even a control, but just a static piece of chrome trim. What makes the mouse scroll is twisting the ball this way or that from the top, as if it were a knob. At first I thought the "scroll ring" wasn't working because I was trying to use it without touching the ball...which does nothing. And now that I've figured out how scrolling works (you rest your finger on the "scroll ring" and push and pull the side of the ball)...I'm not crazy about it. I'm getting used to it, but it's just a weird way to scroll (I can't for the life of me remember how I used to do it on the Expert Mouse decades ago). It does work though.

(Update on the scrolling: I'm also not crazy about the way the KensingtonWorks software handles the scrolling speed adjustment. When you make the base pointer movement speed faster, the pointer continues to move smoothly, but just faster. When you make the scrolling speed faster though, you lose all smoothness - the software makes the scrolling faster by breaking it into successively larger and more jarring jumps. At the slowest speed, it's pretty smooth; at the highest speeds it's no longer really scrolling, but simply jumping abruptly from one screenful (or page) to the next. Increasing the scrolling speed just increases the size of these jumps, but I find them jarring and annoying starting at the second or third lowest speed setting.)

I also had to figure out how to program one of the buttons as a click lock, since Kensington doesn't call it that anymore, but calls it "left drag", "right drag", and "middle drag" (and I have no idea what the difference is between those three - I just chose "left drag" and it's working fine).

So far, those are my only gripes, all minor. So happy to have one of these things again! =) (Did I mention that?)

Works well, but you have to know that a splitter takes an input and displays to all the outputs the same content. A switcher on the other hand lets you switch between multiple inputs and displays to the output what you have selected. If you combine, first a switcher to select which input you want, and then split the output, you can select one of your inputs to display to many of the same content outputs. You should also do some research on the switchers because all I could find were switchers that required a manual selection from your inputs, not automatic. Some were remote control and most only had 2 input sources. Good Luck, Hope this helped.

Pros
*I've tried several different earbuds, and these are good in terms of price and quality at the time of this review.
*I like the volume control and microphone feature, because it is an added convenience, and I am able to adjust without much difficulty
*The detachable clip and hard, protective storage case are an added bonus
*Sound quality and bass is better than expected when I first pulled the earphones out of the case
*

Cons

*The biggest issue I had was having them fit comfortably in my ears and staying in place. This isn't helpful for workouts, and there doesn't appear to be a proper workaround. (Supplemental note: My husband has larger ears, so he seemed fine with the fit when trying them out)
*They do tangle easier than some of the other models I've tried of the same caliber which makes it a little annoying

These earbuds are a good deal for the consumer pocket as of today. If the product malfunctions, I will revisit this review and update accordingly. I did receive these earbuds free for testing purposes for an unbiased review, and positive ratings are never guaranteed.

The prices on big-screen smart tvs are in free-fall these days; projectors are always a bit of a project. But you're sure you want a projector, right? If so this is a great choice. Easy set up, great image, amazing keystoning (more on THAT in a moment), powerful internal speakers, and a decent price point (under $900 currently.)

Setup could scarcely be easier - provided you have your screen and the (not included) input cables/stick - or a wireless dongle. As I already had a projection screen and an HDMI cable for my laptop, all I had to do was switch on the projector, adjust the lens, run the start utility to keystone for the projector being offset from the center of the screen, connect the cable from laptop to projector, then allow the device to find the video source - the device finds the input in a few seconds and is soon streaming video and audio.

The projector's own audio is surprisingly good - and loud. Response to the remote is... a little slow, depending how close you are to the projector. The projector's own audio is great, and as we have it closer to the screen than we sit, I haven't felt the need to connect speakers. Persons with more demanding tastes in audio will of course differ, but the device's own speakers do a solid job.

Video quality is OUTSTANDING. Colors are vibrant and although a light source placed near the screen washes them out, the image is still clearly visible. With a light source more than 10 feet away and even with natural light through windows (at the opposite end of a 25-foot room) the image is perfectly clear; even though as I'm using a white screen the blacks are clear and dark. There was one strange exception to this with a streaming video (Extant) where the darks were warmer in the projection than on the laptop, but we have run other video and also had a DVR player (hooked up via the triple cables), and run DVRS with perfect light levels. I recently got an Amazon Fire Stick, and actually set it up on the projector - setup was easy and there have been no adjustments needed for the streaming video.

The keystoning is an amazing, but somewhat tedious, feature; you can offset the device and still get an excellent image. Using the keystoning feature on the remote, some tweaking gives you a near-perfect image. I say near perfect because when we had the projector placed eight feet back and some feet down to the left of the screen, the upper right-hand corner of the image frame bent inwards - although the cast image itself was clear and undistorted. This was apparently because the projector was not on a perfectly horizontal surface. The real issue was that when the projector was moved back in front of the screen, I had to redo the keystoning manually; holding down the OK key was supposed to reset it, but this didn't work for me.

The projector is relatively light and easy to move around. The feet are easy to unscrew to manipulate the image, but for the afore-mentioned keystoning issue, it was necessary to adjust the surface the projector was resting on; this would obviously be a whole different matter if ceiling-mounted.

I think it's a great projector. So really it all boils down to whether you WANT a projector - the VERY big picture and/or the portability, eh? You don't care about having to control light levels, positioning the device itself (and the associated transmitting device,) maintaining a screen, dealing with multiple interfaces... You're not the complete couch potato, surfing the channels via remote... Not to go on and on - this is a projector, not a tv. You can hook it up to a tv, or a laptop, streaming stick, etc, but - a projector is always going to be more complicated. This, however, is an amazingly uncomplicated projector!

The Tile system isn't perfect but it works (mostly) and to date I haven't run across any better options. So bearing in mind your needs and the device's limitations, it's probably worth getting (at the time of this writing) if you have things you're worried about misplacing.

Pros:

- EASY setup. The time it takes to send an eMail and receive a reply, and a few seconds more. I have heard people say it requires iPhone 4 and up - I have a 5 and everything was a breeze. I didn't use the picture feature initially but it was no problem to update later.

- Decent map feature - good enough to get you in general range of the FIND radius.

- An audible FIND jingle. Just loud enough to hear through a wallet. Louder sure would be better, but it has a tinny high-pitched jingle that's easy to identify once you've heard it.

- It's small enough to fit in my wallet. It's a bit bulky, but it does.

- It's weatherproof and sealed. I haven't actually tested that and don't want to, but it's a nice feature.

- On-phone settings are easy to operate, and allow you to turn off Bluetooth tracking without turning off the iPhone's Bluetooth.

- Easy to assign to other objects as needed (if you don't use the stick pad.) It has a hole, so you don't HAVE to stick it to anything permanently.

- Can add other users (beforehand, of course!)

- It works. The battery is only supposed to last about a year, though (we'll see!)

Cons:

- Bulkier than I thought - not quite as thick as a pen, but almost. About a half-dollar size.

- The FIND process takes a minute or two to adjust and is a little confusing at first.

- The FIND radius sure isn't perfectly accurate. But hey, it's something!

- Battery not replaceable. The Tile people will recycle it for you for a fee, but I doubt that is a rapid process.

I really like it. I don't lose stuff that often, but this is an awfully convenient tracking option - having a general idea is a LOT better than having NO idea at all! And I LOVE the idea of the Tile community! The Tile gives me peace of mind taking things through airports etc. If there's something you think you MIGHT mislay, I think the Tile is worth it.

I used this on a XFX RX 580 GTS 8GB Black edition. In a M-atx case, the stock cooler fans would run full RPM just to keep it at 75-80C under load. Add in 5 case fans (@full RPM) to keep the air flow fresh and I had an annoyingly loud heater just a few feet from my chair. Stumbled upon this in a random search and after reading a few other reviews I decided to order it and see how it goes.

Install was straight forward enough. If you can reapply thermal paste, you can install this cooler. Placing the heat sinks on the VRAM and VRM is time consuming but unlike others I found the supplied thermal sticky pads to be fine after applying moderate force for about 10 secs. Only issue I had was clearance on one of the VRAMs as it sat close to the plate and could only be half covered by a heatsink. Getting the placement on that one took slightly longer but by using a few dry test fits I was able to get it placed perfectly.

The MOSs are on the left on this GPU so I was hesitant but after a week of using it I haven't seen any issues with VRM not properly cooling. Board doesn't support junction temp measuring so I have no hard data on if they are hotter or not, but I do feel airflow around them and performance is still great.

The rad and fan were easy enough to install. In a M-atx case it is tight. It was a squeeze and took a few tries to properly get everything where I wanted but once in I have no complaints. I did hear "coil whine" from the pump once, but quickly sorted out that some pressure was being applied to one of the tubes right near the pump, once I shifted it a little, the whine stopped and never returned.

The LEDS are ok. The controller is adequate. The LED along the side of the GPU mount is a nice touch, really adds a higher end feel to the finished product. Obviously this isn't a high end ARGB controller but its got more than enough setting to make it fit into your overall lighting needs. Personally I just wanted some plain old solid white. I do find the white to be slightly bluish in the fans but I chalk that up to ARGB vs the RGB LED case fans I have installed.

Wiring was tedious but it included everything I needed. Other than taking my time to cable manage and tuck it all away out of sight, it was straight forward enough to wire up. Just double check they all get plugged in! I missed the pump power and on my first start up saw the temps just go up and up and got worried I installed it wrong. Luckily I thought to check the cables right before taking it apart and found the problem.

I did add/change a few things,
-Firstly I used Thermal Grizzlys kryonaut paste instead of the supplied paste.
-I also bought a 4-Pin PWM splitter adapter that allowed me to use the GPUs native fan plug to power the rad and VRAM fans. I can't recommend this enough! Using Afterburner to control the fan speeds really is awesome and allows for easy fine tuning for noise and temps needs.
-I did have to cut some of the metal shroud for the front of the GPU back plate. I didnt want to run no plate on top of the board and obviously it wasn't designed to have water tubes go through it. It was simple and easy to cut but is a permeant mod to make it look better. You can see in the attached pics, some are with the plate on and some with it off.

Speaking of which temps are mind blowing! It idles at 28c (ambient is about 22c) with fans set to 3%. in other words, silent! Under my normal full gaming load it chills at 50c with fans at 50%. Slightly louder but still much quieter than the stock blower! If I turn the fans to 100% it will chill at like 35-37c while full 1080p gaming. I've even pushed the OC a bit, went from 1425 Core clock to 1500, and Mem clock from 2000 to 2250. No way the stock coolers would have let that happen smoothly.

I waited a week or so to write this review just to make sure I was still happy. And I am! I'll update this review with any long term issues or problems so if there is no update, expect that its still just plugging along being super chill.

This is a dual review, as I own both the Contour + 2 and the Contour Roam2. I don't work for nor do I have any affiliation with Contour. I've had the Roam2 for more than 6 months, but held off writing this review until I had the +2 to compare it to. Although I don't own a GoPro, several friends do and I do their video editing so I'll chime in on the Contour vs. GoPro at the end.

MOUNTS:
Contour uses the same proprietary mounts across their lineup, so interchangeability between the two should be fairly easy (but doesn't always work out that way). I've found some to be flimsy(hat mount), while others are damn near bomb proof(suction cup)! The rotating lens means you can mount it in just about any position, however it is difficult to know that you've framed the shot with the correct orientation! Had an important video recorded upside down - laser level only lets you know it's level, not if it's upside down! One of the best features I've found is the ¼ by 20 thread on the bottom of the Contour, pretty much universal to all modern cameras and there's a TON of mounts out there reasonably priced.

SOFTWARE:
The Storyteller program needs to be installed on your computer and is fairly easy to use, but not intuitive, you need to play around a bit before you can figure everything out. The editing ability is extremely limited. (I use imovie). Software is free, and although you can use the camera(s) without first updating I suggest you do that first! The +2 also has an app that I use on my iPhone 5 - it too is free and pretty easy to use - but not as capable as the Storyteller program. The downside is you HAVE to use the Storyteller program to change settings on the Roam2, AND you have to use it if you want to use any of the GPS data with the +2.

ROAM2:
Got this for Xmas last year and immediately swapped the included 4GB micro SD for a 16GB. SUPER easy to use - charge, point, and slide the slider to the on position. Video quality is good, first few outings I had it set for 1080@30 and was very happy. In editing I found one clip I had to slow down and was slightly disappointed at the quality - since then I've got it set for 720@60 and haven't had any issues - video quality is still good (even in slow mo). Low light does induce more "noise" to the video, but if there's ambient light (streetlights etc.) you can still get decent vids. Sound quality isn't all that, it's usable, but in high winds or at speed - forget it. Battery life is really good at around 2 hours. The camera itself is very well built, one of my first uses it got throw (by an idiot) about 8ft into about 4 inches of water over concrete - few scratches, but still kept recording. This led me to look for something to help protect the aluminum body - Glock Tape, works amazing, adds some protection, but most importantly gives it some GRIP!

[[ASIN:B00C7WXTJS 6-Pack Glock Grip Tape - Pistol Grip Tape. * Use on handguns and rifles * Not gritty like sandpaper or skateboard tape. * Does not scuff clothing, holsters, furniture or car seats like those sandy tapes. * Makes chambering a round easier for arthritis s...]]

CONTOUR +2:
Only had it for a week or so, really wanted it due to the Bluetooth (to help frame shots) and was wanted the waterproof housing (worried about watersports damage on an upcoming trip) the GPS would be a plus. Once again amazing build quality - this things tough as nails. First thing I did was hook up to Storyteller and get the latest firmware update - less than 5 minutes later I was off and running! Pairing the Bluetooth took a couple of attempts, but once connected has excellent range (20 or so feet with obstructions - close to 50ft line of sight!). Using the app you can check status of battery, GPS, and memory as well as change settings and start stop recording - wish you could watch videos but oh well. The app has about a one second delay between what the camera "sees" and what you see on your phone - pretty amazing! Attached to my suction cup mount and went for a drive - took about 30 seconds for the GPS to lock on the first time (since then it only takes maybe 5 seconds). GPS is accurate. The video quality is great! Uploaded vid into storyteller and the GPS data was also great - until I exported it then there was a lag of about 5 seconds between the data being displayed and the video. Waterproof housing is bulky, yet seems a bit flimsy - still not sure it could survive 200 ft of water. Came with HDMI to hook up to TV - works really well. Haven't used the mic adaptor yet. Battery life seems to be around 1.5 hours, but spare batteries are cheap.

[[ASIN:B007PUC1UU Wasabi Power Battery and Charger Kit for Contour 2350, 2450, 2900, C010410K and ContourHD, ContourGPS, Contour+, Contour+2]]

COMPARISON:
Even though the video specs are the same between the +2 and the Roam2, the video quality of the +2 is noticeably better - even in low light. Sound quality on both suffers in high winds or speed. They both have the proprietary T-rail mounts on both sides, but the ¼ by 20 thread is about an inch further back on the +2. The Roam2 is waterproof without housing to about 3ft, but the +2 has the waterproof housing. The +2 also allows for filming while charging. The +2 has the HDMI out, as well as a jack for external mic. The +2 has the Bluetooth app, plus GPS - that combined with replaceable batteries and the better video make it worth the extra money.

CONTOUR vs. GOPRO:
I absolutely love the form factor and the mounting options available for the Contours. The Contour line has their own proprietary mounts, but the ability to use the ¼ by 20 thread mounts for other cameras (even the GoPro mounts) plus the rotating lens means there's just more ways to mount the Contour. That being said the GoPro Hero3 flat out destroys the video quality of the Roam2, and slightly edges out the +2. Of course this difference (even over the Roam2) is completely removed once video is uploaded to Youtube or other sharing sites as they compress the video during upload! I've yet to see a GoProH3 recording 1080 go for more than 75 minutes. Sound quality between all three is about the same. The GoProH3 app uses wifi - and has about a 3-4 second delay - still works for framing shots, but not much else. The GoPro also has the advantage in that you can change settings in camera - but it is a complicated affair(the +2 only allows you to choose between two predetermined settings). GoProH3 doesn't have GPS, or rotating lense. Contour recently lowered the price on the +2 it's now $50 cheaper than the GoProH3. Also it seems they changed pricing on their mounts - I went with the Contour line because of the simplicity of their system, more mounts, cheaper price, and the form factor. Now that they're cheaper it's a no brainer.

Let me start by saying I've owned dozens of cameras, about two years ago I stepped up to a Canon DSLR and enjoyed it tremendously. After two years with the DSLR I started looking to replace it with something a little smaller (the size and weight of the SLR making it prohibitive for all my travels/uses). So I sold off the Canon and ended up buying and returning three different point and shoots before finally stumbling onto the NEX-3!

The picture quality easily rivals that of my Canon XSi, yet the size and weight are deceptively small. As much as I practiced and tried different lenses and techniques, I was never able to get great low-light shots from my XSi, with the 16mm prime lens, the Sony constantly gives me great low light performance - without using the flash. Speaking of the flash, I was skeptical at first about the whole detachable flash - for fear of losing it or breaking it. Once I installed it I found that it's really not that obtrusive, when closed (in the down position) it hardly adds any mass to the camera and unless it's in the open position, the camera doesn't even recognize it's presence.

Some have complained about the user interface, while I've grown accustomed/spoiled by manual controls the NEX-3 menu system is really easy to navigate. Even my parents were able to change settings and get some amazing shots without being told how, or looking at a manual. Some of the "helpful" tips are a bit basic, but those can be turned off quite easily.

The "handheld twilight" mode is amazing, taking several pictures at different exposures then combining them into one - why haven't all camera manufactures jumped on this bandwagon? Sure you get some color distortion, but the ability to take a picture in all but the darkest settings and still be able to see what was there is mind blowing. How many people with a point and shoot can walk outside at midnight and take a good picture of the moon? What's that you say? You don't want to mess with a bunch of settings? Just set it to intelligent auto mode and let it choose for you!

Pleasantly surprised, by far the best camera I've ever owned! Cannot recommend highly enough!

Great little ear-buds for the money. Also, although it doesn't say these have a microphone, you can have a conversation with these in on the phone, and my callers say there is less distortion than with my Bluetooth. The sound quality is pretty surprising for the price point.

I'm a die hard 3D fanatic. I've been through it all ( started with 13 Ghosts in a movie theater as a child). Through the years, I've experimented with 3D tech as it progressed. From flickering active glasses to the passive, movie theater style approach . I still have a 3D computer monitor and TV, though they're not set up at the moment. I even have 2 Nintendo 3DS units which was quite an accomplishment being the first, truly mainstream product that did not require glasses to view 3D, and finally, the ultimate 3D experience was/is VR using the Oculus Rift/Quest systems. Yes, it is quite the tech, but wearing the headset is not something you'd want to do for long periods, as it can become uncomfortable , and I don't always like the feeling of cutting off my real world surroundings.

Fast forward to 2021. I had my eye on the Lume tablet, but not at the original price. I already had an iPad Pro which is pretty unbeatable. When I saw the $299.00 price tag (April 2022), it was a no brainer. I always wanted an android tablet as an alternative anyway. The flexibility of the Android OS goes beyond IOS, making it a helluva lot more interesting for tinkerers and people who love to customize!

Well, I'm happy to say, this tablet is beyond my expectations.. Look, if you didn't grow up with 3D tech, and expect Jason Vorhees to jump out of the screen and slice you, then you're not meant for this. Go play in VR insead. When you understand going in, the limitations of 3D, then you'll love this. The 3D is gorgeous, but the tablet's native resolution (2D), will drop dramatically to accommodate the 3D mode (just like it does with passive glasses displays on TVs ). The display will sometimes be dimmer in 3D, but it varies with each app and its contents. 3D Photos look amazing and you hardly hardly notice the dimming, where as some games it's quite obvious, but again, depends on the app. Speaking of which, the game library is not large yet (I think they're around 100 titles at the time of this review). Some games utilize the 3D intelligently and will leave you impressed, while others are too basic or simply not good. Gameloft's Asphalt racing & Architect are both samples of top quality on all levels, and there are few other 3D gaming gems hidden among the crop; I'm still going through them.

Now for some REAL hotness: I just installed Citra, which is a 3DS emulator with an option for Lume 3D. It's still an early version, but quite a number of games already work excellently! Having 3D on a sharper, larger screen with 3DS gaming - are you kidding me? This is amazing.

What I find most impressive are the videos and photographs. It's like, some objects look almost as if they're protruding 4" off the screen. This baby can convert 8K 2D youtube videos to 3D in seconds , or at most, a minute. There's so much to try out on youtube and other social media platforms , that you'll realize, there just isn't enough time in a day. The app is called LeiaTube, which is part of a suite of Leia 3D apps including one where you can even take your own impressive 3D photos and videos with the dual lens camera.

Some of the other pre-loaded Leia apps for the Lume include a viewer for manipulating thousands of 3D objects, mind-blowing community photos and dozens of well-done educational videos covering a wide range of topics, each pretty lengthy! Explore everything from the human body, to heading back in time to ancient Egypt, all in 3D of course.

Want to watch blockbuster 3D Movies? You can head to Leiaflix and for $1.99, you'll have a mini 3D theater right on your lap, and the results are impressive and even more exciting is an app on Google Play called Jellyfin. You also have to download the server software for PC or Mac as well as a custom video player made by a talented individual (check the Leia forums). Now you're able to REMOTELY watch your own 3D videos (and 2D) from your Lume tablet from anywhere in your home over wifi. It's Amazeballs!

The tablet uses a USB type C connector. If you purchase one of those multi inputs to C adapters, you can add a hard drive, USB flash or SD cards so you'll be able to transfer items from your expansion storage to the Lume, or you can download Total Commander, and remotely transfer PC/Mac files to the Lume and the reverse. All from your bed.

And finally - two things that are MAJOR surprises -- beyond the 3D itself are the sound and picture quality. When using the tablet in normal 2D (like any Samsung tab), the picture quality is unreal - it actually gives the iPad screen a run for its money. I mean, this display almost approaches OLED - with crisp, bright and bold colors, and a rich black level. As far sound, we're talking Dolby Atmos. It's the richest sound I've ever heard on any mobile device, and the build quality is solid, like a tank.

So, take away the 3D, and you have one killer tablet on its own. Head to the Google Play Store and go crazy! I hope enough units sell so this unique tablet gets the support it deserves.

So I decided to go for MSI after doing much research on Nvidia Pascal-Powered laptops. I do a lot of 3DS Max work, and I'm a gamer since the 80's, so I figured, this may be the best route. I didn't want to get a laptop which, in a few months, would already be obsolete, so I skipped some of the other current gen models from the likes of Alienware with 970/980 m cards. I didn't give Asus a shot because I've had a not-so-good experience with my current and previous desktops. This is my first MSI computer, and I have to say, the laptop is stunner. The Steel Series keyboard is a pleasure to type on with its generously- spaced keys, and backlit configurable color spectrum while the non-reflective IPS screen is gorgeous, sporting good viewing angles with colors that truly pop. I love 17" screens for gaming when I'm sitting on a recliner, as I don't feel like being hunched over a desk all night. I haven't used it for VR yet, but I did run the Steam VR Speed Test to see where it stands. On my Asus G11CD Desktop (16GB i7-6700 3.40Ghz and Nvidia 970), the results showed my system just making it into the VR ready green band. The same test on my MSI Laptop had the VR Ready indicator near the very end of the green band, almost off the chart. As for Windows 10 itself -- it's up within seconds thanks to the 128 SSD. There's not much to comment on the touchpad. I never use them - they're the spawn of Satan. I always hook up a wireless mouse.

I haven't had a chance to test all of my games yet, as my laptop less than a week old as of this review, but the few I've tried ran smooth as glass. I downloaded the demo of the updated System Shock which has a 2017 release. Using FRAPS FPS counter, I was clocking in 92-120 FPS. Same download on my Asus was roughly 75-83. I've been heavily involved with the Planet Coaster (Alpha) which is more taxing than most high end first person shooters. I am running large simulated theme parks, with very advanced lighting effects and all graphic options maxed out. With Nvidia GSync (this monitor supports it) enabled, I'm getting a solid 60 FPS .98% of the time. In comparison, my Asus using the same dense parks using V-Sync gave me an average of 45-50 FPS

Thankfully, there is not too much on the bloatware end. Most of the included extras are MSI tune-up/tweaking programs and surprisingly, quite useful. Norton Security however, is bloatware in my opinion. It came with my Asus, it came with this MSI, and on both systems, it was the first thing I deleted. I don't need it. I never will. Stop it.

As far as the audio, the Nahimic 2 Virtual Surround is super impressive. I've had other laptops in the past, and they've always sounded like tin can alley. The sound that comes out of this unit is rich, and at times, the surround effect is quite effective. The max volume could use another notch or two, but it's still quite competent. Definitely game and epic movie-worthy sound.

The system remains fairly cool and quite capable of dispersing heat properly. Running the power hungry Planet Coaster Alpha no doubt generates a ton of heat, but it all seems to flow out of the back vents, so no keyboard hot-spots. One issue: I use a very thin, rigid laptop mat so the back vent heat winds up flowing to my knees which can be uncomfortable. The one way around this is pulling the laptop toward you, allowing for about an inch of the mat to stick out of the back as a kind of shield. A welcome addition is the turbo fan which you can easily access from a button on the left side of the laptop. I usually turn it on for about a minute and it diminishes the heat fairly well. One of the included MSI utilities gives you more access to the fan's options. Besides the fan, the MSI Dominator Pro has additional buttons that handle quick access functions like sleep mode, sample keyboard color layouts, and other options. Oh, and if you're thinking about lugging this around to your local coffee shop, forget it....unless you want to attract a crowd of wide-eyed onlookers. Also, It's pretty heavy, as in home gym bicep curl heavy. Unfortunately, the one area I haven't tested (my apologies) is the battery life as I am not one who travels with my laptop. I keep my laptop powered through AC in my living room.

Any regrets? None whatsoever - my jaw is still on the floor, but I have a very minor gripe.

The Laptop has a huge sticker on the base, in front of the keyboard. It's one of those highlighted specs stickers that all laptops generally boast. On the list it shows 120mhz display, yet, the on-line specs shows it being a 60mhz. At first glance, your heart will skip a beat and you'll be thinking... WOW even better than I imagined! That is, until you look close at the tiny word under that feature which says (optional). Really MSI - If you're going to slap a "Look what I have inside me" sticker on my laptop, at least leave out what is absolutely not included.

Absolutely love this monitor. I now have it next to my Acer GD235HZ (4+ years old) and the Asus makes it look lifeless. Yes, the Acer GD235HZ was great in its heyday, when NVidia was still cranking out the original 3D Vision (before light burst), so this was my monitor of choice back then. Over the years, I got into 3D sessions when I was in the mood, but short periods with an active shutter set up will tire your eyes out in no time, AND make you feel drugged. This is with a 120hz display mind you.

The colors on this Asus IPS screen are just so vivid -- text and graphics are super sharp! ! And in theater mode, the black is like velvet! The screen default is very bright, so during non-gaming periods, I tend to drop it down. The Asus monitor uses passive technology which means inexpensive 3D glasses (same as the theater gives out), and longer playing periods. I'll sacrifice the horizontal resolution loss, over expensive active shutters any day. If you sit at least three feet away from the monitor, the 3D looks amazing, unless your're one of these anal journalists who judge it from every angle. Yeah, when I play a game, I tend look directly into monitor, not off from the the side of my desk. If you want to watch a 3D movie with six people, then perhaps a living room, passive TV over 52" would fit the bill. The Asus VG23AH is a monitor, and one that sports a pretty vibrant, spectacular 3D picture if you know how to use it. There are a number of settings which can be tweaked, and if you do a google search, there is a very informative set up guide which is also posted on youtube. In addition to running native 3D programs through TriDef, there is a 2D-3D button right on the front panel. I've never seen this as a button-based feature, but it takes any 2D media and displays it in 3D. A number of TV sets have a similar option, but I've never seen it right in the hardware. The results may vary, but considering the original content is 2D, you'll be quite impressed.

As of now, I have my PC hooked up to it via DVI cable and tried a number of games, including Sonic Generations, the Half Life 2 series and mods, Skyrim, and others. All are breathtaking, but you do need drivers. I already had the TriDef drivers when I purchased it years back, but you will need to lay down $40-$50.00 for a licensed copy in order to take advantage of PC gaming.
I will also hook my PC up through HDMI and try the other modes of 3D like Side by Side, which will expand my capability with 3D content available on the web.

In addition to the PC, I have my PlayStation 3 plugged in through the extra HDMI port, and the PS3 automatically recognized the 3D display, when running a game that supports this feature. There are a good number of PS3 games in 3D and they look absolutely stunning on this monitor, especially the Zen Pinball series!

Oh, the sound through HDMI will come through the monitor's speakers, and it's pretty good actually! Not tinny like other monitors.

Overall, I'm loving this monitor -- once you see IPS you will be spoiled!

Note: I got this off of Amazon's warehouse deals for $191.00 (aka a steal for IPS + 3D, It was classified as "Used/Like New", but it looked brand new to me when it arrived. Everything was still wrapped in its originally manufacture's packaging. A totally worthwhile buying experience!

My three year old i7 tower with its still impressive Geforce decided to freak out and shut down due to the Northbridge turning into an oven. I couldn't get my Asus to stay on more than 3 minutes before it would abruptly shut down. When turning it back on, I would get a NB temperature warning, so I knew it was hopeless. I opened it up and saw the results of the bake off: My passive heatsink was resting on the floor of my tower, instead of its designated spot on the MB. Come to think of it, I did hear this clang sound at one point. I ordered this product in hopes that it would solve the problem and eliminate the need to purchase a new motherboard (I'm not THAT technically good). Turns out - it was fairly easy to put in. I just used some 90% isopropyl alcohol to clean the left over goo from the previous thermal paste, applied the included thermal paste, placed the adjustable metal rods with spring anchors into the heatsink's base, and snapped this baby down. Finally, I plugged the fan into a nearby free power cord, waited about 20 minutes, then turned it on. Drum roll .... perfect! The temperature levels are now safe and I got my main computer back (so long for now backup laptop). Oh, and the fan is super quiet.

Just one note: My heat sink popped off on its own from the drastic heat, so popping in this replacement NB cooling fan was a breeze. If you are removing a faulty heatsink/fan that still happens to be in place, you may need to take the entire mother board out,.You see, those two screw like things (I called them anchors), snap down into holes through the motherboard in order to clamp down the fan. Once they snap down, the bottoms expand so there's no way get them back out except by squeezing the bottom end (under the motherboard) to get them through.

Had a 45 inch Sharp Aquos in the living room for over three years, and always thought it delivered wonderful HD output. On my PC, I own a Nvidia 3D Vision Set for the past two years for my PC gaming. The 3D Vision uses shutter technology, and definitely works beautifully with a 120HZ Monitor. Being a huge fan of all things tech, I've been watching the 3DTV market for the past few years, and finally it happened: Passive 3D! An affordable option which can feed 3D to a group of four+ without making you bankrupt.

I transferred the Sharp to the bedroom, and plugged all peripherals (PS3, 360, HDDVR and Roku) into the LG. Fired it up and immediately noticed how the colors popped. It actually ran rings around my Sharp Aquos! I transferred some 3D tech demos I saved on my PC to a USB drive, then ran them on the LG and was blown away by the 3D quality. Clean, bright and wonderful depth! Next, I popped in a BluRay movie (Monsters vs. Aliens) and again, my jaw dropped. I understood that the passive tech on the LG is suppose to have one drawback: horizontal resolution is decreased in 3D mode, but I'll be damned if I can see any difference. The TV arrived the day after Thanksgiving, so we still had the Thanksgiving Day Parade saved on our DVR. We used this to test the 2D to 3D on the fly conversation and it worked out pretty nicely. It definitely adds depth to any 2D broadcast, but nothing compared to true 3D.

As for gaming, the PS3 recognized I had a 3D TV from the start, and the few games I quickly tried (Wipeout, Uncharted 3 & Super Stardust) were mind-numbinlgy gorgeous. I didn't get a chance to try any 3D gaming on my 360 yet, but that's next!

Overall, I couldn't be happier with my decision to go for this LG!

Some quick notes:
- Unlike my 3D Vision PC shutter set up, the LG Passive does not darken the screen; colors remain bright and vibrant!

- My eyes were able to handle much longer periods of 3D viewing with the passive glasses. The 3D vision shutter would screw me up for the night if I played a long gaming session wearing them.

- The LG uses the same glasses they give out in theaters; go see Hugo and keep the glasses! :-)

- Get access to YouTube on your TV, and search YT3D! The LG Passive supports a number of different 3D formats which work brilliantly with most of YouTube's 3D showings'; there's TONS to see on there!

- The only ghosting I noticed was when you were not watching the TV from a normal viewing angle. For instance, if you stand up and move a bit close, you'll see overlapping images, but who watches TV like that?

- The two negatives: LG supplies a set of two orange and two white glasses. Orange and White? Really? What happened to the black glasses shown on the box and in a zillion ads? No big deal though, glasses are cheap. I found an eBay vendor selling a lot of 10 Movie glasses for $15.00! Try doing that with shutter technology. The USB input does not support DTS sound, so if you have a movie stored on a USB drive, it has to be converted or you will have no sound.

I think I'll just do a simple pro and con list for this one.

Pros:

+ It starts up fast when switched on and immediately reconnects to the last Bluetooth device selected.

+ The ability to store multiple device profiles and switch between them with the press of a button is awesome, and it saves a lot of time over having to open the Bluetooth settings on each device to reconnect.

+ And of course it has a 2.4g wireless USB dongle, so you can use it with things that don't have Bluetooth or which require a stronger wireless signal.

+ There are visible-yet-unobtrusive lights on the top that allow you to tell at a glance which device pairing you have selected.

+ The shape of the mouse fits my hand perfectly and is very comfortable.

+ The scroll wheel is easy to grip and roll back and forth. It has a very satisfying sort of "bump" feeling as it rotates from one position to another, whereas some wheels just turn freely, leaving you little control over how much you're actually scrolling. And most importantly, the wheel doesn't rock side-to-side like those ones that supposedly allow you to scroll left and right but never seem to work except by accident when you don't want them to.

+ There's no branding that I can identify on the packaging, the instructions, nor on the mouse itself. I see this as a pro because well, frankly, a lot of these random brand names are weird and bother me (though admittedly, I did once buy a product on Amazon primarily because the brand name was BULLETFACE *cue electric guitar solo*).

+ I really appreciate how every feature on this mouse serves a purpose. There are no dumb shapes or graphics added just to make it look "cool". It's cool enough as it is.

+ It's great that it has a built-in rechargeable battery and a USB-C port on the front so that I can charge it wherever I can charge my phone. But because there's no battery access door, the dongle rests in a recess on the underside of the mouse and is held in by a really strong magnet. That's better than other attachment methods I've seen where the dongle either snaps in with plastic clips or press-fits into a slot, as those will both wear out and fail eventually, where a magnet will not.

Cons:

- The ball feels a bit loose and rattle-y in its socket. It's not an issue when the mouse is on a level surface, but if you're carrying it around or trying to use it on the arm of a sofa, it can wiggle a bit, which feels weird.

- All but the lowest DPI setting is way too fast for anything I can imagine doing, but maybe I'm just not used to it yet. (Update: I guess I wasn't used to it. I've since moved up to the middle DPI setting now that I've gotten better at making fine movements)

- This may not be a con for some people, but the dongle really, really stays put in a USB port, to the point I was afraid I'd need pliers to get it out (though I managed to do so without them).

- Update: I thought of one more con. It's a shame I can't re-bind the little forward and back buttons on the far left to something more useful, like shift or ctrl-z.

Conclusion:

I'm currently very satisfied with my purchase, and I expect to get a lot of use out of this mouse for years to come. The best thing I can do to thank the manufacturer and seller for making a great product at a great price is to leave my honest feedback to help others find the product, so that's exactly what I've done. Oh, and I swyped (typed via path input) this entire review on my phone's on-screen keyboard using the very trackball I'm reviewing, if that gives you an idea of how comfortable and accurate it is to operate.

I did a good amount of research on other devices before buying this product. I initially wanted a sleek smartwatch that also had great fitness tracking modes, but apparently you either get a pretty smartwatch/OK fitness tracker, or a decent fitness tracker/outdated looking smartwatch. In the end I decided I wanted mainly a fitness tracker that has some smartwatch features, and that I wouldn't use most of the features on an actual smartwatch.

PROS

The app is awesome! My husband is a software developer so I learn a lot about what makes good apps good and what makes bad apps bad. This app is free and user friendly. It has mostly accurate measurements and you can easily track your progress and areas of improvement. It also has a feature that allows whoever you send the link to to track your location, in case you are concerned about getting kidnapped on your run. Very good stuff.

The steps I get seem to be pretty consistent as well as the distance traveled. The heartrate tracker seems to be mostly accurate (checked with manual pulse check).

The battery life is pretty good. Obviously I would use more battery if I am using the fitness modes. Depending on your activity level and use of the fitness modes, the battery could last you all week plus some. The battery charges to full in about 30 minutes.

I like the rectangular watch face and the light green band. I also like that you can change the bands. Apparently for some of the expensive FitBit models the band is not changeable so some people just buy a whole new watch. Like whaaat?

CONS
I like being able to see the texts I get on the watch, but I don't really care for receiving phone calls (I get so many spam calls that I don't even answer my phone lol). I don't think there is a way to say 'no' to having phone calls, so I get frequent notifications to enable phone call permissions. It's not too much of a problem but it's kind of annoying sometimes.

I think the sleep tracker is interesting, but I don't think it is accurate. I think that as long as you are "resting" during the hours that you put as your sleeping hours under Settings, that it considers this as sleep. Sometimes I can't sleep but the device considers this as light sleep. I think this would be an interesting addition, that perhaps it could be integrated: I am a night shift worker and I switch between day/night sleep, so I have to manually enter my bedtimes in the app's User Settings to sleep. I think that if there was an activity button, like when you choose walk/run/cardio on the watch itself, for sleep, it would be easier for me personally. I am not sure if that could be done with a software update or if this is a hardware type thing.

FINAL THOUGHTS

I wear this watch almost 24/7 and I think it has helped me consider and evaluate my activity levels as well as track my improvement. I think that if Garmin made a watch that had the aesthetics and watch interface comparable to the Apple watch but kept the good fitness aspect, I would definitely purchase as an upgrade.

An upgrade of Nikon's original digital-only tele kit zoom, this new 55-200mm f/4-5.6 ($250, street) adds Vibration Reduction and a number of optical improvements for only $70 more. A 3.6X 82-300mm equivalent zoom, it's not expected to be bundled in Nikon DSLR kits any time soon.

Hands on:

The barrel, when contracted, is nearly an inch longer than the earlier 55-200mm non-VR DX lens, but is still extremely light as a result of all-plastic construction, including the lensmount. The large zoom ring's slightly uneven and underdamped turning action is what you'd expect from a lens at this price. The narrow manual-focusing ring is even-turning but also underdamped, with a very short turning radius for fast, if coarse, manual focusing. AF action on our test camera, the D40x, was adequately fast and quiet, thanks to Nikon's Silent Wave Motor in the lens.

In the lab:

SQF tests found Excellent sharpness and contrast at all focal lengths -- an improvement over the earlier, non-VR version of this lens. DxO Analyzer 2.0 tests found Imperceptible barrel distortion at 55mm (0.08%), and Slight pincushion distortion at 105mm and 200mm (0.24% and 0.19%, respectively). All three are also improvements over the earlier lens. Light falloff was gone from the corners by f/5 at 55mm, f/7.1 at 105mm, and f/8 at 200mm.

At the uniform close-focusing distance of approximately 43.5 inches, tests of close-up ability found maximum magnification ratios ranging from 1:14.25 at 55mm to 1:3.8 at 200mm, about an average magnifying power, and not up to the 1:3.4 turned in by the non-VR 55-200mm. DxO Analyzer Blur tests of the lens' first-generation VR system (at 200mm) showed an improvement for three users of about 3 stops of extra handheld sharpness at slower shutter speeds; 4 stops are possible with Nikon's VR II system.

Conclusions:

Even though it's the earlier version of VR, to get any VR at this price is a steal.
