My computer told me this, but it refused to tell me how to fix the problem in spite of tantalizing me with hints. It was a bit like an adventure game in which you have to find the right version of "XYZZY" in order to get things to work. Once I finally figured out how to make my computer recognize the BTD-300, everything went smoothly. It connected with the sound bar and has been streaming music from Spotify to the speaker without a hitch.

The price was quite good, and the size is perfect. It's small and unobtrusive, but unlike some other small-size USB plug-ins, it's easy to insert and remove. It's got a bit of a lip and it's large enough to hang on to.

Until I get tired of streaming music, I doubt I'll use it for any other device, but when and if I do, I don't anticipate any problems.

I have a tabletop radio that gives me weather alerts, but hauling it around with me in case we have to take shelter would be a big pain, not to mention how useless it could be in case of power failure. The CWR 200 sits in its cradle, charging, until it's needed. Then it can be tucked in a pocket or clipped to a belt while you get the family to safety. Wherever you are, it'll be there giving you information you need.

Even at lowest volume it's more than loud enough to be heard. Programming is easy, it charges fast and holds its charge. I get very good reception with it, though I can't speak to what other people might get. That's an individual thing.

For a solid, portable option in emergencies, the CWR 200 seems to be a good choice.

I spent months, literally, shopping for a radio for my kitchen/dining area. I had awful problems with reception with every radio I had in there, so reception was at the top of my want list. Size and cost figured in too, but reception was the key because I like listening to the radio while I work.

Every radio I researched had someone complaining about the horrible reception. Every single one. I was paralyzed with fear that I'd pick the wrong one so I just kept looking, hoping to find one where everyone said "Get it, the reception is fantastic!"

Finally I realized that reception depends on so many variables that no radio is going to work for everyone everywhere and I was able to quit shopping and actually order the Sangean CL-100. The price was good and the size was perfect for the space I had in mind.

I know you're all waiting with bated breath to hear that the reception, even in an old building where it's difficult to get good cell reception, is spectacularly good. It even picks up a lot of the smaller and more distant stations. Tuning and changing settings is relatively simple and the sound quality is good enough for a kitchen radio. It has some serious volume on it, so I can turn it up and listen while I'm making the bed or cleaning the bathroom. No the sound isn't great at that distance, but again, it's all a matter of convenience for this radio.

If you're like me and want a small, simple-to-operate radio that will (probably, no guarantee) pick up your favorite stations, give the Sangean a shot. You could spend more, but do you really need to?

I've had problems with Pixmas in the past, mostly having to do with wireless networks and having to reinstall the software over and over to try to get them to hang on to network settings. I can't guarantee that this printer is going to be any better in the long run, but the set-up actually works pretty well if you use the standard version, not the WPS... and I'm getting way ahead of myself on this one.

To begin with, the printer requires a lot of time for set-up. You're not going to be doing this on the fly, so set aside an hour or so to: 1) remove all the tape of which there is much, 2) read over the instructions 3) install the ink, 4) run a print alignment 5) set up your wireless connection (about which more in a moment) 6) install the software (which takes a good 15 minutes or more), and 7) put the machine (and yourself) through its paces. Yeah, it's going to take a while.

Now I know you can read about the features on your own, so I'm here to tell you about the things that work for me and those that don't. First off, the wireless set-up is confusing. Choose Standard instead of WPS and save yourself some headaches unless you're a computer whiz kid. After the third error message in the WPS set-up I went to standard, entered my pass code and had the connection up and running in about a minute.

Once that was done and the software was installed I fired up the Canon Image Garden. First I scanned an image and attempted to rotate, crop and fix any deficiencies I found. The scan was over sharp and looked a bit jagged, but a little fiddling with the Canon software fixed that. Canon software also rotated and cropped perfectly. One really nice feature is that they remind you to put the printing side of the paper down in the paper cassette. How many pieces of paper will that save?

The biggest complaint I had was that it didn't give me a choice of which paper cassette to use for printing, so I got a ridiculously truncated image on the first try. I believe it chooses the paper based on the size of the image, which I get, but at the same time that limits flexibility in printing. I opened another photo processing program and it allowed me to print from whatever cassette I liked. Coupled with a better suite of applications for correction and enhancement, I think it's safe to say that I'll be using the Canon software almost never.

Printing on plain paper is clearly not going to be as satisfactory as it is on glossy, but in some cases I found it surprisingly good, good enough to give you an idea of what sort of image you're going to end up with when you switch to photo paper. It's also more than good enough for printing out emails and web pages.

Scanning and printing are both pretty fast, another plus. And the copy function works pretty seamlessly without any sort of computer interface. Just punch a couple of buttons and Bob's your uncle! It does take a bit of time to warm up and is a little noisy but no more so than any Canon printer I've ever used. It's not bothersome, in my opinion. You might feel otherwise.

Inks are easy to install, but you'll find refills pricey, no question. I suspect off-brand ones are available or will be soon enough.

In short, it's a good, inexpensive printer for a home or home office. Use photo paper and settings and get the full quality the MG5420 is capable of producing; I think it's pretty remarkable. The photos I printed out are as good as or in one case, better than the original. That's a powerful recommendation in my book.

Right out of the box this clock was impressive because it comes pre-programmed. In fact it threw me for a loop because the day of the week is tied into the date, which means somewhere in there is a program that is keeping track of the year. And here's my first criticism: If the clock knows the year, why isn't it displayed? The instructions suggest that there is a year display but I've found no evidence of one. I have an email in to the company asking about it, but so far no response. If and when I receive one I'll cheerfully update this review.

The clock itself is so large that I initially felt that its primary use is more commercial than residential. But I remembered my caregiver days and realized that this would have been a fantastically useful item for both my parents, but particularly for my mother who suffered from severe visual impairment. I have it set up in my living room in daylight and I don't find the unlit LEDs to be in any way distracting. The clock has three brightness settings (In spite of what some other reviewers have said, you can dim it.) however if you're planning on using it in a bedroom, the lowest setting might still be too bright. And here's where my second complaint comes in: If you want to hang it, there's no easy way to access the controls. It might have been nice to have the dimmer control in an easy-to-reach spot. As it is, you can only dim it with relative ease if you are using it on a flat surface. Ditto setting it, though supposedly there is no need to reset the clock in the event of a power failure. The AC adapter has a good long cord, so you do have a certain amount of flexibility about placement.

As for hanging the clock, it requires two screws. One won't cut it unless you want to hang it sideways, which would be a decorating statement, certainly, but not terrifically useful. Alas, the company has seen fit to include only one screw and one anchor. Kinda sloppy.

Also sloppy is the fact that the box says "calander clock" instead of "calendar clock." Call me a grammar nerd if you want, but that's not a positive representation of the company, in my opinion. It made me wonder if the clock itself was going to be cheap and badly designed. Fortunately aside from the few minor problems noted above, it seems to be a product of reasonably good quality. Time will tell -- excuse the pun -- if it has staying power.

ETA: I set this up in my basement workroom and discovered that while it was unplugged it jumped ahead a few days. Strange but easy enough to fix. What bemused me was that when I went down to the basement and opened the door, the room was flooded with this eerie light, and it took me a minute to figure out that I wasn't being visited by aliens, but that the light from the clock was so bright it lit up the whole corner of the basement. Leave it in a darkened room. Confound your neighbors each night.

It's not often you encounter a power strip/surge protector with twelve grounded outlets. Six is, of course, more common. But the Belkin manages to double the number of available outlets while taking up not a whole lot more space. The arrangement of the outlets is pretty clever, too, with six flanking a central strip of six. Thus there are six convenient outlets for those ginormous transformers we all seem to have so many of these days, and six for regular plugs, so there's no lost functionality to the bulky transformer bodies. It also has two USB charging ports so you can easily charge your iPod or Kindle as I do without using a regular plug.

There's an on/off switch and a pair of lights that tell you if the strip is properly grounded or not. The plug to the wall is also one of those low-profile plugs so it'll fit in the outlet behind the bookcase or the media cabinet without forcing all the cabinets forward. There's also a power cord manager at the bottom that locks your cords in place so they're not hanging all over. And the outlets have sliding covers to keep dirt and small fingers out. Unfortunately only the main part of the plug has a cover. The grounding hole doesn't. Now I don't know enough about electricity to know if this is some sort of oversite but it seems to me that covering the whole outlet would be a better choice. I could be wrong, so don't automatically assume that it's a problem.

Belkin surge protectors come with a limited lifetime warranty on the unit itself, and an equipment warranty which will reimburse you for any equipment losses should your surge protector fail to... well protect your stuff from surges. 3000 joules of protection seems like a whole lot to me, so I'm going to assume this is a pretty good warranty. I don't really know what sort of hoops you'll have to jump through to get your money in case of failure since I started reading the warranty and my eyes glazed over. But it's a little peace of mind for expensive stuff like laptops.

All things considered I think this is a pretty well designed product with a good warranty, and I don't know that you could go far wrong with Belkin, so I'm going to recommend it. There might be better ones on the market, but I haven't tried any of them. And let's face it, it's always good to have a little protection and a couple of extra outlets.

This is a nice cover.  It's a little rigid, but if you work with it long enough you'll probably find it loosening up a bit.  The color is a matte bubblegum pink; not exactly a shade that charms my socks off but it's fine.  Honestly if it wasn't for the fact that it's a green product I'd probably say "Meh, fine as far as it goes."  But I give mad props for anything that doesn't require petroleum.

[[VIDEOID:ce9372435451bc2c3bda4d2794c79f4f]] I am really impressed with this camera. The Flip MinoHd package pretty much does everything the average user needs it to do. It takes high quality video, transfers it to your computer, lets you stitch videos together to create movies, allows you to trim your videos, pull snapshots out of them and helps you share them to various websites including Facebook and YouTube.

The Flip comes partly charged right out of the box, but they do suggest that you let it charge for 5 hours before you use it. I plugged it into a USB port on my laptop for about an hour before using it and the battery was fully charged. Operation is a cinch. Turn it on, point and press the red button. The zoom in button is + the zoom out is -. Delete is a trashcan. How much more obvious can this be? The only problem I have with the recording is that pressing the zoom controls doesn't always produce the desired effect immediately and I tend to get a bit of a jitter in the frames where I'm trying to get it to recognize the command. Of course I'm still getting used to holding the camera, so I expect that I'll get steadier as I learn the feel of it in my hand.

Uploading your vids to your computer is also simple. Again, plug it into a spare USB port and there they are. There's software included on the camera's hard drive, and it's a nice little program called FlipShare that helps you label, sort and share your vids pretty easily. Though again, I do have a quibble with the saving part. It will only let you save to your C drive in the video library. Meh, I figure it's simple enough to copy the vids to another drive when I'm done. The software also helps you cobble together shorter vids into a movie, complete with music -- you can use the tunes they've provided or any MP3 on your computer -- which can be softer than the sound on the video, louder or which can replace the sound completely. Their selection of music is fairly uninspiring, but what can you really expect? When you're done, you can upload or email your videos with FlipShare, or make a video greeting card with one of their templates. I've used FlipShare to upload a video to my Facebook account and it works very smoothly.

As for quality, I've looked at these vids in four different sizes and I have to say that with the exception of the ones I shot at night, the quality even in the largest size is exceptionally good. The night vids tend to be a bit pixelated at the larger sizes, but not so much that you can't enjoy them. I haven't checked the quality on my HDTV yet, but I'm going to guess that it'll prove to be surprisingly good. However, you don't have to take my word for this. The video I've appended to this review shows the same Halloween decoration in daylight and at night. I leave it to you all to judge the quality.

The camera itself is compact, light and relatively easy to handle. It comes with a wrist strap and a drawstring bag. I hesitate to use the wrist strap, though, since a free-swinging camera might end up smashing itself into things as I went about my business. It's fine if I'm actively engaged in shooting a video, but not so much if I'm just carrying it around with me in case I find something to record.

Given what this recorder does, and the simple but useful software that comes with it, I really think the SRP is reasonable. This isn't professional grade stuff, but it's more than good enough for most of us. It takes good quality video and makes it easy to edit and share that video with friends. What more could you really ask at this price point? I am sold on the Flip and I think you will be too.

I love my laptop; it's freed me to work in any room in the house and for that alone I'd nominate it for the greatest invention of the century. ButI don't much like the keyboard and I flat-out hate the touch pad, so I've been wanting a free-standing mouse for a while now. Along came the Logitech desktop bundle and suddenly I've got the sort of flexibility I'd been craving. They aren't kidding when they say it's ready to work right out of the box. I could do all the most basic functions without ever programming a thing. Once I installed the software, I got a lot more control. I was able to program the mouse buttons to give me single, double and right click functions as well as scrolling, the most common functions for my work. The keyboard functions include an easy application switcher, a button which boots up the default email program, and one which I've programmed to open my browser. Another key opens the control panel, and a fifth I've programmed to bring up my documents window -- a huge time-saver for a writer. There's also a key to bring up the calculator. Function keys are similarly programmable, and with the amount of choice I have I could automate all of my most common tasks and still have keys left over. There are also control keys for audio functions, and all the standard keys including a keypad which was sorely missed in my laptop. There's even a key to check battery status on both mouse and keyboard.

One of the things I liked most about the keyboard is that it can apparently be secured against keystroke monitors. Not that I have a lot of concern about that particular issue with my set-up, but people who are working in unsecured office space might well appreciate that feature.

The keys have a good, solid feel to them, and are surprisingly quiet for a stand-alone keyboard. The mouse works beautifully on a bare desk, and has a good hand feel.

If Logitech quality holds true for this duo, I look forward to many years of heavy use for both. At it's current price point, I'd call this set a bargain, and one well worth checking out.
I wish it had other sounds, but a great little clock for the price. Hasn't failed me yet.

I only just got these, but so far I really like them. I usually use AKG, Sony, and V-Moda circumaural studio monitors for music listening and earbuds for walks, runs, or working out.

Highs are very clear, and the hiss of a snair drum or certain consonant sounds (s, f, etc.) come through a little stronger than usual.

My favorite part is that there is a sense of space the the sound. Different vocals and instruments are distinguishable, and it feels like they are spread out in a small room. It's not the big soundstage feeling I get from headphones, but it's far better than I'm used to hearing from an earbud.

Mine fit pretty well right out of the box. They get mildly uncomfortable after an hour or two of wear, and some foam tips would probably be a good investment for both comfort and sound. I have rather large ears, which may be part of why these big things fit so well.

So I'm very impressed so far. With some equalizer adjustments and foam tips, I expect these will get even better. But right out of the box, they sound like something worth more than $20. They beat some old Beats I have, and get close to some Sennheisers I tried iut.

One last note: the 90 degree 3.5 mm jack on the included cable doesn't fit my phone of it is in a case. But it works fine with a headphone amp, computer, or phone without case.

If these break or change with use, I'll post and update.

I don't see myself wearing these in public much, though. More recently, I grabbed a set of MEE Electronics M6 earbuds, which don't cost much more, stay in just as well if not better while running, don't look nearly as silly, and sound considerably better.

So, these are pretty good for earbuds under $10, and they'd be OK for under $20. However, there are better options out there for only a little bit more money.

Even pre break-in, these sounded great: probably the best headphones under $20 I've found. After break-in, these MEE buds were sounding like something that cost 4-5 times as much with a nice, even frequency response that favors bass only slightly. I find them comparable to $60-$80 Sennheisers, my previous favorites (which superseded Sony and Koss buds that I also liked). These MEE buds came with 3 sets (S, M, and L) of your typical soft rubber earpieces as well as 2 sets of the interesting multi-tiered earpieces shown in the photos and a pretty standard cloth case. Between the various earpiece options, it's unlikely anyone will have an issue finding a good fit.

The cord is about 1 m long, which suits my purposes. I like the over-the-ear wire bits, too, as they prevent tugs on the cord from dislodging them. They might be awkward with some kinds of glasses, but my straight-earpiece sunglasses fit over them fine. They can be bent to hang down more like normal earbuds if desired, though.

I'll be checking out more MEE products now, seeing what a great value these were. I still favor AKG and Beyerdynamic at the high end, but for my biking/hiking/running/workout listening needs, I'll probably be coming back to MEE.

This will be a fairly detailed and honest review.

1. Who is this for?
This computer is what I would consider a gateway computer. Those who are looking at upgrading a fairly old or not so powerful laptop and are looking to do a little more productivity, this is a great option.

2. What do you get?
Well you can probably read the description, however it's worth noting. You get an Intel i7 7500u CPU (dual core with 4 threads) 12gb DDR4 RAM, Nvidia 940mx GPU, a 256gb SSD, 15.6" 1080p screen, fingerprint reader, and a backlit keyboard.

The reason I mention all of the feautures is because you would be hardpressed to find another laptop with these features for the same price. To my knowledge there is not laptop on the market for $800 with an i7, dedicated graphics, 12gb of RAM and an SSD. This is really one of the best values on the market right now.

With all of that said, this isn't for everyone. If you want to do extensive gaming, this is not for you. Can it game? Yes, light gaming can be achieved, however it isn't marketed as a gaming laptop. Is this for someone who wants to do editing (video, audio, photos)? Yes, again light editing can be achieved.

What blew me away with this computer is the speakers! They are fantastic! I usually use headphones and would consider myself somewhat picky with sound, and for laptop speakers these are really something great.

This computer is really a middle of the pack all arounders dream. If you dabble in a little of this and a little of that but don't do anything professionally or extremely serious, this is really all you need.

Also, everyone's experience is different. Some hate loud fans, and if this is pushed the fans will be audible. Some don't like that the backlit keyboard times out after 30 seconds of no use. These things really don't bother me.

Lastly, the versatility of this laptop is really great. I've bought tablets and sold them because I couldn't justify having a laptop and tablet, then bought tablets again because I missed the things I could do with them that I was missing on a laptop. This solved all of those issues except size. It's pretty big, which for some is a plus others its not.

Overall, if you are looking at upgrading and don't want to spend $1,200-2,000 on a flagship model laptop this is a great option! I can't recommend this enough.

Software Features:
This AGPtEK mp3 player is a really good alternative to an ipod or zune which is more expensive and offers less storage space while offering the opportunity to drag and drop files into the mp3 player folder directly, once it's connected via usb cable to your computer. This feature is important to me, because not all my music is properly tagged, so music organizing software like itunes doesn't recognise the files. This is no problem with the AGPtEK mp3 player, since I can always manually find the file and drop it in.
Hardware Features: The build is attractive and sturdy. I appreciate the glass display and nice solid but light aluminum casing. The shape is a basic rectangle which works fine for me since I like a minimalist look. One thing I don't like about the build is that the click wheel click very loudly and is a little stiff, which is a hassle to use when you're trying to scroll down your music list.The wheel feels a little cheap, its quality is not on par with the rest of the build. The screen is not as large as a typical ipod's but is sufficient. The title of your song will have to scroll a bit to be read fully, which can be kind annoying. ANother great thing is that you can upgrade storage using a micro SD chip which means you're quadrupling your storage. score!

Music Playback features: They have a nice EQ option if you're into that. The fast forward is really slow. The mp3 player plays a bunch of different formats like mp3, oog, wav, flac, etc... You can also store audiobooks, videos, photos, and record sound. I havn't use these features yet.

Accessories: The arm band is a nice bonus. It fits perfectly and leaves holes for charging and headphones. It holds the mp3 player snuggly. The band is smooth and not scratchy. If you have small arms the band can be pretty big, it's adjustable but there will be somg extra band hanging around. t is fastened by velcro.
The headphones are like $10 quality. They're not bad, but they're not audiophile. They don't fit very well as I have small ears but they'll do in a pinch.

The mp3's battery is very good, I haven't been able to drain the battery completely, but keeping it off, it's been able to stay charged for over 3 days.

I needed covers for two different remotes; as a result, I got to do a general comparison of this cover to a unit from another manufacturer that sold in pairs. While the covers from the other manufacturer were of nominal quality and fit, this one easily it in a few important areas:
1) This skin seems only slightly thicker but holds its shape and resists deformation much better. The thickness matches the button height well, and the holes also have beveled/rounded edges rather than being cut straight through. The bevels provide a nice feel; It feels much more like a single unit when it's on the remote, and it's still easy to tell where the buttons are. The other cover was easier to stretch lending to obvious stress in a few narrow spots when putting it on the remote. Once on, felt too stretchy and mobile on the remote even though it technically fit and the straight hole edges were very distracting and much higher than the buttons.
2) The hole size and the thickness/location of the area for lanyard attachment on this unit is perfect for reasonably easy threading with the cover off or on the remote. The attachment feels like it would be tough to rip out accidentally or to loosen/slip. Due to materials, the lanyard attachment pulls the attachment point evently rather than threatening to cut through the material. The attachment site on the other cover was too thin and had holes that were difficult enough to thread when off the remote; the wiry attachment loop would only take a few hours to cut through the cover.
3) the lanyard seems to be good quality. The attachment loop is not too thin or wiry, and the wrist loop is a cord with a nice feel and enough body to it to keep a nice shape without being too chunky. When attached to the remote, it is secure and structurally sound. The ribbon loop lanyard that came with the other company's cover is obviously sub-par quality, even for bulk ribbon lanyards--enough said.

Overall, I am very happy with everything about this cover. When I find one from this mfr for my other remote, I'll be getting one for it.

This keyboard works pretty well. Good amount of resistance in the keys, and it has lasted me almost two years. It is just now starting to lose accuracy in one of the shift buttons.

Pros: Has lasted fairly well. Keys are lit enough to make viewing easier without being too bright. Convenient hot keys. VERY convenient mute key is the top right corner where it is easy to find quickly. A little "clacky" but not super noisy. Few accidental letter presses. Build quality is pretty good.

Cons: The enter key is according to a non-US layout. The \ button is right beside the enter, and it took me about a year to stop accidentally typing a slash. If you are used to this layout it is fine, but do be aware that it is not the standard US keyboard layout.

Other: the volume knob is very handy, though after a year and a half it mysteriously fell off... not sure if it was misused by my kids or if it was spontaneous.

Bottom line: it's a good build and it should work for you if you prefer this (international?) keyboard layout over the standard US keyboard layout.

Best sounding in-ear headphones I've ever heard, by a mile. I've owned the Bang and Olufsen H3, Sony XBA H1, Klipsch S4, X7, X6i, 1More Dual Drivers, Beats by Dr Dre Tour (wired), and Monster Cable's Jamz and Turbines.

The bass has lots of range and goes DEEP, in some tracks it even reminds me of my Kicker CVR 12' car subwoofer I used to blast about 15 years ago. It is not quite that overpowering, of course, and it balances out nicely with the other frequencies. The midrange is very present and natural sounding judging by how vocals and guitar strings sound. The highs are beautiful, they sound very accurate to me and present no sibilance. The overall sound is very rich and detailed, it allows you to follow specific instruments as you listen, and it even presents some soundstage (which I didn't think was possible in in-ears, maybe my aforementioned B&O H3 had some)

Overall these do have a V sound signature with boosted bass and treble, but not as marked as almost everything else that's in the market. In order to eliminate any fatigue caused by this, I would strongly recommend that you disable any bass boost, make sure you're not elevating bass or treble at all in EQ, and go even deeper and disable default features like Dolby Atmos (Oneplus phone) and even the Hi Fi quad DAC on LG phones (which I've found does introduce a bit of a V curve itself)

Other than their sound these earphones' build quality seems very good and durable. I'm in disbelief they could cost $60. You're welcome

Everything that is included is of adequate quality, and everything was useful. I needed to provide a heat gun and safety glasses (do wear safety glasses, prescription glasses would work just as well, or a face shield--i had little pieces of glass pinging me in the face as I removed the very cracked digitizer).

All told the replacement took me 3 hours to complete. I followed instructions on the iFixit site; there were a few discrepancies but fairly trivial ones, and it included many tips, cautions, and comments, in addition to the directions, that were more than adequate to make the repair fairly easy. As I mentioned, the glass was a mess of cracks, I covered the screen with a couple of layers of packaging tape to hold the majority of shards together as I worked. Once the glass was off everything went pretty smoothly.

The two things which I think should have been included are adhesive and gloves. The glass is taped down, and at least in my case, the tape is almost impossible to recover. The gloves would make keeping the screen and glass free of finger prints. Both would be pretty cheap.

Short version: When used appropriately, this is a great device at a great price. Simple installation options and useful features. Stronger wireless transceivers than my Netgear cable modem/router. The key here is a lot if not most people don't know how or when to use these devices...so I'll try to help with that below.

Long version: Let's assume you're buying this for your home to extend existing WiFi coverage. Before you do anything, conduct an analysis of existing networks in your area and what frequencies and channels they are using. On 2.4GHz, channel 1, 6, and 11 do not overlap. Ideally, you want to be using one of these channels without anyone else nearby using it so go ahead and reconfigure your router to meet that criteria. There aren't any overlapping channels on 5GHz and it may be used less by your neighbors so that could be worth pursuing for you as well. Next, try moving your WiFi router around to find the ideal spot to cover the entire house. If your router has external antenna(s), you can try using a more directional antenna if you think that'll help and your router has connections for it or reorienting existing antennas. If you find a perfect configuration with this that works everywhere in the home, run a new cable to that location for your Internet if necessary and you're done and didn't need this device.

Now on to tips for setting up this device. Use a different SSID than your existing one by appending something like "_EXT". This will help you troubleshoot any issues in the future and help get you on the right network at the right times. Do upgrade the firmware on it after initial setup. Keep in mind, no affordable repeater seamlessly bounces you to whichever device has the best signal at any given second. That is handled by the client, i.e. your phone, laptop, etc. and it's not always perfect. I haven't tried it, but I think this device can be wired to your router. That is the best way to use this, but may not be required depending on your situation. If extending it using only WiFi, put it somewhere that has decent signal already and will reach to where you're lacking signal.

The Power schedule and LED on/off schedules are nice touches. It increased my coverage and bandwidth 5x where I needed it to after an easy 5-10 minute setup including getting the firmware and applying it. I am a former networking professional. I didn't go in to extreme detail because this is a review, not a blog...research anything I mentioned where you have questions and the info is out there. Or have a buddy help you with it or a company that does residential on-site work and don't let them bill you more than an hour and a trip charge.

I had a very specific need in mind when I researched BT transmitters, and I was happy to have found this one that both transmits and receives Bluetooth. I wasn't sure what need I would ever have to receive Bluetooth, but I did need to use it as a receiver, and decided to go ahead and give this one a shot. The price was reasonable without being too cheap. I hadn't heard of the Trond brand before, but I liked that it came with a flexible 2.5 mm connector because I intended to use it on my non-BT FiiO X5 (2nd Gen) which spends much time inside of my pocket (i.e., the flexible cable would be much better than a stiff unit plugged straight into the FiiO).

I liked that there was a switch to toggle between transmit or receive. I also liked how easy it was to pair as no codes were needed. It paired right up to my Bose Bluetooth headphones and within moments I was enjoying the hi-fi sound from the FiiO X5 2nd gen player via Bluetooth via the wireless Bose headphones. This would otherwise be unheard of without a gadget such as this!

I also like the status lights on it. Red = not connected. Blue = connected. Flashing Red/Blue: in pairing mode. Easy peasy. Instructions are emailed to you with your welcome email from TROND. I'd recommend PDFing these so you don't forget, because it's not easy to locate them online.

Once I realized how handy this was, I started thinking of all sorts of uses for this little BT transmitter/receiver. I have paired my laptop to it and use the Logitech Z623 Subwoofer/Speakers set with it, just by switching it to Receive mode and plugging it into the 2.5 mm jack in the speaker. I know I can do the same with the 20 year old RCA receiver as well. I have been considering a few other uses as well.

All in all, I've found this to be an amazingly versatile device that I'm very glad that I bought. Recharging it via micro USB is simple as pie. The battery life is nothing short of fantastic -- I can get 10+ hours of use out of it before I think about charging it. It can be used while it's charging, which is definitely a plus.

If you have any need whatsoever for a Bluetooth receiver OR a Bluetooth transmitter, this is going to be the right device for you, because you'll find yourself finding other ways to use it.

The sound is unheard of (ha ha, sorry for the pun). Nothing compares to the quality of sound that comes out of this little machine, for its size and price. Pair it with a set of high quality hi-fi headphones and some FLAC music files, and you've got yourself an insane little music machine. You'll never go back to Apple or another brand of music player. You'll find yourself hooking it up to your home sound system and playing all of your music through it. I can't say enough for the sound quality. You WILL notice a difference between crummy .mp3 files and other low-quality sound files. You WILL find yourself craving FLAC files, and you will go wherever you can to find them. You might even start converting your entire CD music collection into FLAC, even though you'd already converted them all to .mp3. You WILL find yourself hoping that someday soon, Amazon will start offering FLAC files instead of .mp3s! (HINT HINT NUDGE NUDGE!) ;) Seriously, though, you probably haven't realized how GOOD your music will sound until you listen to it on this FiiO X5 2nd gen. Even the .mp3s sound better. Especially if you use noise cancelling headphones.

I like that you can adjust the configuration and tell it which buttons to remain active when the screen is off, depending on your preferences. I also like that there are several preset themes to choose from. The screen is easy to read and nicely displays album art.

The unit itself has a wonderful weight to it given the aluminum shell. The volume wheel moves easily and there is a slight tactile feedback click. That wheel controls both the song volume and song selection, depending on which screen you're on when you use it. The power on button has a tiny LED light that's blue when it's running and red when it's charging. There are volume up/down buttons beneath the power button and those buttons are some of the buttons that you can choose whether or not to have active while the screen is off.

I'm not sure if I there's a firmware update that needs to be done that could change this, but there are a couple of things that are pretty bothersome in general about this unit:

1) There is no way to search for a song. If, like me, you have more than 5,000 songs, it's impossible to sit and scroll through each album/folder to find a specific song. I suppose if you're some kind of major organization guru (which I thought I was, but apparently not at this), it would be possible to arrange your music folders into genres or some other category to make it easier to get to the exact music you need to play, but if you've moved over from iTunes like I have, you're probably real spoiled with the ability to view songs either by artist, album, song name, etc., as well as the ability to do a search. Here, you're pretty much on your own, depending on how you've got your music library set up. Having purchased most of my music here on Amazon, it's all arranged by artist name in individual folders. I have several hundred folders set up like this, and scrolling through everything with that scroll wheel can take a very, very long time to find the one thing you're looking for.

2) The unit can be quite SLOW to respond to your clicks. It is not touch-screen, and when you click on a button to change tracks forward/backward or to change from looking at what's playing into another option, such as a list of the songs on the album, it can be quite sluggish. Again, if you're used to using an iPod, you'll be frustrated with the lack of responsiveness of this unit. Again, I keep hoping a firmware update will come out that addresses this.

3) Whenever you add music to your micro SD card(s) [NOTE: There is NO onboard storage, it's purely on whatever card(s) you insert into it] you have to completely update your whole media library. This can take a long time depending on how much music you have, so keep this in mind and don't expect to add music and listen to it immediately. In other words, plan ahead for this :)

4) It's not as user friendly as the typical Apple products you may be used to. You'll get used to it, but don't expect the polished feel because of issues like #1 and #2, above.

5) Playlists are not straightforward. Yes, you can be playing a song and add it to a playlist that resides on one of your SD cards. However, importing playlists can be tricky and you may find yourself looking to the internet to help convert your existing playlists from your prior player. Expect to spend some time on this unless you're totally okay with starting over from scratch (I wasn't okay with this). Also, any playlists that you save to your SD card that you've hand-converted do not show up as a playlist on the FiiO. Instead, you have to navigate to the file on your player as if you were looking for a song, and play it as if you were playing a song. Only playlists you've created on the machine show up in the Playlist section, not playlists you've brought in from elsewhere. There is no 'import' feature or anything fancy like that, so you're pretty much on your own unless you add a song one at a time to Playlist 1, Playlist 2, etc. (I do not yet see a way to rename these as there is no keyboard function on this machine, so you're stuck with those names).

I think with time, the FiiO's software will catch up closer to what you're seeing from the high-visibility media consumer based music players, but right now with this X5 you should be more concerned with how WONDERFUL your music sounds vs the issues associated with the frumpy software that comes with it.

I really went through a lot trying to find ways to be able to write for hours per day without getting my hand and arm tired. The iPad Pro 12.9” is where this all took me and now the PAPER LIKE screen protector is my latest aid in this endeavor.

This is day one and I already ordered the 7.9” for same day delivery because I’m so impressed with the 12.9” for my iPad Pro. If you write all day with the Apple Pencil, you need this. You really do need this. Protects the screen. Gives you an anti glare surface, and it feels like paper.

It's a San Francisco Victorian with bent hallways and a nightmare for both cell reception and WiFi range.

I have wanted to get networking from the back of the flat to the front. That seemingly simple concept never works. What I did get to work was to put WiFi in the back, and then a WiFi extender in the front with a 20' antenna extension which then pushed the antenna to the middle. Even that was tricky.

I even once tried a Verizon 4G LTE router to get some broadband in the front. It was expensive and still didn't work. So I pretty much resigned myself to just running cat5e or cat6 cable down the hallway, which is what I wanted to avoid. But right before I did that I decided to give this a shot.

The install took all of 5 seconds, seriously. Plug a box into one outlet in the back of the flat. Plug that box into my switch. Now run to the front of the flat. Plug that box into an outlet. Run the Ethernet from that box to my switch. Plug Linux box into switch. Boot up and test the speed. 53 MB/sec down, 4 up. Pretty much my ISP limit. My only concern is security, but they do have software, but it requires Windows I bet. I use Linux. I'll see what I can do to lock this down. But it does work. Fantastically so. Not sure the front and back are on the same circuit. Guessing they are. Either way, I finally got the front connected to the back without WiFi or a long Ethernet running down my hallway. And that is 5 stars!

I just unpackaged and started using the Amazon Fire TV. Right off I had to do a small update which didn't take long at all. Next there is a neat video that shows you how to use the device. I think this is the first time I have had a video box teach me how to use it with a video. It is a nice touch.

I'm already a prime member, but for those who are not the video spoke of a 30 days trial.

Right off the bat I noticed in the main menu of items to choose from that there are movies, tv, watchlist, video library, games, apps, photo and settings. What's missing from this is the Amazon Music of which I have quite a few albums. I hope we get to see music in some future update. That's kind of a glaring omission in my opion. One star knocked off for that right there.

One cool feature I noted right off the bat is that the device already knows me. I didn't have to log in or do anything.

The watchlist

So I went straight to my watchlist to confirm that it indeed already knows me. It does. And I went to a recent season of shows I am watching where the first two episodes have been watched and the third has not. There is a white bar at the bottom of those watched and missing from the one that is yet to be watched. So I'll guess that is my progress bar as well. Nice touch.

Voice feature

This feature is slightly confusing to me right off. What you do is hold the mic button down until you hear a tone, then continue to hold it down as you speak your question or title search. When you are done talking, only then do you release the button. I kept letting it go as soon as I heard the tone, which causes it to attempt to process the question. So the feature is a little odd, but once you get used to that oddity it works quite well.

I asked it, "what's new this week" and got three suggestions. I further asked it questions like, show me my watchlist which offered me two methods, "watch list" and "watchlist". Neither of which showed me my actual watchlist. Clearly the audio search isn't yet fully aware of navigation.

Purchasing a TV show

Photos

Looks like they have an iOS and Android app that lets you share photos with Amazon Cloud Drive and thus have them available on this device. I'll have to try that out. I'll skip it for now.

Apps

This looks good for now. NetFlix and Pandora are here as well as Hulu. I use all three of those so that's good.

Games

There are good looking games here. I didn't buy the game controller as I own a console already, but I might rethink that.

YouTube

I didn't see YouTube, so I did a voice search and an app popped up. Once the app downloaded and installed, I had to visit an activation page of YouTube to connect it to the device. Very simple and now I have YouTube on here.

NetFlix

Netflix didn't have a simple activate system. I had to punch in my email and password via the remote. Boo! In this era of complex passwords, activation should become a standard function on TV based media devices.

Navigation

The navigation is quite smooth. I guess thanks to some good specs under the hood. This device doesn't feel sluggish at all. Getting to your watch this is as fast as hitting 'home' and then moving up or down from wherever you left off. I can do it in a second. There is also a nice back button so you can navigate backwards. All device should do this. Works perfectly.

Fast Forward

When you are watching a movie, you can fast forward and see a small picture window that gives you a visual preview of the fast forward event. It's really well done. I can quickly find where I want to be and drop off there.

It is so darn difficult to find a good case for a 2.5" hard drive. How does absolutely tooless sound to you? That's what this case is. You slide it open, pop in your drive, slide it shut and that's it. No screws. No screw driver needed. NONE. And it works!! It's a simple design, not too weird. Nice, smooth, nondescript.

I didn't buy mine from Amazon as I couldn't find it on Amazon. I ended up going to my local BestBuy to pick it up. The reviews online were mostly okay except for The Verge which said it was sluggish and basically was down beat on it.

I decided to buy it and if I didn't like it I would be returning it. I picked it up around 5:30PM on the 16th of August which is the release date. The first thing I did was get rid of all the widgets that are on the home screens. I suspect those might slow it down. I kept only one widget which is the clock / weather widget. I then downloaded all my favorite apps and began to arrange and configure it the way I wanted it.

It comes with Polaris Office, which is better than QuickOffice if you plan to create and edit word docs, Polaris is easier. To view documents and complex excel sheets I find QuickOffice often does the better job. I ed up keep both installed just in case.

I installed 14 games on it. All of which perform very well. There are my favorites, like FieldRunners, and newer ones like Final Fantasy, Ski Safari, Nova 3, Osmos HD, Amazing Alex and Zynga poker that I also really like. This quad core eats through anything with ease.

Got the latest Google Maps, which is so fantastic on this. You can save a Map so it's available without a data connection. Perfect for these WiFi devices. I'm a fan of the new Google Play movies, music, books and Magazines too. But if you prefer Amazon or Nook, those are available as always. It comes with the B&N Nook Reader by default.

There are Galaxy Note 10.1 specific apps like Adobe's PS Touch. I've been using Photoshop since 1996 so I am going to carefully review the built in lessons for PS Touch, a mobile version of Photoshop and see how far I can take that. If you are a subscriber to Adobe's Cloud services you're supposed to be able to edit a PSD with PS Touch, save it to the cloud, and then continue to edit it with Photoshop the desktop app.

There is also S Note. S Note and PS Touch are geared to work well with the new Samsung Galaxy S Pen. This was a primary reason for me to be interested in this particular tablet. The S Pen is so accurate that you can hand write whole sheets of handwritten text with it. I didn't try to have it translated into actual text like type written text. I just left it as my handwriting. Really like it.

Now this new Note 10.1 also has a new Muli-tasking feature. I should say that it doesn't multitask any app combo you want. Just a few apps blessed by Samsung which are: The base browser, not Chrome, their video player, Polaris Office, the picture gallery and their email app, not the GMail email app. Their email app can be used with POP, IMAP and Microsoft's Exchange via the built in Active Sync. So I tend to use that email client for work email and I use GMail as my personal email client.

Now, according to The Verge, multitasking was horrible. Not so fast Verge. I don't know what you guys are doing but I multitask'd just about every way you can on this and it works surprising well. I wrote notes while playing video. I played video while scrolling up and down on a web page. I copied text from an email to S Note, which both apps loaded in the side by side both on the screen simultaneously method. I had no trouble at all.

I bought Autodesk's Sketchpad Pro and can draw with that just fine. I also bought Adobe Ideas, but haven't yet played with that at all. Samsung also has their own kind of store and I am going to see if they have more S Pen specific apps. Really like the S Pen a lot. It's exactly like a typical Wacom Stylus. It's sharp, not that horrible eraser head large stylus you get stuck with if you want to use a stylus on the iPad. Although the iPad has Paper by 53, which I wish I had on here.

I'm really just getting started. I'll have to update this review over the weekend. Only played with this new tab for about 4 to 6 hours now.

Check out Google's Currents for news, and Pocket for saving articles for future reading. Both are great on this tablet. I think all the bases are covered with this tablet. Movies, games, magazines, office and productivity, art creation and editing. It does everything. And since it is Android, you have a real file system which makes email a breeze. Love this thing so far.

This is without a doubt the best phone I've ever owned. I dropped the iPhone 4S for this phone. Didn't expect to like it more than the iPhone 4S, but kept an open mind and decided to try it out. Glad I did. The screen on this phone is amazing.

I use Google services like email, calendar and docs. I wanted a more integrated phone and that's what I got. I switched from iTunes to Google Music, which is fantastic. I'm deep in the cloud now and I love it.

Android is freedom. I am using the Swift 3 keyboard. I have a thing for great keyboards and I love how Android lets us choose the keyboards we want.

Next, I went with GoSMS rather than stock SMS. Much better. Using TweetCaster Pro as my twitter client. Using Google Currents, Google Reader and Pocket for daily news. For notes I am using EverNote. For tasks, I went with GTasks to sync with my Google tasks.

Using GMail, and Chrome for Android for email and browser. Google Music for music, BeyondPod as my Podcasting client, and Audible's own client for my Audible books. Google Play Movies for movies and TV shows, Google Books and Magazines for books and magazines.

Google Maps and Places turn by turn directions and finding common places like coffee shops and so on. Facebook and Google plus for social along with the twitter client.

There are tons of games. Cut the Rope, Amazing Alex, Angry Birds, Defender, FieldRunners and so many others. I have about 20 games on this phone. QuickOffice for office documents which ties into Google Docs and DropBox.

There is nothing this phone can't do. And you get an amazing screen that makes my iPhone screen look like a postage stamp. With Apple, I got tired of the same design, same screen, same icons in much the same way. Hello widgets! I have HD Widgets and they are beautiful. My clock / weather widget is big, bold and beautiful. I can even adjust the color of the font!!

All my banks are supported, and Mint is available as well.

Lot's of GPS apps for running. FitBit, Loseit and so on to keep tabs on food intake and calories burned.

I also found this super cool package tracking app called ShipRack. You email a tracking number and they add it to your phones Shiprack tracking app.

Samsung gave me white headphones which have pause / play and forward reverse buttons. So I can control my music from the headphones. I also picked up a pair of UrBeats from the AT&T store, plus a BlueTooth sports headphones for when I run.

This is a great phone for business and personal uses. It's stylish and fast. You won't feel lag and you add more storage capacity for about $30 for 32 more GBs.

Soooo much better than my iPhone. At least I think so. If for no other reason than the email client. So easy to email anything. We have a full file system which makes attachments a breeze. OMG how much I wanted that one feature!

I have bought so many speakers for my office. I just hate plugging in my iPhone when I arrive at the office. I want the podcast I'm listening to to just switch to my office speaker when I arrive. And that's exactly what happens. I do have to turn the speaker on first. At that point my iPhone assumes the speaker is my choice so long as I leave BlueTooth switched on in the iPhone general settings.

I'm seriously considering buying a second one for home now. I'm becoming something of a fan of BOSE. I have a lot of their gear these days. If you're a teen looking for a seriously loud loud-speaker, perhaps this isn't for you. I don't blast music at the office. I listen to a little music and office acceptable levels. Mostly, I listen to Podcasts while on the way to work, and I typically want to finish them as I walk in the office. And I don't want to have to plug the phone into something. I just want the speaker to take over for my headphones. That's what this does.

I wish it had a remote though. I can change the volume from my phone, but the screen goes into screen saver mode and it takes a few strokes to do it. Sometimes I'd appreciate it if it had a mute on a remote so when a phone call comes in I could quickly cancel the sound. I can double-tap the iPhone and get the quick player controls and pause it. Not too bad.

I'd give this a solid 4/5 stars.

This one does a pretty good job.  That said, invest in a set of good headphones.  The built in speakers are there, but the sound is 'small and tinny'. Just the right amount of outlets.  Love the swivelling power cord.  I cannot speak to its ability to protect against power surges (thankfully) as our power grid is very stable.  I use this for the critical equipment in my home office (laptop, monitor, cell phone, tablet, etc.) and so far it's worked very well.

(Sept. 3, 2022) I bought this for a 2008 Thinkpad T61 that dual boots Linux Mint 20.3 XFCE (Ubuntu/Debian based), and MS Windows 10. YMMV if you are using other hardware and/or operating systems.

Linux:
I plugged the dongle in, opened the Bluetooth control panel, and paired the laptop with an iPhone SE 2020 and then paired it with a MPow Flame Bluetooth headset. Both devices worked fine, and the audio was clean and clear.

I shut the machine down and the booted it into Windows 10:

Perfect for my non-Bluetooth equipped car stereo. I'm tempted to buy another for my non-Bluetooth how sound system too!
This Antec Edge 650W 80-PLUS Gold is rock-solid,and very quiet. I replaced an old 350W that was sloooowly fading away.

This project requires you to have good dexterity with miniscule screws, ribbon cables and connectors, and to be comfortable disconnecting and reconnecting various miniature electronics (hard drive, logic board, LCD screen, etc.

There's a how-to vid. Watch it before you order this battery. Go to youtube.com and search on "iPod Photo Repair: How to replace your battery".

The installation went by the numbers. Hardest part was opening the case. I worried the corners with a knife (still have all my fingers!) until it created enough space to fit a tiny flathead screwdriver between the aluminum back and the plastic front. Pried little by little all the way up the side until it finally gave up with a pop. Don't bother using the plastic opening tools, you'll need them after you're in the guts of the iPod.

Total time to replace battery and reassemble: a little less than an hour; 25 minutes of that was spent prying the case apart - I didn't want to destroy the case or my fingers. Oh, and you better believe I tested it before putting the back case all the way back on!

Considering the price, I'm giving this little cam 4.5 stars. The half star off is for a user manual that is not as clear as it could be, and for the non-existent buttons mentioned therein.

As Sean Carter wrote elsewhere on this page,this cam is small, cheap, and "set-it-and-forget-it".

I opened the box (which contained everything in the parts listed in the product description), took the stuff out, inserted a 16GB San Disk class 10 microSD plugged the camera in, and had it working in no time. I set the resolution to 720, set the time and date, and left the other stuff pretty much at factory default.

The bracket is dead easy to mount (vac cup). I ran the power cord up into the roof liner, down the inner rubber gasket of the A-pillar, then used a couple of clips to hide it under the bottom of the instrument panel. It comes out on the driver's side center console and plugs into the power port. I used black duct tape to cover the massive, glowing red LED that is on the plug.

So, basically, once you set it up you just leave it plugged in. It comes on when the car is turned on (or the key is turned to Accsy). Note that the cam will stop recording after a few seconds of no motion - like at stop signs, traffic signals, etc. So you may want to set it so it runs all the time.

It comes off the bracket fairly easily, so you can take it indoors and connect it to a computer to view the video. I connected it to a WIndows 8 laptop and the camera came on and queried if I wanted to use it as storage or as a cam. Since I wanted to playback the video I had just shot, I selected storage.

WIndows recognized it as a removable drive. The video is AVI format, stored in DCIM sub-folders within dated folders.. I played the videos back on the PC. Didn't really look for details, so I'll have to check again for things like license plates, etc. The first couple of videos were very fuzzy. After I took the factory protective film off of the lens it shot very nice clips.

The sound is very soft.

Again, this is an inexpensive camera, but it does every thing it's supposed to do.

* * * * * tl:dr;

Pros: Cheap, Easy to install, set up, use;

Cons: Sound is very soft;

Idiot point: Don't forget to take the protective cellophane off of the lens.

OK, these aren't audiophile-quality earbuds. But they sound just fine, they fit comfortably in my ears, and they seem sturdy enough to hold up well -- unlike those super-cheap earbuds that break the third time you use them. A good option for someone who just needs a decent pair of comfortable earbuds.

I've had this on my iPad Pro for several months now. The first day or so, I felt like it was visually "noticeable" because of there is the tiniest perception of something being between your eyes and the stunning clarity of that screen. However, I stopped noticing that and it in no way has hindered my enjoyment of the amazing visuals my iPad Pro is capable of presenting. Most importantly to me, it makes drawing and writing with the Apple Pencil decidedly more pleasant and natural feeling. Before I applied this screen protector (it is tricky and you need to be very careful to avoid dust, cat hair, etc. being on the iPad screen surface while you're applying the protector), the surface felt crazy slick to draw on...was hard to control the Pencil's marks sometimes. Very happy with this purchase, and like that my screen surface is protected from potential scratches. It's easy to clean...I tend to use lens cleaning wipes on it.

Super bright and work great on my work surface where I film myself painting watercolors while I narrate the process. These along with a few other lights provide high quality illumination and let me produce video that doesn't require any post-processing in terms of lightness.

For the low cost, a very good value. I use them to shoot instructional art videos, mainly of myself painting. With the right adjustments on my video camera, these two lights (along with a supplemental LED bar that is not in this kit) allow me to shoot decently-lit video that requires minimum exposure or white balance tweaking in post-processing. See unretouched screenshot taken from a video made using these lights. In hindsight, I wish I had purchased a 3-light kit, and might actually buy another of these kits. Because more is better, right? :)

The kit did not come with instructions but it's pretty straightforward to set everything up. Took me a minute to figure out that I needed to push the ring onto the light bulb socket to stiffen the soft boxes themselves. I'm wondering if I can wash the softbox diffusers to get the fold wrinkles out and then store them rolled.

When not in use, everything stows neatly in a carry bag for convenient storage/transport. All in all very satisfied. Just a couple of nitpicks: 1) the packaging they arrived in was beat-up and overstuffed; it looked as if it had been opened, unpacked, and then poorly re-sealed; and 2) I thought the lights would be a bit brighter (and wish they were, but they work fine in the configuration I'm using them in).

I already own two full-frame Nikons, a D750 and a Z6. I wanted something small and easy to carry around without packing the larger equipment, something i could have with me from day to day, with better picture quality than an iPhone. This camera fits the bill. I like the retro dials on top (with the option to use the touch screen if you want that), the ability to shoot RAW files, the excellent Leica optics with the very fast f/1.7-2.8 lens. The picture quality is impressive. The camera has excellent features and is fast and quiet. I can't deny that I've always wanted to own a Leica, and this is much more affordable than its cousins.

I was curious and just looked up when I purchased this backpack for my daughter - when she was going into 6th grade and she'll be a sophomore in college this year! She has carried this bag every single day through middle school, high school years and in this past year at college. (Not to mention it's *the* bag she takes on trips and overnights elsewhere.) It's been through rain, sleet, snow and everything in between.

The handle looks a bit worse for wear but is sturdy as the day it was purchased. She's used leather conditioner about twice in these past 7 years, so not a lot of care, and it looks like it will hold up at least another 7. I asked if she wanted me to replace it with another and the answer was a resounding "Nope!" This is probably the only thing I've bought for $99 that's still as useful as the first day I bought it.

A must-have reference for young photographers learning processing. And for me -- multigrade papers weren't a 'thing' when I was doing darkroom work. Excellent photos and explanations for my daughter taking darkroom photography this semester. (I'm surprised it wasn't a required textbook since they use Ilford paper.)

My high school daughter's taking college classes at the local university and needed a nice, portable computer to take with her. I purchased this Asus at Bestbuy on a whim and couldn't be happier! The screen size is a bit small for my old eyes, but perfect for her. She's able to carry it in a small bookbag with ease.

This laptop is not meant to do heavy lifting like Photoshop or major gaming, though it runs all the office programs of OpenOffice.org perfectly fine. (A free/open source program that beats the heck out of MS Office.) The high school requires a google drive account and this laptop is well-suited for it, too.

The only cons are with Windows 8 -- which are only cons if you live in an area like ours where there's no luxury of high-speed internet (SE Ohio): You'll need to uninstall all of the pre-loaded aps so they don't eat your bandwidth. You'll also need to make sure all automatic updates are turned off. Another quirk of Windows 8 is that when you close an ap, they really aren't closed so you have to open task manager to kill them. My new laptop runs Windows 8 (and I find myself using my old Windows 7 laptop more than my new) and when I turn it on I instantly hit the windows-key and "d" to bypass the whole ap screen altogether.

Great little laptop at a great price!

This was the perfect December birthday gift for my newly-turned-8-year-old daughter!  She was utterly speechless when she opened the many layers of wrapping and saw "my own ipod".  Big Sis corrected her: "MP3 Player."  I was very happy that it came pre-loaded with a few songs just perfect for her age.  She and her two companions were able to start dancing to the music as soon as the package was opened and the battery inserted.  I just LOVE this little device.  The built-in speaker is perfect for sharing the tunes.  It gets plenty loud for them all to hear, even over their chatter, but not so loud as to be annoying to us folks.  The speaker sound is quite good for what it is and considering the audience.  (Don't expect it to sound exceptional to the trained ear.)  She also isn't able to turn the volume up too loud with headphones --a nice plus for the young age group.  She loves that she can `shake' it to the next song.  Most of the kids who have this will probably be great at Name That Tune with the fast succession of shakes I've heard..."I can name that tune in one note"...shake to the next!  It comes with all the necessary accessories including software and the cable to hook it up to the computer.  I've used neither of those, however, as it's so easy just to put the card into my card reader and drag and drop the music she wanted.  Though I find it not to be a problem, my biggest time-consumer was downloading a free converter to convert my wma files to mp3, as this player only recognizes mp3 format.  But even that is not a detraction to this great little player.  I've read other reviews that the bottom falls off, etc., but I really don't see how that could happen unless it was forcibly pulled apart instead of the little `twist/click' it takes to remove it and replace it.  It does take smaller hands than, say, my husband's to get the right grip on the bottom.  The design is quite good for the aimed market, namely 6-10 year olds I'd say.  Even younger if headphones aren't being used.  And I'm going to plug the brand itself.  I bought my husband a Sansa last summer because the price was right.  But I was happy with the quality, sound, and size, too.  And after my 8 year old's birthday her sister turned 13 and I got her a different model Sansa--her favorite feature of that model is the FM tuner so she can record her favorite songs on-the-fly (something not even an ipod can do).  I won't be looking at the more (overly) expensive models of MP3s anytime soon!  I highly recommend this player and this brand!

Devices that send audio TO your phone are very rare: This is one of them. It works quite well: Just connect a standard stereo cable (TRS) from your headphone jack (e.g. on a PC or mac) to the microphone input and pair it with your phone. It shows up as BT speaker, and works by default on Android (The "phone calls" setting needs to be on, but it is by default when you pair it).
It looks like there are a lot of other inputs & outputs on the back that could be wired up, but I haven't tried any of them.

This is a cost-efficient way to power the Ubiquiti cloud controller without needing to run a power cable to it. It will also work to power a Lorex Flir surveillance camera. (I used it to test various other software with the camera).

Nice little device. My only niggle is that it has cables coming out both sides and the back, which makes it take up more space than if they were all coming out the back, especially since I have BlueRigger cables, which are quite sturdy, and so they don't bend very tightly--which is a good thing in general, but it *does* require a bit more room!

The touch is great, and the keys are good sized: I can touch type with it, and my hands are not small. I got this one instead of the BlueTooth one, because I can use this one on airplanes, whereas BlueTooth, being a radio, is not allowed. It folds up really nice and small, so it doesn't take up too much room in your carry on, and the whole thing works well on the little table back in "cattle class" during those long flights.

The only reason I didn't give it a 5 is that--with my ipaq (hx2795), it presses the down button when in portrait mode. At first, I thought something was wrong with it, because it keep scrolling things off the screen! Usually I want to use landscape, anyway, but I have to put it into the second landscape mode to line up the IR, which is a tiny bit more work, because the ipaq doesn't let you hold down a button to get there, you have to use the iTask menu. Also, if you are doing a lot of punctuation or numbers, it takes a little while to get used to the function keys, since the keyboard is missing the entire top (punctuation and numbers) row.

That may sound more negative than it really is: I really like this keyboard!

This heart rate monitor is quite comfortable and synced to my forerunner 610 without difficulty. I can imagine that this, as with any elastic bands, would stretch over the years and require a replacement. This does not seem like an easy thing to do, however I'll cross that road when I get to it.

My daughter uses these during school and finds them to be comfortable and they do a decent job at blocking out ambient sound. I tried them out and they are not terrible but I am accustomed to wearing full sized professional over ear headphones running a sound board so my perspective of them is not based on typical end user experience.

I've had this drive for a few years now and while the capacity is more than adequate and the write speeds are acceptable, I confess the design of this thing is consistently baffling to me. Maybe I don't use it frequently enough, but I always forget which portion of the slider to hold onto as I slide out the drive type I need. This is why so many others of this dual type have a slider functionality or dual caps. It's unique, just one I reach for less frequently than others in my arsenal because of the actual design of the drive!

This is a lovely case with a soft fleecy interior that protects my equipment beautifully.  I love the contrasting light blue accents and having pockets on both sides is very handy.  I haven't used the shoulder strap yet, but really appreciate having the option to have one (as well as being able to pack it away when not using it).  Love the handle on the side of the case as well.  Great durable fabric and classy look.

I bought these to use on a flight to Europe, and while these do tend to block out the ambient noise, they can be a little cumbersome to insert.  This is really only an issue if you remove them constantly, but I found myself doing so to either talk to my husband, a flight attendant, listen to announcements, go to the restroom, etc. so having to reinsert them each time was a little annoying.  I ended up using other headphones for the rest of the flight to make things a little easier.  My other issue with these earphones is the cable; it is thin and flimsy, and they could have really gone for a more robust cabling, either a thicker plastic or a wrapped plastic.  I worry about the durability of these units as a result, but will keep them around as a backup option.  The sound from these earphones is pretty good once you get them inserted and wait until the memory foam fills the ear canal.

The noise cancellation and sound on these very comfortable headphones are, well, BOSE. My complaint about them is the swipe and button controls. I find that the smallest angle change can cause a video or song to skip to the next one and the “favorites” button works sometimes and sometimes not making, for example, changing to various levels of noise cancellation unpredictable. Besides being sometimes unresponsive, the buttons are sometimes over-sensitive: I’ve raised my arm to put something on a shelf and brushed a button with my sleeve and toggled the voice activation options many times.

All that said, the battery life, comfort and awesome sound are great. I just wish the controls were better.

I purchase this based on the Audubon Society's reviews and love them. They are a bit on the heavy side compared to the cheap binoculars I used to use but I am pleased with the clarity and easy of focus.

Works perfectly; only complaint is that it is short and required purchase of an extension piece. Recommend it but buy an extender if you don't want to have your computer a couple of inches from the monitor.

They were easy to use, came in a nice case, and connected no problem. I like having the volume control on the earpiece too.

The sound quality is excellent. An equalizer would've been nice but it's really overall a pretty good stereo in spite of that.

It looks nice and is very comfortable, you barely feel it in your ears, looks cool in ear also.

Have been using for 3hr straight and there is still around 40% battery left in the earbuds. The box use type C to charge and its design looks good. This is a pretty good little speaker for the price. I've had it for a couple of months now and I really like how long the battery lasts. It could be a bit louder but in general it gets the job done with no problem.

This was actually a gift for my co-worker and so far she loves it. I helped her pair it to her Samsung S6 and it was very easy. I've seen her wear them on her lunch break listing to YouTube. Most importantly she loves them when she is at the gym. Her last bluetooth headphones were not sweat proof and they started to 'crackle' after a couple days of extensive workouts.
