This bag is beautiful. I was looking at a much more expensive brand-name camera bag when I found reviews for this hand-crafted bag on YouTube.

I bought what ended up being a smaller version and returned it because it didn't fit my daily gear (13" Mac & cord, Nikon body with attached 18-55 lens, zoom, and a macro lens).

I received an email from the company suggesting this larger version, which fit beautifully and is equally as gorgeous.

The bag comes with a removable padded camera insert and four removable dividers. There are two slots--I can fit my laptop in one and files in the other. There's a zipper pouch on the side closest to the body which I'll use for my wallet and/or camera, and a buckled compartment that fits my cords, batteries, and SD cards.

The quality of the padding and leather are beautiful. I haven't used the bag a lot yet, but the hardware feels sturdy and the stitching is really nice .

I was hoping it would serve as a cross-body messenger, but it's a little stiff for that...more like a briefcase. So, it won't be the only bag I keep, but I will enjoy it as a great upscale grab-and-go bag at a quarter of the price of the name brand camera bag I was going to get.

The one adjustment I'll make is to punch a hole in the strap to make the strap fit me a little bit better, as I'm not that tall and I like the bag to fall higher on my hip, but I'm pretty handy and will do that myself. So far, I am very happy with this bag and the customer service.

I'll give it a 5 for beauty, fit, and customer service, and a 4.5 for the adjustments I'll make.

I am a professional photographer. I usually shoot Pentax. I bought a Nikon DSLR as a backup to my Pentax K-1 Mark II. This camera would be used if my professional gear should need repair.

I now have four of these quick release plates. I keep them mounted on my most frequently used lenses and the camera body itself. I've been taking pictures professionally since 1976, so, I've used a lot of big lenses. For clarity and quality of build, nothing beats a prime focus lens. This is a big telephoto 300mm lens. The build quality or Pentax professional lenses is second to none. This one has excellent image quality. The lens barrel is rugged and was made to handle heavy use. This lens is on my Pentax KP body more than any other lens when I am shooting whitetail deer. I've even used it to photograph wild turkey and larger waterfowl with great results.

I have some really expensive lenses in my collection. The clarity of this lens is the best I have seen. The goose picture in this review was shot handheld.

Yes, there are limitations, but, image quality is the reason to own one. BUY this lens, you won't regret it.

I am a long-time PENTAX enthusiast and professional photographer. I bought a new Nikon D3100 in 2014, but, I sold it and returned to Pentax because the wide assortment of superb lenses and I prefer the quality of their cameras. I wrote the book, Frame That Shot, and I have traveled all over the country shooting landscapes and wildlife. I used to shoot PGA tournaments and NHRA drag racing, and extreme sports. Back then, Pentax was my camera of choice. I bought an *ist in 2006 and it is still going strong. So, why the K-50? I am one of those wildlife shooters who likes having the 1.5 lens factor-- since the price of BIG GLASS is really high. I also know that an APS-C sensor puts your image right in the sweet spot of a full-coverage lens. The K-50 has a stainless steel chassis and a poly-carbonate body overlay. The old *ist DSLR had a magnesium alloy chassis. These cameras are durable. My old *ist looks like new and works like new. I expect to enjoy equal longevity with the new K-50 body. I gave my wife the kit lens (18-55mm DA-L) because I have an 18-55mm DA that came with the *ist and I will be using it. I also bought the DA 50-200 ED WR lens (not the cheaper plastic mounted version).

My next investments will be the Pentax 70-200 f/2.8 WR lens and the Pentax 150-450 ED WR (or the SIgma 50-500mm).

My only wish is that Pentax still used the CRV-3 batteries that the older *ist cameras used. They gave my 800 shots on a fresh set of batteries. The K-50 gives me about 450 shots per battery charge. One other thing, I'd love to be able to turn off the LCD by default rather than having to turn it off manually every time I turn on the camera. I won't use "Live Preview" and I have a top-quality Canon video camera for "action" shots.

Pentax, change the LCD to automatically turn off after about two seconds like the *ist and I'll be a loyal customer for life.

A lot of storage here. Great value, and works well. USed to add some songs to be able to play in my car, and it mounted on my windows 10 PC instantly, and was recognized by my car. Sounds good, fast transfer speed. All I need in a thumb drive.

Good comfortable headphones with loud volume no noise cancelling as far as I can tell the over-the-ear design allows you to muffle out most annoying noises for the best sound. These are good entry level earphones for kids. They are smaller, so they fit smaller heads, and the volume limiting feature is good so kids don't hurt their ears.  Seems pretty sturdyily made, and should hold up fairly well.

It's an echo, and it works. For the price it's great deal. Have had no issues with it. As with all dots, the speaker is a bit tinny, but good for a second unit, or if you are like me, you can attach it to an external speaker for more sound.
Good buy

I love my Bose headphones, and was so sad when I was having trouble with the cable. I lost all sound in the left ear.  This cord replaces the breakaway cord that comes with your Bose headphones and bring it back to life.  Just a simple cable can make me so happy. Installs in seconds, works like a new one.  What not to like?

It does what it says, it connects to a computer via USB, or the USB port on a wall charger, and connects to you phone, tablet, or any other device that requires micro USB for charging.  Works with my fast charger and my Samsung Galaxy S7. Also allows very fast connections from the computer to the phone for file transfer.

This is a great cable for extending your headphone's reach. I have a turntable. The problem is that it's on the far side of the room. If I want to sit in my comfy chair and listen to my vinyl on headphones, I'm out of luck. Until now.

This is a sleek and very thin laptop. Because of that it doesn't have all the extras of a desktop or even a larger laptop. It has 3 USB ports, an ethernet port, HDMI port, and a port for a SD Memory card. There is also a headphone jack.

It has a built in microphone which does a pretty good job of picking up voice for skype or video calls and a built in camera.

People have complained about the keyboard and touchpad. I think it comes down to personal preference. I like the keyboard, it has a surprisingly enjoyable click and clack when you type, and the buttons are responsive and comfortable to use. The touchpad would take the most getting used to, but if you ever used a buttonless mouse, then you are familiar with how it works. Basically the whole thing is a button and depending on where you push down on the pad it either depresses the left or right button. You can also pinch to zoom, which is a nice feature for looking at smaller text, though it does become a bit blurry.

Performance is amazing. The Solid State hard drive is amazingly fast and quiet. From a full shut down windows boots to the login screen in under 5 seconds for me.

Screen is bright and the display is rich. Touch screen is probably the thing you may or may not use as much. This comes with windows 8, so steep learning curve aside, you can use the screen as a touchscreen when you are using the tiles or anytime for that matter. For regular use, opening Facebook or shopping on Amazon, you can use the touch screen to scroll, zoom, highlight and click, simply by touching the screen. I dn't use it much, but did find it fairly responsive when viewing web pages, but even more so in programs meant to be touch screen. Scrolling through tile screen is the windows menu is surprisingly fun.

Overall this is a great computer. It is sleek and beautiful, with a wonderful screen and so so buttons and touchpad. Most of the latter comes down to preference. Myself, I like how they are as I've used other devices that behave similarly.

The picture is spectacular. The colors are vibrant, and the darks are dark. Especially if you have it properly calibrated. It's very light for its size, thin and easy to set up. The remote is a bit on the light side, not having a backlight, and the buttons are hard to see in the dark.

The smart capabilities of the TV are fantastic. It comes with programs like Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and iheartradio (all have buttons on the remote for fast access) as well as others. There is also a store where you can access and download other programs like Accuweather and Plex, among others.

It won't quite eliminate the need for a chromecast, as that is just a spectacular piece of electronics, but you'll be using it less and less.

It has 3 hdmi inputs. I use it with a sound bar, as the TV sound is a bit hollow. If you use a Vizio sound bar it will recognize it immediately and you can use the TV remote to control the sound on the sound bar.

The stalk is a bit flimsy feeling, but otherwise a well built TV set. Great picture and wonderful features. The only drawbacks I see is the flimsy stalk, cheap feeling remote, and the IR sensor is a bit weak.

Unit is easy to connect and has several connection options. Cables required for RCA
(good) and optical sound (best) are in the box. Nicely designed and blends into your setup. Can sit on table in front of or under the television. It sounds much better than the stock TV sound. It also connects via bluetooth to your phone or tablet so you can use it as a speaker to play music and such from your phone.

My biggest complaint with the Kindle paperwhite is that it is uncomfortable to read. The straps go around the four corners of the case and hold your Kindle in place snugly. Folding the cover around the back displays a holding strap. I was prepared to give this a poor rating. As other reviewers stated there is an issue with the fm transmitter strength leading to static.

I found there is stronger FM signal if the device is installed away from electrical components. Since most people, including myself, installed it initially on the dash, the radio and other electrical system components caused interference. I moved the device to be on the corner of the rear view mirror and had noticeably stronger FM reception.

The device plugs into the cars cigarette lighter. There is a port on the plug to insert an additional USB charger, so you can continue to use your phone's charger while this is plugged in.

Synching is fairly straight forward. Press the button the back of the device, search USB devices on your phone, and it will pair. The readout is red when not connected, blue when connected.

FM transmitter will transmit on most every frequency from 88.1 to 107.9fm. There is a button on the top to search for the best signal, but I found it was unreliable. It also has two presets so you can set two signals you know to work.

The button on the front lets you switch between playing music from your phone to working phone controls. It also allows you to pause music playback and end calls by pressing the music or phone button respectively.

Since it plays through your car stereo, music and calls play through your car speakers. When you are connected to a clear channel, the sound is clear and distortion free. Phone calls sound clear. There is a small microphone on the front that picks up your voice and I was pleased at the quality of my voice. Every person I called with the device were surprised to hear I was on a hands free speakerphone. They said it sounded better than my USB headset, and almost as good as using the phone's internal microphone.

Overall the base features were very good; music playback and phone features worked very well. There was an issue with the FM signal; there was often static, but found that it was improved by placing it where there was less electrical interference. Once I found the correct place, it was acceptable in that regard. Though I am only giving 3 1/2-4 starts as I am not fully comfortable with recommending it based on that alone.

I've had the Harmony One remote since the day it came out, and now "upgraded" to the Harmony Ultimate Remote.

Build and Setup:
This is a very solid remote. It is heavy for its size with clean lines and elegant design. Inside the box is the powered hub with two remote blasters, remote, base, and power cords for the hub and the base. There does not appear to be a removable battery like with the Harmony One.

Set up was very simple. As I already had my settings in myremotesetup.com, I simply had to log into myharmony.com, transfer my settings to the new remote and the remote was setup. It was very easy.

The difference between this remote and other Harmony remotes is that this has a hub and blaster units that connects through your wireless network to allow you to connect and control your units with your smartphone.

You have to connect the hub and blaster units around the units you want to control. It has to be connected to your home wireless network, which was easy. You can either do it through myharmony.com or by pressing the setup button on the hub and your router (if it supports it) it was that easy.

I have my hub on the shelf with my Blu Ray, Dish Box, and Xbox. The one blaster is near the television, and the other is on another shelf with my Wii and my surround sound box. When you go into advanced settings on your remote you tell the remote to control the devices with either just the remote, with the hub, blaster 1, blaster 2, or all of them. This allows flexibility where you setup and place your devices and blaster and hub units.

Using the Remote:
The remote is easy to use. Many of the major buttons; play, pause, fast forward, volume and such are hard buttons on the remote. The remote has a large touch screen that can do all the other device options you may seem fit to try. It scrolls across several pages: Home screen allows you to choose between actions such as watch tv or dvd, channel favorites (which you program), current action screen that controls actions related to what you are doing, and finally the number screen, here is where you can enter numbers to change channels. This last part is a bit of a pain as when I am channel surfing I like to be able to press number buttons to change channels and you really can't do this with this remote without looking.

To operate DVR like functions you can also swipe up from any screen to access a black screen where you can program gestures. By default you press to pause, swipe right to skip forward, swipe right to swipe back, etc.

Phone App:
The phone app for the android is a bit lacking as it is not quite as sophisticated as the remote itself, but can do most of the actions of the remote as long as you are connected to the same wireless network as your hub is.

Troubleshooting:
The remote is easy to use and troubleshoot, Simply rebooting or re-syncing the remote can resolve most problems I've found. It also prompts you for assistance the first time you add an action or new device.

Overall this is a great remote. This will demand, though, some knowledge on your part as it is a very sophisticated remote. Many problems that occur can easily be resolved by some knowledge of networks, remotes, or Harmony devices in general. If you have experience with this you will enjoy the functions and capacity of this remote.

This is a good voice recorder. Whether you need it to record your voice memos, lectures, meetings, or discretely record your favorite spy, this will surely be a recorder you'll find many uses for.

It feels very secure in your hand, and has a comfortable feel and weight. It comes with a small pouch, which is nice. The record button is easy to find my sight or feel. The volume and forward/reverse buttons are on an outer button from the record button. Play and stop on the left and index and menu are on the right.

f1 and f2 buttons are primarily used for setting mic sensitivity and voice quality. Under Mic Sensitivity you can choose: Dictate (good for personal memos), Speech recognition (turns on when it hears voice), conversation (good for interviews or conversations, auto zoom (good for large areas where there may be close up voices and far voices), and lecture (good for lectures)

You can choose either low quality at 8kbps in Mp3 format to super high quality 192kbps in mp3. There is also a wave format in 1411 kbps. The higher quality you go impacts total record time. You can add a micro SD card for adding recording time.

There are also 4 index folders labeled A thru D. These are for separating projects. There is also a folder you could place music files if you wanted this to be a mp3 player.

There is also a menu setting where the voice quality and mic sensitivity can be accessed as well as numerous other options such as splitting files, display contrast, and clearvoice (an option that improves the sound quality of the recorded voiec)

The unit comes with rechargable AA batteries that will need to be charged when you first open it. They charge with the included usb to micro USB cord. Any other micro USB cord you own will also work. Once the recorder is connected to your computer through the USB cable you can download and upload voice or mp3 and wave files.

The only thing I wish this had was different settings for each index. For instance I would have liked to set index A for lecture mode at high quality, index B for dictate at a lower quality, etc. Once you set a mic sensitivity and recording quality, they are the same for all index until you change them in settings.

Overall a great quality recorder. Great for meetings, memos, and conversations.

Usually I don't like ear buds. They tend to fall out and have sub par sound, but I am quite self conscience about using over the ear phones. These are some of the best ear buds I've ever tried. They fit very comfortably in your ear. The rubber holds them in your ear and blocks out much of the outside sound. There are also a small assortment of rubber insets that you can swap out if you have larger ears or smaller ears. The ones that cam on the buds worked fine for me.

The cloth cord also works great and greatly reduces the entanglement that happens often with the rubber cords and is a nice touch. The sound is great with crisp mid and high range and full deep bass.

If you wear ear buds alot, they are comfortable, and if you don't use ear buds for the reasons that I always steered clear of them you'll find these a great reason to start wearing ear buds.

Though they advertise this pouch as a adequate carrying case for cameras, I found it is also good for my Garmin Nuvi GPS, which also has a camera.  It is rugged and tough on the outside with soft cloth on the inside, as not to scratch any optics or view screens. The double zipper zips closed nice and tight shielding your small camera or GPS in a wrap of safety.  Very adequate for trips where there may be chances for your camera to get knocked around a bit. I like this for that reason.

The Garmin Nuvi 295W is a mid-range navigator with built-in wireless. It features the well-known and reliable Garmin navigation with the added benefit of a slightly updated UI. The icons for navigation within the UI are easier to see and access and are accessed through a touch screen scroll screen on the main screen.

Fit/finish
The unit feels very sturdy in the hand. It's solid feel makes it feel like a useful instrument instead of a toy that many other units feel like. The touch screen has a slightly matted appearance that resists smudges and scratches and glare. When in the cradle there is a on/off/sleep button on the side and the volume buttons are on the top.

Navigation
Navigation is typical of Garmin GPS units. The default setting is driving mode, in which you can choose different route settings such as faster, more direct, avoiding tools, etc. If you know where you are going it may send you a way that you question, but it will defiantly get you there. If you are going someplace you've never been, you can be rest assured that it will get you there. If you need to deviate from the route it suggests the units improved OS offers lightening fast recalculations. Often times the recalculation will take under 5 seconds.
You can enter waypoints or places to go either from the built-in Google search (for places of interest), restaurants, gas stations, police, hospitals, and other places along your route. You can also enter an address and save that as a favorite and give it a name of your choosing.
You can also choose a pedestrian mode. You go to pedestrian mode when you remove the unit from the cradle.

This is useful for geocaching. It also works well with the myGarmin portion of their website where you can download additions, including up to five geocaches in your area at a time.
In either mode you can also enter GPS coordinates. If in pedestrian mode it will show you how to walk to that coordinate. If it is farther away it will switch to driving mode, drive you to a point near the GPS coordinates and then allow you to walk.

Wifi
The unit has built in WiFi. Setup is quick and easy, though the range is somewhat less than that of say what a laptop computer would be able to pick up, but the signal is strong and reliable. The browser is typical of small units like this and can be improved upon. The e-mail application is great and adding a gmail account is quick and painless because the unit already knows the server settings. Just enter your address and password and you are checking your e-mail.
The built-in Google Search also looks for places of interest near you or your route and you can add that to your favorites or waypoints and be off.

Extras
With all Garmins you can go to myGarmin from their website. You can download customizable maps, geocaches, voices, and new vehicles. Connecting is a snap (hint, choose USB Drive Mode) via the included USB cable which also acts as a charger. You can download map updates, software updates, and lots of fun tools.

Final Verdit
As someone who has only used an older GPS unit, I was impressed the this units functionality, build quality, and interface. As with any GPS there are some limitations. These are overshadowed, however, by the extras on this unit and its lightning fast response, interface, and navigation.

A fun tool for any driver, or any geocacher.

This camera is a great camera for the money. It offers affordability, function, and great shots at a wonderful price point. For a bit more than a full featured point-and-shoot, you can get an equally full featured DSLR.

This camera offers ease of use for beginners to the SLR market but also has a full feature set that even experienced photogs would love to have.

I'm not going to get into all the features here, you can read them above on Amazon's product page, but I will tell you that they are there to help you get the most of your shot. You can, of course, control exposure, shutter, and aperture, but you can also control white balance and color modes with a push of a button.

At high ISO speeds you can shoot indoors without a flash, your pictures will turn out beautiful and perfect every time. What once you would need a 80a or a neutral density filter for you can now do with a few brief menu options on the camera.

Another great feature is the live view feature where you can use the LCD screen to see what the camera sees. This is so you won't have to look through the viewfinder and especially useful when doing tripod work.

Also the EF-S mount on this camera will also accept your older EF lenses, though EF-S lenses won't fit on your EF mount camera.

Overall this is a great camera. It offers wonderful features, price, and takes great pictures. So why don't you move up to a DSLR and start taking great pictures instead of just good pictures.

* Adjusting volume control is tricky... the center control knob is low profile so it does not feel effortless to adjust volume or settings.

* Not sure if it has something to do with the iOS 4 update but now my phone is hit and miss if it will charge by the radio. No issues on the audio coming across the usb cable. Don't see where you can use bluetooth to stream audio, yet works fine with the phone.

I've now had this laptop for several months. I can't say better things about it!

The touchpad is sensitive, intuitive, and easy to use. This was important for me coming from a Mac, since their touch pads are amazing. Expectations exceeded. The touch-screen I thought would be more of a novelty, but I find myself using it more and more as I remember that I can actually touch the screen. I'm a graduate student, so it's perfect for scrolling while I have books covering the keyboard or while it's on my lap at an angle that makes it tough to get to the touchpad.

Operating system works well. Much much better than the ASUS Zenbook that I got previously when my Mac died. The ASUS had issues with scaling and screen resolution of many apps including the desktop itself, Chrome, Firefox, and Adobe programs. By this I mean that every time I opened the laptop after sleeping, the scaling and resolution were different than I left it, usually microscopically small, and I do mean TINY. Not just 10 point font...more like 2 point font. It was ridiculous. So as much as I loved the way it looked, I had to return it. This laptop has a less-sharp resolution (numerically, not really visibly), which makes the fonts (like in Adobe) much more legible, even though those (Adobe) are the only programs that do this on the ATIV Book 9 Plus.

Windows 8 is not this computer's fault, so I'm not going to talk about it. You can tweak a few things on Win8 and learn a few quick keyboard shortcuts and life is much better. I do not use the "apps" that Windows 8 touts. They're stupid--just avoid them if you don't like them. :)

Very portable laptop. Light, loud enough speakers that I can set it quite a distance away and still hear clearly, the screen sortof "locks" into position past about 100 degrees (like slightly more than a 90 degree angle), so there's not much jiggling past that point. However, I will note that sometimes, when it's right at 90 degrees or a bit less (like if I'm laying down with it on my stomach) and I move too quickly, it does tend to want to try and close on me. No biggie. Just be mindful.

Also no internet connection issues--again with the ASUS, the internet connection was spotty and would go out periodically (like every 20 minutes I had to restart the internet connection--sometimes it fixed it, sometimes not). My husband is a computer guru and tried everything that the ASUS forums suggested, from uninstalling and reinstalling to updating the drivers, and turning off settings that I never would have been able to find on my own. The ATIV is just peachy. :)

One more thing to note, and I'll update if anything comes of it: The fan, about a week ago, started making more audible noises. Not necessarily during "times of high stress" on the system, sometimes I'm just browsing Facebook with one tab open. I haven't dropped the computer or dinged it around unnecessarily. Husband-computer-guru said this just sometimes happens and isn't a sign that there's something wrong. His has been doing the same thing (he's got a Dell) since about 6 months after he got it.

BUT the fan issue for me only lasted that one day. Hasn't happened again since. So, like I said, I'll keep ya updated. Any more questions, feel free to comment and I'll answer ASAP!

On its own, this is small, lightweight, comfortable, and minimal phone case. It does a fine job of keeping your phone clean and protected. Keep in mind that there are limited colors/designs but it’s not about a fashionable case, it’s about the functionality.
I wanted an inexpensive set that I wouldn't be upset about if they got squished.  They do meet that requirement, but they do still hurt my ears after wearing them for awhile.

These are the best earbuds I've purchased. The volume is a bit low, but I think that its a good thing to protect my hearing. The sounds is still really good, they are comfortable and the battery life is excellent. I think the longest I've used them is about 3 hours, so I'm not sure what the maximum battery life is. Calls are easy to answer and very clear.

I had purchased this to replace another stand I didn't like. The previous one had a goose neck arm, was tall, and had a huge base. Ultimately it took up way too much space and was not versatile enough.

This stand is lightweight, does not take up much room, and can be folded up and taken with you. There is a silicone grippy material on the back to stick to the phone. The phone's usb c port is accessible. It is easy to adjust and has some options for angle and height.

I do wish it was just a little bit more sturdy. If the cradle is extended to it's maximum height vertically, any pressure on the phone will cause the base to move. This can be combatted by simply moving it down at an angle closer to the front instead of straight up in the air. I also wish it was able to extend higher vertically. The height of the phone can go from anywhere from 0" to about 3-4" in the air- depending on angle.

Overall I like the aesthetics, functionality, and the price/value of this item and am very happy. The other style I had actually clamped to the phone. This ultimately did not work well because I picked the phone up frequently from the cradle.

So I did not purchase these, but they came with my DROP Alt board. To me they are asthetically pleasing. The light does shine through the legends if that is your thing.

So two sides of the keycaps meausure aprox 1.35mm which is all well and good. What annoys me is that the two other sides measure 0.95mm. That is quite thin for any keycaps, and it does affect the sound a feel a little. They are perfectly fine for most people and are still way better than most original keycap, but I have become accustomed to 1.4- 1.5mm keycaps as a standard. If my board was not apart at the moment I would take a photo.

I purchased these to replace the Mpow Flame light that I had lost one of the earbuds too. I have gone through a couple of these.

What I do like is the charging case. It is pretty slim, it is USB C, and it also has a display to show how much of a charge it has. This is super helpful. It also has volume and connect/disconnect buttons. This has not yet had any charging issues, but I have not owned it for very long.

Now for what I don't like- They do not fit my ear that well. It may be the shape of hook, the length of the arm from which the speaker is mounted, or some other variable. The hook keeps it in place, but it never feels as if it's in my ear properly. I also think the sound is not so hot, and for 50 dollars I was expecting more. It is a little treble heavy on the heavier frequencies and just sounds like a cheap driver.

My previous headphone was the MPow Flame Lite. The charging case is bulkier and bare and there is no digital display. With that said- these are now 1/3 of the price. What I do like is that they fit my ear like a glove, and the sound quality is phenominal. It sounds like a much bigger driver. I am not an audiophile, but it really sounds great. Maybe it is the mid that come in fuller giving it a rich sound.

I have had some charging issues. Sometimes I find that only one of the headphones are dead and the other is fully charged. However, fit and sound are my most important details so these are my favorite. For the price I can purchase three and keep them in different places. If I lose one or have a charging issue I can replace it with the extra. This makes much more sense than keeping the aI do not more.

Edit: I changed from 3 to 5 stars. I have owned these now for almost one year, and use them probably every day. There has been no decrease in performance or battery life. I was so accustomed to my previous ear buds that I did not like these much at first. However, the sound is balanced, the battery life is great, and I really like the charging case. I have never actually times the batter life, but it is probably about 7-8 hours on a full charge. There are sooo many choices now for bluetooth ear buds, but these are a safe bet and most people should be happy. I am however not an audiophile, and someone who truly is may want to spend more on a Bose, or whatever the best ear buds are nowadays. My previous ones were more bass heavy, but these are better balanced. They do stay in the ear, unless I go to lay down on my back; I then have to push them back into my ear.

I purchased this as a data storage/backup drive for my desktop PC. My main drive is a1TB NVME drive. The data drive I use for movies, songs, and backups and digital images. Since I am not booting with the drive I don't care about raw performance, nor will I pay for it. With that said I am VERY happy with this drive. It only spins at 5400 RPM, so the access time is slightly slower, but it makes no difference to me. Maximum transfer rate is nearly 200MB/sec. High capacity drives have dense platters and are able to pull data faster.

I am a Nazi for eliminating extraneous sound and used to keep my drives inside enclosures to reduce sound. My quietest drive to date is the Samsung HD 503HI, and this is even quieter. I have several large case fans spinning slowly and if I turn them off I can ever so slightly hear a faint humming or click, but otherwise I hear NOTHING.

This is my first WD drive (have always used Samsung). I cannot speak to the drive's reliability as I've only had it for one month. It is labeled for "Surveillance," so if it's meant to be running 24/7- 365 it is meant to get use in commercial/industrial environments.

I think everyone with a desktop PC should adopt this system. It is very easy to backup anything important- save it to your C: drive as well as your backup E: drive or whatever. If one your main drive goes kaput you have the backup to pull your saved data from. You can use flash drives for additional redundancy and portability, but in my experience they are not so reliable.

I own the early Soundcore Motion B. My plan was to upgrade to this for myself and to gift my older speaker to someone else. I opened up the package and tried it out and I was blown away by the sound. It was just so rich and full and balanced. I felt it would be a crime to give my older one away, so I gifted the new one and purchased a second one for myself.

I use it mostly in my bedroom when I sleep I play it all night, but I use it sometimes during the day too. I've taken it out for the day to barbecues and stuff and the battery lasted 8 hours without needing a charge. I'm not sure how much longer it can actually go, because I keep it plugged in at night. The manufacturer states 24 hours. I know I was thoroughly impressed by my original Soundcore speaker's battery life.

It is very easy to pair with the device you choose. There are 4 control buttons on top. The outer case is made of rubber and it is very easy to feel which button is which as each button is uniquely raised out of the rubber. You can play, pause, skip, etc with the buttons on top (the buttons are not dedicated for this purpose) but I have only controlled play from my mobile phone.

I prefer the more classic box shape of the Soundcore vs the other offerings from JBL, Bose, and Amazon.
I would most definitely purchase it again.

So I upgraded my home desk (which was an old kitchen table) and decided I needed to free up some desktop space. Also, the desk was smaller and I didn't want the monitor to be closer to me. What I was most concerned about was the actual distance between me and the monitor. Most spec sheets will list the maximum extension distance- how far the arm can bring the monitor to you, but not how far behind the desk it can carry it. I posted questions on Amazon, but really never got a clear answer for the products I was interested in. (So it's actually approximately 2") I decided to pull the trigger on this one and I'm glad I did. (So it's actually about

AESTHETICS 4.5/5 The center pole is stainless steel and the body is a metallic silver/grey color. I like the look of the pole mount like this, instead of the style where it just swivels at the base. My desk and components happen to be all black and I should have put more thought into the color when I bought this. There is a lot of contrast and I think a darker grey or black would have looked better. This style with the gas spring mount has a very chunky arm, however the arm is completely concealed by the monitor.

STURDINESS 4.5/5 I don't really have anything else to compare it to seeing as this is my first stand. However there is little wobble/bounce with the arm fully extended. I am not worried about this going anywhere. If you have the monitor clamped lower down on the pole you will get even less bounce. I do think that the bottom plate of the C clamp should be larger. My desk is particle board and I did put cardboard and foam in between the clamp and the desk to put less stress at the clamp site. They do make professional kits for this, but it wasn't necessary for this.

VALUE 5/5 I paid approximately $40 dollars and I think it was a fair price for the features and performance. Looking at what is available I think $40- 70 dollar range is ideal for most people's needs at home. Below this and the quality/features may suffer. I don't think it is necessary to spend more than this unless you very frequently need to reposition the monitor. I do not need to move it often.

INSTALLATION 4/5 The directions were not written in very clear English (probably poorly translated from Chinese). However, this was super easy to install and I could have done it without directions. The only issue I had was mounting the VESA mount to the back of the monitor. The supplied screws were too long, so I used my original screws, but they were still too long. The plate that screws into the monitor is thinner than the plate on the OEM stand, so the screws in my case were about 2-3mm too long and there is a gap/play/movement. It's not an issue for the moment, but I will have to get some washers or spacers.
The only spring I had to adjust for my 10lb/27" monitor was the tilt spring. It required about 1/4 turn to get the right tension.

TO SUMMARIZE MY COMPLAINTS/CONS

-Color: I knew this when I bought it so it's not really a con
-Mounting: The thinner VESA plate may require additional modifications
-Clamp: The part of the clamp under the table is a little small. I'd be careful if mounting on very thin surfaces. It may require reinforcement.

Well made case fans are worth the money- they are quieter and move more air. Noctua is among the best in the business. I have an extended-ATX case and am overclocked to the gills. I prefer air cooling. I have a Noctua cooler, several Scythe and Thermaltake case fans, and needed one more so I purchased this. The bios on my ASUS board does a great job of controlling it and monitoring speed. This one is definitely the quietest and it moves a lot of air.

I do like the colors of Noctua fans, but I admit they clash with the other case colors. I don't have a display case so I'm fine with that. I personally choose function over form.

You know, when before this board was to be released, it was rumored to be at the $200 price point. If you purchased quality PBT keycaps and an aluminum case separately, you would already exceed the price. This is probably the best keyboard you are going to get for $130 dollars.

This is my first keyboard with PBT keycaps and while it gives the feel of quality, I'm not sure If I prefer ABS instead. There are several layers of programming possible, and you can program any key to just about any other key, or macro key combinations. Ultimately, this board has more features than I will ever need. I like that there are no feet; it gives typing a very sturdy feel. Unless you like typing at a very high incline, but that would be easy enough to make minor modifications to elevate it.

If you are looking at this then you are probably also looking at the KBP V60, which costs virtually the same. The only reason to get that board is you prefer illumination, ABS keycaps, don't need the programmability, and prefer a lighter board. I also purchased the V60 and am waiting for it to be delivered. I want to make sure that I am making the right choice.

Other boards to consider are the Choc Mini, although this is a lower class board, it may meet your needs. There is the Ducky Mini which has an aluminum bezel which makes it larger which kind of defeats the purpose of the 60% board IMHO. There is the Tex Beetle. These are all at a similar price point and similar layout. I will post back after I have had the V60 for a few days. Who knows, maybe I will actually prefer it. I'm not 100% sure I like the PBT keycaps as they feel like typing on cubes of concrete, although I would be in the minority. Also worth mentioning is that the space bar kind of creaks when it is depressed. I'm not sure if it is the stabilizer, spring, or defect, but it is mildly annoying. (One more thing I want to mention is that my favorite mechanical keyboard ever is the Cherry MX Board 3.0. It is more of an economy board, but the keystrokes are the smoothest, the board is quieter, and it has great low profile keys which really do make typing smoother. I don't know why these have not caught on).

Edit: I wan to add that have since purchsed the Poker 3 LED. It gives typing a different feel. In comparison, the PBT keycaps make the keystrokes feel stiff and mushy. I actually prefer the LED version with the ABS. They are fairly high quality, not the crap you get on a typical Dell keyboard. My preference for ABS goes against the grain as most prefer PBT, but this is all subjective.

I have to say that this is my favorite keyboard ever owned. The look is sleek and modern without appearing like some alien technology. The illumination levels are adjustable and I prefer medium or low (3 levels). I've seen keyboards with something like 200 levels of brightness and I can't say that I see much practicality in that.

The switches in these are of the scissor type which is typical of laptop keys. In my opinion the amount of pressure it takes to depress each key is ideal. The keystroke is short, but I don't feel as if my fingers are jarred at the bottom. It is not noiseless, but not excessive. I find the clicking of the keys very satisfying. I type faster and more accurately with this as compared to some other boards. I'm learning to use a mechanical keyboard, but at this point the Logitech is still my preferred board.

I'm sorry, but I'm not sure if there are reprogramable hot keys. I have Logitech software installed for several keyboards but I can't find the settings for this one. I'm sure this info is easy to find.

In conclusion, this board would be a fantastic upgrade for almost any board, especially the stock pieces of junk that come with desktop computers. I would recommend this over any rubber dome type keyboard. You will find that with the shorter keystrokes your typing speed may improve. Those who like mechanical keyboards may like this as well, although this is highly subjective. Fortunately, many computer stores have this on display so you can try it before you buy it, which is a huge plus. I would rate this 5 1/2 stars if I could as I could not find a single negative thing to say about it. Well, with the palm rest it may take up just a little extra real estate on your desktop than other keyboards.

There is a wireless version which is similar to this, but I like the feel of typing on this better. I used to much prefer wireless keyboards and mice for everything. However, after going back to corded it just feels more responsive. How often do you really have to move your keyboard and mouse anyway? Plus, no more dead batteries.

I did not purchase this through Amazon, but I frequently shop here and wanted to share my review. When I own it for long enough I may add things or change things. The keyboard is kind of attractive, but in a minimalist way. There is no backlighting, no hot keys, and no design features which make it appear to originate from an alien spaceship. I do like the font on the keys and board feels sturdy and well built. The cable is actually detachable which I think is a good feature if you are packing it up or if the cable is damaged. I believe it is a USB to 5 pin flat connector.

I have to say that this is my first mechanical keyboard and I have not adjusted to it yet. My previous one was a Logitech Illuminated Keyboard, wired, and it was very low profile and resembled a laptop keyboard with it's scissor switches. That is my favorite keyboard ever and I would give it 5 1/2 stars. The Logitech had a very short keystroke. The Cherry board has a keystroke of almost 2x the distance, but it actuates half way down. It takes a lot of getting used to not to press the keys all the way down.

I did a lot of research, but unfortunately I did not have the luxury of trying the different types of switches before choosing one. I ultimately went with the brown because that seems to be the most popular for typists and I do not like a lot of clickiness. I do not know if I would have liked a different switch better than this one. I can tell you for the noise level of typing, it's VERY QUIET. It is very similar to my previous Logitech keyboard with scissor keys. One think I like a lot about this is that they keys are VERY STURDY. There is no wiggle. Almost every keyboard I have owned made a lot of noise from the keys rattling and wiggling. These keys travel up and down with the switch and that is all; there is no horizontal movement or twisting. The "actuation" is minimal, meaning the amount of pressure it take for the keystroke to register. I'm wondering if I shouldn't have chosen a different color switch, one that requires more pressure. Some say mechanical board are loud, but this is QUIET, especially if you don't jam the keys all the way down. I wish I had a way of objectively testing it, but it's comparable to your average, cheap rubber dome keyboard. I have no other mechanical keyboards to compare it to.
*I should add that I am a light typer. If you are rough on the keys, meaning you slam them down, it does make some noise. However, it is still not as loud as most of the Youtube videos showing mechanical keyboard noise.

This is a full size keyboard. It's not a ten key less. However, the border of the keyboard extends only an extra 1/2 inch around the keys. I like that it takes up less room on my desktop. I wouldn't mind a few extra media keys or hotkeys, but I don't mind making the sacrifice for a smaller keyboard. I would not however give up the number pad. Even though it's not used that often it's still essential in my opinion. I will break this down in to pros and cons.

PROS:
-minimalist design
-detachable cable
-sturdy board
-very sturdy keys
-quiet and responsive keystrokes ( like the font on the keys)
-low profile (as far as mechanical keyboards go this is considered low profile)
-inexpensive. Costs 30-75 dollars less than other mechanical keyboards, but also lacks some of the bells and whistles
-anti-skid rubber caps and adhesive backing. The board stays put.
Cons:
-minimalist design (I don't care for a flashy, ornate gaming keyboard, but this is a little too plain). It very much resembles the cheap Dell keyboards that came with their low end desktop computers a few years back, in appearance only that is. The Corsair K70 looks like an attractive board to me.
-NO PALM REST! There actually is one for this board, but it has to be purchased separately and it's difficult to find, and expensive.
-no braided cord
- no programmable hot keys or included software
-no backlighting or USB ports

Other Thoughts:
It's awkward pressing the keys halfway down, but I do really like a short key stroke. I wonder of if I would have liked blue or clear switches better, being stiffer and/or giving more feedback. Unfortunately I could not try all of these out before buying them. I may try the rubber stoppers to shorten the keystroke. I have not decided yet if I like my Logitech K740 better yet. I've been using that one for about 5 years.

Edit: I am changing my review to 5 stars. After typing on a Dell keyboard, the dome switches seem extremely hard to press and uncomfortable. I do not think the actuation pressure which I believe is 45g is too little for the Cherry, but I would like to try this side by side with the clear MX switches. It is true that this has no programmable hot keys, braided cord, lights, USB ports, but you go into the purchase knowing this. If you do some research you can find the board for $80 which is almost unheard of for a mechanical keyboard. If some of these features are important to you than you will simply choose a more expensive keyboard. I can find no reason not to give it 5 stars. There is one thing that irks me to no end--- the wrist rest is not included!! It's very difficult to find and the vendors that sell it are charging an arm and a leg, nearly what the keyboard is worth. I purchased an aftermarket wrist rest.

Edit: I've now owned this for over a month now and have adjusted to the keys. At first my typing speed suffered because I fumbled a bit for the keys or missed them, and I was not used to the longer stroke. I have learned to press each key halfway and am typing more accurately. I can no longer use the Logitech Illuminated keyboard, but I returned it anyway because it had some unexpected problems with certain key combinations.

Used this to replace a handset on a 20 year old 3 line AT&T office phone.  I don't know how standardized these things actually are, but if fit perfectly and the sound is as expected.  I was looking at other handsets and some people complained that they did not fit the cradle, which is why I purchased this one.  I would look here first.

I can't REALLY comment on the audio or video quality. It looks as good as it did. I have a TV that has an external media box, which died. So this was the only way I could find to get audio to my receiver. It does it flawlessly and reproduces 7.1 sound enough for my receiver to know to send sound all over. This solves my problem until I replace the TV.

(I have received this product mostly free in exchange for an honest review)
I have been using a 3-in to 1-out HDMI switch for a couple years and recently the media box for one of my TVs died, so put on connected to the single HDMI input. It works just fine, but I have more than 3 devices I'd like to connect and reaching to change the input is annoying.
This has solved multiple problems. having 5 HDMI inputs is a pretty sweet deal. I've only tested 3 of them so far and they work just fine. One nice feature that I didn't expect is that it doesn't appear to let you switch to an input that doesn't have a device even powered on, at least using the remote.
The picture quality is just fine. I have nothing to compare it to, but it looks no worse than it ever did.
The nice feature of my previous switch was that it did not need to be powered. The Koopman one DOES need power. It comes with the micro USB cable and power adapter, but if your TV has an open 5v usb output, that might be more convenient. I had to plug it in. It's a minor annoyance, but if you're low on outlet space, keep it in mind.
It's small and light, so I'll need to anchor it in place so it's not flying off the stand. HDMI cables like to pull things awry. It's almost inconspicuous.
Speaking of HDMI cables, it doesn't come with one. I had expected (and didn't pay attention to the product description - so MY bad) at least a short one.
The remote is tiny. This is great because it doesn't take up much space, but I KNOW I'm going to spend a bunch of events looking for it in the couch or under the footrest or because a spider dragged it into their web in the corner. The remote worked from at least 15-20 feet away (as far as I could comfortably go), BUT, the angle of reception is not very wide. It might be about 60 degrees (I did not pull out the protractor). The box itself had a button on it, so if the remote goes temporarily missing, you can still tap your way between inputs.
I'll give it some time to see how it lasts. If it does well over time, I'll possibly buy another for another TV with only one HDMI input.
One cool improvement would be if it had an audio output, even in only a 1/8" port.

So far, I like this tv. It has issues though. Some strange combo of using Chromecast and turned it off causes it to require being unplugged to get back to the home. It's happened 2-3 times in the month or I've had it.
Sometimes getting back to home is just tricky or lucky.
The home screen is MESSY with too much stuff. I wish we could customize some parts out of it.
Vizio watchfree is cool, but we don't use it. We cut cable long ago and it feels like having cable again, which might be a huge plus for some.
When connected to a sound bar and using apps (mostly casting) to change volume, it makes huge jumps or inconsistent changes.
The app could use traditional arrows as an optional interface.
It would also be nice to have it work with both wired and the wireless networks concurrently, but that's not even common with a PC.
I'll give it more time. If the issue with requiring unplugging continues, it'll be a warranty issue.

The picture looks pretty good out of the box-setup, but I'll eventually tweek it. For a matte screen, it does reflect a lot more lamps/light that I expected.

I found myself needing to teach from home, like most US teachers, because of covid-19. Using zoom and whiteboard software locally, I would attempt to maintain some of the same methods I use in class, but also knew I'd need to do a lot more "showing" for that low ratio of students showing up for conferences sessions. Another teacher loaned hers to me to test for a few minutes. It did the job, so I decided to get one myself.
I really only use Windows for games that won't install/run in linux. My distance teaching wasn't going to be from Windows if I could help it.
This worked right out of the box. It didn't have all the functions, but it worked as a mouse would. It meant I could write (doing math work) in the whiteboard software without trying to do it with a mouse or fumble equations in real time with an equation editor or giving too much away using Geogebra.
I'm also a lefty, so that proved annoying quickly. It defaults to right handed mode, and the body that holds the electronics gets in the way. So I HAD to find drivers. Thankfully at Github (search Linux driver for Veikk-brand digitizers ) there is a driver. Installing was not too bad (had to compile myself - and had to find a fix for something getting in the compile way, search ""FATAL: Module veikk not found in directory" and a potential fix" at github).
Viola! The touch sensitivity works just fine and I can rotate the orientation, by manually editing parameters in /sys/module/veikk/parameters
Great, but then I had to find the GUI, because it kept resetting my orientation setting any time I rebooted. Search "Configuration tool for the VEIKK Linux driver" at github for the gui installer. It gave me hassles to install, but somehow I got it installed. Idon't use it much, but somehow it also keeps my orientation setting correct on reboots, and that's what I cared most about. I could change button configs and the sensitivity curve, but I'm not there yet.
Openboard (foss whiteboard) actually works with the touch sensitivity, but Activinspire doesn't. No big deal. Gimp doesn't until you set it to in device settings. Krita didn't need to be told what to do and works wonderfully.

My complaints:
The PITA driver installation isn't one really. They don't officially support linux - THAT is worthy of a complaint though. For those using linux, I'm going to guess, still, many are used to dealing with this.
The placement of the USB cord is annoying when in lefty (108 deg orientation), as the cord comes in your direction.
The drawing surface isn't huge, but that's a given. The challenge is that the sensitive area goes very close to the edge, making it hard to draw on the edges if you are not using this on a regular flat surface. I'm using it on my lap, most of the time.
The pen is also thick! 7/16" or 11mm diameter. Not super comfy. My hands aren't small. It makes using the buttons a little less than optimal, but I don't use them much yet anyway. I'm sure as I do more art with it than math, I'll want to customize that. I have an older wacom stylus I'll try to locate and see if it magically works. It was a far better fit.
All said and done, I do recommend this. I might even buy one of the larger ones.

I'll update later. First thing I did was toy with it a little to make sure it worked, then I installed Ubuntu 12.04. THEN I found out that there are not reliable drivers for using the optimus feature in linux. I went with this laptop so that I can play one game in particular. After spending HOURS tweeking, installing and experimenting, I'm at the point where I can say, if you plan on using this machine for linux AND gaming, either walk on by, or plan on dual booting or running a virtual machine (which one I've not decided I'll do yet). I THINK if there was the ability in the BIOS to turn off the intel graphics card in favor of only using the nvidia, that might be helpful.
The design is nice, it's fast and it may be heavy by today's standards, but compared to the Dell d810 I'm replacing, this is light.
The price point is, as stated by many before, excellent.

I take away the star for the simple fact that it's FAR too late in the game for nvidia to not have appropriate drivers to support this card fully in linux.

I do NOT want to run windows 7, but it looks like I'll be recovering it and spending hours decrapifying.

Update: May, 14, 2012
I've now had the laptop running a dual boot of Ubuntu 12.04 and Windows 7. I initially tried to just run Ubuntu and gave up on the driver debacle - fail for nvidia - and went back to reinstall. Major advice, when you get this machine, BOOT IT AND MAKE THE RECOVERY DVD SET!!! It took 4 DVDs and actually a little while, but it was the best move. When I went to recover W7, it did not properly use the recovery partition. The DVDs rebuild the partition (and destroy everything else in the process) back to factory. That was ok for me, I was testing and didn't lose anything worth saving.

Boot is fast. Ubuntu shuts down super fast, so the time to switch isn't bad. I play my game (Lord of the Rings Online - mostly set as ultra settings) quit and reboot into linux so I can enjoy my daily computing experience.

The plus other mention is the full HD experience. My previous laptop did 1900x100. I miss the vertical resolution, but am getting used to only having 1080. The screen is great. I do not understand why people like the glossy/glare screens. I hate them. This is pretty matte.

Temperature-wise it runs lap-top ok. The left side vent blows warm/hot air, which was actually nice on my hand in the cold basement during gaming (I'm a lefty - using a mouse).

I'm getting used to the keyboard. I often find it misses some of my key strokes, but I might just need to MEAN them a little more, as I tend to type with a softer touch. This makes the typing experience a little louder than I prefer, but my wife doesn't complain, so it can't be that bad.

I'm a tad less fond of the USB placement. They are toward the front of the sides, which means the USB plugs are close to all my business. If I had the RJ45 connected as well, it would be more annoying wires up close and personal.

As or resources, it feels perfectly adequate for my needs. This weekend I was running about 60 firefox tabs, 10 chrome tabs, a handful of libre office documents, Redblade 3.5 (D&D character generator) running twice via wine, about 15 20-50MB PDFs, ktorrent, and a few other things here and there concurrently without a hiccup. Eventually, maybe I'll upgrade to more ram, but I cannot currently see any reason for it. I also can't see a particular reason to plunk down for a SSD. I imagine the power saving would be nice. I do get only around 2-2.5 hours of regular use off power, but since this is a desktop replacement, that's less of an issue. If it was less than 1.5 hrs, I'd be troubled.

There are several instances where this item is not what was advertised. Here is the list:
Starting with the 26 melodies, this is false. There are likely a possibility of 26 different melodies available in the manufacture of this device, but a random four (4) will be chosen for your receiver. Each receiver mode will have a single melody selection within the sensor that will create a different ring depning on which if he four sensors is activated. Inside the sensor, there are two switches, one for sensitivity, the other which identifies the sensor as number 1, 2, 3, or 4. You can stand in the house (pre-installation) and move this switch, for the single detector package, and select ONE of the FOUR melodies provided, which will then become permanent once your screw the back panel on the sensor, and then screw the sensor to its permanent location. Sure, if you get sick of the melody, you can take it down, and apart, and then move the switch to a different number if you only have one sensor, however, if you order four sensors, each will have their own separate melody for location indication, and these melodies cannot be changed. It comes with four only.

The next problem, is that on the incuded pamphlet, it states that the sensor can be set up in two ways. One way is a straight angle, and from 3.5' to 4.5 feet. This will catch ANY motion, even the wind blowing, becaue this is a HEAT sensitive device. If the sensor has a heat image deviation, it will sound. The wind can do this during any evening or morning where there is a temperature difference between low and high air. The second set up is not higher, still from 3.5' to 4.5', but the sensor is angled diagonally across an area, and tilted downward. This is supposed to make a difference in only showing heat signatures and motion for larger objects.
Now, on the web page, it states that this second setting should be 4.5' to 6' high to achieve the best angle. It also states that the lense of the sensor should not be exposed to direct sunlight during the day as this can ruin the sensor leading to false detetions. It also says on the web page that a solid, non-moving mount is essential for accurate sensor monitoring. Nowhere in the instructions are these two critical pieces of information given.

My father, and octogenarian, was extremely firm in his belief that only the piece of paper in the box with its limited instructions should be believed, not some nonsense on the internet. The company needs to get a native English speaker to update the assembly and information pamphlet included with the device. It is not in agreement with the sales page, and it does not give pertinent information. I explained the differences to dad, and then remarked how his two receivers from a different brand, but also manufactured in the same country were non functional within a short time period when 1. He had them set up straight across at 3 feet high, and 2. They were positioned facing south where the sun shinned on the sensor all day. I got him to conceded that I had a point. These two factors give false alarms to the devices.

After measuring the distances, which was 15' - 20 feet of coverage distance needed, we chose the low medium setting, for 20 feet. We picked sensor melody for sensor 2. We placed the sensor at 5' high, and angled it slightly to the left, not straight across the driveway to the barn. Then we tested. A golfball rolled will not be picked up, so mice and chipmunks will not be picked up. I walked by(I am 5' tall) and it picked me up 15 feet ahead of the mounted position, coming from its distant angled side( its blind side). Dad, 6' tall, walked past it and back. It sounded at the same location as it did for me going by, and coming back, it picked him up twice as far out. Perfect. Driving a car by in either direction gives one sound, not repeated. Some models will sound forever for a vehicle, this one does not if set properly.

As far as it being waterproof, it has only drizzled, not hard rained yet. However, the shield on the top, shaped like a wide horseshoe, both covers the top seams, and covers the sensor well from side sunshine. The four screws on the back panel have rubber plugs in them. The seam for the panel is completely hidden when it is mounted.

With the mounting being so permanent for internal settings, no one is going to get inside easily and remove your battery, or try to turn down the sensor range to sneak by. It has a mini plug charger plug hole and a rechargeable battery. It can be charged in place or you can take it indoors to charge by dismounting it from its location.

I do recommend this unit for simple motion detection, especially since it is easy to install. The receiver has an on/off button, two volume buttons, and AC adapter plug, a low battery warning light from which you will know to go get your sensor and charge it.

If this product has any problems in the next 12 months, I will update this review.

Pro (for me):
Really good, clear pictures
Good image stabilization (hand-holding at 1/15th of a second or slower!)
Low noise, as low as ISO 1600
Large zoom range
Manual focus
DIGIC 6 processor (latest generation)
Very nice screen
P, Av, Tv & M exposure modes
Canon's basically good control layout
Small and light; carrying around a DSLR can be wearying
Wi-Fi is handy
Fits in the same case as my A1100, which was originally bought for a tiny 35 mm Vivitar I carried as a 2nd camera for years. It's marked "Samsonite World Sport, Model #20" if that helps.

Cons:
Not as good a macro capability as the A1100 (which is sterling at that one thing. I'll be keeping it for that.)
No viewfinder (unlike the A1100. It's not needed all the time, but it is handy)
Slow GPS lock in (my Nexus shows 18 or so satellites in view, and took maybe 30 sec. to lock in. The camera took several times that)
GPS power hog. (It appears to suck up a lot of power, turning it on and off a few times did seem to affect battery charge indication)
No auto bracket (To be fair, that's not common on cameras, but it should be. Canon puts it on the similar S110.)
No hyperfocal distance setting (You can do it manually, of course, but, Canon, why not add another click on the focus bar? There's a computer in there, you know)
Lithium batteries (I prefer the A1100's NiMH AAs so you can get a new set at any Staples for cheap or use alkaline AAs in a pinch)

So, with all of 2 days of experience under my belt:
1) Nice easily-portable camera at a low-ish price
2) Power hog, due to inefficient GPS, big zoom, and powerful microprocessor being pushed by video, etc.
I'll update this review someday when I have some durability information.

Update: 4/27/2014 Took a nice long walk, shot 6 min. of 720p x 30fps video and took 101 L-superfine .jpg (4k x 3k pixel) photos. This used up most of a fully-charged Vivitar 1700 mA-h battery. I got a battery warn and shutdown after my walk while reviewing the video at home. The 1000 mA-h stock Canon battery would give proportionately less life. Canon says that the stock battery is good for 210 photos. A 1700 mA-h Vivitar battery should be good for 147 more than that, or 357 photos. That means that 6 min. of 720p video is worth 256 photos! I don't think anyone will be shooting at 1080p x 60fps much.

Another way to look at it is the number of pixels processed per second by any of the 11 modes of the camera. The normal L .jpg picture takes 12.0E+6 pixels/sec (12 megapixels/sec). The least hungry mode S, takes only 0.307E+6 pixels per second. The hungriest mode is the 14 frames per second L multiple shot mode, which takes 168.E+6 pixels/sec. Since this is only in use for a few frames, it's not bad on battery life. The second worst mode 1080p x 60fps takes 124.E+6 pixels per second, 1037% of the normal L photo processing power! The 720p x 30fps mode I used is only 230% of the normal L mode. Remember, though, the single shot modes are on now and then, maybe a second out of every minute at most. The video modes are on continuously.

NB: Good cameras with a lot of features have historically eaten batteries. I carry around a handful for the A1100.

Misc.: I'm sorry to see the little A1100 get superseded; it was a trouper. Its biggest problem was auto-focusing at long zoom, which isn't a problem if you're taking snapshots in your yard, but it can be a problem if you see a magnificent vista before you. The SX280 shouldn't have a problem with that (manual zoom). YMMV

Update 7/13/2014: My one significant complaint with the SX280 was the macro focusing. As I've gotten more experience with it, some of that has gone away. The SX280's autofocus seems to work differently from the A1100's. I tend to use the macro setting less, and let the normal mode carry the freight, except in extreme cases. In many cases, that's plenty good enough. It's still not as good as the A1100, though. In all other ways, this is an amazing still camera. It also still has too small a battery. Canon seems to be phasing this one out. If you need a still camera and can find one of these cheap, you might consider it.
August, 2017 Update: 3 & a bit years after purchase, the camera is becoming unreliable, throwing E32 (lens) errors more & more frequently. That's not a bad lifespan for a point & shoot, especially with a wide-range zoom lens. The error appears to be focus related.
Sept. 2018 Update: I replaced this with a 720. Much better. I actually cured the lens error with some strong blasts into the lens gaps from canned air. That's risky, blowing dust into the camera, but in this case, it worked. The 280 is now my office camera.

...and it works with my Targus Bluetooth keyboard. Actually, it works better than it does with the GP5. The Samsung has some key-mapping problems, probably due to Gingerbread.

As to reading, I happened to be starting a novel the other day, and started it on the Nexus 7. I had no problem. I did keep the brightness on 'Auto', so the light level of the screen matched the ambient light. With the GP5, matching light levels was a little chancy, so I had a bit more eyestrain. (Of course the extra 2" of screen have no bearing on that, right?)

I did try the freebie 'La Luna' video that Google gives away. It watched fine on the 7" screen. The thing I really like is that there is a 7" screen in the weight of a past-technology 5" package. I owned a Nook color for 13 days, but took it back because of the weight and balance. It just wasn't comfortable to hold.

I haven't tried any significant music listening. I suspect I'll still prefer my Clip+ for that. The Nexus is a little large for that purpose. I also haven't tried the camera in any particular serious way. A selfie and a picture of my cat isn't much of a trial. Again, I'll probably use a purpose-made camera for real pictures. I also haven't explored portability yet. In the case, it's a bit bulky for easy transport, whereas the GP5 fits in my pocket next to my cell phone. I probably won't put the N7 in my pocket without a case. It's a little large and fragile seeming for that.

...As to the camera, it's OK, the image quality is fine, but a 7" tablet just isn't a good ergonomic platform for picture taking. This is the best from an afternoon at Mass Audubon's Ipswich River Wildlife Sanctuary.

...And I still prefer my Clip+ for music. I hand to hunt around the Android store for a decent player for my collection which includes WMAs as well as MP3s. Google does not play WMAs (cue prissy, superior sniff). I settled on Poweramp, not because it was perfect, but because it was the first one I came to that was good enough. I've had no real problems with this router. Since I did my homework before buying it cheap, I had read about all of the problems other people have had. In particular, I noted several observations that this device runs hot. That shouldn't be a surprise, since the case ventilation is poor compared to other routers on the market. I put mine in an open space on a wooden desktop and had no problems for a long while. One hot summer day, the router had to be reset, and the case was unusually hot to the touch. I put the router up on a couple of small blocks, to get more air circulation and the problem went away.

My advice, either put it up on spacers like mine, or mount it vertically on a wall or the side of a desk. Make sure you don't block off any air ventilation.

I hope the industrial designer who decided that no vents on the top surface were needed won some kind of artistic award. Me, I'd have laid him off for incompetence.

Update, June 2013: Still working, still needs resetting occasionally. I recently took a vacuum cleaner to all of the vents and the need to reset decreased. Keep it cool.

Update, June 2016: It finally failed, albeit gracefully. Requiescat in pace.
