I headlined this review "Linux loads fine," but with a caveat: neither Debian or Ubuntu detected the onboard wifi card. No prob. I have a USB wifi dongle that plays well with Linux and used that to test the installs.

One of the first things I did was pull the included 128gb NVMe (which is preloaded with Windows) and replaced it with another NVMe stick I had on hand. Then I installed an SSD in the 2.5-inch SATA drive bay. Getting to the SSD bay is easy. You just remove a single Phillips screw and slide a lock switch to the side and the top lifts off the box. Getting to the NVMe socket (which I'd guess most people are probably unlikely to need to do) is another matter. It requires loosening the main board by removing four screws that are accessed by pulling off the rubber bottom corner pads. A magnetic screwdriver comes in really handy, especially during reassembly.

The system didn't detect the replacement NVMe stick I installed. Maybe a compatibility issue, or the original stick is proprietary in the BIOS or something, not a machine flaw. It did detect the SATA connected SSD, so I went ahead. The BIOS had no prob booting from a USB stick. Installation of both Debian and Ubuntu went without a hitch, except for the wifi card issue I mentioned. That's not unusual when installing Linux in machines with recent-generation wifi cards. Sometimes the drivers just aren't available.

The bottom line for me is this mini PC is capable, runs smoothly, graphics look good (but don't expect to run this as a gaming machine), and it is pretty quiet. And Linux will load on it. It would make an excellent Linux-based file server or media server with a hard-wired Ethernet connection. If you just go with the Windows OS and NVMe stick it comes with, it all works right out of the box, and you can add a SATA 2.5 inch SSD for more storage.

The build quality of this little portable recorder is great. It's metal, not plastic, and has a nice heft and feels durable. It looks great. And audio quality is very good. It comes with a micro SD card already installed and ready to go. It also comes with a set of ear buds, a lavalier microphone which can be used instead of the built-in mics, a cord for line-in recording, and a USB charging cord. No charger is included. And it does not come with a protective pouch or sleeve. But it is boxed nicely.

It records in user-selectable WAV or MP3 formats in various selectable bitrates. It has adjustable gain control and a noise reduction function. One important function for voice recording is the ability to monitor while recording using ear buds or headphones, and this recorder has that capability. The display screen isn't as sharp and clear as it is portrayed in the listing photos, but it is decent.

Now for the minor negatives, for which I dinged a star off the review rating. One is the printing labeling the buttons on the one I received is only a little lighter than the color of the recorder, making them very hard to read. That means you have to memorize the button location and functions or keep the user manual handy for reference. And that leads to the second negative, and that is the print in the user manual is tiny. Really tiny. I looked for a PDF version online and couldn't find one. The manual suggests visiting the brand's web site, but neither the manual nor the box provide a URL. Or even the listing brand name (Tenmatec) for that matter. I wound taking photographs of the manual pages with a tablet so I could enlarge them for easier reading. The other minor negative is that it has no USB-C port, only a micro USB for recharging or connecting to a computer for moving files around.

Other than that it's a good recorder. It has one-button functionality (although there is a slight delay when starting a recording while it starts up). Because of its metal construction and heft it feels good in-hand and looks really good.

This charger is heavy duty and well built. Output is twenty amps. Charging cycles (start, fast charge, float) are all automatic. The green light comes on at the end of the fast charge cycle, and the charger switches to float (trickle charge). I checked with a multimeter and three different 12V LiFePO4 batteries. Fast charge brings a 12V LiFePO4 up to around 13.65V. Leaving the charger connected and on float, after a few hours the battery was up to 13.91, almost at 14V. The instructions describe a power switch, but the charger I received doesn't have one. The only power switch is to simply plug it in or unplug it. It has a cooling fan that comes on during fast charge cycle, so it does make a little noise while charging. There's no status display other than a red and green LED (red is charging, red flashing means error, green means charged and on float).
The sound is a little tinny in my opinion but they're loud enough and they come with enough sizes of cones to fit most ears including mine. And the price is really good.

The first thing to note is that this tablet comes with a screen protector already installed on it. But the top protective sheet is still in place. It's to be removed by pulling the tab on it. I didn't realize it was a protective sheet on a screen protector and started lifting a corner instead of the tab and almost removed the screen protector too.

So anyway, that said, this budget tablet is a good value. The screen isn't ultra high definition, but it is 1200 by 800, and that's high definition enough for reading and media. And on top of that it's an IPS display, so the color and viewing angle range are really good. Touch screen responsiveness is okay too.

Build quality is surprisingly good. The tablet feels solid. The speakers and volume are decent. It has 64GB built in memory but only 2GB of RAM, which isn't great, but it works well for most purposes even if operation isn't always smooth. The listing says the Rockchip processor is 1.5GHz, and it seems capable of keeping up with most things. At 1.5GHz, though, It's not a gaming tablet, but it works for browsing and videos and reading.

One place you notice that this is a budget tablet is the cameras. Front and rear, they're pretty grainy and contrasty. But they'll do. And the cameras are located on middle of the right edge in portrait orientation, right where you hand would ordinarily be holding the tablet (if you're right handed).

It comes with a charger and USB-A to USB-C cable, and it ships with Android version 11. There's a built-in user manual app icon. The manual is pretty short and simple. There's a micro SD card slot that works fine. One more thing to note is the included blue light reducing app overlays the screen with a filter that can interfere with screen operation with some apps, Google Play Store being one of them. The solution is to turn that app off while using any apps it interferes with. I found out that unfortunately that app cannot be uninstalled, and alternative blue light filter apps are blocked from functioning with the explanation that they will slow down the tablet's performance. I don't know what's up with that. (You can't uninstall the included user manual app either.)

Holding the tablet in portrait orientation, both speakers are on the left edge (for viewing in landscape orientation), the headphone jack is on the bottom right, and the power and volume switches are on the lower right edge. The USB-C port and micro SD card slot are on the upper right edge.

The manual recommends charging the tablet a few hours before first using. Mine arrived over 90 percent charged so I set it up right away, then charged it.

For the money you get a good, useable tablet with a very good (though not ultra hi def) display and few minor budget tablet quirks. As I said it's a good value.

This review might seem a little overly enthusiastic but I really like this little radio. The second product photo is accurate -- it's pretty much palm sized. But it has lots of fun features, including multi-band tuning and lots of LED indicators and surprisingly loud volume. It will also play MP3s, WAVs, or WMA music files from a micro SD card (up to 256 gb capacity, card not included with radio).

It recharges via USB-C. The battery looks like an old-school flip phone Li-ion battery. Tuning performance is okay. The thumb wheel isn't going to give you fine control when shortwave listening, but the SW spectrum is divided into seven bands so it works. It's amazing this little radio even has SW. FM tuning seems to be assisted with AFC, so it automatically locks in on stronger signals on the band. The built in rod antenna is supplemented with an included clip-on wire extension for use on some bands.

You get FM, MW (medium wave, also known as AM), SW (shortwave in seven bands) , and weather band with several preset freqs. The LEDs indicate current band, power status, and can display battery charge, or function as a VU meter while listening.

It does come with an English language user guide that's pretty easy to understand. The selection buttons are all small (it's a small radio) and dark colored and have only embossed lettering so you pretty much need the guide or to memorize the functions and locations to operate everything.

It does not have a headphone jack or a line-in input. It will not transmit a wireless signal to other devices. But as I said it will function as a wireless speaker. It has a sleep timer, but no clock or alarm function.

It's a tiny speaker of course, but the sound quality and volume is impressive. On certain EQ settings it can get pretty loud. Don't expect full hi-fi audio from a speaker this small, but it is clear and has a decent sound. The sound quality reminds me of some of the better old school transistor radios (the ones that used 9V batteries).

And as I said in the title of this review, this little radio is fun.

Nah the bass ain't boom, but it's acceptable, and it sort of depends on how tight you fit the ear tips into your ears. But these are nice and loud and they have a great high end. You get a lot of bang for the buck -- they're rated IPX7 waterproof, the case has a digital charge meter, and it recharges the earphones several times before it requires recharging (via USB-C). Pairing and operation are pretty simple, and the instruction sheet covers that. You get three sizes of ear tips by the way. My set arrived with the smallest ones already installed, and almost a full charge.

No issues running this cam on Linux. Plugged it in and it worked. It comes with a USB Type C to USB-A cable to connect to a computer. The cable is about 6 feet long.

It doesn't have built-in, onboard light or picture adjustments, but it's high resolution and a good quality picture, and capable of being adjusted via software. It also has onboard mics so sound can be captured simultaneously. Build quality seems very good. It has a simple clamp for positioning it atop a computer display. The gimbal base rotates 360, and up and down, but doesn't tilt side to side. That can be adjusted by simply putting something under the clamp to adjust it. And it can be mounted on a tripod. It comes with a lens cover too.

Overall this is a good portable stand for a laptop or projector or other device. I deducted just one star for a few reasons: It's a little top heavy, especially when a device is on it and it's extended to its full height. The metal edge of the tray could be uncomfortable if you rest your wrists on it. And the lower front corners of the tray are a bit sharp. The only other issue is the tray will slip out of tilt position if you put a lot of weight on it. I think some sort of locking adjuster might have worked a little better there.

The stand was very wobbly when I first assembled it, but I realized the lower tube clamp (the one above the base clamp) wasn't positioned correctly. It should be only halfway on the lower tube, so the upper half of the clamp can tighten on the tube above it. Repositioning it was simple and only required a Phillips screwdriver. After that it tightened nicely and no more wobble.

It does adjust high enough for use standing up. It comes with a carrying bag, a foam pad for the tray, and a couple of elastic bands for securing whatever device you put on the tray. It also comes with a clamp-on phone holder.

The sound quality isn't that of boutique headphones, but these pretty much hit the sweet spot for me. They are excellent for listening to narration or spoken word material or podcasts, dialog-heavy movies and series, and for phone calls. They lack boomy bass and have good high end and a pretty flat mid-range, all of which are a plus for me. They're okay for music, but if music listening is your primary use, you might shop for something else. I'd liken them to the sound of a good quality portable radio with the "bass boost" turned off. And the mic works great for phone calls.

This isn't a full-range audiophile headset. It's basically a midrange speaker. But it works very well for listening to spoken narration, audiobooks and the like. Really handy for side sleepers -- just hang it on the "upside" ear, switch it when you roll over.

Installation requires a power outlet somewhere nearby, because this cam isn't totally wireless. It comes with a 12v adapter. But it works over wifi, so no Ethernet cable is needed. A 64gb micro SD card is included for onboard storage of motion capture video (up to 128gb is supported). Or you can set up an account and upload captured video. The 5X optical zoom makes clear images up to the limits of 5X, then it switches to digital zoom and things can get less sharp.

The FHD IPS display shows pictures in nice color and sharpness. The transitions between pictures are simple and smooth. It's listed as 10-inch, but it's actually a little smaller than that. But it looks fine.

Like some similar digital picture frames, it requires using an app to load photos via wifi, even though pictures are stored on board. It has 16GB of built-in storage. It's not cordless. It uses a power adapter. And it does have a stand.

Good quality walkie talkies. I like that the listing is realistic about the range (about a half mile in urban settings, up to two miles in rural, open country). The lapel mics and separate chargers are a plus.

These also feature wireless cloning. Cloning is simply copying the settings from one walkie talkie to another so you don' t have to manually enter frequency and such.

It's a good set for family use or for small events or business use.

The HD resolution is plenty sharp and the 10.1-inch touchscreen is nice and large for viewing photos. Wifi is required to set it up and load pictures, which are stored onboard after loading. It's not cordless. It uses a power adapter. The frame looks nice and has a built-in stand.

Here are the negatives, and the reason I deducted a star:

It requires the app and registration for loading pictures. The transitions between pictures are not always smooth, and there isn't a lot of choice for them. The color isn't as vibrant as on IPS displays.

You could spend extra money for more resolution and an IPS display and more freedom on how you upload pictures to the device. But for the money, this one works well.
Good wireless headset at a good price with good performance. Audio is very good, and the mic works very well.

This PTZ camera has lots of features out of the box, including motion tracking and low light capability, two-way audio, and of course remote pan, tilt, and 5X zoom. Some things you might want to keep in mind though:

Installation isn't too difficult, but the dome cannot be easily detached from the mount, making it difficult to drive the lower two mounting screws. (Screws and wall anchors are included.) I made a paper template as a guide for drilling the pilot holes and used a small rachet wrench as a bit driver to crank the screws in. A nearby power outlet or extension cord will be needed for the power adapter.

The camera can be initialized using a device (phone or tablet) via WiFi with the CamHiPro app. The app insists on location permission, or it stops setup. I wasn't too pleased with that. However, the camera can be operated and viewed using other IP camera apps, which I think is a good thing. The camera can also be set up using a PC and a direct connection to a router using an Ethernet cable. One is included.

The camera is ONVIF compliant, which seems like a good thing (compatibility with other security cams and such), but one app I loaded warned that ONVIF isn't secure. I'm okay with it for now.

This camera is meant to be mounted in a high position. It can't tilt any higher than level. When zooming, it points downward slightly.

The instructions are pretty clear. I was able to follow them and get it installed and working. The instructions say mount it in a location where WiFi signal strength is at least 70%. And that's what it was at the location I mounted it, and it's working okay, a little better when the stream is set to SD instead of HD.

I can actually type faster on a low profile scissors-switch keyboard than a mechanical. This one is a bargain (especially when the seller offers a coupon for a few extra dollars off), and it has a really nice feel---it reminds me of the much-liked keyboards on vintage ThinkPads. The throw is short and fast. The thin profile means you're not reaching way up (meaning higher above the desktop than your hand position) for keys. It doesn't take a thick wrist rest to get into optimal position, a modestly thin one will do.  It's also quiet. This tenkeyless version has takes only a small space on the desk, and the mouse can be kept closer to it. The mouse is okay, a little slow to wake up maybe, but it works. Incidentally this combo works fine with Linux.

Of course I'm typing this review on this keyboard. I like it a lot. I love the retro-looking round keycaps. They take a little getting used to if you're used to square keys. But some of us are familiar with round keycaps because we were around when there were devices called "manual typewriters" that had round keys that you had to punch hard to activate swinging hammer things to output text onto these white sheet things that we called "paper." Anyone who complains about the clickiness of mechanical keyboard switches (like the blue switches) hasn't spent a lot of time in an old-school office with the banging and clatter of manual typewriters. The loudest mechanical switches aren't anywhere near as noisy. The switches on this keyboard are brown type, so they're not very clicky.

The lighting effects are preprogrammed, and you cycle through them by pressing Fn+Ins. The colors are fixed, meaning each row are single color LEDs, so the effects are really about varying the way they light up. Fn+PgUp returns to the last selected effect. Fn+Up or Down arrow adjusts brightness. Adjust it all the way down to turn off the lighting. Fn+ Right or Left arrow adjusts lighting effect speed. The keyboard I received didn't come with any instructions, so I'm telling you all this stuff in case yours doesn't either.

Obviously at this price the mechanical key switches aren't going to be brand name top dollar switches, but they do have a nice feel. The stabilizers on the wider keys (space bar, shift, etc.) are pretty good too.

This is a wired keyboard, standard USB to computer, and micro USB into the keyboard. A cord is included.

It's a fun keyboard, and as I said in the headline, it's a lot of bang for the buck. I like it so much I bought a second one -- the blue switch version.

I love the layout of this keyboard. I love that it is tenkeyless. I love the action of the keys. It's a membrane keyboard, not a mechanical, but the keys operate smoothly with a relatively light touch. It's pretty quiet. The whole keyboard, though plastic, has a good durable feel.

The only thing I don't like is the built-in wrist rest. It slopes down too steeply to actually give any elevation to wrist position. It's smooth plastic and has no padding. And the keyboard does not come with a front edge riser, only back edge folding supports. I'm using it with improvised front edge elevation and wearable wrist rests. But I like everything else about this keyboard so I may keep using it.

This is a great little device for those muggy hot southern summer days when the air isn't moving much. Bring your own breeze. This portable blower can clip to your waistband, blowing air up under your shirt, or worn around you neck, with the air blowing right up onto your face and head. The stream of air travels a good distance too, so you can stand it on a table or desk near you.

It's rechargeable and runs for hours on a charge. It has three speeds that are selected by repeatedly pushing the on-off button. You can switch it directly off from any speed by long-pressing the button for three seconds. It comes with an adjustable neck strap, a USB-C adapter cable, and a brush for cleaning the air intake grill. In addition to a USB C input, it also has a standard micro USB input (standard cell phone kind) for charging.

When running, the sound it makes is mostly a soft white noise, but on the highest speed I noticed it does have a bit of jet engine whine. Otherwise it works great.

The picture is as vibrant and bright and sharp as advertised. It works with Google, Apple, Alexa out of the box. There's even a Google privacy agreement printed on the outside of the box before you even open it.

It's excellent for movies and streaming video. Gaming performance is very good. Not quite excellent, but very good. It did lag very slightly when there was a lot of action on screen at once.

The built-in sound is decent but you might want to add a sound bar.

The only negative is the screen on the unit we received had two dead pixels but it took some scrutiny to spot them. They're not really noticeable, and not worth initiating a return or deducting a star in this review, but if you're a stickler, you might want to give the screen a close inspection when you receive it.

I wanted something to amplify my phone's ring volume at night so it would wake me up. Volume boosting apps only boosted volume on my phone when headphones were attached. The seem to do nothing for ring volume. So I gave this speaker a try.

It works. Volume depends on what you set on your phone, but it does amplify nicely. It's not overpoweringly loud, but it is a lot louder.

The plug seems a little undersized. It's kind of loose in my phone's jack, and the speaker crackles a bit when I move it a little when it's plugged in. But it doesn't cut in and out, and it works.

The plug is positioned toward the back of the speaker so when you lay your phone down the speaker won't prop it up. As a result, the speaker is a bit front-heavy, so when you're carrying it with the speaker plugged in, the speaker tends to rotate to whatever the lowest position is. Most anything flat can be positioned behind the phone and speaker to stop that though.

Don't expect full-spectrum audio and rich bass. It's a tiny speaker and it sounds like a tiny speaker. But it does provide a nice boost to volume, it's small and convenient, and it's rechargeable.

If you go through a lot of canned air, this blower, though a bit pricey, will eventually pay for itself. It's really convenient since it is battery powered (and rechargeable). It puts out a stream of air that to me seems a lot stronger than canned air. It comes with an extension to reach into small places and direct the air flow.

It is pretty loud though. That's the only negative, but not enough of one to deduct a star.

You may know about the announcement from Lenovo a few weeks ago that going forward the company will be certifying all their ThinkPad and Thinkstation workstations for Linux. This computer is an IdeaCentre, not a ThinkPad or ThinkStation, and it comes preloaded with Windows, but I am a Linux user and I wanted to see if it will run Linux.

First things first: If you're looking for a gaming computer or something to handle graphics-intensive programs, this isn't it. It doesn't have a screaming fast processor, although it is a capable one. The onboard AMD Raven graphics module is pretty capable (I tried it out on a big display), but this model has no expansion slot for a video or audio card or any other such upgrades.

It does have a bay for a big 3.5 inch HDD with SATA connectors. And it comes with a 256GB SSD already installed on the motherboard. It also comes with 4GB RAM (and a second slot to add more), and a wired keyboard and mouse and the power supply. It has four USB 2.0 ports in the back, and two 2.0 and two 3.0 (gen 1) USB ports in the front. Also on the front are a card reader slot, the optical drive, mic and headset connection ports, and the power button. The back also has an HDMI port, VGA-out port, and and ethernet port.

It's about the size of an ITX mini tower form factor box, which is a little larger than a big dictionary. It stands upright, so the footprint is pretty small. And it's lightweight compared to a big desktop box.

I didn't even complete the first boot into Windows before attempting a Linux install. Tapping F2 on boot will get you into a graphical menu for picking your boot device, and F12 will get you into a deeper menu for selecting boot order and into the BIOS.

My favorite distro is Debian, so I thought I'd take a shot at installing it. It was a no-go. It didn't have the drivers for the onboard Atheros wifi card, and apparently a few other things. I actually pulled the wifi card off the motherboard and substituted a dongle and gave it a second try. I got Debian installed, but the machine still froze on boot without ever getting into the desktop environment.

So I tried installing Ubuntu, which, along with Red Hat, was specifically mentioned as now being supported by Lenovo. Success. Installation went smoothly. I was still using the dongle for wifi, so I shut down the machine and reinstalled the inboard card. Again, success. Wifi operated right away.

The couple of minor -- emphasizing minor -- things I don't like is that an inboard white LED glows continually when the power supply is plugged in, and as far as I can tell there's no way to turn it off.

Bottom line here is I think it's a good machine for general use. It's pretty capable, but be aware of its limitations so you won't be disappointed.

The charger comes with 8 AA rechargeable batteries, but not a power supply. Any USB power supply that can provide 1 to 2 amps of current will do. It comes with two cords -- a standard micro USB cord and a type C cord. Either will work to supply power to the charger.

You don't need to charge batteries in pairs with this charger. You can charge any number up to eight at a time. However, the instructions say that a 1 amp power supply is good for charging only up to four batteries, while charging eight requires a 2 amp power supply.

The display is bright and easy to see from even low angles. The display indicates which batteries are still charging, and which are full. The display has a basic progress meter in the form of the number of five bars representing each battery that remain lit as the batteries charge.

As far as the included batteries go, I own several Tenergy batteries already, and they've performed well. I expect these will do the same.

Surprisingly good build quality, light but sturdy. Good raceways for cable management and esthetics---they're easy to route out of sight. The power buttons (including a dedicated LED button) and some ports are front and center on the top for easy access. The cutouts are cut and fit perfectly. Very high airflow design, which may result in some fan/air noise, but that's a trade off. And it's a cool design. Good mid-tower case.

This is a great solution for a remote monitor for video shoots, and it's simple, no wires, no cables, and basically one-button operation. You install the app on your device (iOS or Android), connect the transmitter to your video camera (via HDMI), boot it up, then connect your device to it via WiFi. Launch the app and you're looking live at the video camera output. It delivers 1080p at 60fps and pushes audio to your device too. It's actually pretty awesome.

We gave it a real test in a room full of servers and a lot of potential electronic interference and it delivered a solid signal and connection up to about thirty feet. Beyond that it dropped a frame every now and then, but not bad.

If you're recording video through the app on your device, there's ten-minute limit per file, something to do with restrictions on the app's classification. That doesn't interfere with the camera recording video. It's just a file recording limit on whatever device you're monitoring the video on, if you choose to capture it while you view it.

The build quality is great. It feels practically indestructible. Battery life is solid.

If there is one thing to complain about, it's that the Android app is a bit blah. The iOS version is a lot better.

I got the 8-inch T290. If you are aware of what you are getting for your money, this tablet is worthy of five stars. No it doesn't have the top processor speed or display resolution. It's a budget tablet at a really good price (especially if you catch it on sale), and you get a lot of bang for your buck.

The display is 1200 X 800 pixels which qualifies as HD, but not ultra HD. What counts the most when it comes to font legibility on screens is pixel density. A 1200 X 800 8-inch display has a pixel density of right at 180 pixels per inch (PPI), and that's not too shabby. My 6th generation Kindle Paperwhite has a pixel density of just over 210 ppi, so this tablet isn't too far from that. If small fonts are hard to read, you can scale up the fonts and size of things in the settings.

The display also has good color and contrast, and is plenty bright. The blue light filter app included doesn't offer as many options as I like, so I add one from the Google Play store.

And speaking of that, with an Android tablet (and this one comes installed with Android Pie) you do have full access to Google Play store.

The sound is a lot better than I expected, and that can be enhanced even more with a third party volume booster.

And I find an 8-inch tablet is just the right size. A 10.1-inch tablet is too cumbersome in my opinion, and a smart phone is too small. And an 8-inch tablet like this one will fit in the back pocket of men's pants. (But not so much if you have it in a case.) And at just 12 and a half ounces, it's a lot lighter than a 10.1-inch tablet.

So understand what you're getting, don't expect top of the line, but you get a good tablet for the price.

I'm not a gamer. I purchased this card to add video ports and support for a higher resolution display to a mini-ITX motherboard.  Since this is an x1 PCIE card, it doesn't support high-bandwidth-demanding games. But it works very well to provide low demand, higher resolution support and video port options. The specs say it requires a 300-watt power supply, but that it draws only 25-watts. I'm running it in a box with a 160-watt supply and it's working fine.

I'm glad this ships with three protectors. Took me two tries using two of them to get a good result. The first try I wound up with trapped dust specks because I misaligned the film and had to pull it up a couple of times to align it. That just invited dust, even though I was installing the protector on a very humid day (which reduces static electricity buildup). There was no cleaning it, so I tossed that one. The second time I still wound up with a couple of trapped dust specks, but both are in the display margins so they're not a problem for me.

The air bubbles pushed out nicely.

What I love about the screen protector though is the matte anti-glare finish. There's a tiny bit of trade-off in the form of some barely noticeable blurriness, but the screen overall is much easier to look at and to read.

This radio can be recharged via built-in solar panel (which takes twenty hours or more) or by built-in hand crank, or by the mini USB port. There's a full-size USB port for using the radio's built-in battery to recharge devices. It also can be powered by three AAA batteries (which aren't included).

The speaker is just about ideal for spoken messages like weather alerts, but not high fidelity for music. Forget about bass response -- there isn't any to speak of.

The three bands are FM, AM, and NOAA. There's also an "alert" setting, which I assume means the radio will wake up and start broadcasting when it detects the NOAA weather alert signals. The instructions don't mention this.

The AM band volume is a little low compared to FM and NOAA bands. There's no headphone jack. No text alerts. It's not a digital, so tuning with the wheel can be a bit finicky. The telescoping rod antenna is okay, but you probably have had similar experience that those can be the first thing to break, so it's a good idea to handle that with some care. It also has a built-in flashlight.

Since it's basically an analog radio and not programmable and doesn't have text message alerts, if you live in a severe weather-prone area, this might not be the weather radio you want as your primary radio. But with all the recharge options it might be one to consider as a backup or for carrying camping.

To use the Logitech unifying receiver and link other compatible devices (as well as this keyboard) on a Linux computer, look for and install an app called "Solaar." I found it just by doing a search with Synaptic package manager. Install both Solaar and the Solaar GUI (graphic user interface) to make it easier to use. Once you launch Solaar, you may have to unplug the Logitech unifying receiver and plug it back in to get Solaar to detect it. And you may have to switch the keyboard (or other compatible device) off and back on. Once Solaar is running, it puts a little hiding widget on the lower left of your display screen you can click on to access the settings.

As far as the keyboard goes, it works great and the key action is quiet and comfortable. I like the ergonomics too. I still use a wrist rest since I like more wrist elevation than what the built-in rest provides. All in all it's a good keyboard.

This in-ear headset works great with Xbox, Playstation, and Switch. All the online players were able to hear the mic great.

It also works with an iPad, but the mic was a little glitchy with an iPhone.

The audio from the ear buds is phenomenal---right up there with name brand buds.

The only negative---and it's minor---is the ear buds are a little larger than most. That might be something necessary for sound quality, or for the mic wiring or something. But as I said, that's a minor negative.

Overall this is an excellent gaming headset with great audio both in and out.

I'm not sure about the 42-inch height claim. The one we received measures about 36 inches to the top when fully extended. And it stands about 12 inches tall when closed.

It's well built and durable enough for a cell phone or a pocket camera. I'm not sure it would be stable enough for a tablet, and I'm pretty sure a digital SLR would be too much for it, especially when fully extended.

That said, it's a good tabletop cell phone camera mount, and I think it's more stable than the bendable kind. It has a standard tripod platform and screw, and it comes with a cell phone holder/adapter, and a remote that requires a proprietary camera app. You might want to just use your camera app's timer function instead of the remote. It also comes with a carrying/storage bag.

Compared to the Crucial 1TB M2 NVME I reviewed earlier, this Sabrent 512GB model benchmarks a little faster. And it works just fine on a PCI M2 adapter card, which are only a few bucks. (I bought the cheapest one available and it works.)

The NVME still offers much faster R/W speeds than other drives even when used with SATA 1 (as on my workstation). For example, the SSD I was using as my hard disk benchmarks at about 220MB/second. The Sabrent NVME on a PCI card benchmarks at about 1.5GB/second.

This time I experimented to see if I could get Debian Linux distro running on the NVME on my older workstation.

It took a few tries. Getting the OS to boot directly from the NVME was a no-go. Since the NVME is mounted on an adapter card, I had hoped it would trick the system into thinking it was just an ordinary SATA drive and boot from it. But that didn't happen.

So what I did was installed all the Linux OS EXCEPT for the boot folder on the NVME, and put the boot folder on the SSD HDD. So it boots from the SSD but the entire OS is on the NVME and runs from it.

Step one:

The partition manager in the Debian installer didn't want to partition the NVME at first.

So I bailed out of it and used GParted (Gnome disks utility couldn't do this) to "create partition table" and selected msdos as type. That wiped everything and turned the whole drive into unallocated space. From that point the partition manager worked.

Step two:

From the linux bootable USB installer I partitioned the SSD (not the NVME) with a primary partition labeled (to be mounted) as /boot. (You can make this partition most any size from a few GB on up---the boot files don't require a lot of space.) The remaining space I manually labeled as /msc.

I partitioned the NVME so the installer would put everything else on it, starting with / (root). You can simply make the whole NVME / root and the installer will take care of putting everything else on that drive, or you can do what I did and set up size-defined partitions for /home, /usr, and so on.

After installing the system, the installer asks where you want the bootloader GRUB installed. I selected the SSD.

It worked. The SSD does the booting to the NVME, which then runs the OS. And it did improve speed.

Just to clarify a few details: These headphones have a built-in mic, volume control (+ and - on on the mic), and a four-barrel connector for compatibility with most phones and devices. (I think headphones with built-in microphones should be called headsets, and headphones without mics should be called headphones---just to avoid confusion.)

Like most headphones (or headsets) today, they're set up to favor bass response, which to most buyers is a good thing. The response across the rest of the frequency spectrum sounds well balanced without too much top end.

The mic response is, well, pretty much like a budget phone headset mic response.

They're comfortable (even if just a little tight-feeling on first use) with good padding, and they look and feel well made.

A good choice for people who prefer on-ear instead of in-ear headsets.

I tried this SSD out in an older desktop workstation PC running Debian Linux. I bought the least expensive PCIe adapter card I could find (around twelve dollars) to install it. Even though it has an SSD as the primary drive, the workstation only has SATA 1 and USB 1.1 and 2.0, so I'm used to relatively slow speeds. Once I installed the card and rebooted, the NVMe didn't show in the files list, but it hadn't been formatted. It showed right up in the Gnome disks utility. I benchmarked it immediately, and, wow. Those speeds may not look like much to those who have later gen equipment, but the speeds were impressive for this older system.

It looks like I could have made it my primary drive, but I think I would choose to use this SSD as a personal cloud storage device in a USB enclosure. But enclosures for this particular 2280 (22mm X 80mm) form factor and NVMe are still rather pricey. I'm guessing the prices will come down eventually. Until then, the more economical option is to get an inexpensive adapter card and install it in a desktop PC, or install it in a laptop that has an M.2 slot and will accommodate 80mm long cards.

It looks like a good way to get some fast speeds and big capacity into some older gear. I'll leave the more technical reviews for the more technically minded.

This is a nice alternative to chargers that require you to charge batteries in pairs. There are spaces for eight batteries, and you can charge any number within them, and mix and match AA and AAA. The eight spaces are divided electrically into two banks of four spaces, and the manufacturer says each bank can provide 2000 mA of charging power (which lowers as you add more batteries and the current is divided between them). However, the included adapter only provides only 1200 mA (so says its label), so I'm not sure the math checks out.

I gave it a test with an assortment of different brand and capacity rechargeables, then checked the batteries with a multimeter. Even fully loaded the charger worked pretty quickly and brought each one up to just over 1.4 volts. I have a brand-name charger that will bring them up to 1.5 volts, but that may be overcharging a bit and might reduce overall battery life.

The one minor negative is that the battery icons on the backlit display are pretty much invisible unless you bend down or tilt the charger up to see them. You can see how low the angle is in the photo I uploaded.

Other than that, convenient and reasonably fast, it's a nice charger.

Good crisp audio quality for phone calls. I like an on-the-ear headset instead of in-ear because cell phones have little or no sidetone.

Don't know what sidetone is? Back in the day, land line phone handsets fed the sound from the mic back into the earpiece, so a person could clearly monitor their own voice (and also hear any other sounds that the other party could hear that the mic picked up). That enabled a person to modulate their own voice (instead of screeching in order to hear themselves) and speak much more clearly. It made for a much better phone conversation experience. That feature was called sidetone.

It's a feature that cell phone designers and engineers somehow decided not to add to cell phones, or to make it so low in volume as to be nonexistent.

So until either cell phone engineers put sidetone back into cell phones or headset manufacturers start building it in as a feature, the workaround is on-ear headsets that allow you to hear your own voice while you speak.

The downside is that on-ear headsets aren't exactly convenient to carry around, and they're not inconspicuous. And they can be a bother if you're wearing a hat.

But they do give you some natural sidetone by allowing you to hear the sound of your voice. And this headset from Logitech, as I said, has some good crisp audio quality for phone calls.

Which brings up another point. Even after years of development, possibly the thing cell phones still do worst is make phone calls. The audio can still be garbled and fluttery due to digitizing and signals that fade in and out in strength. So good audio quality---in that mid-range EQ sweet spot---can make cell phone calls a lot more pleasant.

While there's a volume control on the cord, there's no answer button. That's probably a decision to keep the headset compatible with many devices.

Overall, good headset.

I ordered the small version some time ago, tried it with a Linux system, and it's a little slow to respond sometimes, but it worked well enough (and still does). And nothing special was required to get it operating. I plugged it in and it worked. There's no convenient way to customize or modify the operation though---you get what you get. It has a small footprint which is handy for crowded desktops.

More recently, I ordered the large version. It only partly works with Linux. The touchpad part works---the cursor can be moved around with the pad, but the buttons don't work, and no tap-to-click function. I tried it with Debian and Ubuntu installs, and the buttons and click don't work with either. The pad itself works fine when plugged into a Mac machine, so I'm guessing it's a driver issue.

Looking back at all the recordable data storage media formats that have fallen by the wayside over the years, I guess it's inevitable that writable CD/DVD will eventually go obsolete too.

And many of our devices don't come with built-in CD/DVD drives these days, since flash drives and cloud storage and downloadable software and streaming video have pretty much taken the load for now.

But some of us still have DVD movie collections and still have an occasional need for a CD/DVD drive. And this is a good one.

It's USB powered and doesn't need an extra power adapter. It comes with two USB cables --- both USB type A (the regular kind) and type C (the newer reversible kind).

Here are a few of the specs:

Read/write speed is 8X for DVDs and 24X for CDs, 4X for DVD video playback.
USB interface is 2.0 (not 3.0).
It's compatible with Window 10, 8, 7, Vista, and XP, and Mac OS X 10.6 and above.
It has M-disc support.

It comes with bundled software for backing up and encryption that you may or may not want to use.

I'm using this enclosure for an earlier-gen SATA thin profile 500GB Western Digital hard drive and getting great results. The fastest removable media I own is a SanDisk Extreme USB 3.0 flash drive. And with this enclosure, the WD hard drive is hitting read/write speeds that are almost as fast as the SanDisk Extreme. It's not nearly SATA III fast (since it's not a SATA III drive), but fast.

I followed the recommendation of other reviewers and reformatted the hard drive to MBR and NTFS file system before using. This requires using DiskPart or Disk Management in Windows. Instructions are available on the web.

Older hard drives with a thick profile won't fit this enclosure. If you're not sure if your hard drive is thin profile and you don't have a metric ruler handy, if it's a quarter inch or less in thickness (and has a SATA connector) it's thin profile and will fit this enclosure.

I did not get good results testing the enclosure with a desktop computer with only USB 2.0 capability---it was very slow or not even recognized when plugged in. I don't want to blame the enclosure, because I've had similar issues with other brand enclosures and that same desktop computer. But I want to mention this in case you're thinking of buying this to use with a computer that only has USB 2.0. You might do better to get a USB 2.0 enclosure.

Pixels per inch is where it's at!

I bought the 24" 1440 model for one reason: Pixel density.

I'm not a gamer. For me it's all about legible screen fonts for easy reading. And pixels per inch is where it's at. The higher the pixel density, the clearer the type looks. Fonts on a larger monitor with a lower density won't look as clear as a smaller one with a higher number of pixels per inch.

The density on the 24" model (2560 x 1440 resolution) is a little over 120 pixels per inch (ppi). A Kindle Paperwhite pixel density is 300 ppi. So if this monitor is a bit over twice the distance from you as a Kindle Paperwhite, the density and clarity will look about the same.

There is one thing I do want to mention: brightness. Wow this thing is bright. In the early days of LCD and LED monitors, brightness and color accuracy were issues. The brightness issue has certainly been solved, and maybe too well. I have mine set on just "5" on the on-board brightness setting. Occasionally I have dialed it down to "0" and it's still readable.

Creative sells good stuff. I bought a Creative Sound Blaster Audigy 4 sound card with an outboard hub several years ago (Windows XP days). It's still going strong.

This speaker system doesn't disappoint. The wooden enclosure construction (it's particle board) makes for a nice sound. Good response all across the audio spectrum. Highs are crisp, mids are up front and present, and the bass -- well it's better than expected. After trying this system out, a similar off-brand speaker system went back in its box.

Setup is easy. The light show is a cool feature. If there's one thing to complain about, it would be that the cord between the control pod (the volume controller) and the main is short.

Otherwise, a nice-sounding, nice-looking speaker system.

This is a great improvement over an earlier-gen ZINK paper ("zero ink") portable printer we have, which requires a wired connection and a proprietary charger, and no longer holds a charge well.

The HP Sprocket connects and prints wirelessly, charges from a standard micro-USB cable, and has a lithium-ion battery which is sure to last a lot longer.

We had it unboxed and printing in less than 5 minutes. You run it from a free app available for Android or Apple iOS devices. We used the Android version and it works great.

It takes less than 30 seconds to wirelessly send and print a photo. The prints are 2 inches by 3 inches, smooth and glossy, good resolution, and have a peel-and-stick backing for quick and easy mounting. In the long run, the priciest thing about a ZINK printer is the paper, so shop around for deals.

The prints came out a little to the warm side in color when sent "as is," but the app allows a lot of enhancement and has lots of effects you can add.

The Sprocket printer itself measures only 3 inches by 5 inches and less than an inch thick, and weighs about 6-and-a-half ounces. It's very portable.

And it's loads of fun.

Works great for occasional use. I'd hesitate to use this adapter exclusively for an external HDD that gets a lot of use, because I suspect SATA connectors are just not designed for constant plugging and unplugging. USB connectors are, though. So if you're frequently plugging and unplugging your external HD, you might want to go with an enclosure with USB connector.

This is a good entry level gps watch. I use a Nike Run and a Garmin 220 and this one seems to be nearly as accurate. It’s light and comfortable, and the band is soft and doesn't feel cumbersome or sweaty.

The interface isn't super intuitive, but the instructions are clearly written and accurate. As far as the function goes it seems to do a lot better if you sync it with the companion iPhone app. Occasionally it would lose Bluetooth connection – the app has a much simpler and more intuitive interface than the watch face itself. Aesthetically it’s really cool though – when you’re in idle mode the face is black with white numbers, and when you start a workout it switches to white numbers – really easy to tell where you’re at regarding the different modes.

You can program a goal pace, time or distance – bear in mind that there isn't haptic feedback so if you have your headphones in you might not be able to hear the audio cue when you hit your milestones.

Syncing it with GPS was a little frustrating because it seemed to time out – again connecting it to the companion app made this much easier – it only took a couple of seconds.

All in all a decent watch, especially for someone just starting out in the GPS tracking stuff – just make sure to use the companion app.

I first bought the blue LED version of this keyboard, but it was a little too bright for my tastes. I sold it and bought this red version. Much better in terms of brightness levels.

Man, the color-code key label system sure adds some confusion when trying to select one of these things doesn't it? The Blue Cherry keys are the loudest and most tactile --- which I love --- but it just adds confusion when you're trying to pick the LED color you want along with the right color label key action. It's difficult to tell from item listings what the "blue" or "red" is referring to, whether LED or key action.

I experimented with adding O-rings to mine, but they just took all the feel and fun out of it. I like the clicks and clacks and pops and the tactile feedback. Straight out of the box is the way to go to me.

There's nothing like a mechanical keyboard for satisfying typing feedback. And this one is solidly built, with nice heft. And the letters and numbers will never wear off, since they're double-shot molded so the LED light will shine through.

The lighting scheme can be modified and customized for gaming and the like, but I just leave mine all lit up all the time, set on the lowest level.

Great all the way.

Good for the price. They don't enclose your ears, they rest on them. They're certainly not noise canceling. Sound quality is okay, a bit strong in the mid range, perhaps a tiny bit muddy, but clear enough. Don't expect overly impressive bass response and you won't be disappointed.

They fold up compactly, a nice plus, and so is the in-line volume control. A nice alternative to ear buds when you want to listen to something without being too particular about audiophile quality full range sound reproduction.

This is the third Olympus voice recorder I own. The first is a DM-10 that only records its best quality setting with an optional external mic, is a bit complex to operate, and goes through batteries quickly.

The second is a VN 6200PC. It's much simpler to operate. Battery life is longer. But like the DM-10, it only records in WMA (Windows' proprietary audio format). Which has become increasingly difficult to use, at least for me, since it seems fewer apps will load and play and allow editing of WMA files.

This newer WS-852 records MP3 audio in 128 kbps stereo, 64 kbps mono, or 32 kbps mono.

Granted, the 128 kbps setting is not audiophile quality, but it's rather good quality. Good enough for music if you're not too picky.

And on the 128 kbps stereo setting, the device's built in mic array sounded better to me than the DM-10 on max quality setting with the external ME51SW mic.

When I tried that same mic in this new WS-852, the quality was worse, not better. So you don't need it. Good thing, since those stereo mics are getting scarce and a bit pricey now.

On the 64 kbps and 32 kbps mono settings, the results are much better using an Olympus ME-52W noise-canceling microphone. Fortunately they're rather inexpensive. It's a much better sound for recording narration or dictation -- much louder and clearer and more present -- although the built-in mic is acceptable.

I do like that playback of mono recordings does play into both ears of the headphones. A stereo-to-mono headphone adapter was needed for that on the earlier two models I own.

The voice filter setting pretty much makes the audio sound like a telephone, which is a good thing for clarity in speech recording, particularly in rooms with a lot of bass-ey resonance or echo. Of course not a good thing for music recording.

It has a little flip-out stand, which is nice. The 90-degree mic array actually does make a difference I think. It produces a more natural sound than the older 180-degree external stereo mic.

The menu is easy to learn and operate.

It has a slide-out USB plug. The earlier devices require a cable to connect to a PC.

It has ample built-in memory, and also accepts micro SD cards. The earlier two devices do not.

I'm not crazy about the mic and earphone jacks being on the side of this device. The top mounted jacks on the other two recorders are very convenient. I suppose it was necessary to locate them on the side to accomodate the stereo mics.

The built-in speakers on all three devices are barely speakers. Earphones are about the only way to really listen to any of them.

Battery life is much improved. Especially compared to that early generation DM-10, which used up batteries rather quickly.

Why buy one of these when cell phones and other devices can pretty much do the same thing? One reason is that you can continue to use your phone or device for other things. Another is that this little recorder can be tucked in a shirt pocket and used more inconspicuously.

Overall it's a very good device.

Before writing this review I glanced over some reviews of earlier models, and whatever issues previous editions of the Bose SoundTouch speakers may have had seem to have been worked out with this SoundTouch 10.

Setup was simple with the SoundTouch app (available for iOS, Android, and Kindle Fire devices). We had the speaker set up and operating in less than 5 minutes using an iPad. You'll need your home network security code to connect to WiFi and that's about it.

It comes with a remote, but most of the controlling is done from your device (tablet or phone). The remote is handy for adjusting the volume when you're using your device for other things.

The speaker is about the size of a cereal box. The sound that comes out is impressive for its size. I think there's a wee bit of case resonance in the mid range, but that's just me -- everyone else thinks it sounds terrific. It doesn't rival a huge stereo system but it's really, really good.

Now excuse me while I get on my soapbox about monaural. This is a single speaker system, not stereo, and that, to me, is a good thing. I'm a fan of monaural. It solves a lot of issues about speaker placement (trying to make sure they're equally distant), and you hear the full mix as the producers and artists intended. You can move anywhere around the room and not have half the mix disappear. And if you like oldies, particularly from the 1960s, this fixes the problems caused by common pan/mix practices from that era (for example, drums and bass panned hard left, guitars and backup singers panned hard right, lead vocals in the middle). If you listen to mixes like that in headphones, you pretty much have to mix the music down in your imagination since bass/drums are exclusively in one ear and keyboards in the other. Some devices don't support mono audio output (I'm looking at you, Windows phone), and as far as I know no one makes a dual-ear mono headset for phones either. So a mono speaker solves the issue. Okay, that's it for the soapbox. Back to the review.

The only tone control available in the Bose app is bass volume. But since the sound is well engineered, it's adequate. And bass is very audible. Not subwoofer level audible, but it's very present.

The SoundTouch app itself is impressive. It really does make setup a breeze. And the listening options are VAST. Hundreds of radio stations from around the world on WiFi, streaming music services, Pandora, Spotify, and so forth. I used to do a little shortwave listening, and if you're a DXer, this exceeds the capability of SW by far, and every station is digitally clear. And you can connect directly to play music straight from your device.

Just to be clear, the speaker itself needs a wall outlet to power it. It's not battery powered. But everything else is wireless. More speakers can be added, but it's so easily unplugged and moved around that one speaker can easily be sufficient.

Nice product from Bose.

Very nice, sharp picture, bright, and great color. Other reviewers say the built-in OS crashes a lot, but the 32-inch unit (1366 X 768 resolution, 60 Hz) we got worked fine and was stable.

The remote's one-button access to YouTube, Netflix, Vudu, Toon Goggles, Pandora, and Accuweather is a nice feature.

The onboard speakers are tinny, but loud enough. There are lots of inputs and outputs including component audio and video (RCA), USB, HDMI (3 of them), headphones, composite, 15 pin VGA, and an optical digital output.

It comes with remote (batteries included), two feet (which are attached with screws -- a magnetic screwdriver will help because the screws go in small recessed pockets), user manual, and quick start guide. It also has monitor mount screw holes in the back (200 x 100mm spacing).

My one concern -- and the reason I'm deducting a star -- is the WiFi reception. We set the TV up in a room adjacent to our wireless router -- which provides a strong signal to every device through the house -- and only got 75 percent signal strength on the TV, and we didn't get full HD video on WiFi. It seems to need a better internal antenna or something. So it might be best to consider this mainly for LAN cable connections, HDMI, or uses where the TV will be very close to the wireless router.

I'm using mine for a workstation and it is performing like a champ for my purposes. I did try out FSX Steam version and got pretty good performance with scenery set on a medium level. It seemed to strain a little and did some blinking at higher settings.

But for workstation use it's doing a fine job. It's quiet and hasn't overheated once so far.

First thing I noticed on unboxing this projector is it's SMALL. Very portable. It's about the size of a slice of bread and an inch thick. It fits in a jacket or jeans pocket. Our kitchen scale says it weighs just over 10 ounces.

My first concern was that 100 lumens is bright for a flashlight, but not so much for a projector. A home theater projector requires 1200 or more lumens for a nice bright picture. I looked forward to trying it out.

It has wifi, and has a built-in Android operating system (v 2.3.1, according to the manufacturer website.) It has a touchpad on top, along with a focus wheel. No optical zoom wheel or adjustment.

(Just to clear up any potential confusion, let me point out that this is a full color projector. The listing title says "black/white," but that's just the color of the projector itself.)

There's an SD/MMC card slot in back, along with mini-USB and mini-HDMI ports for connecting to a computer, and a headphone/audio out jack. There are laptop-size speakers built into the sides. On one side is an 1/8" A/V in (in case you want to hook a game console, video camera or separate media player to it), the other has a standard USB port for dongles or thumb drives (so you can play videos or other media from them or cards in the SD/MMC slot. In other words, you don't have to carry a tablet or computer to play media, just an SD card or USB drive with your movies on it.

In addition to media, it also has viewing support for .pdf, .ppt/pptx, .xls/xlsx, and .doc/docx formats.

What's in the box:

The projector (of course.)

An HDMI-to-mini-HDMI cable. The big end goes to your computer's HDMI port, the little end goes to the projector. If you have an HDMI port, this will give the best resolution.

A USB-to-mini-USB cable. Same deal -- big end to computer, little end to the projector. Use this to move files to the projector and upgrade software.

Quick start guide and manual (in several language versions). These docs are TINY, with TINY text, difficult to read as a result, and I could find no downloadable PDF versions online. Not even on the XSories web site. (I assume that brand name is pronounced "X-S-ories.")

AC adapter/charger (12v, 2A) with three different snap-in, easily interchangeable plugs for US, UK, and EUR use.

A soft case. The AC adapter was packed in it, but it's obviously for the projector.

What's NOT in the box (but available for purchase separately as accessories):

A 5-way splitter component cable for connecting to component systems.
A 3-way A/V splitter cable for connecting to game consoles, video cameras or other media players.
An antenna for digital TV.
An iPhone/iPad connector cable.
A sound station for audio boosting.
An MHL to HDMI cable.
A VGA cable.

I plugged it in for a charge. I noticed the LED adapter/charge indicator is not very bright. That's GOOD. Shows some thought went into this device. You don't want a too-bright LED competing with your projected image.

After charging the recommended 3 hours, the LED switched from red to green, and I was ready to try it out.

If you want something this portable and convenient, chances are you're not going to be lugging a screen around. That's okay, because there are plenty of things that can be used as makeshift screens, such as walls or poster board or sheets or foam core or large sheets of paper or the side of a tent (or the ceiling, which is awesome for watching while kicked back in a recliner or sofa or such). Or for a better image quality you could buy some projector screen material and just roll it up and take it along and tack or tape it up when needed. A dry-erase whiteboard makes an excellent screen for this projector. That's what I used for most of my testing, along with a wall and a ceiling.

After booting (which takes about 30 seconds) and focusing the projected image, I navigated to the Android OS and activated wifi. In about a minute I was online.

The Android OS is limited. And appears dated. I tried to browse YouTube and got repeated security certificate warnings, so I disabled the warnings in the Android settings panel. Scrolling is done by sliding a finger along the side and bottom of the touchpad. There are no buttons -- you tap the touchpad to click. There are spots on the top for "home," "back," and, I assume, "settings." It's not really easy to navigate.

I went back to YouTube and successfully played a video, but navigating around YouTube was frustrating. The browser wasn't smooth, and the scrolling and such was kind of clunky. I'm not sure online viewing with the built in OS is a strong point with this projector.

Speaking of which, if there's an easy way to install an Amazon or Netflix app (which don't come pre-installed) on this device, I couldn't find it. I suspect it takes one of those complicated procedures like with a rooted device -- using the USB cable and connecting to a computer and flashing ROMs and and such.

I tested playing .mp4 vids and viewing .jpg photos from an SD card, and it readily found and played both. Photos are launched in a slideshow by default, and transitions and view times and such are adjustable in settings. Likewise, it easily found and played .mp4s from a USB stick.

Adjusting things like contrast, brightness, color, volume, and such is a bit of an annoying process. Some are done from the native menu. Other adjustments and setup (such as for wifi) are done within the Android settings menu. And it's not really easy to get things done with the touchpad. There are some pop-up adjustment sliders that will appear if you slide a finger along the right edge of the pad while playing media, but they're still a bit difficult to get used to adjusting.

It gets really warm while operating, and there is some fan noise, but it's relatively quiet. Battery life seems to be as advertised, about 2 hours on a charge, but leaving Wifi on will probably shorten that. If a movie runs over 90 minutes, you're probably better off using the adapter.

The built-in sound is about what you'd expect from a couple of tiny laptop speakers. You'll want to use headphones or run the audio through a system if you want better quality.

There's no optical zoom. The picture size can only be adjusted by moving the projector. Brightness diminishes considerably with distance and picture size. I'd say 12 to 14 feet is about its max effective distance, and at that distance the image is a little larger than 6 feet across. In total darkness you may be able to go a little larger with it.

There is no keystone adjustment either. If you want to avoid the trapezoid, the projector will have to be positioned square to the screen.

The projection lens isn't very wide angle. The distance-to-picture-size (or MTS or meter-to-screen) ratio is kind of small. When the projector is at optimum distance for brightness -- about four or five feet from the screen -- the picture doesn't look much bigger than a regular laptop monitor. Which sort of defeats the purpose of having a projector in the first place. You could just turn your laptop around and show it to the group.

And to go much larger, you're going to need a very dark room and some distance. It's not going to be useful for the typical boardroom or conference room.

About picture quality: I tried it as a display/monitor with two different laptops using the HDMI cable, and spent some time tweaking settings to get the most I could get out of it, and got similar results. It's not HD. It's a tad globby, whether operating on wifi, HDMI, or watching a movie from an SD card or USB drive. Considering the size of the projector I guess it's a bit much to expect genuine hi-res 1080p.

So those are the two negative things -- picture size and picture quality. Kind of important for a projector. But it's a trade off for the super portability.

To summarize, this isn't a productivity or business item. It's a fun item. It will do for movies and images, but used as a computer display/monitor, screen fonts are not clear and crisp, and it is sure to be tiring if one is using it for number crunching or word processing for any length of time. It may be useful for the occasional location presentation to a very small group in a very dark room. But I'd say this one's for movies and pictures or gaming that isn't HD dependent. Even then, don't expect wall-sized projection and super brightness. I'm guessing it will be about half the size and brightness you might expect.

I'm giving it four stars because of the coolness and wow factor -- the smallness and portability -- but with reservations. Since battery life is only two hours, you're going to probably be carrying the adapter with it. And at this price point, I'm not sure what the advantages are except for the exceptionally small size. For less money you can get a 1200-lumen HD projector with many features this projector lacks. So whether this projector appeals to you is going to depend on your intended use and situation. Who knows -- maybe you're looking for a little projector to connect to your computer to watch Amazon Prime or Netflix on the ceiling, or one you can toss in a bag or backpack with some SD cards and take with you on trips. If so, it may be just what you're looking for.

Truly plug and play. Simple 3-cable setup (plus a power cable). Windows 8.1 recognized it instantly, didn't even have to install drivers. Works immediately with Google Hangouts, Skype, and all the conferencing apps we tried.

The instructions are simple and clear. The only real critical piece of information you need from the setup manual is to not attempt to physically move the camera around by hand -- just use the remote control to move it.

The picture quality is impressive. The camera is large and very high quality, obviously has a great sensor. It's tolerant of high contrast environments. We tested it in a backlit environment and faces were still highly visible.

It's HD capable (up to 1080P), it zooms 10:1 by remote control for closeups, shows whiteboards beautifully and in sharp detail, pulls back to a very wide view (we were able to see both corners of a 12-foot-wide wall from only 8 feet away, so it easily would show participants at a conference table), and all camera movements are simple from the remote. Just by pressing one button a few seconds you can easily program a "home" position so the camera can automatically swing back to a main speaker every time you push the button again.

The audio is amazing too. Even standing several feet from the base unit, the person speaking sounds like they are wired with a personal, close mic. This is due to some pretty sophisticated noise-cancelling technology. Room echo is practically eliminated.

Which also makes the speakerphone quality great too. You can hear remote participants very clearly.

I know this thing is built for small business use, but I could see this as a great home use system for online family or friend get-togethers when some friends or family are scattered around the globe. And it would make a superb personal webcam, particularly if you want to be able to pan and zoom in on things around a room or shop and show them in HD detail.

The only minor gripe I can think of is that the camera swivels to a to a down-and-side position when it turns off. A good position -- people won't get uncomfortable seeing a camera pointed at them, and the lens is protected. But is not the position it was packaged in, and you aren't supposed to force it manually, so it won't fit back in the original box for storage.

As I said, that's a minor gripe. Everything else about this system is five star all the way.

This does a good job without vignetting. You get a much wider field of view with a Flip, and the lenses are pretty good quality.

The lens comes with peel-and-stick metal rings that you attach to the camera. The lens then sticks magnetically to the metal ring. It doesn't stick all that firmly -- you could shake the lens off if you're shooting video while running or something. But for most uses it sticks well enough.

I was concerned the mount would not work on a 3rd generation Flip Ultra HD because the ring around the lens on the Flip is tapered, and the metal mounting rings that come with the lens are flat and won't bend to shape. (It comes with two mounting rings, not three as shown in the picture.) I followed the instructions and allowed the ring to sit for fifteen minutes after applying it so the adhesive could set, and the adhesive turned out to be aggressive enough to hold the ring to the Flip. If it loosens later I may reinforce it with some CA glue.

You actually get two lenses that screw together. When you unscrew and remove the wide angle outer lens, the inner one functions as a fixed-length macro that focuses well at around 2 to 4 inches from the subject.

It also comes with a pouch (not a lanyard) and a couple of lens caps that fit rather loosely.

For the price, it's a good buy and really adds some versatility to a Flip Ultra HD. A better fitting mounting ring would be nice, but that might require machining and that might run the price up. It still works well, it's priced reasonably, and I think that makes it a good deal.

Back in the dinosaur days of PC clones and 8086 and 286 processors, backing up data frequently was a habit you really had to cultivate if you didn't want to find yourself groaning over the unexpected loss of hours of work.

I never lost the habit. And it's easier than ever with this tiny USB flash drive.

You can just leave it plugged into a USB port all the time. It sticks out only a quarter of an inch, so it won't get in the way.

It comes with some handy backup utility software. I personally use SyncToy, a free Microsoft app that I'm used to, so I deleted the included one.

It has a blue LED activity indicator, which I still appreciate, since I remember the days when every LED was the same shade of green. And 8GB is plenty of backup space for me, since I work mostly with text.

So plug it in, leave it plugged in, back up your work often, and you won't have to worry about the unexpected crash. They still happen from time to time, you know, even though the dinosaurs are long gone.

Got it even though was skeptical at first. It arrived very quick, packaged beautifully and did not take even a minute to set it up. It easily connected and the sound quality was way beyond what I expected from small speakers. In addition to that the headphones are very thin and soft, so they are comfortable to sleep with ( which is what I originally got them for). I added an outer cover from natural material, as I can not use synthetics and now I enjoying them for my naps!
They work amazingly they have such great volume
It works great makes no noise and feels great on my desk

I've bought these ear buds a lot, and they never fail to disappoint. (With heavy, daily use, and falling asleep in them more nights than not the normal ones usually need to be replaced about once a year, if that often.)
This is the first time I've bought them with a microphone included on them, which I bought for gaming purposes, and they work wonderfully for my needs! I used a free recording program to see what my own voice sounded like through them and it sounds very clear.
They also sound wonderful, and are an all around good purchase in my opinion. (Also, color doesn't effect quality of product received, if you were wondering.)
Cambridge SoundWorks makes good speakers at an excellent price. Nice designs and portability are basis for their success on top of high-quality sound.
As recommended for Synology NAS, both purchased units are working flawlessly. No noise at all. Fast response times. Solid construction.

This is an amazing tablet for its price.

Let me start by saying that this is my first tablet, but I have messed around with a Wacom bamboo at a friend’s house. Based on that small experience, and how I’ve felt about the Huion so far, these are the pro’s and con’s

PROS:
• the price!! This tablet is dirt cheap compared to a Wacom with this size and pressure sensitivity
• the size. I didn’t realize how big 11 inches was until I opened the package. To put it in perspective, the drawing space is about an inch longer than a piece of standard paper and maybe a half and inch less wide.
• the sensitivity— it’s above 8000 levels, so as you can imagine, it’s pretty stellar
• extra nibs and pen holder! I like that it came with 8 extra nibs and that they all fit inside of the pen holder. It added an organized and professional touch. The holder has a weighted bottom so it won’t topple over when the pen is in it, and the holder has a mechanism to remove worn out nibs as well. It’s just nifty

The quick keys seem like they would be convenient but since this is my first tablet I haven’t thought to do anything with them really. I like the shortcut buttons on the pen a lot however

CONS:
• as everyone has mentioned: the drivers. Really, it’s not a huge setback given the low price and the fact that once it’s working, it is WORKING, but I have a frequent problem where the pressure sensitivity will not work when I boot things up. Sometimes the fix is as simple as opening the huion tablet application, sometimes I have to reinstall the drivers. It’s a pain
• the speed. Once I had been drawing with it for a bit it wasn’t nearly as noticeable as at first, but there is a bit of a lag with hand movement and the movement of the cursor on screen. There are also times when it will skip when I’m using it as a mouse, but when drawing, so far no skipping. (I use it with an Intel i5 powered Lenovo Ideapad 330 on Krita)
• if you have the pen plugged in, like someone else said, you can’t have it in the pen stand. It’s just a little odd though, not a real con

Notes:
• it has a very smooth slightly papery finish on the drawing area.
• my laptop is 17.3in and I can lay the tablet on my keyboard and have it almost match the width.
• it easily gets little greasy marks on it, I guess from hands.
The box it comes in is pretty nice, everything is in its own chic black box and it’s all packed down neatly. It seemed padded enough as well.
• there is a USB plug for your computer to enable a wireless connection and there is no place within the set to store it, so I’m afraid of losing it, make sure you either keep it plugged I to your computer, or have a safe place for it.

Should I have any more thoughts as I continue usage, I will update
Easy to use, sound is good and a fair price.

Definitely helps you see objects in the distance more clearly. However, they’re still pretty fuzzy/blurry at about 100 feet. Also the equipment they provide for you to use your cell phone for pics is super cheap, I dropped the tripod 6 inches and a piece broke off. For the price it might work for you, just wasn’t worth it for me.

Good for the price.
It is a little bit loud but not that bad. Definitely for the night though. Fits on my wall and I like my movie night with this projector.

Bought as a gift for my teenager. He really likes them, sound quality is good, crisp. The noise cancellation isn't as good as others he's had. However, the quality is great for the price. Battery life is excellent! He wears these about 70% of his day.

We upgraded from a 48" rear-projection TV that was about 8 yrs old to this plasma model.  We checked reviews elsewhere on this model, and figured we'd give it a try.  The price difference between this model with 3D and a similar model without the 3D was about $200, and we wondered if the feature would be worth it.  We purchased from a big-box store with a good return policy so we could try it out.  Our only concerns were that the 3D capability might be a bit gimicky and the novelty would wear off; and that this model is only 720p; not 1080 like most newer models.
