6- Because the mike is positioned on the outside of the ear peices, not aimed at the mouth, there can be a lot of background noise and poor pickup for calls. I would not suggest these if your primary purpose is to talk hands free.

I would normally ding it a point for being this fiddly, but the sound quality and noise cancelling effectiveness is extraordinary.

I have been using this one and [[ASIN:B01N4DHGN2 Sport headset, Dylan Bluetooth 4.1 Stereo Headset Wireless Neckband Design with Retractable Earbud for iPhone, Android, Other Bluetooth Enabled Devices-White]] back and forth, and I think they both have such different strengths and weaknesses, it serves best to compare them.

If you are only interested in sound quality they are identical (tested on the iPhone 6).

If you are interested in comfort, things change. This one is substantially lighter, which is both its advantage and its disadvantage. If you want to listen in a relatively stationary or low movement situation (lying in bed, riding on the bus, going for a walk) the light weight of this one serves it well. I prefer it in those situations. If you want to listen in a high activity situation (going for a run, working out, doing housework, bending and picking up a lot of stuff) then the heavier weight of the Dylan grants it a stability advantage. This one keeps leaning off to the side when I run with it.

It pairs with two devices. It pairs easily. It looks elegant. It sounds great. It charges quickly. I use it every day and adore it.

The only minor thing that bothered me was the sides are not marked L and R and it takes a bit of getting used to in terms of figuring out which is which.

I've been an avid fan of ebooks since the long gone days of the Rocket and the eBookman, and a fan of the Kindle since the very beginning. This is miles and away the best there has ever been. It is a luxury model, no doubt, but oh is it luxurious.

I like:
The weight. Even in the case it's very light, though if it gets much lighter I'll worry about it blowing away in a strong wind.
The size. It's not going to get much smaller without shrinking the screen.
The interface. I'm sorry, I like buttons. Call me old. I never bent back the spine of a book (horrors) so I can't compare the feel of this to that, but I can say it's nice for a long reading session. The touch screen takes a bit of getting used to, but the tutorial will guide a new user. The tutorial is intrusive at first, but provides useful information and goes away quickly. I will suggest customizing the screen. I hated the default, but you get a lot of options to make it just the way you want.
The lighting is now all but invisible. I was unhappy that you can't completely turn it off as you could with the Nook Glowlight, and turning it down casts an odd yellow light over the page, but it's so even now as to be so unintrusive I barely notice going from sunlight to tunnel on the bus home. With the Nook I'd be thrown out of the book to go turn on the light. With the Kindle, I can keep reading without a pause. It does not have adaptive lighting, but I'm not sure it needs it.
The download speed. I don't know if it's supposed to be faster than the Kindle Keyboard (the last one I had with 3G) but it certainly seems that way.
The battery life. Maybe with this thing going for months we'll finally hear an end to the "but my dead tree doesn't run out of power" nonsense.
Next in series. When you're almost done with a book, it tells you where the story continues. Now the next feature I want, and if it does this I haven't seen it yet, is an alert when the next book in a series I'm following is published. Yes, FictFact is great, but I'm greedy and want it right on the device.

I don't like:
It's not waterproof. There was a lot of hope it would be after the Nook went that route.
It's not solar, yet, but there are rumors of a solar cover coming soon.
It doesn't support Audible and the excellent immersive reading between ebook and audiobook. I have a weird love of that feature, seeing what changed print to audio.
Recommended Content and Reading Lists. I shut this feature off. The information seems scattered at best and gave me no useful information, especially considering how precious screen real estate is.

I had some issues cloning to this drive, but I'm wont to chock that up to trouble with the source drive, which was on its last legs, and not on this drive unless other reviewers experience the same.

Its a fast drive, given it is HDD and not SSD. It is technically slightly lighter than my old drive, but only slightly. We're well past the point of diminishing returns here. I don't see much value in shaving an ounce or so off the weight given it lives in a laptop. It runs quietly, and, for what I'd consider the most important factor, it runs reliably. It has been trouble free since it was installed.

I have always liked Seagate's drives. I've owned many of them, and I've never had an issue. They're definitely a "go to" brand for me. I have no hesitating in recommending this one.

I'm in the process of upgrading a few hard drives that are working fine, but are too small for my needs.  This does fast work of cloning the smaller drive to the larger one, and at least for Windows 10 I do not need to fiddle with the partitions afterwards, which is a big plus.  I did format the destination drive in advance.  I'm not sure if it is required, but it seems to work that way without partition problems.  For cloning, this is a very useful tool.

This was incredibly easy to pair. I paired it with my Kindle Fire HDX and it was faster than any Bluetooth pairing I've ever done before.

The sound quality is astounding. If I put it on the hardwood floor, and if I play something with a lot of base, and it I turn it up about half way, it will shake the floor. The range is equally impressive. It does not go tinny on the high notes. The sound remains clean and clear at all volumes (or did until my neighbor came to yell at me to turn it down). It produces music of a quality one would expect from a full sized unit.

The only thing to be aware of is that the speakers are along both long sides. That makes for fantastic sound, but the device must stand on the short edge while in use, which to my mind is not as stable. It uses a proprietary charger rather than charging via USB. Makes it just a tiny bit less convenient, but not a big thing. That's all I can say against it.

The sound quality is excellent, and be warned they can get pretty loud depending on the source.  They stay in the ear very well.  They are pretty sturdy.  I just find that they become uncomfortable after the first hour or so.  I have sensitive ears, so that might be part of the issue, but I generally don't have trouble with most earbuds.  These just felt uncomfortable, no matter which tip I used, and the tips are fairly atypically shaped.  That may contribute to why they are uncomfortable and why they stay put so well.  They really do a great job of not falling out.  It's impressive.  The sound clarity and range are both remarkable, and what I would expect from a much more expensive pair of headphones.  The high range is undistorted.  The bass is deep and beautiful.

Atmos is the newest (at least at the time of this writing) innovation from Dolby. The idea is, rather than discrete speakers, the system packages sound into objects and has the speakers work together to play the sounds in the way that most recreates what is intended. So in theory you can have as many speakers as you want. In practice, the receivers will support but so many and people will want but so many in their living room. Speakers will always need to have some distance between them or the sounds will blur. The format allows for sound from all directions, including the ceiling and not many people are going to want to hang speakers from the ceiling, which is where a speaker like this comes in.

It has two input pairs, top and bottom. DO NOT plug in the top pair unless your receiver supports Atmos. You can damage it that way. If it does, you put the "upper" speakers into the top pair and these speakers fire upward to bounce the sound off the ceiling giving you the illusion of sound from above.

If you don't yet have Atmos, and you want to pick up great speakers now, and build up over time, you can totally do that with these. You plug in the bottom pair (these will be connected even with Atmos) and let them sit in any speaker position in your configuration. They work well in any standard configuration.

The sound quality is crisp and clear and the range in both pitch and volume is remarkable. The footprint is much smaller than the photo had led me to believe. It looks like an elegant piece of furniture. I love it.

You will need a Philips head screwdriver to put on the base. There are spikes to help balance it on a carpet, but mine lives on a hardwood floor, so I did not attach those.

I used this as an upgrade drive for the PS4. It caused one reboot on installing a lot of software over a slow Internet connection (it was during the upgrade of the software, and might have been caused by that) but it has been running flawlessly ever since.

It is stable, reliable, and quiet.

Don't let the speed be an issue here. Sony bullt at 5400 into the PS4 originally, so it will not need faster, and a faster drive could cause overheating. Two things to keep in mind when downloading the Sony firmware though. First, the folder names are case sensitive. PS4/UPDATE not ps4/update. If you are going to use this to upgrade the PS3, a thing to keep in mind when installing the system software is that the PS3 has trouble reading larger thumb drives. This nailed me when I tried a 120 gig drive. I had to roll back to an 8 gig, that did the trick.

For a laptop or netbook, I would favor a faster drive, but for the budget conscious, this one is excellent.

We have a lot of router noise by my television, right where I wanted to connect my ChromeCast. Now with most other devices, I could just plug in Ethernet and be done with it, but ChromeCast does not support an Ehternet connection. So I picked this up and put it right behind the TV to boost the signal.

Just so you don't make the same mistake I did. If you go modem->switch->router this will work for most devices, but for the ChromeCast you have to go modem->router->switch. ChromeCast is very fussy that way. This is not one of the modems listed as being tested to work with the ChromeCast, but I have it set up and it is compatible out of the box.

What surprised me is that I can get the best signal in the from this device, even on the opposite end of the apartment. It extends pretty far into the hall, and it is sitting in the room furthest from the front door. Because of the low price, I only expected it to be perfectly stable within a ten foot radius or so, which suited the purpose, but it dramatically exceeded those expectations. I was pleasantly surprised.

If I need another router, I'm getting another one of these.

These are very comfortable. I must have small ears, because most in-ear headphones are way too big for me. With the smallest tips these are perfect. They come with three sets of tips, across a decent range. The cord is on the long side, which means I can plug them into the desktop I have sitting on the floor and listen comfortably, not something I can do with my old pair. Even so, they are able to sit in my purse and not bet themselves tangled or wrapped around everything -- which is not a common feature in headphones. I think I must have extra chaos in my purse, because anything that can get tangled, generally does get tangled. Still, it would have been nice had they came with a carry pouch the way the better headphones in the line do.

The sound quality is excellent for the price category. I am very pleased with these.

These are amazing. They are substantially thicker than the cables the come attached to most headphones--more serious stereo equipment--and I was concerned they would not fit in my Nintendo 3DS (which is what I bought them for). No problem. They fit perfectly. I put them in my SteelSeries headphones and the sound quality is great.

SteelSeries comes with this type of cable--only Aiko chewed through them (I have it on good authority that cats don't normally do that, but she won't believe me). Anyway, I tried this on the PS4, which is what I had been using it, with its original cable, for in the first place. The sound quality improved substantially in terms of quality and range. That is, the base was a little deeper with the new cable.

I am very happy with this cable.

I'm torn on this one, and I think it has a lot to do with how it is meant to be used. It is absolutely the best tool for certain types of situations, not so much so in others.

It wraps around the back of the iPad (the iPad Air in my case), and while it is a little difficult to get the iPad in, it holds extremely firmly. It is like a bumper system on all sides, so it adds a bit of bulk, but that can't be helped given the intention of the design. While there are cut outs for the controls, the thickness of the case makes getting to them, in particular volume down, a little difficult. In the hand, it feels like a foam toddler's toy. I would imagine wrapping something like a handheld game system in this type of thing.

There is no coverage on the front, so it cannot be used in a briefcase or tote bag without an additional screen protector. The case extends forward of the screen a little bit (that is to say, once in the case, the screen is sunken in) so even if it falls face down on a smooth surface, the iPad should be fine -- it offers substantial padding -- however, if it falls face down on a rocky or uneven surface, or if something drops on it, it's more than likely going to break. Basically, for day to day use commuting to the office, look elsewhere.

Now, say you put a good screen protector on it and you want to take it into a more challenging situation. You're putting it in your backpack to go camping or hiking, and you need something that can well and truly cushion the blows. In that situation, this is your case, absolutely.

Say you want to let your small child play with it, but you're worried about the kid dropping it on the dining room floor. You want something easy to grip, and something that can keep the device safe from the kind of mishaps the kid is likely to get into. In that situation, this is again, absolutely, the right case for the job.

The only thing to be aware of is that Windows 8 has some difficulty recognizing the 3 gig partition, even on the 64 bit. If this is your second drive, you can use diskpart to get access to the full 3 gig -- just keep in mind this will erase your entire hard drive. Use it carefully. If it's your primary, your best bet is to partition it before you install Windows. If you aren't very technical, and just need a replacement drive, you're better off picking up a 2 TB, which is the biggest Win 8 can recognize without such additional configuration.

The drive itself is perfect. It's fast. It's quiet. It's reliable--I work in IT, and I've found WD drives over all to cause the fewest problems. This one has been put through some very heavy use with no issues.

I received this as a gift, and I could not be happier.

The voice search works when you want it to and gets out of the way when you don't. With some other devices, where the microphone is on constantly, you'll be watching tv and someone will say some utterly unrelated phrase like "potato chip" and the system (XBox, Playstation, whatever) will jump in and wait for you to finish the command. With this, you press the button and it listens. You don't press the button and it doesn't try to jump in to your tv show.

The video clarity is perfect. The audio is fantastic, and it autoconfigered for surround sound. Didn't have to do a thing. Really, setup can't be any easier. Plug it in, turn it on, you are done. I thought I had to unplug to reboot a few times, but it turns out my HDMI cable wasn't in tightly enough. After I fixed that the problems stopped.

If you have the Kindle Fire, you can get xRay on that while watching TV, which is a feature I love. The games definitely do better with the controller. Overall, I think we need to see a few more apps for this, such as Crunchyroll, which are undoubtedly on the way. For performance, for power, for ease of configuration and use, and for overall design, I'd give it five stars easily. This is a fantastic device.

The sound quality on this machine is amazing.

It is kind of hard to set it up. You use a microphone (included) to get the acoustics of the room. This is pretty normal. Then you have to set the sound field to match the source video or audio. That's not so standard. Denon, for example, can automatically detect what the source is putting out and adjust automatically. It took a while to figure out what lined up with what, but once I had it all sorted out, I was a very happy camper.

The range of audio, high to low, is very impressive. The bass is amazing. Naturally your speakers will play a role in this, more so than the receiver will, but with the right speakers this unit is pretty amazing. 7.2 strikes me as odd. There is only one audio channel that goes to the subwoofer, so the same sound is sent to both. Humans can't audiolocate subsonics, so there isn't much surround quality involved.

It supports both WiFi (with a good antenna that sticks up from the back) and Ethernet. As with any device, Ethernet will give you the more reliable connection.

It supports Blutooth, which is kind of cool. I use it to stream Audible books from my Kindle Fire. It's very easy to set up.

It supports passive HDMI, which is really nice. You don't have to have everything turned on if you don't need it. When the system powers itself down, which it does if it is inactive for two long -- say if you leave a video or disk paused -- the screen barely flickers.

It does not yet have support for Sirius, which is disappointing, but it supports other services, such as Pandora and, of course, Sony's own Music Unlimited service.

It was very easy to set up, and very easy to use. The only thing that confused me was the pointer. I was trying to wave it around like some sort of WiiMote. You need to use the arrow buttons to move it. If you plug it in via the serial cable to an Ubuntu box, it shows up as a second desktop. If you plug it in via the serial cable to a Win 7 box, it mirrors the desktop. Of course, this is fully configurable for both. That's the default behavior. If you plug it in via USB, it installs drivers first. You can plug in multiple sources and switch between them at will with the included remote control.

What I like. The picture clarity. It looks like a 720p HDTV. It's not quite 1080, but not that far off, and that's pretty remarkable for a projector. The color clarity trumps that of my netbook. To test it I connected my netbook via HDMI to the projector and projected a movie. At one point there was a distant view of a crowd with pink glow sticks. Where there was a haze of pink lights, all the same shade, the projector showed tiny dots in hundreds of similar shades of pink. I was very impressed.

The speakers are well place, and produce a full range of sound at full range of volumes. You could use this for showing a film to a classroom with no issues. Run through the image options to find the right one. It looks horrible if it is on the wrong setting, but fantastic on the right one. It can adjust the lens to account for uneveness in the surface. That just about everything is included. You need an HDMI cable. The serial cable is included. The USB cable is included. The case is included. The case looks flimsy, but it holds up very well. The ability to freeze frame if you want to do something on your machine, say to set up the next slide or next presentation, without showing it to the room. The pointer controlled by the remote control. It's just one less little thing to forget.

What I did not like. It gets hot fast. The driver install is a little clunky.

This is the best projector I've ever used. I love it.

It's set up differently, depending on which console you want to use it with. For PS3, you plug both the AV and USB cables into the base, and then. You need to go into the settings menu on the PS3 to activate the headset.

For XBox 360, you plug both the AV and USB cables into the base, and the small audio cable into the controller.

For the PS4 or Wii U, you plug the standard audio cable into the controller. That means if you are going to use it for the PS4 or Wii U, you do not need to set up the base, except as a battery charging station. This setup is also used for any portable electronic device that uses a standard headset or standard headphones. Vita, 3DS, MP3 player, Kindle whatever.

For the PC, you plug the USB cable into the base.

I have my base connected to the PC, and often plug the headset into the PS4. It swaps between those two setups dynammically.

The audio quality is exceptional. These are excellent noise cancelling headphones. A yeshiva two blocks away from my house is using an old air raid siren as a shabbos alarm. Imagine how loud that is. When I have these on, and have my game set to a comfortable volume (I do not like it too loud) I can easily hear the game over the air raid siren.

The base is smaller than I expected, so I can seat it further back on my desk, and it takes up less space. The height isn't adjustable, but seems perfect to me. The center lines up at just below eye level. The display is crisp, no dead pixels, and presents clear, crisp images.

I plugged it into an Ubuntu machine, via HDMI, and there was no problem. The monitor was recognized immediately. I needed to reset the screen size on the settings in Ubuntu, but that's very common.

I played some PC games with it, and it's very good, and very comfortable for that.

It's easy to access the ports to plug in headphones or other audio equipment, or to switch out things in the second HDMI port. The menu buttons on the bottom right swap the input feed quickly and easily.

The default brightness setting is "burn a hole in your retinas", which can be a nightmare if you suffer migraines and leave it on that setting. If you change it to "standard", it becomes a beautiful, comfortable, fabulous monitor.

This review is for the Crucial Ballistix Sports XT 16 Gig DIMM kit.

I was a little concerned with the DIMMs as they were a little fatter than normal, but they snapped easily into my Dell desktop computer. Both Windows 7 and Ubuntu recognized the memory at once, with no issues, which really was to be expected.

Often, I'll run multiple VMs at a time. I do software development, so often I'll have one VM running Windows Server 2008, hosting SQL Server, while a second acts as a development box, and a third, which is frequently wiped out and recreated (or really, cloned from a blank copy) acts as a testing machine. Each of these machines gets 4 gig dedicated ram, and I leave the last 4 for the host OS. This RAM has held up to that kind of intense use without any problem. I am delighted.

I also use this machine for intense gaming, and again, this RAM does an awesome job. The memory, left at default configuration, is fast, fast, fast. Again, I'm a happy user.

Overall, I think the product is an exceptional value -- a top performer at a sensible price. The best I can say is, after a while you won't notice it. It will give you solid performance with no problems, and will just become invisible as you. I will definitely be using them again next time I'm in the market for memory.

I use this primarily as a charging station, since it is a USB 2.0 device in a USB 3.0 world, and for that purpose it works perfectly. It's small. It lights up to show that the device is seated properly and is charging.

What I like most about it is the elegant design. On a functional level, one USB 2.0 hub is the same as any other. The only question is powered or non-powered. You can run this one powered for a charging station, or if your device requires it, and non-powered for those devices that draw enough from a single USB port.

What I don't like is the power adapter. It's not standard, or at least it's smaller than anything else I've seen, so I can't just bring the hub and have one power supply for home and one for the office.

The video quality is amazing. It self-focuses, self-stabilizes, self-adjusts for light conditions (and the included light shield is a huge plus for avoiding glare). It hones in on a person and automatically adjusts to focus the image and the sound right on that person. It seems to have a built in wind shield -- wind is the great enemy of microphones. Filming home movies doesn't get any easier, and really, when you're in the midst of your important memories--the ones worthy of recording and keeping forever--you want to live the experience, not fuddle with the camera. This one takes care of just about everything, and it does it so well, you'll come to trust it. It can record for over 11 hours (I tried it and both the memory and the battery held).

The only one nit pick is the projector. You have to start playing the video before you can turn the projector on and tell it the source to project from, so you lose the first few moments of the video. Shoot a little lead time to compensate. That's the worst I can say for this camera. It is otherwise perfect.

In a pinch, you can wall project from any video source with the right HDMI cable. The only trick is finding a wall large enough, and far enough away without obstruction. I have done the lazy trick of watching TV on the ceiling with this.

I'm not sure what the value of a GPS is in a camera, but it has one, and it certainly doesn't detract from anything. WiFi, which makes more sense, is sold separately.

The 7.1 sound is shockingly good. I have a standard 7.1 surround system, and I didn't think the headphones would emulate that with any degree of quality, but I was wrong. They're excellent. Two things to keep in mind. One, your sound card needs to support 7.1. Some laptops don't. Two, you may need to go into your sound options and turn on 7.1. Otherwise, you just get stereo. For the game systems (XBox or PS3) no configuration is required. Just be aware that running the headset might not mute the tv, depending on your setup.

The microphone is crisp and picks up what you say, not your breathing, which is an annoyance with some other headsets.

The cord is long enough, you won't mind that it's wired. It's easy to sit a comfortable distance away from the TV and have ample slack left on the cord. It's a thick cord, and oddly, doesn't seem prone to tangling.

The only downside is the complexity. By being a headset that supports everything, it has a lot of permutations. If you have an XBox with composite cables, set it up this way. If you have an XBox with HDMI, set it up that way, if you have a PS3 with... You get the idea. But once you have it configured in your environment, you'll love it.

I use this with the [[ASIN:B008GFREAU Kindle Fire HD 8.9", Dolby Audio, Dual-Band Wi-Fi, 32 GB - Includes Special Offers]] and it's perfect. Once I paired them the first time (a very quick and easy process) the two find each other immediately as soon as I turn both on. The stand doubles as a case for the keyboard, and then I put that and the Kindle Fire in a netbook sleave and carry them all together. The stand works with both 8.9" and 7" tablets, in both landscape and portrait modes.

It's a full sized keyboard. I am a touch typist, and small keyboards often throw me off. This one is perfect. I hate when, with a smaller keyboard, I either hit the wrong keys or need to look at the keys. With this, I can just type as comfortably as I would at my desktop.

It's too easy to forget to turn this off, which kills the batteries, and it's so convenient it'll see daily use, which also kills the batteries, so I highly recommend [[ASIN:B0030T1NEU AmazonBasics AAA NiMH Precharged Rechargeable Batteries-4-Pack, 800 mAh]] to go with it. I've had a few bluetooth keyboards, and this is the best I've ever seen.

There is a lot to love about this case. It hold the Kindle Fire HD in two orientations. The lower one is perfect for watching a video. The higher one is great if you're pairing the Kindle with a bluetooth keyboard for an ad hoc Android netbook. The case feels good in the hand. It's warm, like a quality journal. The texture is pleasing to the hand and the eye. It's utterly luxurious.

The wake and sleep features work shockingly well. The bands hold the device securely. The ports are easy to access. The speakers are covered and this leads to a slight decrease in sound quality, but hardly noticable.

My only concerns are that even though it can hold the device at a perfect angle for reading, it can only do so in a landscape orientation--leaning it up against the case doesn't hold well-- and that there are no pouches. As with any cover like this, it is of limited protective value. Very small items such can slip under the cover. If you want complete protection, get a slip case.

This is about as perfect as an 8.9" case gets. Highly recommend.

The first thing to know is this is for PC gaming (and other PC use). It will not work on the XBox 360 and it will only work as a voice headset (not carrying game sounds) on the PS3.

The picture doesn't do the comfort of these justice. That microfiber lining on the ear buds feels like velvet. It is so nice on the head. They're light. They're comfortable. They adjust to your head size and are angled just a bit for maximum comfort.

The microphone does not fully swivel. You can only wear it on the one side, but that helps, because the headset will do an excellent job of emulating surround sound and you don't want to hear your enemy coming at you from the left, when in fact they are on the right and your headset is reversed. Don't ask me how many times I've done that. Games are substantially better with surround sound. I was used to "there is a noise somewhere so look around". This takes it to "there is a noise just left of me so look left" which is both helpful and more immersive. These headphones do a great job with that. It is emmulation but the games I've tried it on (mostly with Steam) are able to handle the fact that the PC is performing emulation and accomodate. I'm spending less time wondering what's killing me and more time returning fire.

When I'm not gaming with them, I use them for Skype, most particularly for seemingly endless conference calls. The battery can outlast my coworkers' ability to drag out a call, and with my coworkers, that's impressive. I can walk from room to room, answer the door, get another cup of coffee (and then lunch, and then dinner) and never miss a thing. Moving the microphone up will mute it (great for dealing with whomever is at the door) and the wheel on the side can adjust the volume (perfect for when the discussion devolves into a shouting match). The microphone has excellent pickup.

They're also great for watching videos without distrubing anyone else, and the surround sound emulation works perfectly there as well. There is some sound leak, but not much. For music, they provide excellent range and purity of sound.

Some days I spend more time with these things on my head than off. They're comfortable enough, and last long enough, for me to do that.

FM reception is flat out horrible where I live. It's like a radeo dead zone. My home theater system can pull in nothing. My stereo gets a lot of static. I listen almost exclusively online but I'd heard good things about this radio so I decided to give it a try. The reception was amazing. Perfectly clear. No static on FM at all. It sounds beautiful. The weather feed was full of static, but servicable--I ususally can't pull in the weather band at all. AM is average--neither the worse I've heard nor the best. But then, I don't expect much from AM.

It does the FM1, FM2 trick that some cars do. There is no difference. It just lets them repurpose the buttons. I find it odd, but not bad.

The only think I would have changed is how it hangs. If you don't have a shower hook (I don't) it hangs over the shower head. That tilts the entire unit forward. It should either suspend from the shower curtain rack (the strap is oriented the wrong way to do that--it would try to hand perpendicular to the curtain) or reach a better balance point. That's an issue of aesthetics, not function. I'd be worried about sitting it on the edge of the tub, as it is too likely to fall.

The one trick to remember, when sticking the antenna to the shower wall, is that suction cups don't work as well on a wet surface. Thoroughly dry the wall first, then place it. It helps will the issue of the antenna falling.

Given the price I had two questions going into this purchase.

One, is this really a pair of speakers for around $50? Yes. Two in a box together.

Two, would these be the underpowered tagalongs when compared with the more expensive speakers in my setup? No. Absolutely not. These have brilliant clarity and volume. They are much higher quality then the price suggests.

I'm using them to upgrade a 5.1 system to a 7.1. I could not be more pleased.

The sound quality is going to depend a lot on the speakers, but this device can do any speaker set proud. It delivers clear, powerful audio around the room.

SETUP

The connectors are speaker cables to the speakers and RCA to the subwoofer, no cables included. If I'd have known that off the bat, it would have saved me a last minute trip to Radio Shack. I'm not dinging any points for that, just making certain to mention the need to order cables as well. Grab a lot of speaker wire. You'll get better results if you move the surround speakers well away from the TV. Also, don't leave the subwoofer in the corner or right against the wall. Give it a little bit of space to resonate and you'll get better sound quality.

The on-screen instructions are weird. First it reminds you that you'll need speakers and a TV. Then it tells you to plug in the front right speaker, then the front left. It doesn't give you any more guidance than "go plug it in to the labeled port and make sure that plus goes to plus and minus to minus" so I'm not sure the point. At the end, it uses the included microphone to do a six point test throughout the room to automatically balance the speakers, which redeems the condescending earlier portion. Mine told me I had the wires reversed, so I swapped them and it told me I still had them reversed. I told it to skip that test and everything is working just fine.

POTENTIAL PROBLEMS WITH SMART TV

If you have a 3D TV or a smart TV, you might have problems using any kind of HDMI switcher, and this receiver will cause the same issues. There is a nifty workaround. Plug the HDMI cables straight to the TV and connect only the audio ports of the the device (Blu-Ray player, Sat/Cable, whatever) to the receiver. Then, just set the TV to external speakers, or just mute the TV. Sadly, this won't work with XBox or PS3. Neither put out a dedicated audio signal. For some TVs you can plug the audio out of the TV into the speaker and take care of it all in one shot, but that didn't work for me.

It has dedicated labeled audio and HDMI connections for Cable/Satellite TV, Media Center, Game, DVD, and Blu-Ray. These map up to the remote control and the front panel. There is one auxilliary HDMI port in the front for "other". The remote is clear, and using the device is easy--no games of "which one do I set it to when I want to watch cable?" The only issue I have with the remote is the size. There aren't a lot of buttons, but they're so widely spaced the remote is huge. It gets to be a problem for those of us who graduated from remote boat and are working on remote barge.

NETWORKING

I'm dinging it one star for networking. In this day and age, who puts out a network-enabled device with no capability for WiFi? This device has no WiFi, and no ability to add it with a USB attachment. If you want WiFi, you need to get a network bridge. Given how fabulous Sirius sounds on this system, getting it on the network is a must.

The setup was easy. I found no trouble, no complications, no issues. I just plugged it in and it works.

It streams Netflix, Hulu, and Amazon videos with no trouble. Setup for those was easy as well. My router is on the fritz, and when too many packets get lost, the device drops the connection (can't blame the device--it can't stream if it can't connect to the Internet) but it recovers smoothly. I've seen other devices just fail and return to the menu. This pauses and picks up where it left off once it is able to reestablish a connection.

The image quality is outstanding. The form factor is beautiful. The interface is easy to use. The remote is a little fatter than most, so expect to give it one of the larger pouches in the remote boat.

It does not contain cables, so pick up good ones. I like [[ASIN:B003L1ZYYW AmazonBasics High-Speed HDMI Cable (9.8 Feet/3.0 Meters) - Supports Ethernet, 3D, and Audio Return [Newest Standard]]] Not all HDMI cables are equal. It depends on which specification it implements (these are 1.4) and what part of the specs the cable implements.

I'm very pleased with this device.

I was trying to send a digital cable box to this, and it works, and works well, but set up was a little tricky.

I tried to use the enclosed cables, but that made for a really grainy image off the Cablevision Scientific Atlanta 8300. I was hoping for normal standard definition video. This would have had me reaching for the rabbit ears back in the day. I switched to an S-Video cable, let the enclosed audio cables carry the sound, and that solved it for me. If you see a horrid image quaility, switch cables.

It records easily and well and lets you name your tracks. Pause to cut out commercials but keep the track together. Stop to end a track and start a new one. It's intuitive, easy, and gets the job done. For the price, it's hard to beat.

The picture is astounding. A few friends and I watched [[ASIN:B004K4N64E Tron: Legacy / Tron: The Original Classic (Five-Disc Combo: Blu-ray 3D / Blu-ray / DVD / Digital Copy)]] on this, and althought I love the movie, I couldn't pay attention to the movie the first time through. I was too busy staring in awe at the way the clouds in the distant background moved, or the beauty of the image. I was told passive 3D is an image quality drop from HD because it projects half the image to each eye, but I'm calling that theory out. This picture is glorious.

When it upscales images to 3D it can get a little odd. I watched Naruto on it, and some moments were astounding, and some were just odd, as Naruto's eyes seemed to deepen into layers. Overall, I like the upscale. It's an approximation of 3D, but it's a darn good approximation.

My boyfriend wears huge glasses and these fit over them perfectly. On a lark, I put them on over my largest sunglasses, and they still fit, so if you wear glasses, even very large glasses, and you have any concerns that they won't work well with these, stop worrying.

As to connectors, there is one input for composite in, but it comes with a three-into-one adapter for that. The same for component in. Those are the only cable that come with it, so you will need those. I suggest [[ASIN:B003L1ZYYW AmazonBasics High-Speed HDMI Cable (9.8 Feet/3.0 Meters) - Supports Ethernet, 3D, and Audio Return [Newest Standard]]] as they are reliable and implement 3D transmission well. There are four specifications for HDMI, 1.4 being the latest, and not every device or cable fully implements the specification. The signal will downgrade to the lowest component, and with a TV like this, you don't want that component to be your cable. The difference is substantial.

There are four HDMI ports, and it doesn't seem to like connecting to an HDMI switcher. If you have a lot of devices plugged in, and you often find yourself wondering which input the DVD player is using, you'll love this. First, if a device isn't actively sending a signal, it displays as greyed out, and moves to the back of the list. Second, you can name your inputs. You select them from a list (I would have likes to call one Playstation 2, but had to opt for "Game") but it helps a lot.

The remote is kind of like a Wii controller. You wave it around and it points at things on the screen you can select. Very cute. If you find it hard to use, back up a few steps. It's counterintuitive, but it works. The cursor slows down.

For streaming it has the standard YouTube, Netflix and Hulu among others. The only tiny downside is that it doesn't yet support Amazon on demand videos. Plug in a [[ASIN:B005CLPP84 Roku 2 XS 1080p Streaming Player]] and you're set for streaming entertainment. I am in the process of replacing my router. It's in such bad shape that my Pingtest results range from B- to C when connected wirelessly. Whatever caching the set top does, it can provide perfect clarity even in such adverse conditions. Good to know if your Internet can have "off moments".

The energy star note that came on the TV (the yellow tag required by law that you see on all appliances these days) claims that this TV will have an Estimated Yearly Energy Cost of $14 with a range for similar models (45" - 49" TVs) going from $18 to $51. This is "Based on 11 cents per kWh and 5 hours use per day."

I wish I could give this 50 stars. It's perfect.

The device has exceptional sound quality, for an MP3 player at this size and price, far greater than I had expected. I'm able to listen to it on the platform of a NYC subway station and hear my audiobook over the sound of an incoming or outgoing train. I can't do that with my iPod. The sound for music is just a bit better, richer, than the iPod.

The headphones are nice, with exchangable earbud sizes and decent sound. It's so small and light, it's like carrying no device at all. That alone is heading this in the direction of becoming a favorite.

The controls are good, once you get used to them. It's not so much a touchscreen as a pseudo touchscreen. The up and down arrows on the side are touch screen buttons, but if you touch a track's name, it won't play. The headphone jack is on the top, where it belongs (I do not understand the trend of putting it on the bottom; I know noone who carries their MP3 player over their head). The cable is standard USB mini, nothing proprietary. The one that comes with it is unusably small, but any standard mini USB will work.

The FM radio picks up a good signal, the equal of a dedicated AM/FM radio.

The battery charges quickly over USB and lasts for several hours of play. I got it down to about half after 7 hours of play, but never drained it completely.

Audible content is sensibly organized into its own section, away from the music, so it's easier to navigate.

It's a video player in name only. The screen is far too small. It's only 2 inches. The video that comes with it (avi) has printed text so tiny as to be impossible to read. The memory is too sparse, though it can take a micro SD card.

The main concern I would have with the device is that, if you completely fill it, it won't turn on. It simply reports an out of memory error and shuts back down. Given that it has reserved half a gig for operations, it stands to reason some of that should have been for caching (and while that might sound small, we used to run full computers--OS, programs, data, the works, on 20 meg drives). Were it not enough, more should have been allocated. Normal use should not cause it to refuse to function unexpectedly. That's why it gets four stars, not five.

You know how, with some movies, you can't hear the dialog for all the sound effects? This normalizes (or levels) the sound, so you can. It provides a better-than theater quality sound experience, for those of us who like to hear the dialog, experience the rich tones of the score, and not go deaf. Oh, it can get mighty loud if you want too. User's choice. It delivers a grand sound experience at any setting.

The setup is the "impress your kids" kind. It's easy, but it looks hard. You will need a Phillips head screwdriver, an [[ASIN:B003L1ZYYM AmazonBasics High-Speed HDMI Cable (6.5 Feet/2.0 Meters) - Supports Ethernet, 3D, and Audio Return [Newest Standard]]] and possibly (unless you have HDMI ARC) an [[ASIN:B001TH7GSW AmazonBasics Digital Optical Audio Toslink Cable, 6 Feet]]. Get them on Amazon. Most places charge a lot more for these. My TV didn't specifically state it was HDMI ARC (Audio Return Channel) but it worked anyway. I'm connected via an HDMI switcher, no problem. I just have the switch put out to the sound system, then the sound system put out to the TV. Everything is labelled and color coded, and it just couldn't be any easier. The only "gotcha" is make certain you're on the right input setting. Sometimes it wants TV instead of one of the HDMI ports.

It comes with a remote, in case your remote boat isn't already overflowing.

This is pretty much the top of the line. It's beautiful. It delivers awesome sound. It's perfect. I'm using my TV instead of my stereo to listen to music, because the sound quality of these speakers is that good. Oh, and you can turn the TV off and the speakers on, and the sound will still work.

The setup is super easy. Everything is obvious, and it plugs right into a headphone jack for universal application. Plug the speakers into the back of the box. Plug the wired remote into the box. Plug the device into the wall. Plug the device into any headphone jack. Nothing fancy. Nothing tricky. The box comes with a variety of optional adapters, and even a headphone extension cord for a long reach. The speakers don't have a long cord, but given they are using standard plugs, an extension is easy to find.

It seems like "minimize troubles" is the core principle around which this device is designed. The manufacturer was smart about bypassing potential problems. The plug is two prong, not three, for greater flexibility. The plugs are all universal for easy of finding extensions, adapters, etc. I get the impression the designers spent far more time than most sitting around saying, "What could become a pain about this thing? Let's make sure we avoid that." It's impressive how well thought out the unit is.

I tried it with an iPad and it was perfect.
I tried it with a digital TV and there was a minor whine when there was no other sound coming out. The whine stops when there is a signal, so it doesn't interfere with use. The same with a netbook.

Overall, the sound quality is very good. I would reccomend it. That weird whine is the only issue, and that only barely.

These are amazing. They will fit. My ears are tiny. Most ear buds hurt after a while. With the smallest adapter in, these fit fine. The adapters cover a wide range of sizes, so you do need to test them all and find the best size for your ears. They work in two "modes" and I'm not sure they're supposed to. If you just sort of seat them in your ears, they act like normal earbuds (good for when you need some awareness of your surroundings). If you insert them the way you would ear plugs they act like noise cancelling earbuds (good for when you don't want to listen to the lady on the bus explain the ins and outs of her new baby's diaper). It just depends on how you sit them in your ears.

The sound quality excellent. I needed to turn down most of my devices because these transmit at a good volume--awesome if you like your music loud. The volume can be controlled on the cord. The microphone works nicely--I used mine with a Droid and the sound quality was fine. You can pause your MP3 player by pushing the button on the cord. Perfect for listening to podcasts and audiobooks.

They come with a carry case, which I thought a bit much for headphones, but I think I'll be using it. These are very good headphones, worthy of such care, and I want them to last a long time.

This is by far the best ereader on the market.

The bad.

It doesn't do epub and it doesn't connect to the library. This seems like a deal breaker until you try to borrow a book from the library. I have one on hold now (to read on either the nook or the Sony) that should be available in 39 weeks. I'll probably give up and just buy it anyway.

The good.

The speed. The page turns are as fast as the average person can turn a print page. You won't see that "opening book" message the nook displays. When you tell it to open a book, it opens in less than a second. I keep hitting the page turn key just to marvel at how fast it is. I've never seen an ereader this fast. This is perfect.

Store access. Let me run you through buying a book for the various devices. For the Kindle, if you're on the Amazon site you select your book, click buy now, pick up the device and start reading. For the nook, you buy the book, then you turn on the touch screen that keeps turning itself off, you go into the home screen, go to "My Library", select "Update B&N Content" and wait a few minutes. There is no mechanism to automatically push content to the device. For the Sony (I'm using the Daily Edition, which has 3G), you use the custom software (no way to buy from a website), buy the book, then either transfer it via USB, or go to the device, to the store, log into your account (you need to provide your login information each time you go to the store) find the book you bought and click download, then wait. For buying from the device, Kindle is easy and fast, nook is decent, and Sony is unreasonably slow.

The screen. There is no glare, even with the book light on. It's the crispest and easiest to read screen out there. It's beautiful.

Audible integration. Download your books via WiFi or transfer via USB and listen with your device, either through headphones or the speakers. How cool is that? Now if only there were a card reader to store those larger files.

Collections. I have the Kindle 1, so I was first introduced to collections via Sony. It's great to be able to organize so much content. Here you can organize ebooks and audiobooks into collections together. That's one thing Kindle and Sony both have over nook--they treat content the same. Nook is the only one that doesn't let you annotate or bookmark newspapers and magazines, and who wouldn't want to mark an article to refer back to later?

Ease of use. I handed my Kindle 1 to a woman who was too scared of technology to turn on her own laptop. Her husband had to do it for her. I wanted to show her a passage in the Declaration of Independence, and I had the passage on the screen. I didn't instruct her. Moments later, she turned the page and just kept reading, all the way the end. Then she looked at what else I had on the device. An ereader should be as easy and intuitive to use as a print book, and most of us figured those out when we were about 10 months old. Kindle fits that bill.

Social networking. Post passages and comments on them to Twitter and Facebook. You can see what passages other readers have highlighted. This is particularly great for online book clubs.

More language sets. I'm kind of hoping Amazon will sell Japanese language books in the US Kindle store, or let us buy from Amazon.co.jp.

I could go on and on, but what it comes down to is, when it comes down to the core features of an ereader--buying, reading, annotating, and searching a book, Kindle beats the competition hands down. When it comes to extra bells and whistles--organization, commenting to others, web access, text to speech, Kindle beats the competition hands down.

There is no other viable choice any more. Kindle is just too much better than every other device out there.

The good:

Lane guidance. I like to plan my turns and exits, especially in thick traffic. I hate it when the passenger who claims to know the way suddenly says "Left turn here!" to feet from the intersection when I'm in the right lane and the middle and left lanes are packed with traffic. No more. Tom Tom says things like, "Take a right on 17th street, then a left on Maritime Road, giving me time to get into that left lane." It also gives you lane guidance for exiting the highway, when it's right two lanes for this highway, and middle two for this bridge and left one for the other bridge. You can see on screen, and it tells you aloud, which land you want.

It tells you "left turn here", which is good when the street sign is missing or obscured.

It adapts quickly. It seems to know traffic laws, so it doesn't try to put you the wrong way on a one way the way Mapquest did in the early days.

It tracks your speed.

The route chosen to a familiar location surprised me, but thinking it over, it was the most direct route. I normal go one exit on the highway. It had me go a few very small side streets instead.

It works in or out of the car, for those who want to use it for camping or geocaching.

The bad:

Even on the loudest setting, it's a little hard to hear. The pronunciation is off, which one might expect, but the volume is poor. It's hard to hear, even with no one talking in the car. Good luck if you've got kids in the back seat.

It was a little hard to figure out. It wants the street then the number, and I tried offering the full address. Once I figured it out, it was pretty easy and did a great job.

I plugged it into a netbook running XP, 1 gig RAM. In seconds, it provided a beautiful video quality. The set up could not have been easier. Even though it's an HD webcam, it doesn't require a powerhouse machine to run. The picture quality was amazing.

My only teeny tiny complaint is that there is no easy way to mount it. Otherwise, this device is perfect.

Good brand.  Got these for my hubs.  He said sound quality is good and that they are comfy in his ears. He is 6 '3" and kinda has a big head and ears and these worked fine.  These paired well with his iPad and were pretty much find it and pair it.  Decent sound and noise cancelation.  Not the best of the best, but for the price, these are valued and work accordingly.  My husband's only complaint was that I did not get them for him sooner.  So, there ya go.

We have used Apple Airtags since June 2021 and purchased those directly from Apple. Took a chance on a Warehouse Deal on THIS one and it turned out just fine. THIS purchase will make 3 that we own. They seem gimmicky, but as someone that occasionally loses things in plain site, these items are great, We have a tag on each of of our set of keys and I have one in my wallet.

Having them on our keys saved me one day when we realized the keys had fallen behind the washer/dryer. Playing the sound to find them alerted us to where they were. Having one in my wallet is great when the wallet falls between the seats of the car and keeps me from panicking because at least I know the wallet is nearby and I did not lose it.

These are easy to pair and super useful. We have no regrets with them.

Compared to like products this camera does what others do and beyond with a better value.

Like many, we have been on Zoom for almost two years now. Our congregation has been holding meetings this way to keep people safe. We have learned a lot and changed our set up a number of times to make things better. We added an external microphone long ago. A definite recommendation. This week we went to dual screens. This allowed my husband to pull up talks on one screen and we could see participants on another screen. However, this led us to always looking up, beyond our laptop camera. To me, at that point, we looked weird.

To solve this, we attached THIS camera to the top of our second, higher screen. The zoom on the camera wasn't enough, for us. But we found a way to rig the camera about 2" in front of the higher screen and it is perfect. We are at a great angle, seeing just our torsos, with both of us easily in the view. The light ring is tooooo bright for us and we turned it off (touch the top of the camera).

LOVE the remote. Saves us from touching the camera. I chose this camera based on that alone. Clarity is hands down better than our newer Dell business machine's built in camera. For a high end laptop, that camera always struck me as grainy. THIS camera was super clear. Compared to the other 20 boxes of other Zoom participants, we were probably the least grainy people present. That really sealed the deal that this camera was a keeper.

The zoom on the camera could be slightly better, but that was the only issue. No regrets after fully using it.

Having had a pair of Jabra Active 75t's for the last year (and just LOVE them), I thought it would be nice to try these more updated Elite 3's.

The Elite 3's pretty much behave for me like the Active 75t's. They both fit in my ear fantastically and stay there. They both have exceptional sound quality. They both charge easy and keep a great charge. The case feels cheaper with these newer 3's and the earbud itself feels cheaper. Cheaper, but at the same time lighter which is a good thing. The color offerings are also not as good as the Active 75t's were. With those, I have a color called "Sienna" which is a golden peachy color and kinds really compliments my skin tone and so those earbuds don't stand out. THESE earbuds are dark grey, one of 4 colors offered and just look like standard earbuds in color.

I think the main difference between the two is the active 75ts are more designed to be waterproof, sweatproof, and for sports. THESE Elite 3's are more basic.

I like these Jabra lines because once they are on and music is playing you cannot hear the world around you. Husband's private calls ... GONE. I can be in our small house and he can conduct his business privately. Definitely a plus. Music sounds great, everything sounds great. Have not use them for calls.

Overall ... these are worth the price. Best part is how they fit and stay in my ears. I would not hesitate to recommend these to someone and I, for one, have no regrets.

Easy to set up. Hooked up to a Roku via HDMI with ease. Good smaller sized TV. Picture quality is as expected for an entry level TV. Not a smart TV, no bells and whistles, no bluetooth. Sound is actually not my favorite. THIS Continu.us TV replaces a 21" Samsung TV in our guest room and the smaller, WAY older Samsung has a much better & richer sound than this TV. I am going to have to figure out how to attach an external speaker to bring this TV up to par.

Overall ... If you want just a basic TV, this is it. Nothing fancy, just a TV.

Holds airtag safely and securely.  I do not feel like it will drop out of the case.  These are some on the market that that is the fear.  For me, I can see my engraving through the center of the case.  I can also hear the sound it plays easily, when you are looking for the tag.  Overall ... this is one of the better cases I own.  No regrets.

Let me start out by saying the noise cancelling portion is super excellent.  My husband puts these on and he cannot hear anything but the TV or his music.  He cannot even hear a muffled version of me.  Good?  Bad?  You decide, but as far as noise cancelling it is well above average.  Hooks up wirelessly easily.  Charge lasts a long time.  Comfortable.  to wear all day long binge watching or listening.  We have a couple of other pairs of headphones ... MPOW and Panasonics.  Both good in their own rite.  But these are hubs favorites now and he uses them most often.  Overall ... no regrets at all.

I chose this because I was already familiar with the Onvis brand. We already had two temperature sensors installed by this brand. What I liked about the temperature sensors is, you scan the sensor and they automatically recognize in the AppleHome app on my phone. We do not have a special hub. I like that I do not have to download a special foreign based app (but you can). You don't have to hook up to your wifi and enter in any passwords or enable location services or any scary stuff like that. I will not use "smart appliances" that require a third party foreign app that wants me to enter my wifi password.

So THIS home security device ... it was much the same. Scan the QR code, it is recognized in AppleHome right away and I went to set it up. We have one window in our house that always spooked me because it is closer to the ground and further from the master bedroom. This is where I placed the alarm. It works perfectly. Arm it "night" or "away" and when it is opened it shrieks the most awful noise. Then, you get an alert on your phone. Presumably this would not notify you away from home unless you have a hub, which we do not. But for now, it is peace of mind enough. One extra level of protection.

No idea how this works on non Apple devices. Sorry.

Overall ... this does exactly what I needed it to do and will probably get an additional device in the future. Easy to use and set up. No regrets.

We needed/wanted an external mic to improve our Zoom meeting quality. Our meetings for worship, midweek and weekends, have all been moved to Zoom for the safety of our older ones. When my husband has "parts" to give we wanted the clarity to be a step above what it was. It is hard for US to judge the clarity but we asked others and they thought and they said it was average and above average so I assume that is good.

Easy to set up and use. Pretty much plug and play. Zoom recognized the device without having to install it or do anything special. We just chose the device in the Zoom menu and we were good to go.

So far no complaints ... met our expectations.

Right about the time my husband was talking about how he wished he had a laptop stand (and he started stealing my puzzle boxes to try and help) ... this item came into our lives.

Out of the package it is easy to setup. It is sturdy and holds his brand new Dell Vostro that we just upgraded to. We are weekly Zoom hosts for worship meetings and really had to tweak our world with our internet, sound, video, and lighting in our house.

We actually do not have one complaint about this stand. I am not afraid it will collapse. It is strong and holds the lappie at a perfect angle for our needs. Could easily recommend. No regrets.

UPDATED REVIEW:
Had these for well over a year and they really are my favorite earbuds ever. They stay put and the music and sound quality is excellent. When I have them in I cannot hear anything around me, which makes them excellent living in a small house and trying not to hear important, private calls that my husband takes. When I have these in, I just tune the rest of the world out. Their charge time lasts seemingly forever. I have had no issues in the last year.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
These are perfect for my lifestyle.

The color I chose is perfect too ... I have medium cool skin tone and they just blend right in.

This is the first wireless earbud headphone that has ever stayed in my ear. EVER. They never feel like they are going to fall out. They just stay in effortlessly.

Setup took a little longer than expected. One must download the Jabra app first. It is not just a simple pair. But once they were paired, it was all easy. Take them out of the case and they are on and for me, paired to my phone.

Aside from the fact that they stay in my ear during walking, running, and whatever, the sound quality is very good and music is so pleasurable and crisp. I also like that my husband can have private calls while on the couch (we are in the Covid year after all) and I can put these in and play music and not hear even a smidgen of his conversation. I can just immerse myself in my own little world and he can trust that he is having his space.

I didn't know an earbud could be so good. No regrets here. Would very much recommend.

We have, I would say, a middle class income, and only my husband works. We keep a pretty tight budget and sometimes needs and wants get weighed heavily.

The antenna he had finally started to really not work well and as I was going to purchase it (it would have been $22) he asked me to look for the low profile version. These were the first pair of headphones I ever purchased on Amazon back in 2010. I really loved them as a pair of simple headphones. I have had good success with the Creative Brand. These had good tone and good bass. They stayed in my ears fine and for the price, I believe they were worth what I paid. I would purchase creative headphones again and recommend the brand easily.

I got this surge protector power strip to take in my camper so I can plug my computer or tablet into it.  It is a little big looking at it but I could use it when sitting outside.  It has the requisite AC outlets along with 2 USB outlets.  If I had it at home I could hang it on a wall or my deck as it has mounts for that on the back of it.  I could also hang it on a hook as it has a big hole on one corner that you can string something through.  I am not thrilled by the color as it stands out too much for my needs but if you were using it in a construction setting with other workers you might want to have it noticed so it doesn't get stepped on or rolled over. This was my first telescope.  I have read a lot about telescopes and plan on buying a much more expensive one but then I read that you can take a scope like this and upgrade the eye piece and the finder scope and have something very usable for a basic telescope.  It is below zero here so rather than go outside I did all my reviewing inside looking out my window at the mountain.  The listing provides a great overview of what you get with the scope so I won't detail it here.  I will say that it does comes with everything you need to get ab great intro into having a telescope of this type.  The trip is very shaky  and when you look out at such a great distance any movement of the tripod makes focusing difficult. Using a remote for your camera or phone would work best.  It comes with a phone adapter so I attached an older phone to it and took a couple of nice shots of a portion of the top of the mountain.  Given I didn't have to do much I thought they turned out pretty good.  The focus needs improvement but I guess I wasn't expecting a lot from this lens.  The finder scope is used to first find the object you want to see in the telescope.  It worked fine.  Then you go to the telescope lens and the object should be there and all you need to do is focus, which I did.  Because the tripod is shaky it is hard to get a good focus as just touching the eye piece cause it to shake.  This is a very inexpensive tripod and most good scopes would require a tripod 3 times the cost of this entire product.  For this price you are getting an intro to using a telescope.  With some experience with this I should be able to get better at focusing.  I took these mountain pix with the 25mm eye piece.  It comes with a nice carrying case for the scope and tripod.  There is also a nice small case for the lenses.  The instructions and well done with a nice bird watching book included also.  I will enjoy taking this with me when I go camping where maybe I will see some birds.  I highly recommend this scope as a good start for getting into this hobby.

I have always wanted a little printer like this when I was working many years ago but they were never this small.  Now that I go camping in my RV and work while I camp I may want to print something without having to drag a full size printer along for the ride. I decided to set it up to print from my phone since I mainly use a phone or tablet when on the road.  I downloaded the suggested app and it was easy to get started and I didn't need to sign up or register to do so.  My Bluetooth found it right away.  I selected first to print a photo file and selected low quality as I didn't want to waste ink.  It came out OK.  I next selected a page in a PDF manual that had a [photo embedded in it and selected medium quality and that turned out great.  The only gripe was it only gave me the following places to look for a file to print:  iCloud, Photo, Web and my print history.  I only had a couple things in iCloud as I mainly use Google Drive so I would have to move the document to iCloud first in order to print it.  Photo didn't allow me to browse my photos so I wasn't dure where to go there.  Once I printed a photo inn iCloud then that photo showed up there to print in the future.  I thought that was what the print history was for.  So, the app could use some UI work but I can't complain as everything worked/connected so easily.  Now, the paper.  You have to use their HPRT Premium Multi-Purpose Copy Paper.  It is a bit shiny on one side and more expensive than typical print paper.  This brings me back to you have to really need a niche printer like this to make it worth it.  I cannot sweat these things because I got it to use sparingly while I travel when something just has to be in print form.  I don't even really print much anymore from my home printer so once could say I waste cartridges there.  In summary, if you need a portable printer, that costs more with proprietary paper, for those short run printing emergencies on the road then this is great.  It works great and is easy to setup.

I live in a rural area and find myself in areas with no cell service frequently.  Radios like these can be a lifesaver if you get separated from your group and can't make a cell phone call.  I plan to leave one radio home for my spouse while I go hiking away from the cabin.  This radio has a few functions that are important to have.  First you can set your channel number and be sure to make it the same on each radio.  You can find a channel that sounds the best or just pick a number where you don't hear any other radio traffic (people talking).  In addition to the main channel numbers there are 0-121 tone codes you can select.  This code in addition to the channel number provides more confidentiality to your calls.  The channel and tone code it is set at out of the box is 01 and 01.  You can set the volume.  If you don't want to have to press the PTT (push to talk) button you can set it to Vox and you can talk without pushing a button.  You can still only have one person talking at once but lets say you were doing something where your hands weren't available, like rock climbing or kayaking, you could still respond to someone calling you are start talking and others will hear you.  You should also be aware that each channel may or may not be capable of transmitting under hi power.  For maximum power, use channels 1-7 or 15-22.  To get the most range, be sure that you are using high power mode on the channels that allow it.  If you are unclear what channel someone else is using you can put it into scan mode and it will cycle through the 22 channels until it finds a signal. Lastly you can get weather channels on this so if you are uncertain about incoming weather you can go to an active weather channel and hear the latest forecast for the area.  You can also setup weather alerts so an alarm will sound should a weather emergency be forecasted.  In summary, for the money, you get a lot out of these 4 radios and they will make any trip safer if you use them.

If you're reading this, there's a good chance that you already know that if your devices tend to fly out of your hands and down flights of stairs, or out of speeding automobiles, you want it nestled inside of an OtterBox case, in particular, an OtterBox from The Defender series.
When I first got my Samsung Galaxy Tab S2, the first thing I did was to look for a case, because yes, I'm one of those people that devices seem to fly out of my hands totally unprovoked.
Unfortunately, my choices were limited, hence the cheesy pink case shown.

When this bad boy arrived, there was a sigh of relief, and with great anticipation pulled it out of the packaging.

If you've ever had an OtterBox before, you know that there is always a possibility that it's going to be a bit of a challenge to get your device in the case. That's the price you pay for the ultimate protection. With that in mind I studied the little how-to diagrams as if my final grade depended on it.
Looks pretty simple and straightforward. Better yet, it shows that it can be done without any tools or engineering skills.
The first two steps were no problem. Step 3, on the other hand, proved to be a little more of a challenge.
Okay, a lot of challenge.
You must loosen 9 tabs that are on the perimeter. It helps if you can do them all at once so that the 2 pieces can easily separate. Since it would take a multi-armed deity to accomplish that feat, I tried to do it as the diagram indicated, with my hands. Those tabs do not budge. After much struggling I tried to pry them open with my nails.
Crrrraaaaaack!
Both thumbnails gone in an instant. It was apparent that I would indeed need tools.

As you might imagine, someone who is concerned about her manicure only has one set of tools.
MANICURE tools.

And yes, the cuticle Nipper turned out to be the exact tool that this delicate operation required. As the photograph shows, if you can prxy up those three side tabs and slip your hand in, you can get the rest of the tabs easily.
Don't think you can open just the one side and slip your device in, it's better to remove it completely.

Mission accomplished!
Although you lose a bit of screen sensitivity, all buttons work.
Yes, it's big. The sleek look of the tablet dissappears.
But if you're a butterfingers like me, this is the perfect protective case.

DVI stands for Digital Visual Interface. It was designed, beginning in 1999, to transmit uncompressed digital video.
This cable is dual link which allows resolutions up to 1920 × 1200. It is also 9.8 ft. Cable lengths up to 15 feet will work for this resolution.
This cable is pinned for digital only, no analog, and is used for flat panel displays, digital CRT displays, projectors, HDTV and Video Projectors. Most new high resolution monitors come with HDMI ports. These cables are similar except that HDMI also carries audio signals.
These cables are a high quality, gold plated which reduces the chance of oxidation as long as you don't damage them.

First, the item is advertised as a server cooler. My application as an AVR cooler makes noise an issue to be dealt with. The unit is not designed for standalone operation where noise would be an issue, such as in a non-rack mounted AVR set-up.

My 11.2 AVR system runs hot as anticipated. Heat, of course, kills. So in the move up from a single top-down fan-cooled 7.1 AVR system, I expected to need a rack mount to contain the upgraded power conditioner and Li-ion UPS.

I read 70 dB within 6" of the 4-fan RAISING ELECTRONICS plenum assembly. I measure 60 dB at 3' on the bench. The noise drops to 35-40 dB with the glass enclosure door closed and the addition of acoustic deadening panels within the rack. This four fan plenum is moving a lot of air. Air velocity, not fan motor mechanics, is what creates the noise frequency range. In a server farm application, a 60 dB/blower is typical.

The acoustic deadening panel configuration attenuates the overall rack noise to 20dB from the seating. The overhead 4K projector fans run 30dB at the back of the room. There are few options available to silence the projector. The projector cooling is making more noise than the closed and acoustically deadened rack. The overall room noise becomes imperceptible when the system is pumping speakers.

It's not the silent, single-point thermal management solution for an open-air, shelf-mounted AVR system. It moves lots of air which creates noise. Well worth the investment if you think your application through.

Bose headphones are noise suppression first, sound fidelity second. If it’s sound fidelity you want, buy a comparably priced studio monitor headphone without noise suppression.

I’ve owned and worn out every iteration of the Bose noise-canceling headphones over the last 20 years for jet cabin noise suppression. Commercial airplane cabin noise is a proven travel fatigue-inducing component. A 2-17 hour flight with noise reduction headphones delivers noticeably less flight fatigue.

The QC-35’s are nearly worn out after another ‘million miles.’ They got 5 stars for the Bose attention to long-wear comfort. They’ve been beaten about, dinged, I’ve replaced the ear and head cushions twice. I suspect I have a wiring failure that’s about to reveal itself fully. I use the Bose most frequently without music for just the noise suppression. They work great as a sleep aid in hotels with and without music. Noise suppression is my #1 priority in this category. I have tested 2 of the latest Bose noise suppression headphone competitors. For several reasons, mostly head comfort and suppression extent, they still have a way to go to meet the Bose total experience.
The ambient noise suppression that these new 700 headphones provide is a significant improvement over the QC-35’s. The bass quality of Bose has always been a question mark easily revealed in a sales counter testing for comparison. Honestly, after an hour, the bass issue disappears in the Bose sound ambiance.

As to music reproduction, Bose does not represent the product as a monitor grade headphone. I happen to have a pair of Blue Ella monitor grade headphones. It is an error to compare the Bose work-horse noise suppression headphones that the 700 series represent with studio monitor grade fidelity. There is no question that studio monitor grade headphones deliver superior fidelity for the time they are worn.

Can I comfortably wear the Blue Ella’s on a trans-con flight? No (plus they are prone to a five-finger discount). They simply aren’t designed for hours of head comfort. The Blue Ella’s are fantastic for a couple of hours but are no way suitably head comfortable for a 17-hour flight to Australia.

The Bose 700’s are a clear step up for the QC-35 users. These are lighter on the head, and though they don’t have hingey elements of the QC-35, I’ve not experienced a flexibility problem from this lighter weight and flexible design. They are an improvement in the Bose reputation for the best designed, long-wear consideration.

This review is about what I think >90% of users will care about. The detail specs are a step further, higher and faster and advertised and advertised. The Asus ZenBook 13 has been my go-to everyday toting computer for some 7-8 years.

I have last year’s i5 gen7 ZenBook 13 to directly compare the two.

P.S. This Zen-book has been so good that I had it modified to incorpoarte medical practice compliant HIPA secured software. It's a step function increase in my nightly homework replacing my 7-year old Dell. This laptop is ubiquitously practical with 180 screen twist for descirbing patient procedures. With the med-system handshacks, its like 3x faster than the Dell.

First, this new i5 gen8 ZenBook 13 has a quarter inch all-around smaller footprint. The 1/4" is immediately noticeable from last year’s edition. The 1/4" bezel is noticeably better. As small a footprint as the two have, Asus has reduced the size with no compromise in keyboard utility.

This year's ZenBook is noticeably thinner. Recharge and headphone jack are reversed. This year's hinge is slightly more robust to account for the reduced thickness. The hinge has been a 'should improve' on ZenBooks since inception. This years may solve the issue for good.

The plug-outs are changed. Make sure the output ports are what you want. For my purposes, the addition of a standard HDMI vice last year’s mini-HDMI is an improvement requiring no adapter.
