I get 11 hours out of last year’s battery every day. I can't recall running out of battery on last years on battery save mode on trans-con flights.

Wish it came with Windows Pro instead of Home, but oh well.

Love it. Exceeds expectations. There's no purchase mistake to be made with the UX331.

Performs as advertised. These can get tricky when software is required. This avoids that.

5-star.

The Chrome OS is quick … the light on board memory loves friendly cloud apps.

I count this as head to head competition with the 2017 CES show winning Dell XPS. I have one of those from earlier this year and can say that form, fit and function are very comparable. HP is late to the party and was, therefore, able to deliver the 8th gen I7. Specs are very nearly identical.

From opening the box to Office 365/Outlook load with imports to this review took <15minutes. Maybe a smidge faster than the Dell. A little more bloatware on the HP after you're up.

So, I like what I see. Sound quality is outstanding and the very best I've heard coming out of the 13.3" genre. Screen resolution and viewing angles are outstandingly extending beyond 45 degrees in all directions. All round, very sharp looking 13" rocket for work or dedicated to the entertainment center. The appearance and specs are well covered in the description. It's assuredly more capable than I need. Runs AutoCAD swiftly.

The Envy is the quietest machine that I've seen. The Envy Keyboard is nuanced and is the most obvious difference. I keep hitting '/' instead of '.' for some unexplainable keyboard spacing delta. Keyboard backlighting is f5 ‘on’ or ‘off’ vs Dell's 3 step lighting adjustment. The Dell XPS wins on the keyboard backlight quality, keyboard, and keyboard contrast. HP Envy’s light piping to backlight keys and keytops is a competitive miss in indoor daylight conditions. The key laser etch depth or a backside geometry acrylic problem is biggie for me. The keyboard backlight must be fixed. On the upside, HP has gone the distance and moved the power converter brick away from the outlet junction box to mid-cord. I appreciate that nod to customer convenience.

Both the Dell XPS and this HP Envy are so thin that a standard USB-A is too thick for the available side real estate. Market peripherals have not quite caught up to the USB-C. I can't find a USB-C wireless mouse for instance and that means a dongle on the Dell. The HP Envy, on the other hand, has an interesting USB-A to C compatibility trick via a cool little spring door for the larger USB-A mouse. It's conveniently smaller than the one it replaces.

5-star improvement. I like it.

This is an expensive product that requires a deep dive into utility.

First, I’m curious about the advances in testing/assessing these ubiquitous and seemingly simple lead acid devices and enjoy checking in on the state of the consumer art. Your individual lead acid battery is phantom-like, escaping modern sciences ability to assess the individual battery after cyclic charge and recharge.

As a physicist with extensive multi battery type experience, there are only a few things specifically understood about the multi-cell, lead acid battery … they are generally black, always heavy, with skin burning and ion rich acid reacting with the cation Pb+2. There is a limited life governed by complex, non-linear characteristics. Your service authority is a broken record “it’s not possible to determine remaining life, sorry. Buy a new battery just in case.” The deep science is in the complexity of surge, energy densities and integrity. It’s the ions and cations. Devices like the AccuMaster calculate an average status several different ways.

The AccuMaster BT Digital Battery Load Tester Analyzes 12V 100-2000 CCA Batteries | Voltage, Capacity% Life, Resistance, Cranking Amps | Amp Hours (AH) indeed packs a bundle of algorithmic and heuristic calculations to ‘help’ assess battery ‘health’ for purpose. I have two distinctly different purposes for boat and car, for crank energy and deep cycle. After a season in boat storage, replacing the battery rack is insanely expensive in my opinion but, having been stranded with one-year old batteries, I’m not taking chances anymore … out they go. The car batteries present a different problem with extreme summer heat (deadly!), vibration, and overall alternator/computer behavior.

The baseline battery test on my assortment of batteries today suggests all is well … ‘good’ in fact. With the quantitative baseline, I have a starting position to watch what precipitates.

In the meantime, I will buy a replacement before and no later than the day the existing battery warranty expires. The manufacturer warranty period is a statistically demonstrated random or continuous testing regimen based on the manufacturers variant for, test confidence level, reliability to be demonstrated, the number of allowable test failures and the test sample size.

The BT tester provides a wholly new mechanism to potentially ‘maximize’ the battery confidence at a theoretically minimum cost.

5-stars! Simple, smart standardizing metrics. I like that. Time will tell.

Maybe best in price class. As advertised, better than expected. 5-stars.

I needed the multiport for my USB-C/Thunderbolt 'only' outputting new windows 10 Dell. The Dell is too thin for USB 1/2 ports. I needed an HDMI output and that required this adapter.

I was a bit concerned about the advertised potential downloads and "may not work with" conditions.

No such need here. It's a seamless plug and play device from newest Dell USB-C.

Works great. 5-star.

Fastest new computer start-up ever. From box to MS Outlook inbox in 6-7 minutes … including iPhone contacts & calendar sync, including Cloud sync. This used to take time, hours … days of downloads and starts and restarts. Dell has laced up Cortana to verbally walk through the setup process with the clearest voice and response I’ve seen. Very impressive! Dell is hands down the best I’ve experienced at getting you up and running fast. Minimal bloatware.

My application is business/internet from lap/table to car seat to site. I tote my computer walking miles on the job using various power modes.

I’ve been sold on the 13.3” size by day and switch to my engineering work station by night. If you are looking at a 13.3”, Asus and Dell are the leaders duking it out for market. As I have both, I’ll compare and contrast to answer questions regarding stuff I’ve found important between them

Newest Dell …
- Extraordinarily fast … speed has not been a discriminator for non-game use for some years. I can’t detect one faster than another. It’s just really fast. It behaves like MS and Dell are better integrated behind the scene than Asus.
- Dell is physically smaller and presents a ¼” display bezel to reduce the footprint and shave about ½” off the external X and Y.
- Dell’s LED-backlit display appearance is superb. The 4000:1 contrast is a noticeable attribute. Viewing angles appear to be like >60 degrees all around (outstanding!). It seems unusual that Dell incorporates a UHD graphics card to drive an FHD display ... I suspect a UHD display is coming when competition demands.
- No touch screen. I don’t like the touch screen 95% of the time (thin film over LCD, busy pointy fingers on the screen make stuff happen) … but you pick’um.
- Keyboard illumination has moved into my must-haves. The Dell delivers a different take in light piping. It works OK. In daylight, the Dell keyboard has to be turned off if you want to read the keys. Could be the color or light pipe strategy, the illumination obscures the key characters like an optical illusion. The Asus keyboard lighting is better.
- The keyboard of course feels different. Asus uses membrane switches offering minimal tactile feedback and less noise (I think it’s faster). The Dell is using a spring key switch to provide more tactile feel and audible ‘click’ feedback. User decide. Both work fine for me.
- Integral sound quality is comparatively outstanding from the uber-tiny speakers. Dell has fixed the typical awful anemic 13.3” sound quality.
- The Skype view camera is at the bottom of the Dell display providing crisp up the nose hole vision. Come on Dell! You gotta be kidding! It’s awful. This is not a Skype’r PC.
- Very responsive touchpad. Better than Asus.
- Face recognition is by True Key and works fine. After a couple initial failures, the fingerprint reader works great ... faster than the FRT.
- The 128G SSD might have concerned me a couple years ago. Asus standard is 256G. However, cloud and share applications have become so good and so responsive that I simply don’t store data locally from the start. The paradigm that more SSD is better is obsolete for me. I’m not going to suck up 128G.
- Not initially obvious, the Dell keyboard deck is made from an excellent composite. Water beads up on it, great for sneezes and general hygiene. Easier to keep clean than the anodized metal Asus top deck.

I'd say the chief consideration for the Dell is the USB-C only connectivity that for the moment, must be dongle/hub adapted to your USB A-B, HDMI peripherals. As these 13.3” offerings get faster and lighter, they have to get thinner. This Dell is the thinnest I’ve seen and too thin to even fit a USB-A port in it. USB-C thin is the tech trajectory so get with the program.

So my wireless mouse here is hanging off an adapter dongle. Who among typical users even have a USB-C Thunderbolt device to plug in? The Thunderbolt 3 Type-C ports run at a blazing 40Gb/s transfer rate and support full 4K TV and more … for now, you will need to buy an adapter hub to plug your HDMI, and various collections of USB A and B peripherals. The Dell is significantly ahead of the market here. On the plus side, it’s been a while since I’ve had to do some uncharted pathfinding and the USB-C, Thunderbolt 3 connectivity is going to be interesting for me.

The bottom line … if I need a day with the best display and no mini-mouse, I’ll take this Dell. If I need to be flexibly capable for connecting HDMI and USB A/B on the fly, I’m going to use the Asus. If the newest Asus display stepped up to this Dell performance level, it would be a toss-up. For now, 95% of my ‘joy!’ is in the display and sound quality. The 5% negative includes the nose-hole-cam and its incompatibility with an adult video conference.

Overall very impressive, excellent value for money. Kudo's to the Dell team for this CES 2018 winner!

I had been shopping for a replacement to my >7-year-old Proxima DLP projector in our home theatre. I have out spent the projectors price in bulb replacements. Two bulbs had blown up and smoked the optics. The image had deteriorated to the point that my large theatre room was being abandoned by the family.

The projector is integrated with a professional screen 120" screen and a Denon AVR driving a 7.1 sound system. The AVR solves compatibility issues. Inputs include DVD, satellite, streaming computers and games. Theatre lighting is sophisticated. There are no windows in the theatre. The objective for this Epson 355 was to plug and play replace the Proxima DLP.

This Epson 355 is in a curious competitive space. It’s >$100 more expensive than I would pay for a business projector and a couple hundred less than comparable labeled “Home Theatre” projectors. Its in a sort of demand 'dead' zone that seemed best value for money.

Decision factors for me included price, tech specs (brightness being #1) and integration compatibility. This projector has a 720p resolution. The focal distance is about 18" shorter than the DLP it replaces on a 120" screen.

The installation was simple and more rewarding than weaseling a blown-up bulb replacement. I’m very satisfied with the Epson 355 contrast, color and brightness performance.

It's a game changer over the DLP.

These arrived as a pleasant surprise fitting better than any others right out of the box You get plenty of ear fit accessories to experiment with for the right hold and fit. Finding the right headphone fit for the hard cardio workout has been  continuous search. These are superb. Sound quality is excellent.

First, getting the ear fit right is awkward. None of the earfits really secure them well. These are bigger than ‘buds’. When you have them fitted to your ear in a least worse choice sort of way, the fidelity and most especially the bass is fantastic … as good as I’ve ever heard from such a compact package. But … they are too big/heavy for use on the treadmill. I can’t keep them in my skull.

For non-workout use, these are likely the best full fidelity you’ll find. The ‘earbud for workout’ application just isn’t working for me. If you’re not looking for active wear, these are really superb commuter 'super-buds'
I'm not sure how you can get a better sound out of set earbuds. These are used on iPhone 5. Compared to the Apple buds, there is simply not a comparability in comfort and sound quality.

This replacement is a perfect plug and play compatible match for the Mitsubishi model WD-65831 DLP.

DLP's require that the owner anticipates bulb replacement. Our WD-65831 requires a new projector bulb about every year. If you own a DLP, you will need to plan on a replacement bulb just like one anticipates the burned out bulb in an office projector. Keep an extra in reserve. If you notice that the image starts to dim on the TV, bulb replacement is near. The bulbs can also suddenly blowout with a high voltage arc contained within the fire proof housing. The lamp for large format DLP's demands significant voltage. You should note that the TV has a power kill switch built into the access plate to insure the plate is replaced before the bulb can be energized.

Bulb module replacement has been a nightmare for this Mitsubishi model. There is the slightest difference in the mechanical mating of a replacement module to TV among advertised/specified replacements. Several replacements are advertised as a fit for this model but none have connected until this replacement. Prior to this unit, I had found no housing replacement fit at all ... 4 bulbs expired in the original housing. This one curiously has a red paint dot highlighting the fit key. I've previously had to transfer the bulb to the original housing on every occasion and it is patience wracking requires a third hand.

This replacement works!

... now it's time to get a 65" LCD

7/22/2011 Update:

It died after 31 days. Peculiar. DOA I might understand. Burn out after infant mortality is rare. The bulb was an Osram. Amazon made good on the return.

12/14/2011 Update:

The TV has always been prone to bulb blow after brown-outs with transient spikes that degrade the 850w filament. I have high $$$ voltage protection but no APU able to sustain the TV's current draw. I've replaced at least 5-6 bulbs and suspected that sooner or later a catastrophic blow-up would blow glass through the internal fan and optics. That's exactly what happened this time. I've declared Mitsubishi 65" DLP dead. I'm done with this early generation 'big screen' technology. The LCD/LED/Plasma options for a true 65" replacement that I built the hole around is problematic with the new external sizes. The 60" class is too small, the 70" class is too big for now.

I needed a smaller, fast laptop for many reasons to include practical airplane use and general portability. The 15"+ inch size is no longer usable given the seating squeeze on airplanes. I shopped the 13" i5 processor touchscreens (HP, Toshiba, Fujitsu, etc). I thought the HP was `dull' except for the flip display (on more thought, the pivot mechanism looked like a fragile link and to easy to break), Fujitsu was the best but $500 premium was excessive (apparently it's the last laptop built in Japan rather than China). This Toshiba was about right. There are many tradeoffs to consider.

Toshiba good:
I use the touch screen as a mobile cognitive `whiteboard' for sketching and retaining client discussion. Don't waste $ if you don't need a touchscreen. The touchscreen overlay does reduce image quality.

DDR memory is easily user expanded (unusual for a laptop)

Win score is 4.7 out of the box ... far more than I'd think a typical user would need. Expanding memory should push it >5.0. Beyond that, you'd need a zippy video card.

The unit runs on about 25w in battery mode ... won't set your pants on fire.

The optical drive is internal ... no flimsy tray to slide out and take space, just a slot ... excellent! No other 13.3" has this feature that I looked at.

Toshiba has done the best industrial design job ... it has the best look and feel among the units I was looking at

Up for debate:
2 reviewers have problems with the "flimsy" keyboard and I had a similar first take. I would now couch this element a user preference. Personally, the design parameter, cushioned keyboard works better for my typing style after I've had some time on it. I now prefer it over the ridged keyboards. The Toshiba keyboard is a design element and not a flaw or cheapening. As a 'buyer beware' among the smaller format laptops, keyboard compatibility with the user should be the #1 user consideration. You really need to try before you buy. The Toshiba keyboard does not double and triple up key functions to compensate for the smaller space as others are trying. There is no keyboard 'standardization" in this smaller format. Every manufacturer has a different keyboard configuration.

Don't likes:
The `laptops for idiots' bloatware overhead has to go as soon as you're comfortable. This is not unique to Toshiba. There are 40-50 unnecessary overhead programs that slow startup significantly. They are easily disabled to speed the startup cycle.

Battery life is unusually short at less then 3 hours in full operation. The i5 power wattage consumption vs battery tradeoff should be considered. I've been adjusting power schemes with not much success. For trans con flites you may want to carry an extra pack.

Unexpected delight! = Backlighted keyboard means no ambient light required to work in the dark. I've never seen this attribute before.

I'm 5 star happy ... the price is fluctuating up and down between $400-500. A buyer needs to watch the pricing.

The camera is $[..]for gosh sakes! It's an amazing little piece of technology. The 3X optics and 12.2MP CMOS camera are well matched in the optical train to provide a great image for casual photos adequate for most users. It's the simplest start-up I've ever seen. The viewer LCD provides a maximum size to the package. `The manual' is 7 steps of which 4 include inserting memory, battery, charging battery and turning it on. It's `point and shoot' in the extreme.

I work in the domain of optics & imaging design. My wife has a 5 year old Fuji camera of this same genre that I've gone to some lengths to compare with Nikon and Canon in this low cost market. Without getting technical ... for the old Fuji, there are no user discernable image quality differences. The Fuji optics were superior (i.e. best objective lens light capture and transfer). Take your pick between the 3 on the backend image processing system/PC interface.

My wife has carried the 5 year old Fuji in her purse every day ... that's a technically demanding reliability challenge. Fuji can be relied on to deliver the best value for money in an image capture platform if you're designing a million dollar platform or this $69 platform. You're not paying the premium for the huge advertisement budget of Nikon and Canon when you buy Fuji. I think you just get a better camera.

I can't speak to this unit's reliability for now. A 3x optical train with autofocus, f-stop, etc mechanisms and micro motors are robust to a point. They will all fail, even the highest dollar product, if exposed to the wrong environment (g-shock, sand, salt spray, thermal shock, etc).

One reviewer mentioned software loading problems. I had absolutely no problems on a Windows 7, 64bit OS.

You can't go wrong with this device. It's an excellent camera for you or the kids or the g-kids for Xmas.

Unboxing these was a bit fiddly, with layers of boxing woven though each other and stuck together with stickers. Still easier to deal with than clamshell, and seems recyclable and compact, with one nice little box that would've been reusable if it didn't have a big tab sticking out the top. The only instructions are to put them on and connect via bluetooth, though there is a QR code that takes you to online instructions.

The earbud case is small and smooth, with a button to open. if it were magnetically closed it would be a lot harder to get a grip to open it. The earbuds within are easy to get in and out, which is refreshing. I like the magnetic holding on other brands, like Jabra, my personal favorite, but they can be hard to get out and come out suddenly, which just ends with you tossing them under the oven or something.

Bluetooth connecting was smooth. I like to try all the weird new earbud designs, and I was intrigued by the donut shape of these. They're relatively easy to put on and are labeled with L and R. They don't have a snug fit, but instead just rest in the ear in a way that seems secure. There are some rubber bandy things that adjust the fit to several different sizes.

With the hollow center and more casual fit, these don't have a really immersive and deep sound experience, and they lack more advanced features like noise cancellation. On the other hand, they don't leave you with sore sweaty ears, and it's hard to beat a hole through the center for effective hear-through.

Sound is good as expected, though less immersive. Controls are minimalist, with no buttons and a double tap as the "do something" default for near every function.

They're a good set of earbuds for someone who finds most earbuds too obtrusive.

I've tried several earbuds from Jabra now, as well as several from most of the major brands, and jabra is consistently my favorite.

Unboxing wasn't especially exciting. Minimalist, but well designed paper packaging with a sheet of quick start instructions that could really use a QR code to save us the trouble of searching for the app and trying to make sure we found the right one.

Getting to the earbud case itself, it's lower and wider than the previous generation earbuds I've tried from them. Opening it up was a treat. The earbuds and whole interior look like some kind of stealth technology. So matte black they absorb light. Pulling them out of the case lights up some tiny LEDs to confirm they are on and battery status. They're coated with something slightly grippy, and although they are held in magnetically, they didn't come out suddenly and make me toss them across the floor like my previous pair. They're a bit smaller and better fitting than the already excellent 85t.

Putting them in, they're quite comfortable. A really good size and fit. Immediately a voice assistant will talk you through pairing, which went smoothly. After locating and installing the app, it alerted me to a firmware update. It took a few minutes, but was as simple as waiting for it to finish while keeping the product near and on. Flashing LEDs keep you apprised of progress. The app has instructions and additional options.

Sound on these is great! I think these are going to be my new favorite earbuds. I've tried the Pro version as well, but I like these better. The Pro seems to just switch out the grippy stealth finish for some improved wind resistance on calls, so usage counts.

Controls are easy and intuitive. A clickable button instead of gesture control, so you can tell what you're doing, and don't trigger it every time you brush the hair away from your ear. They're my favorite way to talk on a cellphone too. Nice to have both hands free.

This arrived well packaged and without issues. I've tried out several major brand soundbars in recent years, and I've yet to find any that are as good as the Sonys, at least as a television speaker. I've already got an A7000 that I'm familiar with to compare this A5000 with. It's a step down in price and feature set, but there's more to the differences than that.

The A7000 has cloth speaker covers on top, while this A5000 has plastic. It's my impression that the sound is a bit better out of the cloth, since it provides less of a reflective barrier, but it's also hard to keep clean and safe. Being on top of the speaker facing up, it's right where something can get pur or dropped on it, or a cat walking across it. The hard plastic seems much more resilient. It's also hard to tell on the sound, because the A5000 has two fewer speakers.

The top of this speaker is a textured plastic, like a car's dashboard. Not super fancy, but resilient. The A7000 has very shiny black plastic, which looks very nice and is easy to clean, but also lacks resilience and shows dust more readily.

The remote is infrared, so you need to have line of sight to the speaker for it to work, but it's full featured, even having buttons to control optional additional speakers. which I really appreciate.

The instruction book is pretty good. Setup is easy, especially if you connect it to a television. It'll put the menus right up on the screen. It's really built to be a television speaker with bluetooth and other inputs so it can be used for other things as a secondary purpose.

I'm still trying to figure out what I can do with the Chromecast feature that seems to be present in the speaker, but not in the television. So far I haven't had much luck connecting with Chromecast.

I definitely like the A7000 better, but there's a solid price difference. I love having a second HDMI input, since the way they've got these things set up, it outputs to my Sony television rather than the other way around, so I need to plug in extra devices to the soundbar, not the television, which makes it a weird decision to put so many more ports on the television than the speaker.

Great speaker, but still plenty of things that could be improved in a future version, like more satellite speaker compatibility, some kind of port passthrough from television, chromecast video, etc.

I have quite an assortment of earbuds, and like them for different reasons. My normal fave are a Bose set that has kind of a bigger capsule shaped part and then they fit right into your ear. But, for those of us with small ears, even a well designed set like those can begin to make my ears feel tired after a couple hours.

When those make my ears tired and I still want to be listening, I pop these on. The fit is SO different from any other earbuds I own that they are a perfect alternative for when traditional buds make my ears tired. They are interesting to get on the first time, but kind of brilliant after you get the hang of it. By the time these begin to get uncomfortable, the others feel good again.

The sound quality is not as good as my other Bose buds, but is still better than most brands by a long shot.

I appreciate the innovation a lot. They fit well and stay on.

This product feels different to me than other Sony stuff I've gotten. It's like they've gone out of their way to make everything feel like cardboard. The packaging was like egg carton, and the earbuds and their charging station are a rough lightweight material in a drab color. The earbuds themselves are customizable, but bulky compared to the competition. I find them hard to get out of the container, hard to hold onto, and hard to wear. The noise cancellation and sound are both above average though. I like the charging light on the container. It communicates with color and flashes what the status of the product is, and isn't bright or hard to locate.

USB-C charging makes the base station charge up nice and fast. It holds the earbuds securely, and doesn't rattle or fall open. It's also a nice pocketable size and shape with no sharp corners, making the whole product especially portable. Controls are gesture, rather than button. I'm not a fan of this because I end up doing a lot of swiping and hoping. A click button interface, I can just click it the number of times I know will do what I need, and move on.

I've got a few Sony audio products that I use every day and am very happy with, but with earbuds, I'm sticking with jabra for now. It's a competitive market right now for earbuds. Lots of companies putting out new designs.

Unboxing: This was thoughtfully packaged. The packing materials are egg crate style, but made out of much higher grade stuff. It's solid enough that I doubt there will be any shipping problems even if the box is abused. Everything fits in snugly with no rattle. When you pull something out, and the easy way seems to be to flip the box over and slide it out, it comes out right side up. It's like they unboxed it a few times and adjusted to make it a better experience. It seems obvious that this is the way to do it, but I rarely see it.

There's some thought in cord management for the subwoofer. It's bluetooth, so the signal is wireless. No buttons or switches on it that I've noticed. The cord plugs into the underside and there are channels cut into it to pick which direction the cord comes out. Electrical plugs are angled. Transformer is on the cord, so it doesn't take up huge outlet space. The sound is good for its size, but doesn't match what I'm getting from a subwoofer half its price and twice its size.

The components themselves feel like high quality. Heavy, and with buttons and lights hidden behind speaker fabric. The center speaker has plastic holes on the top for the top facing speakers. I'm not sure how these will do after a couple years of dust.

Instructions are lousy. Pages of legal nonsense and barely enough information to get started, much less figure out how to configure preferences. It managed to sync itself together and play audio just fine, but even the remote just has "universal" symbols for I don't know what. Pushing them does result in an announce voice telling you what you've done. It seems they're for choosing audio source, some presets, and volume. I can't figure out something like how to adjust the relative volume between center and subwoofer, for example, so I guess I just have to hope my source can do that. A lot of devices these days put everything in the app, so I went to check it out. No mention of it on the page here. No mention on the product. First page of the instructions has a QR code that leads to the LG home page (eyeroll). As of now, the product does not appear on their site. Farther down in the instructions is it mentions an app name, which I had to go search for myself.

After connecting to the speaker via the app and bluetooth, I was able to download and install an update to the device. The app has some more features and adjustments, but it does need to be connected via bluetooth, and has no real way to test what you change, so you have to switch the speaker back to your other audio source to see what changed.

Sound is good, but better at low to mid volume. It sounds a little small and localized at higher volume. In its defense, it is small and localized, but whatever tricks it uses to sound surroundy fall off.

I've been waiting for a while for someone to figure out how to do wireless speaker components. I'd like to be able to connect a couple of other good speakers I have around the house wirelessly into this system, but I haven't seen much in the way of cross platform connectivity from anyone yet. Overall, this seems like a nice speaker set for someone with limited space. It's good quality and sounds bigger than it is.

Unboxing: Wouldn't usually make a section of this, but every once in a while a product makes it a pleasure. Especially a weird one like this. It's like unboxing a little UFO. It starts out in something like a hat box with a couple sticky tabs of tape to remove. Wish they could have found a better closure method, but the box is nice. Inside that you're immediately presented with the odd looking earbuds and a starter guide (also round) that has you immediately trying them on and fitting the best sleeve size for in your ear. There are no extra sleeves obviously apparent, so time to dig deeper. Next up is the UFO. A large earbud like this needs a large charging case. This one is round and unzips like some of the nicer headphone cases, but it's also a hard case with lights and buttons. Nothing inside but a charging dock. Under it is a secret compartment (made less secret by the thumb holes for easy removal). At the bottom of the hat box we have our missing sleeves and a charging cord.

Even with a diagram, putting these on was confusing and took four tries. Once they're on though, they are quite comfortable, and I think I'll learn to put them on after a few more tries.

Back to the book, and ugh! now they're telling me to put them in the charging case to pair. But I just finally got them on! &*^@#!

Ok, after getting things paired and back on, I'm able to put them through some testing. I'm not really an audiophile, but I've tried a lot of earbuds. Comfort is good. They don't rely on being stuck in your ear to hold themselves up, so there isn't a high stress point that's going to get sore first. They sound good. Better than most, but not the best I've heard. The control button is on the back of your ear, and I find it awkward and unreliable. Noise cancellation is solid, but like every other one I've tried, it is hard to tell sometimes because it scales with volume. Turning them on in a noisy room doesn't result in a quiet room, but turning up what you are listening to will result in noise other than what you are listening to disappearing quite a lot. There is a passthrough mode if you need to hear what's going on around you, but it doesn't sound very nice.

I like that it's USB-C. No more having to turn the cord over three times to figure out which end is up, and much faster charging. The case has three lights to show you charge progress for the case Each one represents enough charge for one full use of the earbuds. There's also a light on the top to tell you whether the earbuds are charged yet.

It's a solid product. Not my top favorite, but definitely innovative and a competitive offering.

These are overall perfectly okay earbuds, but they certainly don't outcompete some of the similar ones on the market.

I have a set of Bose earbuds, and a Jabra set that I like better.

When I think about beats studio buds, I think about sound quality, and particularly I think about Dr. Dre, and playing some music with a thumping beat. Well, the sound quality on this was not great for listening to music. It's perfectly fine for a podcast, but music felt muted and unexciting through these.

The noise cancellation did work well, so I was impressed with that. And they are very comfortable to wear.

But another thing he didn't really care for with these was that there is no instructions, and there's no way to pair these with my phone without downloading their app. I really don't always want to be forced into using their dedicated app. I appreciate that the app has some settings that are very useful, but I would prefer that be an option rather than a requirement.

They did a quality job on these. Luxury without excess. Packaging is acceptable. The case feels great, the zipper is awesome. The headphones fit in very easily, and there is a mesh pouch inside for accessories.

The headphones have a giant L and R printed on the interior foam, which is convenient to figure out which way to put them on, but isn't visible once they are. The buttons are easy to access, labeled, and simple enough to remember.

Bluetooth was easy to connect and had audio cues.

I'm usually not a fan of gesture controls, but they work really smoothly and intuitively here.

The product itself feels high quality, and they're very comfortable and secure. Noise cancellation is fine, and a nice addition, but I don't find it notable. What was more impressive to me was just how little I noticed the usual irritations of wearing headphones. They don't have a background noise at all, they don't feel like they're going to fall off if I bend over or make a sudden move, they don't press uncomfortably, and they don't make noise when I turn my head.

I've tried a few modern wireless noise cancelling headphones, and I'd say some of the others win in one feature or another, but these are an excellent complete package.

I'm not an audiophile, but I've tried out a good number of different earbud brands lately, all across the quality spectrum. I'm grading on a curve here.

Packaging is sufficient. A few tip sizes, quick start, instructions, and whatever is in that other manual of junk I always throw away. The earbud case is lozenge shaped and pocketable enough. No external lights, which is nice if you're charging it next to your bed, but not so much if you want to know their charge status.

They are supposed to immediately start trying to bluetooth pair with something when first opened, and appeared to be trying to do so. My Surface was unable to locate them. I even tried with a second Surface. I plugged in the case and left it to charge for 15 minutes, and then they paired fine. Overall on unboxing and setup, I'd say they're adequate, but far from exceptional.

The earbuds themselves are aggressively visible. I assume they're trying to ride the I-Pod branding success, but I'm not really feeling it. Despite looking huge, they don't feel huge. They are lightweight and comfortable. They don't feel like they are going to fall out, despite not feeling like they're crammed in the ear. Fit is unusual in that you can turn the earbud like a screw to make it tighter or looser. Sound is good. I'm giving them very low marks for appearance, and very good for fit and sound.

These use swipe style controls, which I despise. I much prefer a physical button that I can just feel that I've clicked. The controls do work as advertised, but there's enough delay that it often takes me a while of swiping my ear and waiting until it gets the message. Mostly irritating when someone tries to talk to me and I can't get it to pause for several seconds.

Range is average.

Overall, Id' say there's a bit of a brand name premium on the price compared to some other products, and I'm saying that as someone who has used Surface products as my primary computers for many years now, but they're not bad. I've definitely tried more expensive earbuds that weren't as good, but of what I've tried, I'm happiest so far with the Jabra Elite series of earbuds.

The downside on this pillow tablet stand is that it doesn't fold flat and store easily. Aside from this obvious issue which really can't be solved on a pillowy tablet stand, this thing is perfect. It is exactly what I was hoping for. I frequently use my surface tablet on the floor, and have found that the hard stands don't have the right angle that I like, frequently collapsed into my carpet, and just feel uncomfortable and cold.

This one by contrast has a beautiful firmness to it, an ideal angle for me, a little lip at the bottom to keep it from flopping over, and everything is exactly what I want in a tablet stand. I'm really delighted with it and anticipate picking more up for my children in time.

This TV made it really easy to sign into my Amazon prime, Netflix, and other online TV accounts. Like many people, we don't just sit around watching TV, we go to a show that we want to watch and the episode we want to view, and we just look at that. This TV made it very straightforward to do that.

It shipped well protected in a box and arrived functional and looking sharp. My husband found it easy to get everything set up, and the picture quality was crisp and clear, and the sound quality was very good. Our other TV is a nicer one from about eight years ago, but this newer one has picture quality and sound quality to rival it, given the increases in technology.

Overall I'm really impressed with this TV and how simple it was to use out of the box, and how nice the quality is overall.

This really added an extra level of fun to our river day recently. As a homeschooling family, we try to get out and about and have adventures that naturally lead to teachable moments, or just moments that inspire curiosity. This surface drone, controllable by our cell phone, was a lot of fun!

This thing is great! The instructions are sparse, so it took a bit of trial and error to figure out what needs to happen. The battery needs to go into the compartment, then have the two sides of it lifted up to go farther in, which is counterintuitive. It looks like those should be raised as handles to pull it out. The battery has an on button as well as the device.

The phone app uses the boat like a wifi host. Registration was just an email address and verification code. The app, like the instructions, is simple and universal symbol heavy, so it takes a while to figure out what you're supposed to swipe where to get everything running. The app defaults to a different device, and doesn't make it very clear that there's a second page you can swipe to to get to this one. When it says swipe right to unlock the device, it means move the little center ball on the screen over to the unlock icon to the right, not just swipe right on the screen.

Once it's all connected and in the water though, it's responsive and competent. I took it to the river and zoomed around on manual. I switched it to underwater photography mode, and it slowed down to a sedate enough pace that I could actually see and control where I was taking pictures, and they came out very nice. Note that this thing doesn't dive, it just zooms around like a boat with a camera that can be adjusted to above or below the water.

Putting it in AI mode and setting waypoints was impressive. I immediately saw a very clear and detailed view from above that looked more like it was taken from a helicopter than a satellite. I was able to set waypoints, and then it very quickly zoomed through them. I get the feeling the accuracy is only within ten feet or so, and it really moves, so be careful with this or the auto-return that it doesn't just slam into something nearby if it's within the margin of error. At one point I grounded it with the auto-return and it didn't quit.

Not a bad product. Most of my complaints are in the instruction clarity department, which is pretty minor once you get things figured out.

Overall it is a fun new toy and will be great to have one more adventurous thing to bring when we hit the river this summer.

I really love this speaker. I already have two sets of Bose earbuds, so I already had the Bose app downloaded to my phone. It was easy to pair and didn't have any issues getting set up. I don't control it through the app, I just control it through the buttons on the speaker itself or just by turning the music on my phone on or off.

I wanted a simple speaker that I didn't need to worry too much about so that I could listen to podcasts and music in the shower, or when working in my vegetable greenhouse this summer. So far it's been great! The battery life has been longer than expected, the sound quality is absolutely amazing for listening to music and has great bass, not any kind of tinny sound at all, and the unit itself seems thoughtfully designed and built to last. It's got a nice weight to it and doesn't want to tip over.

I really appreciate after having a bunch of Chinese made brands in the past, that this one is just straight up quality, everything works, it's easy to deal with, etc.

I haven't truly tested the water resistant capability of it, but after two weeks of showering with it just outside the shower and bringing it into the sometimes drippy or humid greenhouse, it still doing great.

Overall the Bose quality shines through in this item and I've been really thrilled with it for my purposes.

The box took a big gouge in shipping (in just the original TV box), but the TV was fine, so packaging is probably adequate. Unboxing was easy and there was just a bit of styrofoam and minimal cardboard. Be careful with removing the television from the box, because these things are getting thin enough to be bent under their own weight.

It mounted fine on my old wall mount, but required a different screw size. The screws from my previous setup were the wrong size, so you might want to check what you've got and order some so you don't have to wait around.

There isn't much thought put into cable management, so you'll have to come up with your own solution if you don't want cords visible. Power cord is in the lower right quadrant. Most of the other cords are in the lower left, as is a well hidden power button on the back left. The instructions are minimal. I tried hooking my receiver in as instructed to use the television speaker in place of my old center speaker, but it wouldn't work. It may have just been a clash of brands and standards, because every time I tried to switch to using the TV speakers in the options, it would shut off my Pioneer receiver instead. I ended up using the other speaker input, which did work. I can't believe we're in the 2020's and still cramming bare wires in as audio input. I've got a drawer full of various audio cables here.

Turning it on, I was greeted with setup options. The remote seems high quality, but I wish it had some air-remote functionality. Navigating menus with buttons can get a bit confusing. After getting it hooked up to wifi, I was off to YouTube to find something to make sure it was working right before I hooked everything else up. One of those HD coral reef relaxation videos was just the thing. The picture is vibrant! Bright and colorful. The bezels aren't small enough to tile these together, but are very small. My kids wouldn't let me change the video for hours. They just sat and watched the fish. I'm susceptible to the whine some televisions put out, and I've heard none of that. Worked great for video games, though I didn't try anything especially high end. Worked well for computer output. With the exception of that one audio jack compatibility issue, and the different sized screws, everything has worked as expected.

The screen is a speaker, like a modern smartphone. Sound is good, especially at frequencies you would hear from a center speaker. I definitely still wanted my subwoofer and side speakers to round things out, but it's really nice to have the voices from the television coming from where the faces are, not from some speaker below the television.

I don't have a different brand of 2021 television to compare it to, but my impression is that there is a bit of a premium for the brand name, but it's a very nice product. This was certainly an upgrade for me. A lot of progress has been made in the 8 years since I last upgraded.

I had to try this when I saw it. It's a bit like a large sci-fi candle/speaker hybrid. The sound from it, especially in the mid range, is excellent. I like that I can put it on the table at dinner and listen to something, and it seems to add to the experience rather than detract. Voices from a good audio source are good enough to fool someone into thinking someone is there. I'm not at all convinced that their claims about how it works are true. They say the main glass cylinder carries the vibration, but I can't feel it, nor does holding it change the sound detectably. I suspect the convex glass in the middle might be doing something like that.

There are two separate sets of controls simply marked with a + and -. One of them controls the volume, and the other the brightness. Good luck guessing which is which.

It's novel, gimmicky, functional, and arguably elegant.

I have been using this line of mouse from Logitech for many years, going from the original, to number two, and now picking up this compact mouse for my laptop. It is incredibly responsive and is the only mouse I've had any success with for doing CAD work because it is responsive enough to small motions to really do good detail work.

This one is comfortable and ambidextrous. When I'm not using it, often my seven-year-old does for his homeschooling. It works great and we've experienced zero connectivity problems. The battery life seems to be about a week of very active use, or longer if used less frequently. I just plug it in every Saturday and we haven't experienced any issues.

A solid heavy speaker. I really appreciate having a bluetooth capable speaker that is both high quality and plug-in rather than battery. The sound is excellent for music and action-packed television shows, and it has a few corded input options on the back. Setup and connecting was super easy. I didn't get much use out of the app, but maybe it makes more sense with more products of the same brand.

I put it at the back of my living room, which I realize isn't really what it's for, but I wanted to be able to have a speaker back there without having to run cords, and it works fine. The market seems to have gone from 7.2 surround with lots of crummy speakers and cords to all in one center bars. I'm hoping the bluetooth thing will catch on enough that it'll be easy to get and set up decent speakers wherever convenient and let the software figure out where they are.

These are definitely a quality product. I don't think they outperform some of the competitors. They feel really solid. Range is decent. A bit large and heavy. The noise cancelling is just barely worth turning on.

They come with several options for improving fit. I settled on some of the bigger flappy looking parts as being very comfortable. Unfortunately, after wrestling them onto the earbuds, I found that the lid is no longer even close to closing on the charging case. I'd call it an inexcusable design oversight. Lots of tuning options in the app.

Compared to other earbuds I've tried, they sound better and are much heavier than much less expensive brands, but I'm not sure it's worth it. At similar price points, I've tried two other brands. One was even bigger, but sounded amazing (Bose), and the other I found to be superior in nearly every way.

My family has tested out numerous noise canceling earbuds in the last six months, looking for the best ones to fit each member of our household. This set of earbuds was the universal favorite among every member of our family.

For one, the noise cancellation feature is absolutely the most effective noise cancellation we have found on earbuds. Even having it on silent, I was unable to discern individual words from my mom reading loudly to my two noisy children in the other room. With an audiobook playing, I really didn't notice anybody else being in the house, though I could hear them if I thought about it. With music, it was like they weren't there, someone can stand right next to me and talk to me and I can be blissfully unaware.

If you get overloaded from auditory stimulation easily and just need the world to stop making so much noise every so often, these are the earbuds to get.

The sound quality is extraordinarily good on audiobooks, rap music, metal music, and more peaceful and soothing ballads and classical. The base was not overwhelming, nor did the treble get screechy.

It fit my very small ears well, and fit my husband's ears well also, he has a much bigger ear canal size.

The one thing that we have both noticed is that these are also heavier than most of our other earbuds, however even with my ears feeling rather sensitive, it really didn't bother me because they are weighted nicely and fit so well.

Overall, while these could be improved by being slightly smaller and less heavy, these still beat out five other well-known brands in our household for both the noise cancellation and in audio quality.

I needed a little work laptop for running my CAD software. A previous laptop was not up to the task, but this one handled my program as smoothly as my desktop with only very occasional brief lags when I ask it to do something complicated.

When looking at a budget laptop, there will always be some tradeoff, and with this, it has great performance, a beautiful crisp screen with good color, runs quietly, and everything just WORKS. But, no touchscreen. I am used to all of my devices nowadays having that and it took some adjusting to remember just to mouse or touchpad. However, for what I needed to use it for, it is perfect.

Overall I am really pleased that it doesn't feel like it is overheating, the battery life is surprisingly good, and overall I have not run into the edges of the performance of this machine much. Feels robustly built.

I've got a couple of Jabra products, and they impress me with their quality and attention to detail.

It starts at packaging. They come nicely packaged, but not excessively so. Packaging is recycled, and walks you through unboxing and functionality. There is a nice zippered case that the headphones fold up into. The button layout isn't bad, but could use just a bit more labeling on things like the volume buttons. They aren't entirely intuitive, with a column of three buttons, the top and bottoms being volume, while the middle is used for something else.

The headphones are a little smaller and lighter than I expected, but are still made of very nice materials. They have the feeling of a luxury item. Pairing was easy, and if you install the app, it will update firmware for you, walk you through all the functionality and allow you to set button and behavior options.

I keep expecting active noise cancellation in a modern, high end product like this to really silence the background. I'd say it does if you are already listening to something with a little volume, but it doesn't really 100% silence the background if you just want to silence the world and have some quiet. That said, it takes things down about 10 notches, which is enough to stop auditory overload if, like me, you are sensitive to having multiple streams of auditory input coming at you at once. After trying about five different noise canceling products in the last six months trying to find the best one, this definitely wins on the noise canceling front.

These headphones are optimized toward things like answering calls, but are very good for other uses as well. That said, I have a pair of Jabra's ANC earbuds, and I actually prefer them to these for near everything. They're smaller, less obtrusive, sound nearly as good, and are actually more comfortable.

Whoever designed the packaging for this had some fun with it. Opening it all is an interesting experience, in a good way. On the box, it says "thoughtfully designed, purposely engineered, expertly built" I think for the most part, they live up to it. Something tells me they pay their product designers well.

As usual for earbuds, they're hard to pry out of the magnetic case. The case does have a charging light on the front. It's so tiny, you probably won't see it until you plug it in. It's bright despite being the size of a grain of sand. Easy to see, which is nice. Easy to cover if it's by your bed. The case is small, smooth, and well built. More pocket size than most such charging cases.

I tried on the earbuds and the fit is ideal for me, and I've tried about seven brands. As soon as I put them in, they started giving me instructions on how to pair them.

I was irritated to find that the instructions tell me to install an app to get further instructions and functionality. This is typically where things fail, and I was primarily wanting these for a Windows tablet, not my phone, but I gave it a shot. The app does indeed give further instructions on how to use them, and also updated the firmware with no fuss the second time I opened it, complete with flashing purple LED on the case. The app also has a bunch of adjustments to the level of noise cancellation, equalizers, many soundscapes, like rain and pink noise, that work well with the cancellation to block out the world. The button functions can also be rearranged, which is nice because every brand seems to be different, and it's nice to be able to switch it to something personally intuitive.

I ended up connecting them to both my tablet and my phone, and now when I put them on, they say, "two devices connected" If I'm playing audio on my tablet, and then pause it and play audio on my phone, it seamlessly plays whichever is running, though not both at once. I like that I should be able to listen to my tablet and then take an incoming call. I'm not an audiophile, but the sound quality seems excellent to me. I've tried a couple expensive brands with noise cancellation, and it's interesting. It doesn't remove background noise very effectively, but it does a bit. I think it's more that when it's turned off, they use the mic to pump in outside audio so it's almost like you aren't wearing them. Neither mode is especially effective, so I wouldn't buy them for that specifically, but It's a small benefit. It's best suited for making your audio your focus or your situational awareness your focus.

I tried them on a call and it went well. My first time using earbuds for a phone call, and I have no complaints.

Definitely my new favorite earbuds, and I've got pricier ones. So far price has had little impact on my earbud opinions, mostly because design is still so much more variable and important than quality. I've only got two notable criticisms. One, every set I try is harder than the last to pry out of the case. Magnets are great. So is a sleek look to everything. Give us a divot in the case where we can get a finger under the edge. The other problem is range. Range is average, but when I tried walking out of range, instead of announcing the problem and handling it, they just cut out and turned off. I had to actually put them back in the case before they would go back to playing.

Overall, even with a few minor quibbles, these have become my new favorite earbuds, after having about seven (from good brands) in my family's stash to try. They fit well, audio quality is very good, the app actually functions and they are just a very solid, comfortable offering.

As far as I can tell, this laptop functions as intended, but I'm finding using it to be a moderately unpleasant experience. At this price, it's not unexpected, but I'm having trouble figuring out an optimal use for it.

The version of Windows (S mode) it uses, won't install most software. You can only install from the Windows store. The best use I can think of for this is that my dad is too old to learn new tricks and could really use a new laptop that functions better than his ancient one, and can't install malware.

The problem is, people who aren't good with computers generally just want to buy a cheap one because they figure they won't use it much. It's self fulfilling. They aren't generally a pleasure to use. In this case, it doesn't have a touchscreen. These days, anyone who isn't between the age of 30 and 50 is probably pushing on their screen when you tell them to click something.

It includes a full tenkey on the keyboard. I would usually like that. Maybe they just had extra space and figured why not? I can't think of who would need the feature. Everyone I can think of who would want a tenkey would be dealing with either gaming or spreadsheets, and would have a nicer machine. At this point I'm thinking maybe a business that wants to cheaply equip a bunch of employees with something they can't screw with in a way that will be problematic. I think it would work fine for that, so long as there is no non-app software that needs to be installed.

From such a small unit, I did not expect such incredible sound quality. However, I'm extremely impressed with this. In particular, hip-hop and rap music sounds great coming out of it, with the stunning level of base from such a small form factor.

This pairs up easily with my Samsung phone and didn't drop the connection while driving or 6 feet away in the bathroom. I also used it for podcasts and audiobooks while showering, and it worked great for that as well.

Overall I am in love with the simple, space-saving minimalist setup. It is perfect for those of us who, with covid, may need to setup an office in a location not previously meant for an office, because it takes up so little room, is very quiet, and is sized just right in every respect. Strangely, this all-on-one actually takes up LESS room than my old laptop, with a generous screen that is much easier on my neck to work with.

This was very simple to set up. I tried using Cortana with voice controls (the default), and it went really smoothly. I am not very tech-savvy, so that was lovely to find that everything was easy.

The keyboard and mouse are wireless and already paired up so they're ready to go. They seem like they're more suited to a more portable machine. The keyboard isn't bad if you're prioritizing desk space, but the mouse feels flimsy. It's usable, and ambidextrous, but hardly comfortable and the range is poor - I could only geet about four feet away before it didn't work. Since this is a laptop replacement for me (I am tired of hunching over a tiny screen), the range is not much of an issue.

I tried some older games on it like my beloved Portal as well as a kinda ram-heavy CAD program for my work, and they ran smoothly with no issues. Besides the mouse, nothing feels like it was a cheap afterthought.

The screen resolution is more than enough for my needs as a work computer. I don't get a headache, the motion is smooth and not choppy, and the detail is more than enough for my needs. And the touchscreen! It works great! I now find myself trying to touch my other monitor's screen all the time because I have gotten used to the ease of it. It's very intuitive to use.

The keyboard can tuck under the monitor on the base, so if you have a shallow table, it really helps.

This is a great all-in-one and a solid, clean-looking, minimalist/ space-saving option that runs great and works well for most types of work and home entertainment.

Wow this thing is wide. Works great. I recommend reading the instructions before you unpack anything. It can sound like an obvious or easy thing, but I felt like I had to unpack this in the driveway because I wasn't sure I was going to have room inside to deal with it all. It's closer to a couch than a monitor in this respect.

This is about twice the size of any monitor I'd ever unpacked, and the curve presents an interesting challenge. They don't want you to just lay it face down on the floor to deal with assembly, because the arch puts too much stress on the center. The packing materials are designed for this. You can leave it in the foam packing when you remove the box, and it'll hold it steady while you get everything put together and plugged in.

Most of the assembly is for the mount on the back. It's like putting together a Portal gun or something. From the back, it really looks like it was designed by Aperture Science. The main support attachment from monitor to mounting hardware is excellent. Easy to attach, but strongly supportive. After adding some rings and back plates, it's almost ready. There are channels in the stand for cables if you pay attention to the fine print in the instructions before you get too far along (oops).

The most questionable part to me is a plate that goes all across the lower back and covers up the ports. I'm thinking of it as optional. It makes things look nice if you spend a lot of time looking at the wrong side of your monitor, and also never mess with your cords or ports. It's also kind of huge, like the rest of the monitor, so if you aren't using it it presents something of a dilemma whether to keep it around or not.

The swivel mount on the back is really smooth and makes it easy to orient it with a light touch, and it stays put. This is elegant engineering. Getting just the right balance and tension.

We decided to record a sound from a cartoon on this that both makes everybody jump, and makes everybody laugh. When the kids are get a little wild, we pound the button and it seems to distract the kids out of whatever silliness they were engaged in that we didn't approve of. It's also knocked a couple of mild grouchy moods out of people.

We have had in the past a set of four of these that was meant for kids that were very low quality, so to have this one, which is heavyweight, incredibly good quality, re-recordable, and is all done via USB, is amazing. The quality level is absolutely there, and it is something that I expect we will be thrilled to have and use for many years to come.

These are a good value for the price. I've got a competing brand's binoculars that are very similar, cost 25% more, and aren't quite as nice. These Bushnells are clear, bright, and sharp. There might be some color fringe, but if so, it's really small, unlike my others. All the adjustments are firm and smooth, with no rattle. I've got four pairs of binoculars, and these are the first I'd grab on most occasions.

I wanted to listen to some music and audiobooks from my cell phone, and while the included Samsung earbuds were okay, I was hoping for a mild upgrade in both sound quality and style, and these Panasonic ones are great. I have the metallic violet Samsung S9, so this set of earbuds is a similar color tone but a little bit darker, which is great. I like how it color-coordinated, the sound quality is great for listening to pop, dance and rap music, and my audiobooks sound crisp. The earbuds are comfortable and fit well.

These cute little earbuds fit my ears just right, and were perfect for listening to some hip-hop music and then listening to an audiobook from my cell phone. The little microphone picked up a little wind noise, but seemed extremely comparable to the Samsung earbuds that came with my phone in that regard. Everything worked just fine, and pretty much exactly as expected given the price and form factor. This is a nice quality little set of earbuds that is cute and stylish, fits as expected, and has decent sound quality both on the input and the output.

This little set of earphones fits comfortably in my ears and came with a few of the little differently sized cushions so that I could customize my fit. The included microphone worked fine and I didn't hear any complaints from the people I was talking to. And the earbuds themselves had perfectly good quality for listening to some pop music as well as listening to an audiobook.

Overall there were no surprises with these simple wired earbuds. They work great!

I absolutely love this beautiful chrome book. It took some adjusting for me to go from a regular desktop to a chrome book, where everything is done in the cloud, but since I have been using dropbox and other online programs for storage, photo editing, etc., the transition has been overall going smoothly.

The design on this chrome book is incredibly thoughtful. I love that the touchscreen can spin and turn around to lay flat so that I can sit and work with it in a number of positions or different ways. I love the little touchpad, the way the stylus hides right in its little compartment, and everything that I've tried to do has gone smoothly and easily with the amount of computing power here. I've mostly been using this to edit photos and create documents including these photos, and I've also watched a little bit of video online.

The picture quality is exceptional and the responsiveness of the touchscreen has been great, I haven't felt any frustration using it- quite the contrary, everything is gone far smoother and easier than expected, and it just feels like a really high-end machine.

This was an easy plug -and -play item for me. I began by backing up my desktop computer to this, then hooked it to my laptop so that I could access all of my desktop files on my laptop.

I really like the feature where you can charge the laptop through USB-C while accessing files. That's helpful as my laptop does run out of juice relatively fast.

It worked well, worked nearly soundlessly, did not need software to drag and drop files, and overall feels attractive and sturdy.

This is not my only file backup solution, more a convenient way of sharing files from desktop to laptop, and for that it does a nice job. I have experienced no problems and everything has been smoother and faster than expected.

This is such a fun little speaker! The speaker in my truck makes a horrible buzzing noise, so I can't hook my cell phone to it the way I do in my other vehicle, and this little handheld unit really bumps the tunes or my podcast so that I can enjoy rides in my truck. The sound quality is absolutely stunning given the size. It handles everything from radio shows to beat heavy dance music and rap without any distortion or problems, and it gets quite loud. It hooked up to my cell phone via Bluetooth almost immediately and with no problems, and I've now owned it through to cell phones and found it just as easy to use on the second as the first. This is absolutely the best small Bluetooth speaker I've had the pleasure of owning. I had a larger one from Sony about three years ago, and the sound quality on this little unit absolutely beats it.

This is a good sturdy speaker. I like how it has a metal grill over the more delicate parts of the speaker. It prevents accidental damage by my kids and pets, who like to poke claws and curious fingers into our other speakers. The handles built into either end make it way easier to carry, and it has rubber bumpers that allow it to work equally well vertical or on its side. The controls make sense and are easy to use.

The lights are a fun addition, and the option to use the flashy strobe lights is surprisingly fun. I had expected them to be irritating, but turning down my room lights and playing a game of Just Dance with the kids made me wish we had a whole set of flashy speakers. The lights are mesmerizing, more like a lightning storm than a strobe light, and they did a great job programming them to take their cues from the music. There are multiple lighting modes, and they can be turned off.

The only minor complaint I have is the lack of different connector types. It's a big speaker with plenty of space.

Adapters aren't hard to come by, and Bluetooth is a great feature. Connecting a thumb drive full of music was easy and intuitive.

Overall we are thrilled with this addition to our sound system. It sounds great, is easy to set up and doesn't take a techie to do so, and the lights give it an extra boost of fun.

I have a similar monitor from acer that is about 6 years old, it's the exact same size, but the difference between this one and the old acer is night and day. The Acer looks dim, dingy, and yellowed next to this one, and even making side by side adjustments to the two monitors, this Dell really is a huge upgrade in crispness and clarity as well as the trueness of colors.

I like the matte screen and that I don't get reflections on it. And I love the ease of making adjustments to it. I can change the brightness and color tones easily for viewing movies or reading text for a long time. I like the Paper mode of viewing that makes for less eyestrain.

Given the low price and crisp view, I wish I'd upgraded monitors years ago.

I received a sample for review but opinion is my own.

I'm using this for my Surface Pro 3. and I find it adequate. It is tiny and light, but still holds up the Surface. It does multiply the usb port, but if you want to power anything with it, you need to plug it in with to an additional cord. The official docking station for the Surface is very expensive. This is an inexpensive alternative if you just want to be able to dock it at your desk and have enough USB ports for all your peripherals.

This keyboard seemed awfully familiar when I got it. I realized that of all the Bluetooth keyboards I've reviewed, the ZAGG had been the one I'd actually been using for my Surface tablet. The one I'd been using wasn't made for the Surface, but I liked it because i could easily transfer it between devices, it was big enough to type on without feeling cramped, and it had a feature where if you start typing on it while it's asleep, it remembered what you typed and sent it as soon as it awoke and paired, which is a feature strangely absent from many similar devices. I hate how on other keyboards it just skips the first few seconds of what I typed and I have to backtrack.

This keyboard has all the features I liked from my previous ZAGG, but adds a magnetic strip that attaches it to the Surface and allows the keyboard to work as a cover. The key layout is intuitive ans spacious, and the keys have a pleasant texture and resistance and a small click. When the keyboard is closed and used as a cover, it has a texture something between leather and rubber, and will make the Surface sleep when closed and wake when opened. When open, it can either lay flat, or magnet up against the bezel to sit at an angle. Pairing is quick and easy, just a button combo, click it in Bluetooth settings, and then type in a short number sequence.

So far, I'm really impressed with this new way of capturing ideas on paper. While I often use my phone or iPad air to brainstorm, the fact is that my brain just doesn't work as well when tapping things out on a keyboard or using a stylus, as it does when just writing with a simple pen and paper. I also love doing mind maps, but hate the mind map software for entering the information, because it really slows the flow of my thoughts. This is a perfect solution for both.

I began by jotting things down on my to do list for the day, then sending my to do list to the Spark app which I had enabled on my Samsung S6 phone. Whoops! Once I pushed the button to send the to do list to the app, I realized I'd forgotten to add a few things, so I went back, added a few things, pushed a button to immediately upload it to the app via Bluetooth, and realized that I now had two separate notes. This could be great if you like to divide your to do list into multiple parts, such as a shopping list, blog post brainstorming list, and to do list, and would like to upload them as separate PDFs or JPEG's, but because I wanted them combined into one single note, I quickly found and selected the option to combine the two notes into one, which it did flawlessly in just a second. Awesome!

I then opened up the note on my phone, and jotted a couple additions to my to do list onto the existing note. Because I primarily have my to do list on my desk, but frequently need to refer to it when not at my desk, this is the perfect functionality for me. I then sent the note to my email, my Dropbox account, and found it in my free Wacom cloud account.

To answer a few questions that I had before receiving it:

the way it works is that the pen communicates with the Bluetooth electronic pad underneath the paper, so it is really similar to using a normal bamboo tablet except that it has a slim profile and nice surface to where a pad of paper fits perfectly on top and provides a nice writing experience, so you can see what you are writing as you go and have that old-fashioned writing experience.

You must use the Wacom pen and ink refills, because the ink has a copper barrel that lets it communicate with the pad underneath. However, you can use any paper that you want, provided it is the right size and not too thick. There are details about this on the "getting started" page for the spark on the Wacom website.

You can't slide the pad of paper out and use it separately from the laptop sleeve, the functionality is stuck in the tablet sleeve, so make sure you actually want your tablet to be built-in to this. I'm not sure, but I may have preferred the experience of just the pad of paper without the tablet sleeve, but then, it is really nice having the tablet right there for certain types of applications, like when I am sketching out landscape design ideas.

Two things that I am disappointed about:

I don't usually like ballpoint pens with caps, I prefer the retractable type instead.

The text recognition in the app does not yet work, at least not for me, but since this is in beta, I have high hopes that this issue will be solved very quickly. It sounds like this functionality was only just released in the last 10 days.

I had previously tried to use a $200 pen from Adobe to take digital notes and draw out digital landscape design sketches on my iPad air, but unfortunately I found the included apps so complicated that they just weren't worth it to learn given the simple things I wanted to do with it. Adobe's software and interface got in the way between me and my device. I prefer the simplicity of this device so much more.

Overall, I'm thrilled with the functionality and fun of this cool new way of using a bamboo tablet. We have an old-school bamboo tablet in the house, but I never got used to looking at the screen to see what I was writing, even though my partner, an artist, did really well with it. This allows me to come into the digital age with my notetaking and have my notes available across all of my devices, including my desktop via the Wacom cloud.

While it's called a handbag, this elegant and professional hard cased bag really reminds me more of slightly feminine version of the briefcase. I absolutely adore that I can fit my clipboard and portfolio as well as a couple of miscellaneous items in the bag without cramming. The hard case means that my papers are unlikely to get wrinkled, and I just love the structured look and feel of the bag.

While it is made of faux leather, it really feels like it has the buttery texture of real leather. I like that there is a handle for carrying it in one hand, as well as a shoulder strap for if I have to walk a few blocks to a meeting. It's comfortable, beautifully designed, and fills an ideal niche in my professional wardrobe. Though I'm a landscaper, I frequently do landscape designs and consultations, so it's really nice to have something that looks professional and elevates my work so that I can be seen as more of an architectural professional rather than a blue-collar construction worker – in some settings, it is all about the image of professionalism that one projects.

Though I received a sample for review, the positive opinion of this product is my own.

I think you get what you pay for with this projector. It isn't extremely bright, but it is bright enough for a lit room if you use it at a minimal focus distance. It is fine at a greater distance in a dark room and has a large range of focus. It is small enough and very light weight for portability, and it has a good variety of common input ports for versatility. The fan is a bit loud. Small to medium sized text is unreadable due to low resolution.  Overall this is fine for showing some snapshots or a youtube video with friends but not for business or text. I recieved a sample for review but opinions are my own.

This is my second modular power supply from Corsair, and I'm never going back. I always hated having to try to figure out how to secure all the power cords I was never going to use, so they wouldn't fall into the fans. Being able to remove the ones I'm not using is a big bonus. It runs quietly and has the feel of good quality.

My motherboard has a four pin connector that I initially couldn't find, but if you look closely at the 8 pin connector, you will see that it can unclip into two four pin connectors.

My only criticism is that I felt like I had to turn several of the cords over three times to figure out which end went to the supply. All it would take is some colored dots to make it clear where everything goes.

I picked this up thinking it was a monopod, because I love having a monopod that I can set onto the ground and make sure that my shaky hands don't ruin the shot.
