I've become somewhat dependent on the sight of this bright blue radio. Every morning I stumble, groggy-eyed, into my bathroom. Having this clear-sounding radio, blasting my favorite music, is a nice pick-me-up as I shower. But does the design offer me anything more than what I would expect from a typical shower radio?

PROS: It's cleverly designed to mimic the shape of a shampoo. It melds easily into the background. My initial fear was that I would accidentally grab it instead of the real thing, but so far that hasn't happened.

PROS: The sound quality is tinny but quite decent for a shower radio.

PROS: The radio offers a "store" function where you can bookmark your favorite radio stations and get to them fast by using a "recall" button. This is a feature common to most clock radios but I don't spend enough time in the bathroom to use it. I basically stick to one station while showering and can't see myself using the "store" function unless I'm taking a long bath. Still, nice to have that option.

PROS: Great battery life! I used my AA batteries for this and it has been running for months with no problem.

CONS: It's not that easy to see the buttons. They're located on the sides of the device but the positions are not intuitive. I always have to squint a little to see the print above the buttons because the buttons do not stick out.

CONS: "Light up" function. The time display is very clear and easy to read as-is. Since it's not a bedtime clock radio that benefits from having a glow-in-the-dark function, this feature feels extraneous to me. Perhaps it's best for someone who likes to take a bath with candles all around.

CONS: Not space saving. I used to have a shower radio that could be hooked over the showerhead. While the radio is not huge, I still had to move my shampoo and conditioner bottles to make room for it.

Overall it is a decent radio and I have been using it since I got it with no problems.

PROS: Easy to set up. All I had to do was plug the included Bluetooth wireless device into a USB on my Toshiba Windows 7 netbook. Soon I had the pleasure of listening to Youtube videos and my iTunes library through a thumping subwoofer and two speakers.

If you don't expect BOSE quality-like sound, a decent set of speakers for the price. At high levels the sound does get a little tinny, but still represents a major improvement over the sound of the typical speakers provided with a PC. The set is particularly useful if you're throwing a party in your small apartment and want to use your iTunes library as the source.

CONS:
The title of the product is misleading. It is not a true "wireless" device in the sense that the subwoofer and speaker are wired and have to be plugged into an outlet. However, I didn't mind this as many truly "wireless" devices often require batteries or have to be recharged at some point.

Do we need such a big fat subwoofer/speaker? It looks weird being sandwiched between two little ones. The trio takes up a lot of space and is awkward to store. I would rather have had two moderately-sized speakers with good bass. Also, the right speaker is permanently wired to the back of the subwoofer, while the left one is detachable. I would have preferred two detachable speakers.

The instructions are poorly laid out. Instead of having one or two manuals (i.e., one for a quick set-up, one with more detail), the manufacturer chose to scatter the instructions across several small booklets. One had a diagram showing how to connect it with an analog connection while another little booklet showed you how to connect wirelessly. Yet another listed the customary safety warnings and warranty. A waste of paper.

I have owned this plasma TV for only a few months, so it works fine so far. The picture looks great and the sound is decent (especially when hooked up with speakers). But whether it will last for at least 5 years is uncertain, given what I've read about Panasonic and the tendency of today's TVs to give out sooner so that you're forced to buy another one. So, I have my fingers crossed.

Works perfectly with my Samsung S4 mini. I use this old phone as an audio book streaming device (SIM card removed so no phone #) and this battery holds a charge through several hours of listening. The battery initialization was a bit complicated, but important to do for optimum battery life.

Fills a medium room with sound very well with good bass.  Works seamlessly with ipod on the dock.  Also has an aux jack for other audio players (you need provide your own 1/8" patch cable). AC adapter works well.  I haven't tried it just using batteries yet. Remote is small. I used some sticky back velcro to attach the remote to the speaker to prevent the remote from getting lost.

This is a wonderful audiophile turntable
But would not be recommend to the beginner

This is a nice TV, great picture.  However, it is VERY LACKING in HDMI ports, has one eARC HDMI should have at least two and only has three total HDMI ports.  SO, if you use the HDMI eArc port for the sound bar, you only have two left and I use one for a Blu Ray player plus I use a Roku so no more ports for games etc.  Could use bluetooth for soundbar, but if you mute for a few minutes my sound bar (Yamaha) shuts off as no signal to it.  Yes, could use the optical, but then there are other problems with the remote functions.  Prefer the Roku to using some of the TV smart apps, but might look into that to free one HDMI port.
It does what it's supposed to.  Sound quality seems a little lower than the cable it replaced, but not significantly so.

My new state of the art hearing aids came with an accessory that plugs into the tv.  Problem is, my TV has one optical audio jack, and I have a sound bar going to that.  This splitter means I can listen to the TV via my hearing aids and everybody else can listen through the soundbar.  Perfect

I have been looking for moderately priced bluetooth headphones for the gym, ones that stayed in place on the treadmill, and offered quality sound. These work so well. Secure fit--the design keeps the headphones in ear without having to constantly re-adjust. Fine sound --rich bass without mush, clear treble without that tinny sound. 3 equalizer modes that allow adjustment- and you can actually hear the difference and choose the one you most enjoy. The controls are easy to use once your fingers know where to press. The call quality through the headphones is very good. The battery life--have used for a few hours over 2-3 weeks and battery life is still "medium" (nice to be told  where the battery life stands each time you turn these on.) Okay, two side comments: they are a bit bulky due to extensive battery life and easy to use controls, but not to the point of hampering fit, and; the memory foam earpieces  did not work that well for me, and when trading them out to try the regular ones, they immediately ripped. No issue, though, cause i preferred the regular earpieces, and had a chance to order more free as well. All in all, a great purchase at a good price.

Truly surprised by the range and quality of sound from these inexpensive earphones. Using them with a computer with beats audio. Clear lows, crisp highs, no distortion. Very pleased. Fit as comfortable and secure as any earbud I have used.

Back when I used to spend my days fumbling with earbud wires, I wondered "What kind of idiot would pay $300 dollars for headphones, when you can hear your sounds perfectly fine for less than $10?". Even as these products rose more and more to popularity, I scoffed and resisted.

Those days are long gone. After I borrowed them from my friend for a day and tried them myself, I knew why. After getting them, these quickly became a non-negotiable part of my life. I use them to:

- take and receive meetings
- freely go pee, refill coffee, and wash my dishes while listening to a meeting
- go on runs while listening to music
- ignore noisy people around me
- get myself into a state of focus
- calm my anxiety on airplanes
- show people I am not interested to talk to them
- as a fashion statement

Seriously, I wear these so much I think I am developing a bald spot. Maybe that's why all the engineers are bald. The sound quality is superb, and so is the bluetooth range and connectivity. I have since tried the Sony's, Dolby dimensions, the newer model of these, but these are the best one. I have bought a pair for my whole family, and replaced my old pair when it got old without a second thought. One time, I tried my friend's airpods and almost threw up at the sound quality. Not to mention, with this size, they are much harder to lose.

These are my favorite product of the last several years (this, and the divacup) and I would wholeheartedly recommend!

Not so many years ago digital audio devices came with 3.5mm single ended and 2.5mm balanced connections. Then the 4.4mm came on the scene and all my aftermarket IEM got cables upgraded to the new plug end to work with my newer iBasso DAP. But I still had enough devices like FIIO BTR5 that wouldn't accept the 4.4mm plugs so I needed an adapter and this one looked like it would fit the bill. And it works just fine but it is just one more thing I have hanging off my cable and just one more thing to keep track of. Oh well, such is the price for progress I guess.

I was trying to use the older model MPOW but the syncing with the older Bluetooth codec wasn't cutting it. I use this to transmit sound from my A/V receiver to my wireless earbuds for watching TV by plugging it into the headphone jack. Pairing was effortless and the sound quality is much improved over the previous model. It does exactly what I tried to get the FiiO BT transmitter to do for about 1/5th the price.

These stick in your ears like they were glued in and they are comfortable. The only thing I didn't like about them is the fact that if I use them with my True Wireless Earbuds the buds won't sit low enough in the charging case to allow them to charge. Perhaps a smaller size (these are the large) will work. I fear losing an earbud while working or riding my bike so the fact that these stick in my ear so well makes them a must have for me. I don't care too much about how they work with phone calls because I don't talk on my phone and the noise cancelling isn't a big deal so the fact that these fit so snugly adds to the isolation. All things considered I give these two thumbs up and I will get more.

I’ve been on a quest to find the best (perfect would be nice but....) TWE’s in the sub $150 price range. I mainly use them for watching TV, listening to audiobooks while riding my bike and podcasts and some music (I have dedicated IEM’s for serious music listening). I began my search with the Soundcore series by Anker because I’ve used their other products for years and I find their quality to be above average for the money. My first foray into the TWE world were the Soundcore Life A1’s. I still have them and for the money they are hard to beat. Small, comfortable, great battery life and minuscule pill case charger. Also used them for a phone call and they were great for that, but I almost never talk on the phone so .......Next we’re the Soundcore Life A2 NC because I wanted to try noise cancelling. I didn’t really NEED NC but I thought it would reduce wind noise while riding. It didn’t. They also were impossible to get securely in my weird ears. I tried all the different tips and wings but the would fall out on occasion (once into the compost pile while turning that monster). So they went back in favor of these Liberty 2 Pro’s. Initially I was very disappointed. The gimmicky “10 Grammy Winner” EQ settings are ridiculous. And as with all the TWE’s so far none of them give me the volume my 70 year old ears need, but at least these come with the option to run the EQ up to +6 dB across the board so that helps with the casual listening thing. They also came with ear tips perhaps best for a large mouse or maybe a small cat and there was no chance the would stay in so I changed them to a larger set (there are 7 sizes to choose from, all silicone 😢) and they fit better now. They are substantially heavier than the Life A1’s but we’ll see how secure they are as time goes by. I do wish they would offer some foam tip options and I’ll be trying out some Delkoni tips in the near future. As for the Astoria Aural Coaxial Architecture thing, they sound pretty good. Not BGVP DM6 good, but not bad for Bluetooth. The AptX is decent, pairing was simple, the wireless charging is nice, and the packaging was phenomenal for the price. I went for the refurbished set and I can’t tell them from brand spanking new. There really isn’t anywhere else to go with the Soundcore line so we’ll see. Updates coming if things change.

When I bought my BGVP DMG’s a year or so ago the cable that came with them was sub par. Having been in the “audiophile” world for years I was ambivalent about the worth of cables. Many look upon them as snake oil, and frankly I can’t tell the difference when upgrading interconnects on my home theater system. However there is one realm where better cabling shows a marked improvement and that is the IEM arena. I’m not an audio engineer so I can’t explain why they work, probably something to do with impedance, don’t know. All I DO know is that the improvement is astonishing. The soundstage is wider. The mids are crisper, the cymbals and drum head strikes are sharper and vocals are smoother. With IEM’s it’s impossible to do A-B comparisons. It’s not like switching between amps, and one of the things about sound is it’s difficult to “remember”. Given all that and added to the fact that the prices of decent 16 core cables with a myriad of connection options, be it 2 pin or MMCX with 2.5mm balanced, 3.5mm single ended and now Eve 4.4mm balanced there really isn’t any reason to not jump in and find out for yourself. I now routinely buy new upgraded cables for every new IEM’s I buy (with Campfire Audio products being the exception). When I bought the BLON BL-03’s the change of the cable and the replacement of the foam tips with some Spinfit silicone tips (total investment under $60) turned these “budget” items into absolute killers I’d put up against any sub $200 ChiFi offerings. Peace out.

I ordered these to compare with my Philips Fidelio X2HR's. I wanted a closed back to use in situations where the open back X2HR's would be too loud for others nearby. The first thing I noticed when I unboxed them was they are smaller than the Fidelio's, especially the pads. These are more like on ears than over ears. I don't have a big giant head but man these things are small. I can fall asleep with my Philips on and not be bothered but these are going to take some modding to get them comfortable. I was tempted to just pack 'em up and send 'em back, then I plugged them into my Monolith Liquid Spark and ran a few tunes through them. Sweet. Great staging, nice bass, mids and highs are not fatiguing. The bass on The Grateful Dead's "Box of Rain" is punchy and deep without crapping out so that's a good sign. So it's back to Amazon for some Brainwavez pads to see it that alleviates the insane clamping pressure.

I’m an IEM guy. I have tons of $$$ invested in monitors, cables, tips, etc. but recently the addition of a piano to our home for the pre-teens here has made a pair of noise isolating headphones a necessity. I looked at some of my go-to Utoob channels for some direction and these were rec’d by many of those whose advice has been valid in previous purchasing decisions. Zeo’s was pretty stoked on these and the “Black Friday” price below $120 was a clincher. Once again my “friends” were spot on. They are comfortable (once I got a pair of wire rimmed reading glasses). The memory foam microfiber covered pads are good for hours of listening. The sound rivals some of my IEM’s although I find the soundstage to be a bit more compressed. The bass is definitely more defined but that seems to come at the expense of the highs although not in a bad way. I can see why the bass heads are crazy about these. The 35 ohm is comparable with all my devices including the cheap ass headphone jack on my ROKU remote. I did ditch the stock cable for a 1.5M SKS because I don’t require the 12’ cable that came with the cans, although it’s a nice cable. I do see a headphone amp in my future, perhaps the Little Bear B-4X portable tube amp. Lord save me from this addiction 😀

Got these for my twin 4 year old nieces for Xmas. They came with lots of stuff on them, most of it will never be used and was fairly easy to remove. Then there was Alexa. She’s an annoying bitch and won’t be easily ignored. If I wanted Amazon to know every little thing a 4 year old did or said I suppose it would be nice to have but there’s enough crap in today’s world trying to stick their noses into our business so it had to go. Sorry Alexa. It would have been nice if I was given a list of things I wanted that I could choose from but that’s not how things work these days. As for things I do like, the screens are nice and the foam rubber shells should provide adequate protection. And they are so feather light. Makes holding my iPad feel like holding a brick. Would have given it 5 stars if not for the annoying Alexa.

These things were being given glowing reviews from many of the reviewers on UToob whose tastes pretty much align with my own. Get the BLON’s they said. So I did. Get a better cable they said. So I did. Get better tips they said. So I did. $70 +/- a few later and they are almost impressive. Compared to my BGVP DMG’s there is no comparison but for the money I wasn’t expecting them to be. Honestly they sound like an IEM that costs about twice as much so I guess I can’t bitch too much.

Update 01/2020: All my original listening was done using the Radsone ES100 Bluetooth DAC/AMP and while it is miles better than whatever comes out of your smartphone or your computers headphone jack it won't hold a candle to the results you get putting some power to them, and while they don't require tons of power they absolutely shine when you put good CLEAN power to them. Using a SMSL M100 DAC and a Monolith Liquid Spark amp and throwing on a pair of Delkoni tips has made these IEM's into killers. They sound comparable to my BGVP's and damn near as good as my BGEYZ Spring 1's. As I write this I am listening to Pat Metheny's "Road To You, Live" and the presentation and depth of the soundstage is remarkable. I was seriously considering moving these along to thin the heard but I think they will hang around a bit longer.

I’ve been seeing reviews and recommendations from folks I trust praising these headphones and I needed a pair of lightweight beaters I could take out and about so I figured $30 wasn’t too bad a gamble. The lifetime warranty was a nice touch by Koss too. My main music listening is classic rock and jazz and my go to system is a HiBy R6 with BGVP DMG IEM’s but when I’m out doing yard work or just knocking around I listen to podcasts and audiobooks. For these tasks these are excellent headphones. The fit is a little snug but their weight makes that bearable. They are lacking a bit in the upper frequencies but do have a nice bottom end. Overall it was a good buy and I wouldn’t hesitate to buy them again or gift them to friends.

Very nice features, sounds great, 2.5 balanced output! BT v5, aptXHD, top of the line DAC’s, great battery life. So why just 4 stars? The documentation leaves a lot to be desired. The included printed doc was about the size of a matchbook with writing so small it required a magnifying glass to read and for all that effort it basically said nothing. The biggest hassle was the pairing. It couldn’t be less intuitive. I have many BT devices, both receivers and transmitters and this is the first one that required a web search to figure out. Very frustrating. And to enable the BT v5 it requires a ROM flash upgrade so you have to connect it to a PC and follow a bunch of steps that are as intuitive as the pairing. I came within seconds of sending it back but stuck it out because it had some pretty stellar reviews. It turns out I’m glad I did. Once you get it sorted out it is a pretty amazing piece of kit. I use it with my HiBy r6 and BGVP DMG’S as well as my ATH M-50x headphones. I can now roam freely around the kitchen while keeping the DAP safely out of the way. I can plug-in the 2.5mm balanced cable and get outstanding sound with the added bonus of not heating up the DAP (it gets hot when plugged in directly) and the battery life of the HiBy is more than doubled. Both of these bonuses more than make up for the minor degradation in sound staging. I have listened for over 7 hours without the battery giving up, but have not used it up to it’s limit yet so I can’t say how long it will last. Is it worth the Benjamin it cost? Oh yeah.

Update: Upgraded to 5 stars after a month of use. Once the niggling little details were figured out and the unit was set up I can't say enough good things about this puppy. My main reason for getting a BT transmitter was I am going to be doing extensive bicycle touring later this year and since it will be solo touring I wanted good quality music available. I have an extensive library of 24 bit flac's as well as a couple of hundred audiobooks for the trip and while the playback of the books isn't important the music is. I invested a fair amount of cash into a HiBy R6 DAP and BGVP DMG IEM's as well as upgraded cables to connect them. The EarStudio lets me connect via 2.5" balanced with no real discernible degredation in the quality of the playback as opposed to plugging directly into the output on the DAP, and here's the kicker, instead of just getting 6 - 7 hours of playback and heating up the DAP I now get double that without any heat. I can stash the HiBy in a Pelican 1020 case and put it in my top tube bag where it's out of harms way and protected in case of misadventure. The EarStudio has a battery life of around 14 hours (I haven't run it out yet, and I have listened for over 8 hours). Added to that the App that is available for my Android based DAP is amazing. More fiddly bits than your above average geek could ever want. So I gotta give it a 5 star rating. And it's worth twicw the price but don't tell Radsone.

I recently invested a fairly substantial (for me) amount of $$$ in a DAP and IEM’s with all the ancillary cables and a BT receiver and I wanted a safe and secure environment to transport everything in. This Pelican case fits my requirements to a “T”. I can now store everything in one place and take it anywhere without worrying about damage, plus I can listen using the Bluetooth receiver while the HiBy player is secured and out of my pocket. Great piece of mind when around small children and knuckleheads.

I bought this as part of my foray into the world of “higher fidelity” personal audio. I paired this with a pair of Tin Audio T2 Pro’s and a pair of BGVP BGD’s and connected them with the Yinyoo Upgrade 8 Core Silver Plated Copper Cable HiFi Earphone Replacement Cable. I didn’t know what to expect other than it would be better than my $25 Sennheiser ear buds plugged into my four year old Android phone playing MP3’s. What I wasn’t prepared for was just how much better the experience would be. I don’t have the flowery audiophile descriptions to say just how astonishing the music is. The clarity, depth and separation. The placement of each instrument and voice is no longer just thrown into my head in a haphazard manner. Everything is where it should be and the soundstage has made it feel like the distance between my ears has gone from a few inches to many yards. As far as “smiles-per-dollar” goes it’s just nuts. I’ve been listening to music since before Jimmy Page and Robert Plant’s formed Led Zeppelin. I grew up in SoCal and I’ve been to hundreds of concerts, I’ve spent buckets of Benjamin’s on stereo gear and sold stereos back in the 70’s but I’ve never felt this engaged in the music. It’s nice to be surprised. As this is my first foray into digital HiRes gear I don’t feel qualified to say this is better than that. I did have a price point in mind and did a good deal of research prior to purchasing the Topping and I do feel that it was money well spent. I would recommend it to anyone wishing to step up their enjoyment of their digital music. I use it as a portable dac/amp as well as a desktop solution. It takes a line out from my laptop and feeds it into my A/V receiver or my headphones/IEM’s. On the desktop it can remain plugged into the power source so the battery remains charged and ready to go if I want to venture out. I’ve taken it on walks and bike rides and as far as I know the battery is good for many many hours in amp mode only. In dac/amp mode I think you could get upwards of 10 hours before you had to charge it.

I bought these at the same time I bought the Tin Audio T2 Pro’s to do a comparison. The BGVP’S cost exactly twice what the T2’s cost as I scored them from Amazon with the $20 discount. Quality wise the two are comparable in the materials used. The ear tips with the BGVP’s are superior and the cables seem to be of a higher quality, as one would expect for their respective price points. Sound wise I have to give the edge to the BGVP’s. The bass is cleaner with a tad more punch. I’m not a big bass guy so for my tastes in music (classic Rock, blues, jazz and some classical) they are perfect. Where the BGVPs really shine is the top end. They have superior “shine” with great staging and depth. I’ve only had them long enough to preview a couple of albums and if the only get better with some burn in then I will be a happy man. The big question is are they twice as good as the T2Pro’s. They cost twice as much after all. My first instinct is to say yes. If you have a budget that keeps you under $75 then go for the Tin Audios. I still say they are the best IEM’s for under a Benjamin. If you can toss in a few more frog skins you won’t be disappointed with the BGVP DMG’s

Update: I’ve had these now for about three weeks and have used them for about 100 hours, give or take, and I’ve experimented with the different tips and barrels and I have replaced the cable with an upgraded offering from Yinyoo audio (reviewed elsewhere) and I have found what suits my tastes best. I’m still impressed with the warmth and staging presented and with the gold barrels and silicone tips the fit and comfort are outstanding. I have fallen asleep with them in on a number of occasions and was surprised to wake up realizing that they did not disturb my sleep or cause me discomfort. I have used them for 5 hours or more at a time without really noticing them. I still feel that for the money spent which even with the cable is still well under $200 that you’d be hard pressed to find better. The majority of my listening has been done using an Android phone playing 16 & 24 bit flac’s through a Topping NX4 DSD DAC/AMP. I use the HiBy music player and I also subscribe to Tidal’s upgraded service and have access to MQA files if I listen on my Win10 laptop. The thing that surprises me the most is that now that I have upgraded my hardware I have found my musical tastes have expanded considerably. Next up is the HiBy r6 DAP and I’ll do another update after test driving that in a couple of weeks.

I bought a second set of small speakers for my home studio for editing (IK Multimedia iLoud) but they use RCA connectors and my monitor controller (really just a mixer) only had 1/4" available. I could have gotten an RCA cable with 1/4" adaptors but this seemed like a better solution. Everything sounds great and I enjoy having a smaller setup just for keeping my ears safe while editing.

Got these just i time for having to work from home with a ten-year-old in the house. :-) They feel great and sound really nice. I like having the option to use them corded and I love the hard shell case they came with.

This is exactly what I was hoping for. I recently bought a used GH4 from my stepson who had upgraded to the 5. The only problem was he had lost the original battery charger. In researching online I found a lot of other products that came with batteries but those batteries didn’t last nearly as long as the original. I am 99% sure these last just as long as the original equipment battery so not I have three batteries (the original one and the two in this package) and a charger at a great price.
This is a cute small radio. I use it mainly to listen to stuff i stream through bluetooth. It connects quickly and effectively. Sound quality is okay, not the best but works for me
This camera is good and small. Picture clarity is amazing and it delivers what it promises. Have not tried out the other functionality yet, but will update when I do
If you hate buds, this item is for you.  It's comfortable and compact, and carries good volume and reliability at minimum cost.
Nothing more to say, perfection.  Sound is impeccable, clear unbelievable really from just this base.  Cannot wait to hear it with the base and ones ordered to finish it.
works well. Stays in my ears which was an issue I had with a different pair of buds. Still doesn't cancel out the water noise though. Maybe what I want doesn't exist.
What else to can I say - sound is very good, more than adequate to what it's needed for (movie watching).

Enthusiast of World of Tanks BEWARE! I am not the only one out there to report serious problem with the game vs. this card (and more nVidia cards in general).
I have had World of Tanks crashes on EVGA GeForce 9800 GT and they, unfortunately, continue to happen on this very card - my newest MSI N650Ti-1GD5/OC GeForce 650Ti. They happen regardless the driver version (usually at the beginning of a battle), and they do still occur with the newest 314.07 drivers, though less frequently and at a different moment.
Worked with World of Tanks support and we went through several iterations, including clean re-installations (incl. registry cleanups) of the game/drivers in different combinations, underclocking, etc., but that did not help at all.
To be fair - the card never gave me problems with Portal 2, Order of War, Medal of Honor and a few other games needing solid 3D rendering - it appears to be issue with World of Tanks game in particular.
Not sure whose fault it is: 1) may be game developers, with whom nVidia claims to have business partnership), but, equally valid, 2) it may also be nVidia drivers that crash the program (the issue seems to be reported more often with newer nVidia drivers by multiple players).
Anyway - if you're into World of Tanks a lot - I recommend picking up some decent Radeon card - the one I have on the other PC (HD 6870) never gave me any issues with my favorite game.

EDIT as of 08 March 2013:
I added one more star and here's why:
1. The crash of World of Tanks occurs due to client (program) issue, which was admitted couple days ago by the developer's support folks (they're still working to resolve this, with me). So, as this is not the card's fault I am adding one star, especially that graphics is really stunning (especially for such a price point!).
2. Why not 5 stars? Well, I would, but then one thing stands out - if you want to keep that (factory overclocked) card stable, you need to speed up the fan a bit and that makes the card pretty noisy (louder than a fully spinning DVD drive, in my instance)! So if you do not mind it (or you have a well noise insulated computer case) then go ahead with it.

First of all, kudos to Amazon for the shipping service and ease of the process. I also purchased Squaretrade warranty for the peace of mind, but even without it, the Amazon delivery service did not get me any troubles. White glove level, indeed.
The TV - as the other reviewers said - MUST "CURE" ITSELF for at least a couple days of use. At first, the colors were not good and contrast/brightness did not seem to do well, but after two days (two evenings, rather) of regular use with a DVD player it stabilized and works very nicely now (comparison was easy while watching the "Rome" episodes that have identical beginning).
I do not own Blu-Ray player so I'm not sure if black does better there, but on DVD it is just OK and on Netflix is terrible - I guess these types of TV do not ever reach the blackness of a tube TV, but still, this one is satisfactory on the DVD; works for me (Netflix is to be kicked out, I think...).
One thing I can't figure out - or it may be TV's flaw - is how to adjust TV's resolution when DVD plays low resolution movies (home-made from VHS, VCD, etc.) via HDMI cable. My TV is 42". Resolution is fine when VCR (hooked up via RCA) plays, but same quality type of movies do not seem to do well when they go through HDMI, too much pixelization. The TV does not have an easy adjustment of the resolution itself and working it out through DVD is too tedious and time consuming. Panasonic could think of some sort of resolution enforcement that a user can set up from the remote - it would be good thing to have.
Overall, nice set and I will enjoy using it for the next (hopefully) 10 years or so.

IMPORTANT UPDATE (21-Dec-2011): In order to connect to an external stereo receiver/amplifier one needs an optical cable (like the one I bought: [[ASIN:B00168NFCU 2PCS 12ft Digital Audio Optical Fiber Toslink Cable]])and digital-to-analog audio converter (this exact one: [[ASIN:B0053VKP8S FiiO D3 Digital to Analog Audio Converter - 192kHz/24bit Optical and Coaxial DAC]]). I hooked it up and was able to watch all things from my laptop on TV, such as YouTube and enjoy external speakers quality through an amplifier. However, I encountered, at one point in time, a serious issue of lack of sound when streaming from Netflix (the one going DIRECTLY to TV via VIERA Link, as I have it connected to my network with Ethernet cable). Only the TV speakers were playing sound then, even as THEATER was set up as default speakers, but external speakers were mute. Laptop (connected to TV vis USB) still played well through external speakers, which indicated that optical cable and converter were working fine. Interestingly, after playing something on laptop (even music, any sound) and staying at the same input channel (i.e. in my case HDMI2) then switching to VIERA Link Netflix stream, it suddenly restored the sound going to external speakers! So it looked like you need to "purge" your optical cable & converter (however irrational that seems, we're talking 'digital' here!) in order to get back to the VIERA Link Netflix allowing the sound to go through the optical cable again. When TV was switched off, however, then VIERA Link Netflix again muted itself to the outside world and only played on TV speakers (regardless the settings). Intrigued, I called Panasonic and the solution was found! Here is what you need to do if you come across the same issue:
1) Freshly turn on the TV;
2) Switch to input (HDMI) which you know works with the optical cable out (in my case it is laptop connected to HDMI 2 port);
3) Open the MENU and select Audio/Advanced option;
4) While there, go to the audio input setting "HDMI 1-3 in" (in my case it is HDMI 2 in and it is the only highlighted one, because you're in it; look at #2) and - IMPORTANT - select COMPONENT (so switch it from DIGITAL);
5) Exit the menu and start VIERA Link, select Netflix and... ENJOY IT!
No one knows why this setup works, but it does ONLY before you start up VIERA Link tool, so this sequence above is important. I tried to change from Digital to Component while inside Netflix already (playing movie, mute to external world) and it did not work; I had to exit Netflix and go to menu to change that, then it did work. Of course, if you want to get back to your laptop and enjoy the external speakers, repeat steps 3 & 4 and change back to DIGITAL. Just a few clicks, but much less pain than trying to "purge" the line each time with playing something on my laptop and then going back to VIERA Link...
I hope it works for you, too! MERRY CHRISTMAS TO EVERYONE!!!

The size of the projector is not as small as the pictures make it seem. Though it is not advertised as a pico projector, I expected it to be smaller. With that said, the projector is not so large that it would be hard to transport or store when not in use.

Unfortunately, I was not able to get the Wi-Fi feature to work with my Iphone. This is not a dealbreaker for me, as I plugged a Roku stick into the HDMI port and the system worked well.

I was surprised by how good the native speakers sound. I found watching movies enjoyable and voices were easy to hear. There are adjustments for the bass and treble levels in the menus. The unit has a headphone jack in the rear which makes hooking up an external speaker set up a breeze.

The fan on the unit is very quiet and is not distracting while it is in use.

While I really like this projector, there is a large downside. The lack of keystone correction is a huge oversight. Placing this projector without keystone adjustment means the projector has to be directly in line with the viewing area making it necessary to use a tripod in most instances. Having to bring a tripod along, makes the unit less portable.

Overall, this is a small projector with a great picture, as long as you can place it in the perfect location without much ambient lighting. If WEWATCH added keystone correction and refined the mirroring feature, this would be a 5 star projector.

This Honeywell smart home security starter kit has a great video and is easily expandable.

Each item in the security kit was simple and clear to find since they were labeled in their own little box. There is an instruction sheet that is quite large for the info that it holds. The instructions have nice graphics and it is spaced out well so it is very easy to read. The instructions are simple for initial set up. Though I would appreciate another manual to help with the “extra” things it can do. I relied on the Honeywell videos and reviews (video and written) by other people to get it functioning with all the bells and whistles. I could see the need for a manual for those less tech savvy.

The base station could be a little smaller but it looks very nice in my kitchen and blends in very well. It’s a nice design with only one button, for the speaker. You can touch the top to check how it is working and run your finger around the top to change the volume. The camera is small and has a privacy ring that can be twisted to block the camera. It would be a nice feature if I could twist the camera from the app in case we forgot to open it when we left.
The middle mesh part is the speaker and it has a good range of volume and the sound is good.
The bottom has a light inside and it changes colors when you choose the different settings. It also lights up to help when you set up new devices.
The base has a backup battery. You will get an alert when it doesn’t have power. This has been handy when there is a storm so I know when the power goes out and when it is restored.

To start the set up I downloaded the Honeywell app. It was easy to use and is a nice looking app. The main page is very simple. When you go to the settings that’s where all the extras are.
My husband also has the app on his phone so he can use it just as I can.
Set up was very easy besides having troubles with it connecting it to my WiFi. I decided to wait till the next day and it worked after a couple tries. I don’t have a fast internet so that might be why. I haven’t had any issues with the connection since set up. Besides the WiFi wait it was about 15 minutes to set up the app and base.
The key fob was very easy to pair up and only took me a couple minutes to have it ready to use. Nice to have when a babysitter comes over.
The access sensors were very easy to install and set up. I didn’t need the extra piece. It only took me a few minutes to stick them on and pair them. I did use painters tape to attach them to my doors and frames. I am worried about the tape they have ruining my stained trim. I haven’t seen any comments about it. I also wanted to try it on other doors and windows first.
When you open a door or window in home mode it chimes and sends you an alert. When you open in away mode it will sound the alarm. I wish the door sensors were a little smaller or gray. They stand out too much on my wood trim and door. If my trim was white they wouldn’t be very noticeable.

The camera is very clear and has a wide angle so if you position it right you can see a lot. You can switch the video to full screen and the picture is still good. You are also able to zoom in on the video in the app and it has options to take a snap of the video, talk through the base or have an alarm go off. Sometimes it takes a while for the video to load or it will just turn off. I am assuming this is from my slower internet. Usually after a few tries I can get it to work. Also there is a delay in the video and the movement is jumpy, this could be due to the slower internet also. You still get a good picture of who is there. I was impressed with the night vision.

The motion detection is a nice feature when you are away. I have been trying to figure out the best setting while we are at home. It will send me alerts all the time when we are home. Most of the alerts are during the people detection time. Maybe because our camera covers so much of our main area. I do like that how the people detection can let me know who is in the house and I don’t have to look at the video. When it detects motion it will take a short video clip and save them below the live video. You can scroll down to look at the older ones. It looks like the clips are saved for a day. The people detection is limited to 2 hours. But I did notice that you could set it for the morning then when that time was over you could change it for later in the day. You would have to remember to change it but good to know if you wanted it on for longer or multiple times in the day. Not sure why they don’t have an option for more time.

The geofencing didn’t work well for me. It would switch to away mode even when the phone was close to it. We’ve decided to turn that feature off. It’s easy enough to turn it to away with the app, key fob, or talk to it. We are at home a lot so it makes more sense to do it manually. But I could see it being a great feature for people gone more during the day.

The kids like the Alexa feature that it comes with. They can ask the weather, time, kids jokes. I use it for the timer and to ask it questions. We had problems with playing songs. It wanted us to subscribe to amazon music. We have found other ways of playing music but it’s not very easy. Alexa seems limited but still useful. I like that the security base links to my Honeywell thermostat (it was very easy to pair it) and I can tell Alexa to turn it off or change the temperature or use the same app. I would like to get other devices that link to it. Overall it is easy to use and looks nice. It’s nice that you can have a security system that is easy to use and it doesn’t have a monthly fee. I don’t usually need all the security features that this security system offers but it’s nice to have it set up and ready for when I do.

I noticed a 1 star review, missing 8 GB SD card. This card was glued to the inside of a business card which would be easy to overlook or throw out by mistake. I fall in the camp that with no instructions, 4 stars is as high as I can go. I had a couple of false starts which would have been avoided with a nice diagram. That avoids any language issues
1) Screw goes thru bottom plastic plate and run a nut down as spacer
2) Add the new add on board and the four tallest extensions. I had one extension a little short.
3) Add your Pi 0 board, the top plate and final four nuts.
First power on test failed to find network adapter. I tried power on the RasPi and a second attempt with the power on the add in. Neither brought up the network or the wireless keyboard. Power to both boards did bring the keyboard online, but not the network.
I ended up taking off the top plate and after verifying the top hat pins were seated properly, hand tightened all of the standoffs. I also grabbed the included power supply and cable to eliminate variables and here I had success. My guess is that I just hadn't tightened the boards down sufficiently, but now that it is working, repeatedly, I don't feel like testing power adapters.
I like the case, easy access to SD card, I doubt I will stay with the 8 GB card. Plenty of room for air to circulate and avoid overheating.
One last lesson learned. Before I celebrate a $5 computer, I need to think about all the addons that are required. I will be looking for a project where this could go headless.

After I looked around a bit. It turns out that a (headphone amplifier) of any good quality, is way expensive. Ok, that is the first strike on other people. Then, those other people are not powered by the usb. I've got enough wires around my desktop, the usb powered of this little gem, was the deal maker for me.
Then the next step. I got this. And I'm already loving this on paper. Then I use it and it's nice. I just got a set of 600 ohm headphones. And a motherboard cannot drive those very good. So this little powerhouse, make the volume come back. And if I like the volume on my 600 ohm cans. Most people use 32 or 80 ohm. I have to think this is way to loud of an amp. Those people will never go full throttle.
There has to be some bad. What is it, Mike? I've been using this for about 12 hours. And I'm impressed. But then. A cracking, and a hissing. Maybe it is just on that one video, I am hoping. Nope. It's for real. So I switch out the usb wire they shipped with. For a usb 3.0 one. And yea. I know this product is only rated 2.0. But 3.0 is backward compatible. And the cracking and hissing is gone. I didn't want to lose this. And now, I won't.
So, takeaways from my experience. Save yourself the time and just buy a 3.0 wire now. I read a couple other reviews that had this problem. I never saw that anybody "fixed" their issue. I was determined. I wanted this to be true. It is great after all. A good wire is like $10 for 3 feet.

Sony Cyber-shot DSC -H 55.
I have owned two other cameras in the past. My last Camera, before this one, was a 12 Megapixel. And I thought it, at first to be ALL THAT. This was only because my previous camera had been a four Megapixel. I was so impressed with the increase in the resolution that is all I could see was the ability to crop photos to a better end then I had been able to. After the newness had worn off I began to realize the Cameron was just a lemon. So with this camera, that mistake will not happen again. The (14 Megapixel) of this Sony camera is not that different from my (12 Megapixel) camera that I am replacing. So I will look past the resolution difference with ease.
However the (10 x) zoom lens is NEW. Not only to me, but to all (point and shoot) cameras I have ever seen. Now, the 10 x zoom lens that I am talking about is NOT digital zoom. But rather, purely optical. There is a digital zoom offered in the menus of this camera. But I simply turned this feature off. If I want to do any digital zoom, I'll do it in Photoshop on my own time.
Other perks include; a battery and charger. The battery is lithium. And knowing that a lithium battery must be conditioned before its true capacity can ever be obtained. And even before the battery had been `conditioned' it was still able to take approximately 400 shots. And of course four or five HRS of me playing around in the menus with the features. And I know from past experience this can be one of the biggest power drains on a camera battery. And this is only the first cycle. I don't foresee a need in my future to buy a spear battery.
While I am on the subject of batteries, I need to mention. The battery charger is a cute little thing. The part of the plug that actually goes into the wall will fold into the plastic housing. So it is not a burdensome piece of machinery to store. And the whole thing is extremely small. It is only 3"x2"x1". To me that sounds ridiculously small, and if it were not right here in front of me I might not even believe. But it is true. It will fit in my small camera case, instead of the drawer. I already have enough mess around my room.
Also about batteries, there is a handy little gauge, on the LCD screen, that reports the amount of battery left by a four bar indicator (like a cell phone).
I spoke earlier about the massive zoom lens. But I didn't even tell how this camera can also take a macro picture up to about 8" away at full wide angle (zoom out). The 8" I just spoke could be off a little by + or - an inch. The manual that could tell me for sure is over there in that box, and I am over here. And I'm a lazy person.
I'm really impressed at how small this camera is. It will fit very nicely, with lots of room to spare, in my chest pocket. I do wear a 2X shirt, but there is so much room left over, I bet you could fit this camera in a large size pocket. I haven't had a chance to test it; I'm just using my best estimate. On outings, being able to tuck this camera away in my pocket will be way awesome. And it is so light weight.
And it weighs very, very little for such a nice camera. I have a cordless optical mouse hooked up to this computer. So by comparing weight, the mouse is the more heavy of the two.

Although others have reported success with this, I am getting messages on screen that audio is not available over HDMI. I do not believe this device is HDCP compatible. On some broadcasts (e.g. Internet TV) the sound comes through HDMI just fine. However, on DVR playback of network TV, or Netflix streaming movies, no sound comes through HDMI. I have to connect Toslink IN and OUT to get sound OUT to the the TV.

If this device was HDCP compatible, I would expect it to output sound through the HDMI connection to any compatible device, including my plasma TV.

Before getting this switcher, I ran my DVR with HDMI out to the TV - video and sound,- no problem. After putting the device in line between the DVR and the TV, HDMI sound no longer goes through. So I believe the problem is in this device.

Conclusion: It works, but only if you add Toslink connections for sound.

Correction: I later discovered that if you change the switcher from one source to any other then back again, it "finds" the sound. Many times, I turned on the TV and the DVR and got no sound. I added the Toslink cable and got sound. However, I now conclude that a Toslink cable is not needed. The switcher does work as advertised, but you may have to switch it to another source and back again before it will pass sound through. A minor inconvenience, but not as bad as I initially thought.

I carry a circular polarizer up there, along with two spare Canon batteries. These headphones work very well, are about 1/3 of the price of the Bose, and come in a very convenient travelling case.  Independent reviews indicate the Bose headphones do a better job of noise cancellation and I do notice that it doesn't always block out a loud TV, for instance.  I have no regrets on the purchase though and am very satisfied that I am getting my money's worth from them.

Indoors: Each unit sounds very different depending on where it is located. For the Emberton, it sounded a little too bassy in most locations and the mids and highs sounded drowned out because of that. The Bose also sounded a little too bassy but was more even on the mids and highs. In particular, the highs sounded great indoors. In certain spaces indoors, the Bose might have had the most even sound but only when standing right in front of the speaker. The JBL Flip 4 did not go as low in frequency response to the others however there was more clarity in the mids and had a more stereophonic sound. The Flip 4 in most cases sounded too bassy indoors (and I don't mean low bass but mid-bass). The Emberton sounded as one of the best when placed in the middle of the room. Outdoors: The Emberton was definitely the loudest and had the most bass and sounded better outdoors and had the best low frequency response as well as loudness. In some cases again, the bass drowned out the mids and highs. I liked the JBL Flip 4 outdoors for having a stereophonic sound and clarity in the mids and highs however the bass did not extend as low as the other 2. The Bose did not sound too good outdoors (worst of the 3 outdoors) and sounded the best indoors in particular situations. The Bose outdoors also did not perform well when not standing right in front of the speakers while the other 2, you can get pretty good response at different angles. As far as loudness and bass, the Emberton blew the other 2 away, but did not have the stereo spaciousness or mid/high clarity of the JBL.
Sounds amazing outdoors especially by a wall, but sounds muddy indoors for some reason. Don’t understand why.

I am a limo driver and depend on this thing all day. I am very satisfied with it except for a few issues.

The good:
-Map graphics are great and shows direction of streets. In regards to information - I prefer the map format and image scheme/theme over Garmin any day. In fact bought and returned a popular Garmin model.
-Graphics for real-time moving travel graphics is also superior to Garmin.
-Size is just right as it does not block too much on my windshield.
-Display is configurable.

The bad (minor issues):
-May lose satellite reception in extremely bad weather, or extremely tall and dense buildings (like in the Wall St. area of NYC). However this was the same case for the Garmin models.
-Traffic is a joke. Rarely does it show accurate information in NYC. In fact, I just use it without the TMC cable, since it speeds up the processing. (Also note - Lifetime traffic only means that you get the RDS-TMC receiver cable. You can just buy this cable on Ebay for $15 or so for the "lifetime" service. Lifetime maps on the other hand is very valuable.)
-Screen calibration (if needed) is very involved.
-Suction requires really clean windows and may be difficult to twist on in some situations.
-Does some inexplicably bad/strange routing in a few cases. Maybe due to some errors in the mapping.
-Gives too much weight to certain major streets and avenues in regards to how fast you can travel through them, when in fact they can be very slow to travel through; again, just due to bad data.
-Occasionally has wrong address issues; again, data.

Laptop is very well ventilated for cooling with perforated holes on top and bottom and has vents on the sides and back of laptop. It’s covered in mostly all aluminum for a premium feel. Durability: This laptop has a solid tank like construction comparable to the way Alien laptops are constructed. However, the display has some flex but that is to be said for a lot thin and light gaming laptops. Quality control issues are a concern from some posts, but these sound like issues that would present themselves right away once you boot up and can be returned or replaced in the event that should happen.

Noise: For basic daily non-gaming use, the fans runs fairly quiet even with 40 chrome tabs running. By comparison, my 9370 laptop has the fans running pretty noticeable with 40 chrome tabs. Fans run loud when turbo is enabled but the noise is on par or below comparable gaming laptop noise but most gamers wear headphones when playing games on a laptop.

Display: The 1080 IPS 144Hz near borderless display matches well for this tier of gaming laptops and is pretty decent, Although it was mentioned in other posts about brightness levels, it is plenty bright for indoor use. There are some screen backlight bleeding but it to be expected and is not noticeable or impacts my daily use.

Keyboard: One of the better keyboards for a thin and light along with good 1.7mm of travel and solid feedback. I was disappointed that I could not change the volume up, volume down, and mute key on the right to page up and page down.

Gaming Temperatures: The idle temps I was getting is between mid 40s to high 50s. Fan kicks in around mid 40s but is barely audible. My max Unigine Heaven benchmark max temps are 89c CPU and 75c GPU. However, average temps are around 5-15 degrees during the benchmark.
Upgrading the ram or SSD will be a pain due to the inverted motherboard. I hope this design trend does not continue with future laptops.
However, despite the difficulties involved in upgrading, there may be no need as the ram and drive space size should be sufficient for most people. The dual channel ram of 16GB is enough for most games and use cases, while the 512GB of NVM SSD drive is a pretty decent storage space by recent standards.

First, there is a huge difference in power between the Supercube III and the Supercube I. Even though the Supercube I doesn't seem that much bigger than the Supercube III when it's placed into position, the Supercube I is in fact a whole different animal!

Now that I have the Supercube I for six months I'm ready for a review. I do believe that it takes about 100 hours of paying time to get these subs broken in. Someone reviewing them the day after they set them up is not doing the sub justice.

Personally I find the Supercube I's base to be clean and crisp. I've had a Martin Logan Dynamo 700 and other DefTech subs and prefer the Supercube I to all of them. In summary - GREAT SUB! But unless you have a really, really big listening environment to fill you could probably get by with a Supercube II or III.

The Fuji F70 EXR has features which clearly depart from the "same old, just a little better" way of doing things. For one, it puts the camera's digital nature front and center and manipulates images to improve them. Starting with the common auto red eye reduction, extending to pixel binning for high dynamic range or low light shots in EXR mode, as well as merging multiple shots in the natural light flash, pro low light and pro focus modes. Couple such digital magic with a great new sensor and a good zoom lens, packaged into a very small, attractive camera, and you have a real winner. In Auto EXR mode it even switches automatically to macro mode when needed, a feature I wanted for the longest time.

My favorite mode is EXR high dynamic range. On a recent trip through the Southwest US I pretty much left the camera in this mode with the Velvia film simulation (i.e. vivid colors), and all outdoor shots turned out great. Stunning, vivid colors, good detail in highlights and shadows, and nothing overdone. Simply cool!

Originally I bought the F70EXR for low light shots at work because the new sensor and software promised to yield better results than older PnSes, and it does. I have sharp handheld shots without flash that I simply have never been able to take with any other point and shoot (or older SLR for that matter). I alternate between EXR high iso/low noise, natural flash and SP night modes for this, depending on the situation or how much time I have to think and plan.

Overall, this camera is fun to use and gives great pictures almost all of the time.

Pros:
small and light
great auto modes, especially high dynamic range EXR
nice 10x zoom lens - love the range
great sensor, larger than average for PnS
smart software
fast focus and time to shoot
high quality bright display

Cons:
pronounced purple fringing (chromatic aberration) around bright, high contrast edges
finicky zoom lever - I wish it had two levels of sensitivity

Quibbles:
mode wheel turns too easily for me
some modes have overlapping features, makes choices confusing (e.g. Astia film simulation for soft tones vs. two portrait modes which promise soft skin tones)
multi shot modes are impossible if subject doesn't hold absolutely still
on/off button somewhat difficult to find by touch for me
would be nice if the lens defaulted to somewhere between 35 and 50 mm equivalent focal length instead of the very wide angle 27 mm

These are around the same price as all the junky Chinese wireless earbud brands on Amazon but sound much better, are much more reliable, and are made by a company with good customer service that stands behind their products.

Ankers has several wireless earbuds with the cords that go behind the neck but only these, the spirit, the spirit pro, and the spirit x are worth considering for purchase. Their other earbuds are older models that cost just as much but have less features and weaker specs.

The bass on these is weak but I use these mostly for working out and for that it is fine.

I already have a pair of Apple EarPods but I wanted another wireless pair of headphones as well so I could switch back and forth while the other pair was charging.

These do not work with Apples w1 chip Bluetooth protocol, only apple and beats headphones work with that standard right now so those wireless headphones brands will sound better than anything other wireless headphones will with Apple products.

They also do not have aptx, which is the best sounding Bluetooth standard for anything other than Apple.

Ankers spirit pro headphones do support the aptx standard and supposedly have better bass than these so those are that models advantages.

However the spirit pro cost twice as much as these and only supports Bluetooth protocol 4.1 while these headphones support Bluetooth protocol 5.0.

Why is that important? Because the 5.0 protocol is the new “low energy” Bluetooth standard. Meaning that if you have both a device and headphones that support it you will get much more play time out of the same size battery.

Ankers other most recent model of earbuds, the spirit x headphones, have the same specs as these headphones in terms of the protocols they support but have a different form factor, obviously, and have 10mm drivers while these have 6mm. They also have a little more battery life.

I think I might buy the spirit x headphones as well in order to have a backup and to compare their sound.

As an Apple user the spirit pro headphones are just not worth the extra cost for me since I will never use the aptx protocol and they do not even support the Bluetooth 5.0 protocol.
If they were Bluetooth 5.0 compatible I might consider spending the extra 25 bucks in order to get that extra bass.

While these don’t sound spectacular they will get great battery life when I use them with devices that support 5.0 Bluetooth and they are very affordable.

I want to quickly rant about amazons policies and the flood of cheap Chinese products on here.

Why is this?
Because the Chinese brands pay “click farms” to leave hundreds or even thousands of 5 star reviews.

The fact that many of them say the same things over and over and that many of them are written in broken English are other obvious clues.

I reported a few of them but Amazon does not take them down because Amazon cares about money and absolutely nothing else and having millions of people purchase this Chinese junk off their website makes them a lot of money.

It really sucks because good products, like these anker headphones, are barely visible in amazon search results because reputable brands don’t pay click farms to manipulate amazon search results.

It’s the consumers that lose in the end when their headphones, or other cheap Chinese products, break a few weeks after use or maybe never even work to begin with.
And you can bet that half of the time the companies selling this junk on amazon will simply disappear in order to avoid accepting returns and then reappear later under a new seller account to sell more junk through click farm manipulated amazon search results.

Of course amazon will find itself on the hook for some of these costs but apparently the money they make off of allowing all of this Chinese junk to be sold on their website under false practices is much more than any costs they incur.

These practices that amazon allows, and this one issue about manipulated search results is just the tip of the iceberg, hurts not just American consumers it also hurts American companies.

I have unusual needs for the Kindle Touch. It is my study device. As an autodidact moving along in years I found that lugging a lot of textbooks/reference books/dictionaries around was getting in the way of learning. Sure, I can use a laptop for lots of online material to study but when I'm comfortable in my easy chair and the laptop is in the other room I just don't want to get up. Enter the Touch. I am reading philosophy and studying Latin on my own. I have loaded the Touch up with many free or low cost books on Aristotle and St. Thomas Aquinas. I have many personal Latin documents, some Latin readers and texts, Interlinear translation of the Douay-Rheims Bible, etc. Now I discover that I can save web pages in html file format and convert them to mobi format for the Touch and end up with "live" links to hundreds of web pages I am interested in using in my studies. I have sent these documents to the Touch either using the email forwarding capability or the conversion program directly(Calibre-free download. A terrific program recommended by a Kindle Touch tech services guy. Wouldn't be without it!) The Kindle Touch when hooked to my home wireless network downloads web pages very fast. I can look up anything I need on Latin grammar from the web and even bookmark pages I want to save for later use. If I'm out and about I can find any free Wi Fi location and log on and do the same.

The things that are invaluable and a couple are unique to the Touch--the Fire, or the iPad 3 cannot do them, are:

1. Change the default dictionary to Latin, or any language for which you can get a digital dictionary that works with Kindle Touch. I have two Latin dictionaries that cost nearly nothing! This is a great help to anyone trying to translate and learn a new language. If I can't find it in the default ditionary I am using I then work the magic of...............

2. Web search for Latin words. I can get Google Translate, the Whitaker Latin Dictionary, Perseus Latin Word Search, etc through the browser. Pages I want to use often I can Bookmark and open them through the Menu screen for the Touch. Then, and this is crucial...........

3. You can expand browser pages by a couple of taps or by the expanding finger touch move on the screen. Many Latin words are displayed in tables that are actually images and are really too small to deal with. Just hold your finger/stylus on the screen, the box pops up and the little magnifying glass with + sign in it appears. Press that and Voila! the image now fills the screen in comfortable text size. This can be done with books too and makes tables of conjugated verbs, noun declensions etc from texts and web pages super readable and thus useful.

4. Notes. Press an word that I want to look up later, type a note about my thought(s) or that I want to translate off the web later on, save it and then look up later in View Notes and Marks for the document/book I am working with. A great way to study!

5. The reading screen is so comfortable to use. Absolutely no glare and I cannot say that about Kindle Fire or iPads--anti-glare covers are a necessity with them. Just try to read something with the Fire on sunny day while sitting in the car waiting for your spouse to get finished shopping. Not easy. With the Touch it is simplicity in itself. Just turn on and read.

6. Many books have an interactive "live" table of contents. If I really want that in a book I download a sample first and check. If it doesn't have one I may not buy although you can navigate with page/location numbers if necessary. Just a bit more awkward.

7. Amount of stuff on the device. I have over 4000 pages of the works of St. Thomas Aquinas, Aristotle's complete works of his major writings, again nearly 1000 pages, several very large Latin textbooks, other philosophy books, three different copies of the Bible, etc etc. Probably approaching 7-8000 pages of material ALL AT MY FINGERTIPS!........Plus the web when near Wi Fi and connected.

My wife received her Touch from me for her birthday. She is a voracious reader of thriller/mystery novels, the Vince Flynn, David Baldacci, et. al., genre. Since she got the Kindle Touch her reading speed has increased noticeably. She can make the type as large as she wants it to be, adjust the interlinear gap and look up words she doesn't know with the default English dictionary that comes with the device.

Finally, I can charge my Touch, use it everyday, web time, download time, reading time and a lot of just looking at the screen "think time" I charge it about every two weeks. She does the same, maybe less frequently because she doesn't make the Internet demands on her device that I do on mine. The Fire or the iPad--admittedly devices with much more capability for complex displays, videos, etc can make 7-10 hours before a charge is required. That can be a problem for people on the move.

I am sure I will find other great uses for this device. So far, I can find no knocks at all. My wife had to exchange her first machine because the touch screen wasn't quite right. That was a snap. I have contacted Kindle Customer/Technical Service Support about 7-8 times with questions or wanting to return her first device(which was replaced with the new one by overnight shipment!!!!!!!!!!! At no charge. Had the new one before we had to send the old one back. That is customer service.) The people I have talked to are well-trained, smart, very easy to talk to and polite beyond my experience on the web. Amazon customer service is superior. That is a major selling point as well.

I do not work for Amazon, never heard of them until a few years ago and nobody has helped me learn to use my Touch or my wife's either beyond a few calls about things that were actually easy to take care of if I had only read the right page of the manual. I would buy Touch again in a second! I purchased this amp for a "zone 2" application - 6 separate patio and pool speakers. The flexibility of the configuration of the amp is superb. You could power up to six separate stereo outputs (12 speakers) or as in my case, bridge each channel and power six speakers with a high power output to each speaker. Keep in mind that in bridged mode, the speakers must be 8 ohms or more.

The input flexibility is also superb. There are two separate bus inputs, as well as individual inputs for each of the six stereo channels. Each channel is individually selectable; bus A, bus B or dedicated line in for that channel. Additionally, each channel has its own gain control, so individual channel volume can be adjusted, allowing for a perfect balance of volume to each stereo pair.

In my case, there are six speakers total, three stereo pair. I have fed the Left zone 2 preamp output from my receiver (Yamaha RX-A1080) into Bus A and the Right zone 2 preamp output into Bus B. I then assigned the six bridged channels to Bus A and Bus B alternating; Channel 1 to Bus A, Channel 2 to Bus B, etc. and used those to power the left and right speakers respectively. This arrangement gave me three stereo pair to different areas of my patio/pool, with each output individually adjustable.

The sound quality is crisp and clear. I'm sure this amp is good enough to pair well with audiophile grade speakers, as well as high quality ceiling mount and outdoor enclosures as in my application. It's not a massive powerhouse, but for my application, the power is more than sufficient.

The only complaint I have is that the auto-on feature requires a significantly high input level to fire. I sometimes have to turn the zone 2 volume on my receiver up to about -20db to get the amp to turn on, and then adjust the zone 2 volume back down to my desired listening level. However, this is better than the sensitivity being too low, and having the amp turn on when it's not supposed to. The auto-off feature works perfectly...the amp goes into standby after a few minutes of no input. Build quality is also impressive...it has some heft to it for sure.

Overall I'm very pleased with this amplifier and highly recommend it for similar multi-zone applications.

My work bought each person in my branch a pair of QC25’s from Amazon. I also own a set of QC2’s.

I have to say, whether I’m wearing my QC25’s or QC2’s, I love my Bose QC headsets and will not travel without them. I also use them for work, not just at work.

Since I have both a pair of the old and new, I thought I’d do my own comparison:

1. Equally comfortable

2. In a quiet environment, where noise cancelling isn’t really a factor, I think the sound quality (even of the older QC2’s) is pretty comparable. If I were thinking about upgrading just for sound quality, I don’t think I would.

3. Noise cancelling has definitely improved in the QC25’s over the older QC2’s. In a noisey environment where noise cancelling matters, the difference is noticeable. The QC2’s are good, the QC25’s are clearly better.

4. The QC25’s will work w/o a battery. If the battery dies in the QC25, you will have music, just not NC. In the older QC2’s, the headphones would not work at all w/a dead or no battery.

5. QC25’s have a mic for taking or making phone calls. The QC2’s did not.

6. The case is smaller, but just as protective for the QC25’s. The QC2’s do not fold up as small.

7. They both look good.

8. The prices really haven’t changed over the years.

The bottom line, I love my Bose headsets, both of them. I would absolutely recommend buying a set, particularly if you have a need for a set of quality headphones at work or for travel.

For me, after reviewing the older and newer QC headsets, I don’t think I’d upgrade until the older QC2’s stopped working. I think that Bose headsets are built so well, that time doesn’t diminish the quality and utility of Bose’s older products.

I will note that I had to return the first one I got due to a stuck pixel, but the second one looks great and has been performing well for several months. One additional note: If you are running your audio through this monitor, there are times when after rebooting the computer, the audio sounds garbled. It'd pretty and very gold but it looses sequence at  a hight rate. Don't move it a lot or you will have sequence all over the place.

Wow, I'm impressed. needed quick rough-and-ready 'DSPin' for two gigantic PA subwoofers. Using cheap iNukes for amplification, this analog Filter was the most simple solution. I was skeptical, thinking I would need more options for fine-tuning. However, with this filter I was able to perfectly select the low bass I wanted.
I still would like to know what this filter actually is, a bandpass? Lowpass? Because while intuitive, the 'frequency' knob doesn't make any sense. Is it the lowpassed frequency? or the center of the bandpass? Or bumped up frequency? I would like this to be a bandpass, because you need to cut off the low-frequency information going into your big subs (18" or 21"), I typically use 25Hz and up, otherwise you might damage the driver with overexcursion. So Rolls, it works great, but what is this thing doing? I haven't measured the frequency response, which would probably give me some insight here.

So far so good, this thing has mindblowing sound quality, which is the reason why I bought it. It's a fairly recent development that 'powerful' Class-D amplifier are getting cheap. I use Class D amps in my Pro Audio, and it's just the gold standard now if you carefully pick your brands. I'm using this one of KEF LS50s, which I wanted to provide with 100W/Channel amplification (8Ohms Impedance). Now, realistically the AIYIMA A07 will not put out 300W/Channel so I would not recommend using this little amp to power your Hifi-towers which have significant bass. Bass will eat a lot of power, ultimately reducing the total SPL you will get with this amp when you crank it all the way. And when you crank it all the way, you'll run into a potential problem (which is why I'm saying 'so far so good'). This has nothing to do with the Power supply, but more with Power dissipation. Somebody in the internet took the A7 apart and noticed a rather small heatsink located close to the capacitors. That's not ideal, heat will dry them out over time. If you want to run true 300W/Channel you need a fan or a big heatsink. So enjoy the clean Audio for speakers rated up to 100W but don't push it, you won't be happy as the A7 might just quit or even pose a fire hazard. Or modify it and cool it properly and then crank it.
