I was reluctant to try but after hearing a friend's rave reviews about a certain name brand version of a bone conduction headset I was compelled to give it a shot. I wasn't willing to go whole hog given the price, but after a lot of research I narrowed it down and purchased these.

I'm just going to lay it out... these are PURPOSE BUILT.

One must have reasonable expectations of the technology. One must match their specific purpose with this solution for it to work.

PROS:
1) They are comfy, It takes some getting used to, but after a day or so, you hardly notice they're there. It can get a little sweaty but not any more than say wearing a pair of sunglasses. Still they're lightweight and you'll hardly notice you're wearing them.
2) I wore these for 9 straight hours on and connected to my laptop. By the time I turned them off they were showing nearly full battery power left. Granted it was a slow day and I didn't have much in the way of meetings but it beats having to charge them midday. I imagine on a busy meeting day I'll be cutting it much closer or will need to top it off at lunch. But hasn't been that way yet.
3) The audio is not bassy or broad, but I get clear meeting audio and do not want for more. It is not hifi and won't do justice to music or movies or the like, but figure if you needed to make a phone call, or listen to an audio book or podcast, or if you have zoom meetings all day, this fits the bill. It's like listening to an in ear headset but with nothing on your ear pressing down on it. It also does not obstruct any external noise. I can still hear the sizzle while I'm cooking.
4) The range is impressive and connection is stable. I'm able to go anywhere in the house even on different floors and I stay connected and the audio doesn't clip or stutter.
5) Controls are easy to find and use. Pairing was also easy.

CONS:
1) Like I mentioned before the audio isn't great so it won't replace all your headsets/headphones/earbuds, just the ones you use for whatever you need it to do.
2) At high volume the transducers vibrate on your temples and tickle some. It's like having a broken woofer cone on a speaker except its pressed to the side of your head. Just gotta remember to turn the volume down or perhaps turn down the bass balance on your audio device.
3) Proprietary charging cord. As much as I like the magnetic cable (how easy it is and that there's no jack to wear out), the fact that I must have THIS cable to do the charging is a worry, but since I keep everything work related with my work stuff its not a problem for me.
4) I do wish they were "louder". You can cheat a little and place the transducers right over your ear canal but they're still not as loud as speaker based headphones. In my home office, they're fine. Hanging out outside in a busy neighborhood, no big deal. In a noisy restaurant, its a challenge, for me at least.
5) Lastly, they don't do a great job of noise cancellation. Your audience will be able to hear everything. And my office which does have a little echo... well that echo comes through in these.

CONCLUSION:

I'm pleased with these as they're comfortable and make work communications and audio easy. I will be using these as my primary headset as they're the only ones I can wear all day and not notice. I've got my old Jabra earbuds as a standby in case I'm going to be in a noisy environment but in most cases that can be helped.

I did have a pairing issue but the seller's CS got back to me immediately and solved my problem faster than I could have asked for.

For the price I could not have asked for more and have no regrets!

I have much nicer LED photography lights. EDIT: I have some nits to share as I believe they are important:

1) The included USB wall plug is nice and convenient as there are two slots and it powers both simultaneously, but over the period of about two months of frequent use, the plug just died. I verified by swapping out with a different one. It's just not tough enough and to make things worse the inside of the plug had browned, I'm assuming because of heat generated in the plug. Please be careful.
2) Regarding the aforementioned plug, the included one is great since it appears to provide a full 2 amps of power to each plug. This is an important point in that if you use a lower rated 0.5 or one amp plug, you'll notice your lights just don't get very bright at all.

As a result, I'm downgrading to 4 stars because on the basis that it does its job it is just fantastic, but in the manner that the included power plug needed to be replaced, I'm pushing it down, especially since I have safety concerns.

In the days of COVID... this is how the story begins. Let's set it up. Combine the elements of Work from Home, quiet space at a premium, available enclosed semi-outdoor space, and awesome weather, and you have a situation where the enclosed patio becomes not just ideal for the day-to-day work schedule, but it becomes AWESOME! Only problem is the wifi is on the other end of the property with a solid home construction bulkhead in between along with a sheer wall and other means of interference. I was dropping Zoom meetings, getting late messages, I had a solid 4-5 seconds of speech delay, and my phone would not alert me to anything.

At that point I thought, maybe the router just isn't strong enough. It's only about 40 feet away but still. So I took a chance on a reasonably priced and well-featured (this one) version of a wifi-extender and I am now at full speed. No drops, no lagging, full speed even through a VPN connection. I wasn't sure this was going to be the answer to my speed issues since the base connection isn't terribly fast, but it absolutely worked.

I do need to bring up a quick caveat... the word "extender" may be misleading. The means of extension is by acting as a relay. Thus in order to connect to the home network via the extender, you actually need to connect to the extender instead. If you are prone to moving about the house/property/office, and you need the strongest available connection, you may find that you need to manually switch back and forth to whichever is strongest in the particular location you are at in relation to either the wireless router or the extender. For my purposes this was fine since my work computer stayed put... I just had to switch wifi networks on my phone when I worked in that location.

I certainly didn't expect anything of audiophile quality or anything astounding. Knowing how much I'm spending is the context for the review.

It's a good pair of headphones.

They're lightweight, comfortable, the earpads stay reasonably cool, the cord is just long enough to listen to at a desk (and that's a good thing), and they sound awfully good for what I paid. They also look pretty okay. The fact that they fold flat is a nice little bonus but for a pair of utility headphones, I think these are a home run.

So as a sound engineer and a musician I would put it this way. They're not high fidelity headphones, nor do they work for performance. They won't work for reference/studio work at all. They're too flimsy to call a solid pair, but for casually listening to music while multi-tasking at home or for watching a streaming video, these do just great. I think there are a number of good headphones like this one you can get for less than $20 or so. This one is up there and I would buy it again if I needed another.

I'm not a fan of the ultra-thin profiles of most tablets. Understandably if its a smart phone you want it to slip into a pocket easily but with a tablet for home use there isn't much occasion where it needs to be ultra-slim and consequently unwieldy and as secure as a wet bar of soap. That being said, I know these are meant to be travel friendly and as such I'm glad that they are small and sleek and, in the case of the Lenovo M8 HD, power misers as well. I'm okay with this because I occasionally travel with my tablet and because the remedy for the non-tactile properties of the ultra-sleek tablet is a silicone case like this one. They're not expensive, they do a darned good job of protecting the tablet, and they make the tablet much easier to handle in and around the house.

Normally I don't look for a feature rich version of the silicone case. It's usually going to be just a simple stretch into place "skin" of sorts where corners are protected and screen is recessed to where it is protected from drops and such. Those usually hover around the $10 mark or so. What intrigued me about this case was the rotating stand and the handstrap feature. I use the tablet in bed often as it sits on my nightstand. I also occasionally use it in the kitchen or bathroom too. So those features would undoubtedly come in handy. My first thought was that paying double the cost was a little out of form but that was followed by, "what's another $10?"

The case installs in parts that are intuitive and easy to fit. Some stretching is required and some massaging of corners to get everything to fit. But once in place everything fits perfectly. Buttons work great and have good feel, the power jack is covered by a silicone flap which is easy to access as needed. Cameras front and back show fine and the speaker is exposed. The case itself is nice and hefty, easy to carry, non-slip in enough areas, and dare I say "bouncy" in all the right places.

I removed the shoulder strap retainers that came pre-installed as I don't see myself carrying the case that way. I put those away with the shoulder strap as a just-in-case item for later. The handstrap adjusted with velcro easily and the stand works great. The fact that the stand/strap mount rotates 360 degrees is awesome as it adapts to whatever angle your hand is at whatever orientation that you're standing the tablet on any flat surface. This was of instant benefit as I slipped my hand in and it felt both comfortable and secure.

The one feature I do wish it had was covers for the cameras. I ended up 3D printing some covers for it. I also feel like there is little to no bezel clearance for a tempered glass screen protector although the case itself has enough flex to accommodate it anyway so I'll be adding one in the near future. That being said the case provides a substantial amount of protection for the screen as long as it gets dropped on a flat surface. Conclusion: Well worth the money as it is grippy, wieldy, standy, grabby, and functionally perfect.

I had some several years old PNY Anarchy sticks of a higher rating that have degraded over time and were causing periodic BSOD errors.  I finally got fed up and bought these actually very affordable RAM sticks and replaced the old sticks.  Problem solved and the performance so far has been great.  Granted its only been about three weeks but compared to the old state of my computer this has been amazing.  I can't comment on anything like gaming performance as I haven't put it through its paces but for all else these seem more than adequate.

It takes some getting used to. I have three of these Anker ergos. Two are wireless and are in use at work. One is wired and on my gaming rig at home.

Gaming: My normal mouse is a Logitech gaming mouse which had been my go to for many years. It was fast accurate and had plenty of built in controls for everything I needed. This mouse also has all of the relevant controls and the resolution button is less likely to get accidentally hit than on the Logitech. It does still get hit here and there though. I also find that the vertical style while more comfortable is not as ideal for gaming but honestly speaking is a small niggle in that the comfort is far more appreciated than the slightly awkward hand position (as movements need to be very fast). Is this up to par with other premium gaming controllers? I have my doubts, but it is certainly comfortable and as a wired controller is adequate for sure.

Everyday: Just yes. Especially considering the value. It is both affordable as an ergonomic mouse and comfortable. You may need to make adjustments to your seating angle as the tendency is for this mouse to be most comfortable when your forearm is almost flat on the desk surface.

Look and feel: It is not an especially heavy mouse. But it does have a level of refinement expected on something more costly. It is also well designed and not obscenely gaudy like a lot of products these days. The rubbery matte surface is pleasant and tactile and the buttons are responsive and easy to actuate. The mouse is somewhat full-sized. I don't want to say large because I have small-medium hands and I can use this just fine, but by no means do I have small hands. Those who have small hands might find this more of a challenge to use though I don't doubt you'll get used to it. The primary buttons and grip would be fine, but the locations of the scroll wheel and the forward nav button are a bit of a reach.

Like I said I have three of these in various formats and love them all. Other than my ultra compact travel mouse, these are used on all of my home and work devices. At such a reasonable cost you can't lose by at least trying it.

So this is what I experience everyday. The bluetooth connection is fast and solid. The sound clarity and mic clarity are excellent. The battery life I'd say is fairly average but also as advertised. Once you get used to the buttons this headset is very easy to operate and the earpieces are comfortable for hours. The on/off sound+vibrate are cool sounding and the headset tells you the battery level when you either power up or hit a volume button. You can also switch between Active Noise Reduction On, Active Noise Reduction Off, and Passthrough modes all of which are useful in different situations.

Whereas I normally use a $300 pair of active noise reducing on ear headphones for travel, I took these to London and Paris and they were flawless on every flight. There are cheaper options out there but get these!

I always like using a rubber coat on my tablets/phones. It doesn't need to do anything special because I use these tools around the house. For this tablet I just need to make sure I don't destroy it if I drop it.  That being said its a nice little bit of extra security for a costly piece of sensitive electronics.  The rubber is somewhat soft and because of that its very easy to install but its also somewhat wiggly.  The corners stay in place fine but it does want to slip a tiny bit on the long edges. Once I installed my tempered glass screen protector it moves off a little more even.  BUT - the holes for the speakers are well placed and don't interfere with sound at all, the raised parts for the power and volume buttons are easy to find and tactile and they work just fine... no guesswork.  And the 'kickstand' which I didn't care about when I bought it was actually a nice little bonus.  Because of the stand it doesn't lay flat on its back but after a day or so I found that to be preferred.  Five stars because it does what it promised and there are no bad surprises.  Would buy again!

I want to preface this review with a quick note; I returned mine shortly after receiving. This had everything to do with the feature set that I was looking for and not with the quality or performance of the item.

Within the price range that this dashcam is offered, this is a fully-featured and functional dashcam. I did a considerable amount of research about several of the more affordable offerings and determined that the LEVIN dash cam seemed to satisfy and could be a solid investment.

The product pictures appear to be taken at an angle that make the item appear to be much bigger and bulkier than in hand. In reality, the LEVIN Dash Cam is slender, small, and discrete. The installation is not dissimilar to other models and is very quick and easy.

I don't want to comment on the actual performance because I had a very limited experience with the item. But according to the research I did while shopping for a dashcam, the image quality and video performance was satisfactory if not very good. Nevertheless, consider this just a vicarious assessment.

The physical buttons and layout are good. The button click action is substantial and assured and the buttons themselves are easy to find and depress. Unlike the dashcam I upgraded to, finding a button doesn't necessarily require direct sight as the button layout allows for easy tactile navigation of the control panel. My upgrade item however has a touchscreen with no physical queues as to where specific controls are located.

Lastly, the reason why I returned it... no wifi. My primary reason for investing in a dashcam was an incident that my cousin had. His dashcam had captured a traffic accident in which he was not at fault. The other driver of course dishonestly tried to establish fault by my cousin, who promptly downloaded the related video content to his phone, showed it to the responding traffic officer and sent copies to both the reporting officer and his insurance company. While the content can easily be obtained from the onboard storage, the ability to share and view that content on the fly allowed my cousin to establish non-fault and include it as part of the LEO's official incident report. Wifi is the feature that made this possible and because of my cousin's experience, it's one that I didn't want to miss. I do wish however that my new dashcam had the capacitor feature that the LEVIN has.

Aside from lacking the wifi feature, this dashcam is everything I would need it to be. It's also more affordable that most given its feature set. Even if you were to upgrade at a later point, I don't think you can go wrong with this one. Unless price is not an object, if so look to this model as a good pattern for the kinds of features you'll want in a more expensive model.

I've been using an older Onkyo 5.1 for awhile now.  It was a good one, but this Yamaha has so many more features than my older receiver.  For what I like it for, classical music, its great.  I prefer straight through sound fields rather than the custom ones, but certain ones work great.  It also connects to my PC through HDMI and runs all 5.1 channels.  The YPAO feature made configuring the speakers a snap!  It really only took a minute to set it, and if I ever have to reconfigure I just have to do the same 2 step process.

No frills banana plugs.  These are easy to put together with just a screwdriver (and assuming you have a wire stripper).  They don't look all that great, but WHO CARES... they go in the back of the receiver, right?  They work.  If you're running more high end equipment, spring for the upgrade.

My coworkers are jealous.  Its quiet enough that I forget to turn it off sometimes and the speed is just right to cool down when I've been active around the office. If you're going to plug it into your tower that's on the ground you may want to get a USB extension cable. I have a USB hub on top of my desk and it hasn't been a problem.

Easy to install, although the instructions are a little funny.  After installing the first one six months ago, I haven't had to replace it once and the first one is still going strong even with daily use.  Do be sure to be in a nice clean dust-free environment when installing, preferably without any fans on or wind blowing.  Does not reduce the sensitivity of tactile input at all and the clarity of the shield does not reduce the view of the screen either.

Wow for the size it sounds great. I like that it isn’t big and bulky. Clip it on your belt and it’s barely noticeable. I would buy a lot more of these it needed.

I love it, I really do. It works wonderfully and is such a super adorable color! It does have a bit of a funky smell but then again anything plastic/rubber and so on does for a few days when new. My top ten include dogs, sewing machines, houses, my bed, a few trips, and my Kindle. I love my Kindle so much that I actually bought a Kindle edition of a big, heavy, expensive book that I have in hardback just so I don't have to carry it around. It has taken just one month for me to only want to read with the Kindle. It's going to save lots of bookshelf space, my bookshelves are jammed. I love being able to use the dictionary and look up many more words than I used to. Yes, you know the meaning from the context, but it's fun to know the etymology. I took Latin many years ago and frequently consider the root meanings of words, and having the Kindle dictionary makes this easier. Wikipedia is wonderful, too. I looked up the Magna Charta while I was reading a book that mentioned it, and found when it was written, what it was about, etc. I have also looked up some cities to find demographic and weather information.
The ability to change font size and page justification is a good feature. It is important to realize, however, that you can't change justification if the book wasn't formatted to allow that. You get those giant gaps on some lines when it's in full justification. If you use a small font, it's not so bad. Most of the books I have purchased allow left justification, and my guess is that more and more books will be formatted that way, which generally eliminates those gaps. You can get the first chapters of books as free samples, and see how they are formatted, as well as whether you like them as far as writing and subject is concerned.
The next thing I plan to do is put some of my music from my iPod onto the Kindle so I can listen to background music while I read. I understand you can't control the order of the songs, so I'm only going to put on classical music that is not distracting in and of itself.
Getting more books fast is great, too. I forget the name for the phobia that is the fear of running out of things to read, but I have a small case of that, and Kindle is the cure.
Traveling is much nicer when you don't have ten books in your book bag.
I'm asking for an SD card for Christmas from one of the grandkids (it's very inexpensive) so that the Kindle will have even greater capacity.
When you go to the Kindle store from your Kindle, there will be recommendations based on what you have bought, just like there are when you go to Amazon online. However, online you can say "not interested," but on the Kindle, you can't. You get the same recommendations over and over. It would be nice if you could delete recommendations from your Kindle. But, hey, that is definitely just a small thing.
Another thing that would be nice is a password for 1-click ordering from the Kindle.
I'm retired and on a relatively small income. If I lost my Kindle and couldn't afford another one, I would go back to work just long enough to get the money to replace it. That should tell you how much I love it, 'cause I sure don't want to work anymore!

I bought this camera about 8 months ago to keep in my purse. (Completely protected in a hard case.) We also have a 6MP digital Canon SLR we bought in 2003 that was SO expensive at the time, and this camera is BETTER and 1/4 the price (over $1000 vs $266). The 10x zoom is the equivilant of a 280mm zoom lens. Obviously this camera also has 12MP. I can't believe you can get this kind of MP and zoom in a pocket camera. The color and clarity are excellent, even when using it as a camcorder. It picks up the various hughs of a rainbow better than my naked eye. I have recently used the "sun" (bright) mode taking photos of the snow, and it is an unbelievable difference from using a "regular" mode, which is just all bright white. Our SLR does not have a pre-set "sun" or "bright" mode - you would have to manually configure such a thing.
The camera itself is compact and sturdy. The viewing window is huge and the controls are user-friendly. The on/off, photo snap, and zoom are all convient to the trigger-finger, but not so close that you accidentally bump one while using another. I do dislike that you have to change from "picture taking" mode to "picture viewing" mode to delete a photo you just took if you don't like it, but this isn't a major issue for me.
I only have two complaints. One is, you cannot zoom while you are using it as a camcorder. You need to zoom to the level you want before recording, and if whatever you are recording moves closer or further from you, you are, well, SOL! I don't think it is a limitation of the hardware, I think they just didn't include it in the internal software. Second, the battery doesn't keep a very good charge after just 6 months. And I was NOT using it extensively in either photo or video mode. The battery is not part of the warranty. But you can pick up knock-off batteries (which reviewers say also only have a rechargable life of about 6 months) for $6-$7 apiece, vs the "Canon" brand battery at $40.

We ironically bought this radio just in time to get it home and receive an alert. I'll tell you now that we live in a major city and are therefore not far from NOAA transmissions, so I cannot comment on how great the signal strength is further away.

This radio is water resistant and comes with a heavy-duty belt clip and 10-second blue backlight, and therefore is probably great for outdoor enthusiasts. It's not lightweight, but rather obviously durable, quality parts. It also has two built in alarms (and a snooze!). We've not used these since we have a regular alarm clock, but this feature would definitely come in handy on a camping trip along with the backlight.

We had no problem using the SAME technology to program our county and a few surrounding ones, and receive just those alerts. We keep this radio on the "standby" mode so it only comes on when an alert is transmitted. Also, the volume can be set anywhere between whisper quiet and unbelievably loud!

One thing it is missing that I have seen on more expensive models is the ability to pick which warnings you want to hear. For example, it would be nice to just get tornado warning alerts at night and not thunderstorm warnings also. But we didn't want to spend the extra money for something that insignificant, and this radio has served us fine.

While it's not one of these vaccuum power models that do everything but, the dishes...this one will suit your needs if you're not opposed to spinning the record yourself and drying them your self. P.S. (Update to earlier review from March 2013 - added April 17th, 2013)
We found that the records only get as clean as you are willing to put forth the time and effort for. Since we wrote our review, we've seen and used one of the fancy automatic ones and believe me, this one does the job, better, if you're willing to put in the effort, without the over the top price tag. It uses the same cleaning fluid as the expensive motorized ones and does an even better job because you can pay attention to details and especially dirty spots, are cleaned easier with this system.
We also use the glue method when a recording is exceptionally dirty. Amazing! Wonder who thought this up? But, it does pull the dirt right out of the grooves! Between this system and the glue method (we use plain old white Elmer's School Glue) you can't get your recordings any cleaner. As SOON as we have a clean record, we play them into our computer, run them through our program to eliminate pops, clicks, and etc... and then download them as MP3 and/or put them on a CD. Then we put the records in a NEW sleeve to keep them clean and put the cover, old sleeve (if it's collectable) and the clean record in a new paper or static free plastic sleeve to store them until they are sold or needed again. If you're going to invest the time and money into old Vinyl, make it worth your while.
We also like the fact that you can re-use your fluid more than once and you can keep an eye on it and know when you have to change it. We have a recipe for the fluid but, it's also easily found on YouTube. This is the most economical way to clean vinyl you'll find and it probably does the best job, as well.
It seems now that Vinyl is seeing a resurgence now that these youngsters have found that MP3's are not the sound sensation they were led to believe they were! Some vinyl, no matter how popular, due to copyright laws and problems, will never see a new vinyl groove or cd pressed of them so we need preserve as much original vinyl as possible. This is the best way to do it at present!
One note, be careful NOT to wet the record labels. We do quarter turns and wait for excess to run off before turning again, but, you experiment and see what you come up with. If you find better ways, we'd love to hear about them!

The quality

Quality of Life Cons: (basically super nitpicks. Feel free to ignore. The case is great!)

I made up cables for power for my Skywatcher EQ-6R Pro mount. These connectors fit perfectly.  Just PAY ATTENTION TO POLARITY. I've heard you can fry your mount control board if you apply reverse polarity. So check, and double check before powering the mount.

Worked fine once I realized the cable is a UART and I had to install a driver for it. Was having trouble, getting error messages, checked Device Manager, and realized there’s a UART in this cable, which requires a driver. Looked it up on the web and found one, but it wouldn’t auto-install. I had to manually install it. Suddenly, COM4 appeared and there was the mount. My mount is an LX200GPS, and I still need to connect the handset for this to work, sadly. Meade has discontinued making the Autostart II handset, so the mount is doomed to become obsolete unless someone else makes handsets or an emulator. This cable works fine, though, once you figure out the driver software & install it.

These cameras are amazing. Get a 32GB chip, put CHDK on it and you can do awesome stuff with this camera. I bought two for my family's trip to Alaska, and we snapped thousands of photos. Here's a neat trick: You can use these cameras as low power microscopes. Put the Macro setting on, take a photo as near ask the thing will focus, which is pretty close, then hit 'Play' and use the zoom lever on the shutter release to zoom in and get a microscope view of what you took the photo of.

Also, with CHDK on the SD card, you have a built in intervelometer for taking time lapse sequences.

Good quality material-sufficient thickness to make a good screen protector and be reasonably easy to apply. The end result looks very good.

Pros:
-Comes with lint removal cloth
-Easy to use, rigid squeegee to push out bubbles
-Several pieces of tape to remove lint and dust particles from the underside of film while applying THIS IS A BIG DEAL and it's the first I've seen with this addition...

Cons:
NO INSTRUCTIONS INCLUDED so if you haven't applied one of these before you'll be lost and need to search on-line for how-to
Protective film only on ONE side. This is an issue because the squeegee applies pressure to the upper surface of the protector and can, if pressed with enough pressure mar the finish of the protector's surface.

QUICK HOW TO APPLY INSTRUCTIONS:

WHAT YOU'LL NEED:
a) One wide piece of baking parchment paper (18 inches) cut to a length of about 24 inches OR two pieces of standard width waxed paper cut to 24 inches long.
b) Some spray cleaner for eye glasses is nice but you can window cleaner IF you don't use too much (really just a spritz on a paper towel will do.
c) All the pieces from this kit laid out on the work surface (see step 1, below)

APPLYING THE SCREEN PROTECTOR (DON'T TOUCH THE STICKY SURFACE WITH YOUR FINGERS)
1) Do this on a dust free (or relatively so) surface. That means don't do it on top of your table cloth. Do it on a table top or counter top.
2) Wipe the table or counter top with a slightly damp cloth to remove dust particles then dry it with a piece of heavy paper towel.
3) Spread out a piece of wide baking parchment paper or two overlapping pieces of waxed paper (this is your work surface)
4) Take another paper towel and spritz it VERY LIGHTLY (half a spray or less) and wipe the iPad's screen and case. Get rid of all the smudges, dust and finger prints and be sure the screen is as dry as possible--completely dry is best.
5) Using the same paper towel, wipe the top of the screen protector sheet lightly and make sure it's dry. Do the same to the side that you will peel back before adhering the protector to the iPad's screen. This gets rid of stray dust particles and a bit of the static that builds up on the screen protector sheet.
6) Lay the iPad screen facing up onto the parchment or waxed paper surface and wipe the screen gently and completely with the dust removal cloth from the package. Be sure to get rid of any dust you can see (there's some you cannot see--more on that later)
7) Pick up the protector sheet and grab the tab with the number 1 printed on it.
8) Gently pull back about half an inch to one inch of this protective covering to reveal the adhesive side that will be placed against the iPad's screen.
9) Place this uncovered section on the iPad's screen at the correct end (remember--the camera hole and home button hole do go an specific ends so do this correctly.
10) At this time there may be some bubbles between the sheet and iPad screen. Gently push them out with the squeegee. It's easier to do this when you catch them near the edge that is just beginning to adhere. You can always pull the protector up a bit to get rid of bubbles.
11) PATIENTLY AND SLOWLY keep pulling the protective sheet back and off of the stick side of the protector sheet, laying the protector down a little at a time and using the squeegee to push out bubbles as you go.

THE TOUGH PART---
THERE ARE ALWAYS SOME MICROSCOPIC DUST PARTICLES THAT FIND THEIR WAY BETWEEN THE SCREEN AND THE PROTECTOR SHEET. THIS IS WHEN YOU USE THE DUST REMOVAL TAPE STRIPS.

A DUST PARTICLE CAN LOOK LIKE A BUBBLE. THIS IS BECAUSE THE PARTICLE IS 3 DIMENSIONAL AND AIR DOES SURROUND IT. YOU CANNOT SQUEEGEE THEM OUT.

THESE PARTICLES STICK TO THE UNDERSIDE OF THE PROTECTOR SHEET NOT TO THE iPad SCREEN.

DO STEP 12 BELOW IF YOU HAVE DUST PARTICLES.

12) Get a piece of the dust removal tape-pull it off the sheet it ships on. Hold it with the stick side up. LIFT the screen protector sheet just high enough to get the piece of tape under the protector sheet until you think you're in the correct spot. Stick the end of the tape strip to the underside of the protector and then pull it away. This should remove the dust particle IF you carefully noted the location of the dust particle. This part takes a while and can be frustrating. I learned to live with two or three because some just won't go away. IF A DUST PARTICLE will not come off with the supplied tape, try some scotch tape or a short piece of clear packaging tape-the adhesive is a bit stronger and can pull particles off that the tape strip included in the package will not. Fold over one end so you don't stick it completely onto the sheet as doing so will force you to use another protector.

13) Keep removing the protective sheet, laying the sticky side down onto the iPad's screen, using the squeegee to push out bubbles and the tape to remove microscopic (almost dust particles).
14) Finally the entire protective sheet will lay flat on the iPad's screen. Use the squeegee to push out any remaining bubbles.
15) Use the dust removal cloth from the kit to buff out any smudging caused by over zealous use of the squeegee.

Final note: The whole process takes at least 30 minutes and can take up to 45 to do carefully and properly to produce a result that is bubble free and has as few dust particles between the protector and screen. Take your time, be patient. Have a stiff drink AFTER your done.

After messing around with two of the cheap Asian manufactured antennas with rotors (neither of which actually rotated right of the box) I finally coughed up a bit more change and bought this one from Winegard. I should have done this is the first place. In less than an hour I had removed the cheap Chinese junk antennae and replaced it with this one from Winegard.

I googled something like "correct direction to point antennae for maximum reception of San Francisco HDTV stations." I found a web page that had all the stations in my area listed and the direction in degrees around 360 from North to which to point the antennae for maximum reception. I then downloaded a free compass app for my Windows phone, and put as much of the antennae together before taking it up to the roof. Once mounted on the pole with the mounting hardware and tightened just enough to allow me to move the direction of the antennae, I fired up the compass app, and found my heading (324 degrees). I rotated the antennae by hand to that approximate direction, adjusted it a couple of times and then tightened it down all the way.

My HDTV (and probably yours) requires me to do a channel search after installing a new antennae or rotating an existing one. It's the way these sets find signals and add them to your list of available channels. I've got all the national network channels, including three flavors of PBS (nine total channels), have clean reception of CBS, FOX, NBC, ABC and a host of other stations I never knew existed before--61 channels in all.

Winegard has been making antennae of all varieties since I was a kid (a very long time ago) and they are known for excellent design, quality and for working well. This company knows how to build a great antenna so if you're looking for one to replace your cable provider with an outdoor antenna and streaming video from the net (like Amazon's Prime) this unit makes a great choice.

OTHER STUFF TO CONSIDER:
--I don't have a direct line of sight to Sutro Tower, where all the major networks and other stations have their antennae and that still did not keep this antenna from working.
--If you're a long way away from the TV station transmitters you may need to add a preamplifier unit to the installation. You'll know you need one if after installing your Winegard reception is still not great. You can find them here at Amazon.
--If you live in an area that doesn't have one huge tower all the stations antennae mounted on it like Sutro here in San Francisco, you may also need a reliable rotor to turn the unit. Again you can find a great one made by Radio Shack and sold on Amazon.
--Plan on another $50 for a heavy gauge 5 ft. pole, and an additional $50 for each additional 5 ft section. Even factoring in a preamp, a rotor and some lengths of pole, you're still going to come out way ahead of your cable bills.
--The higher you go, the more sturdy a mounting you'll need so there may be some costs for guy wire, screw eyelets, roof sealing compound for around the hole the screw eyelets make in the roof.
--This antenna does not come with any 72 Ohm coax so you'll need enough to run from the antenna to the set. This also means some crimping tools for the end hardware.

THAT WAS THE WORST CASE SCENARIO:
--Reality is the further you live away from the broadcast stations and if the stations transmitters are not at a central location, the more stuff you'll need to consider before buying this or any antenna.
--You'll likely end up needing the antenna, a 5 ft. pole, some coax and connectors, a piece of free compass software for your phone, or an old compass (remember those). If you figure a total budget of not more than $150, and factor in about 90 minutes of your time to assemble, install, and adjust direction you're likely to have enough left over for some good beer.

FINALLY:
All the essential hardware needed to mount the antenna to the pole and connect it to coax is included with the antenna. I had no missing parts.

For the money, this is a great value.

I tried a lower-end model of the Boogie Board and wasn't satisfied because there was no way to save my notes. In my work I have to plan menus, estimate quantities of food, jot down some new ideas and scribble some diagrams. These I needed to save for use later. The lower-end model did not save and was defective out of the box. Amazon gladly facilitated my return and refund so I could get this model.

The Rip does exactly what I need it to do. I can make notes and doodles to my heart's content, press the Save button and my current page is saved to internal memory where I can access it later on my PC (I run Windows 7 so I can't comment on other Windows versions). Everything you need is included in the box; you get the Rip, a very sturdy stylus, a USB cable, some instructions on its use and two coupons for additional software. One is from the manufacturer, I think its name is Studio Notes. I'm using the fully loaded trial version presently and what the software does is run on my PC, take my notes and scribbles onto the computer's hard drive and from there with the click of a few menu choices converts it into Word-ready text--like you actually typed it at the keyboard--opens Word and puts the converted notes into a new document.

This software takes my very, very sloppy handwriting and converts it almost error free. I'm amazed since I've worked with character recognition software programs since the late 1980s. In my opinion, if you need to take your notes into Word or other word processing packages via RTF, this software is a must have. It's not cheap and it's priced in Euros so I can only estimate that its cost, with the discount from the in-box coupon of 25%, is around $60. There are other apps as well, including one that is a calculator capable of some rather complex mathematical operations.

The second coupon is for Evernote, a cloud-like app that enables sharing across multiple platforms and locations. I have not investigated it yet. I have used Evernote for the PC and never really put it under any sort of stress.

There is one glaring omission in the design of this product and I've listed it under CONS below. All-in-all this is a product I highly recommend, it's useful, sturdily constructed and solves a problem I had keeping track of random notes and sketches.

PROS:
--Holds a charge for a very long time

--Saves documents in the mostly universal PDF format

--On-board drivers install into Windows flawlessly

--Sturdy stylus

--Rugged USB cable

--Integral part of a total solution this manufacturer is creating

--Good depth of available add-ons

CONS:
--I gave them just FOUR OUT OF FIVE stars for missing this most essential function--once you save a page of notes and diagrams to tablet memory there is no way to get back to any saved material until you're once again connected to a PC or Mac. It is not like a lined pad which allows you to flip back a few pages and revisit a topic during a meeting, when developing a lengthy meeting agenda or process and want to see if you noted a particular item further back, or some other complex process in which you may be involved. They really, really should fix this. I hope when they do, the fix will be made available to those of us who purchased this product pre-fix.

--You cannot password protect the device

--After you move your notes from the Rip to your PC, and the notes are no longer in tablet storage there is a glitch I have had to remember to work around. When tablet memory is empty and you create what is your first note, then press the Save button on the Rip, the Save light does come on but the document is somehow missing from tablet storage when I connect to my PC. This is most inconvenient as the first page of anything generally is the summary/overview of what will come next. THE WORK-AROUND seems to be to save a junk document BEFORE you start to create your real content. I write the word JUNK on the first note page, press Save, watch the pretty green light. Then press Erase and start my actual work. The JUNK file never shows up but the first page of what I've worked on does. It is possible that I'm doing something wrong but the documentation is so bad I can't figure out what it might be.

--The documentation is virtually worthless even though it's provided in about every language known to mankind. You have to really scan the pictures to get what it's trying to point out.

--The tablet only recharges when connect via USB to your computer. If you're on the road without your PC, I think you're pretty much screwed. I haven't actually had this happen yet and as this is the case I am diligent about making sure it get charged regularly.

--You do not have the same amount of space as on a regular lined piece of tablet paper. Nor does the tablet's line thickness seem as easy to control as the specs lead you to believe. Line thickness is about 1 to 1.5 mm.

NONE OF THE CON POINTS is a reason to pass up this product if you want to get rid of your paper note pad and random pieces of paper notes. It is a very good product at a very reasonable price taking into account its functions. Aside from the foregoing, yes you can get similar software for your tablet PC, either Android or iPad. However, as I am not willing to take the risk of losing a piece of equipment costing in excess of six or seven hundred dollars as well as the value of the information stored on my tablet PC this is a good alternative. I can afford to lose or have stolen an item of this price and I won't be using it for storing sensitive client or personal information.

If you buy the Rip, pop ten or so extra bucks for the neoprene sleeve; it fits the unit snuggly and doesn't let it fall out. It does make getting the tablet a bit harder to get out, yet I'd rather have a snug fit than a broken Rip.

For the price, this is the 3D plasma to own. Panasonic makes the highest rated, best plasma displays on the market for the middle-end consumer and even higher-end sets. The GT30 has taken some hits due to its black-leveling during scene transitions. This seems most notable to those who may not understand or have the know how to alter the video settings properly; I DID notice this occurring when video output is set to "standard", once you tune the display properly, there should be no noticeable or any flickering between darker scenes to brighter transitions. To go into great detail on how to properly set your TV would be worthless, a "good" picture varies person by person but this preliminary issue should not deter one from purchasing this set.

With that out of the way, consider this: you will not see a better high definition plasma display on the market. At the GT30 price, you are not going to get 3D quality, HD quality, feature set and value any where else. If you have not been to any store to view other brands competing with this set/price, do so and do yourself a favor. Once you see a GT30 set up properly, showing the same content as other brands, there should be no questions left to answer. The display owns. From blu rays to PS3 to Wii to regular DVDs, I have not scene until this plasma a more OUTSTANDING visual display. Blu Rays appear as though people are standing in your living room.

the most noticeable attribute of this plasma, at least to me, is the quality and richness of the depth in the display. Its simply amazing. Looks like you can reach your hand into the background and touch things. And no, I am not talking about when 3D is on, that is another story. In pure HD form without 3D, the depth, black, and richness of this display is simply jaw dropping. Your friends will not understand what they are looking at. To note, a HD gaming system looks simply unbelievable. You will be playing your games for the "first time" all over again.

The bad: THE SPEAKERS ARE DOWN RIGHT AWFUL. if you do not have some sort of surround sound system, or at the very least two channels (front left/right) the speakers sound terrible, they may as well sold it without them and saved a few bucks. You will need some sort of sound bar or extra components to get anything other than dialog. And the dialog is barely satisfactory; no bass, tiny highs, bad spacing and underpowered.

3D: Panasonic has the best 3D on the market. Compare it with Samsung or Sony. There is no comparison. View them back to back and you will find that Panasonics 3D technology, although requiring ACTIVE shutter glasses, reproduced 3D images in HD form where as others may not. Samsung for example, 3D reproduction looks like cardboard paper cutouts with no depth and lacking resolution. Not in the GT30 however. The 3D is amazing and even the 2D->3D reproduction (taking standard 2D video and artificially creating 3D images) adds incredible depth to your viewing experience, albeit not so much "pop" off the screen. Worthy to note is that 3D viewing does produce a somewhat dimmer display, not sure if this is due to the glasses tint or how their system works, but overall when 3D is on, expect a less vibrant picture from non-glasses viewing.

Overall, theres not much out there for the GT30 price that offers screen size, content and value. Above all else, picture quality should take the cake here. Please check it out in a store and make your decision. Cant beat this set. On a side note, internet connectivity works flawlessly, I wired the TV with a ethernet cable, which, you should do if you expect the highest speeds and purest connection. The TV synced up with zero glitches and loaded youtube, pandora and amazon with the ease of touching 1 button.

Excellent buy, sound is its largest demerit but can be remedied for a couple of bucks. Good luck!!

UPDATE: after running these for just over a year - lets clear up alot of the ASTOUNDING reviews. Realize that to get the best sound out of any speaker does not begin with the speaker itself but with the amp/receiver that pushes them. I would NOT buy these to plug into some home theater kit bundle receiver - that wont cut, even just on the power rating alone. One of the main reasons why I wrote a favorable review is due to the fact that the Sony's are connected to Yamaha's highest - rated receiver which pushes a clean 140w x channel. Thus, my review may not be a typical review of what to expect in sound quality. That said, the Sony's do an incredible job managing sound in their application as a part of my 7.1 setup, much of that can be chalked up to a quality amp which makes the 7000's sound so much better.

Cut to the chase: these speakers require a heck of a lot of EQ'ing (and power) to sound GOOD. You most likely will need a subwoofer to assist in most situations. They are a perfect set of cheap speakers to complement a smaller home theater system (im not talking like 2-inch cube Panasonic bundle kits, but a nice polk or JBL mid line 5.1 speaker system). In buying these speakers, its a great addition for music listening. Standing alone, not sure the Sony's can work a room without the help of other components or a fantastic top-shelf amp. For those that dont care or just want something tall to fill an entertainment setup, the Sony's are perfect.

Verdict: good budget buy, but do not expect the world out of the box.

I am impressed by the frequency response of the 7's. The low end is fuller of course and they handle the power coming out of my 7.1 receiver better. However, im less impressed with the mid range. Its not as dead on as the 6's and if you move about the room, the harmonics and sound direction change too much. The high end is nice because the speaker is taller than the 6's. I can't tell any difference between the hi's in the 6's and the 7's. The low end, like some reviewers have stated is in fact BOOMY; but this is what you get with a budget EIGHT INCH woofer. Smart and precise equalization is required to get the 7's sounding really good. I spent an hour doing a manual EQ setting distance, independent speaker levels (like LF, RF, LR, sub ETC) EQ'ing each, and finally arrived at a sonically sound room. I then used the Yamaha's auto tune function with microphone to see what the receiver would come up with. To my surprise, pretty similar settings. Where the 6's did not leave many dead spots in basically a perfect 15 x 15 room, the 7's left many pockets of dead air, especially dead center. Took alot of sub & front tuning to clear this up.

In conclusion: I honestly would purchase the SSF-6000's again as their sound is warmer and more even. Those handle 180W, the 7000's handle 200W. If you need a broader bigger sound for a bigger space, the 7000's will do the trick, but i find they initially lack smack and punch in the low end and the mids are scattered. I have a JBL powered 12 inch sub (their higher end) and it helped but did not fix the booming, still working on the tuning. Make sure you have enough power from your amp to these things, they need it. I decided to see what my [...] would buy, the Sony's do no disappoint, short of spending 1200 on a pair of floor JBL's, these do just fine in their own right.

As many have already written this watch has software issues. It does not display pace accurately. There's absolutely NO EXCUSE for Garmin releasing a training watch that doesn't know a person's pace. That's the sole reason this is getting a one star rating. On top of this, it is a simple software fix that they have still failed to make.

There is a simple work around: don't display pace and instead display lap pace. Lap pace has no issues and accurately describes your current pace. All the other pace features also work. Lap pace, ave pace, last lap pace are all accurate. The fact that everything else works fine shows to me it is just a software issue that Garmin could pretty easily fix if they bothered to spend 10 minutes on the issue. I probably would have given it four stars without this issue.

Why I really, really like this watch:

I bought this to supplement/replace my 405CX

The display is bigger and better. You can display four metrics at a time across four screens - so 16 metrics. The font is BOLD and easy to see even in tough conditions. While working out, you can hit the down or up arrow to more quickly get the screen you want to see. Also, even at its smallest, the font is bold and readable even to old eyes that don't see up close so well. The font describing each display is too small for my eyes to see when I have contacts in. So, I need to memorize which spot displays what. Still, this is sooo much better than the 405CX. On that watch, I can only see the big middle display with my contacts in.

The watch vibrates alerts. This is awesome!! I hate watches beeping at me and in loud conditions I would miss the beeps. I much prefer the vibration and I just turn off the audio alerts altogether. Also, the watch now alerts you (via beep or vibrate or both or none - your choice) when it has a GPS lock. The 405 never did this. Awesome improvement.

The battery lasts forever. Well probably not forever but you can use it for an entire day with GPS. The manual claims 22 hrs - I've yet to use it up when I started fully charged. The 405 claimed 8 hrs but it was really more like 6. Also, the 910 can be turned off so you can NOT waste the battery during travel time to your work out starting point.

It shows your recovery heart rate about one minute after you push 'stop' if you don't do the reset count downtime. Someone else mentioned that here. It a wonderful feature and not mentioned at all in the promotional material or users manual.

No touch bezel. The touch bezel in the 405 and 510 is a miserable feature. It has a life of its own in humid conditions which pretty much describes most of the heavily populated USA during most of the months of the year folks train a lot outside. The 910 completely relies on pushing buttons so now it only does things when you WANT the watch to do something. Also, the start/stop/lap/reset buttons are on the face of the watch. Everything else is on the sides. This keeps me from accidently hitting the wrong button when I don't mean to.

GPS programming seems smarter than the 405 / 510. With the 405 or 510 if you stop your movement and forget to hit stop on the watch it will keep adding distance. (For example, you can sit on a bench for a 15 minute break and it will add 0.5 miles to your distance.) I think this is because of GPS not knowing your exact location so it keeps seeing you as 10-20 feet from the last place it thought you were and keeps adding this up even though you are not moving. The 910 seems to do a lot less of this. It's still adds a bit of distance but over a 15 minute break it might be 0.05 miles instead of 0.5 miles.

Other things to note:

This watch is NOT smaller than other Garmin watches but it does stick out from your wrist less but to make up for that it is wider and taller. My guess is that it weighs pretty much the same. If you have a tiny wrist like mine, it can actually be a bit too big for your wrist. I got the cloth strap - this makes that issue much better.

I have not used it for swimming and I don't think I'm going to. It's not worth the risk if there is even a chance of screen fogging.

The manual not very useful. It doesn't show all the features. It is close to unintelligible. If I hadn't already had the 405 and was sorta familiar with how Garmin watches were organized, I'm not sure if I could have figured this out. Garmin's online help is no better.

Hint for female users: I skipped the heart rate monitor that came with the watch and instead got the original plastic hr monitor. I take off the strap and just place the main plastic part inside to top of my bra. It works great this way and is much more comfortable than having a strap wrapped around me and much easier to get in and out of and you don't have to find a private place to do it. I'm not sure if this will work for all women but it might be worth trying if you hate have a bra, HR monitor strap, plus shirt all binding around you like I do.

I got this GPS watch back in September 2010. I use it at least once a week, mostly for hiking, not running or biking. It's a useful little gaget. Sometimes I get frustrated with it because it tickles the ideas of so much more that it could do if fully reliable/prorammed.

Pros
-Up to 4 customizable display screens where I can choose to display 3 fields to display the ~40 metrics the watch keeps on my workout (Current Pace, Average Pace, Pace last lap, etc.)
-Relatively small (I know some might quible about this and smaller would be better but I remember doing field research with a GPS device in the 1990s that was less accurate and weighed about 3 pounds.)
-Pairs with lots of other gagets - heart rate monitors, foot pads, etc
-Hey, it's a tiny little GPS device on your wrist!! It's just fun knowing all these details about a work out I used to have to guess at or spend a great deal of time trying to calculate
-Garmin website where all your activities are downloaded and comparable, trackable, etc

Cons
-Battery is flaky. Specs promise 8 hrs, I rarely get 6 hours. I feel silly quibling about this too since my old research GPS ate ~10 AA batteries a day but it's annoying. I wish there was a better, smaller battery that lasted longer
-Watch does not turn off and thus eats its short battery life even when you don't want it to.
-I must remember to turn GPS 'off' to save battery life. If I accidently leave GPS 'on' while driving to my hiking start point, I can use up 30-50% of the battery life before even starting my work out.
-Poor downloading of activities. The ANT transfer fails a lot of the time. I get frequent error messages requesting I send stuff to Garmin Technical Support. They help but it's annoying to have to go thru this process. I just want a reliable transfer. I recently hiked the Grand Canyon and cannot for the life of me get that work out to transfer to my computer. I can see it on the watch but the computer refuses to download it. The watch won't give elevation info on past works outs - only the computer will. Not being able to see this special activity is obnoxious.
-It doesn't like slow people. Since this is designed for runners and bikers it seems to have a hard time tracking slower paces. Even when I'm fairly confident I'm hiking a consistent pace, the watch will vary from 15:00 min mile to 25:00 min mile - so it's tough for me to know. Overall average pace is more reliable than current pace.
-Distances are not particularily accurate. My 405CX consistently gives different distaces than those posted or those on my hiking partners Garmin 410 forerunner. Someone isn't correct. (FYI The 405CX's distances are less than those posted. The 410's distances are less than 405CX's)
-Garmin website now uses Bing maps instead of google maps. Bing's are worthless compared to google. I can't figure out how to get it to switch back.
-Garmin website defaults to making all your workouts and details public. I'm still not sure if I've set everything to private or not - there's more than one setting. Hey Garmin, some privacy please!!!
-Display changes even when you don't touch the watch in ANY way. It sorta has a life of its own at times. It goes to the navigation screen all the time without being asked. Other times it seems determined to show the clock instead of my workout screen.
-Banner displays pop up on watch screen and won't go away. For example when it's detects a heart rate monitor it beeps at you and displays a reminder accross the screen. There's no way to get the reminder to go away leaving the screen unreadable for 15-30 seconds. If you work out with other Garmin people, this can get tedious, as it goes around 'detecting' everyone else's gagets constantly.
-It reminds you continuously when your battery life is going down. I'm on the trail, what do you want me to do about it? There are no outlets!! It seems like it wastes quite a lot of its remaining battery beeping at me every 10 minutes telling me it's about to die.

Anyway, I've rambled enough. It's a fun gaget but what it can do reminds me of all the things it can't do or doesn't do well yet. I'm hoping Garmin continues to improve its offerings. Having this level of detail is just awesome!!

Great wireless camera/doorbell. Hardware/software this is ideal. We live on a busy street so we were getting lots of notifications. The software allowed us to adjust where the camera sensed motion, cutting down "false" notifications. Easy to use.
Easy to setup and install. Took maybe 15 minutes from opening the box to having it up and running.
Convenient set-up and access via phone (iOS and Android) app. Added skill to Echo, so when someone sets of camera or pushes doorbell, we get a notification via Alexa, and an image on the Echo show. You can adjust how often and what notifications you receive in the app.
Night vision is pretty good as well. Another nice feature is you can access a "live" view anytime, notification or not.
Audio works well, so if you are in the basement, garage, at work, shopping you can talk to whomever is at your door.
If you carry your phone everywhere or have a smart home speaker (Google, Echo or maybe Apple?) you won't need the additional chime, phone and speakers have a decently loud sound.
I would suggest getting a second battery if you have a busy street or lots of activity. The app notifies you in plenty of time the battery is low and needs to be recharged (only takes a couple hours to fully charge). But a second battery extends the life and less work (but to be fair, one screw using included driver, slide off plate, slide battery out, set to charge and reverse process to put battery back in. With two batteries, the whole thing takes about two minutes. With one, you simply have a non-functioning doorbell/camera for a few hours. No biggie, just FYI.
Also there is an an App called Neighbors free to join and use. It lets you share "videos and notifications of criminal or suspicious activity. So if someone in your neighborhood is broken into or home is vandalized they can share the video and/or share a notice of the incident. Lost dog, share. Delivery thieves, share. So both kinda cool and scary.
Now the BAD. To access the video you have to pay a monthly fee ( now if you access the video within the first 30 seconds or so, you are golden, but if you have your hands full, or can't access your phone, you can't see the video, or back it up. While the basic few is like $40 ish a year. Higher for the next tier up. That is forever. And no easy way to back up to a local storage device. All files are on Rings servers.
Now if you know that up front, and $40 is no biggie. Then 5 stars.
But for me that is an issue.

I have had this unit for about four years now. Never a problem. I use it for storing media files and my digital Paintings. It was used for four years on a MacPro 3,1, connected via USB 2. Upgraded the drives over the years, so now it has two 4TB and two 2TB Seagate HDDs.
I just purchased a new (to me) MacPro Trash Can, so I will try the USB 3.
This enclosure is heavy, and not bad looking. The plastic faceplate comes off easy (as it was probably designed to do, to allow easy changing the Hard Drives). But again chances are once you get the drives installed and settings just so, you will not be messing with the door/faceplate. it has tow plastic pins on the bottom and a "latch (Spring loaded)" press and it pops off or on.
The power cord goes in the side, which is weird but not a deal breaker. And unusual configuration, but it is pretty solid and really I don't really mess with it very oftern).
Three fan settings and yes two of them are not quiet. I leave mine on auto and unless I am working on a hot day, moving or writing tons of files, don't hear the fan at all).
The LED lights are not an issue for me, but I could see where in a dark room it would bother some folks. (electrical tape if it really errkks you).
Getting the settings the way you want them takes some trial and error, but once you have them you will most likely not mess with them again.
Drives are easy to add or remove, a couple screws, slide it in the slot.
I have found that if the drive has been formatted and contains data when you add it, you have to force mount it, but once that is done no issues.
So if possible initialize the drive in the enclosure.
This is ideal for novice of mid-level tech geeks, or folks who have a large media collection (Music, movies, photos, etc).
I have hooked it up directly to my Mac Pro and my Wireless router (Orbi) so anyone authorized to access the network can access the media files on it. So my Photos on one drive, Movies on two drives and music on the last drive.
I would highly recommend this to anyone wanting to create a media server.
It DOES NOT have RAID built-in, it can be added via software, but, for a few bucks more you can get the RAID version of this.

A lot of folks are complaining about the "feel" of these keyboards, these, by all accounts are for kids or seniors, or disabled. That being said, yes the keys require more pressure to push down, no they are not just barely touch and letters appear. disabled and seniors (my in-laws) have a difficult time seeing small keys, so the larger keys. As they have limited feeling in their hands and fingers, they need to feel like they are applying "pressure" to the keys. When they used a "touch" keyboard they had nearby characters popping up all over the place, since they could not "feel" when their fingers touched a key or keys. Same goes with some little kids, once they get the hang of the keyboard they have no problem with the soft -touch keyboards.
I purchased one of these a few years back, still working fine. For me, who is used to a soft touch keyboard, it does get a bit frustrating pushing down on those keys. BUT it is not meant for me.
From my experience recommended for little kids, people with disabilities, or seniors.

Trying to decide if we were ready to cut the cord, we installed this antenna to see if we could get all the local channels. We got 40 digital channels about 20 miles west of Washington DC and the major networks are crystal clear.

The network towers we use are clustered together about 20 miles away. We have 2 or more topographical obstructions between our house and the towers (no line of sight). The Noise Margin on the networks is 35-40 dB. TVFool.com listed my location as "yellow" (which means use an attic antenna or higher). The cable drop is about 25 feet and I did not use an amplifier.

This antenna is supposed to be omni-directional but we did experience occasional signal drop on the networks with the initial "eyeball" installation (which was off about 15 degrees). Standing directly under the antenna and looking through a compass I had my son walk through the yard until he stepped into the path to the towers. Then I had him stand still, facing the antenna, and rotated it until he told me it was pointed straight over his head. That seemed to fix the signal drops. Given all the factors of our situation, I am probably maxing out the performance of this antenna. If I have any issues I'll just buy the add-on the reflector shield to increase directional performance...but for right now I don't need it.

Installation was easy (I just mounted it to the Direct TV mast). This antenna is small and light which was a big plus when climbing up a 25 foot ladder.

So far so good!

This is the highest end 12GB RTX 3080 you can get from Asus.  The first thing you need to know is that this thing is power hungry and will create more heat because of that. Something to note if you are upgrading from a lower end GPU. The dual bios switch comes set to performance mode which has an aggressive fan curve and will run cooler but louder.  The opposite if you switch to quiet mode.  This is more of an enthusiast's GPU and if you are looking for quieter and cooler then I'd recommend the Tuf series.  It actually doesn't run very hot, it just sheds it's heat well, so you'll want be aware of that. With a few tweaks it's possible to get your fps into the realm of 3080ti and 3090 land. It's rigid enough that I don't notice any sagging in my rig.  Coil whine?  None here. Luck of the draw?  Maybe. But having a higher end PSU (you get what you pay for) and not daisy chaining the PCIE cables does help.

This card has one of the best air coolers you can get in this price range.  This thing runs cool and quiet and because of that leaves some headroom for tweaking.  It is power limited so there's only so much you'll get, but it's a decent performance increase with very little to no noise associated with it like the other brands (I've tried most).  No hint of coil whine either, which I found is usually associated with your PSU anyway.  Runs good at stock speeds.  Doesn't require extra tweaking to control temps, the factory fan curve is good.  These 12gb variants are being discontinued, so if you don't want to wait for the 4k series and can get one at a decent price then go for it.

This being the first time I have used an ergonomic mouse I had certain expectations regarding how it would solve the problem I usually have with mice. While it removes the pressure points from the center of the wrist the tilt move that point to the bone on the side of your wrist. This is easily cured by a cushioned mouse pad. So why then use it if you still need a soft spot for your wrist? Ease of use! The mouse has a variable sensitivity rate that is nice and high for us power users (move the mouse a fraction and you can span the entire screen), or dial back the sensitivity for doing very fine and slow cursor movements. The two buttons on the side are excellent as the back and forward buttons. I have become an active user of the back button. Saves having to move the mouse to the screen icon to go back.
The Bluetooth connection works about 90% of the time. When you walk away for a bit, or don't move the mouse for a while it goes to sleep. Which requires you to hit a button to make it wake back up. On my Linux environment that translates to a few seconds of time wasted on movements and button play to get Linux to realize the mouse is in play. Using the USB adapter for 2.5Gz communications, there is no waiting for anything to wake up. It simply works. Downside: it eats another port on your computer. If you have limited ports but also have Bluetooth, your best bet is to keep it on Bluetooth.
Overall I have enjoyed its speed and button options. Work very well for what I do. Takes a little getting used to but you'll be a pro in a short amount of time.

This enclosure/cable worked perfectly and allowed me to recover a failed external drive.
My 6 month old external Seagate 1 TB USB drive failed. The drive inside the tinny Seagate case was a 2.5" Toshiba SATA HDD that seemed to be spinning OK so I assumed it was likely that the junky interface had failed and not the HDD itself.

Summary:
I bought this kit because I needed to recover the data on an 80GB Hitachi 1.8" Drive from a dead Vaio notebook. No setup was required after I finished installing the drive in the enclosure, and it was recognized and read on my XP machine without a fuss. The enclosure is a thin aluminum extrusion with channels on the inside. The end caps appear to be pot metal castings. One end cap contains the interface board with LED activity light and the USB connector. A USB cable is provided. The kit is cheaply made but did what I needed.

Installation:
Installation consisted of mating a flex cable and connector, sliding the drive and active end cap into the enclosure, and screwing in the end cap(s).

It takes a bit of care and patience to insert the flex cable into the connector on the drive, but I was able to get it done in a few minutes.
The cable needs to be made to assume an S-bend after attaching it to the drive so that the entire assembly will fit into the box. That is best accomplished by gently pushing the end cap and HDD together and guiding the cable into an S. I suggest you place the assembly next to the enclosure first so you can see how much length the bend will need to take up. It's not much. Then, slide the drive into the enclosure followed by the cable and end cap, gently guiding the cable bend as needed. Make sure the end cap fits properly in place before and while you install the screws.

Here's the part I deducted a star for: The screws go into unthreaded channels in the enclosure and their alignment is less than perfect. It took quite a while and a better screwdriver than is provided to get the screws fully seated. YMMV.

If the drive rattles around more than you like front to back, you may wish to install one or two of the stick-on rubber bumpers that are provided onto the far end of the HDD or the inside of the blank end cap. Be aware you'll have to deal with two more screws if you put them inside the end cap.

I'm an amateur radio operator and generally use headphones, especially when trying to understand weak signals. I wanted something to give my aging ears a bit more volume when I need t. I also wanted to be able to share what I was listening to with visitors using additional headphones.

I haven't actually measured the dynamic range of the HA400 yet, but this past weekend's experience makes me believe it is excellent within the boundaries of the levels that come out of the headphone jack of my receiver. I noticed no distortion during operation.

I believe the HA400 is a good choice cost-effective choice for amplifying and splitting a single audio stream into four headphone-level stereo channels.

Be aware that it requires 1/4" stereo plugs to mate with. You will need adapters if you have cords with 1/8" plugs. The unit comes with a wall wart power supply with a generous length of output cable. There is no ON/OFF switch.

FWIW, I'll be ordering one or two more HA400s for use with our home entertainment equipment. I ordered this unit from Amazon on another account, hence no "Verified Purchase" notation. The price was competitive and delivery reasonable.

The unit was easy to install and worked well as a 56K data modem under both Windows Vista and Mac Snow Leopard (OS X 10.6). FAX mode was not tested. We needed dial-up access to use for one location that we visit only twice a year. Our travel computer is a dual boot Macbook Pro with both Snow Leopard and Windows Vista OS available. I decided to install the modem under both OS.

Installation on the Mac side consisted on plugging in the modem, letting the Mac find it, and filling in a few setup blanks under System Preferences.

Installation under Windows Vista required first running the provided CD (to install drivers), shutting down the PC, then plugging in the modem, restarting the machine, and filling in a few setup blanks.

The written and on-screen instructions were clear and easy to follow for both the Mac and the PC. An important thing to remember for the Windows installation is to run the CD before plugging in the modem. The written instructions are clear on that.

Instructions are provided for Windows 7, Vista, XP, 2000, ME, and 98, as well as Mac OS X 10.5, 10.0x-10.4x, and OS X 9.x. It installed fine under Mac OS X 10.6 using the 10.5 instructions (basically do nothing :-)

The modem performed equally well under both Vista and Mac OS X 10.5, connecting to and using a dial-up ISP at close to 56K rate. We have not tried to use the FAX features. I can recommend the unit as easy to install and use under Vista and OS 10.5+. I expect it will work equally well for other NT based Windows OS as well as Mac OS X from 9.x to 10.6, but cannot speak from personal experience.

FAX Update: I used this modem with my Mac as a FAX machine when I needed to FAX something and my PC's FAX interface was FUBAR. The modem worked fine. I simply selected "PDF" and then "PDF FAX" in the Mac's print dialog. Then I filled in the pop-up form and sent out the FAX. Easy no-hassle process.

My mom ordered 2 of these thinking she'd be able to play music out of both of them at the same time from her iPhone. They come in the mail and we cannot figure out how to do this at all, and the instructions that came with them were unclear, as well as what we found online.
After a few hours of trial and error, this is what we figured out:
Pair both of the speakers to the iPhone
Make sure *one* of the speakers in connected (the other may not show anymore/doesn't have to be connected)
On the *connected* speaker, press the play and + buttons simultaneously (a sound will play)
On the other speaker, press the play and + buttons simultaneously (the same sound will play with some additional beeps)

Play music and they should work! This worked best for us when only one iPhone was connected/paired with the speakers at a time.

Hope this helps someone else!
