I'm really pleased with these headphones except for one thing: The Macbook Pro I bought these to use with is only Bluetooth 4.0, and apparently this causes some conflict because I have to remove and rescan for the headphones every time I use them. I really do think this is the culprit, not the headphones themselves, because the instructions clearly state they should be used with the same version of Bluetooth on the device.

I bought the headphones because my soundcard has gone grouchy and screechy, and I was trying to avoid getting it replaced. Considering this is an early 2013 MacBook Pro, however, maybe it's time for me to think about upgrading....

The headphones themselves fit my small head well, and they stay connected throughout our 1200 square foot house. It's only when I try to go outside that the connection is lost.

Because of scoliosis that makes sitting straight up in a chair painful, I do all of my small press work kicked back in a recliner with a wooden lap desk straddling the arms of the chair. I've got redundant cloud-based backups set up for my most important data, but I wanted to have a Time Machine backup as well. My Seagate 2TB portable was taking up valuable lap desk real estate (I have to have a graphics tablet handy for design work), so when it crapped out on me, I started looking for something else that might work better.

This little Ultra Fit is working just fine. I had to reformat it for my MacBook Pro, but after I did that, setting up Time Machine was easy. I excluded superfluous non-work items (movies, photos backing up to Google Drive, and my archival book files backing up to pCloud and the SDHC drive), so I can actually get a decent number of backups before Time Machine starts knocking off the older ones. And there's room for me to work on my graphics tablet.

Another reviewer said it's flimsy so best for leaving in place, which is exactly what I'm doing. I haven't had any problems with it so far, and it was a small price to pay for the extra insurance and peace of mind.

This is actually about 4.5 stars because they still need to work on the trackpad driver. I love love love the tablet itself in all respects and especially love the shape and handling of the stylus pen. I was (rarely) using an Intuos Pro L, and that pen was just too unwieldy for my hands, so when the dog got it and chewed it up, I bought this tablet instead of spending $68 on a new pen. (My illustrator-artist son will be happy to add the Intuos Pro to his arsenal.) I work in a recliner with a lap desk straddling the chair arms with a MacBook Pro (15"), 2TB backup drive, and smartphone stand on it, and I wanted a graphic tablet I can integrate into my workflow. This is almost perfect for my needs.

Here's what I think needs immediate improvement, like last week!

1. I was getting a "no-can-do" Funk-clunk sound every time I pressed one of the Express Keys or tried to scroll on the trackpad. The functions work, I just get the audio feedback that they don't. I'm dyslexic enough without having to deal with this. I went in and set my alert sounds to Frog, which is not as objectionable to me to hear with every move, and turned the volume down where it's barely audible, but that means when actual notifications I need to hear occur, I won't hear them. So this needs to be fixed. Or is my product defective? I'm curious to know if others are experiencing this.

2. I'd tell you the driver version that I downloaded 3/16/2018, but the Huion website has not added the link to this tablet driver in its regular listing of product drivers so I can't find it again. It took me a lot of searching to find it to start with. They need to fix this for a better user experience for those who do not have DVD drives so have to download the driver, or who want to easily check for driver updates.

3. As others have said, the two-finger up/down scrolling on the trackpad majorly sucks. If I take the sensitivity all the way up to the top, it will scroll three or four lines at a time, but if it's at a sensitivity that allows for varying brush strokes, it scrolls one line at a time. I was trying to set up Express Keys to scroll a page up or down at a time (accessed with the fn key on my Macbook Pro) to compensate for this, but the fn key is not included in the setup for keyboard shortcuts. For now, I'm using space and Shift-space on my laptop keyboard to scroll up and down in those programs (like Gmail) that won't respond to click/dragging the scroll bar with the stylus. Click/dragging to scroll with the stylus works well in some programs. I don't want to waste two Express Keys for something one ought to be able to do with trackpad gestures.

4. The pen nib works as a left click in some programs if held down, but not all of them, so I had to sacrifice my lower stylus button to be a left click; the upper stylus button is a right click, and that seems to be the very best use of that button for me. I wanted to put Cmd+S (save) on the lower button so if I hit the button by mistake it would do something useful, but I guess I'll just start getting used to that button as a fall-back when a pen-nib left click does not work. I do very much like the feel of this stylus.

I really like having the top row of the Express Keys set up like this:

UL: Cmd+- (zoom out) (default)
UM: Cmd+0 (fit to screen)
UR: Cmd++ (zoom in) (default)

The bottom row I'm going to live with for a while to see if I like it or need something else. I mainly do photocompositing sorts of work, so the left and right buttons are often-used commands, but they are also easily accessible from the keyboard without having to put the stylus down:

BL: Cmd+Z (undo)
BM: Cmd+S (save)
BR: Cmd+J (copy layer)

The BM key is the least useful for me because it's so easy to just hit Cmd+S on the keyboard to the left of the tablet. A special request, if even doable, for a future driver update would be to give us the ability to combine Shift, Control, Option, and Command keys from the keyboard with the express keys, which would extend the flexibility of the tablet's Express Keys mightily.

Now, this seems a natural for combining with Affinity Designer's one-letter shortcut keys, so now I'm going to make the time to learn them all. I have not tested how the brushes work yet because I don't do a lot with brushes, but layer-level work seems to be handling super-well. I've also done a bit in ON1 Photo RAW 2018, and so far, so good.

In short: I think this G10T is a fantastic product that, because it's just been released, will need some driver tweaking until it can be the mouse/MacBook Pro trackpad replacement I really want to get used to using all the time. Super build quality, super easy/clean to use, but iffy in the trackpad department.

Even though my mirrorless 4/3 camera has wireless, I found myself not remembering to transfer photos and it being a hassle when I did. I was nervous about buying this card, but so far it is working great for me. This morning, even with my camera turned off, I got a notification that my MacBook Pro is connected to the Eyefi Mobi card, ready to begin transfers. And my initial transfers when I installed it yesterday worked seamlessly, placing my RAW folders automatically into my custom import folder on my Mac; I chose to enable the date folders, but you can turn that off if you don't need them.

My beef is mainly with the software, which seems rather poorly programmed. When I first downloaded the Eyefi app, prior to ordering the card, to see how it worked, it installed fine and offered me the card activation screen. I didn't have the card yet, but there was no way to close out of the screen so I had to leave it hanging until the card came. Then activation was easy, but following the prompts on the activation screen resulted in nothing transferring. After going through all the troubleshooting on the website, it still would not transfer, and rebooting and reloading the Eyefi app did not fix it. Finally, I just clicked "Next" from the hung up activation screen, where I was offered to create an account and got the free year of the cloud service. I did so without difficulty, rebooted, and THEN the app recognized the card and began the transfer. Keenai (which acquired Eye-Fi) needs to work on this.

I've tried so many different types of headphones, from very cheap to uber-expensive, and even bluetooth hearing aids trying to listen to music while working or exercising. I've been frustrated (infuriated, really) with most of them. I have very small ears, so most of the over-ear or on-ear headphones I've used have been just way too bulky, hot, and uncomfortable. But the earbuds and earphone-type headphones have been majorly aggravating and just don't sound very good. I did find a pair that stay in my ears, but then I have to remember to charge them repeatedly. Why does it have to be so hard?

Well, it doesn't with these C6 headphones. They are the perfect size for me. After I've had them on for a while, I don't even notice I'm wearing them except when I notice that I am not fatigued from listening. I hadn't realized it until I listened to some of my music with these headphones, but a lot of the headphones I've tried really muddy the sound. A lot of these bass-boosting devices trash all the dynamics and make it difficult to cleanly hear the words and notes played. Some of them even further compress already overly compressed music, which makes for horrible listening fatigue and also risks hearing damage. So when I first put these C6 headphones on, I thought they weren't very good with the bass because of all the other nuances of the music I was able to hear! It didn't take long for me to adjust.

I absolutely love the way these headphones keep the music from being too loud. I've been sitting here listening as I write this, now a few hours into wearing them, and I have absolutely zero fatigue and am really enjoying being able to play album after album. Folk, Rock, Country, Alternative Rock, all sound really good. I'm not an audiophile, but I've done some computer-based recording and sound editing and think these would work very well as monitors. I'm picking up on L-R panning and other sound engineering methods used by various artists that I hadn't realized were there before.

Also, I have to credit these headphones with my discovering Play Music for Chrome. I've been listening to music with Amazon's music player, but under these headphones I thought the music sounded horrid. I realized it was a matter of the acoustical space, so I went out hunting for something that would allow me to add a little reverb. And found that Play Music sounds fantastic with these headphones! I don't know what they are doing differently, but the difference in quality is amazing. And they actually fit on my recliner-desk beside my 15" MacBook Pro, beside my Time Machine backup drive, when I have to take them off for any reason. I love them.

UPDATE: Oh, shoot. I don't know what I did, but I've apparently ruined these headphones. There are small wires extending from the headset part to the ear cups, and I must have tugged on one of the cords enough to short something out. This resulted in my losing the high mids and frequencies above it. I went to the site myNoise dot net and tried to calibrate to these headphones, and there was literally nothing there in the top three sliders. I might have questioned if it was hearing loss (which I do have), except my other headphones don't completely lose those frequencies. Bummer. I was so happy with them. I had to knock off a star.

When my dog chewed up the cord to my 2012 Samsung Chromebook, instead of getting a new cord, I decided maybe it was time to get a new Chromebook. After reading all the "top five" reviews I could find, I decided to get this ASUS Chromebook Flip because of the excellent build quality compared to the others and the features. My partner has a Windows-based ASUS tablet this same size that he has really loved, so I knew the ASUS brand would be dependable. However, I didn't realize that this one would be the same size as his, but had I been thinking clearly I would have realized I would not be happy with the smaller keyboard size.

When the Flip came, I was definitely impressed with its build. Everything the reviewers said was true. I was thinking about sending it back, but then DP mentioned that he wished he had an ASUS like the Flip that could run Linux; apparently, he's going to sell his other ASUS because he's quitting Windows and the other ASUS machine has something proprietary about it that prevents him from being able to install Linux on it. Other than that, he loves it. He said he didn't want a Chromebook. But I searched and discovered that Linux CAN be put on the Flip and told him so, so he happily took it. I don't think he realized, either, how great a Chromebook is when you're cloud-centric like I am, and like he's increasingly becoming, so he casually mentioned to me last night that he might not even put Linux on it. There's no reason why he couldn't boot Linux from a flash drive, I don't think, if he wants to leave the Chrome as the main system OS.

This MP3 player, which I was given at a discount in exchange for my honest review, is sleek and lightweight yet potentially—via a firmware upgrade that I hope Lonve will consider—very powerful. (See my photo of the player lying on top of my MacBook Pro trackpad to get an idea of its size.) It can be listened to without hooking it up to anything else, either with wired headphones or through the surprisingly good-sounding on-board speakers. The view screen when the player is powered on is quite readable, and I love how the surface of the screen becomes a classy grey-bronze mirrored surface that is so clear you can use it to check your appearance. The ability to add up to a 32GB SDHC card you've preloaded with music or video is a great feature.

The included wired headphones are better than some I've listened to, although I prefer another pair that fits my tiny ears better; unfortunately, those are Bluetooth, so they won't work with this player. I will likely listen to the player my itself, with no headphones, through its speakers.

I can't five-star love this player because I can't set the time to a 12-hour clock and it doesn't allow for adding playlists, which I was thinking it did. Maybe I'm missing something, but I can't even start an album folder playing by tediously navigating to it in the Explorer; it appears you have to navigate all the way into the files in the folder and then start it playing, although I haven't even been able to get this to work. It takes too many steps and is so very aggravating that I usually just quit trying to play either music or video.

What really shines on this player is the radio. I'm sure reception will vary depending on where you are, but in Lexington, KY, I can pull in NPR very clearly and easily. It would be nice to be able to store favorite radio stations—if there's a way, I haven't figured it out after days of fiddling with the player—but I'm happy that I can leave it sets to my main station and it always comes back there even after I've powered off and then back on. If you're a person who likes to listen to the radio at night with the lights off, going to sleep, but don't like fooling with headphones, this will be a great little player for you.

The Game feature has a neat little Tetris-style game that's amusing while stuck waiting somewhere. The Photo feature is nothing to write home about, but it can be used to show off a few photos of your pets or kids or maybe a logo or graphically produced emergency contact info. There is an Autoplay Time setting you can set in the Settings/Photo. The text feature allows for reading text files, so you can take along a grocery list or study notes. I started to knock off an extra star (down to three) because of something I really dislike about this player, and that is the dedicated left-side button (one of only three) that seems to serve no purpose but to turn on the voice recorder. When I press it by mistake or forget that the On/Off button is the button on the right, not the left, the Recorder comes on. Then I get a file format error when I try to get out of it. It would have been better, I think, had they used that button for something more likely to be used constantly (Explorer with the ability to set either the internal C: card or the external D: card as the default for the button maybe) or, better, allow the user to define the function of that button via a Settings selection. I want to be able to disable the Recorder completely, although I know some people will want to have a recorder. But I hate it.

You do have the option of upgrading the firmware, but the instructions are very poor. When I select Upgrade in Settings/System (which you reach by scrolling down to the end, near the Language setting), I am warned to connect to USB. When I connect the USB cable to my computer, however, I get the Connect screen on the player and there does not seem to be any way then to access the System/Upgrade selection. The instructions, such as they are, are clear in how to navigate through the features and which of the two non-Recorder buttons (middle, right) to push in connection with the up/down, left/right arrows. But, needless to say, there are bugs in the player I am reviewing. Lonve has been good about getting back quickly with answers to questions, though, so I'm hopeful they'll work hard to get this one right.

I've had the opportunity to review three different G.G. Martinsen players, and of the three this one is my favorite. I brought two of the players, pre-charged, to review at my sister's where I am staying a week while she had and recovers from surgery, and the one thing I can say right off the bat is that I wish the charging cable was of the ubiquitous Micro-A type and not the mini type, which I did not think to bring with me. The [[ASIN:B016F4AGLC other player]] handles like the [[ASIN:B0173CW2CQ first one]] I reviewed for G.G. Martinsen, but I will have to wait until I get back home to do anything other than test the recorder and FM radio on this 16GB player because I have no cable to copy music onto the player with!

Anyway, unlike the other two players, the controls on this one make sense and handle more like what I'm used to. The instructions that come with this (that I also left at home!) were well-written in English, unlike so many products coming out of China these days. But I haven't needed the instructions to figure out how to use this player or change the settings. The first thing I did was set the Power Off and Sleep settings to 0 so the player won't shut off unless I flip the manual switch to turn it off. I have been listening to this player while I've been writing reviews, and I have had absolutely no cutouts with the FM radio even though I'm in a condo sandwiched on all sides by other units and this place is bad with reception of cable TV and other radios. I like that the station stays selected even when you power the player off and on again.

The control dial is easy to see, with a top Menu button, left and right arrows, and a pause/play button on the bottom (something the other players did not have). The round button in the middle has a good tactile feel, and even in the dark it's fairly easy to feel where to press for the different functions. I'll have to re-read the instructions to understand fully when to use the center button and how.

The little piece you can thread a lanyard into is plastic, but I don't think it will break easily unless you put a lot of stress on it. The player comes with a pair of original Apple-style earphones, which are great for walking outside where you need to be able to hear sounds around you while listening to music. The headphones are not the best in the world, but they are a nice additional feature and good to have in situations where you wouldn't want pricier headphones to get ruined (the gym, outside should it start raining). Of course, your listening experience will only be as good as the wired headphones you plug into this player. It really is a whole lot of bang for the buck and an attractive little player. I have the turquoise color, and it's really nice.

I put links to the other two players I have reviewed so you can compare them. What I like about this one is it doesn't have that gimmicky bubble-gum type selection screen but, rather, just has a list of the different features and functions. The list is easy to read and looks more businesslike and professional than the more cartoonish screens of the other two players.

I have been offered three different G.G. Martinsen players free or at a discount in exchange for my honest review. I like this one better than the first one I got ([[ASIN:B0173CW2CQ an 8GB player]]), but because I went into detail in that review on the different functions (that this one also has), I've copied the functional descriptions from that review below. I'll just compare this one to the pink one in terms of what's different.

I like the black color of this, the ability to put it on a keychain or lanyard, and how small it is, but I don't like the way it all handles nearly as much as I do the [[ASIN:B0168C6MB4 16 GB player]] that I will review separately. The controls and settings are just awfully fiddly and not terribly intuitive. That you can add up to 16GB extra memory via an SDHC card (for a total of 24GB) is a boon, and that's the only thing I like better about this player than the 16GB one; the latter does not have an expansion slot. It's a useful thing if using a player like this when exercising if you can swap out different kinds of music for different types of activity—what works for running or walking will be different than what you'd use for swimming or dancing, for example. But still, these players all hold a decent amount of music natively, and you can also copy a ton of files to it if you're using it to double as a flash drive.

Here's the original functional review for this type of player:

The first thing I tried was the FM radio, because I was really doubtful it was going to work very well in my bedroom, but I was able to pull in NPR and the voices were crystal-clear. The earphones that come with this look really cheap, but they sound pretty good. As with any earphones, they don't cancel surrounding sounds, which makes them perfect for going out for a nice brisk walk. I actually prefer earphones to earbuds because earbuds never fit my ears right. These are like the original Apple earphones, and they stay in my smaller ears really well. I think it's a nice touch that these earphones are included with the player because you can use them in situations where you don't want your really good headphones to get lose or ruined. The device has the following menus, accessible by pressing the Menu button, then the right play button to cycle through them.

SETUP: It's very fiddly trying to set these settings. It takes a lot of trial and error to get it all to work. These are the settings: Clock, LCD Set (not sure what this is), Language (came set to English), Power Off (I can't figure out how to get into these settings to set the times to zero so the player doesn't shut off too soon, so this is why I'm knocking it back to three stars), an Online Mode, Firmware Upgrades, Memory Info.

MUSIC: Navigating through music is straightforward cycling through folders and files. I set up a Walking Songs folder and also dragged my whole Collective Soul Folder with Subfolders to the device, and I was able to navigate between the folders before playing. Selecting specific songs is more difficult. I've never learned how to create playlist files (I know, I know), so I can't say if those will work. There is a funky little equalizer animation on the screen when you play a song.

VIDEO: There's actually a nice music video included on the device, and it will play over and over if you don't stop it. I can see that this might make it possible to put together a loop of items to keep a child entertained on a trip, but it might also have utility for studying, memory work, a flash-card-like experience, or the like.

RECORDER: What it is. Records in .wav format at 32kbps. Great for quick reminders or embarrassing your friends.

VOICE: Used to play back recordings.

FM RADIO: Works great on the stations I've tried, without an antenna of any kind. I may have to start listening to more radio while I'm working.

PHOTO: A simple photo viewer, so you can keep all the pictures of your pets or kids that you'd normally have in your wallet to inflict on the people you meet. I'm just learning about QR codes (scanned my first one on my phone the other day), but I would think you could generate QR codes to carry on this device as well. The device does not recognize .png or .eps files, but it reads .jpgs fine, even larger ones (which do take a bit more time to load).

EBOOK: This is for reading simple .txt files. Don't think you can put anything proprietary like Kindle ebooks on it; it didn't read the .mobi file I copied onto it, or the .epub, or the .pdf. But who'd want to read a whole big book on such a tiny screen anyway? Use the EBOOK capability to take grocery lists or short paragraphs of instructions with you.

GAMES: I almost forgot the games. I'm not a game player. There are a handful of games that I haven't bothered to look at.

This player is not a super-fancy high-end piece of electronics, but it's a lot of bang for the buck and also something you wouldn't die over if you happened to lose it. Of course, you can always use it instead of a flash drive to take files with you different places for subsequent transfer. So it's a lot of functionality in one small package.

I have had a terrible time with trying to wear bluetooth headphones to listen to TV, given that my ear canals are tiny and my hearing is poor. I got some very pricey bluetooth hearing aids, and the range on them is just awful. The on-ear and over-ear headphones are very bulky to wear, and most of the headphones won't hold a charge long enough for me to get through the whole night of TV watching. I picked up these bone conduction headphones on a Woot sale to try them to see if there would be any difference. I like that you can wear these with hearing aids.

I really wasn't sure what to expect, but I have to say that the clarity of the sound makes it possible for me to understand speech on TV without having to read lips. I can keep the volume relatively low and still understand what I'm watching. DP can talk to me when he needs to without having to wave his arms at me to get my attention, and I know that I can watch TV now without disturbing him.

I was able to pair these pretty quickly with my Amazon Fire TV and a bluetooth transmitter that I use when watching cable. The latter took several tries, but it did finally pair. I'll have to get used to how to switch between the two devices, because you can't connect to two bluetooth devices at once. The rockers on the left and right earpieces are intuitively placed—up volume forward, down volume back; skip ahead a track forward, skip back a track back—and the end buttons work to answer/end a call or pause/resume playing music.

I cannot wear these headphones at all in the manner you're supposed to, with the battery compartment at the back of my head. I simply cannot hear anything this way, and that may be because my head is so small. I AM able to hear, however, if I sit the headphones on top of my head&see my photo—and they clear my glasses this way. It's a little unstable this way, so I just use a headband to hold it securely in place.

This review is for the VicTsing Wireless Bluetooth Car Stereo Audio Adapter/Receiver (ASIN B00LWY8Q6S). I notice reviews for a lot of other products from this company are rolled into the reviews page.

I've been given the opportunity to review a few of these car kits in exchange for free product. Unlike some, which were powered through the cigarette lighter and as such are clunkier and less sleek, this one is first charged via USB and then you remove the charging cable and plug it into the audio-in port of your car. The sound then transmits from your phone to the receiver and the sound comes through your car's stereo speakers. If you do not have a 3.5mm audio port in your car, this will not work for you, but if you do, the device is very tidy and unobtrusive and easy to use. Pairing is simple, and I had no trouble with it.

This is one of those products that fills a need, and it fills it well. But make absolutely sure your vehicle has a 3.5mm input (headphone) jack before ordering it! I didn't realize when I agreed to review this bluetooth car kit that our 2007 Toyota Tacoma truck radio does not have one! I had to find a neighbor with the requisite jack in their vehicle to test it to see how it would work. And it works as advertised, routing the sound through the car's speakers, which is rather cool. Imagine driving along a highway with your co-workers, having a conference call with the office. That is really a nice thing to be able to do. And having a quick-tap means of answering your phone while on the road and being able to talk without having to hang onto your phone is much safer

Don't throw away the instructions for how to pair two devices at the same, because it's kind of tricky. Stick them in your glove compartment so you can refresh your memory. There is a specific sequence you need to follow to be successful in pairing two devices.

Because I was imposing on a neighbor, I could not test the voice quality when talking on the phone to someone via the smartphone's mic. It goes without saying, though, that you should have your phone close by. One of those dash or CD-player mounts ought to work fine, and then you can feel like you're riding in a much more expensive car when you use this Tendak car kit. But, again, and I can't stress this enough: Check to be sure you have that headphone jack first. I'm bummed out that I'm not going to be able to take advantage of this neat little bluetooth device.

Okay, I am not an audiophile. In fact, I have cookie-bite hearing loss, which makes it very difficult to listen to anything without either the voice range being too hard to hear or all the frequencies outside of my bitten-off range being way too loud. But I'm starting to exercise indoors more (just moving around, "dancing," is my favorite activity) and have purchased several sets of Bluetooth headphones to try to find something that would work for me for that. This review will briefly compare (to the extent of my ability to describe the experience without audiophile-type knowledge, and also in view of my planned use) three sets of Bluetooth cans, in descending order of quality and expensiveness:

Parrot Zik 2.0
Phillips SHB9100
Alpatronix HX110

I tested each of these by playing two songs ("Money For Nothing" by Dire Straits and "Love and Affection" by Joan Armatrading), both of which have a decent range of complexity but not so much that my ears would get too fatigued too quickly. Also, please note that I have a small head and small ears; the fit of each of these is good on my head. All but the Parrot Zik are on-ear; the Zik is over-ear. Only the Zik requires an Android or iOS app to get the best sound, although all can be used no-frills. I think the Zik is the only one with noise cancellation.

First, the Alpatronix. If you're going to ruin a pair of headphones during a workout, these are the ones to do it with. The overall effect of these is a kind of "wall of sound" that gives you the illusion of a large, expansive sound. After comparing them to the high-end Parrot Zik, however, it soon became clear to me that little details and nuances of the music are lost. If you're sweating to dance tunes, however—especially if you're going to a gym or anywhere else that losing an expensive pair of cans would be a disaster—these are the ones I'd go with. And they are small enough, I believe, for a middle-school child. The range of the Bluetooth is not great. It cuts out badly when I'm in the kitchen or bathroom, where there are appliances in the path of the signal. And of the three, this is the only one that cannot be used wired.

The Phillips headphones are a discontinued model that I've had a while. They used to be my favorite, but that was more because of how comfortably they fit, not how discriminating I am musically. The cup covers feel buttery. The sound is okay. They don't feel as boosted as the Alpatronix ones, which can be a good or a bad thing, depending on what you're after. The on-ear cups fit snugly but don't press to the point of headache, and the headband is sufficiently adjustable that people with larger heads would have no trouble with them. The Bluetooth range is just a tiny bit better than the Alpatronix. If I had to pick a word to describe the sound of these, it would be "smudged." Again, depends on what you're listening to and what you like.

And now we get to the Parrot Zik 2.0s, which are the real point of this review. At first I had a very maddening time with these, so much so that I started to just write them off as impossible. You must have an Android or iOS phone or tablet to be able to install the app that allows you to do all the fancy Concert Hall, Equalizer, Noise Reduction, and Tuned By stuff, and that's a challenge for me because I don't really use any of those. (I have a MacBook Pro, which I tried first without the app, both plugged in charging and via Bluetooth. It was okay but not hundreds-of-dollars okay.) But I do have an up-to-now little-used Android Jelly Bean tablet that I downloaded the app(s) to for testing.

CRITICALLY IMPORTANT: Don't do what I did, which was follow the directions to download the Parrot Audio Suite; the only one in the Google Play Store did not end in a "2" but maybe the Apple Store has the "2" version mentioned. The Audio Suite app did not work at all with my headphones, so I went back and got the Parrot Zik 2.0 app. I had both apps on my tablet, and they were apparently conflicting badly, because all I got was constant cut-outs and garbage. I called Technical Support to find out what I was supposed to do, thinking maybe the headphones were defective, and they said to completely uninstall the Parrot Audio Studio, remove the pairing, and just use the Parrot Zik 2.0 app. When I did that, BEAUTIFUL!

Those little details and subtle nuances I mentioned before? I can hear them. I can manipulate the speaker placement through the Concert Hall effect (my sweet spot is actually closer to 60%, not the wider placements many of the Tuned By presets favor) and also the equalizer settings. If I knew what I was doing, I could tune everything to help compensate for my cookie-bite hearing loss. (I'm thinking a visit to an audiologist to get a current printout of my range of loss is in order.) I love that I can just tap the right ear cup to pause the music without taking off the headphones (why would I bother with that if I don't have to?), and the directions make sense; up to up the volume, down to reduce the volume, swipe back toward the back of my head to go back, swipe forward toward my face to move forward to the next track.

Okay, though, here's what I don't like. The controls are very sensitive, so every time my little dog (who sits above my head on my recliner as I work) moves his tail, the music is paused. It would be nice if this could be better controlled to a degree with an app or firmware update. I've got everything disabled in the app and it's still a problem. Also, I started out trying to use just a finger to swipe, and this requires starting right in the center of the cup or it doesn't work reliably. (You have to look in the mirror to locate the center of the cup, and that's not going to happen.) I finally figured out that a flipper-like movement with all my fingers works better, but it's going to take some getting used to. And the app really needs work. My main request is that I'd like to be able to adjust speaker placement and room size (Silent Room, Living Room, Jazz Club, or Concert Hall) without losing the other Tuned By preset settings that I've selected/downloaded. If nothing else, at least don't block out the preset's visual information in the equalizer window so I can see roughly how to duplicate the setting as a starting point. A "duplicate/revise settings from Tuned By X" in Producer Mode would be a marvelous enhancement. Also, I wish the app would auto-rotate like all my other apps do. Because now I'm going to have to use this tablet more often. I'm going to have to start listening to music every day, and not just while I'm exercising either. The Ziks sound that good.

This timer is a good size with a very readable LED display and a strong magnet on the clip on the back to hold it to your fridge or whatever a magnet will stick to. The buttons are large and accessible, and it's really no problem to set it up. It beeps loudly when the time is up, so there's little danger you're not going to hear it from an adjoining room.

Strangely, on day one (unlike with some timers I've used), the first three or four times that I held down the hour, minute, or second buttons to speed up the counting and turn off the beeps, it just froze and stopped counting. If I pressed the button over and over to advance the counter by one, it worked—beeping annoyingly loudly each time, of course. I was about to give it a two-star review and throw it away because I couldn't stand it, but I put off doing it and just stuck it to the top of my stove. A week later, after I'd used the stove several times and the timer probably got exposed to some heat, I went back to try it again so I could write this review and the fast-count sans beeps feature worked. Weird. Maybe it was just stressed in shipping and needed time to settle down....

A few things I really do dislike is that it's easy to reset the time by mistake if the grey button on the left gets slid up; the modes are manually set with this button. (That approach to the modes could be good for the technologically challenged, though.) Also, if you overshoot your mark on the time, there is no way to go backward; you have to go forward until you come back around to where you were supposed to have stopped the first time. The clip is a little too sharply angled, so when you stick the timer to a surface with the magnet, the face slants down somewhat, but it's still visible; really not that big of a deal.

Another thing, as I've remarked about another MeasuPro product: the how-to info on the packaging is white letters on light grey, which is practically unreadable for anyone, not just people like me with old eyes. (The company told me they were correcting that with the other product, so I expect they will do the same with this one.)

I played with Sony's HDR-AS30V and its accessories for a few hours, then took it with me (in its optional camcorder case) to videotape, and take photos for, a Christmas party. This is a nice little video camera as long as you are clear on what it's going to be used for. It's really not a replacement for a digital camera.

First, the accessories: Sony was kind enough to send me the camcorder cradle, wrist band mount, head band mount, and tripod angle mount to test with the HDR-AS30V, along with a package of the pretty essential anti-fog sheets. The video camera itself comes with a waterproof casing for underwater filming. The camera sits inside this case, but you can take it out to put it in the camcorder cradle instead (which is not waterproof, of course). In its waterproof casing, the video camera mounts well on any of the mounts. I tested the wrist mount on my chiweenie puppy (7 lbs.) but he didn't like it very much and it rolled around. On me, it's fine, also, but I don't do anything that would warrant my using it. The head mount has a wide band that fit to my head securely, but I don't do things with a helmet on so I couldn't test how it works for that.

Before I left for the Christmas party, I charged up the battery and replaced the 8GB SDHC card that came with my video camera with a 32GB one. I spent about half an hour with the video camera in Interval/5-second mode snapping photos and about 45 minutes non-stop videotaping activity. I really wasn't happy with the quality of the photos, however. I thought I had set the camera to its highest quality mode, but apparently I had not. I wound up with a lower-resolution appearance to the photos that really don't look all that good even onscreen. Another thing I did not like is the fisheye-like distortion at the edges, warped-looking (bent) walls and doors, and an odd color cast. Like I said, this camera is not a replacement for a digital camera.

What the HDR-AS30V shines at, though, is precisely what it's made for: rapid action shots from the perspective of the wearer. The video camera has good stability and the fisheye effect enhances the (for lack of a better word) intimacy of the action shots. The GPS capability and log is a really geeky thing that could even have some diagnostic utility for sports people. All in all, it's a lot of capability in a very tiny package that won't weigh or slow you down.

To be honest, I'm not likely to do much in the realm of action shots. I did find the camcorder case to be very lightweight and easy to use over several hours of time without fatigue. The battery held up during that time, and so did the 32GB storage. Extra batteries can be purchased cheaply, so you can always be ready to go. When I got back home from my party, it was just a matter of plugging in the USB cable into my computer and importing all my photos and movies using the PlayMemories software. I wouldn't give up Photoshop for PlayMemories, but it serves the purpose of importation well enough.

I think what I enjoy the most with this video camera is taking slo-mo shots of my puppy running around, tearing the throat out of his floppy dog, etc. The slow-motion and slow-slow motion modes take more juice, though, so it's good to have an extra charged battery on hand.

Okay, I'm not one of those who streams a lot of movies because our internet service is a little erratic in the mountains. We get way too much lag if we're trying to use more than a few devices (computers) at the same time on our wireless network, so essentially we have to power down everything else if we want to stream a movie. But given the opportunity to review this projector, and especially if I download a movie to my computer instead of trying to stream it, I have to say that it's a really nice experience for a movie night with DH. Even without a projector screen, projecting onto a buff-colored textured wall, the image is not bad at all. You do need a darkened room for the best viewing experience, of course, and I'm sure the image would be a whole heck of a lot better with an appropriate screen. Our Roku box works just fine in either of the two HDMI slots.

It takes some fiddling to get the settings just right, but you can start out with everything set to auto and then go from there. (The manual horizontal/vertical adjuster on the projector itself does not work, however, if you set the H/V extended settings to auto.) Don't attempt to do anything until you've checked the product manual for proper positioning and adjustments. Projectors like this, while in some ways easy to use, are not completely plug-and-play. Your environment, positioning of furniture, lighting, and distance of the projector from the wall/screen all will have an impact on the quality of the viewing image. Movie houses take down all the lights and have curtained walls for a reason.

Our living room is fairly cozy (small). We have a 65" wide recessed area in the wall across from our seating area where we have our 22" daytime "while working" TV set up for background-watching news or listening to digital music, and this room is where I work on my laptop during the day. I was able to get the image from the projector to almost fill this wall width and float above the top of the smaller TV so we don't have to move anything when we want to watch a movie on the weekend. Of course, the image can go considerably larger (up to a barely imaginable 300"!), but in our case that would take it out of the recessed area. If you don't have a suitable home theater-style or outdoor setup, going larger can be like sitting in the first few rows of a movie theater: headache-inducing.

I found the projector to be a little noisy unless set on the energy-saving setting. Also, I discovered that closing the lens shutter in the front turns off the projector, resulting in the need to re-download a streamed movie. The remote that comes with the projector provides access to most settings you would need while watching various media without having to go into the Menu settings on the projector itself. You can also hook up a sound system to it, which I would want to do if setting up a dedicated theater space. Ideally you'll want to have your power access nearby, installed in the floor or the projector cabinet, and that's not something we're going to do. So now we've got the projector sitting on the coffee table in the middle of the room with the cords running to a surge suppressor lying beside the sofa. That's not a setup that would work for us unless we're actually sitting down watching a movie. If you're going to dive in and do the dedicated home theater thing, be prepared to spend some money to do it right.

I've used a Chromebook, I've used various Kindles, but this is my first experience with a tablet. The Android OS is still pretty alien to me, and I'm still knocking around in it, discovering how it works. So it's probably not fair to review the tablet itself based on my own inexperience with the OS. But this tablet is high resolution, easy on the eyes, and amply large. I love that it senses the ambient lighting and adjusts automatically, because my Kindles don't do that and I have to take the brightness up and down manually.

One thing I don't like about it is that it does not use Flash so you can't play anything that requires Flash. Any attempts to add Flash give you messages that Google or Adobe have decommissioned Flash and will not use it. I spent several hours nosing around in the forums looking for a solution, and even found some cautions that I could hurt my tablet by trying to install a Flash player, so I didn't do it. Sure, geeks and power users may laugh at this, but I don't want to mess with it. But what this means is that I cannot watch Amazon Prime movies on this tablet, which is a real bummer. In the forums I found discussions about this; it's apparently a problem with Amazon, not anybody else. They have not developed an app to allow playing their instant videos on Android systems. Somebody said they were hoping an app would be out by 2014, but that there was no guarantee; that Amazon is probably trying to protect its Kindle market by not releasing an app. So my normally high estimation of Amazon is knocked down a peg for absence of an app. Hopefully they will rememdy this soon.

The first thing I did was order a rooCase for it, but I discovered that the cut-out in the rooCase for the rear-facing camera vignetted photos and videos (imagine a black circle around the edges). So I took the plunge and ordered [[ASIN:B00BP54KNM ASUS Official Folio Keyboard Case for MeMOPad Smart ME301 Series]], and that's given me a completely different experience with this tablet. It feels more like my Chromebook, if a little less stable in my lap. I like the soft-touch ON button on the Folio keyboard case because, without it, it's kind of hard to turn on the tablet. There are a few Bluetooth connection issues with the Folio keyboard case, but that's for another review.

One thing that is weird to me about this tablet is that you are not supposed to leave it plugged in to the charger. I'm used to leaving my Kindles plugged in overnight, but with the Asus tablet you're only supposed to leave it plugged in for eight hours at most. (And if you get the Folio keyboard case for it, you use the same charger for both, one after the other.) The screen is more responsive to touch than my Kindle Fire, but still there is sometimes a lag that I haven't quite gotten used to yet. I think it's like learning to drive a new car: you just have to get used to the way it handles, and then you can groove right on into it.

It is definitely easier on the eyes than a 7" screen. Again, the auto-adjusting brightness is a major boon. I love that I can pick it up in the middle of the night, read or browse for a while, then close it up in its case (which auto-offs) and go back to sleep. I'm still not sure I'm in love with the whole tablet concept, but Google Voice definitely makes it easier to use it. For the money, I think this Asus offering is a very good value.

This projector is very simple to set up and use. You'll be tempted to just plug and play, but it's important to read the manual so that you understand how placement and distance affect the quality and size of the projected image.

I don't have a lot of experience with projectors, but one thing I've come to understand is that you should choose the lumens based on your planned use of the projector. This projector is perfect for professional presentations done in a less-than-dark setting, such as a workshop or training session. Even with the lights up, you can see the projected material very clearly, and the color brightness is truly a knockout. I've had the opportunity to compare this 3000 lumen professional projector with the [[ASIN:B00EU9V3VW Epson V11H562020 PowerLite Home Cinema 2000 1080p 3LCD Projector]], and the latter is far better suited to a home cinema experience. Don't just assume that higher lumens means better. I find the [[ASIN:B00E87E1ME Epson EX6220 WXGA 3LCD Projector, 3000 lumen color, 3000 lumen white (V11H550220)]] really too bright for an evening home viewing experience, even after adjustment.

This projector comes with a professional-looking black shoulder-bag-style carrying case that makes it easy to port to sessions, and it is lightweight. You won't have to look like a dufus lugging a heavy projector around, and it has an understated look in its case that doesn't scream "steal me!" Ideally, you'd want to use a projector screen, but if you are trying to project onto a flat white or pastel (say, library or hospital or computer lab) wall, it will be fine without a screen.

Epson's projectors are consistently rated highly, whether it's the lower-end ones or those that cost thousands of dollars. You really can't go wrong with them. There is no comparison between a projector and a printer, but if this projector is as reliable as the Epson printers I have owned over the years (as I expect it to be), it will represent a very good value.

DH is the one who will be putting this projector through its paces over time, as he does workshops for writers learning to use the internet and various cloud-based software to their advantage. If he has anything negative to say about it, I will come back here and post it, but so far he's loving it. Its image is really crisp and readable, and it's truly easy to use. Bravo, Epson.

First off, let me say that if you have an iffy wireless connection, as we do at home, you are not going to be happy with this product. We live on a mountain where the only way we can get high-speed internet service is by bouncing the signal from a north-facing satellite onto our south-facing one and hoping for the best. But there are other ways we can use this Push2TV device.

It is very small, so it fits easily into a pocket. Someone with a WiDi-capable laptop can take this device along to display a computer's contents on a large-screen TV with HDMI, assuming the TV is already on the premises. It would have utility for doing on-the-road workshops, training sessions, classes, tradeshow displays, or meet-up meetings; the site could provide the TV and the person providing the content could bring the laptop or WiDi-enabled smart phone and the Push2TV (plus cable, if needed). You do need a good wireless signal, but if you have that and the requisite equipment, you're good to go.

I am director of a small publishing house. I've been using a $1,000 MacBook Pro 11.6 (Lion) laptop for over a year, with the Chrome browser, Gmail, and GoogleDrive as my online backup for laptop-based files of importance. I got accustomed to the trackpad (I switched the scrolling direction) and haven't used a mouse since I got my Mac. I do book production and cover design on it, sitting in the living room recliner (too far from an electrical outlet to use the adapter) but the battery runs down pretty quickly.

I wanted this Chromebook as a second machine for starting and ending my day: browsing and doing the cloud-based work I have to do, like accounting in Wave, managing social network-based marketing, ordering books, searching for cover art, reading manuscripts in Submittable, handling email, etc. My Mac with Adobe CS5 is essential for the actual book design and production, so I basically reserve its battery now for that.

What is amazing to me is how similar this Chromebook keyboard is to my MacBook Pro. The only time I realize I'm not on my Mac is when I hit what, on the Mac, is the caps lock key but on the Chromebook pops up apps. (There is no caps lock key on the Chromebook; supposedly you can press both shift keys at the same time to effect caps lock, but I guess I don't have the right touch because I can't get it to work.) Another slight difference is in how click and drag works; on the Chromebook, you hit the trackpad with your thumb, then drag.

Those who have already gotten accustomed to using Google-related commands for email, clearing the cache, and the like will be good to go without any learning curve. Chrome extensions and apps, of course, work as expected. (I am SO glad I had the prescience to realize a year ago that I definitely wanted to shift to a cloud-based approach!)

Now, a word about the quality of the monitor. I find the type on the screen to be MORE readable than on my Mac. It is much crisper and high-definition. The colors don't match between the two computers, but I'm not sure it's the Chromebook's fault. The Chromebook does seem to be able to sense how to adjust brightness based on the conditions of the room, which is helpful. Sometimes, however, my eyes start smarting, something that happens when I'm working on the Chromebook, but not on the MacBook Pro. I don't know what accounts for this. The sound is better on the Chromebook than on my Mac, especially if I use good headphones. When watching a movie, the color is a bit washed out compared to the really garishly brightly colored sets, but I prefer that.

I'm probably more of a power user when it comes to the user end of a computer, but I don't try to get in and hack things like some people do. Developer mode, need for static IP address, etc., I'm clueless about. But this is a well-built, fast, mostly no-fuss, low-cost and very light-weight piece of work with a long-lasting battery, which is exactly what I wanted. That I also got a seamless experience shifting from one machine to the other for a quarter of what my MacBook Pro cost? That's priceless!

I got this cable because I work in bed (no jokes, please) and there are not adequate electrical outlets near my bed. I was thinking I could use this cable with my computer to charge my Kindle Fire, which I could sit on the dresser; the charging cable that came with my Kindle Fire is too short for that purpose. However, the business end of the cable does not fit my Kindle Fire. It doesn't fit my Kindle 2 either. It's a good little cable, but not what I needed for what I wanted to do.

This TV is just the right size for my bedroom, and the picture is of very good quality. I don't have cable in my bedroom, but I like my little all-to-myself cave and wanted to be able to at least watch DVDs in my bedroom. The TV was on its way before I saw the reviews saying the DVD player does not work. Well, all I can say is, mine works just fine! I'm wondering if maybe the DVDs weren't inserted correctly (the shiny underside of the DVD must face out, toward the front like the TV screen does) or if people were trying to play Blu-Ray discs in the DVD player. (Geez! At the exceptional price of this TV, one should not expect a Blu-Ray player!)

I hadn't really planned to do this with this TV, but when it came I unplugged my little purple Roku box (which is only capable of 720p) from the livingroom TV, plugged it in to the RCA TV, and it just fired right up with no problems whatsoever! It was already registered, so even the last movie I had been watching was set to resume right where I left off. Being an Amazon Prime user, the Roku opens up all kinds of content. Now I'm hoping to snag a really good deal on one of the 1080p models so I can get the full benefit of the higher resolution of this TV. I pulled up Pandora and let it play through the TV, and the sound was good enough that I listened to it for quite a while. (Speaking of listening, if you want to, you can set the TV to sound-only mode so the video is not on. This saves even more power than the energy-saving setting.)

The TV is lightweight enough that I could literally unplug it and the Roku box, carry it all into the kitchen, learn to cook along with Julia Child, then bring it back into my bedroom to watch movies. It would be no harder to do this than moving a laptop, but the screen is bigger and easier on the eyes than my laptop screen and the sound is better, too.

The sound at first seemed a little harsh to my ears, but I set it on the "Soft" sound setting, which minimizes treble and accentuates the bass, and it was perfect. Also, when I first did the setup, I scanned Air channels because I wasn't hooked up to a cable (or an antenna for that matter), and it didn't find any. I was afraid it wasn't going to work, but putting in a DVD automatically switches to DVD mode. Also, hitting Input on the remote pulls up the various input sources, and that's how I figured out that I needed to select HDMI to make my Roku work. Duh.

I don't think you can beat this TV for the price. It's a tidy-sized TV you can tuck in just about anywhere, is a breeze to set up, and just works out of the box. I have not tested its use as a separate computer monitor for my laptop yet, but it does have a PC input mode. The manual's not the best I've ever seen, but it's serviceable. The various connections diagrams are exceptional. Most people who have any experience at all with electronics should have no problem figuring out what they need to do with the setup.

I am an amateur photographer—so amateur that I've rarely used my [[ASIN:B0035WTVUK Fujifilm FinePix Z700EXR 12 MP Super CCD EXR Digital Camera with 5x Optical Zoom and 3.5-Inch Touch-Screen LCD (Silver)]] because I have not yet bought a tripod and I'm unsteady. When I got the opportunity to review this one, I jumped on it, not realizing that it costs more than three times as much as my camera! I'm not going to address cost versus features, as other more professional photographers here have done; but, clearly, this tripod is intended for professionals who aren't afraid to spend their bucks on professional-calibre equipment.

Still, what I really like about this tripod is that it's going to be a boon for doing macros and odd-angle shots, both of which are what I am most interested in learning how to do. This tripod positions so easily and fluidly, it actually gives me confidence I didn't have before. I do book cover design and particularly like disconcertingly cropped photos; however, working in 300 dpi for print, I rarely find photos large enough to allow for the kind of cropping I'd like to do. With this tripod, I can get the odd angles and perspectives I want to start with. I can also see myself using it to record intimate events (where the important participants all fit into the view window) such as small musician jam sessions, poetry readings, or writing workshops. As another reviewer helpfully noted, there is no pan arm with this tripod, so anyone wanting to use it for video requiring panning needs to find something else.

My first GPS unit was a [[ASIN:B00426C3FI Magellan RoadMate 9055 7-Inch Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator with Lifetime Traffic]], which I was given to review (as in this case) for Amazon Vine. I was so tickled with having one finally that I gave it a higher rating than it deserved. Now I know what a really nice GPS unit is. This Rand McNally feels in the hand like a sturdy tablet PC, and it even has an amply large, stowaway stylus on the back. The mount that comes with it did not attach properly to any surface in our Tacoma pickup truck, but I expect it would work on a larger/flatter dash. We will probably pick up something like this for it: [[ASIN:B003Z4TPPO GPSHDCS7: Extra Large Hard Shell Case For Garmin, TomTom, Magellan GPS with 5" ~ 7" Screen]] if it will fit. (If you know of a good wallet for this product, please leave a comment.)

This Intelliroute GPS is targeted to commercial cross-country truck drivers who must maximize the efficiency of their routes, be able to report their expenses, make notes, and have access to information like truck stops and weigh stations, weight restrictions, altitude, terrain, sunrise/sunset, longitude/latitude, speed limit and acceptable over-limit amounts, detours, and other bells and whistles. Multiple-stop trips are easy to plan and rearrange, and all is visible on the map. A very handy feature is the ability to have both a truck and a car tracked by the GPS, with the ability to eliminate the car or the truck from the mileage reports. The lightest truck weight is 5,000 lbs., and our family Tacoma is well under that, so we just set it at the minimum truck weight.

We like the male voice, which is crisp and understandable, but the female voice is nice, too (and far superior to that Magellan woman). Announcements of distance to turns and destination are brief, informative, and (also unlike the Magellan) very precise. We have yet to be routed into a corner and made to loop back, which was a frequent and infuriating experience with the Magellan GPS.

There is only one weird and peculiar thing about this GPS. I could not for the life of me figure out what the little blurry icon-blob thing was that shows your position until I just happened to look at it when turning a corner. It's a helicopter! I don't know if this is supposed to be a "cool" factor for truckers perched up high over the passing cars or if it's supposed to suggest that there is a helicopter over your head with your GPS navigator calling the shots through a megaphone. Well, when you think about it, it IS rather cool!

If the [[ASIN:B0064GON5C Rand McNally TripMaker RVND 7710 7-Inch RV GPS with Free Lifetime Maps]] is anywhere near as nice as this Intelliroute truck GPS is, we want one!

I am disappointed with these headphones for only one reason: My ears are small, and because of that, these headphones will not snuggly "hang" over my ears like they should. (Children would have the same problem, I expect.) If the over-ear part of the headphones were a little more moldable, I might be able to make them work for me; the extra ear gels themselves are helpful in getting a good fit into the ear canal, but that doesn't keep them from falling off of me. This is why I'm knocking of a star but, again, the problem is not with the headset but with my own anatomy!

With that caveat aside, I love them! For a gardener who wants to listen to something outside while working, the FM radio works just fine and the yellow rubbery cord keeps them around your neck even if you do knock them off. The U.S. Military-grade protection features (against dust, moisture, and shock) make these headphones stand out from the pack.

The Bluetooth pairing and sustained connection with these is better than any other Bluetooth device I've ever used, although I tend not to use Bluetooth unless I'm up and about in the house doing chores. I also don't make or get a lot of phone calls, so we don't even have a cellphone account and depend on the occasional VoIP to get the job done. Meaning I haven't tested the headset features at all.

But the sound is crisp and clear, without mud, more like monitoring headphones used in the music industry. I feel no pressure when wearing them (holding them to my head with my hands, of course, to keep them from falling off of my teensy ears), and I know they would be very comfortable for me in daily use. Maybe I can come up with something to rig them with so they don't fall off. Because I really do like them.

UPDATE (11/1/2014): I'm getting complaints from my partner about how deaf I am and how loud I crank up the TV, so I figured I'd better get some headphones to use with my Samsung Smart TV (which is not Bluetooth-capable, so I'll have to get a transmitter). I gave up trying to use Bluetooth such a long time ago that I didn't realize these headphones were Bluetooth! I was hunting all over the place for a pair of wireless headphones with the look and feel of these, and in the process, I rediscovered these are Bluetooth! (Heck, it's been three years since I first got these, so forgive this little old lady for not remembering.) Anyway, I realized there were (were) two problems with me using these as anything other than wired. First is that the signals (the blue or white lights, which flash or breathe depending on what you're doing) can't be seen if they are under your fingertip. So you have to make sure you don't completely cover up the light. Second, it really does depend on what kind of Bluetooth-capable device you use. To test these, I paired them with my new MacBook Pro Retina. My old Mac didn't do very well, kept dropping the sound, couldn't stay paired, etc. I got a new MacBook Pro, now running Yosemite, and I'm sitting here listening to Pandora coming all the way through about 15 feet and a thick wall and it's great! And this is the "discontinued" set that I've had all this time. They charged up in very little time, too. So if you can get 'em, get 'em.

Because of very small ears and ear canals, I cannot successfully wear the in-ear headphones, but most over-ear headphones with decent sound that I've tried have been too unwieldy and uncomfortable to wear. Not these. The ear cups feel like memory foam covered with soft, breathable leather, and they conform to your ears, making for a pleasurable listening experience. They fit snuggly without pinching, and they have little brail-like raised nubs on the left side of the headband so you can tell in the dark how to put them on. (The wired cord fits into the right-side headphone cup, which is where the rest of the controls are.)

The wired sound is fantastic. I can hear all the nuances of the music even when it is turned down quite low, which is the way I prefer to listen to music; otherwise, my ears start hurting even at moderate volume. The wireless sound is also good, unless you walk too far away from your computer. I walked from my bedroom past the bathroom and into the kitchen, and only when I got into the kitchen did the sound start breaking up.

I had a terrible time getting the bluetooth pairing to work, though. (The instructions are terrible, and one should not have to go hunting all over Philips' website for the proper PDF to download just to get the headphones up and running the first time. I gave up looking and asked on the Amazon Vine forum to see if anyone else reviewing these headphones had found the requisite information; fortunately, somebody had.) I first tried pairing them to my MacBook Pro while visiting my sister in Atlanta, in a condo sandwiched between other condos, and could not get them to work at all. I had resigned myself to using them wired, but when I got home to my rural house, I was able to get them to connect and work by first deleting the original pairing and starting over. I don't know if I was experiencing interference or not. I have always found Bluetooth to be quirky, so I don't blame the headphones for what's clearly a Bluetooth issue, but Philips would do well to explain this most maddening aspect of their product a little better in a printed product insert.

Another thing that is badly explained is the setup for both input and output. I have not had the opportunity to test the internal headset/microphone and I'm not even going to try because I'm afraid I'll screw up the output from the headphones. I'm just using my computer's internal mic for any conversations I might have.

My hat size is 6-7/8 (man's small), to give you some perspective on how these fit. With the headphones adjusted to their most compact size, they fit me perfectly, so there is plenty of expansion room for larger heads. They might be too large for a younger child, however, and I know some children are into gaming. So keep that in mind.

Installation is straightforward, and you should definitely download the THX software to get the full benefit of these headphones. An icon for it was not automatically added to my desktop, but I was able to find the software in the Creative folder (it's not the Alchemy one; I don't know what that is). The software allows you to adjust and save equalizer settings as well as game-enhancing features under the TruStudio Pro tab: crystalizer, surround, bass, dialog plus, and smart volume. Each of these can be adjusted in percentage increments, so you can tweak them to be just perfect for whatever game you are playing. Clicking the play button on this tab loops a sample video with sound to allow for experimentation. A VoiceFX tab allows you to morph the sound of your voice using a bunch of presets so you can freak your friends out! I like using the Deep Voice preset, because I sound like a man when I answer my Skype phone.

The ear-surrounding cups cradle my ears for an immersive sound experience and are not too heavy, so (except for the cord attached to a USB port) I can forget I am wearing them. How I'd love to have a wireless pair of headphones that sound this good! If the ambient air is hot, the headphones can feel too hot, but I don't have that problem most of the time.

The adjustible microphone piece is detachable, and all sound input is muted when it is removed. For online conversations, the sound through the mic is sharp and clear, and the piece is flexible enough that you can put it just about anywhere. I've already lost the little foam mic cover, though, because it slips off a little too easily.

As far as attaching to your computer goes, you have a USB plug-in with a small rectangular THX TruSoundPro module attached. Your headphones, with separate (thankfully color-coded) mic and headphone plugs, plug into this module. When I forget I am wired and walk away from my computer (as I too often do), the headphone plugs pull out of the module first, leaving the USB plug in my computer, still sensing the headphones are plugged in. That's a boon. Volume adjustment wheel, mute switch, and a handy shirt clip are built into the cord, which appears to be of a decent length. (I've left my cord bundled and tied because it's plenty long for desktop use without undoing it.)

The sound and fatigue level (or lack of it) have surprised me with these headphones. My hearing has always been sensitive and I have to keep my volume turned really low to be able to wear headphones for any length of time. With most headphones, turning the volume down that low means I don't get shooting pains in my ears but the sound is tinny and practically inaudible. With these, I can turn the volume down quite low and still hear the nuances of music while still being able to hear voices clearly. Best of all, I can wear them for hours without fatigue and NO hearing-loss-signaling pain. Often, I will suddenly realize I have on the headphones and that people in the room with me cannot hear what I'm hearing. It sounds like the sound is filling the room and not coming through the headphones.

I'm giving this case four stars only because I'm not in love with it. I have an AmazonBasics leather camera case that has two features that this Case Logic case does not have: a velcro belt-loop mount and a slot through which I can thread my camera's strap. I hadn't realized how important the strap slot was to me until I switched to the Case Logic case. After a week of use, I tired of having to stuff my camera strap into the case before I zipped up the case, so I reverted to the AmazonBasics one. I'm now using the Case Logic case to carry the wall charger for my Fujifilm FinePix Z700EXR, and it's perfect for that.

All that said, this camera case is a good one for compact digital cameras. The color is visible and sexy without being too loud, and the case is hard (but slightly flexible) so it conceivably may protect your camera a little bit better than the AmazonBasics leather case will protect mine...although the AmazonBasics case seems plenty protective for my needs. What you wind up getting is really a matter of personal preference. You can't go wrong with either of these cases.

Once calibrated, this PC tablet works wonderfully. It is responsive to the stowable stylus or a tap of my fingernail, and I can even scroll with my thumb after adjusting the right edge width. The screen is sharp and clear, and it's speedy enough for pleasurable surfing and blog-reading, which is what I mostly want to use it for. I have not watched any HD movies on it yet, although the sample movie clip included with the computer shows what it's capable of...and it's gorgeous.

But I have a problem with the Archos 9. Because there is no fan, which makes for a very quiet experience, the lithium battery does get hot when held in your hands. Now, maybe there are people who will use this computer by pulling out the little easel-like stick in the back, but not me. I want to curl up on the sofa with it like a book. So I could see immediately that I wanted to rotate my Archos 9 PC Tablet's screen to portrait orientation so the battery would be at the top and not bother me so much. Well, doing so was a BIG mistake. Once you rotate the screen, it's pretty much impossible to recalibrate it; trying to move the cursor is like trying to walk without an inner ear: Directions ceased to make sense and I'd skew off East (or was it West?) when I meant to move North. It was all I could do to manage to restore the computer to its earlier state.

The little end piece of the easel-like appendage pulled off and I had to super-glue it back on, but that wasn't such a big deal. This appendage also stows into the back of the computer, and it can be pulled out short or long depending on whether you are watching a movie or trying to type on the on-screen keyboard. I can see it for watching a movie, but there's no way I'd ever try to type on the on-screen keyboard. Hunt-and-peck with the stylus is quicker. Needless to say, I will reach for my laptop if I have to do much typing.

I installed Skype, but it was too slow to show video unless I stopped everything else from running. This is fine with me, however, because I prefer to use Skype without the visuals. Google Chrome runs very well on it. I found I preferred the software keyboard (which you can drag around the screen) to the one that pops up when you press the keyboard key. I found that by keeping the former loaded and minimized to the tray, I can get around and do things online pretty efficiently. I just wish that battery didn't get so hot OR that I could easily/reliably rotate the screen to portrait. I gave this computer four stars because, on the whole, it's quite nice. But I must say that I am not likely to reach for the Archos 9 very often because of the discomfort from the battery heat when holding it in my hands. If they will come out with a software upgrade that will make screen rotation practical, then I will be a lot happier with this tablet PC.

A word to the wise: Immediately when you take your Archos 9 out of the box and get the software installed, you need to back it up. Don't wait a second longer than you have to. I was able to restore mine to its pristine newly installed state, but had I not backed it up, the whole thing would have been trashed by my little screen rotation exploit. You don't have a restore disk with this product. So be careful.
Very comfy fabric and non-irritating to have on for hours. It is adjustable for big heads and doesn't hurt at all. Its worth the big bucks for it. Sound quality is as good as it'll get for $100.

Great product.  Limits the volume which is a great idea.  Too many folks increase the volume too much (e.g., to drown outside noise) which can damage long term hearing.  I bought two for both daughters and they use all the time.  Recommend vs normal headphones for kids.
Connects to my phone easily and the sound quality is great!  Great price, too!
I bought this as a gift for someone who has a podcast.  He said the sound quality was great.
The sound quality is great and it does a great job with noise cancellation.
I like that this Fire TV stick can also control your TV power & volume.  Our WiFi is spotty causing connections to be lost/buffering but we’ve noticed it happening less than our original stick.

I have had this for a year or two and love it. It plays loud and battery last me all day. I put it in the cup holder of my tractor and listen to music from my phone while I work. It does great. One day while working I noticed it had bounced out of the cup holder. When I found it, I had apparently ran over it mashing it into the mud. I cleaned it off and it still works. It's a little dented but it matches the tractor better now..LOL
It is portable and easy to take with you. I use it in my workshop, on the deck while grilling, and while soaking in the hot tub. Great purchase for me!

Bought this to accompany my Panasonic Plasma TV. Both work great together along with the cable box. The features are great and for the price you can't beat it. Now with the push of one button my system comes on along with cable and TV. I didn't want the wireless speakers and enternet, hard wired is always better! You get better sound and no cracking and popping from wireless interference. Would recommend this to anyone. The unit looks like new, no scratches or flaws.System is a refurbished but you would never know it. Perfect!

I've been using phone bluetooth professionally (required by work conditions) and personally for years. This product seems to work as well as one I paid 4 times as much for that a puppy chewed up. It does take some practice to adjust to this type of ear piece and it probably isn't going to work for everyone in every situation.  I have built in bluetooth in my car so I am a safer driver. However if my girlfriend calls and my wife is in the car it gets a little too cozy on car speakers.  Just kidding, I don't have a girlfriend. The only downside to this was I ended up with two clocks, two calculators, etc., etc. Easy enough to realize that happened and delete the Moto versions. One side note is that the phone came preloaded with some Microsoft applications (Office, OneDrive, LinkedIn, and Outlook) in a folder labeled "Aplicaciones de Microsoft". (haha, a little French humor in a review about a Spanish language phone with an American english option ...).

The other important news is that the phone within a day downloaded Android version 10 (it shipped with 9). Even better, this will keep the phone fresh enough for the next two years.
