We have Consumer Cellular, which resells both AT&T and T-Mobile services in the US. We've been using the T-Mobile variant, as it does a better job of supporting WiFi calling than AT&T. The only odd note on WiFi calling is that when I choose "WiFi preferred", the phone seems to want to default back to "Cell preferred", but it will dial using WiFi if there is no (or very poor, as in our case) cell service in the area. Overall, you can't go wrong with this phone. Just don't expect a US warranty experience, as it's not in the normal sale area if you buy it in the US. We needed to save some money, and I'd heard that Over The Air broadcasts included channels you wouldn't otherwise get. My Dish TV account provided local channels and a whole bunch of channels I didn't use; but the OTA feature really helps!

I paired the Zinwell digital / analog converter box (highly rated, outstanding Amazon price) with the Radio Shack Antennacraft® HDX1000 Amplified HDTV Antenna (also highly rated). You should know one thing -- the mast size for the Dish TV is larger than the mast size for the Antennacraft antenna, so you can't just remove the Dish and replace it with the Antennacraft on the same mast. But it is an easy install.

As a trial, before going up to the roof (2 story house), I set the Antennacraft in the downstairs window that has a view to the southwest (the direction our local TV stations broadcast from). Without the Zinwell, you're limited to the low power analog stations (mostly Spanish language, a few home shopping stations). I think I got about 6 stations. Then I plugged in the Zinwell in line between the antenna and the TV (after disconnecting the Dish TV feed), did a scan, and had 20 channels. Repeated the process upstairs (remember, we have a 2 story) and had 22 channels!! All the local tv stations (NBC, ABC, CW, ION, PBS, etc.) that broadcast digitally came through great!! Unfortunately, it started raining :( so after the rain stopped, I only got as far as getting the mast installed outdoors before it got too dark. It won't take long to finish.

Only one Zinwell related item: You're supposed to be able to choose the feed from the Zinwell to the TV to be either Coax or the Composite (yellow video, red and white audio). I couldn't get the composite to work in setup, but the coax worked just fine. Haven't had a chance to see if, once programmed, the composite would work, or if for some reason I hooked it up to my tv incorrectly (hard to imagine), but ... since the coax works so well, and video and audio quality are great, I'm money ahead and not complaining!!

So when do I break even? $80 antenna plus 2 $40 boxes = $160; Dish TV was costing me about $55/month (yeah, once you've been a subscriber for a while, there's essentially no customer retention policy, so, good by Dish!! -- and that's probably true for Directv and Comcast, too). So after 3 months, essentially at the start of January, I'm home free!! Thanks, Amazon, you're helping me save money, and that's really great!!

NOTE: I only ordered one Zinwell to test out things, now I've ordered a second for our other TV (didn't want to put too much at risk if it didn't work, but it works great!).

NOTE 2: The gov't coupon program is long dead, no hope of getting $40 off on one, just be glad if you waited that these things are as reasonably priced as they are.

Basic Information: I have a 2-3 year old Toshiba laptop running Windows Vista 32 bit. I have an AMD Turion(tm)64 X2 Mobile Technology TL-58 running at 1.90 GHz, and 2 GB RAM. I'm current with all the Windows updates (SP2 for Vista 32 bit). I have a 200GB hard drive (really 184 GB) with 125 GB free.

Step 1: Unpackage the usb device, plug it into an available USB 2.0 port -- that's the minimum spec USB, and it probably wouldn't work worth a darn if you have an older PC / laptop with a much slower USB 1.x port.

Step 2: When Windows detects it, put in the supplied CD, point to the CORRECT drivers folder. Windows will start working on installing the drivers. It took mine several MINUTES to install the drivers -- like maybe 5. I thought the system had locked up, but no, the drivers are apparently fairly extensive. When done, it told me it was done and the device was installed. To check, go to the Device Manager (if you don't know how to do that, maybe you shouldn't be trying to install new hardware). Under "Sound, video and game controllers" you should now see two new entries (assuming you still have it plugged in): "VC600", and "VC600 Device". You need both. If they have yellow warning triangles, your device driver is not installed properly.

Step 3: You COULD install the software that came with the CD. It IS a choice. But probably not a good one, from what I've read. My Vista based laptop has Windows Movie Maker installed, so it's possible to use that for video capture. But I followed the advice of another poster, and downloaded the ABSOLUTELY FREE WinAVI Video Capture software. They also sell some editing software, but the Video Capture software is on a separate webpage and is totally free. It worked extremely well, and was fairly easy to install. Once installed and running, I found that while I do have a Logitech Webcam also installed, the WinAVI defaulted to that as it's first choice of video capture. Across the bottom of the WinAVI Video Capture control panel, there are several menu choices -- choose "Options" to make the changes. It has several tabs. The first tab is "Devices", which specifies the capture device you want to use. If you don't have a webcam attached, most likely the VC600 will show as the preferred capture device. I had to change mine from the webcam to the VC600, a simple enough choice. The second tab is "Encode", and this one is critical. You have 10 choices for output, from AVI to MPEG to DVD, etc.; do some web reviews to see which one works best for you. There's also an "Encoder Setting ..." button, and this one allows you to choose video quality. Default is Medium, one of 5 choices. The Help menu is adequate, and may help you make your decisions. Finally, there is a "Storage" tab, which allows you to specify the directory to write the captured video to. If you want to use an external hard drive, for instance, you'd want to point to that. My internal hard drive had ample storage, so, on to video recording.

Step 4: First I plugged the Red, White and Yellow jacks into the TV OUT jacks. My TV (a Toshiba 27" tube HDTV), had a lot of jacks, but most were INs, not OUTs. In fact, I only had 1 set of OUTs. Everything else was an IN. I teed up the DVR, started the movie playback, and hit record on the WinAVI Video Capture control panel (the red push button on the left). About 1-1/2 hours later I came back, the movie ended, and I hit the STOP button on WinAVI. The movie was saved, good to burn to DVD. At a medium quality rate, it was only 777 MB. I'm sure the two higher quality settings would drive the storage higher. At highest, it may be up to 3 GB per hour. That's why you need a lot of RAM and a lot of free hard drive space.

NOTE: I didn't use the S-Video plug, instead I used the YELLOW jack for video. IF YOU USE THE S-VIDEO JACK, YOU STILL HAVE TO CONNECT THE RED AND WHITE AUDIO jacks. S-VIDEO means VIDEO, it doesn't mean VIDEO AND AUDIO. If you recorded and didn't get audio, check to see if you hooked up the Red and White jacks.

Step 5: My movie had ads, you can then import the saved movie into Microsoft Movie Maker, start the movie, and split it every time an ad starts and ends. Toss the ads, and you have an end to end movie without ads!

I've burned two movies so far (1 with ads, 1 without), and my next step is to burn to DVD. Product works very well; I only rated it 4 stars because I didn't try the included software.

This Vivo Mobile TV Rolling Floor Stand is a tremendous value. It is strong steel, well finished and just right for rolling my 40" Vizio (which weighs only 17 lbs) around the patio for outdoor viewing at the optimal position and height. It looks great and functions flawlessly. It assembled easily. Though it comes with a sheetmetal wrench and a 4mm Allen, I used my own 8mm and 10mm sockets to speed assembly. And a 17mm end wrench to tighten the caster jam nuts. Sadly, one tiny nut was missing; I found a replacement from my personal metric collection of miscellaneous nuts and bolts. Pay close attention to the graphical instructions. I assembled the base upside down before realizing it was wrong. Easily remedied. Also comes with a collection of TV mounting screws, washers and spacers.

I was going to mount the TV on the wall, but being off to the side and quite high, that would very much limit viewing angles and no doubt strain necks. What I really wanted was to have the TV in front of me, wherever I might be sitting and also be able to optimize for group viewing if necessary.

This little cart is exactly what I wanted. It has 2" high quality urethane casters that roll effortlessly and silently on smooth surfaces. They aren't cheap hard plastic wheels. Each caster's threaded stem screws into a tapped hole. A jam nut on the threaded stem allows you to adjust the casters so all four are on the ground, then tighten the jam nuts to lock the adjustment. No wobble! You'll need a 17mm end wrench to tighten the nuts. Two of the casters are equipped with all-lock brakes that prevent both rolling and castering so the TV stays put if desired. When I'm done, I can simply roll the TV out of the way or into the house for safe storage.The base measures 18x20 inches. My 40" TV is 36" wide. You might think it would be top heavy or unstable, but it's not for me, especially as I have the mast set to near its lowest position.

The sturdy steel telescoping mast allows me to lower the TV so that the bottom edge of the 40" TV is 24" inches from the ground -- a few inches above coffee table height. This allows a very comfortable viewing angle when sitting in my somewhat lower patio chairs. In other words, it puts the TV at a very comfortable height to avoid neck strain.

The mount is adjustable and accommodates the 200x200mm Visa mount hole pattern on my TV. It can also handle 100x200 or smaller. Other stands have very large mounting bars. This one is small, simple and compact. Be aware its max Visa mount pattern is 200x200. You can adjust for level and tilt. It can tilt up about 15 degrees. It does not tilt down. The tilt is controlled by a knob. Be aware the TV is more or less permanently mounted onto the mast and the mast is bolted tightly to the base using five fasteners with locknuts: it does not come apart easily. If you want to disassemble this device for travel, you'll need to add thumbscrews.

I did not want extraneous things like extra shelves for a DVD player. It's clean and simple. Its price is very reasonable. With all the nuts and bolts tightened securely, there is no wobble anywhere.

Couldn't he happier. it's well engineered, strong, lightweight and portable.

This ultra thin 16 gauge speaker wire is just right for getting sound to speakers where you don't have basement or attic access. Our ceilings are at 10 feet. I thought I would have to feather the edges of the tape using drywall compound and prime everything before painting, be we were having a party and so I went for it and put two coats of latex wall paint directly onto the white plastic tape. Amazingly, the paint adhered and dried so perfectly I simply cannot see the tape, even though I know it's there.

You can see it if you're close enough but the fact is, people do not inspect your wall/ceiling interface, looking for defects. It's there but invisible for all intents and purposes.

To attach normal speaker wire pigtails so you can plug the ends into the amp and speakers, I used a razor knife to split the copper away from the white insulator on the top and the also from the double stick tape on the bottom, leaving bright pure copper exposed. Using a "spare hand" clamp on the bench to hold the tape and wire with an alligator clip, I soldered lengths of 16ga speaker wire to the two copper conductors, noting which piece was going to be red and which black so I could maintain proper polarity. The copper solders like a dream as it's very thin and heats rapidly, making for an excellent solder joint. Soldering also keeps the overall size to a minimum. If you can, do your soldering on a bench. Soldering after installation is possible, but much more of a challenge at the top of a ladder.

Overall, this material is excellent. It seems expensive, but it's no worse than buying surface conduit after you buy the wire and the conduit and its connectors and elbows. And you can definitely see the surface conduit. This tape disappears.

I spent hours in my attic carefully waling on roof joists and contorting myself like a yoga instructor around air conditioning ducts and trusses. It was really tough. And that was for the parts I could get to. Two of my speakers were simply out of reach no matter what. This tape saved the day.

The final option was to cut a large hole int he ceiling drywall so I could literally put my shoulders through the roof. I might have been able to thread the wire that way, then patch the ceiling or call a drywall guy to put the piece I'd have cut out back in.

For now, the tape is great if you can handle 16ga wire and not require 12ga, which would have been better of course.

Be aware the tape is about 2-1/4" wide overall. It arrives rolled up on a 3" core. The adhesive side is very aggressive, but can be pulled off to reposition if necessary, It's surprisingly difficult to apply the tape perfectly parallel to the ceiling.

Okay. At first I was not impressed with the Harmony Ultimate. After getting the system up and going, however, I love it.

Desired goal: control two entertainment systems in two rooms with four remotes -- two in each room.

3/29/16 update: I thought having a single remote talking to a single hub was a drawback. But the app on my iPhone is so effective, it's really a second remote for no extra cost. I don't even touch the actual remote that came with the system. That's for the wife, who has taken to the system easily and understands how to work it. I now love my system. Five stars.

3/17/16 Logitech Ultimate Remote w/Hub
Cons:
1. Only one remote can be paired with each hub. Want the wife to have her own remote on one side of the room and you to have another, both controlling the same equipment? Forget it. You can't.
2. Two hubs cannot talk to each other. So you buy two remotes and two hubs, thinking they will talk to each other over WiFi? Forget it. They can't.
3. Pricey at list. Acceptable when on sale ($120 off is nice)

Pros:
1. Excellent phone app. You do all programming from the phone after you create a Logitech cloud account. This gives you control of your system if your phone can reach the internet.
2. Excellent desktop app. Logitech has given up trying to use browsers; you use genuine local apps on your phone and laptop.
3. Easy to set up: Enter MFG and Model number for each device. Done. Full remote buttons download for each device.
4. Touch screen on both the remote and the app has "gestures" with one- or two-finger swiping to control devices. This is nice and unexpected.
5. Colorful
6. Recharges in the cradle -- no more AAA batteries!
7. Wakes up when you pick it up
8. Backlit buttons
9. Haptic feedback when a virtual button is pressed
10. Phone app is great for setup and works as a second remote.

Setting up the first remote was wonderful and very exciting. I couldn't wait to expand the system with my second hub and its remote to create a really capable, flexible system. When the second hub failed to talk to the first hub and I discovered that I had purchased two systems that cannot talk to each other, my elation went to mild disappointment.

Sequence to set up:

1. Create an account with Logitech Harmony at myharmony.com
2. Download the Harmony phone app and download the desktop exe to your laptop.
3. Log in to the account
4. Name and connect the first hub with you WiFi router password
5. Add devices to the room's hub by entering the Manufacturer and the Model number for each device
a. These devices can be far more than AV devices, including lights, blinds, thermostats and other things to a limit of 15.
b. Each device can be renamed for accurate familiarity
6. Create "Activities" for the devices you want to control:
I.e., "Blu-ray Living Rm"
a. it will ask first, "what devices are involved in this activity?"
b. checkbox "AV receiver Living Rm," "TV Living Rm," and "Blu-ray Living Rm"
c. the app asks, "Which input for the TV?" and "Which input for the AV Receiver?" and "Which device controls the volume?"
d. click "run test" to see if everything shuts off and turns back on correctly
e. if it's good, click "yes." Good to go to create next activity.

After you get one room's devices entered and working, if you have a second hub and remote, program it separately in the next room. You can rename the hubs using the desktop exe, but not from the phone app. This is very helpful if you are using the phone as a second remote. You'll have to switch hubs on the phone if you go from one room to another.

You can reorder the activities on both the phone and the remote for most logical order for that room
You can edit buttons and gestures and more.
You can add delay time if a unit needs more time to warm up before it can receive a command
You can change the timeout for the remote to go into standby
You can use your phone as a fully functional remote, but you do have to select which hub you want to talk to.
The Hub connects wirelessly to your WiFi router. It also acts as a giant IR blaster to send commands to the devices. It also has two 2.5mm mono sub-mini plug sockets and two "mini blaster" IR emitters that plug into these sockets so you can send IR to other places.

If you have a device in another room that needs to be controlled, you can extend one of the mini-blasters using an inexpensive 2.5mm extension cord like the 5-meter [[ASIN:B003OSR5TE kenable 2.5mm Stereo Jack Plug to 2.5mm Jack Socket Extension Cable 5m (~16.5 feet)]] or a wireless remote IR extension system like the [[ASIN:B0087S9CJ2 Monoprice 109194 Wireless Dual Band IR Remote Control Extender Upto 328-Feet]].

This wired or wireless extension to another room would be moot if the hubs talked to each other.

What Logitech needs to make happen is to allow multiple remotes to talk to multiple hubs and for the hubs to talk to each other. They've been promising this added capability since at least 2013 on their forums, but so far, it's one remote to one hub and workarounds.

Logitech should not market this as "Ultimate." It's very capable, but also not quite as flexible as required.

Pros:
1. The radio receives AM very well.
2. Audio quality is excellent
3. Unit is very small -- fits in your palm -- and very lightweight. Can fit in a shirt pocket.
4. Supplied rechargeable cellphone battery -- no AA cells to throw away!
5. Charges via USB
6. Line In (so you can use it as an amplified speaker for another device) and Earphone Out
7. Can record radio broadcasts
8. Can set timer to record (use "Alarm" setting under Sys Settings to set on- and off-times and whether to record the radio or not)
9. Can record via the internal mic if you just want to record meetings or other audio -- not super high quality though.
10. "Lock" button is handy so accidental changes are not possible. (See #4 below)
11. Can program a maximum of six timed events. For instance, Power On at 9:05 AM; record radio; Power Off at 10. Power On at 10:05AM record radio; Power Off at 11; Power On at 11:05, record radio; Power Off at noon.
12. Has provision for a wrist strap, though it does not come with one. It's so small the strap I added is very handy.

Cons:
1. Cannot program a particular station to record; it records the last station listened to
2. Thus you cannot program more than one program to be recorded, unless it's on the same station or you remember to switch to the desired station before it goes into record.
3. Navigating and deleting recorded programs is clumsy -- but not too bad after you get used to how to delete.
4. If you are listening to a recording and accidentally rotate the selector knob OR press the "fast forward" button too briefly, or seemingly touch any button by accident, it goes to the next recording and if you return, it loses its place. If you were listening to a three hour recording, and you were at, say, 1hr 37min, to return to your former listening position, you will need to hold the "fast forward" button seemingly forever to get back where you were. VERY ANNOYING. A solution is to record a three hour program in two 90-min segments. Easier to fast forward if it loses its place.
5. Fast Forward should go forward in 15-sec increments at first, then, when pressed longer, switch to 1 min per second or faster. It would be better if there were dedicated buttons for Previous/Next and Fast Forward/Fast Reverse.
6. Buttons are a bit too small and too close together. Very easy to press the wrong one. Would be better if they were grippier rubber. And if they lit up.
7. Volume buttons are directly above the power button. Not good in the dark. None of the buttons light up. Having the buttons light up at the same time as the display lights would be a tremendous improvement.
8. Strangely, the AM radio receives broadcast AM signals cleanly. But when recorded, I hear a "Morse Code" beeping that is really annoying. No idea why.
9. Bitrate for radio recording is preset at 32kb/sec wav files -- pretty low. You can select higher recording bitrate qualities if you are recording audio directly via the mic, but radio recording is stuck at 32kb/sec. Thus recordings are not as good as the original broadcast, but acceptable.

By far the greatest improvement would be to allow faster fast-forward so I can move through long files faster.

Second greatest improvement would be to add Bluetooth so I could listen with my wireless earbuds.

I bought a micro SD card for the expansion slot, but it apparently does not come into play when recording. I think it's designed for you to put your prerecorded music or other files on the card, then play them. For my usage, it was a waste of money. The card just sits there, unused. Many, many hours of recording at 32kb can be recorded to the internal memory. Certainly enough for my purposes.

Overall I am very pleased with this radio, especially the rechargeable battery. I use it six days a week to timeshift talk radio.

The ball mount allows you to adjust the phone's angle for easy viewing. It easily removes and stores fairly compactly in my hard case, a Cases By Source B14105 Blow Molded Empty Carry Case, 14.99 x 10.5 x 5.125, Interior

Best of all, my gimbal rig is all one-handed now, still very light and compact and gives full remote control of the camera while safely holding the phone in perfect position.

Works well with the TASCAM DR-70D recorder, which requires a wired remote.

This is actually an IR unit that slips into a holder. The holder has the belt clip on it. Its bottom hinges open, allowing the IR unit to slip in and the hinge snaps closed to secure the IR unit inside.

The IR unit is powered by its own CR2025 battery. The belt clip adapter has some kind of IR receiver inside that converts the IR to hardwired impulses. The converter gets its power down the wire from the DR-70D's 3/32" stereo mini plug's socket. Cable is about 9 feet long.

This softbox comes with two diffusers, a fabric grid, a speedring and a case. The four rods are 1/8" spring steel with ends that make them larger to fit into 8mm holes in the speedring.

The fabric is stiff, with an aluminumized interior and black exterior. Two small heat vents are cut into the long sides (most likely the upper and lower sides) with little velcro doors so you can open or close them as required depending on how hot your modelling lights are.

The speedring comes with a removable Alien Bees steel insert. The insert has an outer diameter of 5.967" (151.5mm). The inner hole is 3.44" (87.5mm). (You'd think there would be some sort of standard diameter for speedrings so a variety of inner adapters could be interchanged with various speedrings. No such luck. Apparently their diameters and adapters are all over the place.)

Softboxes can be floppy things when broken down. Rods can separate and get lost. I have found it's good to sew the rod ends into their pockets at the diffuser end of the box. That way the rods don't fall out in transport and handling. Nothing slows you down like having to re-seat the rod in its little pocket.

When collapsed, the lightweight nylon carrying case is roughly 8"x23"x3". The case has a velcro flap to keep everything inside and a convenient carrying handle.

The main reason I purchased this light is for its grid that controls the light spill. The grid really helps to keep the back light off the background and out of the lens to control flare.

The only problem is that my strobes do not fit the Alien Bees flange adapter. It would be nice if they offered different speedring options.

This is an excellent lens. Roughly equivalent to a 70-200mm in full frame 35mm photography, it's much smaller and lighter, and integrates perfectly with the Panasonic GH4 with stabilization and autofocus working flawlessly.

The only problem is that I keep grabbing the wrong ring for focus and zoom. They are very close together and feel very similar. I've found a [[ASIN:B00JH0GHYM ePhoto DSLR Camera Follow Focus Lens Zoom Smooth Focusing Handle Lever Flexible Gear Belt Ring FFBELT]] really helps, especially when I'm shooting tripod-mounted video interviews. I can see the zoom handle and know which way to push it to go in or out. In that mode, I'm usually using a follow focus gear knob for focus, too. I wrapped a [[ASIN:B005GKAFWM Lensgear Medium Plus Sized Lens Gear for Follow Focus, 9.25" Long x 0.35" Wide]] gear tooth strap around the lens and sewed the ends together instead of using the supplied tiestraps so the strap would lie against the lens with a lower profile and allow it to store easier by not snagging on the storage bag.

Comes with a 58mm front lens cap, a rear cap and a drawstring bag that has no padding, but allows the lens to get about as small as possible in the bag while offering adequate protection from bumps inside the bag. Don't drop it, though: it offers little impact protection.

The images, even at 4K, are terrific and the f/2.8 aperture holds true throughout its zoom range. Can't say for sure that focus holds throughout the zoom range; have not done detailed testing.

A friend told me he acquired a "fluid ball head" but I hadn't used one. The idea intrigued me, especially for video use.

Though this 6664H head has mixed reviews due to inconsistent manufacturing quality, I took a chance and bought one in December, 2012 -- 18 months ago -- and it's still working fine.

I had purchased the [[ASIN:B002SXMRQM Induro CT-214 8X Carbon Tripod 4 Section 61-Inch Max Height 26lb Load]] and it needed a head. The compact and extremely lightweight CT214 is simply amazing for field or studio still work.

For serious video work, I rely on a much larger and heavier [[ASIN:B003VQXWZA Manfrotto - 504HD,535K - Tripod]] that pairs a Manfrotto 504HD fluid head sitting on Manfrotto 535 carbon fiber legs. It's much lighter than older video tripods, but the combo is relatively giant and heavy, though it has a 75mm ball head for horizon adjustment and sliding base plate and counterweight springs for better balance.

As camera technology get smaller and lighter, the supporting equipment technologies are becoming lighter and stronger. Aluminum and steel are replaced by carbon fiber and magnesium.

This 6664H head on the Induro CT214 is surprisingly good for video! I first discovered this when I wanted to shoot video with a Nikon D800 at a balloon festival. Who wants to cart around a monster tripod, lenses and a heavy camera body?

I grabbed my "still" tripod/head (the Induro CT214/Fancier 8886H combo) that weighs all of 5.9 lbs, is only 27" long and 5" in diameter in its Induro nylon carrying case.

Amazingly, with a 70-200mm f/2.8 Nikon zoom on the D800 (and with a [[ASIN:B00D3551NU Brand New Photography & Cinema VF-4 Universal LCD View Finder WITH Extend Bracket]] loupe on the back of the camera to boot) I found I could actually pan the 6664H smoothly, even without an "official" head and pan handle. I was smoothly tracking ducks swimming in a marina with a doubler on the 70-200.

Yesterday I had to shoot a sporting event at the beach, this time shooting 4K with a Panasonic GH4. The GH4 is even smaller and lighter than the D800 rig and was even easier to pan and carry. The whole thing was a bit over 6 pounds! I carried it all over the beach for five hours. I was able to move rapidly amongst hundreds of people with minimal intrusion.

There are four knobs on the head:

The top one is for locking the Arca Swiss-style plate onto the head. The plate itself has a flip-up lever that allows attachment of the plate to the camera without a screwdriver or coin. It holds firmly. A safety button stops the camera from slipping off the head should you loosen the locking knob. You must positively press the button in while sliding the plate to remove the plate from the head.

Three unmarked knobs on the lower body control the head itself (kind of wish they had labeled their functions, but I can do that):

1. The large knob locks the ball solidly from rotating in its socket.
2. The small lower knob locks the panning motion
3. The small knob opposite the large one controls drag

In operation, I fully loosen both the large locking knob (#1) and the small lower pan lock knob (#2), then snug up the #3 knob to adjust the amount of drag. Panning works amazingly well, especially if you're not zoomed to a long focal length. Simple pans with normal/wide lenses are quite effective.

I realize the fluid movement is achieved via some viscous grease that may fail over time, but the head still works pretty well in my opinion in reasonable temperatures. I have not used it in extreme cold where the grease might become too thick -- but I have used it in very warm temps and it still worked well. The grease has not leaked out at all.

As you can see from the picture, it has a marked base in degrees, should you wish to pan incrementally for time lapse or panorama shots.

No bubble level, but there's one on the Induro and the artificial horizons generated by the D800 and GH4 are great for getting the camera level in a hurry. With the right amount of drag, I just push it into position and it stays for the 15-30 seconds I need for any given video shot.

For such a reasonable price, the 6664H is very hard to beat.

Smallrig rod accessories are very well made and should last a very long time. They look good, have no sharp edges and come in a large variety of sizes and uses.

And when you tighten them to the rod, they really grip. Not going anywhere.

One of their best features is the adjustable thumbscrew. It gives you excellent leverage, but if it runs into anything you can pull up the spring-loaded handle and reposition the handle to clear obstacles.

Machining is uniformly excellent and precise. Threaded holes are in logical places and allow a lot of flexibility in mounting.

This particular mount can fit onto the front of the Panasonic YAGH audio/SDI unit so I can mount rod directly to the YAGH.

Unfortunately, this mount raises the rods a bit higher by a few millimeters so the rods are less than the industry standard 85mm below the center of the lens.

Notice the rod sockets are not in line with the machined slot.

If you want SmallRig's solution for the YAGH, consider the Model 1421 mount. But it departs from the normal rod system and instead of having slip-fit sockets with thumb locks like this Model 1266, the sockets are threaded with an M-12 thread (about 1/2" dia but metric). The design gets rid of the thumbscrews and cleans up the tight real estate under the lens, but you need to buy another set of rods as only SmallRig rods will fit, and only aluminum ones at that.

If you need to contact them, they get right back to you, too.

This auxiliary lens support is superb and works extraordinarily well.

If you want to put a long lens on your DSLR or Panasonic GH4, and you have a 15mm rod system, this is indispensable if you want to achieve a solid rig, especially during focusing or zooming.

Pros:
- Solid machined aluminum with hard black anodizing
- No parts can escape; it's cleverly assembled as a unit
- Thin profile (about 5/16" thin); it fits under the lens, supports and doesn't take too much room
- Quick disconnect from the 60mm-spaced 15mm rods, but attaches firmly
- Adjustable height
- Locking knobs are easily accessible, not under the lens; no tools or pesky allen wrench required
- One knob locks the device to the rods, the other locks height
- The height locking knob bites into a machined groove so as the aluminum becomes nicked by the lock, it still allows for smooth movement up and down. This is good engineering.
- The brilliantly-designed rubber hold-down strap is about 3/8" wide and adjusts to any size up to my 4-3/8" diameter [[ASIN:B004JHY5LU Rokinon 800M-B-AI 800mm F8.0 Mirror Lens for Nikon (Black)]]...which really needs this support at that focal length.
- Mounts faster under the lens than fiddling with a bridge and 1/4-20 bolt, should the lens have an aux tripod shoe, which many lenses do not. Much faster to mount my 70-200mm Nikon lens that if I bolt it down via its tripod foot.
- Works with any lens as long as there is a part of the lens that doesn't rotate that you can wrap the rubber strap over; you obviously cannot strap this to the focus or zoom rings
- Is amazingly stable; the rubber strap really holds, even though it's flexible
- Goes on and off in a flash
- Stores compactly
- Light weight and simple

Cons:
- The rubber strap, I fear, will only last so long, and will eventually rot or harden and crack. It is a molded strap that is attached to the device at one end via a hinge pin that doesn't appear to be removable. Even then, I'm sure a small bungee or something else could be pressed into duty. And if I keep it sealed in a ziplock poly bag away from UV and ozone, it should last years and years. Also, don't keep it under tension; let the rubber relax between jobs.

- A bit pricy in absolute terms, but in relative terms compared to other supports I shopped for out there, this is a bargain. Some are hundreds of dollars. And Amazon got it here in two days.

Bottom line, this firms up the lens, especially when equipped with a follow focus unit, eases downward pressure on the camera flange and allows steady tracking when using a good tripod and head.

Couldn't be happier.

This unit supplies adequate wattage at the proper voltage to power my Nikon D800 when fitted with the expensive Nikon EP-5B power adapter battery eliminator [[ASIN:B004FPQH5I Nikon EP-5B Power Supply Connector]]. The EB-5B has a very custom 4-pin connector on it that I didn't want to cut off. This Kapaxen EH-5 EH-5A power supply comes with the mating connector that fits perfectly. They snap together very firmly and are not likely to disconnect easily.

If you want to save half the Nikon's cost buy the Kapaxen version of the EP-5B [[ASIN:B00A8SLDUA EP-5B Replacement Power Supply Connector for Nikon 1 V1, D7000, D800 and D600 Digital Cameras]] or buy the power supply and EP-5B together [[ASIN:B00A98VZPW Kapaxen EH-5 Plus EP-5B AC Power Adapter Kit for Nikon 1 V1, D7000, D800 and D600 Digital Cameras]].

If you have long video shoots or time lapse jobs, this will keep the D800 going at a reasonable price.

In my opinion, this unit makes the GH4 into a professional video camera. However, it's certainly not perfect. I begged the Nikon guy at NAB 2013 to build something like this for the D800, but nothing yet. Panasonic is listening. I'm commenting here because as of June 4, 2014, you cannot download the YAGH manual from Panasonic's website for details you may need.

1. Cost

It's more than the camera body, which is to say, really expensive. I can only hope the YAGH will fit future GH5 and GH6 camera bodies. Please, Panasonic: don't obsolete this thing.

2. Power

There is no internal battery. It has to have external power, supplied via the industry-standard 4-pin XLR. This is good and bad. Stated power requirement on the bottom plate is 12VDC at 1.4 amps.

Power is applied to Pin 4, Ground to Pin 1. (Pins 2 and 3 are not used.) The manual says voltage can vary from 11VDC to 17VDC. This means any professional AC camera supply or brick battery like an Anton Bauer 14.4VDC. (I'm using a 12VDC battery pack built from ten NiMH D-cells and supplies 10,000 mAhs.) You'll need a 4-pin extension power cord and drag the power supply with you. Hello battery belt? Sort of going backward. It would be great to have the ability to add lith-ion batteries somehow but perhaps it draws too much power for smaller cells.

The external power powers both YAGH and the GH4 body.

Once the YAGH is attached to the camera, an "Interface Unit" menu appears on the "Motion Picture" tab. There are many options. One setting allows you to set low battery warnings at 11, 12.5, 13.5 and 15 volts. This is very professional.

UPDATE Sept 26,2014: I built a 12VDC power supply from a computer monitor power supply and a 4-pin female XLR jack. I also have a 14.4 volt battery power supply. I found that if I leave the battery warning set to 13.5 for the one power supply the 12VDC power supply won't work. The battery warning settings actually stop the camera from working. Be sure to set the battery warning levels to match the batteries you are using.

3. Fan

Yes, it has a fan. You can barely hear it (can't hear it six inches away), but hot air blows out the left side when it's plugged in. I assume there's a lot of electronics inside to supply all the outputs. Have not demonstrated the fan can be heard by the camera-body's built in stereo mics.

4. Inputs:

a. the 4-pin XLR power plug

b. two, 3-pin XLR audio inputs, switchable between Line (0dB), Mic (-50dB) and 48VDC phantom power. A stereo/mono switch sends the signal from a single mic to both left and right channels. You can select which mics to use: the built-in stereo camera mics or the XLR inputs.

c. time code-in on one of the BNC connectors

d. the micro-HDMI plug that transfers the HDMI camera output signal to a full-sized HDMI on the YAGH unit. This HDMI interface is implemented clumsily; I hope there is a better reason than engineering laziness. It's basically a short Micro-to-Full HDMI extension cord. The dovetailed arm that sticks up on the unit holds the micro-HDMI cord with a plug. You mount the camera to the unit, open the rubber door on the camera's left side so that it sticks straight out of the camera, then slide the YAGH's dovetailed micro-HDMI plug into the camera, then tighten the tiny thumbscrew. The rubber door disappears into the dovetail arm and is not removed or abused by being bent back too far. This sturdy plastic arm with its metal dovetailed very definitely protects the extremely fragile Micro-HDMI socket on the camera body. (I personally would not directly connect a cable into the camera. One yank and your camera is broken. I thought the Mini-HDMI plugs on Canon 5D's and Nikon D800's were bad. This Micro-HDMI is even smaller and weaker. The YAGH solves the problem.) It would have been better if Panasonic had routed the signal through the bottom of the camera, but that would mean another 15 pins down there, and it's already crowded.

e. One drawback of this HDMI interface method: if you screw the dovetail in, it takes up the whole left side of the camera and you cannot pivot the flip-out viewfinder down at all and upwards only about 5 degrees. The whole point of the pivoting viewfinder is the ability to frame low- or high-angle shots. If you don't need to remote the HDMI to the YAGH (say you're using the audio interface and DC in and not monitoring via the HDMI) you can let the dovetail hang there, flopping in the wind, and allow the viewfinder to rotate.

5. Outputs

a. full-sized HDMI socket under a rubber door on the left side outputs 4:2:2 8bit or 4:2:2 10bit. You can't record both internally and externally if in 10bit. You access this setting while in "Creative Video Mode." The 8bit is good for sending to an external monitor while recording to the card.

b. 4, SDI BNC connectors under a rubber door on the right side, marked 1, 2, 3 and 4. They output different signals based on the resolution of the recorded signal.
- any of the four BNCs can output a 1.5G HDSDI signal if resolution is set up to 1080-29.97p.
- 3G-SDI is output on BNCs 1 and 2 if you record in 1080-59.94p or 1080-50p
- 1.5G-SDI Square Division (whatever that is) is output on all four BNCs as a group if you want to output the Cinema C4K (4096x2160-24.00p) or Broadcast 4K (3840x2160-24.00p/23.98p/29.97p). Apparently you will need all four BNCs to get enough bandwidth to send the 4K signals to an external monitor or recorder.

UPDATE: the four BNC SDI outs supply "QuadHD" -- that is, each delivers one fourth of a 3840x2160 picture or, four 1920x1080 streams. If you have a device that can accept QuadHD, you're in business.

6. Plug and socket covers

Minor point, but of some concern. The camera is not waterproof but is touted as "splash proof." To achieve this, rubber doors seal the camera all over. The bottom of the camera has two rubber seals that cover two sets of contacts -- one with five, one with 18 contacts. The YAGH unit has quite exposed corresponding spring-loaded pins sticking up. When you attach the camera to the YAGH, you obviously need to remove the four covers. There's no place to store them. You will want them if you split the units apart, especially the camera seals.

7. Audio Controls

a. two 8-segment LEDs indicating level: 4 green, 3 yellow, 1 red.

b. two approx. 1/2" diameter knobs to adjust level, shielded by a clear cover so they won't get hit accidentally yet are easy enough to adjust during a take without shaking the camera or making noise

c. brightness is adjustable to either "Hi" or "Low" via the Interface Unit menu item under the Motion Picture tab

8. Mechanical

a. two locating pins register to the camera body and are held tightly via the 1/4-20 tripod socket. It really becomes a single unit

b. Both 3/8-16 and 1/4-20 threaded tripod mounts on the bottom. There's also a hole for the tripod plates that have an anti-rotation pin. Having both 3/8-16 and 1/4-20 allows you to use two screws to mount the YAGH to your tripod plate so it cannot rotate.

c. two 1/4-20 threaded holes are supplied on the lower front of the YAGH to allow mounting a set of matte box rods, once some third party supplier starts making the rod/rail adapter. The two holes are exactly 32mm apart and centered 85mm below the optical center of the lens, conforming to the 15mm Light Weight Support (LWS) standard.

d. It's still not too giant for hand holding, but it's getting there. It's really designed to be tripod mounted.

e. Because the YAGH extends forward of the camera and slopes downward, if you use one, the Metabones Speed Booster tripod foot must be removed for the adapter to fit the camera while attached to the YAGH. Fortunately, Metabones allows this and supplies necessary Allen wrenches and caps.

Overall, the YAGH is useful -- allows (well, requires) external power for long runtimes, protects the camera from HDMI socket damage, outputs all kinds of signals up to true 4K via SDI, allows timecode input and allows professional audio inputs.

However, if you don't need external power, SDI-out or HDMI-out, a simple audio interface like the JuicedLink Riggy [[ASIN:B009YLRZFE JuicedLink RM222 Riggy-Micro Dual-XLR Preamplifier with Phantom Power]] or a Beachtek [[ASIN:B009R89SNQ BeachTek DXA-SLR MINI PRO HDSLR Audio Adapter]] might suffice to get pro audio in.

Pulled it out of the box. The wife said, in a very disparaging tone, before I even plugged the sound bar in, "WHAT is that?"

I put it back in the box and will give it to my brother, who had asked for something to help them hear their TV better. The soundbar was half off on a daily special deal and Yamaha makes good stuff, so I jumped on the offer.

Thus I can't actually tell you what it sounds like. But it's small and beautiful. The piano black finish is truly like a mirror, arriving with a laminated tape coating to protect it. It has two optical inputs (one marked Blu-ray, one marked TV) and one coaxial digital input (marked STB for set top box), a remote control and it can be mounted on the wall with a couple of screws.

Really wish I could have heard it in my own house. There seems to be a genetic disposition in women against anything electronic that is designed to reside in the living room.

I record interview audio for video/DSLR shoots professionally. My go-to system begins with a Sennheiser MKH416-T short shotgun mic into a Sound Devices 302 mixer (which can power the T-power mic), the line-in into a JuicedLink RM222 then into a Nikon D800, then recording to the HDMI output to an Atomos Ninja.

To monitor, I plug my trusty MDRV6's into the monitor out of the 302 mixer, which is listening via its return to the headphone output of the Nikon. With a knob turn, I can then listen to any of the mixer's three inputs directly or to the camera's return confidence feed.

If it sounds good in the Sony MDRV6's, it'll sound good in the edit.

Yes, there are way more expensive headphones, but I know how the MDRV6's sound, I trust them, and they never break.

The biggest problem is coworkers "borrowing" them and not returning them. Write your name on them in large letters.

The only thing problematic with these stands is that they are 40" long when closed and difficult to pack and carry simply because they are so long. (To carry them effectively, you need a light stand bag. I can vouch for the Hakuba 400 -- sturdy, good zipper, good handle, a shoulder strap, good padding and with external pouches for other gear -- but it's 46" long. There are other offerings at Amazon. But I digress.)

This stand is excellent. It extends to about 13 feet tall! Or it can be used as a wide-stance light stand or it can be converted to a boom for holding a shotgun mic or you can use the built in clips to hold a diffusion panel or reflector.

It's a bit fragile compared to a solid steel C-stand, but it's also lightweight and more compact, except for its length.

There are two extensions in the base and two extensions in the boom.

There is a threaded hole in the end for attaching a counterweight and a cross-drilled hole for attaching weights. As with any boom, balance is key. don't expect this to hold up a ton on one end of the boom without counterbalancing it at the other end.

I use it all the time for holding a shotgun mic. It would hold a small hairlight too.

One trick: be sure to tighten all the knobs after you fold it up. They rattle loose and back out. You'll lose knobs and washers and possibly the built-in clips that hold the diffuser/reflector.

Following a very precise installation sequence video on YouTube that happened to deal with my exact model of Lenovo X220T laptop/tablet, I had to remove the keyboard, and move components about to get to the socket so I could install this drive.

It installs like RAM under the keyboard: it is pressed into a socket and then secured with a single screw in one of the holes. My computer did not come with such a drive so I had to find the socket. Be prepared to undo and reinstall various ribbon cables and antenna wires/connectors.

Now I have two drives -- one for the system and one for data. This C: drive is much faster on bootup than the original spinning drive.

The hardest thing was getting the computer to recognize the new drive. I then restored from a backup image and updated. Good to go.

Shooting video outdoors with a DSLR requires, obviously, proper exposure. When shooting at 24 (23.978) frames per second, the normal shutter speed should be 1/50th of a second (1/60 at 29.97 fps). If the camera is set at the lowest ISO rating of 100, in bright daylight the f/stop would be around f/22. If you want to operate at wider aperture to achieve shallow depth of field, you need to cut the light.

This variable density filter allows such an adjustment. The problem is that it cuts the light by rotating two polarizing filters against each other. Polarizers can be tricky and, by design, modify the quality of light. Thus it may act unexpectedly.

One downside is that the front of the filter is not threaded and my 77mm model is a larger diameter than the 70-200mm Nikon zoom it fits on. So now the bayonet lens hood won't fit. Now I'm outdoors with a filter on the lens and no hood to block flare. There aren't any hoods that naturally fit the filter so you need to tape a hood to the outer ring or use a matte box.

Unbeknownst to me, my dog had chewed through the low voltage side of my existing power supply and the X220 laptop simply quit. I bought two new laptops (one for me and one for the wife), only to find a few days later that the pooch had been the culprit. The cut was hiding under the velcro strap on the wire. Oh, well.

This power supply has the old laptop working just fine now, and for a great price. Not sure how long it will last, but I also repaired the old supply, so I have two...and two new Win8 laptops that smoke the old laptop, so it's all good.

UPDATE 1/3/14
While this unit powers the computer well, when I attached the Lenovo X220 Tablet to a Dell U2410 external monitor via either Displayport or DVI, a tremendous amount of RF noise instantly occurred on a nearby AM radio. It was so noisy I could not hear the radio over the static. And the noise was strong enough to reach most of the house. Not good.

I unplugged this unit and used the original (repaired) power supply instead and the noise completely went away. Obviously, this unit's design is different from factory, even if it still works. But the RF noise only occurs when an external monitor is attached. Perhaps a ground loop.

Had to pull a star from five to four.

Almost all the other viewfinder magnifiers out there are primarily for Canon and have fit issues on a Nikon. I saw this Carry Speed VF-4 at NAB 2013 on the last day, but they were sold out. They are finally restocked and offered a $50 coupon promotion.

My VF-4 arrived yesterday via registered US mail. I had to sign for it. I was glad I was home or I'd have had to stand in line at the post office which, believe me, is not pleasant.

The VF-4 is exactly what I hoped it to be.

- adjustable -- the mounting brackets allow precise positioning for the D800, but also for a variety of other cameras. Brackets allow a broad range of left/right and up/down adjustment, then can be locked very securely in place with Allen head screws (Allen wrench is supplied.)
- sized right -- you can see the entire D800 LCD screen, yet still easily reach all the control buttons on the camera back
- built-in diopter adjustment and good optics -- the screen is sharp corner to corner
- comfortable, durable eyecup -- the eyepiece becomes an extension of the camera. (See attach user photo.) When you hold it against your face, the camera becomes much more steady, allowing much better handheld video shots.
- built-in eyepiece shutter -- if you inadvertently let the sun shine into the finder, be aware that by design you have a magnifier focusing that sunlight onto the surface of your LCD screen. It can burn a hole in the LCD like a kid burning ants with a magnifying glass on a sunny day. Get in the habit of closing its shutter or flipping it up if you're outside.
- flip-up hinge allows quick direct viewing if desired. In this mode it becomes a sun hood that should allow better viewing in bright sun.
- when flipped up, it has an angled design to allow fingers to access the screen if your camera has a touch screen
- eyepiece and brackets easily and quickly removed via a single knurled knob if you need to switch to the pentaprism eyepiece to shoot stills
- all brackets are precision machined. This is not a mishmash of flimsy sheet metal and plastic
- bottom mounts to a machined block that firmly attaches to the camera's tripod socket. This block has a slot machined into it that receives the bracket that holds the eyepiece. This means a couple of things: 1) you don't glue anything to the camera to mount the finder, 2) if you buy the bundle that comes with the extra long bracket (or buy the long bracket later) you can mount this eyepiece to the camera even if it has a battery grip installed. Very cool. I know of no other eyepiece that works with a battery grip that doesn't require you to glue/double side tape a frame to the camera, and none of them fit the D800.
- the mounting block that fits the tripod socket has six 1/4-20 threaded holes machined into it for mounting tripod baseplates, but is also machined so the mount is itself an Arca Swiss-style quick-disconnect dovetail plate. If your tripod head has that style quick-disconnect, you are good to go. With the multitude of baseplate designs out there -- even within the same company (Manfrotto, I'm talking to you and your 50 different plate designs!) -- the Arca Swiss is a welcomed standard for quick disconnect plates. Check out [[ASIN:B0086AJ4AS Desmond DAC-02 60mm QR Clamp 3/8 Inches with 1/4 Inches Adapter and Level Arca Compatible for Tripod Head]] as a possible quick-disconnect base.

UPDATE:
The baseplate needs work. It needs to be thinner and it needs to allow the camera to center left/right on its tripod socket.

If you use this accessory in a camera rig that has a 15mm rod system, it is most likely designed to require the camera to be centered left/right on its tripod mounting socket so the lens is centered on the rods. This baseplate has 6, 1/4-20 aux tripod sockets, but none is centered on the camera's tripod socket: they are either approx 5/8" left or 1/2" right of the actual tripod socket.

This off-centeredness also stops the tripod baseplate from mounting parallel to the camera, at least if you use the set of 1/4-20's on the right. When mounting my Manfrotto 504Plong tripod plate to any of the right set of holes, it becomes canted, causing the camera to tilt and not have a level horizon. Not good.

The plate is also quite thick -- .569". This thickness raises the camera significantly in the rig, making it difficult or impossible for rod-mounted follow focus and lens hoods to line up properly.

Sadly, the supplied baseplate works, but does not mesh with standard video production accessories. It appears I will have to machine a custom plate. What a pain.

Still, while not the least expensive, it was definitely worth waiting for. An outstanding accessory for the Nikon D800. A joy to use in bright daylight, hand held and for critical focus.

I bought this to go between my Nikon DSLR and my juicedLink preamp. It's compact and stays out of the way, and has 90° molded gold plated connectors. If you are bringing audio into your DSLR this cable is a critical component that needs to be top-quality. This one fills the bill.

The Canon HFS100 camcorder requires the battery to be in the camera in the camera plugged into the wall to charge the battery. If you want to charge the battery in the wall or while driving in the car using the cigarette lighter outlet you need this charger.

One thing I noticed is that it's very tight to attach the battery, at least at first. Initially I thought the charger didn't work, but then I realized the battery was not fully attached. A firm push, and the battery snapped home. The charger's light is green until you attach the battery. After attaching the battery and while charging it turns red. When the battery is fully charged the light turns green again.

The battery I charged was completely dead. After charging, I put it on the camera and it indicated 100% charge.

What I really needed was the ability to charge in the car. This charger allows me to charge both in the wall and in the car. It's also lightweight and easy to carry.

Best L Series Charger:

Pros:
- charges two batteries at a time, sequentially
- charges batteries fast
- analyzes the battery's internal chip... a button allows you to select which battery to interrogate
- indicates how many hours and minutes it will take to charge each cell to Normal or to Full (nice to know it would have been full in five minutes if you're in a hurry and need to pull the battery off the charger)
- can be used as an AC adapter for most small Sony camcorders:

We have had one at work for years. Bought one for myself as the number of Sony L-Series powered devices I own has increased.

Simple the best charger out there.

This mount arrived with my Lilliput 7" HDMI monitor. Sony L series lithium ion batteries fit it perfectly.

Pros:

- reliable battery contacts
- power-out coaxial socket; no wiring required (5.5mm x 2.5mm)
- included power out cable
- multiple mounting options

Cons:
