UPDATE:
There is a second "Con:" When the battery is mounted, a green LED lights up to indicate charge state, I believe. If the battery goes dead, it turns red, I think. Haven't really let the battery go dead but it does briefly flash red.

To power this LED, there is a rather complex circuit board inside the unit that seems to do nothing but make the LED function.

In other words, if you leave the battery on the adapter, the LED stays lit, draining the battery over time.

I wanted to build a 14.4VDC power supply for my GH4 YAGH unit.

I mounted two of these adapters onto an aluminum plate and wired them in series to do so. I wanted more reliable contact than the coaxial power connectors (which can be pulled out by accident) so I pried open the cases (which isn't easy), unsoldered the wires inside and removed the circuit boards and coax connectors. Then I directly soldered a wire to the contacts so one battery's positive contact flowed into the next battery's negative contact. I then soldered the positive wire to my camera's power cable to the unused positive contact of one battery and the unused negative contact of the other, providing double the voltage of a single L-type 970 battery.

Now the two batteries together provide the 14.4VDC I need in a compact, high amp-hour, inexpensive unit.

I like using L-Type Lith-Ion batteries because they power other devices I use -- small monitors, my mixer and external recorders. They are widely available, lightweight, inexpensive, charge quickly and reliably, do not have memory effect and hold a charge on the shelf for much longer than Ni-Cads. I'm told they actually work better if you leave them on the charger, too.

One of my favorite Nikon lenses is an old 16mm fisheye from about 1977, I think. It has two problems: it is a fisheye and curves straight lines at the edges and it's a non-CPU lens, like many of my aged old Nikon lenses. Non-CPU means I have to remember to select it from my list of non-CPU lenses using that menu feature of the D800, and that there is no focus assist. It's full frame, however, and now that we're back to shooting full FX 24x36 sensor, the old lenses are making a comeback.

That 16mm fisheye costs a pretty penny today and the 14-24mm Nikon f/2.8 zoom is even more. And I'm sure they are both fine lenses.

So I bought a Samyang/Rokinon 800mm f/8 mirror lens for two bills and said, "that ought to be fun, even if it's not that great a lens for such little money." Funny thing: it's a pretty good lens.

That good purchase experience allowed me to select this 14mm Rokinon f/2.8. It is surprisingly good considering it's one third the cost of its Nikon equivalent. Even wide open at 1.5 feet, it is tack sharp.

The main difference between this and the Nikon is that this Rokinon is a fully manual focus lens while the 14mm Nikon is auto focus, although I'm not sure how accurately a 14mm lens can focus automatically. I've often simply estimated the distance and set the lens to that distance using the barrel markings. The focus ring is a pleasant long throw, with the ring rotating about 270 degrees around the lens from infinity to .28 meters (less than 1 foot). Focus drag feels silky smooth. Focus happens internally -- the front element does not rotate.

This Rokinon has a clickstop f/stop diaphragm. It also has a chip in it, giving it enough smarts to qualify as an AI-S lens. To use it on a D800, you have to set it to minimum aperture (f/22) or you get the flashing "fee" in the viewfinder. Ah, takes me back....

Setting it to f/22 (marked in orange) tells the camera what f/stop the lens is working at and allows control of the f/stop from the front selector wheel on the D800. The focus indicator in the eyepiece also works -- you see the left/right arrows and the little ball that verifies it's in focus. It also automatically records f/stop and focal length data in the metadata with the shot. In other words, it's a real lens, just without auto focus, for one third the cost. Old Nikon AI-S lenses have a little lock that holds the f/stop ring at minimum aperture that's not present on this lens, but the click stops are secure and the f/stop ring stays where you set it.

The front element is radically curved and is protected somewhat by the flower petal shaped built-in lens shade. Be careful: that front element is really exposed to the weather.

The front lens cap is terrific and very well designed. It's a durable hard plastic unit that slips over the flower petal lens shade and snaps securely in place against detents in the the lens shade. You have to squeeze both plastic flush-mount buttons on the front edge of the cap to release it. It won't fall off by accident under any circumstances. Only drawback it that it's about 1-3/8" deep and 3-5/8" diameter, so it doesn't exactly slip into a back pocket when it's off the lens.

The cosmetics of the lens are appealing. Even has a brass/gold colored band around the front that mimics real Nikon lenses. The focus ring rubber grip is good and the the body of the lens, minus the front element, is about the size of a 50mm f/1.4 lens. Focus distances in feet and meters are clearly engraved. One nice thing it has that I wish all lenses had is the focal length clearly and largely printed on the side of the lens so you can tell at a glance what it is. Nice. The mount is precision machined and fits the camera like it should. There are five little electrical contacts that interface with the camera body to communicate exposure info. For transport, it comes with an unpadded velour drawstring pouch. May want something a bit more padded if it's bouncing around inside a camera bag against other gear. But the bag's adequate, folds flat when not in use and is compact.

As for performance, I'm not going to go into lines/per millimeter sharpness. What I can say is that it's great for architectural interiors and wide, WIDE rectilinear shots. And in analyzing a snap of my dog I pushed in on his eye as far as I could looking at the D800's rear screen and could see the finest of eyelashes, showing off both the resolution of the lens and the remarkable resolution of the D800's 36 megapixel sensor. The lens distinguishes itself from all the wide/medium wide 24mm/35mm lenses out there. Do I really need to have a heavy, giant, hyper-expensive zoom lens that zooms 10 whole millimeters from 14mm all the way to 24mm? Not hardly. If I need serious wide angle this 14mm will fill the bill nicely, even wide open.

No filters for it, of course, because the front element is so deeply curved.

I'm particularly interested in using the 14mm for video shoots, which I use the D800 for more than for still photography. I'll be able to see the whole world with this lens, even in the most cramped of situations.

This will be a fun lens. Highly recommended.

Hakuba makes a great case. Durable, padded, extra pockets on the outside and on some models on the inside too. Shoulder strap. Strong handles and zipper. They are tapered as if assuming tripods are larger at the head. This is usually true, but video tripods with floor spreaders attached can make the feet of a tripod much larger than a simple set of sticks.

One of the nicest features is that these cases come in four different sizes to fit a variety of equipment. This model 200 holds a 100mm bowl alumInum tripod sans head. I have another larger model that holds two brolly umbrellas, two extension cords, two large 85watt fluorescent bulbs, two light stands and two bulb socket adapters. A whole lightweight soft lighting kit in one case.

UPDATE: after installing the latest map update and waiting for a very long time for the install software to do its thing and worrying if it had actually finished the install because after about an hour my computer said "the application has unexpectedly quit," the device seems to be working perfectly.

Overall, I like the 2595LMT. It boots and finds the satellites faster and has more information available.

Pros:
1. I can press the lower left "Arrive time" button and change it to a variety of readouts: miles remaining, altitude, time via.
2. Voice command works, mostly, especially on simple commands like "Go Home." More complex commands, like an address, return a wide variety of responses, most of them wrong. (Why it's searching the entire United States when it knows where I am and should be looking locally is beyond me.) I liked the old way of narrowing search to State, then City, then Address. Now it just asks you for the whole address, which it likely doesn't understand.
3. It's slimmer and lighter.
4. Easy to import my favorites from my old Nuvi into the 2595LMT. Using a PC, after plugging the old Nuvi into a computer using the USB port,

a. Navigate until you find the "current.GPX" file on the old Nuvi and
b. Copy it to your desktop (this is also a way to make a backup should you desire.)
c. Rename the file: replace "current" with any word you want, as long as it's not "current") so that it is names "anyword.gpx"
d. Attach the new Nuvi 2595LMT to the computer and navigate until you find the folder with its "current.gpx" file.
e. Copy the "anyword.gpx" file from the desktop into the same folder where the "Current.gpx" file resides.
f. Disconnect and restart. All the old favorites will be added to the current list in your new Nuvi.

5. It doesn't say "recalculating" when you disregard its directions
6. It has lane indicators: a series of arrows in the upper left that tell you which lane to get into to make the next turn. Very cool.
7. Touch screen allows scrolling like a smartphone, at least on some screens.
8. Allows you to add/edit shortcuts like a PC. You can create and move icons around so that you can get to a particular feature with one touch.
9. Micro-SD card only
10. Bigger screen
11. 3-D view of the road
12. Speed limit indicator and simultaneous readout of your actual speed that turns red if you exceed the local speed limit. (I wish it bonged quietly when the speed limit changed to remind you that you have to go slower or can go faster.)

Cons:
1. Sadly, on my unit (even after map and software updates) when I say, "Find Place" it immediately crashes and reboots. And if I say, "Find City" it ignores me, even if I ask it to find New York or Los Angeles. I may try reinstalling the software in case it loaded incompletely for some reason. (UPDATE: I waited a couple of weeks and tried updating the maps again. This time it fully installed and happily all the voice commands now work very well. This alone is a good reason to get is unit. Typing while driving is difficult and dangerous. Voice command is simply wonderful and something I've always wanted in a Garmin.)
2. Stuff has been moved around so that the interface is a bit foreign. For instance, "Favorites" are now "Saved Places" and trying to save or edit a saved place is confusing until you get the hang of it.
3. Doesn't have a powered cradle anymore, only a standard mini-USB on the back. Not a real problem, but it's slower to hook up and remove. I used to be able to drop it on the cradle and go. Now I have to find the end of the cable and thread it into a small port on the back. Minor.
4. The traffic function in my opinion is a joke. Driving LA freeways at most times involves congestion and some delay. It's simply the way it is. The Garmin hates congestion and is constantly trying to get you around it. Thus it's constantly bonging and telling me to get off the freeway to take surface streets, assuming they are magically uncongested when in reality the surface streets during rush hour are ten times worse. I'm pretty much going to ignore its traffic suggestions and may turn it off altogether. If you buy the amazon basics power cord [[ASIN:B003N2POXK AmazonBasics Vehicle Power Cable with Mini-USB Connector for GPS and Other Mini-USB Devices]] it doesn't have a built in traffic receiver and thus defeats the annoying and constant attempts to route you around congestion. Simply put, don't believe the alternate route is going to save you any time. Getting onto surface streets during rush hour is a recipe for even longer delays.

I like this radio for AM reception. Comes with an AC adapter that also charges the six nickel metal hydride (NiMH) AA cells if you buy and install them. You must throw a little switch (one time process) to tell the radio which type of cells are installed (regular or rechargeable) so the radio doesn't try to recharge the non-rechargeable cells.

One flaw is that it does not have a handle for convenient carrying. It is portable, after all. It's not that you can't carry it, but it's not very "grippable" and a handle is way better. I bought one of these radios for my 90-yr old dad, who was grabbing it by the buttons and accidentally reprogramming it. The handle assures it stays set properly and won't be accidentally dropped.

I epoxied an auxiliary handle on, as you can see in the photo. The handle is simple white plastic door pull left over from a prefab storage cabinet. Seems to stick fine using two-part 5-minute epoxy adhesive.

One other nit is that the volume control knob is very easy to adjust. I'd like it to have a bit more resistance so it stays at a set volume.

Also, it's not smart enough to ignore weekends. I use it as a clock radio alarm. My other clock radio knows not to go off on Saturday and Sunday. This one I have to un-alarm so it doesn't go off on weekends, and I have to remember to re-alarm it for Monday.

Still, audio quality is great and AM reception is very good.

I wanted to hear and see Skype on our Sony XBR7 HDMI-only capable 1080p TV, fed from a Lenovo X220 convertable laptop/tablet running System 7 64 bit Ultimate through the DisplayPort. I also wanted to watch some YouTube videos playing from Firefox and hear their audio on my big living room audio system. No such luck.

When first plugged in, I remember briefly seeing the TV via this DisplayPort adapter in the audio device list, but the next time, the TV disappeared and is nowhere to be found. Not in the audio control panel, anyway. It's just gone.

I first chalked this up to the Thinkpad weirdness, as its internal audio card/mic doesn't work with Skype either. If I plug in an external Logitech webcam, it works seamlessly. Internal camera/mic, nothing.

Sony audio problems aside, the video looks great on the big screen, though it overscans a bit and cuts off part of the menu bar at the bottom.

One reviewer said he could see his TV in the list of audio devices and was able to configure its audio to satisfaction. My Sony TV does not show in the Lenovo audio devices list, though it does show as a generic PnP monitor.

I plugged the HDMI cable into a tiny 7" video monitor and whatdayaknow, the audio came through and the device showed up as an audio device. Then I plugged it into a 20" Vizio and sure enough, it works fine too. Same with a Samsung LCD. Three monitors out of four work. The Sony is the only one that doesn't. Hmmmm.

Sooooo, I'm guessing there's something about Sony's DRM or some other HDMI protocol blocking the computer from seeing the TV. I set all the TVs for internal speakers. Routing audio to an external amp is another variable in the equation.

Nothing wrong with the adapter that I can tell, it simply doesn't see certain Sony TV's.

These came with my Zen X-Fi, that was retired when I got my iPod and that was retired when I got my iPhone 4, which is the closest thing to a "one device to carry and do most everything." But Apple earphones are sound leakers, don't fit ears very well and really don't stop ambient audio to leak past them.

These Creative earbuds seal into my ear canals wonderfully. They come with three sets of ear buds in different sizes for different sized ears. They have a full rich sound with good bass. They are very responsive, delivering plenty of volume. I wear them under my ear muffs when doing yard work and can listen to podcasts even when mowing the lawn. They work well on airplane trips.

The cords are silicon and do not easily tangle and come untangled easily.

The strain relief on the plug could use some help. I had to coat it with silicon sealer to reinforce it when the cord frayed and almost broke. Now the plug is ugly, but strong.

I bought some Klipsch S3's thinking they would be better, but no, these little Creatives beat them hands down.

Zen X-Fi 16GB review 2-28-09

Had the Zen X-Fi 16GB for two months of daily use now.

The device is well built and solid. It needs a silicon skin for protection, though. That is extra but highly recommended so your expensive player doesn't slip out of your pocket.

First, the buttons are too flat and are not illuminated. Sounds like a small thing, but flat black metal buttons against a black metal background in the car at night are very difficult to find and press. If the buttons were transparent and had the tiniest LED behind them, they would be a lot easier to manipulate accurately.

No Bluetooth--I'm getting very tired of wired connection to my car and headphones. LOSE THE WIRES, Creative! The earphones that come with the Zen are terrific. Really good quality. But the wires are tiresome.

Though I'd rather have Bluetooth, Zen is Wi-Fi capable. You can wirelessly hook to your computer's wireless router and play or copy files back and forth, but it's so frustrating to make it function it's virtually useless. USB cable is the way to connect.

As part of Wi-Fi, Creative does provide something called "Media Server" that you can access via your internet connection wireless router if you're in range and properly connected. After waiting a couple of minutes for the connection to be made, you can listen to propaganda from all kinds of politically correct content like NPR, the BBC, Australia's ABC and KCRW. Yes, master: I hear and obey. Mostly a waste as you can't really select content you want, only what they supply. Definitely politically correct. And boring.

It has a kind of chat texting capability but that's what phones are for these days and the Zen's dinky keyboard just doesn't cut it. The keyboard is laid out the way it is so it can emulate a phone keypad when you're in chat mode. Too frustrating to use. It's why QWERTY keyboards are on phones now.

Bookmarks. A few minutes after being shut off, the Zen forgets where you were when you shut down. If you fire it up an hour after shutdown or dock it to your computer to upload new content, it starts playing the last file you opened from the beginning. This is a bit frustrating when you're part way through a three hour podcast. So Creative allows you to set a Bookmark from within the file you are playing. It's quick and easy once you figure it out. I use it all the time now. This allows you to set a point in a podcast so you can return to it later. But while you can set the bookmark from within the file, you have to navigate to the Bookmarks screen to select the bookmark when playing back later. Not very intuitive. Took me two months to realize the usefulness of the feature. Why doesn't it simply remember where I stopped listening by itself? My DVR does. Just resume from where I left off. But no.

The lower left button is programmable. It's called My Shortcut. You pick from a list of available functions and set it. This allows you to go to a particular favorite screen or function once you decide what that is.

The Zen first and foremost is marketed as a video and MP3 player. What I wish it could do is have a "skip forward" ability (again, like my DVR does) that allows me to skip forward 30 seconds or a minute (or a user defined amount) so I can move forward in predictable amounts instead of holding the fast forward button down. If it's going to be called a "player" of any sort, it should have a variety of player controls. Skip forward/back should be available. Firmware upgrade wish, Creative.

Speaking of the fast forward button, the longer you hold it, the faster it goes. It starts by forwarding at a slow rate, then speeds up until you are jumping forward minutes at a time. This is good for zooming to a point quickly. But if you want to go forward, say, seven minutes, holding the FFwd button down too long will launch it into hyperdrive and you'll be at 10 minutes or more into the file, then have to rewind/search back. Somewhat of a pain. No. A real pain. Let me skip forward or back in 30 second increments.

A great feature is its built-in speaker. It sounds like my transistor radio from my childhood. This feature was the main reason I bought the Zen: you don't have to use earphones if you don't want to. It is a great and rare feature among MP3 players. A pocketable mini boombox.

Creative's Centrale "iTunes wannabe" software is dreadful. I tried it for awhile, then uninstalled it and now just drag files to the device.

Video screen quality is very good but 320x240 is still a bit small. Diagonally it's 2-1/2"; 2" wide x 1-5/8" high. It's also the old 4:3 aspect ratio, not the modern 16:9. If you're viewing a 16:9 video letterboxed, you are looking at one tiny video.

The video player (as opposed to the music player) is very weak. Windows Media Player 11 it ain't. Another key reason I bought the Zen is because it promised it could play a plethora of video formats. Wrong. I have dozens of wmv video files which exist in many sizes and bitrates from thumbnails to HD. Unfortunately, almost all of them need to be converted via Creative's stand-alone converter app or Centrale into squeezed-down bitrates and 320x240 size. This process is clumsy and slow.

If virtually every file needs to be converted in order to play, it's not really playing the advertised list of formats: it's playing the format Creative has selected and must be converted to. Often, even if I render out a wmv directly from my video editing software to Creative's parameters, it still won't play properly without conversion. Yet another marketing promise dashed to pieces.

The Zen allows me to delete files directly from the Zen if I want to (as opposed to needing to plug into iTunes to delete or add). This is good.

It has a built in mic and audio recording capability and you can program the "My Shortcut" button to start the recording process immediately so you don't have to navigate to the recorder's controls.

It has an FM radio that only works if the ear phones are plugged in because the wire becomes the antenna. What I'd really like is an AM radio, though, for news, talk radio, traffic and weather. Who needs FM? That's what your MP3's are for in the first place, right?

The unit has an SD card slot, but it's not well integrated. Content on the SD card does not appear in the normal file list. You must navigate to the card and browse it separately. Worse, when you do that, it comes back with "There are no playable files in this folder" even when I know I put mp3 files on the card that the player can play. You have to use the "Import" function to move files from the SD card to the player's memory in order to play them. Think of the SD card as an aux thumb drive, not as expanded memory, except it doesn't even work like that, actually. If you think you can buy the 16GB and "double" its memory capacity with a card, think again. It's more of a gimmick than a useful feature. More Creative fluff that is long on promise but short on delivery.

By the way, when you plug the Zen into your computer's USB cable the Zen does not mount as a drive (what Windows calls a "Local Disk.") It "docks" as a "Portable Media Player" according to Type in Windows Explorer. This means you can't play directly from the player. If you click on a file on the Zen from within Windows, it moves the file to a temp folder on your C: drive before playing. Not a big deal, but if you intend on connecting the Zen to a USB input on your car stereo or computer, I don't think your stereo will be able to see the Zen's contents. While the Zen is docked to the computer, all the play buttons are disabled and the display indicates "Docked" until you unplug the device. On the other hand, you don't have to unmount the device. Just pull from the USB and go.

Poor Creative. Always trying. Never quite getting there. Won't be long now and a phone will do it all. Look at Sony Erickson's W760, iPhone or Palm Pre.

After I took delivery of my $500 Denon AKDL1 Cat-5 uber-cable, Al Gore was mysteriously drawn to my home, where he pronounced that Global Warming had been suspended in my vicinity.

Yes, I had perfect weather: no flooding, no tornadoes, the exact amount of rain necessary, and he pronounced sea levels exactly right and that they were not going to rise within five miles of my house.

Additionally, my cars began achieving 200 mpg and I didn't even need gasoline. I was able to put three grams of cat litter into the tank and drive forever.

What's more, the atmosphere inside my home became 93% oxygen and virtually no carbon dioxide. In fact, I now exhale oxygen.

One heck of a cable.

Didn't notice any improvement in audio quality though.

The $800 Apple iCable is clearly superior.

The Zen Xtra (any capacity) appears to be the only portable MP3 player on the marker that features Time Scaling. Time Scaling is Creative's term for the ability to play a file back faster but without distortion. Voices don't sound like the Chipmonks, they just talk faster. For music buffs, that's useless--who wants to hear a song faster? But for podcast listeners, it's quite helpful. A two hour podcast that consists of talking can be sped up significantly.

It's amazing how the human brain adjusts to the faster talk rate, too. I've read that some studies claim we retain more by listening to a faster rate of speech.

Time scaling means more information in less time. If you have many podcasts you'd like to hear but only so much drive time to hear them in, this feature is great.

I don't know why Creative doesn't include Time Scaling on more of their products. It's a firmware feature. They make a ton of devices, but only the Zen Xtra has Time Scaling. I don't know of any other device out there that has it, including iPods.

To experience how Time Scaling works, try it on Windows Media Player 10. Open an MP3 voice recording and go to "Play Speed Settings" and move the slider to 1.3 or 1.4. At 1.4 a 60 minute show plays back in 42 minutes.
I really like my new laptop. The sound is incredible! The picture is amazing and the speed is way better than my last one. I would recommend!!

I have several relatives who have either the Echo or the Dot and enjoyed playing with theirs so I went ahead and got one for my home.
I'm so happy I did! I'm enjoying learning all Alexa can do and am really impressed with how well it sounds when playing music. The speaker quality alone is worth the price. Love the shopping list feature and am learning how to use it with my Tv's.

These ear cushions were perfect for my Bose QuietComfort 2 headphones! The original ones were disintegrating everywhere, what a mess! I watched a video on how to replace and did it myself with no problem at all. Now my headphones look brand new! So glad to find this kit.

I was having issues with connecting my MacBook Pro to the gym speakers for two Fridays to the point I had to use the portable speaker in order for me to teach my class. Ordered this iPhone adapter and it worked perfectly as I was able to connect my phone to the gym speakers.  The sound was great, no crackling noise, & no short. Happy students all around.

We have several Alexa devices in our household, two Echo Spots for the nightstands, Echo Dots and an Echo Show 1st Generation.
All of them have the same problem, despite the equalizer the Alexa voice sounds muffled and is sometimes really hard to understand. We tried to adjust the equalizers of course (turning the bass all the way down, treble up etc), but it all sounds the same more or less.

This last prime day I wanted to give the Echo Show 5 a shot as an replacement for my nightstand Echo Spot. You would think that the speaker is better because of the bigger size but sadly it's the same muffled sound when Alexa talks. It's disappointing.

Hopefully the next generation will be better.

I purchased them to be able to listen to my sleep relaxation at night and so far they work great.
They are very soft and I don't notice them when I lie on my side.

Too bad that they don't have volume control.

I ordered this little nut speaker to be able to listen to sleep meditation at night without having to have my phone so close to my head and to be able to leave my phone on the charger.

Frankly I expected a low quality speaker and was a little worried I would just be able to hear some muffled mumbling.

But WOW... this little nut speaker is fantastic! I can hear the voices loud and super clear. I'm absolutely thrilled!

So not only does it look super cute but it also delivers high quality sound.

Highly recommended!

I love our Echo Show, we hooked it up to the Echo Connect so now we can even use it in emergency to dial 911 or any other phone number.
The sound is crystal clear, better than the Echo Dot.

After reading all reviews of video home security systems, we decided on this one.  Good Choice!  The system was easy to set up and install and went in with no problems (other than the work involved to do it right).  I did not hook up to the internet as we don't remotely view the images.  This eliminated the need for a router and simplified the install.  The system produces sharp, clear images and the 8 cameras provide full, all around coverage for our home.  I did purchase the system with factory installed hard drive for image storage.  The Smonet 8CH 960P HD wireless system now compliments our home alarm system and allows us stored images if something does occur.  By mounting the cameras strategically on the corners and over the doors, we now have complete video coverage of our home and property.  HINTS: If you are not comfortable working with electricity and confident of your work, hire a licensed electrician to install receptacles in your attic (2-2gang boxes( 4 plugs per box) are all that is necessary with an 8 camera system).  Since the camera power chord is only approx.. 10 ft. long, I purchased the necessary DC extension cables on Amazon (Hanvex HDX50W 50ft 2.1mm x 5.5mm DC Plug, Hanvex HDX20W 20ft 2.1mm x 5.5mm DC Plug, Hanvex HDX12W 12ft 2.1mm x 5.5mm DC Plug) in amounts necessary to reach the central location in my attic to which I ran power and installed the 2- 2 gang boxes.  FIRST, HOOKUP ALL YOUR CAMERAS AND INITIALIZE THE SYSTEM BEFORE BEGINNING THE INSTALL- THIS ASSURES THEY WORK AND CONNECT BEFORE YOU INTALL THEM!  Write a number on the camera body w/sharpie so you know where each goes outside.  After that, it's just installing and hooking up the cameras, putting power to them and viewing your home/property.  To be fair, the only downside is the ethernet plug attached to each camera.  It's molded into the power cord and requires a larger hole to be drilled to slide it into the soffit.  I remedied this by getting a sheet of vinyl that matched the color of the soffit and cutting circular discs that I silicone over the holes.  Bug entry denied.  LOVE THIS SYSTEM.  It's pretty much plug-n-play for me since I didn't intend on remote viewing via smart phone.

I own the Bose QuietComfort headset, which is fantastic for use at home or on planes, but it's just too cumbersome to lug around New York City. I've been contemplating the MDR-NC10 for use on subways and general wanderings around the city for some time now, but held off in part due to some of the negative reviews on this website. When I saw the updated MDR-NC11 for sale at Brookstone, I thought, with their 60 day satisfaction guarantee, I could try them out and always return them if I didn't like them. (I do not work for and am not in any way affiliated with Brookstone; just like the fact that they have a realistic product return policy.)
In a word, this set is great! I don't have this uncanny ability to tune out noise, an ability which most New Yorkers seem to possess intrinsically; I need a little technical help, and this set does it. Anyone who has ever ridden the NYC subway knows that it creates some of the worst noise pollution of any public transit system, but with these earphones, even when just seated snugly in my ears, much of that noise is kept out of my head.
I have used it to listen to music that I previously could not expect to enjoy outside of my own four walls. Minimalist acoustics in tracks like Famous Blue Raincoat (Leonard Cohen), Drop (Red House Painters) and Colorblind (Counting Crows) are just some examples of music that I can now clearly hear while riding a rush hour train! Even the subtle string arrangement in the latter half of Famous Blue Raincoat is clearly audible. Amazing!
To be honest, I'm not entirely sure how the NC10 and NC11 differ technologically, but comparing the actual device to pictures of the NC10, Sony seems to have made it a little bigger/bulkier, which I don't understand. Given the size of the new control handle, you could have fit your standard play, stop, next track, previous track, etc. buttons of a portable device remote control on there. The relative weight with the required AAA battery means that you have to find a really good place to attach the clip or risk having it come undone due to gravity. Definitely an aspect that Sony could improve. The other thing I would have liked to see is a control for what appears to be a built-in bass boost. It helps with some recordings, but sometimes you just want to turn it off.
By default, the earphones have M size buds fitted. S and L sizes are included in the package. I found that I needed M for one ear and S for the other in order to have both phones sit comfortably but snugly in my ears. It's worth spending some time to figure out the right combination to maximise the satisfaction you'll derive from this set.
Overall, I'm incredibly happy with these earphones and think I should, with their help, be able to endure New York for a few more years yet! :)

I'm using this hooked up to my desktop computer, and I've been happy with it.

The Good:
Very small, works well, has the features I want (headphone jack, sub out, optical + usb + analog in)

The Bad:
There's a single knob that it uses to control everything - volume, equalizer, input, output, etc. Thus it takes a few extra steps to, say, change from speakers to headphones or vice-versa, which is why I knocked a star off the "Volume Control" score.

Other Notes:
1: I haven't actually tried to compare sound quality between this and some of my other amps.
2: I was getting a very soft clicking buzz in my headphones. The volume knob didn't affect it, and it wasn't always there. After some experimenting, my best guess is that it was some sort of interference coming through the power line that wasn't being filtered out by the power supply. Plugging the unit into a filtered power strip (a Rocketfish 8, if you must know) seems to have resolved the issue.

I'm using this with my computer to drive my speakers & headphones, and it's worked out very well for me.  I haven't had the chance to do a rigorous sound quality test (yet), but it seems good so far. It has all the connectivity I need, including a sub out and the headphone jack.  Controls are reasonably intuitive, and so far it's worked perfectly.  If you're looking for a small budget amp for 2 channels + sub, I'd recommend including this one on your short list.

After watching and reading a lot of reviews and doing what limited listening tests I could, I picked these over several others in this price range. I'm using them with an SVS SB-1000 Pro sub. I was immediately impressed; they're a significant step up from my ELAC Debut B6.2s, and I really like my 6.2s. The Uni-Fi seems to have better resolution and isn't fatiguing at all. I haven't been able to do a fair comparison yet, but the Uni-Fis+sub (total around $1100) seem to sound at least as good as my older 'good' speakers (>$2000 for the pair).
FWIW, my other serious candidates were the SVS Prime, Wharfedale Diamond 12.2, ELAC Debut Reference 6.2, Polk Reserve R200 (which doesn't seem to be available yet), Klipsch RP600M (of course), and a few others. I think any of them would have also been very good choices.

I'm using this to drive a couple of bookshelf speakers (Elac Debut B6.2) for my TV, rather than listen to the tinny built-in TV speakers. Setup went smoothly. I've seen comments on the 2120A model that the speaker connectors were too close together, but that doesn't seem to be an issue on the 2120C.

The Good:
It's very slim
It works well
Reasonably clean interface (though I haven't tried to change the settings yet)
Nice, sharp, readable display
If necessary it can get very loud with those speakers.

The Maybe:
I haven't done any side-by-side listening comparisons against other amps, but the sound seems good to me.
I couldn't get the optical connection to work with my TV, though I'm really not sure if the problem is the Fosi unit, the cable, the TV, or me. For my use, this isn't critical and the analog audio connection is working just fine.

The Odd:
Some of the buttons on the Fosi remote use the same command codes as some of my TCL TV's functions. Specifically, if I'm using the Roku Media Player on the TV, then the down-volume button on the Fosi remote makes the Roku Media Player app scroll through its options. And at least once, the power button on the Fosi remote turned off the TV. I don't think this is going to be a problem, just an odd quirk.

The Bad: Nothing actually bad so far.

It seems a little pricey compared to some of the other small Class D amps out there, and I wish it would play MP3s directly, so I knocked a star off. But it's a good little unit, and I'm glad I bought it.

It seems to be a good-quality, well-made cable, but I wouldn't use it somewhere that would require frequent plugging and unplugging because the RCA connectors are very, very tight, so it's difficult to unplug them.  Arguably, that suggests that it's a better connection, but AFAIK I've never had connector problems with less-aggressive RCA connectors, and I suspect that the 3.5mm end is usually the weak link anyway.

The Good:
-They sound good. They're not audiophile speakers, of course, but they sound much better than some of the other outdoor speakers I've heard, and better than any other outdoor speaker I auditioned in this price range.
-They're rugged, which you really need in an outdoor speaker. It's not just rain, after all; an outdoor speaker has to contend with errant footballs, rough handling, curious animals, etc, any of which would break a normal indoor speaker. These have a metal grill and very sturdy build and should stand up to almost anything.
-I like the mounting system; very flexible and well-engineered.

The Bad (and these are minor)
-Very cramped, awkward space for the binding posts. I use banana plugs because I need a quick, easy way to hook them up (standing on a ladder, fumbling around behind the speaker) and there's not enough room back there for normal banana plugs. I wound up buying some right-angle plugs (I got the Monoprice), and those resolved this for me.
-Sound quality is good for an outdoor speaker in this price range but if you don't need a rugged speaker, you can get much better sound for the price. As I'm writing this review, the ELAC Debut 2.0 B6.2 is on sale for about the same price as these Atriums, and the ELAC has much better sound. Of course, the ELAC probably wouldn't survive a night on my patio.

Bottom line: If you need an outdoor speaker in this price range, this speaker would be my recommendation.

The Good:
I was a little surprised at the sound quality from this little unit. After a fair amount of testing, I decided that I prefer it to to my Yamaha RX-377, which is a traditional (class A/B) amp. Yeah, the RX-377 isn't a high-end amp, and the Yamaha does a great many things while the Loxjie does only one thing, but the Loxjie does that one thing better, IMHO.
This may be the world's cutest amp. I'm not sure how functional the form factor really is, but I still like it.
Very small; this would work great for, say, a computer desk if you wanted to use traditional speakers instead of powered speakers.
Build quality and packaging seem to be surprisingly good.

The Bad (and this is exactly per the product description):
Only does one thing, and that may limit its uses. No remote (which rules out a lot of uses for me), no headphone jack (which may limit its use with a computer), no sub out, only one input.

I'd also like to note that I haven't had some of the issues that others had. At this price point, and from a relatively obscure brand, I'd sort of expect some quality control issues, but mine has been great so far.

I've only been using this for a couple of days, and I've used the Aux In and USB (for MP3s) but not the Bluetooth yet. I also haven't tried the USB port with a computer, so I don't know if it will do that.

The Good:
It sounds good, and it gets pretty loud.
It's TINY!
It does come with the a power supply. One of the other reviewers speculated that when the price went from $49 to $69, they added the power supply, and I believe that's correct. It's 19V, 3.42A and that's only 65W, so in theory it's keeping the amp from reaching its full output (50W*2 + 100W for the sub = 200W), but in practice, it's enough to be painfully loud in my cluttered garage.
Lots of stuff in a tiny package - 3 inputs (bluetooth, aux, USB), Sub out, headphone jack, etc.

The Bad (and none of these are critical):
Build quality, as you might expect at this price. For instance, when you push one of the little buttons on the front, the whole column of buttons moves a bit.
Interface is a little odd and feels unfinished. For instance, when you change the volume, it seems to go into 'volume change mode' for a couple seconds and you can't skip to the next track or change EQ.
Another interface gripe: When you turn it on, if you'd been playing MP3s, it immediately starts playing where it left off. This can be a little jarring if you're not expecting it.
Occasionally (maybe once an hour) when playing MP3s, there will be a short glitch in the playback.
The "manual" is a piece of paper that basically refers you to their website, and their website doesn't seem to show this particular device.
Nobsound . . . don't actually have model numbers? It's hard to look up reviews or basic information about the various Nobsound boxes because they don't seem to have unique model numbers or even descriptions. Something like "Nobsound DIA-3455A," perhaps, would be nice.
There are only 15 steps to the volume. If you want the volume to be fairly soft, there's a good chance that, say '2' will be too soft and '3' will be louder than you want.
MP3 playback works fine, but the micro-USB port limits the number of things that you can plug into it. I have only 1 thumb drive with a micro-USB connector, but an OTG micro-to-Type-A USB cable lets it work with 'normal' thumb drives.

The Odd:
The volume level goes from 1 to 15. 15? I guess it's 4 better than 11 . . .
Like one of the other reviewers mentioned, my Samsung TV remote control also controls the Nobsound amp. Samsung On/Off -> Nobsound Next Track, Samsung 1 -> Nobsound change Equalizer setting, Samsung 2 -> Nobsound volume down, etc. It's a remote for an older Samsung TV, so maybe it's not an issue with newer ones. I don't have the TV in the same room as the amp, so this is not a problem for me.
The equalizer settings work for USB (my testing) and Bluetooth (according to others) but not for Aux In. I'm leaving it to the default 'Nor' equalizer setting anyway, so this isn't a problem for me.

Bottom line: No regrets about buying it. Of course, it doesn't have the full flexibility (and smooth interface) of a 'real' full-size receiver, but for a lot of applications, you don't need that. I think this would be best suited for a situation where you're not switching inputs so you only ever change the volume. For example, I use 'normal' speakers with my computer rather than 'computer speakers,' and this would be a great little 2.1 amp for a setup like that. Similarly, if you wanted to hook up a decent pair of speakers to your Amazon Echo Dot (Alexa), this would be a great little amp for that.

This J-Pipe antenna mount was purchased to support an FM antenna that will be connected to my stereo receiver. After examining many other J-Pipes on the internet, this particular one met my requirements exactly. It should be noted that the material is of excellent quality, coated to withstand severe outdoor weather conditions; the wall thickness is substantial as well. Additionally, this J-Pipe is reversible. I fastened the curved end to the pivot/mounting plate which enabled me to secure the pipe in a vertical position yet it was offset enough as to not interfere with the side of my house. This resulted in the pipe being held close to the side of the house with a portion of the opposite end extending beyond the roof line. This is a great feature and should not be overlooked. The mounting bracket is steel and can be secured onto any flat surface in a variety of positions. I'll be capping off the top to prevent inclement weather from entering the pipe. I've also wrapped tape on top of the unused holes on the antenna end.

9/12/2015
Final Review:
Have now completed the installation and hookup of this antenna. The first test was to listen to Mixed Bag, 90.7 FM which was always full of static. Now this station comes in crystal clear, loud, and strong. Note that I decided to mount this antenna on the side of my house, just beneath the peak of my low roof facing the back yard. I had a quantity of twin 300 ohm cable which I wanted to use. Using a 300ohm/75ohm converter, I simply attached the end of the cable to the two 300ohm screws, protecting the connection with electrical tape. I measured and fabricated a wood mounting plate (see photo) and then screwed the mast bracket to it from the back. The wooden support board was then lag screwed, in turn, to the outside of my house just below the peak using 5" long screws. I then installed the antenna and mast, after reversing it. It now extends upwards vertically yet does not interfere with the roof line. The versatility of the mast permitted me to accomplish that.

(This review is preliminary. I assembled the antenna but am not yet ready to install it.
Assembly tips:

- Both curved antenna segments are secured to the antenna cross bar with the supplied hardware.
- The ends of one (bottom) segment are held in place with two phillips head screws. First, remove the curved metal clamp. line up the holes in the segment and, maintaining hand pressure on each segment end to ensure that it is seated firmly into it's curved metal seat, insert each screw and secure. Do not over tighten these fasteners. This is the "bottom" of the antenna, opposite the 75 ohm connector side. Attach one leg of the segment at a time.
- The ends of the second (top) segment are held in place with two hex head nuts. You will note that each nut is topped with a rubber 'O' ring. This is used to keep the nuts from threading off until assembly. Do not attempt to re-use these as they are not spacers or washers.
- Again, seat the ends of the antenna segment firmly in place, aligning the holes over the studs. Holding down the segment, install each nut. Do not over tighten these nuts.
- The closed loop ends of each antenna segment may now be gently guided in front of the black plastic locking clips. Once the looped ends are in position, firmly, yet carefully snap them into place. The circular antenna shape has now been completed. If assembled patiently and slowly, damage should not occur to the antenna.)

I have a 2006 Volvo S60R (with a factory sound system and 10cd changer and cd player but no aux no usb, etc) and I have a Samsung Note 10+ (I've had Notes since the Note 3 and am one of the millions angry about the loss of the built in AUX). I've had my car 2.5 years and initially installed a GROM aux adapter ($70)-Volvo 01-07 Auxiliary Input Adapter Kit) because at the time I had no faith in bluetooth so I declined the even more pricey $140-"Select Volvo 01-07 Bluetooth Hands Free Car Adapter Kit". Now with my newest phone I'm hating that I have to chose between audio or charging. I've been watching the price of the bluetooth grom adapter, but then amazon notified me that this Echo Auto was discounted to $19 and I wondered if it would work instead.

My top priorities are sound quality and ease of use. My car has an exceptional sound quality as is. I watched some review videos and though no one could confirm if it would do what I need and do what I need hooked into the existing grom adapter. For $19 it was worth a try.

It comes in a little box with everything you need. I ignored the vent holder and the aux cord and took it and my phone out to my car. I took the aux from my grom out of the aux to usb-C adapter that goes into my phone and plugged it into the Echo Auto. I took the power cable and attached it into my existing usb power supply. It powered on quickly and lights started flashing. I added the device in my phone's alexa app. It went through the set up (wants location and bluetooth access at all times). It then played a test sound and then considered itself a successful install even though the test sound only played out of my phone's speaker not the system. It even told me I could unplug and get rid of the aux cable as it wasn't needed. I then spent a drive struggling to get it to work. The aux cable IN MY CASE is definitely needed for it to work. Eventually when I had force closed the alexa app several times and fought with it to just open something to play (it wants you to only use alexa type stuff- music on amazon music or audible books). It wasn't until I ran my errand and came back into my car and turned it on that it automatically loaded and started to work.

To be clear, I want to listen to my music (on my phone's samsung app), or listen to youtube videos (on my phone's youtube app), or listen to podcasts (on my phone's beyondpod app), occasionally I will also use the audible app.

I don't want to talk to it or use it as I would my echo dots in my house. The only linkable music services available in the alexa app are a)apple music, b)spotify, c)pandora, d)deezer, e)siriusxm, f) tidal, and g) vevo.

95% of my music is on my samsung music app but if you plan ahead and get stuff in external apps going before you are ready to drive you can do it.

One thing that annoyed me is that when I did use a recognized source (audible), it stayed in my status bar and you can't get rid of it you just have a pause and play button, you have to swipe and close multiple alexa app windows to get it to go away.

The music quality is perfect (but this is likely related to my grom and has nothing to do with the echo auto). I am super thankful I found a cheap option that lets me play audio via bluetooth to my car stereo from my phone. I realize I'm not using it for what it's meant to be used for (voice command and alexa use) but I did do some testing and with windows at least half down and my car's eVolve exhaust system it worked about 85-90% of the time.

It never asked me about my amazon/alexa/echo/google accounts at all so you have to set your home and work from scratch.

In conclusion, this would likely be less complicated for someone who's system is less complicated and it seems to work as it's supposed to and is malleable enough to trick it into working in circumstances it wasn't meant to.

This little speaker got very heavy use (and abuse). It's lasted through 4 different phones, two laptops, one AIO, a tablet, and 4 different homes/apartments. This week it finally died (won't charge, if plugged in will turn on for a second, flash red light, die). I thought about getting another one but they're no longer carried by where I got it from and there were some limitations I'm going to try to upgrade from.

With a full charge it would last anywhere from 6-10 hours depending on volume (I would play an audiobook overnight while in bed and to save my phone battery use this). Volume/volume control were good, at my last apartment the shower was very noisy and it had to be on max volume, at my newest place I can have it at 70% and hear fine. Quality is good for the size and price, nothing deep/majestic, it's a little tinny, but I mostly use it for audiobooks and podcasts and it's fine. You can adjust the volume using your phone/device or the buttons on the speaker.

The suction cups never worked for me, I always used the hook. It's been exposed to 5 years of 1000% humidity during hot showers, drops in the sink, getting rained on, etc. No rust or issues.

Connectivity is finicky, most of the time if it's turned on and I turn bluetooth on on my phone and select it, it connects within a few seconds. Occasionally and randomly it won't connect and I have to manually make the speaker seekable and then repeat the process. It is a long press to turn on and off and connecting does take several seconds but there's a confirmatory beep when it does. Range depends on a lot of things. In some apartments it worked fine on all floors and all rooms. In other apartments it struggled and faded out when going upstairs or right outside the house.

Good value, not for audio-quality-philes, puts up with a lot of humidity and abuse.

The sound and volume control are good. I had to have it on max

I borrowed my father's truck for the past month to move. This camera is ESSENTIAL. I don't consider it cheating at all it's brilliant! It engages within a second of shifting into reverse. The picture in bright, dark, or dim light is excellent. Rain/snow doesn't affect it's use other than if the camera is buried it obviously needs to be unburied to work properly. I will 100% buy another of these when I eventually get my own truck and if I lived in a city I'd install one on my car as well (despite the fact that I have a rear and front dash cam already- that camera pretty much sucks in anything but perfect light and screen size is too small to use for parking).

I purchased this because I work long hours and have an older rescue dog with mild separation anxiety. He's been doing well and I go home half way through the day but I often work 12-14 hour days. It also helps with home security.

I am very happy with the product. The set up went OK, I downloaded the app, powered on the device, it connected to the wifi easily, but the final set up step where the camera has to read/scan a QR code to finalize, didn't work for several minutes. Finally it read the code and the app started. At this point I had to force stop the app and restart my phone before the app would work (it would show my device on the home page of the app but selecting it would cause the app to force close.

The app is pretty easy to use though settings options are minimal/lacking. The app opens showing all your NetVue devices. It shows how many new motions have been recorded. Clicking on the device brings up the active current camera. You can scroll backwards in time by dragging your finger on the timeline on the bottom of the screen. Flipping your phone automatically sets it to full view in landscape even if your phone is automatic portrait (at least for my android Note8). Clicking on History from this screen lets you view all the saved motions detected. Some are stills and some are video. I've found many where there is nothing really happening so unless a fly or one of my fish in the fish tank in the distance is setting it off I don't know what's setting off the motion capture.

Tapping on the current video gives you an option bar- which includes mute, sound/speaker, full screen, screen shot, and record video options.

The settings menu while in the current video view in the upper right corner gives you: Device information (ID, name, firmware version, connection mode), Shared Users (I have none), Motion Detection (on/off, motion time, motion zones, sensitivity), Cloud Service (24/ recording), Notifications (motion detection push function on/off), WiFi, Time Zone, Flip on/off, and Remove Device.

On the main current camera view the other option is the menu button in the top left.This brings you to your account menu page. It shows an avatar image for you, and has 5 options- NetVue (takes you back to your camera view), Motions (takes you to all your recorded motions), Account (username, name, change password, payment info, order details, log out), Support (FAQ, call, live chat, feedback, my feedbacks, user terms, returns/replacements), and About.

I have not had to use the call/chat features of chat but the FAQ has only 9 items and none of them helped me during set up or use issues.

There is a free 30 day trial of 24/7 cloud saving/recording. You can also use a micro SD but I haven't tested yet how long it takes to fill a 256 GB card which I will do in the future. The charge to continue cloud coverage is $5/month or $50 a year. Payments accepted are WeChat, Alipay, or a bank card (discover, visa, MC, Amex, JCB, and Diners Club Int'l)

Back to the device. The image quality is great, it automatically goes to grey scale in low/no light situations. There is a very brief delay when you drag horizontally to turn the camera's view. The two way speakers work well. My dog is mostly deaf but if he's in the room he can hear me. I wanted to be sure he wasn't restless, barking, or having anxiety and this lets me keep an eye on him easily. The only limitation is when I turn the camera to face the far corner of the room where my couch is, the light coming in from the window behind the couch kind of blinds the camera to seeing the couch during day light (until night vision is activated). There is a noise when the camera turns but it's not a big deal.

This is a very helpful and high quality device with a great camera that was a very fair price. I'm unsure if I will continue cloud service at this point I need to research the NetVue company and cloud security and other options first. This is a very small, unobtrusive devise.

Skip to below the row of stars if you want the meat and no background "bun". I am not a gamer. Unless you count the fact that I still have SNES ROMs along with Doom, Panganitzu, Snarfs, etc on my hard drive that I haven't actually played in a decade but restore from computer to computer as I age out of a mixture of nostalgia and fantasy of free time suddenly spontaneously occuring in my life. With that disclaimer out of the way, I have purchased "gamer"-focused computers for the past 3 times now. This is my first AIO. This is also my first submission to the inevitability of horrid newer Windows versions (I was content with XP, thank you very much).

Almost 6 years ago my $1600 HP laptop died in a foreign land while I was starting vet school. I maniacally shopped- read reviews, created spreadsheets, poured over data as I do for all purchase from a $10 toaster to a vehicle. I chose an MSI GE70 2OC i7 laptop. I can't stand slow. The big turbo exhaust fan was attractive too, as I was at school near the equator and it was perpetually 88 degrees or higher. I was mocked by my classmates- literally all of which had macbook airs or whatever apple's slender little mass-produced silver computers were. They asked why I needed a computer like that. But as time went on on our mostly TV less island, my full size screen was envied to watch movies on and my processor handled ENORMOUS picture-saturated 500-plus slide Powerpoint presentation notes seamlessly while everyone else's struggled to load. I use my personal computer for work (I'm a veterinarian), for pleasure (I write, I still dabble with web and graphic design and art), and for storage (4 TB of vet school, pictures, videos, and fully scanned and digitized documents of my entire life).

My MSI was abused, traveled to and from the US twelve times, was exposed to excessive heat and humidity for 3 years, lugged to and from and around center city Philadelphia for my clinical year, was dropped, and infected with garbage third world school programs and systems. After 6 years the deciding factor for retirement was that for the past year it can't keep time. Every start up it reverts to a random day time way in the past. It loses time within minutes. I have to hard-set time and run 2 programs to keep it running correct... until the next restart or shutdown. (PS yes I've wiped and reinstalled this thing, changed main battery and internal battery, etc etc).

I started again maniacally researching options and initially wanted something more flexible. The flipping and convertible laptops were OK, but I already have a Note8 phone (long live the Note!) and had a Note 10.1 2014 edition tablet the second it was released in 2013. They definitely helped in vet school and clinical year and now in the real world both career and regular life-wise (what little there is). I somehow stumbled upon All-In-Ones and somehow they stayed as a viable option. I'm at the point where I really can go on vacation for a few days to a week or so and not actually need a laptop, I can catch up on work (online patient records etc, emails to patients' owners, etc) and can do it very efficiently on my phone, especially with a bluetooth keyboard. So it seemed like it would be OK to come full circle and back to a fairly stationary "desk top". So I took the plunge.

I watched the price of this machine for months. It was not available through Lenovo itself with the enhanced SSD/HD size. Finally, a perfect storm of well-timed paycheck and $200 promotional discount on top of lowest price in 4 months pushed me to make the purchase. Oh what a can of worms. The first order (dramatic leading music here) shipped on time and then got stuck. It did not arrive the scheduled second day. UPS claimed holiday delay. I went to sleep that Friday night disgruntled I'd have to wait until Monday. Little did I know. I awoke Saturday am to an email from Amazon stating a refund had been issued as the item could not be delivered. (Record scratch noise). I simultaneously called UPS customer service (still showing in same place still in transit), and Amazon customer service chat. An hour later it was Amazon that informed me the item was damaged and being returned to them as the sender. I related this to the UPS dude on the phone and he was offended, saying, no proof or record of any damage and just a holiday delay, still in transit, don't worry my pretty little head. I left off with UPS and explained to Amazon that I need a computer not a refund. They instructed me to order a new one. I checked and the price had jacked up more than $200 and there were only two left and the original order's cost hadn't actually been refunded yet. I then proceeded to fall into a rabbit hole of customer service emails with Amazon. Eventually I was told to click on a provided link to purchase a new order and promised that if I purchased the computer again through Amazon through that link, they would knock off the price increase ($200) and refund shipping costs and I was told to choose expedited shipping and email them back when the order was placed so they could issue the reimbursements. I did so. They responded with "we don't do that". I responded to THAT. Eventually I was told that the order was still pending and things couldn't be adjusted until it was processed. It then showed processed and shipping label created. I contacted them again. Now I was told it was "too late to adjust as it was no longer pending but already shipped". (SERIOUSLY?) Back and forth 8 times, with seemingly every other person promising me refund interposed with those claiming "against" policy. On 12/5 I was told that it would be processed and would I like an immediate amazon credit or issued back to the card number. I responded. 36 hours later, nothing, not a word or a refund. I restarted customer service discussions. A dolt told me I had already been refunded the entire cost of the order. I wasted more time directing them to the provided new order number not the old. Another day of silence. Then, I was told I was given wrong information and no price adjustment could be made. It escalated between email and chat and eventually an awesome supervisor (thank YOU Anubha!) took care of everything which was a relief because I spent a day and a half setting up and transferring files and enjoying the new computer but I was ready to wipe it all and send it back rather than pay more than full price. The item came in it's own obvious and exciting packaging. It is slightly over 39 lbs. The box dimensions are 801x282x590 mm (315.5 x 111 x 232.3 in for you majority Americans). The poor UPS guy looked absolutely frazzled with holiday spirit and asked if he could just slide it into my house. Box has nice hand-holes which made it easy to pick up. When you go to open this though, the push-through flaps for the hand-holes need to be pushed back out or you can't get your new computer out of its cocoon. It is well packaged. It could probably drop, get kneed, and tipped over without any concerns (don't test that). I don't see how my original order could've been damaged unless it was impaled by a forklift or fell out of a UPS truck on a highway and got hit by more than 2 armored cars.

The box includes the computer itself, the base to install on it, and a wired keyboard and mouse I immediately put to the side for CommunityAid. The bag the actual computer was in had clearly been opened before as the printed sticker holding it closed had been repositioned with residue glue and text from the label next to the current position. Computer itself was mint with all the protective stickers in place and not a mark. Beautiful, though I seem to be in a red and black schemed rut with my computer choices made solely on performance/power/storage.

The base is easy to install with the two included nice little screws- no tools required, reminds me of the handiness of Ikea, dare I say. The power plug is at the bottom of the back of the base. This prevents the device from being pushed absolutely flush against a wall due to the rigidity of the exiting cord. I immediately plugged in my Logitech wired backlit K740 slim keyboard and my wireless ancient $5 HP mouse. I started up the beast. Very quiet and everything was plug and play. Not a single click or install required for the mouse/keyboard. Set up was quick and easy with a lot of unchecking of bloatware (the stuff they openly identify anyway). Instead of using old discs, I downloaded the most current drivers for my (wired) Samsung CLP printer, (wireless) Canon Pixma IX 6800 printer, and (wired) Fujitsu ScanSnap S1300i scanner. So easy and smooth, no issues. They all worked like happy family members who could all finally be in one home now (not enough USB ports on previous machines for them all).

My first experience with Windows 10. Blech. Lots of deleting, uninstalling, and Cortana was exorcised before the immediately offered Windows update was at 2%. Mine turned on with version 10586 of Windows. It offered an update to the most current (15063) which would take up a gulp-inducing measly 40 plus GB. Sigh. They do this right at the beginning so that you're rendered more accepting and ambivalent by the amazing display.

It is gorgeous. Enormous. Sharp. Extremely bright. As others have discussed, changing brightness is annoying as it is not available through settings or as a hard button. You have to access it by opening Lenovo Nerve Center -> Display Settings. I'm not sure if a keyboard dedicated button would work, my keyboard's volume buttons work but it doesn't have display buttons. You can uncover a keyboard shortcut eventually in the Nerve Center: Alt + I increases brightness and Alt + D decreases. At the lowest setting it is comfortable even for my tired, dry, sensitive eyes, in the dark.

It is as fast and peppy as I had hoped. I can multitask writing emails, viewing huge digital radiographs ("xrays"), downloading/uploading photos or video, watching movies, and transferring gigs and gigs of files all at the same time elegantly. The radiographs look better on my screen then they do at work on the actual radiology viewing screen, and instead of crouching and angling myself to examine them I can smoothly and with the touch of a single finger, tilt this screen to the best angle.

Photo editing is amazing but I sadly couldn't bring my Adobe PS CS3 with me.

This machine is very quiet, although, on the second day I started to notice the fan running. It is a unique sound in my opinion compared to all the other towers and laptops I've ever experience. The best way I can describe it is, it sounds like you are hearing through closed windows, your neighbor down the street running a generator. I hope this is normal and not a sign of bad things. It's quiet but noticeable when its on.

The sound... I am by no means a sound system snob (except when it comes to my vehicles). This computer's sound is lacking. It's OK for movies and background sounds, it just resembles an inexpensive bluetooth speaker. The enhanced setting is a bit murky and the normal is fuzzy/dull. I haven't discovered if you can customize anything yet. I don't particularly care, just the price of this device made me hope for better. The sound in my car (2006 Volvo S60R with factory dolby surround sound 11-speaker using just a grom AUX input to listen to mp3s on my phone) sounds WAY better, but I do realize this computer is trying to put out "surround" sound from a single plane of speakers.

Although it's still the honeymoon I'm really hoping I continue to enjoy this computer and stay satisfied with having chosen an AIO. With the power, speed, and storage I am hoping to get many many many years out of it (with the cost, many many many many many years). 2006 Volvo S60R with factory HU with Pioneer sound system and 6 cd changer. I watched numerous GROM and non-GROM youtube videos and thought myself prepared. Factory HU removal went delightfully quickly, with my manual transmission in neutral and e-brake on I didn't have to shuffle or wedge it out like some videos suggest who want you to keep changing gears to get it out. That being said I'd recommend putting down a cloth or something to protect your interior from dings during this process. I do not have an interior tool I use an excellent and inexpensive spatula from Ikea (swedes are ingenious). First step was popping out the surround from the shifter. Next 2 T25 hex screws. Next stereo glides out. Process was very fast and left me feeling over confident. Install was a breeze, took 10 seconds. Here's where hell broke loose. All the videos claim "plenty of room behind the stereo to tuck the device". What happened for me was no matter where I stuffed everything back behind, that stupid stereo would NOT fit back into place! I was furious and was using my feet against it when I took a breath, went inside (my dog was watching me from the window with a judgemental look in his eyes), and got a drink of water. Then I went back out and tried to be calm. I now realize that the extras my car has (no factory navigation but extra wires and plugs for back up park assist camera if one is ever installed) were just the tipping point for stuffability to get everything back in. I took my time, tried shoving things more to the left than the right which had always been suggested in videos for the S60, and finally things clicked back in. It was at this point that I was concerned all my shuffling and stuffing may have caused a loose connection so I double checked and tightened clips and plugs and did it again. Thankfully everything went back in again. PS I also drilled a small hole in the back of the storage slot to the left of the stereo for the plug to come out of since its right below where my Spigen magnetic phone mount is in the vent above. Before I did this I really electrical taped the plug into the Grom unit so no amount of time or jiggling would get it loose.

I reconnected the battery, turned the car on, plugged in my phone, set it playing Vast's "I'm dying", turned the stereo's settings to CD mode, and.... some crazy hip hop dance song came blasting out. Thankfully someone had left a CD in the stereo and I was not on the CD changer mode but the CD mode and after removing the disc and switching to the correct mode, wonderful music poured from all the speakers. Stunning quality and so happy Grom exists. I debated installing the full bluetooth aux microphone version but this is all I need. I will say my Note 8's speaker phone quality is apparently not great for callers on the other end but this could be due to my car's elevate exhaust background noise. Maybe one day I'll spring from the version with the mic but I'm very happy with this and don't talk in the car hardly ever.
