The HDD fit great without a screw in sight and mount in a what that makes connecting them really easy. They are also rubber mounted to help quiet the HDD.
All the screws are in little baggies with a sticker saying what they are for.
The CD/DVD drive mount has to two sets of holes for mounting. One set of hoses is in set positions, and for me they put my drive just about right with the front of the case. But there are also longer slots for the mounting screws so you can slide the drive back and forth to get it to sit exactly where you want your CD/DVD drive fit in the front of the case.
There is room for cabling to run next to the motherboard sides keeping cables away from the top of the motherboard. There is a lot of room under the top of the case (if you don't use extra fans there) to coil up extra wire/cables. If you wanted you could do a very clean cable installation.
It's VERY easy to plug in the ATX power connector and more important easy to take off (which was a real frustration on my old case)
There is a lot of room in general to work in this case for a micro ATX case. You can take the top off and both sides to work inside the case.
The thumb screws holding the sides on are nice and large and both sides come of easily.
This is the first case I have had that has dedicated brackets for 2.5" SSDs. The brackets have rubber grommets you attach to the sides of the SSD. That then slide into grooves holding the drive loosely by the rubber grommets. Seems overkill for a SSD drive that has no moving parts but it works.

A few random thoughts

The top can be a little finicky to get off. But on the good side it fits well when it's in place. Sits nice and flat etc.
The plastic slide that latches the top in place is a very simple plastic latch and can pop out pretty easily. ( I don't know where/when I accidentally popped off but when I went to pickup the top the latch was on the floor) But it does what it is supposed to do and has not come off in normal use.

The bracket to hold the expansion cards in place is a clever design (no screws) but takes two hands to close and you have to wiggle the cards/brackets around a bit to get to get the holding mechanism closed again.

A solid 5 stars from me

Update after a week. I have finished my install. Installed the SSD. Replaced the back 120mm fan with a 140mm fan I got here on Amazon a very slim one the Prolimatech Ultra Sleek Vortex 140mm. It gets great reviews and really compliments the insides of the case since it doesn't look clunky. The stock one worked fine and was quiet but since there was room for a 140mm and I wanted a 4pin fan to plug into the 4pin header I decided to 'upgrade'. It's a little quieter but the stock one was quiet enough that being 'quieter' doesn't make a difference if you are a couple of feet away.

I have had these a while now, and I recently bought two higher priced models from the same company (the VC02 and VSD1). After wearing those for awhile I thought for sure I would hate these after listening to the better ones. But I didn't/don't. They still have a pleasant sound to my hear. They don't have the same quality as the more expensive ones but these still sound good for what they are. And at $20 I won't cry myself to sleep I lose or break them. So I take them places where I would not want to take the better ones.

While not as HiFi sounding as some other cheap phones, I like these enough that I bought a 2nd set. The 2nd set had more bass than the first set, almost too much, but not so much that I didn't like them. If I lost them I would replace them.

These might not be for everyone. They have a strong but tight bass. Not boomy or tubby but the bass is there. I really like these phones for rock music and because they have plenty of bass I don't have to turn them up looking for bass.

5 stars for value
4 stars because there are other phones with a cleaner sound (try the Koss KSC75 for a more hifi sound for cheap)

Good cable, but just so some of the other overzealous reviews don't lead you astray: don't run this cable in walls or from one room to the next because it is not riser or plenum rated; it not having that rating means it could spread fire or put off excess toxins in smoke in the event of a fire. And, Oh my God, don't think you can use it for electric cable: there's more to a cable than the thickness of the wire that makes it safe for electricity - mostly the temp rating of the sheath.

Also recognize that this is copper clad aluminum. Pretty normal for this type of speaker wire, but still not as great as pure copper.

All that said, this is nice cable for what it is. 12 gauge is generous for most speaker applications and the clear sheath looks cool in some cases, like short runs across floors for your front speakers. And it seems like a reasonable price.

I have multiple reels of CMR rated speaker cables for my whole house audio system, but I can most definitely always find uses for this cable, especially for speaker hookups within a room.

What a great thing, proper high-res PoE cameras like this one. I learned a while back not to care if the brand was generic, because all these things are from the same 4 or 5 OEMs. You can search for which pretty easily, although some of the really new "brands" like this one may not show up.

Regardless, this had the minimum specs (and also basically the maximum available) I wanted for my new home's camera setup, and it is also white, to blend in with the fascia boards it is mounted on. I got it up high enough into the recession on my porch roof that you can't see it from the sidewalk - at least if you're my height - but it can see you. And you have to be discreet in a nice neighborhood: I don't think people want to feel like cameras are a necessity. But you never know. And good theives would be scoping your property out ahead of time, so in my mind a purposefully discreet camera would say, "there are lots of security features here you probably don't know about".

Anyway, it works with my off-branded NVR, which I believe to be a Uniview OEM. I have it so the cables go into a hole in the fascia and the camera covers the hole (I was able to make a generous sized hole, thankfully, due to the large mounting plate (not too large, but basically the diameter of the camera). I really needed that larger hole to pull my cables (this is a very old house, so getting the cables run inside columns and underground and all hidden was really a feat).

It has what I'm not gathering is standard equipment on a good PoE camera - 3 cable ends - one for RJ-45, one for external power if you're not using PoE, and one for a reset button which I hope I won't need since it'd be a bit of a pain to get to.

If you can't hide your cables completely, you can also run them out the side of the baseplate. The camera is essentially infinitely adjustable with very large range. This seems basically the same standard design as all my old analog cameras from my last system on my last house.

I believe you can get this to show up on an app all by itself if you don't use an NVR, which is an awesome feature if you only have one camera or a few by the same brand. I'm also sure I can get this set up with my QNAP NAS if I wanted to, but when I played around with that on my last camera, I wasn't super-impressed (plus, I'm not about to pay for additional licenses on this stystem that is going to be augmented many times). Since I knew I was going to use the NVR, I just went right to it with this camera.

The NVR way sort of automatically makes a VLAN on your network so your cameras aren't taking up IP addresses and getting in your way. You can also set it up so it takes a regular IP address on your regular network and your NVR sees it and records over the network. There's less traffic eating up your other connections if you go straight to the NVR, though. Personally, I don't need a lot of IoT IP addresses obfuscating my network when I'm trying to track down a new device or other computer. But the variety and versatility of these setups is unmatched compared to DVR systems (although those are perhaps unmatched in their simplicity...but you can make the NVR thing as simple as you want to as well).

Anyway, I love the camera. Love the security. Love being able to see if I have a package. Love being able to see what cars are in my driveway. Love having great newage features on an old house.

I used to hate this style of CMP. I used to refer to them as "plastic fingered crap" (yes, these are metal). And that's because telecomm rooms maintained by multiple personnel are always full of beat-up components and poor cable management.

So when I got one of these (a plastic model) for my home cabinet, I realized it actually is quite nice, for a couple reasons: One, I'm taking care of this, so I won't be forcing it too full or anything like that. And I won't be opening it up every day or forgetting to remove abandoned cables, etc., so I think it will hold up and work as it should for a long time to come. And two, since as a homeowner, I can't avoid having some consumer equipment which doesn't all fit on a rack properly, I can legitimately use (and forgive myself for using) the holes (passthroughs) in the back of this to run cables through the rack space to hook up those pesky consumer devices that don't all have their ports appropriately in the front of the equipment.

This one has metal fingers, which is nice. Now you really don't want to pack them too full or you might be more likely to damage some cables, but that'll hold up nicely and help avoid having them get malformed over time.

Nice product.

These are rolled on both top and bottom, which is the single best quality identifier I can think of for something static made out of metal.  A flat plate would be easy to warp or bend if treated improperly.  These will keep their shape well and look good in the process.

So far, so good.

I only have one PoE camera so far, but have used many DVRs and analog cameras in the past. This was a good and inexpensive way to get started (I'm starting on a new old house with brick walls, so I have to get motivated to find ways to run hidden cables all over again) and utilize/recycle a legacy surveillance hard drive.

I looked into Uniview and different hardware OEMs after reading another reviewer's comments. It seems that every brand of camera and NVR I've ever heard of (or haven't) is from 4 or 5 main companies, most assuredly Chinese, and more or less the same. I almost think that is probably a good thing since you're getting more sophisticated software and better interoperability than if all these companies had to write their own apps, etc. The only very negative thing I could find is if you're trying to abide by the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), or just trying to avoid supporting China in general, then this badge swapping is obfuscating the process. It'll be hard to know when you're getting chips from Huawei, etc., and yes, they may be giving themselves access to your cameras. I don't put them in the bedroom anyway.

The camera I have is from a different OEM, and it has its own web server, app, etc., but it only has local (i.e., SD card) storage, so if you don't do paid-for-cloud, you'll want to have an NVR. The cool thing is that you can use the integrated PoE switch OR NOT. So if I want to use the camera's associated app or just keep access to its configuration via its web server, then I can just power it via another PoE switch, and then direct the NVR to its IP address to record. This still eats up one of the NVR's channels, I believe.

If you hook it directly to the NVR, the NVR forces you to give it an IP on a different subnet, which may be good for security and clearing up your IP scheme, but then your only access to the camera will be through the NVR. I think I'll end up doing this anyway, because I realized at some point that I don't need all these 4k video transmissions running through my network clogging up various links. The good thing is that - although I haven't necessarily gotten everything exactly as I want it yet, it was still easy to get this working without issues. Pretty sure once I settle on an architecture and setup for my cameras, they'll all just work indefinitely without maintenance.

I assume* that if you have wireless cameras, they'll work with this NVR as well, just by IP address. That's something to think about.

Now, I also tried my camera with my QNAP NAS, and had quite a few issues, and really didn't like the result, not to mention they'd charge you for licenses beyond the few that come with the actual NAS. I've already ruled that out - beyond just the fact that it creates a burden on my consumer grade servers - and will be much happier with this NVR.

If you're not IP/network capable, you may prefer to buy a package preconfigured to work together, which will likely be as plug and play as a DVR system, but buying separately has its advantages, too, such as picking out specific cameras for specific places, using existing hard drives and other hardware, etc. And beyond that, I'm guessing there's a lot of cool stuff I just haven't figured out yet. Like, can I record over the network from here to my NAS or other storage if I want to? And where's the web server on this thing? I feel like that should be easy enough to turn on and set up so that I don't have to run down to my telecom room to play with this. Yeah, it came with a CD, but finding a CD reader is more onerous than running down to my telecom room.

Anyway, I like this thing a lot, and it seems like a very inexpensive entry point. It's a lot like every DVR I've ever used, just with a built in PoE switch. I'm guessing most NVRs are the same as well. Just wish it was rack mountable...

Fantastic camera. One of those items that screamed quality right out of the box. Good build, compact size, and has a waterproof connector for your Ethernet cable. Can be mounted where the cable comes through a hole in a fascia board behind the camera or where the cable comes out the side of the base. Base is infinitely adjustable. Camera has slight overhang on the top to keep water off the lens. Three pigtail cables - RJ-45 female connector can be the single cable if you have PoE or you can power this via a 12v power adapter or cable (local or centralized) for versatility.

This is my first IP camera, but I've used many analog cameras and DVRs.

I've hooked this up three ways: By itself, to a switch on the same network as a stand-alone NVR, and to a switch on the same network utilizing my QNAP NAS as the NVR - in each case powered by PoE. Here are some details I've figured out in the process:

---By itself: You can view it quickly and easily without delay with the App, which seems to have all the things you'd expect from a camera viewing app. I assume you can record to or snapshot to an SD card from the description, but I'm going to record to my network, so I didn't try that feature. This was just plug and play, worked super easy.

What I love is that once you figure out the IP address, you can access the camera via a webserver, which pretty much future-proofs the hardware. I despise "smart" devices where you need an app, because then you're at their mercy to run their app on whatever OS they decide to use and they can force you to make accounts, update, etc. Having this open to the user/owner is the way to go. Bravo.

And that web server is full featured. I was able to play around and do everything here before I bothered downloading the app.

Note that - like every camera I've ever used - the viewing software sends a substream which is lower resolution unless you demand the higher resolution. With the app you can see low and medium resolution, but 4k has trouble playing over WiFi (or else it's just smart enough to realize my screen can't support it anyway). Just pointing this out so you realize if you're seeing pixels, that doesn't mean the camera isn't actually recording at 4k.

---With NVR: I recently acquired a cheap 8-channel 4k NVR that I believe to be a Uniview OEM. I added a hard drive and put it on the same network as this camera. The NVR has an 8 port PoE switch built in, but it must also be a router, because it wants to use a different subnet if you put the camera on the NVR's switch. Otherwise, you can easily point the NVR to the camera via IP address.

So...if you point the NVR to the camera via IP address, you can view the camera from its own app or from the NVR app. I assume this still takes one of the NVRs 8 channels. This might be useful if you want to give someone access to just one camera on your network. But it occurred to me that, setup this way, you have constant data streaming over your network, and after you add quite a few cameras in 4k, this is going to start adding up.

If you put the camera directly on the NVR, you'll have to change the IP manually to match the subnet, or maybe you'll somehow get it to work through the NVR or with DHCP. I hadn't bothered spending time figuring this out yet because at the time I thought I'd just use my other switch, but I'm thinking once I get more cameras, it'll probably make more sense to put them directly onto the NVR and ...actually, then I won't have to change my entire IP scheme since I won't have so many new devices to organize.

I'm certain I can get it all working in unison with no problem, but it is more complicated than if you just buy an NVR set with a bunch of cameras already ready to work together. Either way shouldn't be a problem if you have IP knowledge, but I'm guessing a random homeowner might prefer a set.

---Using my NAS as NVR. Hmmm...a little disappointed with QNAP in this regard. I mean, I have three NASs, and I'm assuming they all have 2 licenses included, but to combine them into one program then I believe requires yet another license. I'm not into licenses, even if they're a one time deal, because that means you need accounts and if something happens where they're lost, you can run into all kinds of other issues. I just think consumers need to stand up to this sort of thing. But anyway, I had two included, so I tried it out:

I realized that this is a lot of work for my little consumer grade NAS, and even if I had a more hardcore NAS, I'm not sure I want resources being used all the time. It seems like I couldn't get it to use H.265 compression, nor could I get it to record at the higher resolutions and frame rates. Again, I didn't play with this too awful much once I got it recording and working because I already realized I definitely like the stand alone DVR better. The QNAP even had extra stuff to download and windows to pop up on your PC and all this other stuff. Just not as streamlined as I had hoped.

----Conclusion is that the camera is awesome. I'm not sure many are any better at this point. If you want something that just works easy and you don't know much about networking, you may wish to just buy an NVR set. But if you are IP capable, I think buying components separately could be a great way to go because you can really customize what you want to do. But as always, more options with networking means more potential headaches. But I am pretty certain that once you get it working the way you want it, you should be able to forget all about it and have it work indefinitely.

Oh, and after all that, I shouldn't forget to point out that I'd be thrilled to have this all by itself watching my porch just so I can tell when there's a package out there. My Ring (that came with the house) can't even see that because of the angle it is set at.

Of course you can just use these as couplers, but you can also use them as keystone jacks in some* wall plate installations, or you can fill in patch panels equipped with keystone jacks.

*please note that these end up being a lot deeper than a punch down jack, so I don't recommend them for most wall installations, especially if there's anything making your wall cavities even more shallow than the standard 3.5" (my plaster walls are less due to the lathe). You definitely need the low voltage open boxes in that case, and then you may bend the cable too roughly behind the boot if you have to squeeze this into your wall cavity.

Even so, still many uses around the house.

First, I'll just tell you that, yes, this computer is incredibly awesome. Then I'm going to nitpick it as much as I can just to give you an honest perspective and hopefully some details you haven't already figured out.

My last primary home laptop was an Alienware 17. It came out after Windows 8, but it ran 7 because everyone still hated 8. I knew it was getting old, but I didn't want to give up that super-high-quality feel. That computer was really large and substantial, which was both a fault and gave it a luxurious feel that I thought couldn't be reproduced. ...a long time ago, I had no real opinion of Asus, but then my Dad actually got a ROG at some point and I was sort of amazed that this brand that I would have almost considered generic at the time put out such a fine piece of hardware. So when I had a chance to get this computer, I knew it was good enough to replace the Alienware. And it is, absolutely. This computer is about half the weight and much smaller, but it still feels substantial and "super premium". This does have a compressed keyboard (the Alienware actually was wide enough to have a separate number pad), but it's spread out enough as to not be cramped or annoying. And thank God the Delete key is in an intuitive place! (I find that a problem with many laptops). As always, a new touchpad takes some getting used to, but I have it configured how I want it now, and I even finally gave in and started doing two-finger scrolling...

I need to get these gripes out of the way, although they apply to almost all pre-built computers: Too much crapware and ads that won't let you alone at first (RE: McAfee), but not nearly as much as a lot of cheap computers. I hate that Microsoft won't even let you use your own hardware without getting you to make an account for their stupid software. I'm not sure you could even start using this computer if you don't have an active Internet connection (or they're making it harder and harder to find a workaround, but I'm getting too bored and jaded to bother fighting it anymore). Windows 11 at least seems to work well and look good, but they still have some super annoying features from trying to be too much like Apple. I just can't stand that we have some settings under Settings and others under Control Panel. I hate the Apple feel of Settings, but to have to use both is just stupid. Then you can't ungroup icons in the taskbar and I hate the button to turn off Wifi because it's too easy to hit. This is not a phone! OK...point is, I wish MS would respect its customers the way they used to.

On to more specific nitpicks:

1) Once in a while, I still turn on the number pad on the touchpad accidentally. This is a super cool feature, but I'm not sure if I'll ever get used to using it for typing in phone numbers and stuff like that. The overhead on having to tap and hold the corner first if a bit much, and then it's easy to forget to turn off. Of course, if you're doing spreadsheets, you'll probably be thrilled to have that on a midsize laptop.

2) As usual, the included control center software, "Armoury Crate", is quirky in how it works with Windows. As with my previous Alienware, it's now only the second computer I have left such software installed and allowed to run (not sure you could get all the lights working otherwise), but it takes some fidgeting to get used to, and I had some issues with WiFi not coming back on and stuff that I attribute to this. At some point, you just have to give Windows back control of the power settings. Once I got it all working in harmony (basically just using "Armoury Crate" for the lights) it's doing fine. I'm still not convinced about leaving the other Asus software on there - it keeps bothering me about updating, but it seems redundant not only to Windows, but to Armoury Crate as well.

3) The Screen doesn't tilt back quite as much as I'd like it to. I'm glad it seems to have a sturdy mechanism to hold it in place, but I could use just a few more degrees on a day like today: Sitting in a super comfortable chair with my leg crossed at 90 degrees, back of the laptop on the leg. I can still use it fine, but a few more degrees would be ideal.

4) Another common problem: I wish they'd put twin power ports on the back and side of the device so you could pick which one you wanted to use. The battery is great, so I'm not using power now, but power out the back doesn't work with the position I'm sitting in described above. Also, I put it back on a small table near the couch when not in use, but it's slightly annoying to plug and unplug. Much of that has to do with the fact that there is a "goiter" (I think it's used to cancel out capacitance, but I'm not sure) on the power cord right near the barrel jack. This is just in the way and gets caught on the back of the table.

BTW, the power brick is huge, which doesn't surprise me, but I absolutely love that you can plug in with power delivery, which means you can use this with a proper USB-C docking station. I guess you'll still want the power brick for hardcore gaming, but I love the option.

5) No USB ports on the right side. Not a big deal, but sometimes you want the option depending where you are or how you're sitting. They use the space for some add-on thing they want to sell you instead...

6) I get sick of trying to keep up with WiFi, but I actually just got a WiFi 6E AP, and it's awesome to be able to use it. I think they really did get rid of some latency there. It's pretty awesome when things get noticeably better. And I haven't even gotten the AP working optimally yet...

Also 2.5Gb LAN port. I don't have a 2.5Gb capable switch yet, but I'll have to work on that because my AP has a port for that as well...

7) I know everyone wants to hear about game performance: I haven't been able to bog this thing down with anything. I can play 2020s era games and have it transcoding for Plex in the background, and it barely spins up the fans. I mean, I can't give you anything but anecdotal evidence, so I'll leave that to professional electronics reviewers, but I'll just tell you it is as awesome as they say. At this point in time, I don't think there's anything this can't handle (at least that you'd likely be doing at home). And, just as importantly, it really is quiet and doesn't seem to run exceptionally hot, either. My last laptop could get so annoyingly loud.

8) Battery. I was surprised to see the battery's Ah rating was barely higher than my previous computer, but then even more surprised how much better the power must be managed, because it'll more or less last all day if I'm just doing work-work (like spreadsheets and boring stuff) and web browsing. So it has the feel of a great all around, everyday type of computer (and you can even turn the lights off if you want to be low key), but then you can instantly turn it into a real powerhouse. You can have a profile for use with a docking station for work, one to maximize battery life for leisurely web browsing around the house, and one for use with the power brick as a gaming rig. Versatility is fantastic.

9) I had some weird quirks early on, and called customer service. One thing was the WiFi I was talking about earlier and one was the screen doing weird stuff. I partly called customer service just because I wanted it on file that I was having issues in case I did need a repair. Normally I wouldn't just because I normally know better than they do... But I got a real person quickly and he gave me non-condescending advice and made a file for me. I just had to do some random driver updates and it seemed to work. Now, I don't think things should ship needing updates, but...at least they have real customer service.

Well, I could probably pontificate for 10 times this long, but the conclusion is that after the minor pains of changing computers and getting used to some slight hardware differences, getting past the frustration of Microsoft and a few typical antivirus program ads, doing little tweaks to get the touchpad working for me instead of against me, and screwing around with updates until my problems went away, I am 100% happy with the computer. Not just happy, but thrilled. This is the kind of hardware that once you experience as your own, you really can't go back. This not only has all the computing power and features you could want, but it's also cool in every way.

First of all, I love that this company uses all the highest quality ingredients to make a good cable (pure copper, proper rating, UL listing) and then they have no need to hide anything (they make some CM rated cable that they tell you directly can not be run in walls. Generic companies try to hide that from the customer, which is actually a really dirty trick, since many people are not aware of low voltage cable ratings).

You can see the specs for yourself. This is fantastic cable. But it is - it's not a trick. Shielded cable is a tiny bit harder to deal with, if you're not familiar, BUT there are definitely situations where it is advantageous. I'm dealing with a new (for me) old house now with solid masonry walls and no clear path from basement telecomm room to attic, so I'm actually considering running all my cables outside in a downspout (meant for the situation, similar to how they do with HVAC lines). The problem there is you want to ground everything or risk equipment damage. The best way to do that is with shielded cables and then a patch panel that accepts sheilded cables and bonds to a good ground. It'd be pretty foolish, I think, to run a bunch of category cables outside with no way to ground them.

There are codes and standards for separation between telecomm and electric, but a lot of times you'll want to be safer than that by using shielding as well. And, of course shielding decreases crosstalk between parallel cables.

There's really no point in buying cheap cable. You'll only regret it later. And most of the price is in the copper...

This is not really beautiful - there may be better options out there in that regard.  But it does offer about the best volume for cable pass through that I can imagine.  And it certainly looks better than a blank hole in the wall.  I do like that you can have the bump-out facing inward or outward.

This is a cool idea and - as a tool nut - I'm thrilled to have them. But...I'm still not certain as to when you need them except if you just don't have a ratchet around or if you have a very limited volume for a tool to-go bag (which could happen).

I say this because once these are attached to the correctly sized wrenches, they really aren't any more shallow than even my cheap, stamped, Craftsman ratchets. The wrenches are, of course, and these are very low profile, but by the time you get the bump-out to hold a socket, they seem the same size.

They use a rubber washer to hold the adapter to the wrench. That's understandable, but you know those wear out after a while and it isn't really idea, although I'm not sure there's a better option that doesn't increase the depth. They do give you some extra rubber washers, but that just makes me sigh, as I have all kinds of little bags of consumables in my tool chest that just add clutter.

I do like these a lot. They're great quality and they're just cool. I'm still struggling to see the real purpose however (hey, if you thought of one, let me know - I'm open to suggestions!)

This is actually meant to mount inside your PC and attach directly to the USB bus for control, but will power 8 fans attached directly to it.  It uses all interior PC pinouts, and it's really quite slick, sure to please any gamer or PC build nut.  I am actually using it to power fans in my (relatively stark) equipment cabinet, using a server to power and control the unit.  This was quite a fun project to get set up and working, and I like to be able to control and monitor from my main house server.  I really didn't need a ton of airflow in there since it's in a relatively cool basement, so 8 existing fans is more than enough for me.  Definitely a nice piece and with a good GUI (interface).  Allows plenty of fan control.

This is the no-BS line from Cisco. Enterprise features, but nothing proprietary, no forced contracts, no stupid power port that requires special power cords...

You can hook this up and it will work right out of the box, just like an unmanaged switch, which will make network setup and augmentation very easy. Once I signed into the box, I pretty much had to change my password, but then I had a world of options at my fingertips that I could change at my leisure. There were a few things I wanted to configure right away, and plenty of others I realized I wanted after doing some research. I still have plenty to learn and play with when I have time I want to spend on this.

I do believe you can use Cisco command line to configure these, but it also has a very familiar (to other consumer/business equipment) GUI that is intuitive to use. I will say, though, that the GUI it can be pretty cumbersome if you want to use it to go through and turn on a feature on every single port individually. Part of the problem is that you have to save each port individually and then use the drop-down to do the next port. This switch can be a little slow to respond and therefore frustrating when changing multiple features in a row. I also have a 350 series 10 port switch that does NOT have that problem. I am not sure if it has more resources available or just has less to keep track of because of having fewer ports., but that might be a consideration if choosing between the 250 and 350 series. And if you use command line, you might not care at all...

Oh, and you have to do the "save to running config" thing like you do with the Enterprise stuff. Seems strange, but I guess it more or less makes sense why. But at least in this case you can just click apply...and then go up and click the blinking disk to save (to running config).

I am using this in my telecomm closet, which manages to keep nearly all the ports in my house hot. I'm using ports 25-27 as a 3Gbps link to my Cisco 350 series switch in my external cabinet, which connects my servers with multi-Gb links. This is all new functionality for me, but something I've been looking for for a long time.

Here's some random stuff I figured out along the way:

-I am using 10Gbps copper DACs between the two devices. They do negotiate down to 1Gbps, they are cheaper than buying multiple SFPs, and I can use them later when I get 10Gbps ports (so the only reason you'd use fiber is if you needed a >100m link.

-Port trunking works between DAC and regular Cat6 (apparently it won't work with fiber SFPs mixed with Cat6.

-Not sure what I was doing wrong before port trunking on another switch, but I couldn't get anything better than high-error best effort to work as far as speed. On these 250/350 Cisco devices I'm using, all four of my trunks are working perfectly and clearly working at full speed without uncorrected errors (if any at all).

-There are "green features" included, but off by default. The one looks at link length and lowers power on those links if less than 50m. You can only use this if you turn off the Energy Efficient Ethernet standardized protocol, which you might do if the device you are using doesn't work, but I haven't found a case where it correctly reads my link length (and my testers do figure out the correct length, so I don't get this). The other green feature is Energy Detect, which I've turned on across the board, but it's hard to tell if that really saves energy or not, because it just is "on" when the link is down.

-The ports are counted strangely. Port 1 is the top left. Port 2 is bottom left. Port 3 is top second from left, etc. This caused me some brief confusion. The great thing is that you can name all your ports in the GUI so that can make things a lot more clear for you, especially if you keep all ports in your building hot or if you at least keep most of the devices static.

There are a ton of features here, and even more on the 350 series. If you're deciding between the 250 and 350 series, I suggest you do some serious homework to figure out if you actually need the 350 series. Here are just a few of the things I noticed the 350 series has that the 250 does not (not a comprehensive list):

On the 350, you can set link speeds lower on LAGS, use protected LAGS, more LAGS, UDLD, Ethernet tagging, VLAN mapping/private VLAN, lots of VLAN grouping options and more VLAN settings in general, and ISCSI status for QoS.

Oh...worth noting is that the 350 series apparently allows many more trunk groups than the 250 series, which only allows 4, so I would not necessarily want a 250 series for my 24 port switch if I didn't have my servers separate on the 350 (yet it seems unlikely you'd need more than 4 trunk groups on a 10 port 350).

One thing I don't like is that on some rack mounted equipment, you have one set of "wings/ears", but multiple positions/mounting options. These mounting brackets at least are included, but seem like they'd only work with this switch AND you can only put them on in one position, which means the switch will protrude about an inch forward in your cabinet (Well, you can also mount the switch backwards, if you consider that helpful). It would be better to have the option of recessing the switch an inch if you needed to. I also wish they could recess the power supply port on these things since - even with the heatsink on the back of this - the power cord is still the thing making this a tight fit in my closet.

Despite those two nitpicks, there's really nothing about this switch I don't love. Yes, I can absolutely imagine this to be a great line for a company to use, and I think I could even get a robust network up and running without too much stress or trouble. But there are plenty of other real-world applications for a home network as well: setting restrictions for kids or renters or whoever from getting to all areas of your network. There is all kinds of port security features here, protected ports, and VLAN features, so you should be able to do just about anything you want to do with these switches. Also QoS, traffic limiting, etc. I love having these features at my disposal, even at home!

This is like getting nearly everything you'd get with Enterprise Cisco switches, but without all the awful proprietary nonsense: no licensing or forced accounts or anything like that - and it even comes with a power cord. AND that power cord - and the attachment point on the device - is industry standard IEC type and withOUT the Cisco notch! That's good, because I am using this with an IEC style PDU.

I believe you can configure this with standard Cicso command line, but it has a GUI very similar to other business and consumer products, so you can configure everything at your leisure and with just a search engine to figure out some of the protocols you may not be familiar with. Importantly, though, is that it just works when you hook it up - just like an unmanaged switch - and you can take your time with everything else (you should sign in and it will more or less force you to change the password right off the bat). There are a few "wizards" to help you through some common functions as well.

I'm using this in a small server cabinet, which is outside of my telecomm closet. I have three sets of 2x1Gbps port trunks for the servers, which all have two network ports, and then I'm using ports 8-10 as a 3Gbps link to my Cisco 250 series switch in the closet, which connects to all the end user devices. This is all new functionality for me, but something I've been looking for for a long time.

Despite those two nitpicks, there's really nothing about this switch I don't love. Well, okay, I'd like some 10Gb SFPs, (which are available in this line). But having some real Cisco equipment is actually all it's cracked up to be!

I had actually made something like this to run some fans in my custom equipment cabinet. This is a lot cleaner and nicer, however, without needing all the splices and everything else.

The connection points are surrounded as well, and should accept the entire connector; that seems like a luxury, but I do wonder if there are times where it will be too small in the interior to accept a male connector.

Regardless, most of the time, this is a great way to power a pair of fans. Supply our own 12v rectifier.

These seem like great fans, but another reviewer pointed out that the specs on the box are different than the product page - these no name companies really need to fix those supply issues. It just goes to show that sometimes you aren't buying a specific product, but whatever that seller has in stock.

Anyway, in this case the fans seem great, most importantly because they don't seem very loud. Again, like that other very thorough review pointed out, they'll last a few years, so probably can be thrown out along with your computer after you've given the whole setup a good life.

At time of writing, this is going for $30, but I think it may have been $20 previously. I was surprised to see those prices, because it seems pretty sophisticated. I don't have an Apple watch, but I don't imagine it does much more than this (although I could definitely be wrong). It's a shame that wearing a watch sort of irritates me because I can see a real point to having this, surprisingly.

I think the Apple watch may have wireless charging, whereas this uses a magnetic cable with a USB port on one end. This can be just a little tricky to ensure it's charging while on its side (I guess face down is fine, but then you can't be 100% certain it's actually charging), but you get the hang of it quickly.

You get a surprising amount of information on the small face, and then a few scrolls in whichever direction can give you more information. You get use to that very quickly, too, and it is, in fact, very intuitive. You can always find what you want before too long.

The main face can be flash updated, meaning you can download different themes to the device. There's a couple neat ones, but nothing too exciting. I'm guessing there may be user uploaded versions for the Apple version (or maybe not, as Apple always locks its stuff down too much), and that could happen here, too, but I'm guessing not as many people have this, which will lessen the available "content".

The step count is the main thing, along with the time. The watch usually pops on for you to see it when you raise it to look at it, but not always. Usually a shake will turn it on if it doesn't notice you raise your arm. If nothing else, you can press the button. It's a fine line, because too many false positives would also be annoying.

It seems to last a very long time, like many days. And the battery indicator has five segments instead of the three that some devices have, so you get a better indication of when you'll have to charge it.

I'm not really convinced it's super accurate with my steps, but I'm not sure the Apple version would be either. And then it makes a guess on your calorie burn based on steps, which is just for fun as far as I'm concerned. It can do a bunch of other stuff if you hook it up with your "health" app, but I never bothered setting up that app in the first place.

Other convenience factors include it vibrating when you get a call or text, which can help you notice calls and texts, especially if you have your phone on vibrate all the time like I do (and for that reason miss a lot of calls). You can also read your text messages on here, although not really so well that you wouldn't just pull your phone out of your pocket if you actually want to read it (although knowing if you can ignore it can be helpful). You can also control your music to some degree and tell your camera to take a picture, which will be wonderful if you're one of those people always taking pictures of themselves (of if you just want a picture of you and your friends without having to have someone stay behind to press the button).

It also has a timer. Some of these things require the app to be running on your phone (I'm not saying which ones for sure because I think the manual said the camera shutter wouldn't work without the app, but it does). And there is a "find phone" feature which I can't figure out how to get to work, although I haven't tried much. I mean, it's bluetooth, so if the phone is far away, it won't help you anyway.

The watch and the band look just like the Apple version from what I can tell. The band also comes off easily, so I'm assuming it can be replaced with anything that fits the Apple version, but double-check before you count on it.

Overall, I like it a lot. I'd never consider the Apple version, which I assume costs hundreds, but for a fraction of that, I think it's a pretty cool toy.

I received this item through the Amazon Vine program, although the usual green writing may not be shown. The review is specifically for model: GS305EPP.

Port Binding: I noticed that the Netgear chart shows for the "plus" series of switches, that only models with 16 or more ports support port binding. However, through the web interface, I was able to do a single instance of port binding (it looks like it allows you to bind up to four ports, although I can't think of an instance where binding more than two ports on a five port switch would be worthwhile). I learned some quirks about port binding in the process, that using 802.3ad with multiple Linux servers doesn't allow for more than a Gb of data in any one direction anyway. BUT this switch does apparently support balance-rr, because I could get almost 2Gb/s over a 2Gb aggregate link. I think my hard drives in those machines were maxed out at that point. As I understand it, balance-rr has a high error rate because it uses striping and not all machines support it. But it was working quite nicely with my NAS units and this switch (I was expecting the 8 port switch, which would have made that setup more worthwhile because I could fatten the links on all three servers.

Although my current Netgear Pro AP does not have two ports for binding, I did have an AP before that supported it, in which case that feature on this switch may be an excellent option (particularly considering it is PoE). I haven't done the math for myself, but I think that port binding is almost a gimmick on APs because there is so much overhead on WiFi that even if your AP has a throughput in the multi-Gb range, enough of that is overhead created by the AP that you're not actually getting that much data from one computer to another.

Insight and Web Interface: The Insight App shows this switch (and my Netgear APs) as having "limited support" (just shows basic device info and a link to the device's webpage), so they're not really trying to get users of the "plus" line to subscribe to that in perpetuity.

And you don't need the app to use the switch. You don't even need the configuration page, really: I just plugged this into my old 24-port unmanaged Netgear workhose and it picked up an IP from the router and worked just like an unmanaged switch until I decided to give it a static IP and manage it.

I was really surprised how many features are packed into the management software, considering these are Netgear's lower line of managed devices. But most of the stuff you'll see on huge enterprise devices is here as well (well, it's been a while since I've been inside the big enterprise stuff, but all those goodies reach us as consumers before long).

The web interface is just like any other network device - you can reach it from any webpage and it is super GUI - probably just a little more than I really want it to be, but it is very intuitive and you can find everything with a few clicks. I say "super GUI" just because it looks fancier than I need it to. And one thing I find a little irritating is that when you expand one box, it collapses another, so you can't look at everything at once. This doesn't really matter, but I'm old school where I just want substance over style and even style that doesn't sacrifice substance still looks like they're trying too hard.

PoE: Clearly, on this 4+1 port switch, all four of your devices can use a full 30w each, so this is non-blocking in PoE+ as well as throughput. At time of writing, the 8 port with the same power budget was actually cheaper, so you might consider that, even if you can't use all the ports at full PoE.

What is great about this, is that besides just being able to add APs and IP cameras to your network (or even lighting, etc.), you can turn them on and off from the web interface. So I can keep my main AP on PoE (and therefore on my telecom closet's backup power supply), and then turn my detached garage's AP on and off from the web interface rather than having to go down to the basement and plug or unplug the PoE injector every time I want to use the garage AP (I just turn it on if I'm going to be working out there and might need to watch some "how-to" videos or control my audio system from the local LAN).

*Netgear, if you're listening, I would love to have a super lightweight (and free) app that works remotely (when not necessarily on LAN) to turn ports on and off for exactly this type of reason.*

Construction: Solid device, very dense and professional looking. Plenty of lights that tell you a lot from a glance. Power supply is external and about as big as the device itself. Would personally love a way to rack mount this AND the power supply (for maximum flexibility) in 1 RU, but of course I realize most people don't want to waste a whole rack unit on 5 ports. But for the space both pieces take up, it's about a mid size unit that could be mounted with "wings". It does have four-way keyhole mounts for wall-mounting.

Background: I have great experience with Netgear for my home (but way better than most homes') network. I'd definitely use all their devices were I doing work for small or medium sized businesses. I like them just a tad less when they start trying to sell you subscriptions (which is what I hate about Brocade and Cisco, along with all the proprietary garbage), but for the most part, Netgear is inexpensive and quite reliable. I've had a 24 port nonblocking unmanaged Gb switch running 24/7 in my dusty basement for over 15 years without a single fault AND they still sell that model. Their APs are the best I've had, and I don't think I've ever had a Netgear item break on me, period. I have had lots of other home/SMB stuff break or otherwise have strange issues, though.

That said, there's a lot of no-name PoE switches on the market right now. I don't need any of those handling my low voltage needs OR my data. And they won't beat this line on the price by too much anyway.

This is an excellent device which adds a lot of versatility to your network.

Of the giant bin full of different sized cable ties, I didn't have any this length; they are surprisingly short.  But it's actually quite welcome, since ties of this width I rarely use for anything requiring a longer length, which means less waste.  There is nothing noteworthy about them - positive or negative - compared to other ties.  Very useful.

This is really quite large. I mean, that's a good thing if you have a lot of AC adapters that all manage not to block each other on here (and some still will), but it's not great when depth is tight behind your stereo or wherever you're trying to hide this. The flat plug is much appreciated, as is being white. The USB ports are becoming still more useful, but I wouldn't get them unless you plan to use them (like, if you're using this in a static setup with no need for ports, why waste even a tiny bit of power - and space). And the switch is good for some scenarios and terrible for others, so contemplate that as well before you jump into anything.

It's very lightweight. I guess it doesn't need to be heavy.

I'm sure they do it for shipping purposes and to appeal to homeowners without tools, but I don't like that they give you multiple short pieces instead of fewer long pieces that you could cut down to appropriate size. That just means you need more couplers; each additional coupler decreases the appeal of the final installation.

Honestly, I hate surface mounted conduit. But there are times when it is required, and in those cases better than nothing. I own my home, so of course I put all permanent links properly inside the walls, but even then, there are times when the Cat/RG/other jacks are not directly behind the furniture holding the devices that need the cables. In these cases, I prefer to mount these with screws, and then caulk and paint them into the painted baseboards so they blend in better, although they have made these with tape for truly temporary installations.

There is just one connector for an inside corner and an outside corner (on the x/z axis). And in my opinion, these are the only two you should really need, and you probably need more of them. I am never going vertical up walls with cables; I just go from the jack along the baseboard to behind the furniture...if I need more than that, I'm afraid I need to just stop being lazy and tear down a wall or something.

I get that if you are in an apartment or a rental property, you may need more flexibility with this. But in my opinion, if you can't do a proper wall-mount TV install without surface-mount conduit, then you should just use a TV stand as God intended because this is not enough to make cables acceptable in such an install (although honestly, it is better than nothing).

I thought I needed a replacement for my actual amplifier, but it turns out that even though my power injector was working, there was a short elsewhere in its circuit, so I was happy to be able to change the whole setup out with this.

I had to use a separate diplexer to join my UHF and VHF antennas since this didn't provide both inputs. Unlike my other amp, though, this has an LTE filter built in - a product of its newness. The power injector is much simpler and smaller than my other one had been, with the actual transformer in the plug itself. The short length of cable is much thinner than RG6, however, which makes me wonder if that is a source of db loss. Anyway, seems to work just as well as my other one. Even though I watch very little TV containing commercials, I quickly noticed how annoying it was to not have instant background noise.

Signal gauge is just a bit gimmicky, at least in my case where I'm pointing between two cities and trying to get as much as I can from each, which doesn't equal maximum signal according to this gauge. But that's okay. Use "TV Fool" and a compass, and you won't need a gauge, but it won't hurt.

This works just fine, so I sort of hate to give it less than five stars, but considering how long it is, one would expect you might want to run this under the floor or through some walls or whatever (mine is from my set of stereos to a computer in the basement), so for that scenario, this "braided" sheath really isn't the best choice.  Anyway, works as expected.  Keep in mind that it a stereo model, so it will not accommodate your stereo headset with mic (mic would require an extra conductor).

I have these on all my incoming connections - cable Internet, TV antenna group, and Sirius antenna. Remember that this is not a substitute for a proper direct ground connection for an outdoor antenna or a utility (ISP)-provided (out of your control) ground. However, I do appreciate them as extra protection. They need to be bonded to ground, of course. In my case, I bond them all to the Telecommunications Main Grounding Busbar (TMGB) in my Telecom Closet (TC), which is bonded to the Main Building Ground (MGB), which is essentially the main power panel in most residences. Ideally, to ensure equalization, the TMGB and MGB would also connect to the same actual earthing rod outside.

Just sayin'...these are only as good as how they are installed.

Great shape, very much like the classic and ubiquitous Logitech. I like that the pairing device is on-board. Lightweight and simple, a mouse is important for me if needing to get serious work done, especially anything with CAD or Visio.

The big question you need to ask yourself is, do you want a Bluetooth version or one like this that has its own receiver. It seems to me that if you always use this with the same computer and you have Bluetooth built in to the computer, then you probably want Bluetooth. Conversely, if you want this to use with multiple computers and/or you don't have Bluetooth built in to any one of the computers you will use the mouse with, then you'd want something like this. This is because pairing is easier in a case such as this, and drivers usually aren't an issue. Bluetooth usually isn't an issue either, but it might get irritating with frequent changing of machines. At least that is my experience.

Does not come with a carry bag, surprisingly. Mouse roller also functions as a button, as it should. It has an on/off switch on the back, which is nice for saving battery life and being able to leave this hooked up to a permanent install (although with a permanent desk setup, I personally stick with wired).

This is useful. I have a laptop acting as my music server, and at some point I managed to get the audio to output via both HDMI and the headphone jack. Of course HDMI is preferred to the primary stereo, but the analog is just fine for the stereo-only amplifiers. That said, I won't in a million years remember how to get Windows to work for me again, and it might just be a fluke that it does work. This would make that problem a moot point.

But it still helps me with a problem - for some reason my primary stereo's second zone cannot play anything except if the input is analog (unless it's the same as the first zone), so I actually needed to make two different inputs to that stereo in order to be able to use the second zone completely independently as God intended.

Complicated. But whatever works. Seems like you have to switch between A/V and optical outputs on this thing, which is fine. Also, it come with a charger, and a USB to barrel adapter. Nice to have that USB flexibility since a lot of stereos and TVs have ports capable of supplying power.

Picture here on Amazon of product is a little strange, making this look like a double-stack device. That's just the front and the back shown in one picture.

Good, simple power strip. Glad it has keyholes in the back, because I use them like that sometimes.

Sometimes you want a switch, sometimes you don't. Sometimes you want it to light up, sometimes you don't. This one doesn't light up. If I want a switch to turn off equipment, I often want to keep it off most of the time, so I want the light to be able to see it. On the other hand, if I keep the equipment on most of the time, then I don't need extra lights being powered (no matter how insignificant).

14AWG conductors and ground mean you can get the maximum out of most household circuits (because most are 15 amp). I don't like any extension cords or strips less than that to avoid voltage drop, overloading, etc.

Love the flat plug, especially for semi-permanent installations.

Wish the cord was more white considering my trim is white, but it's close enough to not annoy me in most cases.

This is great for me and my constant reconfiguring of my whole-house Audio system (since I haven't just broken down and bought the really crazy-expensive stuff with relayed inputs yet). If you have a good audio card with optical or coax outputs on your server, you can transfer that directly to your (multiple) stereos and let the stereos decode them as God intended. Although it'd be nicer to have something like this that could have pass-through HDMI and strip out the audio for multiple outputs that way.

Anyway, you can have both coax and optical inputs on this, but you can only use one at a time with a manual switch on top. Power is USB; comes with cable and charger. Likely you can power this off one of the stereos or the server itself if you have a setup like mine (and that part is a plus).

This works, and it can be useful.  Nothing too exciting, though.  Be aware that I have had luck in some instances just using a Y-cable to get two outputs out of one input.  For example, I have two analogue audio sources split with a passive Y-splitter to two different amplifiers.  Once amplified, any loss from the split becomes null.  But I have had times where I couldn't get that to work well, so I thought I'd ensure I had one of these around...but in the situation above, it actually offers less functionality since you have to pick one or the other (so try a splitting cable first).  Of course, this also works for times when you only have one input and you have two sources.  So, can be useful for sure.

Although 4k bluray encryption was cracked about a year after these onerous HDMI consumer requirements were put into place to protect against piracy, be advised that you'll need equipment above and beyond this to rip encrypted discs.  However, if you want to capture OTA video or your video game or other similar feeds, this will help you accomplish those goals.  It works, and I normally give 5 stars to cables (and similar things) that work, so...5 stars.  No complaints here.

This is great.  For some reason, it never occurred to me to look for third-party label cartridges.  I'm sort of a compulsive labeler - especially for large cabling projects - but I'm also loathe to pay a premium for refills when the labeler itself was very reasonable priced.  Now I don't even have to worry so much about typos that require a reprint.  So far, so good.

I love that these exist. This is my second one, and I didn't even realize they existed before I got my first one - it's almost too good to be true. Apparently there is some chip in the one end that uses a tiny bit of current supplied by the device to convert a signal to an optical signal, which can then travel further thanks to no impedance on it (due to it not being a wire anymore) and also no interference between pairs.

But they really work. And this cable really works. This is a good looking, seemingly high quality model, BTW. To be clear, HDMI cables are really iffy, and so are the devices that transmit and receive. I've long had a few long runs within my house of regular cables, and some thing will work while others will not. And of course 4k signals need better fidelity than 1080p or SD, and when you add in ethernet, ARC, etc., those full featured signals tend to degrade quicker. But I had a NAS with video card in my basement that just wouldn't send a signal all the way to my TV until I added one of these cables, and now it works perfect. I subsequently used THIS cable to test that run before I ran it to replace the standard cable at the rear of my TV room for just plugging in random stuff to diagnose or test, play with, whatever. Works great.

Just remember to put the correct end of the cable toward the correct device (doesn't matter with standard cables, but does with these), and get one long enough. Honestly, it shouldn't be a problem to add an extender before the transmitter, but better just to have it long enough in the first place when possible.

Great cable. A godsend.

I generally give working cables and similar stuff five stars if it works as expected.  It does, and I also like the form factor and the pigtails on this thing.  Super useful for hooking up anything that "used to be cutting edge", now that you're lucky if a high end receiver or TV even has composite anymore.  Definitely one to keep around for all future generations of electronic equipment.

And here I've been using electrical tape all these years. I guess if you ever actually want to use your web cam, this makes a lot more sense. And for my Surface Pro, I definitely want the rear camera (at least) accessible. Does a great job for this purpose.

I've seen some others, and these seem to be a bit smaller, but still provide an adequate sized hole under most circumstances. These also come in stackable, individual plastic cases, good for stocking stuffers and good for storage because you should be able to find them later easier than if they were by themselves.

I was definitely surprised how inexpensive and still pretty good this dual monitor mount is.  Admittedly, it is not as slick as the ones that cost 4-6 times the price, but it is still relatively acceptable in most situations.  As another reviewer mentioned, I'm not certain it will hold the weight of some 27" monitors well.  I've seen better cable organization, although this one's is not bad, and it does not seem as smoothly and infinitely adjustable as one of the high end models.  All that said, if you just have two mid-size monitors you want to mount in very static positions, this is a great way to clear up some desk space.

Very basic, but very useful set of headphones if you're stuck using a lightning connector. I really hate Apple for this (as well as many other things), but if you you're stuck, you're stuck. The only thing I can say is that now you'll need a second set of headphones for a mini-plug anywhere else, including the plane. So you might prefer a lightning connector to mini-plug adapter. But these are at least reasonably priced enough that you can probably afford a pair of each, although it's still annoying to have to drag both around.

The ear pieces are comfortable and nice. The headphones themselves sound fine, although of course no headphones are really amazing, especially the ear-bud type.

Giving this a five as I normally do for the extended category of cables that work as expected.  Granted, legitimate uses for this are few and far between, but of course this is a good way to add an ouput when needed.  I also think that it's good to have an in-line signal boost when low-level signals for very long lengths, especially in an extended whole-house Audio system that includes a detached outbuilding and other such applications.  Simple, but works as expected if you have a need for it!

I hate to rely on my phone for music, and I also don't like taking the time to pair it with every rental car I use, especially when I get a stubborn rental car that requires me to be in park (even if I am the passenger).  Anyway, for the longest time I took CDs with me on travel, but now it's rare to even have a CD player.  This is a great solution, especially since this model has SD card expansion.  When a car doesn't want to read via USB, you always have the line out for backup.  And even if you are using this via USB, you can leave a cable extending from the device so you don't forget to take it with you at the end of the trip.  Simple device, but very useful in the right situations!

I have multiple receivers as part of my whole-house audio setup. Splitting the analogue audio out jack from my server works, but will not deliver high definition music details for the actual receivers to decode as this will. If you have a sound card on your server with optical out, this device can deliver even more interesting features to a custom audio setup.

Comes with a USB cable, but you provide the power supply. This is fine in some cases where you can tap a receiver USB port. Keep in mind that some receivers will fight with you constantly to try to connect to any USB port you're just using for power. Might want to test that out before you get your heart set on using a receiver USB port for power.

Device works as expected.

These work perfectly as expected.  Have to always keep adapters like these around because I do not like to have compatibility issues.  Even though the old-school mic plugs are more rare on consumer equipment than before, sometimes manufacturers think there stuff will look fancy if they use those types of plugs.  All four pieces that came in my set work perfectly.

Want to extract your audio channel from an HDMI device to use on an older stereo? Here you go. Want to use a newer computer as a music server, but Windows keeps wanting to default to the HDMI port - here's your chance to extract that channel instead of fighting with WIndows all the time.

Also, even some flat panel TVs fail to have HDMI ports - I have one. Here is your chance to add whatever you want, even make it a smart TV. Does its job as expected.

These seem like a steal when you consider they're a tenth of the price of one of the famous brands I can think of. The noise cancellation function is a bit of a white noise injector, and if you use it while playing music, the music actually sounds a bit different (although I honestly can't tell which way sounds better). The noise cancellation does work pretty well, enough to get annoyed looks from people when you inadvertently ignore them.

I like that they fold up, although it doesn't work miracles in the room saving category. They also aren't anything super fancy in the looks department, although they don't look bad (to be honest, I tend to think negatively toward someone when I think they have a product that isn't worth what it costs, and just for the sake of showing off or being trendy, RE Beats).

I do like that these have both Bluetooth and auxiliary. This makes them good for a plane, since sometimes you'll want to use their screen and other times you'll want to use your phone. Any model that doesn't allow for both probably isn't worth considering.

Definitely worth looking at this considering the very reasonable price without sacrificing any functionality from what I can tell.

Update: I do really like this computer. It has smoothly integrated into my home network and I now quickly go to it for quick and easy browsing and/or controlling stuff in my house (particularly if the main computer is in use by somebody else or for some reason tethered. The great thing is that with the full power of Windows and third party software, it can be whatever you need it to be. The one negative I've found, though, is that the delete key is under the backspace key where you expect backslash to be (which is in turn beside the right alt key). For this reason, I've accidentally went into sleep mode a few times, which is annoying. You can turn off the power key (while running) in windows, but the delete key still isn't where it is supposed to be.

Original review:

Surprise! I actually love this computer.

I mean, I am a bit of a power user, so I have a big gaming laptop and a couple of servers throughout my house, not to mention a few purpose-built niche laptops. So while I was a bit skeptical of this machine before it came since I saw the low price tag, I think it's awesome for the right purpose.

I mean, I totally get what "Chrome Books" are trying to do - be low price, low weight computers that run basically "from the cloud". But who really wants a computer running Android? I mean, there are phones for that. So running Windows 10 is a great idea. (Not that I love Windows 10, but if you install Windows Classic Shell and tweak, tweak, tweak away...turn off all permissions, get rid of all the stupid crap they're trying to sell you, use an offline account, then it is almost as good as Windows 7).

Anyway, you don't get a lot of fancy new stuff, but what you do get is important: 1080p screen, mini-HDMI out (odd choice, would have gone for micro or even full, but whatever), 2 USB 3.0 (No C), a micro-SD card reader, headphone jack, and a M.2 expansion port.

64GB of ROM is pretty small, but they installed so little bloatware (just one program to make the touchpad better - I uninstalled it because I didn't recognize it, am paranoid, and figure I can adjust it with whatever is built into Windows) that you have ~45GB free. Should be enough for stuff like MS office and other junk you may want. But you know what, I have a 36TB NAS, and Windows works flawlessly with it, so if I'm using this as a home machine, it's not a problem. I don't much care for public cloud, so if I want to take this on the road, I can always stream (usually still reach my NAS) or just throw in an SSD (by the way, it only takes the small form factor) or a giant micro-SD card (although admittedly either of these factors takes away the fact that this item is inexpensive to begin with.

6GB of RAM is sufficient for a computer that is not meant to be a workhorse.

It's really thin and light and with a real keyboard is just delightful as opposed to dealing with a tablet; a tablet always disappoints me when I'm trying to get something done quickly. It also boots up fast due to NAND memory. It doesn't even look cheap or anything. It actually looks pretty good.

It has a regular "wall wart" type AC adapter instead of the usual laptop power brick. I like this, but the cord is a little short (on the other hand, it is likely easily replaced with something in my electronics closet) The barrel adapter goes into the right side of the device (which is not abnormal, but less normal than the back or the other side in my experience) and the unfortunate part is that it will partially fit into the stereo mini-plug port for headphones on the same spot on the other side, which is likely to cause some confusion.

The only apparent downside is that the keyboard seems...like it vibrates slightly. Like it's not held in tight enough or something. I mean, it does have nice keys and overall I like it, but it just feels slightly weird, although still much better than a tablet roll-out keyboard.

I actually really like this little machine. Not for my main computer or my only computer, but definitely for easy browsing, or a multimedia machine for a teen, or a school computer, a travel computer, whatever. I'd use it for plenty of things, happily.

If you're cool with the memory - and living off a NAS, an SD card, or the cloud - and you're looking for something small and usable, definitely give this some consideration.

This is a pretty fun toy for the price. It's not like those multi-hundred dollar units that some speed boats have equipped (although truthfully I don't know much about those or what kind of additional hardware is needed).

This uses a weighted sonar device with a bobber and a long cord to attach to the actual electronic device, which thankfully has a nice strap. There is a mountable holder for the sonar device, but this can also be used to mount it to a stick if you want to push it around in the water (especially if you're in a kayak or something like that). I mean, you can imagine that there is work involved if you want to scout out a large area around you. And you can also imagine that there are some false positives and it is not super precise all the time, but it does give you an idea about what to expect, and at least you can find out for sure if the area you are at is completely devoid of fish.

The device itself is fine, but nothing fancy in build. Just very basic. It uses AAA batteries, which is always annoying, and they'll get eaten up fast if you don't keep the backlight off. Of course it would be preferred to have an internal battery charged via USB.

Should be fun for any kayak or small boat fisherman.

Update: I really love this machine. You give a lot of things five stars if they're really good products, but this one deserves bonus. I've been slowly going through the full 200+ page manual to make sure I don't miss any features and to get the most out of this thing, and I'm continually thrilled. Also, I give a lot of things controlled by apps low ratings because I tend to hate screwing around with my phone, but in this case, the Yamaha AV controller app only adds to the value, with the best part being you don't NEED it to take advantage of all the receiver's functionality, but it's a joy to have sometimes to make fine adjustments without having to turn on the TV. I really like it for adjusting net radio stations and stuff like that or fine tuning music sounds - again, without having to turn on the TV. This also makes up for the one negative I mentioned below about not being able to change all the settings from a web page. Great stuff!

Original review:

Before this, I had two Sony receivers in my living room. My secondary is a much older model - about 12 or so years old - that does not have HDMI and I use it for my whole house audio system. My primary is (was - it just got replaced) a 3-5 year old Sony model that is admittedly in a lower class than this Yamaha receiver (the secondary was in a higher class in its time, I think).

While I usually have all Sony stuff, I was completely willing to try another well-known Japanese brand who specializes in receivers and amps. And - it's just awesome. Totally. Not a single regret about the switch. The RX-A880 gave me back everything I lost going from my older, higher-end Sony to my newer one, AND it gave me so many nice surprises on the way! As anyone can tell you that it sounds good and looks good, I'll concentrate on this little details that I discovered during setup:

1) Besides the seven HDMI inputs, it also has a composite video, a component video, two optical audio, one extra (second belongs to component) coax audio, and two composite audio inputs, not to mention phono.

The great thing is that you can assign different audio inputs to any of the video inputs. So, for example, I decided to keep my Wii around since I now have a component input (and it takes up almost no space), but the cable is component video with composite audio, but the component video input on this has coax for the audio. Bummer. But no, you can change it. Example number two is I have a computer in my telecom closet hooked up to this with both HDMI and line-out audio. For circumstances too complicated to define here, audio does not output via the HDMI. But because of this feature, I can make the audio appear when I select the HDMI input OR when I just want to listen to the audio directly (with no HDMI output). Perfect.

2) 9 Speaker outputs. First, I'm so happy to have the 2-zone thing back (my secondary receiver has it, but my other, newer Sony did not - it only had A/B speakers that shared an amp). But this one you can actually have 7.1 AND a second zone (although you can't play them at the same time. This is really cool if you want the best of both worlds. I don't know if I can find a place for two more speakers in my setup, but ...it's nice to have the option. Supposedly, this all works automatically. I imagine it could work fine, but I am unable to try it at the moment.

3) 2-zone done better. My older Sony had 2-zone, but the controls were - frankly - atrocious. It was always confusing, even for someone like me who can be a super A/V nerd and memorize anything. The way I use it now is just to keep the remote on Zone-2, and do Zone-1 on the unit itself.

This Yamaha, however, has a simple switch on the remote, and you're either controlling one zone or the other depending on that switch. Simple and effective. You can also control it from the unit, unlike the older Sony.

4) 8 custom presets, all controlled directly from the remote. Another 8 for Zone 2?!

The one complaint I read by a reviewer was that you have to scroll through all the inputs from the remote to get to what you want. But that doesn't matter for two reasons: first, you can change the settings to skip anything you don't want. But, second, with 8 custom presets - and each with their own remote button - you probably don't even ever need to scroll through the inputs anyway.
