And the custom presets are great. You can turn on and off a bunch of features like whether or not it changes your HDMI out settings, if it uses your YPAO settings, extra bass, which speakers it uses, etc. And it even can link the second zone!

Two great examples:

I can't stand to watch regular background TV with the surround sound on because it makes the commercials that much more obnoxious. But of course I like big booming bass and surround for movies. And it's also annoying to switch the unit off and on all the time, especially if you want to use control for HDMI. So I have one preset for very flat TV sound using just the front speakers that is clearer than-, but no more annoying than-, my regular TV speakers. Then I have another preset for surround sound and big bass for movie watching.

I have one preset for straight music just in zone 1. Then I have another preset for straight music in both zones one and two. It turns on zone 2 automatically. I could not figure out how to make a preset just for zone 2, but it seems that when I am controlling zone 2 on the remote, I can make 8 more presets just for zone 2. You can not adjust these presets via menu, from what I can tell, though.

5) 14 character names on the front of the unit in dot matrix. My other receivers were all limited to 8 characters. You can see all 14 at once, which is great.

6) Much more robust networking. I haven't played with this too awful much yet, but it seems that if you start listening to a playlist or an album on your NAS, then the next time you go back to "server", it will start playing where you left off (well, the song you left off at will start over again, instead of at the exact moment you left at), but at least this way you don't have to turn the TV on just to play some music. I suppose you could create a playlist of all Death Metal, and then you just have a stream going whenever you want it. It also seems like you can actually sign into Pandora and all the other stations and listen to your own account. And all the Internet/Network stuff is a separate scroll-through than the other inputs. I really like how that is set up.

6) The "program up/down" buttons on the remote can be programmed to do about 10 different things. I picked to have the dialogue increased or decreased for when you can't hear what people are saying even though everything else is loud enough. To be clear, I think this depends on if the dialogue is known to the decoder. I haven't tried all the other options yet.

7) Remote is awesome. Besides what I mentioned above, you can also make some changes to the red/green/yellow/blue buttons, but I wish you could really program those completely to your liking. Everything is laid out nicely, and the second zone even makes sense, as I mentioned above.

8) I realize the second HDMI output would be great if you also have a projector or something like that. With it, you can have access to all your devices without having to rewire anything. Haven't used it yet, but am glad to have the extra functionality.

...

There's plenty more, but I'm forgetting some of the details right now. I've only played with this thing for a few days, but I like it more and more. The one thing that is missing is that you can't change all the options via the webpage. You can change some, but I liked with my newer Sony the fact that I could look at and change all my custom presets without having to turn the TV and go through all that. I'm only comparing this to my two Sony units so you get my frame of reference, but realize this Yamaha model is in a higher class than those. Regardless, I love this thing, and it has a lot of great functionality and no serious drawbacks that I've noticed yet. Recommended (obviously).

This is a pretty nice headset.  I really like that it can be wired as well, because most of the time I wear headphones is on a plane (and their screens usually take wired only.  Plus, then you don't have to worry about power.  They sound good and work as expected, but I've seen some of higher quality and some that fold up and are more compact, so I guess being being spoiled for choice leaves me jaded to headphones.  Certainly not a bad choice if the price is right.

I am super happy with this computer. It's really a work of art, and I say this as a guy who has an Alienware 17 from a few years ago.

Even counting for inflation (i.e., the fact that specs and hardware have gotten better in the years since the A17), I think the specs are dead on with what you get out of an Alienware. But while the build quality is just as good - and just as impressive - it is so much lighter and more portable (not that I really care, mind you, as I don't travel with my home laptop). But you really don't lose anything - besides weight - because the Asus is a strong machine with everything you could want (including the space for an extra HDD, which until now I had not seen outside of the Alienware...of course now that you can just get chips for ROM, this is becoming more normal).

I love the tactile feel and the fact that it is still a real laptop that can be upgraded easily. I don't want a slick tablet that won't come apart for serious computing and gaming. I want a real laptop. I want this. They keyboard is probably the best built-in I've ever used (which is even more impressive when Surface Pro-type keyboards are becoming more and more common).

And the touchpad. Oh, the beautiful touchpad with it's real buttons. How anyone could want a tap-to-click-only touchpad is beyond me. And you know what - right out of the box - I didn't even change the configuration of the touchpad to keep it from doing obnoxious things to me like clicking all over the screen with my palms. This is probably one of the reasons that this was the quickest setup-to-acceptable laptop I've ever had:

Usually, I spend a week not wanting to deal with a new computer and getting everything configured right, and then a whole day complaining about all the crapware I have to get rid of and trying to find stuff and get it set up right (typically exacerbated since Windows 10 is still sort of annoying when all you want is Win7 back...). And then it's another week until I finally work up the muster to go fix the touchpad settings. I cursed less with this laptop than any other, ever. And after just an hour or two installing the must-haves, it's all ready to go, and works fantastically.

Install Windows Classic Shell right away if you want to avoid as much of the Windows 10 garbage as you can. Don't do an "online account". Remove onedrive and the other MS crap that tries to get you to always be online and buy their stuff and treat you like you're using a tablet (this is a Windows problem, not that of the Asus). Remove included Macafe (now is a good time since it never wants to allow the software I will next install) Then get rid of the one Asus program that is like a store. Now just add the software you actually do want and you have a darn near perfect computer. Really nothing to annoy me. And it is as perfectly responsive as anything you could ever want.

Keyboard is awesome, like I said. Most tactile keyboard ever on a laptop. I couldn't find any software on the machine to change colors and stuff (I may have deleted it immediately while trying to get rid of minimal bloatware, but I don't think I did). So I downloaded ROG aura (and a different Aura program that did NOT work right) and then you have your full keyboard color controls. It seemed like that other program was for syncing with other light-up devices, but it would not allow me to control all four sections of the keyboard independently (even though I think it was supposed to).

I'm getting a full 60 frames + on every one of my new games I run on this. It reminds me why a specialized rig like this is better than consoles. 1080p is still amazing, even (and especially) thrown onto my Sony TV. No problem with any of my controllers or accessories. Bluetooth setup is so mature nowadays.

Yeah...the only thing that isn't perfect on here is that it runs Windows 10. But let's face it - Windows 7 is still too outdated now to go back to, so there really is no decent alternative. But at the same time Win10 really does what you need it to do - I've already established my network links and have everything just the way I want it. Even the Wifi is up to date and good enough now (paired with my 1750 SMB AP, which only runs this computer and my phones because everything else is wired in the house) that (under the parenthesized conditions) you really don't have any need to ever plug in a cable.

Oh...the included master controller software has the fans up on high performance right out of the box. Fine for gaming, but just let Windows control the fans (setting is easily available in the software) when not gaming. You can't give this computer a real workout without gaming, so you won't need the fans cranked up all the time. It stays peacefully quiet.

You get a computer like this, you have the best. Even running games, it'll be reasonably up to date for years. I love it.

Works perfectly - plug and play - with my QNAP expansion card for my NAS by the same manufacturer. I'm using this as cache and I can easily notice the difference, especially when seeking for multiple small files. QTS has an option to cache only small files or everything that goes through - I like the small file option, as those are the ones more likely to be accessed frequently (whereas videos you are likely to only watch once). I suppose that decision also can be based on your cache:storage ratio.

The other great thing is that you can set up even the cache as RAID so you never have to worry about data loss if an SSD chip would fail (not that I'm expecting that). Very happy with the noticeable performance upgrade thanks to this WD NVMe M.2 SSD.

These are nice speakers for a ceiling (or, possibly walls). They will take up the entire 3.5" cavity inside drywall walls, so don't expect to be able to use these with plaster and lathe unless you're using them in a ceiling.

They attach sort of the way an "old work" plastic electrical box does - with tabs that you tighten from the front via screws. Those have enough depth for plaster and lathe, but the speakers themselves are close to 3.5" deep. You can take the grill off from the front to spray paint it.

This is my second pair of in-ceiling speakers, so I can tell you the two I've installed are both about the same installation-wise. And they both sound similarly good, but deep bass is left to be desired, so plan for a subwoofer if you desire and can. These things are looking for a restricted environment, so they sound better if you can put some insulation above/behind them or ensure the area they are enclosed in is relatively tight (think of a subwoofer box you'd make for a car and how each has a specific volume recommended - I didn't see a manufacturer recommended volume for these, but you can guess they want to be enclosed).

Overall a very nice product.

At the current price tag, I am pretty amazed at these, considering the other type I have is (or more likely was) closer to $300. The other had a well-established brand name, although I don't actually remember what it was. They are actually pretty similar, with the other having decent instructions, feeling just slightly more solid, and better cable management overall.

They both have to be messed with, tightened, and tweaked to get them to work the way you want them to. Thankfully, I don't need either to be constantly moved, but constant re-positioning will be challenging on either stand. Both of them, you don't have to put a hole in your desk. You also need to be very careful (with both of them) to position your cables with just the right amount of slack so that they don't look stupid, but have enough slack to reposition when necessary without stretching the cables.

I like to use two small TVs to use as monitors and run 2 no-nonsense (i.e., thin) HDMI cables, coax, an audio cable, and the power to each. That way, you can set the desk up to accommodate two different docking stations. Don't forget Ethernet if the TVs are smart (mine are not, but they have PIP). If you really take your time, you can fit all that stuff in, and hopefully never have to re-run cables, because it is sort of a pain (but well worth it). Get black cables to match.

While I am fan of conduit rather than direct buried, I want to get Internet to my Dad's external garage without a lot of hassle, and since I know he's never going to go through with getting rid of the second meter on the garage to hook up a sub-power panel (which would make running conduits worthwhile), this seems like the best way, especially because you can really direct bury something much easier and with less ruining of grass than by putting in proper conduits. The fact that the cable is already connectorized makes it a little more complicated, but with such tight specs, I'd rather it be factory connectorized anyway.

The cable works, which I didn't doubt, although I don't have the equipment at home to test it at 10Gb. What I will tell you is that outside plant cable generally has sheathing meant for weatherproofing and rodent protection, and there are codes about patching over to inside cable when you enter a building due to the sheathing producing toxic smoke in a fire. The packaging on this cable doesn't mention its sheath's construction, but I wouldn't run this through the walls of my house. Building to building with a close termination point on either side is the way to go.

Even if I could beam wifi over there, wifi is never as good as Ethernet anyway. Certainly not as these claimed speeds.

In my situation, it is what I need to get the job done as easily as possible. I don't know if they make mini cable ploughs that are rentable or cheap enough to buy, but that is my next assignment.

I am impressed right off the bat with just how many useful accessories are included right off the bat. The description says it does not come with an SD card or AAA batteries, but mine did, perhaps for review purposes, although the box did not look like it had been opened. Seems like it would come with that stuff, so perhaps other reviewers might clarify. There is a case and two separate pouches for the wider camera lens and the microphone.

Functionality and video quality are pretty good. I guess the only drawback is that this almost seems like a throwback now. For still pictures - on a vacation or a great hike where I want to take great pictures - I still take along a small camera instead of just my cell phone, but the truth is cell phone cameras are getting so good now that I wonder when that will no longer seem prudent. And with that said, my small camera takes such amazing (not studio quality) HD that I wonder when something like this would really seem like the best thing, especially considering they both take SD cards and length is only limited by SD card capacity.

It certainly does seem like a more professional camera in its size and shape, but mostly because that style has been the trend for some time now. But in a way this style is already starting to seem outdated, like a throwback. I also noticed, just now, that even the really big name manufacturers have this style in 1080p for comparable prices.

I'd definitely give this thing a look. I would have totally loved it a few years ago. The mic and extra lens still feel like premium features, but I'm rarely the one to set up for photos and video footage, as I usually just do landscapes or great spontaneous moments. This may be a fantastic alternative to giving kids your phone - or a phone - to play with. Seems like a good way to encourage their inner photographer without it leading into a bunch of cheap phone games.

Camera has mini* USB and HDMI ports (as opposed to micro) - just when I was wondering what I'd ever do with this one mini-HDMI cable I have... Mic takes 2xCR2032 batteries, which are included, and should probably last, as I don't think mics eat up much power. Has a curled, springy, analogue audio cable with stereo mini-plugs on both ends to connect the mic. Also has an external battery charger.

One of my fans was making horrendous noise, to the point I couldn't stand to have the computer running, even down in the basement. I picked these fans from this vendor because they were cheap and I figured I'd get the pair and change them both out while I was at it (I also used some new thermal paste on the heat sinks while I was at it).

The operation went well, and now I have my server back up, thank God. Fans fit totally perfectly, but the inner fans are slightly differently shaped then OEM, to no detriment that I can tell. They are quiet. 3 pins, like the original. I'm happy.

I have a lot of styles of headphones, and I now know what this type is perfect for: exercising. Maybe you and everyone else already knew this. But if I'm running (or elliptical-ing), regular ear buds may fall out, and bigger headphones can fall off or at least get uncomfortable sweaty. Obviously, you don't want a cord connected to your phone for exercising, so these hit the sweet spot in all those ways.

They are very comfortable as well. The ear pieces that come connected are a perfect fit for my ears, and already offer real sound-proofing from the outside world (warning: you may appear to be an annoying millennial if you walk around isolated from the world with these all the time). They are comfortable, and I love the easy way that the ear-hanger pieces are removable. I also like that you can tighten up the connecting strap. There must be a cable in there, so I hope it doesn't wear out this way, but it seems to be pretty durable, so I guess it will be okay.

Actually, these are great. The charging area is barely large enough for the micro-USB port, but the battery lasts for quite a few hours. Not as long as some headphones, but the low weight is key here.

Also good for: watching movies or listening to music on planes if you have your own device. No cord to slow you down when a seat-mate wants to get past you, and they're comfortable enough to fall asleep in, unlike over-the-head headphones.

Oh, I saw a review that said the bass was poor. I do not agree. Music sounds great in these. They can operate on low power because they are so far up in your ear. Be careful to keep them at a reasonable level.

I would recommend these to friends.

This TV makes me feel bad for ever having given another product 5 stars. It is really just about perfect. Instead of wasting a lot of space talking about the quality of the picture (believe me, it is there), I am going to concentrate on some finer points, particularly those real and perceived weak points:

(This is replacing a 2009 Sony Z-Series TV, which I also love and still consider a fantastic TV; it was the first year of Internet-capable TVs if I remember correctly, and I used the DLNA features with Universal Media Server, but could never get a Plex profile to work right, so I am happy to have a newer TV that supports Plex via App, besides for the 4k, HDR, etc., etc. I have a bunch of other TVs scattered about, but the other two I use most are less expensive Samsung Smart models from five or so years ago.)

Back to (possible) negatives:

I wasn't sure I would like the stand and style. I always hated those Samsung TVs with the plastic grey legs, and I thought this would look too much like that. I thought my ideal stand was either a perfect 90-degree version of the Sony A1E, or perhaps the A8F, which I had my eye on due to its very low profile, minimalist stand. Anyway, this one looks so much better in real life than I expected. It's actually metal, and fairly dark. Placed on low furniture, it looks great walking by, and sits at the right height while watching. I guess it is made to fit a Sony sound bar perfectly (I use full surround setup, so I don't care). But I am much, much happier with the looks than I thought I would be. If that is your hesitation, go check it out in a store (before coming back for the right price).

Thickness: its thicker than some, including last year's 930E, but the way it angles out from the back gives a much sleeker appearance than you may expect just from looking at the dimensions. You only see its thickness at about 80 degrees to the side. Overall, it sits back far and takes up little extra room than it has to. The TV looks as great off as it does on.

I read a professional review that mentioned the picture doesn't look as good from a side angle. I guess that's true, but it's not nearly as drastic of a change as it sounded from the review. In fact, one of the best TV seats in my house is about 30-degrees off-center, and I don't see a difference from there at all. At 45-degrees, you start to see a difference.

Above mentioned professional review also mentioned the Android TV thing can be a little clunky. I don't feel it, to be honest. It's been nothing but good surprises for me. One thing that could be improved is customization of your home screen. You can re-order some apps, but I haven't figured out how to delete the shortcuts for stuff that isn't even downloaded. And I'm never going to play goofy games on my TV (besides real video games), so how can I get rid of that whole section that is taking up space. You can block recommended content, so after them pushing some crapware on you initially, you can basically run add-free. Looks like you'll probably have to sign in to Google, though, but you can make a new account just for your TV (which is what I do for every device).

The downward facing ports look really good with the cable management, so good that I really don't want to use any of the side inputs for permanent setups. For that reason, they should have put the IR blaster and composite input facing down as well (not that I need them, as I don't have cable, but some people will).

Not that I even checked my link speed, but manual says Ethernet port is 100mbps. Can't imagine you'll ever need more than that unless you expect to run uncompressed video without a converter.

The remote is nicer than I expected, but still not as nice as my old one. Plus, although it has Bravia Sync, it doesn't easily just control my stereo the way I would like it to (as my old Sony TV did).Not sure why there has to be a Google button on the remote. Or even Netflix. These should be programmable. Actually, four programmable Apps and/or Input buttons would be greatly appreciated in their place.

That's about it for nitpicking. Here's some things that are totally awesome (besides all the obvious):

It can read all commonly used containers for video files, including *mkv, and it can decompress 4k HEVC (H.265) video natively. So even though my NAS cannot transcode 4k on the fly, if I set it to run at full quality, the TV does it just fine! And since H.265 was made because of 4k video, here's hoping we don't have formats this TV can't play any time soon. This is just fantastic to me, as I really love my NAS' Plex server function. You can also play up to 4k H.265 video right off a hard drive via USB.

My UMS media server is showing up under Video devices (which is where the DLNA servers show up), but you can't see the files. I haven't messed with it much (because now I don't care), but I assume they'll get a profile working before long.

I love the built-in TV guide function and also the way you can browse other channels along the bottom of your screen without changing the channel. These are both great features (the TV guide function on my old TV was abandoned after a few years, but I expect this one will continue to operate). I do not have or want cable, so now I have the features that are nice to have with cable without the burden of slow response cable boxes and the burden of dealing with Comcast.

I haven't even tried out the professional settings (or even messed with anything but motionflow) because the TV is impressing me every second it's on. Again, as this is the first 4k TV to reside in my house, I guess I should be amazed. But the blacks as bars on movies wider than 16:9 are so black you don't notice them. Space scenes are to die for. 4k is done right here: this is the high end of quality, about the only thing worth removing my old Z-series for. I just love it. It looks amazing on and off, and does everything I want it to do (mainly Plex, and Netflix is nice now and then as well). I'm so happy that Plex works so well with this TV without an expensive NAS upgrade, even with movies encoded at 2160p and 7.1 surround. Just fantastic.

It's better than I expected even from Sony's almost-second-to-flagship model. About as high end as they come before they jump up drastically in price. I wouldn't have anything less on my primary TV stand, and I don't need anything more. Highly recommended.

While I might give this product four stars for being so basic and catering to the "just playing music off my phone" crowd, you can't argue with a product done right. And actually, for those who just play music off their phones, this is a huge step up from some Bluetooth speaker that so many people seem to have resorted to.

Basically, if you want a decent stereo for a room with no TV and you don't want to stream over the network (yes, you can do it through your phone, but that seems onerous at best), this is likely the stereo for you.

I like the Sony heft and quality, as well as classic design. I like that it has quite a few inputs including one with ground, and that it has an aux-in port in the front.

I love that you can do two sets of speakers, if you want to fill a large room evenly or if you want to cover two areas independently. You can also change from speaker A to speaker B to A+B to off via the remote, which my higher end 7.1 Sony stereo's remote cannot do (and that is annoying).

This is about perfect for my workshop (no TV, Internet streaming device nearby to give a physical output).

Speaker terminals are the cheaper-than-usual-for-Sony spring loaded type instead of 5-way posts. This is the least-premium feature of this stereo. No AM radio if you care.

I would sort of like an Ethernet interface, but properly accessing it without an external screen (which would require a video output that this receiver doesn't have) would be limiting.

Personally, I hate Bluetooth in this application, especially via phone, because you move to another room, the connection dies. I know a lot of people get through their lives with just the music on their phones, but there's always a better way. If you have one of those setups where you have a music player hooked to this and you can control that with your phone, that would be a pretty good setup.

Beautiful and robust receiver at a low price point if you don't aspire for other options. Great for a workshop or other TV-less space.

Great hard drive, performs as expected with very fast speeds.  Great to have the encryption package.  The look and feel is odd - it all feels mostly plastic, but it seems as if you should be able to pull the two haves apart.  The good thing is, it is easily identifiable compared to the many other hard drives I have laying around.  Quiet and powered via USB.  No flaws that I can see.

Super fast.  Super small.  Just copying a file at what seems like the speed of light was enough to sell me.  There are a bunch of spec indicators on this SD card, but it is a few speeds faster than what is required to record 4k video.  I have an older card that can do it, but this one actually feels faster, if I am able to perceive differences once you get to this high speed.  Wonderful that it comes with the full size adapter, as some high end cameras still take full size SD cards just so they don't get lost!  It will somewhat protect your small card as well.  Great product.

This is a nice little set of radios, improved from my last three-pack of similarly priced Motorolas, but has some room for improvement.

Goods:

+ Good size - small enough, but big enough to fit in your hand comfortably like a radio should. Yes, it could be smaller, but at some point you don't really want smaller.

+ Some basic options to customize, mostly the noises the radios make. LCD screen shows you what you need to know.

+ Batteries can be charged while in the radios via standard Micro USB adapters - two are included. One charges one radio while the other charges two simultaneously.

+ Belt clip included. Head sets can be added.

Bad:

- While it's great that the battery packs can be charged via USB and the chargers are accepted worldwide (whereas my previous set for work had barrel connections to the charger and I burnt one out the first night I tried to charge due to being in Europe, the battery/charger setup is still imperfect for two reasons:

1) Battery packs are not three separate batteries that could be charged with other chargers and switched with other batteries (think Eneloop). My Garmin topo GPS came with actual rechargeable batteries that could be used elsewhere. This makes sense when you want to be able to carry standard alkaline batteries for emergencies/backup. These battery packs are great that they can be replaced with AA when necessary, but not as good as standard, replaceable rechargeable batteries (but you can use rechargeable batteries as your backup batteries).

2) N-MH doesn't make sense for this application because these are the type of batteries that develop a "memory". If you use these every day for work, then you want to recharge them every night. Actually, you would be inclined to recharge every time you want to use them, period, to be sure you get the most from the batteries. But because of the memory, you really want to discharge them fully. The appropriate type of battery would be Li-ion, because they would be chargeable every night AND would last longer. This is the biggest negative to this rig. If the battery packs were Li-ion, I would not care that they are packs versus separate batteries.

- Belt clip should be taken off to remove battery cover without beating the two up. This is apparently an obvious issue to the manufacturer because they have a protective piece of plastic between the two for shipment.

Neutral (strange):

Two standard USB chargers included, at 500mA output each (1A would be minimum standard and expected these days, but whatever; they may have done this to avoid overcharging overnight). Both have the same rated input, but the output is the same (samex2 on the 2 output charger). That actually doesn't make sense, unless the single charger is half as efficient (or they are just too lazy to change the nameplate). Not really sure what's up with that, but I sort of like the 2-output charger. I expect most people have so many USB chargers laying around that they'll use whatever is at hand anyway vice these.

Unlike all the other coax cables I've seen from AmazonBasics, this one has five thin cables feeding through a nylon sheath.  This nylon sheath is not quite as slick and naturally "greased" as the others, but I can see how it provides protection to the individual cables inside.  This has a different style of RCA connector as well, but they are subtly color coded and connect well.  The audio cables are tied and labeled separately from the video cables, so you won't mix up the reds.  Another winner from AmazonBasics.

I'm totally impressed with this sub. I always see Boss branded items and think they've got to be bad considering how inexpensive they are. No way. This sub is impressive right from the start: the magnet is much larger than expected, the dual voice coil @ 4 ohms each is the most versatile type available on the market, and it delivers serious bass, even with just an old Rockford 300w RMS amp (I'll admit, I assume the RMS power is low on this item relative to peak power because it is not listed, but when talking about this wattage, who even cares?). I'll be anxious to try it with a newer and more powerful amp.

Oh...the lights are actually done well. Not cheesy at all. The whole thing actually looks great. And super inexpensive. Good deal.

Mine came with the latest firmware (1.0.6.02) but the backup flash memory contains version 1.0. I have had no problems at all maintaining connectivity and up-time.

I am an EE who does communications projects as a profession. I don't do wireless often, but I am more or less up to date on its features. Frankly, I was pretty stunned by the amount of menu options you can set on this thing. I wasn't expecting such an overwhelming mass of things to update myself on and tweak, especially considering this is marketed more like a small business brand than an enterprise level brand. Impressive. You can check the data sheet for a full list of features.

To counter that point, it's not a super easy device to navigate. Not that it needs to be if you have full time IT guys working on it, but I often consider what hardware a small business might use (when I'm picking parts for my house) if the owner or another employee would be taking care of the network on the side. It can be done with this, but it will take some time to figure everything out if you want to utilize all the advanced features. A perfect example is, it comes working out of the box needing no authentication to associate with the AP. Fine, but I'm looking for that setting for what seems like forever, feeling like I've lost my mind. It's under the Virtual AP heading. I'd normally expect it on the same page as you enable each radio, right up front and center. But at least it's there...

And there are pull down boxes to change from one radio to the other, and you cannot see the settings of both at the same time in most cases. This also causes you to forget to save changes, stuff like that. These are just some examples. Nothing major. The more important take away from this is that there is a lot of substance there, but it doesn't have that super easy to use GUI that Linksys home products often have (However, there is a fine line when a little GUI becomes too much).

The speeds are really here, though! I'd swear I sense a difference with my meager 30Mbps Internet connection getting to me faster. It's only slightly perceptible, but I suppose if AC really cuts out some overhead and always sends on a broader channel, it could be true (I think it is, but I'm being careful not to "imagine" things).

Note that this is true AC, but it is not the end-all highest level of AC available. It uses the minimum required 80MHz band for the 5GHz radio, but the standard allows for up to 160MHz. You can get a lot higher throughput as well, although only with more antennas using the broader spectrum. I believe the 5 GHz band on this can deliver only 1300Mbps to another single device or multiple devices maximum; the other 450Mbps is from the 2.4GHz radio.

Still impressive. Really amazing to think you can get true greater-than-wired speeds this way (I'm assuming small businesses and homes are still using 1Gb ethernet connections) considering I've always touted wired as better in every way. However, you need channel bonding equipment on both ends to do it (If I'm running a small business, I may be using an unmanaged Gb switch without that feature). Keep that in mind. Otherwise, you'll get loops and other problems. Bummer. I am unclear if this feature works with other brands' products because there are a few proprietary channel bonding methods out there.

It can be mounted so that it looks good to a wall or a false ceiling with the included hardware. A little lame is that it does NOT mount to any type of electrical box and they just tell you to drill a hole for the cables to come through. That's not very professional to me, because pulling cables through a random hole distorts that hole over time, making upgrading or maintenance difficult. It may also damage cables depending on the wall material. Not a huge issue, but lowers the professional vibe of the product. It looks pretty decent, though, but it's bigger than I expected.

Even if you have the newer, higher amperage version of PoE that this requires, they still advise you to use the AC adapter as a fail-over. Better would be both ports provide power via PoE at the new standard, share the lower power of the old standard, and if one fails, the single port keeps it alive fully with the new standard or at reduced capacity with the old standard. Then I could make some use out of PoE injectors I have laying around and it would be more backward compatible with older Telecom room equipment.

Overall, I think it's a pretty great product at a very reasonable price point at this point in time. I think it could definitely accommodate medium or even large businesses if implemented properly.

Cheapest I could find, came in a reasonably short time, works as expected, and even has a semi-rigid protective sheath I haven't seen before on an optical *audio cable (it helps you avoid overstepping the optimal bend radius).

I also have an Alienware 17 with GTX 880M GPU. Comparisons are somewhat unfair considering the nearly $1000 price difference, but I believe they may be helpful to a prospective buyer:

You can look at specs and framerate comparisons of the GPUs all over the web, but my experience is that both deliver seamless perfection in the newest games. If I'm dropping some frames with either, I don't notice, but I often like to play on my TV, and I know I lose something there. I am also not obsessed with gaming like some, so I'll concentrate on some of the other factors.

The displays themselves are both fantastic, and I cannot distinguish a huge difference there.

The GTX970M included with this machine does make a noticeable difference in terms of power consumption, as this machine is much thinner and lighter than the AW. At the same time, it feels slightly less robust because the entire chassis is not metal.

I don't like the CD drive placement on this machine, as I keep popping the slot open from time to time.

USB 3.0 is on only one side of the machine (2.0 port and card reader on the other side). AW has two ports on each side.

What I really like about the AW is that it has a second full size HDD slot for added versatility. It's the only laptop I've ever seen with that.

There are no obvious annoyances with the touchpad or keyboard as far as accidental hitting a key or something not working correctly, which I've seen with other laptops. I am not thrilled with the placement of the delete key on this laptop, and I don't really like the fact that the arrow keys are scrunched up with the numbers and other keys, either. By contrast, I believe AW got their layout perfect, including their four programmable keys.

Lights. The keyboard by itself may actually look cooler on the Apache because the lights are in the height of the keys. BUT, there are only three zones, compared to AW's four, plus multiple chassis zones. I really love the light-up touchpad on the AW. What really annoys me about the lights on this keyboard is that despite the controller software that allows lots of per-key and per-game customization, there is no setting that allows the keyboard to turn off at the same time that the screen goes blank (or any time for that matter; you have to wait until the computer goes to sleep). I have it rigged to change from one profile to a dark profile when I press the special command button, but that's not seamless.

Windows 10. Actually, I love that I got the AW at the time when they were still loading Win7 (Win 8.1 was out, but nobody wanted it). I'm still not thrilled with Win10 due to their moving some settings out of control panel and into settings, getting rid of other settings altogether, still having a ridiculous start menu, and wanting to control your life as if you're some dumb tablet/phone user. I installed Classic Shell to get my start menu back, messed with the control panel and settings for a long time, turned off everything they were "offering" me, and I have this working just about as good as a Win7 machine. Oh yeah, and I ditched MS Edge; God, what was wrong with Explorer? Anyway, if we're stuck with it, may as well make the best of it.

Very little crapware on this machine. On most computers, I disable even the proprietary controls since most of them do nothing. This machine has a System Control Manager that doesn't do anything that Windows Power settings cannot do, but it confuses things and messes up my settings, so it will be turned off. The other stuff seems harmless so far.

I was telling someone that computers like this are a status symbol to some people (like cars are to some people). And it came with a key fob, like a car... Oh yeah, this and the AW both come in fancy packaging, including a suitcase-style box that you'll be tempted to keep, but practicality keeps me from doing so. However, you may want it if you frequently transport your machine. Also comes with the largest - but not softest - microfiber cloth I've ever seen (the size of the screen).

In conclusion, you can see that there are a few minor things I prefer about the AW. Are they worth an extra thousand bucks? No. This is an impressive machine that can handle anything I throw at it. It should definitely be on your consideration list.

I'm replacing my Sony STR-DE998 7.1 120w/ch. receiver with this (approximately 10 year newer) model from what I believe to be the same price class. Were this my first receiver or if I were upgrading from a cheap unit, I would probably give this five stars. But when you get a newer and/or better model of something from the same brand, you expect to get everything and more. I found myself giving up a few things, which in some cases requires a work-around. I'll list some of them here to give you an idea:

NOTE: I have a lot of good things to say after all these minor negatives, so don't get too pessimistic. I love Sony products, but that just makes the minor negatives stand out to me more...

1 - The biggest thing is that the extra two channels you may not use if you only have 5.1 around your TV (in my case, due to a smaller space and not wanting to be ridiculous with how many speakers I have one of the main rooms in my house) cannot be dual-zoned. Yes, you can do the A/B/A+B front speaker thing, but now you cannot have a separate source playing out in the kitchen (zone 2), whereas I could with my previous unit. And then, if I ONLY want to play what used to be the second zone (my kitchen), I have to switch it to a mode that doesn't use the rear speakers, lest I annoy someone in the primary zone not using this device.

Worth noting is that the previous unit had a really clunky interface for zone 2, and I'll probably be able to streamline this new switching a little bit thanks to the three custom preset buttons on the remote (of course, I'll probably have to use all three, leaving none for other applications).

2 - Fewer audio-based inputs. Yes, you can change some inputs in the main menu to show up in your "watch" or "listen" categories, but if I want to LISTEN only to something on the "video" input (which is one of only three RCA inputs), then it's a crapshoot to get to it with only the remote (i.e., it was expected you'd have your TV/monitor on to get to this input. This is because there are buttons on the remote to take you directly to some sources, but not others, and no single button to switch through them all (However, with my Sony TV remote, I can actually switch through them all).

3 - Speaking of remotes, I love the remotes of all my other Sony equipment. Why is this one so "un-commanding"? Not only is it smaller, less attractive, and with less buttons than what I would expect, it doesn't even attempt to be the one-size-fits-all solution to your AV needs.

If you do have all your inputs going through this (which I don't, actually: I still like to be able to watch TV or anything else without having to turn this on, so I route through my TV) and you do have a TV that can control your cable box fluidly (good luck with that), and you do have a Sony TV remote that can switch over to control your amplifier pretty easily, than you may be able to get away with one remote. But that's a lot of "ifs". This remote doesn't even have channel +/- on it, so it won't be helpful at all. Luckily, I can mostly control this amp with my Sony TV remote.

That's the other thing - unless you have all those other minor compatibility issues - some mentioned above - resolved, you're still not getting a seamless solution that makes you want to keep this on every time you're watching or listening to anything (I cannot stand how some channels up the volume of commercials, and I find them all to sound particularly obnoxious coming from all speakers). I don't have cable, for example, so I always need to switch TV inputs to get back to watching TV.

4 - It has network capability, including DLNA, but it does not run apps like Pandora locally. It doesn't do any video over the network. My first-gen Smart Sony TV doesn't play *.mkv files natively, so this would have been the perfect gap filler. It's an AVR, so why not fully do the video?

5 - No more switched power outlets. No AM. No 75-ohm coax for FM. Seems like less inputs in general (I have three analog audio sources, so now there is no place to hook up my old 400-disc DVD carousel via digital coax since the digital coax can only be assigned to those otherwise analog inputs).

6 - Neither unit has a wired IR input port, which matters only if you want to hide all your components or keep them in another room. I don't really need it, but you'd think it would be included.

OK, lets talk great things now:

1 - Fantastic sound. More power than you'll probably ever use if you value your hearing. Even if I had a full-out home theater room, this would be good enough, with all its adjustable speaker configurations.

2 - I love its wired network interface (it only has a 100mb connection because it knows it won't pull video over the network anyway). Yes, it can also be used wirelessly.

Here is where I note that I hate wireless except where absolutely necessary. Beyond my opinion (moving toward fact) is that I have noticed the Bluetooth on this does not have the same distance as some other connections because I have it in a credenza. I expect similar issues with wireless, especially since you put this with a bunch of other electronics and they all create EMI as well as clashing radio frequencies...

I have no problem pulling audio from a Win7 machine, even without having purposely set up a media server on it.

3 - With this, though, I do very much appreciate the Bluetooth, both Tx and Rx. I have wanted that for a long time.

4 - One of the best things is being able to set all the options on the TV menu. That was so horrible trying to navigate the menus on the device before. You can still do them that way with just the device and the remote, but in most cases you won't want to. Most of the settings are set and forget. They're also a lot easier to set up, especially since the unit will do it for you with the included mic (that it knows where my speakers are is pretty impressive).

5 - The unit itself looks great with its classic 17" width and sleek design. The LCD is only dot matrix; could be fancier, but it's okay.

In conclusion, I do actually love the unit. I take most receiver/amp features for granted, so I didn't list every little thing as a positive. I was slightly disappointed in a few instances, but the unit still has all the important basics of functionality for audio/surround sound. My incessant yearning for more is perhaps my own problem.

If you've looked at the inputs and features on this machine and it does what you need it to, then I would definitely recommend it. You will not be disappointed in the sound or quality.

I've said it a thousand times: "I think I could really get into (real) photography, but I just can't take another hobby that requires me carrying a whole bag of equipment across the world. If I get a DSLR, I won't take it to the places that I'd like to use it the most." Well...I think they made this camera just for me. I believe this camera to be capable of "real" pro photos, just the same as if I bought a DSLR and a single lens, which many people start by doing. It also makes a startup punk like me look like a pro, much to the chagrin of the real pros.

My other cameras include a DSC-H20, which is an older Sony model with a 10x zoom lens, multiple point-and-shoots, and a waterproof/shockproof Panasonic that I really like for my basic, worry-free shots.

My main question about this camera was, why does it appear to be Sony's flagship compact camera in every way, but yet it doesn't have the 30x optical zoom lens that some of the other Sony's have (or even the 10x of my DSC-H20)? I knew there would be an answer, but to find it, I had to start digging into camera specs, something I've been meaning to do for a while.

First, pro photographers tend to think that if you're using much zoom under most circumstances, then you're just being lazy. You need to get closer. In a landscape shot, zoom tends to flatten things out. I may have never noticed this, or WHY this is. You know, you go on vacation, take a lot of pictures, come back and some look great and others look bad. Maybe it's true that every time I zoom in on a landscape, I'm really just ruining my shot.

The other thing is aperture. Aperture basically tells you how clear the background of your picture will be versus your foreground (I'm just learning this myself, so camera pros, feel free to comment with better verbiage), a lower number being better if you want a totally clear picture, and the lowness of that number being what you use to compare the quality of lenses. It's also good to have a high end on the range because that allows you to take those artsy photos with something super clean up front and a blurry background. I've also seen some neat head shots taken that way, where even some hair starts becoming blurry.

Anyway, the low aperture on this camera is 1.8 all the way zoomed out, and 2.8 all the way zoomed in (you can set it as high as 11 in either case). This is a tight range with great numbers (notice that even here, you lose a little bit by using zoom). My camera with the 10x zoom has an aperture equal to 3.5 all the way out, similar to the 30x zoom cameras Sony has now. It makes a big difference, even to my amateur eye.

This camera, and my subsequent research, has allowed me to let go of the 10/30x zoom. Yes, those cameras are great, but this is the flagship mini for a reason. Now I understand. Just taking random pictures in my neighborhood, although so boring compared to my favorite International backgrounds, I can clearly see a quality difference.

The other main spec for cameras is shutter speed. This can be set for 1/32000 of a second all the way up to 30 seconds. The quickest shutter speeds will capture an instant in time without blur, while the slower ones will capture more action with some blur. They are also good for low light scenarios to expose the shot to more light. Very slow speeds should be used with a tripod or the camera set down someplace. This camera makes a noise (not an obnoxious one) when on auto and using a slower shutter speed, to keep you still. It's very intuitive and works well.

While you will get better shots than you ever had before using this camera on auto, the dial wheel allows you to set either aperture or shutter speed as a priority and leave the rest on auto, perfect for people that want to understand what a real camera can do, and who want to set up pro shots without yet knowing everything.

The controls on this thing are awesome. I love that there is no touchscreen to fight with and that everything is so intuitive. Great praise to Sony for knowing what fads aren't worth it. (One fad they did latch onto is that 180 degree rotating screen, which really is fantastically convenient and feels quite strong and well done). While we're talking about it, they also put in the fantastic viewfinder and the pop-up flash, which all completely recess into the body of this thing (an amazing work of engineering art).

Speaking of the flash, you won't use it often. Even on a cheap camera, I try to keep the flash off, but this thing does an amazing job of using ambient light for exposure (I believe this is the third pillar of photography). I swear, I have never seen such clear pictures in very low light. Instead of being grainy, I can pick up minute details (even zoom-able), and they appear brighter than the actual place they were taken. This, I believe, is because of the 1" image sensor they are touting. I'm impressed.

The 960fps thing. With only two seconds, this may be hard to set up the shot you want, but 2 seconds seems a lot longer in 960fps. Even just shaking your leg on camera, you'll see the odd aftereffects of your socks moving like you never did before. Stupid example, but that's the point: the details you get from 960fps slow-mo are amazing.

4k video. I really didn't care about all this until some guy at a conference pointed out how 4k has been used for pro video for years. Instead of multiple cameras to cover a hockey game, for example, you could just use one and zoom in on anything you want and still have high-def video. I realized we probably will move over to actually using it at some point. Well, here's your chance to actually use that 4k TV. It's awesome. It really is.

A note on SD cards. While most devices can read SDHC cards, which went up to 32GB, the reason they want you to have a SDXC card (which can be from 64GB to 2TB in theory) is because the speed ratings are higher. You need the speed rating of 3 (>100 Mbps) to really use these big data transfer functions. I suspect the 960fps is all that can be held in RAM, and that those speeds are way too fast for even the newest and best card (hence the 2 second limit on 960fps).

Suffice to say that I love this camera. I appreciate each of its mechanical and electrical features and how they're perfectly integrated to make this small, marvelous camera. Even in the leather case (not included), it's about the same size as my H20, certainly portable enough to have it when you want it, but with enough features and technology that you're not sacrificing anything in your photography.

These may be the best sounding headphones I've been able to try so far, which is saying a lot. You definitely pick up all the little oddball sound effects happening in the background of your music, stuff that I realize is easy to miss even in higher end stereos. They also look really good: simple and classic, the way I like it. These are worlds apart in both respects from all the Beats headphones you see that succeeded solely from marketing and bad trending. It's also nice to have the digital-to-analog converter inside since lossless music is becoming more common thanks to memory being so cheap.

The bad news is that these are sort of a one-trick pony: no mic, proprietary connector (which can be justified since it supposedly draws power as well, but then why no mic and additional features), no ability to charge phone while in use (why not have an input to charge both simultaneously on the cable or the actual headphones?). So you're just getting music, and just from your phone. Of course most people want it that way.

The perfect external 3.5" hard drive for purchase at this point in time as far as I'm concerned: they include controller software *if you want it*, but they don't try to persuade you to use it, instead taking the simplistic approach, which is plug it in and use it! I would never use software to run a hard drive anyway.

Also, 4TB seems to be the sweet spot right now for price/size ratio for external 3.5" storage (3.5" drives always require an external power source, whereas 2.5" external drives - which are sometimes slower - usually do not). I like that you can leave it plugged in, but it only powers on when you attach the USB cable.

USB 3.0 really is a vast improvement over previous versions. I'm dumping all my files from five other drives on this monster, and 500GB are transferring through the computer from one drive to another in around 2-3 hours, both large and tiny files.

Worth noting is that the case seems very thin around the drive, which is probably good for heat dispersion, but will not provide the kind of protection you'd want if you were constantly transporting this drive.

I now have on here hundreds of seasons of TV shows, most in HD, nearly a thousand movies, most in HD, hundreds of music albums, books, maps, comics, software setup files, etc., and I STILL have room to grow. To get all these things consolidated and organized - and all accessible with a single drive powered up - is really fantastic.

Since most externally mounted surge protectors require two dedicated breaker spaces anyway, I really like that this one fits right inside the panel, made for QO by QO. The rating is in the basic category of protection, and anything greater would require an externally mounted device. I figured that the power in town where I live is decent and the chances of needing higher protection are slim to none.

I moved the two breakers under my main 200A breaker to make room for this (I'm in the process of installing a sub panel with generator input anyway, so the timing works). Installation was literally plug it on like any other breaker, then I trimmed the lead down to connect with the closest spot on the ground/neutral bus. That's about two to three minutes if you have the spaces already available.

I like the extra peace of mind, considering I'm already suspect of electronics that use all push button controls with nothing mechanical (my high end range just stops responding sometimes and I have to go turn it off at the breaker for a minute to let it reset). For the price, why not?

This product can be flush mounted as shown or surface mounted by removing the cover. When surface mounting, it can be connected directly to your panel with the threaded nipple attached. It recommends two dedicated 20A single-pole circuit breakers to connect to, which should be - if possible - right under or right above the main breaker in your panel. There are four 12 AWG leads to connect, which are 18" long and can be trimmed - two hots, a neutral, and a ground.

I understand the pain of the other reviewer who mentioned a warranty issue. Frankly, I never really believe warranties that promise coverage above the actual product in question (that is, since the warranty supposedly covers the equipment that this device is protecting). No company would give up thousands of dollars on a $30 item. So this - along with any surge protection device - is for peace of mind. It is also a common idea (I know from reading other surge protector reviews) that one cannot know if the item you have is really working...but I see these types of devices in most military and commercial panels, so it's not like they're selling snake oil. I think a whole house surge protector is an item worth your investment.

This fits in the basic protection category with protection to 26kAmps/phase. It will work with any panel and it is inexpensive compared to most models. My only reservation is that some panel manufacturers make a device with comparable protection that fits in the panel and takes up only two breaker spaces. This, on the other hand, still requires two breaker spaces (breakers purchased separately). Worth looking into if you are looking for this level of protection. Also worth noting is that if you are going with an externally mounted device such as this, you can acquire a much higher level of protection for additional money.

Good product, easy to install, and provides the highest level of installation flexibility. Worth knowing what options are available so that you get the exact installation you desire.

This cable has everything I want in video surveillance cable: it is slick and easy to pull without lubricant, but remains flexible and robust without kinking easily. It is pure copper; some other cables are copper clad aluminum.

Also, the power cable is 18AWG, which is good for power transmission up to 2 amps (for this reason, I suggest using this for all your CCTV runs, even if you have some free (probably 22 AWG - good for up to 0.92 amp) cables that came with your security package - this will allow you to be uniform and ready for any potential upgrades. (If you really want to be ready for the future, run some Cat6 at the same time, which you can use for PTZ, audio, and upgrades to IP cameras). BTW, the free cables that come with the packages share the ground conductor, which can make installation messier and annoy you if you are a perfectionist.

It pulls apart easily, but only when you need it to. The cable is marked by the foot and the box has a place to write how much is left. It was also easy to connectorize with the RG-59 BNC compression connectors I bought here on Amazon.

My only install tip is when you cut the end with your coax tool, ensure that the stranded ground cable (outside the dielectric) remains to make a ground with the connector, but that none of the strands remain long enough that they can come in contact with the 20AWG signal conductor when connectorizing.

POSITIVE:

I had been expecting cheap looking/feeling components because one review mentioned that that was the case, and because I am unfamiliar with the brand. Contrarily, every single element of this package feels of good quality. The main units are well formed and have all the ports, buttons, and LEDs that you could want for the application; every cable you need comes with the package, they are good quality, and they even include hook and loop mounts for the IR receiver and transmitter; the on screen menu is simple but well done, and even translucent over the video you are watching; the rectifiers are the type that can fit on most power strips; the unit uses wireless N technology on ~5GHz; the two devices are pre-paired; and the packaging and included literature even looks good.

Nothing about this unit seems cheap.

NEUTRAL:

I'm guessing the reason that some people cannot get an acceptable signal is because they are experiencing interference with their WiFi network; this can be rectified in some cases.

Common consumer frequency bands are ~2.4GHz and ~5GHz. Most new wireless access points/routers transmit at BOTH frequencies, but usually, either of them can be turned off if you go into your router settings (usually 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1 from a web browser by factory default). A lot of people have all their electronics clumped together near the TV, so this could be especially burdensome in that situation. Many routers automatically change bands within the given range to avoid interference, but I cannot know what exact frequency these run on. Try turning the 5GHz band off on your wireless access point/router or move other 5GHz wireless devices away from these.

I didn't experience any problems turning my two 5GHz wireless access points on and off from different locations around the house. I could get plenty of signal from the basement up to the second floor and over a room with no problem, this even going through a few layers of plaster, which - as a non-porous material - the manual warns you may degrade the signal.

NEGATIVE:

Well, all wireless things are finicky, as are shortcuts to doing things in most cases. This works well, actually, but I did have trouble with both my computer and my DVR:

My computer's HDMI output, like most, tells the computer when something is plugged in, so the computer changes its mode. But since the connected hardware (the transmitting unit) is not using the signal immediately, the computer didn't recognize it. I had to first get the computer used to the setup by plugging it directly into the TV's HDMI port and then quickly switch ports to this unit. But then I had trouble with the audio as well. It took a while, but I eventually got it. The problem is, I suspect you'd have this problem every time, so I do not recommend this for use with a computer. I'm guessing a cell phone's micro-HDMI port would have the same problem.

I also couldn't get this to work with my security system's DVR, and I suspect it's the exact same problem, since the DVR does function like a computer in many ways. However, it is clear to me that this is primarily made for a cable or satellite box.

Again, less finicky than I expected. I am unsure if the correct hardware exists to make the computer recognize this device when plugged in via HDMI.

I hate to leave two things turned on all the time, especially because the radios will always run and consume some power (admittedly little, as both units consume around 5 watts when running, probably less than one when idle).

UNSOLICITED ADVICE:

1. I let the cable company slide when it kept jacking up prices and charging me for sports networks that I never watch. But when they started encrypting their signals to force every TV in every house to have a box attached to it (so they could make it easy for you to buy Pay Per View), I finally had enough and cancelled my cable. Those boxes are so slow and unresponsive, not to mention ugly and make your TV work less well than it should. I installed an antenna system in my attic (actually, in my case, above the 8' mark of my attic, so no usable space was wasted) and now I get around 45 free channels, and all the networks are in HD. Best thing I've ever done. If you own your house and/or will be living where you are for a while, I encourage you to do the same. Check out tvfool dot com to start your research (free). Or just cut the cable anyway because you're tired of being lied to and price gouged.

2. I ran proper in-wall cabling systems for a home network, security system, multiple video systems, and whole house audio system all at the same time. Second best thing I've ever done. You wouldn't believe how often it comes in handy and you'll never need finicky shortcuts again. If you own your house and are decent at DIY, I encourage you to do the same. More is better; run more cables than you need, because running them is the hard part.

Everyone is going to tell you this camera is awesome. It is. I'm going to concentrate on telling you some details you may not know:

- I'm an Electrical* engineer, but I am so impressed with the Mechanical* designs of this unit. It's amazingly small, but they've thought of everything to make it easy on the user, from battery pulltags, to grommeted permanently attached covers, to hold switches, mini displays, and options galore...

- ...and to keep it small, they actually had to make a separate tripod mount, that connects at two points, but only requires one screw (that you can screw with a coin), all because the unit is so small that it couldn't accommodate a full depth standard tripod mount screw...

- ...and then there is a baseplate that accepts that standard tripod screw, and once it is attached to that baseplate, you can attach it to either the flat or curved adhesive or Velcro-belt by a very strong friction clip. This friction clip is also accepted by the (not included) wristband offered by Sony, which does not come with its own friction clip (so don't lose the one that comes with the camera)...

- ...all this screwing and unscrewing could almost become annoying. But then you have the waterproof case. This case has a built-in tripod mount, but is barely larger than the camera with tripod mount attached, so why not keep the case on all the time for that extra layer of protection? I like the idea. And then you can keep that mounted where you want it, and remove the camera as necessary to charge or pull out the SD card.

- The strange thing about the case is, it's only rated (per Sony; they say "to their* specifications) to 5m deep water for 30 minutes. That's the same rating the camera itself has, but by looking at the case, I'd expect it to make it down to at least 10m for as long as you want with no problems. I think they're just being super careful, but I know from experience that companies don't like to make dramatic claims as to waterproofing because they end up with all sorts of warranty claims (both legitimate and illegitimate) to sort through. Even so, I love the double protection...

- ...Meanwhile, the wrist-mount monitor is rated down to 10m. Remember that Wi-Fi doesn't work under water, so this is probably only going to do you good at the surface anyway...

- ...The monitor works well, and picks up your camera right away after first connection. The buttons are fairly intuitive. Remember that the camera itself simply will not be as easy to playback/review as a regular camcorder simply because there is no room for all that mess on this tiny camera...

- ...And also remember that - even though this camera is totally awesome - it will not necessarily replace your camcorder if you care about things such as zoom, instant local playback, etc. Ideally, you'll have both for different functions, but if anyone can pull off the ultimate all-in-one a few electronic generations from now, it's Sony. The point here I want to highlight is NO ZOOM.

- You cannot record in XAVC S unless you have an (micro - it takes micro SD or the newest, smallest Memory Stick) SD card "greater than class 10". Even if you have a fancy class 10 SD card that claims to be faster than the rest, the camera will give you an error and you'll have to record to *.mp4. I didn't even know they had classes above 10, but the best they have out right now is UHS-3, which costs around $28 bucks for brand name 32GB, whereas a the same brand/size in class 10 is now around $15. I recommend getting the largest decent name UHS-3 you can find to accommodate this camera, which is probably going to cost $50-60 for a 64GB.

- The accessory options available for this thing are endless, from suction cup mounts for your car (exterior or interior) to your bike handles (the included curved base works on your bike handles, but not as perfectly as the vise strictly intended for that use), wrist mounts, snorkel goggles mounts, and the list goes on infinitely. Sony included two of these for my review, and - as you probably expect - the Sony branded stuff is sublime.

- At the time of writing, Sony's website does not yet have a full manual for download, but there is some barely helpful Q&A page you can get to with the link in the included paperwork. While there is tons of paper included with the camera, it's mostly useless; I wish they'd just give you the full manual and only include one language per box if they need to reduce paper use...

- ...I wanted the manual because I sort of expect there are more connections you can make with WiFi (i.e., connect to computer to download files) and other options that I am so far unaware of. Frankly, the best way for me has always been just to take the SD card to the computer and use the best freeware you already have on the computer (like VLC Media Player).

Conclusion: Sony products have always impressed me, and this camera (and included accessories) get me excited about the company in a way I haven't been since I bought my Z-series TV years ago. They clearly still make the best stuff when they try. Although this is not the perfect camcorder, it is the perfect action cam: the size, options, and quality speak for themselves.

...Satan really is talking to me through my music. I didn't realize she meant it literally, but I can hear it clearly now, along with all kinds of blips, bops, and sound effects that I never knew were part of my favorite tunes. Indeed, the noise cancellation abilities as well as the clarity of the full range speakers contribute to my music sounding better than ever.

These have the overwhelming feel of a set of headphones meant for an actual audiophile, or at least an adult who can afford and appreciate high end quality. I did notice (and scoff) that Sennheiser is also trying to appeal to the type of silly young people that walk around shut out from the world all day by showing how they overextended themselves on a (fools only) status symbol. But hey, they didn't go too far down that road; I assure you these are the type of headphones that can be taken seriously: the materials, construction, comfort, and fit all exude quality, while remaining understated.

I have the "i" version, but they work just fine with my Blackberry, including the volume buttons. The third button, which apparently works for iphone by a series of presses and/or holds, does pause/play my BB when playing music and bring up the voice activated search when on the home screen. If I had an iphone, I probably wouldn't deem it worth bothering to remember all the commands, but they are there.

The headphone end of the cable takes a smaller four-pin (left, right, mic, ground) connector than the phone end, so your existing cables may not work, although you can use standard extensions if necessary. The headphone end is a twist-lock that I've seen before on other headphones, so I'm sure you could get a new one if necessary. The actual headphone cable is the high quality, flat, matte type. The controls are up fairly high, and I wish they were removable, i.e., you could have your pigtail with a female end connected to the headphones, and then use whatever cable you want with or without the controls as applicable. Just a thought...

They are comfortable, but not huge enough (these are the XL version) that my full ear actually sits fully inside the round earpiece (that's okay, they are big enough).

Extremely nice headphones.

Works as expected.  A lot of background noise and it increases the bandwidth necessary when remotely viewing your sub-stream, but it connects intuitively and fits basically inside your camera mount.  Run any two cheap copper leads and splice on half of an RCA cable to either end to connect to this.

[Update: Check the comments section if you are interested in my experience with their customer service.]

I'm replacing an everyday ~$400-500 Compaq home laptop (contained a real Intel processor, not just a Celeron or equivalent) with this computer and using it the same way. Here's what I've discovered:

Before, if I started to get download speeds upward of 1Mb/s, the fans would spin up and I'd get worried it might explode. Performance monitoring would show the CPU being used 80% or more. I never bothered trying to decompress 1080p H.264 *.mkv files locally because they would drop a bunch of frames and it would look worse than streaming with a bad Internet connection. And transferring between multiple drives was clearly limited by the processor and not the USB2.0 ports.

Now, I can easily sustain 3Mb/s download speeds for hours, decompress 1080p from *.mkv files without a single dropped frame, and transfer quicker than USB2.0 would ever allow with these USB3.0 ports, all simultaneously* and without the fan kicking on past low. All that, and the performance monitor is showing less than 40% CPU usage and NO GPU usage. Oh yeah, and all the while, the LED lights all over this device are going nuts and generally looking cool.

Frankly, I don't have the juice or the requirements necessary to bog this thing down. But that's good - that means it should be a good number of years before it begins to feel dated. Suffice to say, I can do all that other stuff in the background as a server function and never even notice it while I'm surfing the web or processing documents.

It's bigger and heavier than my previous laptop, but I find that doesn't matter at all. It doesn't really take up any more room where it sits in the living room, and once the lights go out, it fits in with its classic black look. And it is clearly a quality product, so it looks better and fits in better wherever it is. It's also more comfortable on my lap because it doesn't get hot easily (never that I've seen) and it doesn't have any sharp edges.

I was worried about battery life, but I easily get three-five hours out of it when I take it to the kitchen to browse the web before dinner. And that's with all the LEDs on and most of the defaults selected. I'm fairly sure I could get a clean five hours by tweaking the settings. And I would imagine that this battery should keep its life longer rather than degrading over time like most cheap laptops. I say this just because cheap laptops always have you tethered to a wall after a couple of years, but I suspect that is because they also use cheap batteries. Nothing about the Alienware is cheap, so I suspect the battery may always give me that same capacity.

I love having a big internal HD and some (actually, plenty) solid state memory on different drives. It has some automatic configuration set up, but it still shows as two drives. I'm sort of unsure how that works so far, but I'll probably figure it out over time. It'd be nice if they told you exactly what they were doing and let you input how you'd like it configured.

Gotta admit, I love all the lights and stuff. They do look cool and you can turn any or all of them off, or have them go out when the computer is at rest or whatever you want. However, the back has lights and an alien head; I wish you could turn on the alien head and the other lights off. Regardless, it's a heck of a lot cooler than a piece of fruit back there.

I love 1080p screens even for regular computing because they are perfectly compatible with most TVs, which are large monitors most people already have around.

This is one brand I sort of like, too. I remember one project I had, I worked out of an Internet hall in a hospital because I didn't have an office. One kid used to come in after working the night shift with his Alienware and play games all day long. He didn't have a car, though. Although I still don't get his priorities, I always remember that kid with the awesome computer. And it is some kind of nerd status symbol that makes being a nerd cool somehow. Does that make any sense?

Anyway, now for the small annoyances:

-It comes with a giant Dell rectifier pack that is probably larger than necessary for everyday use. I don't think I'm sucking down much more power than a normal computer when just browsing the web. Regardless, it has that blue LED ring around the end that never goes out. That can screw up your color scheme if it does not involve blue (you could cover it in electrical tape if it annoys you). I guess it's better than having something proprietary that would be hard to replace, but something to note.

-Looks like the motherboard can handle 32GB of RAM, but to upgrade to that, you'd have to throw both existing pieces out, which is wasteful. I could be wrong about that - I suppose it may have four slots; someone please comment if I am wrong. I always want to get the RAM maxed out right away, but my estimate from looking at other models is that upgrade will cost another $500 or so right off the bat. [Update 20 July: Check the comments section - sounds like it is four slots, which makes this nicely upgradable! Another reason to love it...]

-No PCMCIA slot. I know they're not used often, and most things can be done via USB dongle. But an external card reader is annoying. This is a big computer, so there should be room in there someplace.

-Comes in a giant box with padding on the inside, presumably so you can transport it for gaming. Should have made this a real thin, fairly cheap aluminum box, so it would be more worthwhile keeping.

That's about it. Everything else about this computer is amazing. Recommended.

I am very pleased with the functionality and expandability of this system given the very low price point.
