The AF120's were not all that impressive at first sight. Granted, the packaging is excellent – as upscale as what you would expect at this price point. The earphones themselves are, for lack of a better word, rather bland. While I’m not a fan of the over-the-top school of design, a little more flash would have been nice. On the other hand, these are in-ear, so there’s not much that can be seen when in use.

But on to the important issues. Comfort is excellent. The kit includes a wide range of tip sizes so I can’t imagine that there’s an ear out there to which these can’t be properly fitted. Personally, I’m a huge fan of the Comply tips. They fit well, are comfortable enough to literally wear all day long, and maintain excellent positioning even when I’m moving around. But, if you prefer silicon tips, these comes with those as well.

What was not initially comfortable was the over-the-ear cable. It’s pliable and does an excellent job of keeping the earphones properly positioned, but for me, they took some getting used to. I still can’t say that I love them with regard to comfort, but a do appreciate the benefit of having it.

The cord is very good, with a stout fabric cover over the lower portion that gives it durability without making it hard to manage. The upper portion is less protected, consisting of just twisted cable. I like the look, but since I’m usually hard on cords, I would have liked more protection throughout.

The sound quality is outstanding provided you’re looking for accurate response rather than over boosted bass. That’s not to say this lacks bass response – it’s more than ample. It’s just that it provides a more neutral, clean sound rather than rattling your molars. The same for the mid and upper ranges. Listening to string and flute sonatas was just delightful, with crisp sound throughout; vocals were equally outstanding.

These also work and play well when cranked up past the volume point where you should be keeping below to save your hearing. At my age that’s not much of a concern any longer, and it’s great to blast these without it resulting in any measure of distortion.

Complaints are few and mostly nit-picks. I don’t care for the fabric case. It looks nice, but I’d much prefer a hard case for greater protection. It could also use a bit more padding on the over-the-ear lasso. As mentioned earlier, more protection on the cord would be a plus, especially given the price point of these.

While these issues bring my rating to 4.5 stars, I’ll round up to five since overall, I’m very pleased with these earphones. If you’re looking for a true, natural sound (and can deal with the price of these), they should absolutely be on your short list.

This is a decent PC monitor that doesn’t excel in any area but, at the same time, doesn’t fall flat either (except for sound quality). It’s a good choice if you’re looking for an inexpensive, wide-screen monitor that comes in at under $100.

The build quality is what you’d expect at this price point: pretty basic and simple. The casing is all plastic, and rather cheap feeling plastic at that. It comes with a very basic stand that allows a limited amount of tilt adjustment, but no swivel or monitor rotation. There are no mounting holes on the back to facilitate a wall or stand mount. There are also no convenience features, such as a USB hub. It also lacks an HDMI port.

On the plus side, the power cord just plugs into the monitor without the need for a transformer or wall wart. The overall monitor profile is pretty slim, and it is very lightweight.

Setup is very simple. No tools are needed to attach the stand (just push and it clicks into place). It comes with a VGA cable, a 3.5mm audio cable and a power cable. Although it includes a DVI port, it does not come with the cable to use that. It also does not come with a user guide (other than a one-page quick setup sheet) or a driver disk. Both are available as downloads from the HP site. However, neither are really needed.

I hooked it up to my laptop via VGA to use as a secondary monitor. It auto installed under Win 7, so it should be able to do the same for 8 and 10. The recommended resolution is 1600x900 at 60Htz.

Right out of the box the settings were eye-searing bright, as is typical with manufacturer defaults since they want their monitors to stand out when on display in a store. Changing the settings is pretty easy – the menu button brings up the full list of options; you select the one you want; then adjust with the +/- keys. You can experiment at will since there’s also a choice to return to factory defaults should you get lost in the weeds with changes. The adjustment menu is pretty extensive for a monitor at this price point. You can adjust the usual brightness and contrast, and also color temp, image control, and even turn off the blue LED power indicator (yes!). Unfortunately, the control button labels are impossible to read (black on black) but there’s only a few buttons, so it's not tough to figure out.

The image quality is decent once it’s been properly adjusted. It won’t wow you, but it provides good performance on both images and text. I was happier with the text performance than I was with video (it has pretty limited black levels) but, for an everyday, inexpensive monitor, it’s more than acceptable.

The speakers are very, very basic. Tinny to the point of being useless. I’ve gotten better sound out of a $5 set of basic computer speakers.

I’m giving this 4 stars since, even at this price point, HP could have done a better job with the overall look/feel of the monitor, have included some additional convenience features such as a swivel, USB hub, and/or an HDMI port. Features that could have been dropped are the internal speakers, which are useless for anything other than to hear system beeps. Still, even as-is, it’s worth considering if you’re looking for a no-frills, no-fuss, inexpensive monitor.

This is a nicely made water bottle with a number of nice design touches. The overall look is very striking – it’s a jet black with a flat finish that does not show fingerprints. Plus, the flat finish makes it more grippy than other bottles I have that have a polished finish. The build quality feels very good – it has a nice, solid feel to it.

It comes with two spouts. One is for cold drinks, and it’s the standard flip-up spout. It has a plastic straw so you don’t have to tilt it to take a drink (which is great when driving). The spout is a lime green which looks great against the black finish, and has a ledge so you can flip it up with one hand. I especially like that the straw is easily removed for cleaning.

The top cap is plastic, but has thick threads that feel pretty sturdy. It also has a thick o-ring at the top to keep it sealed. I shook a full bottle quite hard with the cap screwed down and had zero leaking. There's a loop at the top that can be used as a finger hold. I wish the loop was a bit bigger, since it's a pretty snug fit for a finger.

It also comes with a stainless steel cap that has a wood top for when the bottle is used for hot drinks. It also has a thick o-ring to prevent leaks, and has a thick stainless loop at the top to make it easy to remove. The wood top makes for a nice looking accent. The carry loop is great -- wish the cold cap had a similar loop.

It also comes with has a neoprene jacket to help increase insulating capability. It’s thin, which is a plus since it doesn’t add much bulk to the bottle, but still helps with insulation. The jacket is black and has the Boje logo on it. It looks OK, but to my eye it would look better with a smaller logo.

Performance has been excellent. I use it mainly for cold drinks, and it keeps the water cold enough to prevent the ice from melting for a couple of hours in a hot car, and maintained a cool temp for a couple of hours after the ice melted. There has been zero condensation on the outside of the bottle even when left in a hot car in humid weather.

It’s too hot out to try this with hot beverages, but based on the cold performance, I expect the hot performance will be equally as good.

It work well, looks great, has some nice design touches, and offers both hot and cold options. It's a bit pricy for a water bottle, but the build quality and options make it a decent value.

This is a rather unique take on a traditional power strip. Rather than be designed as a strip, it’s a tower, with two outlets on four sides, plus a bank of four USB outlets in the front. The design is perfect for plugging in “wall wart” transformers, since even the largest ones allow you to have access to all 8 power outlets.

There are three on/off switches. Two are on the top, with each controlling four of the power outlets. The third one is below the bank of USB outlets. Thus, you have a lot of flexibility in turning on/off outlet banks. That’s a big plus for me, since I use this as the power source for my Li-Ion chargers, and don’t like to leave them in use overnight. The independent switches allow me the flexibility to turn them off, but still leave 4 outlets on. The same for the USB outlets – I can turn them off rather than have to unplug the device being charged.

The outlets and housing feel pretty sturdy. Where the build quality could be improved is the base and the switches. The base has some measure of non-slip padding, but it’s still a bit slidy on a smooth surface. It would benefit from better grip plus a wider base to give it more overall stability. The on/off switches for the power outlets feel (and sound) rather cheap. They have a positive click to them, which is nice, but the feel is really “plasticy.” They work fine (at least so far) but the way they sound and feel don’t give me the warm fuzzies about a long life span.

The USB outlets output a total of 2.1A. That’s fine for a single item or perhaps two, but the charge speed drops way down if you have more than 2 items plugged in that have a high draw.

I do not know if this has surge protection. The product description says it does, but nowhere on the box or the brief instruction card does it mention surge protection as a feature, nor does it describe what type of surge protection is offered. I would believe the product box before the product listing, so I think it’s a safe assumption that this does NOT have surge protection. The only feature noted on the box is that it has overload protection, which appears to be some type of resettable breaker. As noted in the product guide:

"When power socket overloads, the protector -- a white or black pin -- will kick in by popping out automatically and cut off the power. When this happens, please unplug power socket, unplug the high power consumption device that connect to it, then reset the overload protector by pressing the overload protector button back."

I didn’t factor the potential omission of surge protection into my rating, but did factor in the build quality issues. Those bring my rating to 4 stars. Still, it’s a very useful and novel design that is a great way to have access to 8 outlets while using “wall warts” and not have it take up much floor or desk space. The multiple on/off switch options are also a big plus.

These are telescopic glasses – basically a set of binoculars that you wear. Although they may look like the magnifying optics that help with close-up work, they are not. These are for distance vision. It’s a good product if you want to have distance vision but do not want to have to hold a pair of binoculars. However, that convenience comes at a cost: a narrow field of view.

The build quality is pretty good for the price point. The frame is sturdy and doesn’t twist or bend in use. The nose pads and arms are comfortable to wear. It has enough weight that you know you’re wearing it, but I can wear it for extended periods without anything cutting into my nose or face. That being said, I do wish it had spring-loaded hinges on the arms. That would provide for an additional measure of adjustability and comfort.

The optics are also very well done. I can’t tell for sure if the lenses are plastic or glass, but it performs at such a good level in terms of clarity that I would be surprised if it were not glass. The focal action of the lens is also very well done, with smooth, fluid operation to adjust the focus. Each lens can be adjusted independently.

The kit comes with a lot of extras. There’s a set of rubber eye cups to help block side light and aid in comfort, an extra set of nose pads, a cleaning cloth, a pretty nice case with foam cutouts for all the items, and a set of five magnifying lenses that screw on to the main lenses. The latter is where the first problem crops up. You get five different magnification (2,3,4,5, and 6) but only ONE of each. Thus, if you want to use them, you’re limited to using just one eye. It would have been more useful to have a smaller set of adapters and get TWO of each mag power. As it is, the mag attachments have very limited use. I tried them out, and then didn’t use them again.

One item it lacks is an instruction guide. It does have one, but it is all in Chinese. Not much help for me!

The other issue is the field of vision. It’s narrow – very narrow. You’re dealing with tunnel vision when wearing these. It gets way worse when using the mag attachments.

Lastly, you can’t wear these at the same time as regular glasses. I’m a glasses wearer, and it got tiresome having to switch between these and regular glasses. Regular binoculars, in contrast, can easily be used when wearing glasses.

It’s hard to come up with an overall rating for these. The build quality and optics are easily 5 star worthy given the price point. The ease of use (if you don’t wear glasses) and comfort are 4 to 5 star worthy. The mag attachments are 1 star, and the field of vision offered is 3 stars. I’ll average those together and give it 4 stars. It’s a good product if you want to have distance vision but not have to hold a pair of binoculars, but will be out-performed by even a low-end pair of binoculars.

Bottom line: Overall, this is an excellent laptop/tablet setup. The screen is simply gorgeous, the speed is excellent, and it easily morphs between a laptop and a tablet. Windows 8 can be a bit of a pain, as can some of the hardware design quirks, but overall, I’m finding it to be a solid performer. It's a good choice if you want a tablet but don't want to give up the functionality of a laptop.

Full review: It’s been a couple of years since I tried out a laptop/tablet “convertible” type system, and things have certainly improved for the better. This Asus is a fully functional system in both its tablet and laptop modes.

I was a little disappointed when I first opened the box since it was not packaged in a “high end” (ala Apple) manner. It was packed well in terms of protection, but it was pretty utilitarian. I also thought it was unusual that there was no setup or “welcome” sheet/poster packed with the hardware.

The utilitarian feel went away once I started using it. The overall fit and finish is excellent – very solid feeling. It is thinner than I expected – folded up it’s just a bit thicker than my older tablets. The tablet portion alone is sleek and solid. You do notice the weight when using just the tablet, but it’s not bad. My only quibble is that the tablet case is slippy in hand. The keyboard has non-slip feet on it that keep it well-planted, but when using just the tablet, it’s slidy. I’m shopping for a case or skin to help with the hand feel of the tablet.

Setup was straightforward, with Win 8 going through the usual setup process of a couple of minutes to get the basics taken care of, then an hour or so of having it fetch and install all the needed OS updates. I used Win 8 for a bit when it came out, but mostly work with Win 7 machines. It was a pleasant surprise to see how well Microsoft has buffed the rough edges off of Win 8. I can’t say that I love it (I'm more of an Android fan when it comes to touch screens) but it’s a very workable OS that is (mostly) easy to use. Granted, the very first thing I did was install Chrome since IE is a total pain, but overall, Win 8 is not bad. But, I want to keep this review focused on the hardware rather than Win 8.

The shining star of the tablet is the screen. It is absolutely gorgeous in terms of resolution, be it text (which was a treat for these old eyes since young programmers seem to think everyone can read 2 point type) or video. The viewing angle is excellent, the colors are rich and vibrant. Asus did an excellent job with the screen.

The touch sensitivity of the screen is also excellent. I don't use a stylus and am able to reliably hit everything I aim or swipe for. That’s saying a lot given my less than nimble fingers.

The keyboard is good but not great. The key feel is decent, as is the layout, but the keys and the frame feels cheap compared with the more solid feel of the tablet. The touch pad is decent, but there's not much need for it given the excellent touch screen. The docking between the tablet and the keyboard is very well made – easy to attach, pretty easy to detach, and it maintains a very secure grip. I had no problems switching between the virtual and the physical keyboard (which uses Bluetooth to connect with the tablet).

The tablet has no fan but does not heat up much. I can feel some warmth on the right side of the tablet back after it has been operating for a few hours, but it’s just warm, rather than hot. And I certainly don’t miss the fan noise. The internal drive is solid state, so there truly is zero operating sound. The claimed run time of about 8 hours is accurate.

The operating speed is snappy. I noticed zero lag time switching between apps/programs, and no significant slowdown when running multi-tasking programs. I attribute this to both a decent speed for the processor, plus the solid state drive.

The sound quality is just OK. It's pretty clear, but sounds tinny and lacks any measure of punch or bass. That's not surprising given how small the speakers have to be. The sound quality is adequate for basic audio, such as watching a YouTube video, but for anything else you'll probably want to use an external speaker. I paired it with an external Bluetooth speaker for streaming music, and even though the external speaker was not high end, the sound quality improvement was significant.

What I don’t care for is how USB devices are connected. It has a dongle which attaches to the tablet. It works, but it’s ungainly. I would have loved to have a conventional USB port built into the tablet (or keyboard) even at the expense of the needed extra thickness. On the plus side, the dongle worked fine with every USB device I tried it with (various external drives, printers, camera). In addition to the USB output it can read an SD card plus has an HDMI output port.

It’s a bit of a pain to open the tablet when it’s docked with the keyboard and folded up. The hinge tightness works against you when trying to get it open. Lastly, the charger has a wall wart on the end which can be problematic when trying to plug it into a loaded power strip.

While there are negatives, they are mostly of the irritating nature rather than the truly interfering nature. This is a solid device that provides excellent functionality as a tablet and provides good laptop functionality. The Win 8 OS allows you to use the full range of Windows application software plus an extensive number of apps. While it won’t fully replace a “real” laptop since it lacks items that I would want in a laptop (such as a built-in DVD drive and a better keyboard), it offers far more utility than just a tablet and does so at a good price point. The negatives drop it to 4.5 stars, but I’ll round up to 5 stars since the screen is truly outstanding.

I use an extension so I can wear corded headphones while on the treadmill at home, since the treadmill noise makes it impossible to listen to music any other way. The problem is that the cords get jostled and stressed quite a bit, and wear pretty quickly.

This cord, however, is far better made. The jacket is braided and very sturdy, but remains pretty flexible. Both the male and female jacks are firmly attached to the cord and are also very sturdy. I didn't encounter any static or pops with this cable, which is a first for me with any other cable.

It is a bit more expensive than other cables, but the build quality is very much in line with the price point. I'm very impressed with these, and would highly recommend them, especially for applications where the cable gets stressed, stretched or jostled around.

Bottom line: This is a lot of fun! It’s perfect for hobby work when you need to take a magnified photo that’s beyond what you could do with a macro lens. Setup and use is straightforward, but there are some limitations. Still, a great value for the price point.

Full review: This provides the ability to take magnified photos or videos in a self-contained, easy to use unit. The build quality is pretty good considering the price. There is some wobble in the support bar, and the focusing knobs are not high-end in their operation, but overall, I found it delivered more than I expected at the price point it’s selling for.

It only took me a couple of minutes to assemble the hardware (no tools are needed). The software loaded quickly and easily from the included DVD. The software is very straightforward to use – there’s a limited set of options which are all pretty much self-explanatory. There’s also a decent user guide on the CD as a PDF file.

The camera plugs into a USB port to communicate with the software plus pull power for the LED lights. No external power is needed.

I had some problems running the software on an XP machine. Most of the time it worked fine, but it would occasionally crash, usually after snapping a series of photos. Clearing the crash required unplugging the camera from the USB port and plugging it in again.

I then loaded it on a Win 7 machine and had no problems. My XP machine is pretty old, so it may be a PC hardware issue rather than an actual problem with XP. In any case, it was smooth sailing on Win 7.

The first step that you need to do is to calibrate the unit using the included calibration scale. That was a bit challenging, and the instructions could have been a bit better. Calibration is not essential, however, unless you want to ensure your magnification settings are accurate. If you’re just looking to use this as an easy macro camera, then calibration is not as important.

I had no problems snapping photos, which can be done using a trigger on the USB cable or by selecting the photo icon on screen. You can also select from four resolution modes (ranging from 1.3M to 5M).

The software also has a pretty decent set of annotation tools. The menu comes up when you double click on a photo, and allows you to add text, lines, arrows, freehand drawing, etc. It’s very basic, but perfectly fine (and fast) for pointing out a feature in an photo without having to use something such as Photoshop.

There are some limitations. The LED lights are OK, but not great. I found I got far better photos using an auxiliary light in addition to (or in place of) the built-in LED lights. The built in lights are not as bright as they could be, have a limited light field, and have some hot spots that can impact photo quality.

There’s also some wobble in the frame. Not a lot, but enough that you need to be careful not to knock the unit out of focus at high magnifications. The focus controls (there’s a course and a fine focus control) are OK in terms of smoothness, but certainly not what I would call high-end.

While this would not serve the needs of highly exacting, precision work, it is a fantastic help for hobby work. I use it to take photos of various RBA builds, and it's worlds easier (and better) than using a macro lens. It delivers a lot of value for the price, and I would highly recommend it.

IP cameras have always been a total pain for me to get up and running. There’s always something that goes wrong, and I end up spending hours getting it to work. This model, however, was a dream to install. The installation quick-start guide is very clear, and offers two options: installing it if you have a D-Link router; or installation with a non-Dlink router. I used the non-Dlink router approach. You download an install program from the Dlink site that walks you through the installation in a clear, easy step-by-step fashion. I had it running in a couple of minutes in hard wired mode, and a couple minutes more to get it to run wirelessly. Very impressed with how easy it was.

The build quality of the camera itself is pretty good. It’s very lightweight but still feels sturdy, and comes with a stand that has a ball and socket joint so you can rotate and position the camera pretty much any way you would need it. The only hardware issue that I didn’t care for was the power cord. It’s rather short (about 4 foot), which limits where I can position the camera. A longer cord – at least 6 foot – would have been a lot nicer.

Using the camera is both easy and frustrating. There is a mobile app, but it’s really only to view the live feed and take snapshots on demand as you watch the live feed. For finer controls and adjustments you need to use a PC and the My D-Link site. That’s where things can be frustrating.

For example, on the settings page there is a clear section dedicated to email notifications with a checkbox. It is strongly implied that checking the checkbox will allow you to receive email notifications after you have set parameters for either motion detection or sound detection. However, after I set parameters for motion detection and then checked the box for email notifications, I did not receive any emails. After doing some searching via Google I found out that I needed to access the "advanced settings" and set up email there too. This was a far more complicated process and required more online research, but after a little bit of trial and error, I got the email notification working. You’ll need info such as the SMTP server address for your email client, the SMTP server port number, and two email addresses for yourself (one for the sender email; the other for the receiver email).

Why a product with such an easy install process has such a complicated usage setup (with much of the info needed not present on the D-Link site) is frustrating.

Once I got the email notification working, I could choose to have it send me an image at the moment of detection, or a set of 6 images (3 images just before detection and 3 images just after detection, at ½ or full second intervals). I can have it always on, or set it to detect only at certain periods of each day. So far I tried the 6 images option and have it always on, and that's worked out reasonably well.

Night vision and day vision seem to work well, with an acceptably clear picture. I have noticed that some times the view remains in night vision mode even when the room is sunny. Not sure why that is happening. Regardless, the picture remains clear.

It cannot record video captured since the camera does not have an SD card option.

You may need to play with the motion sensitivity adjustment and area of sensitivity to get something that works to your preference. I've found that sensitivity definitely needs to be adjusted higher for reliable night views, which means fiddling with the settings each day. While d-link allows you to adjust motion sensors on a day/night basis, it doesn't let you automatically set sensitivity for different times of the day, so that still has to be a manual task.

Although getting some features working is frustrating due to the lack of info on the D-link site, the overall ease of hardware installation, decent build quality, and good picture quality earn this 4 stars. If the D-Link site was improved this would be a five-star camera at this price point.

Overall, this is a decent monitor provided you’re not looking for a high-res PC monitor. I’m using it mainly in its TV mode and have been very impressed with the picture quality. The built-in tuner works well (with one exception, as noted below) producing a rich image. It’s also very well suited as an extension for a small screen device, such as a tablet. I’m using it with my Kindle Fire (via HDMI), and it provides for an excellent viewing experience.

Although the native resolution is 1366x768 pixels, the screen size of 24 inches is small enough that the lack of full HD is not missed. What I did miss is the lack of adjustability of the stand. There’s no tilt or swivel – the stand just holds the screen in a fixed position. It really interferes with proper positioning if this is used as a PC monitor, and is also a problem when using it as a TV. While I don’t expect a lot of extras at this price point, the lack of any measure of adjustability is a big oversight.

If you’re familiar with Samsung TVs, the menu system and remote will be straightforward. If you’re not familiar with Samsung TVs, the menu system will take a bit of time to master with all the nested menus. There are a number of short cuts for various picture modes (such as “sports mode” and “movie”) which are simple to select. Once you get more familiar with the options you can delve deeper and make more specific tweaks.

The sound quality is not great – pretty tinny sounding and there’s little bass. An external speaker is highly recommended if you want to get any measure of impressive sound out of this.

The TV tuner is easy to program with channel favorites. I’m using it with an over-the-air antenna, and have been pleased with the number of channels and the signal strength. There is, however, an annoying long lag between pressing the channel up/down button and having the channel lock in.

The remote is typical Samsung – lots of buttons that are all the same size. Workable, but nothing special.

Considering the price point, I find this to be a 4-star product. It would be a 5-star one with the current feature set and limitations if the price were $50 or $60 less; it would be 3-stars should the price go past $225. A worthwhile choice for TV or small screen mirroring provided you can live with the limited adjustability.

This is a relatively easy way to convert vinyl LPs to digital files. While the software (which is included) takes some time to master, and there are some build quality issues with the turntable, overall it’s a good performing system for the price.

The turntable is self-contained and includes two speakers. You can use this just as a turntable, with the sound coming from the built-in speakers. The audio quality is pretty decent, with the main limitation being that the volume can’t be turned up very much. It’s loud enough for general use, but if you want room-filling sound, you’ll need to hook the turntable up to a receiver via the jacks on the back of the turntable. Doing so greatly improves the sound quality, as you would expect.

The build quality of the turntable is decent but not exceptional. On the plus side, the case is pretty solid and looks attractive. The size is compact – it’s smaller than a full-sized LP. The cover is nicely designed so that you can lower it with a record playing since there are cut-outs that allow the record to stick through.

On the downside, the damping control is rather fussy and balky, and the arm is very lightweight. The stylus itself is OK – nothing special, but clearly not high-end either. The turntable automatically starts rotating when the arm is positioned off the holding stand. It can spin at 33/45/78 speeds, so it covers all the bases. Considering the price point, the build quality is OK. An audiophile would not be happy with this at all, but for general use it seems fine.

I found the included software rather challenging at first, mainly since I’ve never used such a system prior to this. It installed fine on a Win 7 machine, and had no problems interfacing with the turntable. The challenge was with all the options but, if you take it slowly (and don’t mind some trial and error experimentation) it gets the job done. The resulting files sounded better than I expected, especially given the poor quality of the source material (decades-old records that were not stored with a great deal of care).

It’s not a high-end device but for the price I think it’s a great value and a fun item to have if you want to convert your aging vinyl to digital. While the build quality issues bring this to 4.5 stars, I'll round up since, for the price, it offers a lot of functionality.

I was rather surprised when I got this with how small it is. I knew from the product description that it would be a little guy, but didn't have an appreciation for how small it was until I got it. It's a cube that is less than 1.5 inches on each side. Very compact, but it feels very solid and well-made.

Despite the compact size this is a solid performer. The video quality is quite clear and vivid provided you keep the cam steady. That's not easy to do if this is handheld given the small size, but it's designed to be mounted (there's a magnet in the base plus there are a variety of options available for mounting. Note that the mounts are sold separately).

The sound quality is good. Not spectacular, but reasonably clear and on a par with most cams I've used that have an internal mic.

Getting to the SD card is where the small size does cause a problem - it's not all that easy if you don't have nimble fingers (which I do not). You need to open the access door (which is sealed for water resistance) with a coin.

It doesn't have a lot of features which I find to be a plus since it greatly simplifies operation - the interface is a single button that turns it on/off, takes a still or starts/stops video recording. Can't get easier than that!

Minor quibbles aside, this is a solid performer and one that's well worth considering if you're looking for a very unobtrusive cam that's easy to operate (other than getting the SD card in and out). 4.5 stars rounded up to 5 due to the performance at this price point.

This is a decent set of macro extension tubes. The build quality is decent for the price – while the body is all-plastic, the bayonet mount rings are metal and make for a pretty secure attachment. There are three tubes – 13mm , 21mm and 31 mm – which can be used individually or in combination with one another.

I didn’t have any problems using these with a 5D Mark II and a variety of Canon lenses. Some did require a bit of finessing to get them to make a solid connection. Given the price, that’s not unexpected, but it still lowers my rating by a star.

It comes with a thin cloth storage bag that is rather baggy and cheap feeling. I fount it easier to just store the tubes in the box and toss the storage bag.

It’s not pro-quality gear but it’s an inexpensive way to add extension tubes to your setup to experiment with. If you find them to be something you’re going to use often you’ll want to step up to a better quality set, but for a starter set, these are pretty good.

I've tried some low-cost in-car cams and have been unimpressed with the build quality or video quality of the devices. The Thinkware 550 was a marked departure - it feels very well-built and solid. I'd rate the build quality up there with a decent conventional camcorder, such as a Sony. It also looks very attractive - they did a great job with the design.

This is not an "action cam" type of device for uploading videos of during stupid stuff onto Youtube (sorry, showing my age here - I probably would have done the same had cams been around in my youth). Rather, it's a cam for automatically documenting events that occur while driving (such as a crash or other incident) without any need for user action. Video files are time and date stamped, and assigned a location using GPS. It's more of a "black box" type recording device for a car rather than a "fun time" action cam with a car mount.

You can also use this while parked and with a rear camera, but both of those require additional items not included with this package (hard wire install for parking use; a separate camera for rear view use).

Installation is easy but also a little bit tricky. The mount is a plastic cradle with an adhesive backing. Once you determine where you want the cam mounted (up on the windshield is the recommended position) you peel off the backing on the adhesive pad and stick it to the windshield. It's a permanent mount (well, you can remove it from the glass, but it can't be reused). Easy to do, but tricky in that you really need to take some time before committing to a location and think through where the power cord needs to be routed.

The unit is lightweight (5.1 ounces without the cradle) and seems to be holding well to the windshield even over very bumpy terrain.. The manual suggests leaving the cam off the cradle until the adhesive has cured for 24 hours. I didn't see that tip until after I tested its holding ability over broken road. So if you miss that tip as well, it doesn't seem to be a problem.

The cam does not have a built-in battery. It must be powered by an included cigarette lighter adapter (known by "power ports" these days, but I still call them cigarette lighters). The adapter is very nicely made with a stout cord. That's good for longevity; not so good for routing it so the cord is not visible or in the way. There are some adhesive tabs included to lasso down the cable to help make for a neat (or semi-neat) install. I'll probably add some electrical tape to neaten up the install a bit more.

The manufacturer also cautions to make sure the power port you use gets shut off when you turn off the engine. The cam can continue to pull power if the power port is live, potentially draining your car's battery.

It automatically powers up when you start the car. It can be manually turned off (or back on) as well. It offers two recording modes: continuous (which is in one minute segments) or on-demand (you can manually start and stop). It also states that when there is an impact, the cam will store the 10 seconds before and the 10 seconds after in a secure memory folder. I'll have to take their word for that - can't really test that out! Under normal circumstances, when the micro SD card fills up it starts overwriting old files.

A micro SD card is included along with a reader. The card holds the user manual and the software, so it can't really be used to store video files. I used my own card reader rather than the one included since the included one was too tiny for my clumsy fingers to deal with.

There is no viewer on the cam - you have to take out the SD card and pull up the files using the included software. That for me is the biggest problem and limitation of this device. You have to trust that it's working since there's no confirmation other than the indicator lights and prompts. Nor can you set the camera specs unless you have access to a PC.

On the plus side, the lack of a screen means there's no risk of driver distraction while the cam is operating. I can't fault that. Still, I would have liked to see a design that has a screen that remains off until the camera is out of the mount so it can be used in-car to change settings or review stored video. That maintains the lack of driver distraction but still allows for better use of the cam while parked.

What makes up for a lot of these shortfalls is the video quality. Great - really great. Crisp, clear and sharp. It provides a panoramic view (the specs say 140 degrees) that easily covers the full view from the windshield. You really won't believe this is from a car cam. It dealt with head-on full sunlight pretty well, and did a decent job at night. I did get a fair amount of reflection off the windshield at night, but the video was very workable.

The included software installed fine on a Win 7 machine after I suspended Avast from running - this software does not want to work and play well with Avast. I even had to keep Avast suspended while running the software. Not tough to use - got the hang of it from just trying out menu options and playing around. It will ask to install an update right off the bat.

The video quality and overall "forget about it and it just records" type of operation are strong pluses. The power cord, mounting system, and lack of a view screen are problems. Weighing everything together gets me to a 3.5 star rating which I'll round up to 4 stars since the video quality is so nice. If you can live with the limitations, this is well worth considering.

These are very handy to have to minimize (or eliminate) cord tangles. The coil is tight and holds its shape well. When "at rest" (e,g., not stretched) the cable is about 26 inches end to end. You can get it to 12 feet if you stretch it out fully, but the coil strength is such that it will pull whatever it is attached to. If you need the full 12 foot length, it would be better to get a non-coiled cable.

The ends are well attached, and the wire sheath seems pretty durable. Zero complaints about quality -- no crackling even when I jostle the ends while they are plugged in.

A great way to add some positioning flexibility for attached speakers without having to deal with excess cable that gets tangled. Highly recommend.

This is a great set of cables. The build quality feels very solid -- well attached ends and the wire jacket is thick but still bendy and resistant to kinks.

I got two cables in two separate pouches. One has straight connectors on both ends; the other has one straight and one right angle connector. It would have been better to have both cables have one right angle connector since that's a great way to minimize how much the cable extends from the deice it's plugged into.

Other than that quibble, zero complaints. Work great without any static, and the build quality should be able to deal with the rough treatment my cables tend to get.

This is one of the more attractive mini bluetooth speakers I’ve come across. It’s more stylish than the typical mini cube design, with an attractive grill and a metal casing that feels good (plus hides fingerprints). There’s a red color insert under the grill and the black/red combo works well. There's a large non-slip insert on the base that works very well in keeping the speaker from moving around. It’s compact, measuring only about 3 inches long, 2 inches wide and 2 inches tall.

The controls are pretty intuitive. The vol up/down buttons can be hard to see since they are not raised buttons but are built into the case. Great for aesthetics; not so good in terms of practicality. All markings are black-on-black – again, great for how it looks, but not so good for clarity.

Pairing was simple and straightforward. The operating range is quite good, with zero dropouts at a 20+ foot range.

The sound quality is good, but not great. There’s ample bass – impressive, in fact, given the size of the speaker. However, the mid and upper ranges are rather muddy, making the overall sound quality just average. Given the price, I expected better sound quality than this. It’s not that it’s bad, it’s just not any better than cheaper bluetooth speakers I've used.

It only works in bluetooth mode – there is no 3.5mm jack for a direct connect. So, if you want to use this with a non-bluetooth device you’re out of luck.

It comes very nicely packaged, which is a plus in my book. It comes with a charge cable and a hand strap to help tote it around.

The looks and build quality merit 5 stars; the sound quality is only average at 3 stars. Overall rating of 4 stars. It’s a good choice if you value aesthetics and can live with average sound quality.
[Sample provided for review]

Overall, this is a decent full-size USB keyboard. The keys are nicely sized and have a medium length throw. There’s little tactile feedback, making the keys feel rather mushy. But, on the plus side, it’s 100% silent in use – no clicky sound of any type.

The layout is a standard QWERTY with a separate number key pad and F1 to F12 at the top. There’s also a separate pad for cursor up/down/right/left.

The back light is very nice and has the unique feature in that you can change the color. There are several to pick from including a “mixed” mode that has several colors making for a rainbow look. Color selection is easy via a dedicated key at the top of the keyboard. Just press it to cycle through the colors. The back light can also be set to off.

The build quality is decent. It’s all plastic and pretty lightweight, but durable enough for normal use. There’s a kick stand on the back that folds out to prop up the keyboard at a comfortable angle, and non-skid feet to hold it in place. I had no problems with this staying put even when banging away at full typing speed. There is some flex in the frame when typing with force, but nothing horrible.

There’s a small area for resting your palm, but it’s rather short to provide much (if any) ergonomic support.

It does not have any indicator lights such as for caps lock, num lock, etc.

Installation is simple on a Win machine -- just a plug-and-play with no drivers needed.

While the overall design is nice and I love the back light feature (plus the ability to change colors), the lack of tactile feel and the lack of status indicator lights drops my rating to 4 stars. Still well worth considering as a replacement full-size USB keyboard, especially if you’re looking for a 100% silent keyboard.
[Sample provided for review]

This is a more upscale version of the “pop up” speakers that have been around for a while. It adds some useful features including an SD card slot to play mp3 files directly and more advanced controls, such as a toggle switch for track skip and a mute button.

When compressed it’s very compact, measuring roughly 2.5 inches in diameter. While it can be played in its compact mode, the sound quality is not all that great – very tinny with little bass.

The sound quality improves significantly when it’s popped open. That increases the height to about 3.25 inches. That doesn't seem like much, but it makes a huge difference in sound quality. The bass is far more pronounced and, while the mid and upper ranges are still somewhat muddy, it’s far more pleasant to listen to than when it is folded up.

Given the size, I’d rate the sound quality as very good when it is in its pop-up mode. This is not a room-filling speaker but it sounds a whole lot better than the internal speakers in a tablet.

It is a direct-connect only speaker – it does NOT have bluetooth. It comes with a 3.5mm cord that is permanently attached to the base of the speaker. The cable can be stowed in a grove on the base of the speaker. The attached cable is a plus and a minus: you’ll never forget to bring a cable along, but the cord is only about 5 inches long, which made it backward to use on some of my equipment. I like that the cord is attached, but it really needs to be a bit longer.

The build quality feels pretty solid. It’s all plastic, as expected, but it has a nice feel to it. The bellows section in the middle feels like it is build solid enough to last a while. Plus, the fact that you can close it up easily for transport gives me some measure of assurance that it will survive being tossed around a bit. For the price, I’d rate the build quality as very good.

There are less expensive pop-up speakers available, such as the Xboom. I have one of those as well, and when comparing the two side-by-side I thought the sound quality was bit better on the Sonpre. The Sonpre also has more features than the Xboom (the mute button in particular is a welcome addition) and has longer battery life. So, while it is a few bucks more, it does bring some additional features to the table.

Although the short cord drops my rating by a star, this is definitely one to consider if you’re looking for a decent sounding pop-up speaker.
[Sample provided for review]

This was one of the easier RAID external drives I’ve set up. It’s not quite a plug-and-play operation, but pretty close.

The enclosure is metal and feels pretty solid. Unfortunately, the solid feeling does not extend to the ports (USB 3.0 and eSATA) and especially the power jack. There’s some wiggle to the ports which does not give me confidence that they are well-anchored to the point where they can survive any measure of rough treatment. Then again, plugging/unplugging the connection is not going to be something that’s a daily occurrence. So, while it’s concerning, it’s not a deal-killer.

The front cover (which you remove for drive insertion) is plastic and cheap feeling. It’s held in place with a single small screw. The drives (I’m using some old Seagates) fit fine into the bays.

The fan is reasonably quiet and runs intermittently. It seems to be able to move enough air to make a difference, but I can’t give temp readings on that to prove the point one way or another.

The indicator lights on the front are way too bright – the usual blinding by blue light that seems to be the trend these days. I want the feedback of an indicator light, but dial down the brightness, please!

It comes with cables for both eSATA and USB installs, which is nice, as well as three different power plug configurations for US and overseas power outlets. The latter seems to be a bit wasteful, but I guess it’s easier for the manufacturer to include all three rather than have three different product versions. The transformer is pretty compact and is inline, avoiding the dreaded wall wart at the end.

It offers RAID 0 and 1 options, plus a JBOD mode. Switching modes is easy, but requires two hands. With the unit powered down you select the RAID mode using a slider switch (which, like the ports, has a rather cheap feel), press the Set button, then power on.

No problems encountered in running this – works as it should. I did have some write errors but that was due to my drive acting up and not an issue with this device.

It’s simple and straightforward to use. While this is not the most rugged enclosure out there, it’s workable and earns 4 stars in my book.

This is a great idea: the combination of a USB 3.0 hub and a gigabit adapter. It's a perfect space-saving option -- the overall size is just a bit larger than my gigabit adapter and I get 3 USB 3.0 ports as a bonus!

The build quality is very good. It seems odd to use the word "stylish" to describe such a device, but this is quite stylish -- the case is black with a steel gray brushed top (which looks like metal, but I believe it is plastic). The case is sturdy and has tight seams, and the USB and RJ45 ports are well-anchored. The connection cable is short (about one foot long) but very stout with an well-made USB connector on the PC end.

Setup is quick and easy. The hub portion is a straight plus-and-play install on Win 7 (and, I would imagine, other Windows versions as well). The Ethernet adapter requires drivers, which are supplied on an included CD-ROM (which I'm pleased to report is a full-size CD rather than those mini ones which are such a pain to use).

The hub is passive (no external power) so there are limitations as to what it can support. I didn't have any problems using it with low power draws, such as thumb drives.

It comes with a brief, but well-written user guide.

Well-made, works great, and a easy, compact way to add two different functions to a laptop (or any other PC). Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]

This review covers two different models of the Arctic fan:

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>Model with USB hub:
I have been using the original ARCTIC Breeze for a while and have been very pleased with its performance, and especially pleased with how quiet it runs. The Pro model builds on that and adds a few more useful features.

Unlike the original model which had a bendable stem with a USB plug on the end, the Pro has a base so the fan can be positioned away from the USB port on the PC. The attached power cord is a little over 5 feet long, making it possible to put the fan on my desk and plug it into the PC on the floor.

The base also has 4 USB input ports, so it works as a USB hub. It has a 5V power input jack if you want to turn this into an active hub. The power adapter to do so is NOT included.

Unlike the single-speed original version, this has a knob so you can vary the speed. It's not precise, but there is a somewhat noticeable difference between low and high. It's a continually variable speed - you can turn the dial to whatever speed you like.

Best of all, it's just as quiet, if not quieter, than the original model. That's the biggest plus for me by far, since the cheap USB fans make a racket. This just makes a low-pitched hum. The build quality is solid - the base is sturdy, and the bendable arm holds its position well.

One negative: the packaging. It's in a clam shell package that is a major, major pain to open!

While it's more expensive than the original, the added benefits of being able to position it on a desk and use it as a hub makes the upgrade worth considering. Highly recommend.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>USA EDITION:
I've have (and use) a couple other Arctic USB fans and have been 100% satisfied with them. This new version (their "USA Edition") has a couple of improvements over past designs.

The base is a metal plate which increases the fan's stability when you're bending the stem to point the fan. The on/off/speed dial switch no longer has a lit LED ring around it. I never found the lit LED ring to be bothersome on the other Arctic fans, so having or not having it is not a big deal to me.

The base also does away with the USB hub connections that other models have. That's keeps the base more streamlined and allows it to have a lower profile. It also does away with the clam shell packaging, instead using a very easy to open box.

The build quality of this, like the other Arctic fans I have, is excellent. The stem is bendy by stays put where you want it; the operating sound is pretty hushed; the on/off/speed control works well. The overall design is attractive, with a red/white/blue color scheme and graphics.

It moves a surprising amount of air. No, it won't blow your hair back as a Vornado fan will, but this makes a noticeable difference in circulating air. The size makes it very easy to find a spot on your desk to position it.

While I can't speak to the long-term reliability of this as of yet, I expect it will last for some time. I have an Arctic fan similar to this that I've been using almost daily for the past 1+ years, and it still works as good as it did when new.

Looks good, works well, and easy to use. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]

This is a well-designed outdoor speaker. It looks far better than I expected given the price point. Nicely molded plastics with perfect seams. I’m especially fond of the way they put bumpers on both the top and the bottom, so you can flip it over and still have non-skid feet on the bottom.

It has a novel design feature in that there’s a large slot through the speaker through which there’s a lanyard (which is included). Great feature for ease of carrying this around.

The sound quality is pretty good. It’s a bit muted sounding, but the bass response is excellent – better than expected given the small size.

The controls are all on the same end, and consist of an on/off button, a micro USB input for charging, and a 3.5mm input jack for direct connects. The ports are covered by a rubber flap that is sturdy and well-anchored to avoid it getting lost.

I had no problems pairing this with a couple of tablets and a phone. The bluetooth range is very good, with zero dropouts at about 25 feet. As expected, the direct connect option worked perfectly.

The only negative is that it lacks volume control. But that also eliminates a set of buttons on the speaker, and thus eliminates a potential point of water entry.

I think this is an excellent value for the price point. Solid construction, very respectable sound quality, and an innovative design that makes it easy to take along. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]

This is a really novel design for an otherwise typical product: a bluetooth speaker that floats!

The casing appears to be very well made with tight seams. A lot of attention was paid to ensure it can be used in the water: the battery compartment has a threaded cap with a water-tight seal, and all the buttons are molded into the casing to prevent any water intrusion. The only place water can get in is through the speaker grill on top. That’s not a problem, however, since the grill pops off (no tools needed) so you can drain the water out.

The styling is very nice. I have it in white/orange, and it looks like a mini beach ball. Very attractive. I also like that the button labeling is clear and easy to read -- in addition to being molded into the button, labels are placed on the housing.

It uses 6 AA batteries (not included). The batteries are the only area where I had some difficulty. The compartment is wide enough for 3 batteries, so you need to stack the batteries on top of each other. That can be a bit challenging, but not a significant downside. It would have been wonderful if this used a lithium battery that could be removed for recharging instead of having to deal with 6 AA size batteries.

The speaker paired very easily with a Samsung phone, a Nexus 7 and a Kindle Fire. Zero problems with any device.

The sound quality is impressive – solid bass, and very ample volume. It’s not audiophile-level (nor was that expected at this price point) but I’d rate the sound quality as excellent for a mid-range priced outdoor bluetooth speaker.

Operation distance is also excellent. I had no problems at all maintaining a solid connection at 20+ feet from the source device. It also worked fine with the source device indoors and the speaker outdoors.

Other than the minor issue with the battery compartment, I’m very impressed with this speaker and give it a solid 5 stars. Highly, highly recommend!
[Sample provided for review]

This is a speaker that you can't help but call cute! It's styled much like a toy, but I mean that in a good way - bright color (I have the orange, which looks great) with a chunky top handle and base. It's a nice change from the usual black/grey boxes that all look the same.

It offers the ability to be used in bluetooth mode and directly connected to a device via a 3.5mm cable. Both options work very well. No problems pairing it (tried it with a couple of tablets and a Samsung phone), and (as expected) no problems using it as a direct connect. I found the bluetooth range to be excellent - had no problems using the speaker outdoors while the tablet was in the house about 15 feet away.

The manufacturer says the case is watertight and it certainly appears that's the case. Very tight seams throughout, and all the ports have a plastic flap that keeps them protected from the elements.

The front panel controls for volume, power, etc. are large and have a positive click. The lettering on the buttons, however, is grey on grey, so it can be hard to see in low light. But, since there are only 4 buttons, it's pretty easy to figure out which one to press even if you can't see the label.

It runs either on batteries (not included) or using a 5v transformer (included). It takes a lot of batteries to power this - 8 AA's. The battery compartment is hinged so a screwdriver is not needed when you need to pop it open for a battery swap.

The sound quality is very good. It's a single small speaker, so it does have limitations, but I found the quality to be better than average compared with similar single speaker systems. The bass response is excellent, especially when the speaker is placed on a table so the tabletop can help serve as a resonating platform. The mid range and treble are a bit weak and muddy sounding (especially at higher volumes) but again, for a single small speaker, I'd rate the sound quality as very good.

Misses for me are the fact that it does not have an internal rechargeable battery pack. I'd expect to see that at this price point. While it does come with a wall adapter, the fact that it is waterproof means many people will be using it outside where an outlet may not be handy. The 8AA batteries it needs means that you're carrying around a lot of batteries to do a swap.

I'd also would have liked to see some type of a grill over the speaker, again since this is most likely going to see a lot of outdoor use and could get knocked around a bit. As it is, the speaker is fully exposed, so a hit to the speaker face will do some damage.

Given the price point, those two negatives knock this down a star. Still well worth considering, however - great looks, solid build quality that will withstand the elements, and a nice sound.
[Sample provided for review]

This is a really nice looking mini speaker that is styled after a guitar amp. It allows you to connect any portable device that has a 3.5mm connection. I used it with a couple of different tablets (Fire, Nexus and iPad) with great results.

The build quality is impressive for the price. It’s mostly plastic, but feels very solid. The plastic has a leather-like pattern imprinted into it, again keeping with the overall amp theme. There are non-slip pads on the base that grip well on a tabletop.

I love how easy the controls are to use! No fumbling around with mini buttons – nice big old- style knobs you turn. The settings are marked 1 to 10 (sorry, no going to 11).

The sound quality is pretty good. It’s somewhat tinny and gets harsh at loud volume, but for normal listening it puts out a more than acceptable sound. The bass and treble controls make a noticeable impact on the sound – more so than I expected given the price.

There’s a cutout on the top to hold a phone. This is not an active dock – all devices are attached using a 3.5mm cord. The cutout is just that – a simple cutout that holds the phone.

It can be powered by 4 AA batteries (not included), a wall adapter (included) or a USB cable (included). I use it mainly with the wall adapter, but it’s nice that it can be made fully portable with standard batteries.

Misses are mostly minor. The battery door is held on with screws, so you need to have a screwdriver if you want to swap out the AA batteries. Also, the flap covering the “dock” port on the top is on the flimsy side.

This is something that you get more for the look rather than the sound quality (although the sound quality is pretty good as well). It’s one of the more novel looking small speakers I’ve seen, and well worth a 5 star rating.
[Sample provided for review]

I’m really impressed with these earphones. Usually with mid-priced earphones you have to qualify the sound with the phrase “for the price.” Not with these – they put out sound that rivals earbuds I have that cost 3 to 4 times more.

The clarity is spot-on. Nice crisp treble and midrange, but not at the expense of a goodly amount of bass. Not skull-shaking bass, but clean, non-boomy bass that rounds out the sound perfectly.

The overall build quality is excellent. It does have a potentially polarizing feature: a flat cable. Personally, I really like the flat cable. The style is helpful in keeping the earbuds in place (since these are over-the-ear style buds) and helps keep cord tangles to a minimum. There’s also a small slider on the cable yoke that can be adjusted to keep them secure when wearing them while in motion. However, others who have borrowed these from me were not as enthused about the flat cable. No one hated it, but the reaction was occasionally on the lukewarm side.

Wearing comfort is another point where these excel. Lightweight, nice ear canal feel, and solid sound isolation. It comes with a variety of tips to ensure a good fit for pretty much anyone. I’d suggest trying a variety of sizes since bass response and sound isolation are affected by how well these fit in your ears.

Also included is a nicely styled case that holds the earbuds plus the accessory tips. It’s well-made, attractive and designed for actual use, with small mesh pockets to hold things in place.

The 3.5mm plug is angled to make it easy to use plus stay out of the way better than the conventional straight type plug when using it on a small mp3 player.

Try as I might, I can’t come up with a single negative about these. Built well, sounds great, and thoughtful design touches throughout. Collectively, that makes these one of the best values in earbuds I’ve run across so far, and I would highly recommend them.
[Sample provided for review]

This is one of those earphones where nearly every piece of praise has to be qualified with “for the price.” But that’s not a bad thing. I like and appreciate high-end earphones but I won’t take a pricey set with me to the gym since there’s a good chance it will get broken or lost. At the same time, I don’t want to listen to the rough sound that the $10 or so buds produce.

This is a great compromise. They sound far better than you would expect give the price but they are no so pricey that it would be a tragedy if they get dropped and mashed by a treadmill (which has happened to me), dropped in the pool (also happened to me) or left behind/stolen (fortunately, not happened to me as of yet).

The build quality is pretty good for the price. The cables are on the thin side, but well-anchored. The 3.5mm plug is angled which makes it easier to plug in, and also keeps it from sticking out too much on an mp3 player. It does not come with a case or any extras other than a set of various sizes of tips.

Comfort is a feature that does not have to be qualified by price – these fit very well and are so lightweight that I don’t even notice that they are on. The set includes a variety of tips to customize the fit to your ear. Since bass response is partially dependent on a good ear fit, you’ll want to experiment with the various sizes of tips to see which offer the best feel and bass response.

The sound clarity is quite good at low to mid volumes. They get rather harsh at louder volumes – these are not earbuds that like to get pushed much beyond a middle of the road volume setting. But while they are in their comfort zone in terms of volume, the sound is clear. The bass response won't shake your skull, but it's decent. Sound isolation is also pretty good.

These won’t thrill you with superlative sound, elegant design or impressive looks, but their performance and build quality are impressive for the price point, and much better than the typical low-end earbuds. Well worth considering if you’re looking for an inexpensive pair of earphones.
[Sample provided for review]

I’m very pleased with the quality of this case. It looks nice and is well-built with tight, even stitching throughout. The case material is listed as leather, and both looks and feels nice.

The frame of the case doesn’t interfere with swipe motions (the Nexus 7 has two top frame swipes that call up different menu panels). All cutouts to access ports and buttons are properly positioned.

There are a series of holes on the back of the case for the Nexus' speakers, and the sound playback is decent – I didn’t notice any unwanted muffling. The magnetic front flap stays closed, and turns the tablet on automatically when you open the case.

It did take me a moment or two of fiddling to figure out how the case doubles as a stand. An infographic about that on the case packaging would have been nice (had to go back to the product listing for some guidance). The stand feature works, and allows you to prop the tablet at three different angles.

The table frame insert can also be completely detached to allow you to move the Nexus into portrait view when using the case as a stand.

The only miss is that I would have liked to have one of those stretchy elastic bands on the back so I could slip my hand through when holding it. But overall, I found this to be a good case and a good value for its price point.
[Sample provided for review]

This is one of the better sounding shower radios I’ve used. Although it’s pretty compact (roughly 3.5 inches square and 1.5 inch thick) the sound quality is pretty impressive given the constraints of a single rear-facing speaker. The volume can be raised to a point where it can be easily heard over the sound of running water.

The overall look is nice. The build quality appears solid, and the colors look nice (a baby blue dial, with the majority of the radio being white). It uses 2 AA batteries which are not included.

Reception was decent. It has an internal antenna, so how the radio is positioned is critical to pulling in the station you want to pull in. It can be hung from a hook or the shower head using the included loop, or it can stand up on a shelf or tub edge.

The big negative is tuning. It uses a rotary dial to set the station. It’s not very precise – it’s very easy to overshoot or undershoot the desired station. Once you tune it to the station you want it stays put, but getting there can be a challenge.

This is a decent choice if you’re looking for a low-cost shower radio and tend to listen to the same station all the time. However, if you like to change stations frequently, the tuning can be a bit frustrating.
[Sample provided for review]

I use earbuds a lot since I typically prefer the lightness and ease of use compared with traditional headphones. Right out of the box these were a bit puzzling as to how to position them for use. But, after a bit of fiddling with the over-the-ear loop, it becomes clear.

The in-ear comfort is good. It comes with a variety of ear tips including two types I’ve not used before: a double flange silicon tip and a triple flange silicon tip. The flanges allow the ear bud to make a much better seal in your ear canal. That not only helps cut out ambient noise intruding, it also improves the bass response. I found the double flange works best for me, but the variety of tips included appears sufficient to fit pretty much any ear.

It also comes with an excellent case for storage, and adapters for airplane use and for 1/4 inch plugs. I especially like the case since it’s small enough to make it easy to carry along (roughly 3.5 inches by 3 by 1.5 inches thick) and is reinforced to avoid being crushed. It has mesh pockets to keep everything stowed, and looks nice to boot (black with red contrast in the middle). All-in-all, it’s a great kit in terms of useful accessories.

I’m not as pleased with the cord. While I like how sturdy it is, it has a “Y” link that always seems to be in the way when I’m working out. I got used to it eventually, but a more streamlined cord system would have been a better design approach. Another negative is the 3.5mm plug. It needs to be seated just so or you get sound cut-outs or static. I tried it with several devices to be sure the issue is with the plug and not the device. A more robust plug is needed for this – you shouldn’t have to fiddle with it to get it to seat properly.

The over-the-ear loops are also a bit annoying at first. Granted, that’s certainly due to the fact that I usually use standard in-ear buds without the loop, so any type of loop feels weird to me at first. The material is soft and bendy, so you can position it in any variety of ways. It could benefit from some additional padding. On the plus side, they do hold the buds in very well. Quick head movements that would have loosened an in-ear bud didn’t jar these loose at all.

Now for the really important feature: how they sound. In a word, excellent. My benchmark for moderately-priced earbuds has been units made by RHA out of the UK. These sound nearly as good. Very clean sound but still ample bass provided that you select the right tip. For me, the standard tip (the one installed as delivered) gave me very little in terms of bass. Selecting a different tip to provide a better ear fit did wonders for bass response.

They are a bit more airy than the RHA sound. That could be a plus or a minus depending on your preferred type of music. Very heavy bass music is not a good match for these. Pretty much everything else is, and I appreciated the enhanced clarity. It’s the type of sound that, when you hear it, the first word that would come to mind is “clean.”

They look odd, make take you a moment to figure out how to position them, but provide a very open, natural sound. It comes with a well-designed kit of useful extras. However, the plug issues, the cord, and the ear loops collectively knock it down a star. Still well worth considering, however, and I would certainly recommend them.
[Sample provided for review]

This is proving to be a very nice update to the original Nexus 7. I had no problems transferring over my apps and information that I had on my original Nexus. My only quibble about the process was that it didn't duplicate the way I had arranged certain groups of apps on the screen, so I had to spend some time to recreate that.

The speakers are still located in the rear of the tablet, but are more powerful. Not a night and day difference, but audio plays clearer and louder. Still, to really enjoy a movie, you need to get an external speaker (either hardwired or bluetooth).

The overall speed is improved, including browser performance (which was already quite good on the Nexus). Other improvements include better screen resolution. It’s also slightly smaller and notable lighter. Collectively, these improvements are, for me, worth the price to upgrade.

This is a well-made all-purpose tablet. While I very much enjoy my Kindle Fires as well, the Nexus does not disappoint.

Note: be sure to update to android 4.4 when you get it. Very easy to do, and worth the time.

The key word throughout this review will be “impressive.” Apologies if you get tired of hearing it, but these are some impressive headphones.

They come packaged in a very well-made hard-shell carry case. I can tell that someone was thinking of the little things when these were designed, since the small pouch that holds the cords has velcro on it so it can be affixed anywhere in the case. It may sound silly to point out such a minor detail, but I’ve found that when so much thought goes into the little things, the actual product is going to be outstanding.

Comfort is wonderful. The ear pads are nicely plush and molded themselves around my ears. That not only adds to comfort, but it totally shuts out ambient sounds. Dead silence when the headphones are on.

There is a downside to such nicely-fitting foam: heat build up. These do contribute to “hot ear” and I found I needed to take them off now and again to let things breathe a bit. I think that’s a very small price to pay for overall comfort and sound isolation.

The headband is also padded with what seems to be the same material in the earcups. Very comfortable even for those of us with, how shall I say, rather sparse growth in the hair department. The earcups have the usual up/down adjustments. But, unlike other full-size headphones I have, these fold up so they can be stowed neatly in the case.

The overall design is clean and generally attractive. The metal machining is not as outstanding as it is on high-end headphones, but it is far better than I expected given the price.

The headset uses a detachable cable, and it comes with a nice variety: a 1.2 meter (about 4 foot) flat cable, a 3 meter (about 10 foot) flat cable and a 1.2 meter round cable that has a mic and remote for smart phones. All the cables are well-made, with solidly attached connectors.

I did notice one quirk: the flat cables won’t work with my original Kindle Fire. They work with everything else I tried them with, but only the round cable worked with the Fire.

Now, as to sound quality. Hate to use that word again, but I’ll have to say impressive. Strong bass without any muddiness or booming, clear and crisp mid and upper ranges. Just a treat to use. I listened to a wide range of offerings including Stanley Clark (the twang of the bass strings was just a joy to hear so clearly that I couldn’t help but to play it over and over), bass-heavy rock, classical music, and movie/TV dialog on devices ranging from a cheap mp3 player, to tablets (Fire, Nexus) to a Denon receiver. In every case the headphones never failed to delight.

I have headphones from Sennheiser and Shure that cost 3 and 4 times as much as these, but offer only sightly better sound quality. As such, these are one of the best values in a closed back headphone I’ve come across as of yet, and I would recommend them highly.
[Sample provided for review]

Overall, these are a decent pair of bluetooth earphones. The build quality is good for the price, with sturdy arms that fold so the headphones can be stowed easily in a carry case (or pocket). The ear padding is on the thin side, but there's enough to maintain comfort for a reasonable amount of wear time.

The sound quality is more than decent for the price. They won't stun you with huge bass and crisp mid and upper ranges, but for general all-purpose listening (e.g., music, movies, etc.) they get the job done well.

It paired easily with a Fire and a Nexus. The operating range is quite good - I had no problems maintaining a connection from the opposite side of a large room (about 20 or so feet).

Misses center on two issues: controls and the case. The controls are small and unobtrusive, which is nice from an aesthetic standpoint - the headset casing looks sleek. However, in actual usage, it can be hard to find the proper button by touch alone. Some type of tactile cue would have been nice to ensure you get to the right button each and every time.

I also think the case could have been better. While it's stylish (sort of a triangular shape) with a crease in the cover that adds visual interest, there's no mesh or straps on the inside to hold the headphones and/or cables. The end result is that while the case looks nicer than others I've used, it's not as practical or functional. I find that to be a significant issue since I use these type of headphones away from home (e.g., at the gym, while exercising, etc.) and the carry case gets used a lot.

Given that these are priced the same or a bit higher than other similar bluetooth headsets, these misses warrant dropping the rating by one star. However, they remain a good choice if you're looking for a generally inexpensive set of headphones - they sound pretty good, seems to be well-made, and have a good operating range.
[Sample provided for review]

Summary: This is an impressive performing flash given the price. It doesn't hit the mark set by the Canon Speedlite line of flashes, but it also doesn't hit the price tag of Canon gear either. It's a good choice for a starter flash for those on a budget or if you don't have demanding and exacting requirements for a flash. Also cross shop this with the Neewer 660. While the latter lacks a few of the 680's features, I found it easier and simpler to use.

Full review: In many regards this flash is similar to the Neewer model 660, which I also reviewed. This adds some useful features, such as multi-flash, stroboscopic flash, second curtain flash, high speed synch and flash exposure lock. It also has an autofocus assist beam with a range of 2.3 to 20 feet. The downside is that the controls are more complicated to use than the 660. Although the 680 has an LCD which normally would make usage easier, I found the controls on the 660 to be more straightforward. Granted, this complexity is also a factor of the additional features of the 680.
