Like the 660, it is noticeably larger than the Canon Speedlite, but not heavier. The larger size may cause issues when used on smaller cameras (e.g., could topple over). No problems on any camera with some heft to it.

The build quality is the same as the 660, which is pretty solid. The head articulation/adjustments also work well with generally smooth action and positive clicks. The construction is nearly all plastic, but the hotshoe is metal. Considering the price, I have zero complaints about build quality.

Again, like the 660, it comes well packed for protection in transit, and has a cloth bag for further protection against scratches while being tossed about by UPS. Sounds like a minor issue, but I think it's important to note since I buy most of my gear online, so security in transit is an important factor.

I successfully used it with the following Canons with zero compatibility issues:

Rebel XT (original model)
40D
5D (first gen)
5D Mark II
Powershot G10

Like the 660, it does NOT offer a wireless mode. Off-camera usage requires a pc sync cord to tether it to the camera to the flash. However, unlike the 660, I could not use it as a slave flash with the Speedlite transmitter.

Of the two, I'd recommend the 660 over this model as a starter flash given the greater ease of use of the 660. You'll lose a few features that the 680 has, but the gains in usage ease offset the losses. But either are good choices for a starter flash to build experience without breaking the bank, and I found both to be 5-star products.
[Sample provided for review]

Bottom line: While the features and build quality of this flash are not suitable for pro (or "prosumer" use) this provides quite good performance for the price, and is well worth considering for casual photography needs.

Full review: I've spent a lot on Canon gear over the years and have never been disappointed with the performance or quality of pretty much anything with their logo on it. This Neewer 660 flash, while not up to the standards of a Canon Speedlite, provides pretty good performance at a great price point.

The overall build quality is better than I expected. It feels pretty solid, and the head articulation/adjustments also work well with generally smooth action and positive clicks. The construction is nearly all plastic, but the hotshoe is metal. The only part that felt somewhat "cheap" was the locking ring above the hotshoe. Works just fine, but it would have been great to have that be made of metal, or at least some sturdier plastic. But considering the price, zero complaints about build quality.

I also don't have any complaints about the packaging. Yes, that's often a minor issue, but given that I get 95% of my gear shipped to me, it's something I pay attention to. This comes well-housed with cardboard protection plus is wrapped in a velvet-like pouch to guard against scratches. Not as robust packaging as Canon, but effective. The included manual, while brief, is well written and actually readable (a rarity these days with low-cost electronics!).

It is noticeably larger than the Canon Speedlite, but not heavier. The larger size may cause issues when used on smaller cameras (e.g., could topple over). No problems on any camera with some heft to it.

I successfully used it with the following Canons with zero compatibility issues:

Rebel XT (original model)
40D
5D (first gen)
5D Mark II
Powershot G10

The display screen is easy to use, and the buttons are intuitive. For example, a quick hit of the plus or minus button adds/cuts the strength of the flash. There's a zoom mode for accommodating differing focal lengths which is also easily adjustable on the fly by a button press.

Adjustments include 90 degree vertical rotation, and 270 degree horizontal rotation. As noted above, the rotation action is pretty smooth, and the adjustment clicks are easily felt. It includes an off-camera stand and built-in diffuser and reflector cards.

It does NOT offer a wireless mode. Off-camera usage requires a pc sync cord to connect the camera to the flash.

It is compatible with the Canon Speedlite ST-E2 transmitter. I used the transmitter on a 5DMarkII, and the flash fired just fine.

While I'm not going to be tossing my Speedlites anytime soon, this provides good functionality and build quality at an impressive price, and I would not hesitate to recommend it as a starter flash, or a flash for anyone on a tight budget. Five stars.
[Sample provided for review]

I've tried a couple of the USB fans and have found them to be loud, ineffective at moving air, or unwilling to hold a set position (and sometimes all three at the same time). This fan, however, actually works. And it works very well!

The build quality is impressive given the price. The gooseneck stalk is sturdy, and holds the fan in the position set without drooping or creeping down over time. The noise output is minor - you can hear it, but the sound is very muted and not at all objectionable.

What really impressed me is the amount of air this moves. It actually moves enough air to make a difference, which is something that is not often seen in a USB personal fan. Great for the office, but also an effective cooling fan when exercising on something such as a treadmill.

I'm using this by powering it with a powerbank. Very little battery drain in use - I left it running overnight attached to a small powerbank (8400mAh) and the power indicator on the powerbank showed it was still at the 75% level.

Best USB fan I've used bar none - highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]

I've used several compact speakers over the years and they all were decent performers. Nothing to compare, however, with my favorite desktop speakers, the Bose Companion 20. While this speaker doesn't hit that mark either, it is absolutely, hands-down the best compact mono speaker I've used.

It's tiny. And I mean TINY - just a bit over 2 inches in height, width and depth. As per the name, it's a cube. About as unobtrusive as you can get.

The build quality is excellent. It feels solid and well-made. It also comes very attractively packaged in a clear, thick plastic box. While I would normally scold a company for what could appear to be wasteful packaging, in this case the packaging is useful: one of my primary uses for this speaker is as a take-along for my laptop, and the plastic case makes for excellent protection against the bangs and dings suffered by my laptop bag. So, in addition to making it look upscale, the packaging has an actual use down the road.

Setup is simple - plug and go. It has three outputs - 3.5mm cord for something such as a tablet, a USB port for a computer, and a 3.5mm cord for headphones. Covers all the bases as to potential uses.

I did most of my testing and playing with this attached to my laptop. Outstanding sound quality that is crisp, clear but still has decent bass. I used it mainly for listening to podcasts and webinars (some of them actually work related!) and the sound quality was miles beyond what I was getting from my laptop speaker, and significantly better than the lower-end portable speakers I was using.

Now, the Cube doesn't sound as good as the Bose Companion 20. That didn't come as a surprise since the entire speaker is about the same size as just the power converter for the Bose. The size of the Bose make them non-transportable; the Cube is a very easy device to take along with a laptop.

It does not have a volume control. I don't miss it when using it with my PC since it's easier to fiddle with the sound level from the PC rather than have to use the speaker. I can see that as a negative, however, for other uses. On the other hand, a volume control device, be it a knob, wheel or button, would detract from the clean, simple design lines of the Cube. So, an equitable trade-off in my opinion.

This is one of those products that I really can't come up with a single negative other than the fact that it is pricy. But, if you value good quality sound but have to keep the speaker as small as possible, it is worth the cost. This is about the same size as the small take-along speakers that run in the $20 range, but provides sound quality that is miles beyond what they offer. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]

This is a really nice laptop desk. The first thing that caught my eye was the construction quality. The table is metal and solid - no flexing at all, and built to take a pretty good pounding. The top has a "dimpled" finish that is stamped into the metal, so it's not something that will wear or fall off, like those stick-on pads.

It comes with a small side panel that can be hooked onto either side to use a mouse, trackball or other such device. It is also metal and very sturdy. It also has an adjustment knob so the extension can be tilted.

The desktop is about 16.5 inches wide and 11 inches deep (not including the extension, which is about 6.5 by 6 inches). It's a nice size for even a large laptop.

But what really sets this apart is the legs and how easy they are to configure. There are push-in buttons at the leg joints that allow the legs to be folded as needed. They click into place securely - no matter how much I jostled the table, the legs stayed firmly positioned where I put them.

On the downside, the legs are plastic. They are sturdy, but metal legs would have been wonderful.

The top has a raised lip on one side which is nice for holding the laptop if the table top is inclined. It also has a built-in dual fan to keep the heat down from the laptop. It runs off a USB port (cable is included). Unfortunately, it does not use a standard micro or mini USB input port on the fan but rather a pin-style port. This means you'll have to be sure to take the included cable along since you won't be able to make do with a standard USB cable.

The fans run very quietly. I didn't find the noise at all bothersome or even really noticeable. My laptop fan is actually louder than the desk fans.

Very pleased with this desk - very handy addition that has ample adjustability to keep my laptop positioned for easy use, and solid build quality to last for some time. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]

I've been using an Altec Lansing iM227 (a model that is no longer produced by Altec Lansing, but comparable models are still offered) for a couple of years and have been very pleased with it. The Xboom, however, gives me much the same performance at half the size.

The sound quality of the Xboom is impressive for the size. It puts out nearly the same bass level as the iM227, which is surprising given how small it is. It does suffer a bit in the mid and upper ranges, which do not come through as clearly and sharply as the iM227. But the output is more than adequate for enjoyment.

I really like how the two halves of the speaker can be closed up and turned into a small ball that is only about 2 inches tall. Very compact so it easily fits into a bag or jacket pocket - this speaker is designed to be carried around easily. It comes with a decent cloth pouch plus a USB charge cable.

While it will work when it is in its compact mode, for best sound it needs to be unlatched so it expands to about 3 inches tall.

Unlike the iM227 it has an internal battery (the iM227 runs on 3 AAA batteries). That's both good and bad: good for ease of use and compact size; bad in case the internal battery fails, which renders the speaker useless. The Xboom has a stated run time of "up to 12 hours" according to the specs, which is pretty accurate - I got about 10 hours out of a fresh battery. Recharge time is about 2 hours.

Operation is very simple: plug in the attached cable to your device (I'm using it as a speaker for a small mp3 player), turn it on, and listen. The Xboom has a volume control, which the iM227 lacks, and an on/off switch. There's a power indicator light on the bottom of the speaker.

Unlike the iM227, the Xboom can be daisy-chained to other Xbooms for a bigger sound. I only have one, so I can't say how well that works, but it's a nice feature.

Complaints are virtually nil. If I had to come up with something, I'd say that it would be nice to have the power indicator light on the top rather than the bottom so it would be more easily visible as a reminder to power down and save battery life. Minor point, however.

While the sound quality of the Altec Lansing is better, the size and convenience of the Xboom makes it the one I'll take along with me and use more often. Very good value for the price, and I would highly recommend it.
[Sample provided for review]

A power inverter for your car is a very handy device to have. It plugs into the car's power outlet (which I still call the cigarette lighter) and gives you the ability to plug in an AC powered item. There are limitations, of course - you're not going to be able to plug in your refrigerator, but for low power demand items, it can be very helpful for power when you're traveling or for when the lights go out at home.

I'm very pleased with the Sabrent. It offers a decent amount of power - 300 watts - which makes it far more useful for the things I'd like to use it for than the lower powered inverters. However, the larger capacity comes with a larger size. The unit is about 3 inches wide, 5 inches long, and 1.5 inches thick. It weighs a hefty one pound. Not a small and inconspicuous device by any means.

All the controls and ports are located on one end, which makes it easier to deal with the large size. There's an on/off rocker switch. I wish it had a more solid "click" to it - it has a rather soft touch, so it can be inadvertently switched on/off when moving it if you grab it the wrong way. It has a single 3-prong female outlet to power an AC device, and 2 USB outlets. The USB outlets are a nice addition, since it can be used to charge phones, tablets, etc. without having to unplug the inverter and plug in a conventional car USB adapter.

The housing is plastic but appears pretty sturdy. The plug that goes into the cigarette lighter is decent. Works fine, but feels a little on the flimsy side compared with the overall unit. The cord could also be a bit thicker for greater durability or, ideally, coiled so it does not get tangled. But quite workable as-is and MUCH easier to deal with than an inverter that does not have a cord and plugs directly into the car power outlet.

Performance is very good. I had no problems running a 60 watt cooler using the inverter. Power delivery seemed fine and steady. I don't have test equipment to measure the power quality, but the cooler ran at a steady pace.

The inverter does get pretty warm in use, and has an internal fan that kicks on to keep things cool. The fan can be heard, but the sound is not what I'd consider to be noisy.

It's important to know the power demand of whatever you're plugging in, plus keep in mind that some devices, such as coolers, have an initial surge demand. For example, a 60watt cooler may use 60 watts when running, but will pull 100+ watts when it starts up. If you try to run something that attempts to pull more than the inverter can supply, the inverter will shut down for safety (both for itself and the item attached). According to the specs, this can handle a surge of 350 watts, but I'll keep any surge loads I put on it at not more than 300 watts to be safe.

Although 300 watts won't go far, this is a handy item to keep on hand not only for power on the road, but also to serve as a power source (albeit limited) when the household power goes out. While there are some faults with the unit, overall it is a good performer and a decent value for the price. 4.5 stars rounded to 5.
[Sample provided for review]

While I'm quite comfortable using an SLR, I've not been all that handy with a camcorder in the past. It's been a few years since I used one, so I was curious to see if user-friendliness has kept pace with technological advancements.

With this model it has. I found it very easy to use right out of the box with just some minor trial and error. I did end up reading the manual (which is pretty decent) but the main functions were pretty self apparent by just fiddling around with it a bit. The menu structure is logical and well presented; the screen is clear and easy to view.

The overall build quality is excellent. It feels more substantial in hand than I expected at this price point while retaining a very lightweight and easy to carry profile. I like the button placement - feels very natural in hand.

I love having the internal memory for storage as well as the little touches, such as a built-in USB connector. These features help make this a grab-and-go type of device, which increases the likelihood and ease of bringing it along and capturing video. (Note: you can also use a plug-in memory card should you want to.)

The video quality in good light/outdoors is excellent - very sharp and clear. Low-light performance is a somewhat grainy but quite decent. Stills are pretty decent. It won't put an SLR to shame, but it's more than good enough for casual snapshots. The internal mic works well and is more immune to wind noise than I expected.

My only significant disappointment with the cam is the projector. Wonderful idea, but the actual performance is lackluster. The projected video is hard to see clearly if there's any appreciable amount of light in the room. The 100 inch projection spec is wildly optimistic if you expect to actually see what is being projected.

Given that this cam does everything else so well, is so easy to use, and a breeze to tote along, I won't detract any stars due to the shortcomings of the projector feature. This is a great cam for the novice cam user (such as myself) or even an intermediate user. However, if the projection feature is a primary need, this may not be a good cam for your needs.

I'm really impressed with this bluetooth receiver. Unlike another brand I tried, this offers outstanding sound quality, which is my main reason for using it.

It's very straightforward to set up. Just plug in the receiver (it's very small - less bulky than most "wall warts" that are present on power plugs), pair it with your bluetooth source, and plug the included cables into a stereo.

I'm using this with a Kindle Fire 8.9. Pairing was quick and simple.

The connection to the stereo can be done via a single cable or using a two cable (L/R) setup. Cables for both options are included. I'm using the L/R option, and plugged the cables into the TAPE input on my stereo receiver.

The sound quality is excellent. It is very hard to tell the difference in quality when streaming audio via this receiver versus playing a CD on the receiver. Movie dialog was outstanding as well.

The fact that it does not require a battery is a plus and a minus. On the plus side, no need to worry about recharging or swapping batteries. On the down side, it was a bit of a problem for me to get the cables routed since the wall outlet near my stereo is not easily accessible. I wound up running a short extension cord so that I could plug in the receiver close enough to the stereo so that the L/R cables would reach.

As a bonus, it includes a USB port so you can use it to recharge your phone/tablet/etc.

That one minor issue aside, I'm very impressed with the performance of this product. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]

Although this is a very compact speaker (roughly 4.5 inches long and a little over 2 inches tall) it puts out a surprisingly decent sound - better than I expected given the price point. The treble and mid range were pretty clear, and the bass, while a bit light (unavoidable given the compact size) is more than adequate for casual listening.

Usage is very straightforward. I had zero problems pairing this with a Fire 8.9 tablet and a Nexus 7. The Bluetooth range is excellent - no dropouts even with the tablet on the far side of the room (a good 30 feet from the speaker). It also has the ability to direct connect to the sound source via a standard RCA cable.

The build quality seems solid, with nicely finished seams on the plastic case. The controls on the back (on/off, charge input and RCA in) and are clearly marked. The volume, pause, etc. controls are on the top and are very nicely done - they light up with a red light when touched. Very clear, easy to use, and attractive to boot.

It also comes with a decent carry pouch, which will come in handy to protect it from scratches when carried in a backpack. The "manual" is sparse, but is not really needed -- very easy to figure out how to use this. It comes in a sturdy box, which is good for not only storing it, but also to help prevent shipping damage. (Alas, there are also some unfortunate spelling errors on the product info printed on the box.)

My main complaint, and the reason for a loss of one star, is that it has an internal, non-removable battery. Eventually the battery will fail (e.g., not be able to retain a charge) rending the speaker useless (or requiring a constant tethering to a power source). While non-removable batteries allow for a more compact size, I'd be more than happy to trade some size for the ability to replace the battery.

That one issue aside, this is a very nice speaker for the price.
[Sample provided for review]

Earbuds are my headphone of choice, and I'm rather particular about comfort since there's nothing worse than a poor fitting bud. These Onkyo earbuds fare very well with regard to comfort. They are very lightweight, but stay put even when exercising. There are an assortment of tip sizes so you can customize them to fit your ear. For me, the middle-sized one was a perfect fit.

I really like that these have detachable cables that can be replaced. I've ruined more than my share of earbuds due to breaking the cable, so that feature will probably come in handy down the road. The cable itself appears stout enough to withstand all but the most rigorous strain.

The sound is good but not outstanding. Nice separation, clear mid-range and treble, and a decent amount of bass. But when comparing the sound of the Onkyo to my other less pricy earbuds (such as the RHA MA350) I was not wow'd by the Onkyo as being significantly better. A bit clearer, but very close in terms of sound quality.

Granted, the Onkyo have, to my eye, better styling than other buds, and the replaceable cord is certainly a big plus. Those issues, plus the comfort factor, warrant a 4-star rating. But to get 5 stars at this price point, more is needed in sound quality than delivered by the Onkyo's. Good, but not 5-star superlative.

This is one of those products that is good to have, but even better if you never need to use it since you'll probably be using it when the electricity is out. It offers a lot of functionality in a compact size: a flashlight, AM radio, FM radio and weather band radio. It runs off of an internal rechargeable battery that is kept charged either via solar power, USB connection or by cranking the handle. It can also serve as a source to charge a cell phone (albeit with very limited capacity to do so since the internal battery is only rated at 800mAh).

It works pretty well. The flashlight is very bright - had no problems lighting my way down a dark stairway and in a totally dark room. The radio is OK. The reception is spotty and it only picked up a few of the very strong stations in the area. It's very susceptible to positioning - moving it just a couple of inches turned a clear station into static.

Cranking the handle to keep it charged is pretty easy. It turns easily and the handle is comfortable. According to the manual, one minute of cranking equals 30 minutes of flashlight use or 20 minutes of radio use.

This is a good product to keep on hand in case of emergency, such as a bad storm or extended power outage. It won't keep you cool in the summer or warm in the winter, but at least you can see where you're going and listen to the radio. Definitely worth a spot in the emergency kit. The only shortcoming is the somewhat limited radio reception.
[sample provided by manufacturer for review]

This is a simple, but very handy device to have. It's basically a sound card that you can plug into a USB port to connect speakers or headphones.

I'm using it with my laptop since the speaker/headphone ports are tough to access. This makes using headphones much easier and with less cord tangle.

It's quite compact - about 2 inches long, one inch wide and a half inch thick. Very easy to fit into a laptop bag and carry it along. The ports are on the end, and the top has buttons for volume and mute. Although the buttons are black on black, they have white icons printed on them so it's not hard to see which button you want to push.

Installation was plug and play on a Win 7 system. No fuss, no muss. Sound quality was very good - just as good as the internal sound card.

It's a great solution for laptops or desktops with ports that are difficult to access, or a cheap and easy solution for a defective sound card. Highly recommend.
[manufacturer provided sample for review]

For the price, this is a decent set of gaming headphones. The build quality is perfectly fine for the price point. It doesn't feel as rock solid as more expensive brands, but feels like it will certainly stand up to normal usage.

The comfort is borderline. It feels fine for up to about an hour of usage, then the ear cups start to become somewhat uncomfortable and the headband pinches a bit. It's not the best set for hours and hours of usage, but for "normal" wear times I didn't have any problems.

The sound quality is quite good. Nice amount of bass response without sounding muddy. I also found it to have more than good enough sound quality for watching movies, with the dialogue coming through clearly. It's not the best for listening to music (the mid and upper ranges are a bit constrained) but for it's intended purpose of a gaming set, no complaints at all regarding sound quality.

My major problem was with range. I love the fact that these are wireless, but placement is critical. I'd lose the signal if I didn't vary much from a specific spot near the wireless adapter. Moving just a bit out of the "zone" killed the connection. That was a disappointment since, while I didn't expect to be able to roam around the house with them on, I did expect to be able to leave my chair and go a short distance without breaking the connection. No problems with signal strength when seated or within a few feet of the adapter, but hit and miss when moving more than a few feet away.

Other than the range issue, this is a pretty good value in a gaming headphone set.

This is one of those "why didn't I think of it?" type products. At first glance, it seems quite simple - basically a mini tripod with attachments that allow you to mount a tablet or phone. But after working with it for a while, it's clear a lot of thought went into this.

The tripod is well made and sturdy, consisting mainly of metal. The ball joint at the top is controlled by a built-in key that allows you to loosen and tighten it so it stays put. Each leg extends independently, so you can set the tripod so it is tilted upward (for example, to position a tablet so you can watch a movie at your desk). The attachment screw base has a rubber non-slip insert to protect whatever you're attaching against scratches. It includes a lanyard, but you can easily remove it (which I did) if it's not needed.

The tripod is very compact -- folds up to about 4.5 inches long and about 1 inch wide, so it's easy to carry. With the legs fully extended it is just under 9 inches tall. The legs have a thick rubber tip that keep it well balanced and positioned. I was a bit concerned that the legs didn't have locks, but the tension of the pull out extensions was more than adequate to keep the legs extended even when it was loaded down with an 8.9 inch Kindle Fire.

Impressive quality given the price - much better than expected.

You can also use the tripod as a camera tripod since the attachment screw is a standard size. It worked fine with my Panasonic and Canon point and shoots.

But the star of the show is the clip. You attach it to the back of the device case (you could attach it to the device itself, but it's not recommended) using an adhesive pad. The pad is removable, but is not reusable, so you want to give some thought before you stick it to the case. Once attached, it fits into a "smart mount" that, in turn, attaches to the tripod. Sounds kind of complicated, but it's very simple to use. There is an included instruction sheet, but you can pretty much puzzle it out by just looking at it.

The clip and smart mount are plastic, but seem more than sturdy enough for the job. They clip together with an interlocking system that kept my Kindle very solidly positioned while I was using it.

The only negative I see is the adhesive pad. As with any adhesive, you need to clean the point of contact very well (an alcohol pad is included in the box) and let the adhesive cure for 30 min. I think it's a safe bet that some people won't do both those steps, which opens the door to a significant point of failure.

But, provided you read the instructions, this is a very nicely designed and useful product. Highly recommend.
[The manufacturer provided the product for review]

I needed a cheap pair of bluetooth headphones for my Nexus for traveling, but didn't want to make too many compromises in favor of cost. These turned out quite well.

I was concerned about other reviews noting that the one-size-fits-all aspect of these headphones might be a problem with those with larger noggins (I am one of those people), but did not have any difficultly wearing these headphones - it fits with room to spare and parks securely around my ears.

The sound is decent - better than I expected given the price. I like that you can make volume adjustments with a push of a button on the right-ear side.

The headphones recharge via a USB port to your computer (or use the USB on any plug adapter that you may have for your other devices -- I used my Amazon Kindle plug adapter), with an indicator light changing from red to blue when it is fully charged. I'm not sure of the total battery life, but I've used them for six hours in a single stretch, and they still were going strong.

I also tried walking around and away from my Nexus 7, and the headphones still worked fine. I didn't test the absolute limit of its range, but I got a good 20 feet away on the same floor without a problem.

The sound and build quality won't knock your socks off, but for the price, it's a great performer. Definitely recommend this as if you're looking for a good value in a bluetooth headphone.

Out of the box, you must charge it for at least 4 hours (the light will turn green on the back of the device when it is ready). Once it was charged I was able to pair it with my Google Nexus 7 with little difficulty.

The build quality is pretty good. It feels reasonably solid in hand, and the plastic shell is nicely made.

I found the manual to be easy to follow. You have to switch the button on the back to "on", then hold down the power button for 8 seconds to get it into "pairing" mode (not the usual 3 seconds to simply turn the device on). Then initiate pairing on your device (in this case, my Nexus 7) and it's ready to go.

Sound quality is good, and pressing the - and + buttons adjusts volume. The peak volume is impressive, which I like because my primary use for these speakers will be to hear over exercise machines. It also works well in the shower, and it's more than loud enough to hear over the shower spray.

The manual says the battery can provide about 25 hours of use when fully charged. I haven't timed it, but it does seem to last a good while. It lacks a battery gas gauge, so there's no way to determine how much battery life is left.

There is one issue I've been having with the speaker - stutters and skips. I determined streaming quality was not the issue and the speaker was correctly recognized by and paired with my tablet. I was able to fix it once by unpairing the speaker from my tablet, and then pairing it again. On another occasion I went into the Nexus 7 settings to disconnect and then reconnect the speaker (as opposed to fully unpairing/pairing it) to get the audio to play smoothly. It's a little annoying to have this extra step, which makes this a 4 star experience, but ultimately not a deal-breaker for me.

It's a capable speaker that provides the portability and audio volume I was looking for.

[The manufacturer provided this product for review]

I've been using a clip-on light for my Kindle Touch when reading at night. It works, but I don't like that there's a separate piece of equipment I need to keep track of. This all-in-one solution has proven to be an effective way to light up the Kindle without having a separate light.

The case itself is nicely made. The cover is soft and cushy; the interior is a nice "suede" type material that wont harm the screen. All the stitching is even and tight. The Kindle fits in easily and is held securely. The cover has what I assume is a magnetic closure. It works well, and keeps the case closed in transit, but opens without having to undo any snaps or zippers.

The light is attached on the back of the case. When needed, you undo a protective flap (has a snap button), flip the light over the top and secure it in place with a "hook" that's built into the top of the case. The on/off switch is on the side of the light housing. Takes only a couple of seconds to get it into position.

The light is more than adequate for reading is a dark room. It uses 2 button batteries (CR 2032).

IMPORTANT: my case came with a plastic protector on the batteries to ensure the batteries remained fresh in transit. This must be removed before use or it will appear that the light is non-functional. Unfortunately, there are no instructions about this (I guessed it was the issue when the light would not turn on).

While it's great to always have the light as part of the case, the downside is that the light housing creates a bulge on the back side of the case. That makes this more cumbersome to toss into a briefcase since it increases the width. But, for me, it's a fair trade-off since I don't have to remember to bring the light with me.

I'll give this 5 stars, but 4.5 is a more accurate rating since it should come with instructions with regard to the battery. I also think the battery cover should be thicker (no problems so far, but it's a thin plastic) as well as the lens cover (very thin plastic that bends easily). Those quirks aside, I'm finding this to be an excellent case for my Touch.

[The manufacturer provided me with a case for review purposes]

Overall, this is a fine case for the 8.9 inch Fire HD. The overall quality is quite nice - I have other Marware products for my Kindle Touch, and it's good to see that they are continuing to maintain a strong focus on product quality. All the materials feel nice; the stitching is tight and even; there's ample cushioning for tablet protection while maintaining a slim profile; and the elastic strap holds the cover closed in a secure fashion.

I also like how Marware packages their products with a minimum of packaging waste but still ensures the product can travel through the mail without being dinged up. The package is also easy to open - no fuss, no muss.

I initially had some difficulty getting the Fire into the case. The Fire is held in place using a plastic cradle, but it seemed to be too small. I had to (gasp!) resort to reading the user guide that came with it, and found out I needed to position it in a certain way and then snap it in. When it is properly inserted you'll hear and feel a clear "snap" at each of the four corners of the tablet. When properly installed the case holds the tablet very securely. I shook it vigorously (over a thick cushion in case it failed) and the Fire stayed put.

My main quibble is with the rotation feature. I was really looking forward to this since some apps only run in portrait mode; others only in landscape. While the rotation feature works, it is very stiff - you really have to twist hard to get it to rotate. It's a two-handed operation: one hand to rotate the tablet; the other to hold the case while you're turning.

The bottom of the cradle has a tab that fits into a slot on the base of the cover to prop up the tablet. This works in both landscape and portrait modes. There are three tabs so you can adjust the angle.

There are cut outs for the power and HDMI ports. I had no problems accessing any of the ports, power button or volume controls while it was in the cover.

Since I often end up having to charge the Fire while it is in use, I rotated the screen so the power plug is at the top. That allows me to keep the tablet propped up on my desk in landscape mode for video watching, but still use the power cord.

It also offers an auto on/off ability - the Fire turns off when you close the cover, and wakes up when you open the cover. It's a nice feature and it works well.

It has a slot on the cover so you can fit your hand into it for ease of holding it. That has value, but what I would have preferred to have instead (or in addition to) is a pocket on either the inside or the outside to hold items such as a cleaning cloth. This is not a huge problem, but I'll certainly miss that since the case for my original Fire has a outside pouch that is great for holding a cleaning cloth and a small stylus.

I'm going to give this 5 stars, but 4.5 is more accurate given the reluctance of the rotation feature. But, since it does everything else very well, looks good, and feels nice, it's closer to a 5 rating than a 4.

As with the original Fire, the out of box experience is very nicely done. Very straightforward process of just turning it on and letting the tablet register and update itself. It took about 10 minutes (with the majority of the time waiting for an update to download) and it was ready to go. It picked up all my original Fire music and books from the cloud and most of my Fire apps. I was disappointed to see that a couple of my favorite apps (TED Talks and Play Music Videos Free) were judged not compatible with my new Fire. Hopefully updates will be coming soon.

The screen is delightful! Crisp and clear, and a marked increase in resolution versus the original Fire. Videos on the HD Fire are simply amazing.

The sound quality is also a marked improvement. While it was pretty much mandatory to hook up an external speaker for the original Fire, the new Fire puts out pretty decent sound quality all on its own. I still hook it up to external speakers (I'm partial to the Bose Companion 20) for movies and music when I'm at my desk, but it puts out more than adequate sound all on its own.

Response time is more snappy than the original Fire, and the carousel is easier to navigate (smoother scrolling). Picking up a WiFi signal seems to be better with the new fire - I'm getting all signal strength bars displayed in areas of the house where I could only get 2 or 3 bars with the original Fire.

The form factor is great for video watching. The extra screen size makes a big difference. The other huge advantage to the size is typing. It's MUCH easier to see and use the onscreen keyboard than on the original Fire. I had no problems typing without a stylus; on the original Fire a stylus is a must.

So far I don't see many misses other than a hard-to-find power button. The casing and build quality is not at the same level as an iPad, but neither is the price. I'm very pleased with the price-performance level of the HD Fire.

This is not replacing my original Fire - I'll continue to use that for most of my book reading and when I need portability. For everything else, the larger screen is well worth the additional cost.

I have a Nexus 7, the iPad 2 and an HP Touchpad and the Fire is my favorite by far. Not because either the original or this new Fire are the best in terms of build quality or speed or tech specs, but for one simple reason: the Fire makes it so incredibly easy to avail myself of entertainment and content. The tight link to the Amazon ecosystem is, for me, a huge plus - it keeps my entertainment pipeline full of things I want to read, listen to or watch with little or no effort on my part. And, best of all, a lot of that content is free through Prime.

Love it, and highly recommend.

Overall I'm very pleased with these ear buds. They are my first pair of bluetooth buds and it has been wonderful to not have to deal with cords, especially when working out. I can't tell you how many times I've hit an earbud cord while exercising and ripped the ear bud from my ear. A real pain in the neck (and ear!).

>>>Pros:

Comfort - These fit very well in my ear. There are different tip sizes to create a good fit and, after trying them all out, I went with the medium size. Very comfortable to wear even for long periods of time.

Stay put - I've yet to have them fall out even when doing aerobic exercises or while on the treadmill.

Sound - they sound pretty good. The sound is not as good as my favorite (and inexpensive) corded buds ([[ASIN:B0053R0WWG RHA MA-350 Aluminium Noise Isolating In-Ear Earphones]]) but they are a solid B+ performer with regard to bass response and overall clarity. Keep in mind that good bass response is affected by how the buds fit in your ear, so it's important to try out different tip sizes to see how they affect sound quality. They do get harsh at loud volumes, but for normal listening they are more than fine for my non-audiophile ears. They do reasonably well at blocking out ambient noise.

Setup - I found it straightforward even though I've never had any experience with setting up bluetooth earbuds.

Size - nice and compact so you don't get the "radar dish" look that larger units can have.

Durability - they have a "sweat proof" guarantee which is nice (although I imagine, like most guarantees, there are some loopholes). Overall build quality is good, with a very solid feel to all components.

>>>Cons:

Battery life - The manufacturer claims a battery life of 4.5 hours but I've yet to get more than 3 hours off a single charge. Plus there's no warning about battery life (until you're almost fully discharged) or a visual indicator of how much charge there is left.

Usability - the buttons on the buds are too small, making it difficult for me to push the right one. A lot of fumbling and mis-presses, making it often easier to deal with volume changes on the device, which kills some of the value of having wireless buds. I guess I lack the nimble fingers of the primary target market.

But overall, I'm pleased. The pros outweigh the cons, and I think this is a solid 4-star device.

Overall, this is a very nice golf GPS for the price. I was a little worried about it being too complicated to use, but the manual explains all the features in reasonably good detail. I found it helpful to keep the manual with me the first couple of times I used it on the course to refer to, but after a few outings I felt comfortable using it.

I had an initial problem with the battery life in that it quit on me after about an hour of use. After leaving it in the charging cradle overnight, the next time it maintained its charge for a full afternoon's use. I've used it (and recharged it) several times since then and have had no problems, so it seems the first time was just a momentary glitch (or perhaps I didn't seat the charging cable firmly enough).

I very much like that it does not require a subscription to use, nor does it need to be tethered to a PC for the initial setup. It has a pretty extensive database of courses (Izzo says on their website that they cover 90% of the courses in the US). You can use their website to look up a course to see if it is included in the database.

Sat acquisition times is quick - took only a few minutes to get a lock and find my course the first time I used it. Acquisition time was even faster on subsequent uses. It uses a SiRF Star III receiver.

The display is clear even in sunlight, but it is a bit small for me. I don't usually have my reading glasses with me when I'm outdoors, so seeing the distance numbers took quite a bit of squinting. Granted, if you don't have aging eyes you won't find that to be a problem, but it would have been nice to have a larger display.

I also didn't find it all that comfortable to wear. It is lightweight and not too thick, but the strap was not very comfortable. Plus the greenish/yellow accent color (found on the inside of the strap and the sides of the unit) didn't appeal to me much - rather garish looking to my eye.

The warranty is only 90 days, which I think is too short given the price -- a year would be more appropriate.

But those are minor quibbles. Overall, the functionality is great - quick to acquire sats, accurate distances and straightforward to use. Considering the price of other brands, such as Garmin, this is a great value. Definitely should be on the short list if you're shopping for a golf GPS.

[As an aside, it's a real bear to the product out of the clamshell packaging. I didn't' factor that into the rating, but set aside some time to wrestle it out of the plastic jail it comes in should you buy one.]

I'm very pleased with this external hard drive. The price for the 3TB version was very reasonable, and, like another Seagate external drive I have, it was a snap to install. Just plug it in, and you're done! I wish all peripherals were this simple.

The drive comes with utility software but it is not necessary to use it. That's a big plus for me, since I have my own utilities that I prefer to use for backups and file management. It is also unnecessary to run any installation software - just plug it into the PC (I'm running Win 7 64 bit) and it works.

File transfers are speedy, and the overall fit and finish is very nicely done. It does generate some heat, but no more than other external drives I've used. Very quiet operation.

Highly recommend!

This is a good choice if you prefer your tablet case to be thin and minimal. It offers some level of protection, but mostly along the lines of preventing scratches and scuffs. It won't protect the Tab against any rough handling or drops. The thinness also eliminates any additional storage space/flaps/pouches.

On the plus side it's nicely made for the price (assuming you purchase it at the discounted price and not the list price). The stitching is even and tight, and the overall feel is pretty nice. It's very muted in appearance, which I see as a plus - I don't care for the covers that come in bright, flashy colors or designs. Granted, some may describe the look of the case as boring with its gray and black colors, but I would say it's classic.

The cover feels nice overall, and not at all slippery in the hand, as other cases can be. The stand feature is OK, but you're fighting the thinness of the case. Thicker cases offer more stability when you have them propped up. It works adequately as a stand, but it's not it's strong suit since the "nubs" that serve as props are too thin to maintain significant stability.

A decent value if you like a thin case design.

Overall, I'm pleased with this surge protector. It has 10 outlets to plug in all the various devices that accumulate around the entertainment system with 2 of the outlets spaced so they can deal with the wall-wart plugs.

What sets it apart from the Belkin surge protector that it replaces is its attractive design. I can't hide the surge protector due to the way my equipment rack is set up. The Belkin looked like a typical office surge protector -- functional and utilitarian. The AR, however, has a much sleeker design, with glossy black panels and silver accents. No, the aesthetics don't add anything to its functionality, but it is much nicer to look at.

What does add to the functionality over the Belkin is the 6 foot cord that is very flexible, with a flat front plug (e.g., it plugs into the wall without sticking out, so you can use it in an outlet that is behind a piece of furniture). It also offers 2 USB charging ports, and has inputs for coax and ethernet cables (2 sets in/out for coax and 1 set in/out for ethernet).

I can't speak to its claim of improving the picture and sound. My setup looked and sounded great before using the AR; looked and sounded great after using the AR.

It's priced higher than a generic surge protector, so if the aesthetics and design features are not of value, it's not worth getting for any potential video/sound improvements. But, while I can't give it a first-hand recommendation as to picture and sound improvement, I can give it a strong recommendation for looks, ease of use, build quality and overall design.

The only quibbles, and the reason it dropped from 5 to 4 stars, is that for the price, there should be more than two wide-spaced outlets, and more than 2 USB charging ports (ideally located at various points around the unit).

RHA provided me with a pair of the MA450i to evaluate, and after putting them through their paces, I'm very impressed.

The fit and finish is excellent -- they have a very solid feel to them. The manufacturer states they are machined from solid aluminum which no doubt contributes to the how great they feel. I also love the braided cord. I'm not all that careful with earbuds, and the cord is always the first to go. The braiding is the same as is found on their MA-350 model which I've been using extensively for a couple of months, and the cord still looks like new.

I also like the fact that they include a total of seven sets of rubber tips. That's an important feature since sound quality for any earbuds (not to mention comfort) starts with a properly-fitted tip that sits properly in your ear.

Noise isolation is very good. Not 100%, but they cut down outside noise very well when I used them outdoors (traffic noise) and in the gym (equipment noise).

It includes an inline mic/control so you can skip tracks and control volume on Apple devices. I used it on an iPad and everything functioned as it should. It also includes a mic, but I was unable to test that since I don't have an iPhone.

So they look great, are comfortable and are sturdy. If you think the catch is in the sound, you're wrong. They sound tremendous. Very full bass, strong mid-range, and clear upper ranges (although the latter is slightly clipped at high volume). Really impressive sound.

I passed them around to my friends and asked them to estimate how much these cost. The lowest estimate was nearly 25% more than the actual cost, and the highest was nearly triple. Like the MA-350, these sound as though they cost far more -- they really set the mark for sound at their price point. When you add in the build quality and comfort, it's an outstanding value.

My complaints are minor. I'm not happy with the placement of the inline control. It's located about 6.5 inches from the right bud. While that placement was probably selected for proper mic performance, it does make using the track controls a bit awkward -- those would be better served by having the control a greater distance from the earbuds. Also, as with the MA-350, the right/left markings on the earbuds are almost impossible to see (black on black writing). I put a dot of paint on the right bud so I could easily see which was which. While I appreciate the sleek design and color scheme, some R/L color coding would have been nice.

Highly recommend!

Summary: These sound far better than you would expect given the price. Excellent construction quality, including a nice stout braided cord. A bit muddy at high volume, but outperforms other earbuds that cost much more.

Review: I tend to be hard on my earbuds. Even when they come with a case I just wind the cord around the MP3 player. So I was impressed right out of the box with these since they come with a sturdy, braided cord. Very resistant to kinking, and the thick diameter gives me confidence that they will stand up to my less than gentle handling. Despite the braiding and thickness, the cord remains highly flexible.

It also comes with two extra sets of rubber tips (small, medium and large) to help get a good fit, and a cloth pouch for storage.

I had a bit of a struggle replacing the rubber tips. They pulled off the ear buds easily, but getting them back on was a bit difficult. I found that inverting the tip (e.g., pulling back the portion that goes in your ear so it exposes the inner tube) made it a bit easier. The rubber tips stay firmly attached to the post.

Very comfortable. I had them on for 90+ minutes at the gym, and had zero soreness. They also stay in your ear very well - not even a good treadmill run jarred them loose.

Nice sound isolation. Even with modest music volume I was not bothered by ambient sounds.

Attractive styling. Granted, you can't really tell that since most of the device is hidden in your ear, but they do look nice when not in use.

So it does a great job with comfort, styling and usability. But how does it sound? In a word, impressive. I was not expecting a whole lot - basically thought these would be a small step up from something such as a stock iPod set or low-priced offerings from Sony, Skullcandy or JBL. Very pleased to find that the MA-350s are so much better! The sound is very rich and full at low to modest volumes, with excellent bass and good mid and upper ranges. It did degrade somewhat at higher volumes, with the sound becoming more muddy, especially in the mid-range.

These compare very favorably with my current favorite pair of modestly-priced buds (Creative Aurvana). The MA-350 offer better bass and a better/more comfortable ear-fit. The Creative's offer better sound clarity at high volume, and better vocal clarity, especially when using them for movies rather than music. But it's close - you would think that both should be priced about the same given their similar performance.

Really pleased with these, and highly recommend.

[Product provided by the manufacturer for review]

I've been thinking about getting a Roku for some time, so when it was a Gold Box deal I took the plunge. I'm now kicking myself for not buying it sooner - this is great! Rather than be limited to streaming on my laptop, I can now stream from Amazon Prime and Netflix on the TV, plus have the sound routed through my home theater setup.

Setup of the Roku was about as simple as could be. I was up and running in less than 30 minutes, with a large portion of that time spent downloading updates or figuring out how to route the cables so they would not appear as attractive playthings for the cats. I hardwired this into my router rather than go wireless since the router is just a few feet away from the player.

I hooked the HDMI cable into my home theater receiver. I really can't tell the difference between streaming and playing a Blu-ray or DVD in terms of sound or video quality. My internet connection is 30Mbps.

I was surprised at how small the box is. Just a few inches wide and about an inch or so thick. I think the HDMI cable weighs more than the actual device. Very easy to find a spot to put it.

The remote is OK. I wish the buttons were a bit larger and/or were backlit so you can see them in a darkened room. It's usable and functional, but pretty basic.

Highly recommend!

I was really surprised to see how well-made this extension cable was given how little it cost. Both the male and female connectors are high quality, and the cable itself is quite beefy (about 1/8 inch in diameter). The cable thickness does make this a bit less flexible than thinner versions, but it will also stand up to stress much better. I uploaded a picture of the cable ends since there is none in the listing.

Sound quality is fine -- I don't notice any difference plugging the speaker in with or without the extension.

I'm using it with a Kindle Fire and an external speaker.

Summary: This is an excellent projector for basic needs. It projects well even in lit rooms, is easy to set up, and takes up little space. Not the best in terms of color matching, but just fine for standard business presentations.

I'm very pleased with this projector. I'm using it in the office for run-of-the-mill PowerPoint presentations, and it works very well for those. No more having to have people huddle over a screen - everyone can see the images at the same time!

Setup is straightforward, as is hooking it up to a PC (a Windows 7 laptop). The projector is compact and lightweight, which is good, but I would be concerned about traveling with this. It does not seem rugged enough to withstand much abuse. I'll be using it in the office 95% of the time, and only taking it to a client site once in a blue moon (and only local clients at that), so it should be fine. If you're a regular traveler at the least you'll want to get a very good case.

The picture quality was pretty good. Images are very bright and easy to see even in a lit room, despite the fact that I'm projecting it just on the wall, rather than on an actual screen. Quiet when running, and it has an "eco" mode that uses less electricity (and supposedly also extends the lamp life).

My only quibble is that the colors are a bit off. Not way off, but enough to be noticeable on images such as logos where I had a point of comparison. A bit of fiddling made it better, but it still was not perfect.

This is not a significant issue for my needs since I'm only projecting PPT charts and graphs where spot-on color matching is irrelevant. But, if you have more precise color rendering needs, this may be too basic of a projector for you.

Excellent choice if you need a basic projector for the office that works well, is easy to use, and won't break the bank. Highly recommend.

I tried the first generation Kindle but didn't really care all that much for it. While I loved the screen, it just didn't feel right, and remember thinking this would be perfect if it had a touchscreen.

When the Touch was announced I ordered this along with a Fire with the thought that the Fire would be for me, and I'd give the Touch as a gift. The Touch got here this morning and I opened it up just to make sure it was OK. It looked so nice that I carefully peeled off the plastic just to try it out for a few minutes. After all, one wouldn't want to give a gift that didn't work, right? Well, it's now been a few hours and several chapters of a few books later. I'm keeping it. A second one will be on order for Christmas giving.

Why keep the Touch when I also have a Fire? If you skip over the obvious answer (I just love electronic gadgets) the e-ink on the Touch is much better in terms of clarity and lack of glare. Not that the Fire is bad. It has a very clear screen, but there is some glare. The Touch is better for reading under all lighting situations, and remains highly readable in direct sun. I can't imagine getting better screen clarity than this for black and white text.

I also tried reading it while on a treadmill (a situation that usually gives me a headache when I tried it using the kindle app on my Touchpad) and it was quite pleasant. Best of all is that I can zoom up the text size so I can read it while it is on the treadmill reading stand (it's too far away for me to read hard copy unless it's in HUGE type. Getting old is _not_ fun).

But the strength of the Touch is also it's biggest problem for me - black and white. I read several magazines each month and reading them in B/W is lackluster at best. Magazines are more enjoyable on the Fire, especially publications such as Wired.

The touch interface is great. So far its been very smooth and glitch free. Love the feel of the screen - has a bit of texture to it. I have to say, however, that I am a bit concerned about the screen longevity. The Touch overall feels a bit fragile and less "solid" than the Fire. I'm not deducting any stars for that since it's just an impression, but it will be interesting to see if the durability of the Touch screen is better/worse/same as the Fire (and vice versa). I'll be getting a case for it for sure since it's going to be getting bumped about.

I'll be using the Fire mainly at home and for reading material that works best in color (and, of course, video - need to relax the mind with mindless entertainment as well!). The Touch will be living in my briefcase for reading while commuting (I take the bus and subway, so lots of time to read) and for killing time prior to an appointment. The longer battery life and smaller size makes it a better traveling companion than the Fire. I don't have the Touch 3G version, so I'll have to make sure I keep a few books on my to-be-read stack so I don't run out when I'm out of wi-fi range.

Granted, if I could only have one device, I'd stay with the Fire since that offers more entertainment options, albeit at twice the price. But the cost is not excessive, so I treated myself to both. With a Fire and a Touch I've got all bases covered (until, of course, the next glittery gee-whiz piece of electronics comes out...).

I've been using a Linksys router for years and it never missed a beat (their wireless G model with the two antennas). But, after upgrading my Internet from DSL to cable, I thought a new router would be in order.

Before buying one I searched for reviews from computer and tech magazines/sites. Talk about confusing! I'd read one review that gave a sterling endorsement for a particular router; then another review from another site that gave the same router a horrible review.

Since my router needs are pretty basic (just use it to share Internet access) I concentrated on ease of install issues. In that regard there was consensus about how easy Linksys is to install. So I went with them again, and selected the 1200 model since it gave me all that I wanted/needed at a good price (but, to hedge my bets, I got it at a warehouse club so I could return it easily).

So happy with this router! Installation was SO simple -- if you can plug in a cable you can install this router. But, should you want to tinker with settings, you can also access the full, detailed configuration menu and tweak settings to your heart's content. I think it took me longer to open up the box and unwrap the router and power cord than it took to actually get it to work.

Performance so far has been excellent. I put it on the ground level of my house and have no problems getting a strong signal in the basement and upper level. I did find that it helps to put the router in the middle of the house rather than against a wall for best signal strength throughout the house.

Considering that my Linksys G is still cranking along after several years, I'm reasonably confident (or at least hopeful) that this will last me an equal length of time.

If you're looking for a solid, easy to install single band router, this is it. Highly recommend.

I have an iPad and an HP Touchpad, but the Fire has quickly turned into my favorite tablet for entertainment activities. The reasons are simple - it makes it incredibly easy to access movies, TV shows, books and magazines from Amazon, many of which are free under Prime. I can hold it for hours without it getting uncomfortable, the screen is great, and the overall look and feel of the operating system is intuitive. Storing and accessing content on the Amazon Cloud is also a seamless, simple process.

I was concerned about the screen size since I've become used to the larger tablet screen sizes of the iPad and Touchpad. I'm finding that the benefits of a smaller screen size (easier to hold in one hand and light weight) outweigh most of the disadvantages. I miss a larger screen the most when I'm reading a magazine or a newspaper, but the copy remains highly readable even on the smaller screen.

Sound quality is decent with the onboard speakers. Nothing spectacular but workable. I find a decent set of headphones/earbuds to be a worthwhile addition. The touchscreen is also not without an occassional glitch. I get the same "lack of a final polish" feeling using this as I do with my Touchpad versus the more slick feeling of the iPad. But none of these issues impact usability, and I'm willing to let some factors slide in exchange for a more affordable price.

Is it an "iPad killer" or an "Android tablet killer"? No. But why is that even an issue? I wanted an easy way to avail myself of the benefits of Prime membership (most notably being able to stream shows and movies for free) and the Fire accomplishes this very well. It comes at a price that's a lot easier to handle than the iPad, and a level of ease of use/functionality that's easier to handle than Android tablets.

None of the so-called limitations of the Fire detract from my using it. Yes it has limited onboard storage but with the way the Cloud is integrated, I've not had any difficulty using that as a way of storing content. Plus, when Amazon stores it, they deal with the issue of backup. I also don't miss the 3G connectivity. Sure, I'd love to be able to connect anywhere, but I will not pay the prices charged for data connectivity. I never use the 3G on my iPad for the same reason - just costs too much!

I'll certainly keep and continue to use my iPad since I use that a lot for work. But when I'm done with work and want to have fun, the Fire will be in hand. It's cheap, works well, and provides access to virtually unlimited video and print entertainment. For me it's a perfect fit.

This seemed to be the perfect solution to a problem I was having with obtaining Internet access in my basement. The router is located on the upper floor of the house and, while access is fine in every room above ground, access in the basement has been minimal at best.

Installation was very straightforward - just plug one adapter into the router, the other into the wall socket, and plug in whatever device needs access into one of the three plugs located on the wall socket device.

Overall it works pretty well, but is highly sensitive to noise or heavy draws on the power line. For example, I have a dehumidifier in the basement. When that kicks on, I lose the connection. Sometimes it is regained all by itself, but most of the time I have to either reboot (or power cycle) the device that is plugged in, or unplug and then re-plug the adapter. I tried moving the dehumidifier to a different circuit than the one used by the powerline adapter, and also tried plugging the dehumidifier into a surge protector - no difference. So, I make sure the dehumidifier is off before I use any Internet device.

I've had the same issue with other appliances such as certain vacuums - turn them on, and the connection is lost. There have been no problems with appliances operating in other areas of the house, such as the microwave, laser printers, etc. Just happens when you use the appliance in the same room as the powerline adapter.

But, other than these powerline induced interruptions, the device works well. Speedy connection - can't tell any difference between this and any other WiFi connected device. Well worth taking a look at if you have some WiFi dead zones in your house. Just keep an eye out for someone who is about to use a vacuum when you're at a critical spot in the movie you're streaming!

I jumped in with the throng of people buying this at $99 and have been really pleased with it. I also have an ipad and this is clearly no where near as polished in terms of both the operating system and the overall design. But, for the price, it's been a lot of fun.

I've been using it for the following:

> general web surfing - fast page loads, nice scrolling. Having Flash enabled is a nice feature and puts this at an advantage over the ipad (at least for the sites I usually frequent)

> watching Amazon Prime videos - no problems encountered at all

> Angry Birds - it's a free app

> Kindle - while the Kindle app is not as nice as it is on the ipad, it is quite usable.

> misc. apps - the app selection is not deep, but there are several nice ones. I've been using Accuweather, the Fidelity market monitor, the Washington Post reader and a few others. All free from the HP app store.

> email - while tablet-based email is a bit of a pain due to the cramped keyboard, it's not bad. Setup of a Yahoo account was a snap.

If you only use it for web surfing and the Kindle app you'll get your money's worth. At the regular price there are better choices. For $99, you can't beat it.

Tip: I found the Touchpad fits very well into the Joby Gorillamobile Ori for iPad holder (the one they make for the original ipad). Fit is a wee bit loose, but still secure. The on/off button on the case works with the Touchpad, and there's a cutout that lines up with the USB power port. The volume switch on the case works fine for lowering the volume, but you have to squeeze it somewhat to raise the volume. The Joby line is great -- if you can find one used for a bargain, go for it for your Touchpad. Note that Jobi makes two models -- you want the one that works with the original ipad.

The Logitech Cooling Pad N200 is a simple padded platform your laptop rests on to keep the hot underside of the laptop from roasting your legs. It connects to the laptop with a USB plug, and draws power from the laptop to run a 2-speed cooling fan (controlled by a switch located on the USB plug).

The pad works splendidly. The fan makes only minor noise in operation even at the highest speed (no more noise than the laptop's own fans make when they engage), and I am completely protected from the heat from the underside of the laptop. The bottom of the pad is nicely padded and is comfortable in use. I didn't have to adjust my position at any point, as I often have to do with the laptop alone, when I need to shift the underside's "hot spot" to another area of my legs.

I can't speak to how much this drains the laptop battery since I very rarely use my laptop without having it plugged in via an AC adapter (my laptop battery is failing and can't run for long without being plugged into the wall).

If I had one nitpick, I would suggest to Logitech that future models have some sort of attachment feature that would allow the laptop to be securely attached to the pad. At present the laptop just rests on top of pad, with the USB connector serving as the only connection between the laptop and the pad. I'd like them to be more securely attached to one another so it's less cumbersome to carry the laptop to another room. But that is a minor issue, and I am otherwise very pleased with this.

Highly recommend!

I needed an inexpensive DVD player to use in the basement, but still wanted to have good picture quality. I gave this a shot (bought it used) and have been more than pleased with the results.

Setup was a snap if you have an HDMI port (basically just plug in the HDMI cable, plug in the power cord, and you're done!). The on-screen setup menus were decent. Lots of options to choose from including several picture quality choices. The manual sort of explains the options, but some "lets see what this does" is helpful as well, especially with the picture quality options.

The player feels a bit "tinny' but that's pretty much par for the course for low-ended DVD players. The remote is decent - the buttons could be bigger, but it's acceptable. No eject button on the remote, however, which was an unexpected omission.

The picture quality is excellent - rivals a much more expensive Oppo DVD. Much, much better than I was expecting at this price point.

I've tried to unlock this to play region 2 disks but have had no luck. Tried a couple of options listed on AV discussion boards, but so far nothing. If anyone has had success unlocking this to play something other than Region 1 discs, I would love to hear how you did it.

Overall, a great DVD player, and a good value even at the regular price. Highly recommend.

One of the most important attributes for a headset is comfort. I've tried a few over the years, but always have found them to be a pain (literally!) if they are worn for more than 20 minutes or so. I'm very happy to report that the Moto is a dream when it comes to comfort - had it on for a three+ hour drive, and didn't even know it was there. Plus, it didn't cause a problem with my glasses, unlike other models I've tried.

Set up was very straightforward - basically just follow the prompts and it works. I didn't try out the text-to-voice feature but it sounds interesting. Not really something I would use since I don't text much at all, but if you're text-heavy, that feature would certainly be of value.

Audio quality was excellent. Had no problems hearing callers even with music playing in the car. Range was also very good.

My complaints are two-fold. First a minor one - this comes packed in what I would consider to be wasteful packaging. Looks impressive in a clear, thick plastic box, but the amount of materials used for packing is unnecessary. I did not, however, deduct anything from its rating due to that.

What did cause a loss of one star was the mic pickup. In a quiet environment it was fine. But, in a noisy environment (such as outside, in a crowded restaurant or with moderate-level music playing in the car), it picks up so much background noise that people had problems hearing me. To ensure this was actually the case, I loaned it to a friend and had him call me so I could hear for myself. It seems that the mic is either way too sensitive or not sufficiently directional - it truly is hard to hear the person's voice when they are using the headset should they be in anything other than a pretty quiet environment..

But, that aside, this is the best headset I've used to date. Especially recommended if you have had comfort issues with other headsets or are a glasses wearer.

UPDATE: This also works very well with an HP Touchpad. It's slighly smaller than the ipad so the fit is not as tight, but still quite stable. If you position the Touchpad correctly the on/off button works fine, and the volume button sort of works (can lower the volume easily but raising it requires a bit more effort).

Original review:
This is probably the most useful accessory I've every used for the iPad. Truly amazing in how it can be folded and unfolded to provide ease of use regardless of how you're using the iPad.

All the options make for a bit of a learning curve, however. I tried to follow the diagrams in the user's guide, but didn't really "get" how to use this until I watched the manufacturer's video. Highly recommend that as a guide to how to get the most out of this stand.

I'm especially pleased with being able to use it as a stand for viewing a movie (the position they call "Popcorn and a Movie" in the manual). Excellent when more than one person want to view the screen.

I can't comment with any degree of certainty as to it's longevity since I've only been using it for a few days, but it seems very sturdy. I'll update the review should that assumption prove faulty.

My big question is whether it will fit the iPad 2. Clearly it will cause problems with the cameras, but it is such a tight fit with the iPad 1 (which is a good thing in a case for security) that I'm hopeful that it will work with the iPad 2 with (perhaps) a bit of padding to make up for the thinner profile. I'll update with my experiences with the iPad 2 later this month once I have one in hand.

But regardless of fitting other models, this is an outstanding accessory for the iPad 1. Highly recommend.

I'm a huge Lensbaby fan. I've been using them with my Canon SLRs almost since they first came out, and have assembled a pretty extensive collection of them over the past few years. Yes, I am a lover of blur. It's one of those creative effects that you either love or don't (although I certainly will admit it can be overused with some horrible results). I've recently been playing around with Micro Four Thirds cameras and was thrilled to see that Lensbaby came out with a model specifically designed for the MFT format.

Quick primer for those not familiar with a Lensbaby: it's a very simple device that allows you to tilt the focal plane of the lens to shift focus to any area of the frame and produce a smooth blur effect. It can be in a small or large part of your photo depending on which of the several aperture rings you choose from (all supplied with this Lensbaby) and how much tilt you apply.

This particular version of the lens, called the "Composer" is part of Lensbaby's new Optic Swap System, which allows you to use any one of several optics (plastic, glass, double glass, pinhole/zoneplate) that you can easily swap out of the main body. This comes with the double glass optic - the other optics have to be purchased separately.

The new Composer design allows you to lock the tilt into place for some level of repeatability in your shots. A lot more convenient than earlier versions of Lensbabies, which required you hold the tilt with your fingers. Now it's just pick your aperture and your optic, tilt, and snap away!

This lens comes with an extra you can't get with other Lensbabies for other camera formats - the "tilt transformer." This is an attachment that will allow you to use any Nikon-mount lens as a close approximation of a tilt/shift lens (only close, since you really only get the benefit of tilt and not shift). With this attachment and a "regular" lens, you get a movable sliver, a line of focus, as opposed to the movable point of focus you get with a Lensbaby Optic. Same basic principle, but it produces a slightly different look.

Build quality is good. There's a lot of plastic in it, but my other Lensbabies have performed very well over the years with zero problems. The product comes nicely packaged, but only has minimal instructions. That's not really a problem since the company website has a lot of resources on how to use Lensbabies, plus has photo galleries, forums, instructional videos, and a lot more. Very nice resource if you own one. If you're not sure if a Lensbaby is for you, that should be your first stop to see what type of effects their products can produce. I've spent a lot of time there, and it has been time well spent. The company itself is excellent when it comes to customer service. I've contacted them a couple of times with questions, and they answer emails promptly.

This lens is versatile, and is more convenient to carry (both the Lensbaby as well as a MFT camera itself). I've found with all my gear that convenience of toting it means I'll carry it more often, and thus have more opportunity for taking great shots. The tilt transformer is a wonderful addition - you can play around with a tilt lens at a fraction it would cost you to buy a real tilt/shift lens.

While pricy for a Lensbaby, when you add up all the features it brings to the table, I find it to be a real winner. Highly recommend if you have a MFT camera.

I wasn't all that sure about what SlotRadio really was when I bought my SanDisk player, but am really pleased that it has it. Great concept - basically it's like listening to the radio without commercials but also no monthly fee. The songs are grouped into 7 playlists, and you can skip from playlist to playlist or song to song. However, you can't go backwards or replay - you can only skip over a song. So, if you hear something you like you can't replay it until it comes up again in the rotation.

The song order appears random within each playlist, which helps avoid getting bored with the tunes. I've had this for a couple of months and listed to it for many hours, and still find it enjoyable given the number of tunes on the chip.
